the cross as she has done?”

That I had been more or less influenced by my friend’s experience is shown by another diary

entry written shortly afterward:

“Eleventh month, 17th, 1849. Sometimes today, as I have been thinking about it, it has seemed

almost as if it would be right for me to put on a plain sugar-scoop bonnet; but I hardly dare

believe that so great a favour would be granted me. It is strange, even to myself, that I should

long so for the time when I might make this sacrifice, though in truth it would be no sacrifice.

People generally feel so averse to these bonnets, and I, too, did, perhaps a year ago; but now I

long for it so earnestly that I fear I cannot judge calmly and clearly about it. Gladly as I would

make this and any other sacrifice which God might require, I know how terrible it would be to

run before I was sent, and to do what God had not required. Sometimes it seems I cannot wait

any longer — that I must do something to gain the salvation of my soul; and if God requires

nothing, I must offer something myself. And yet that I dare not do. Oh, I feel that I could love the

cross and even the shame, if only God would lay them upon me; but patience and quiet waiting

are my duties now.”

It is evident from this extract that the martyr spirit had been aroused in me, and that I longed to

do something difficult for the sake of my religion. But these feelings soon passed, and the

“sugar - scoop” bonnet I both dreaded and desired never adorned my head. I was a healthy young

creature, full of animal spirits and absorbed in the joys of outward life. My conscience was

always easily quieted, and for the most part, I passed my girlhood conscious only of the ordinary

claims of everyday duty, which my training and the compelling Quaker atmosphere around me

had made almost second nature.

fields.title: Chapter 10. The" Hat Testimony"
fields.body_html:
art of the testimony to “plainness of apparel” was the testimony ag ainst what was called

“hat honor.” Quakers believed that since taking off the hat was an outward sign of

reverence toward God, it was not right or appropriate to give that same gesture to human beings.

Barclay said, “He that uncovereth his head to the crea ture, what hath he reserved for the

Creator?”

Because removing the hat was considered a mark of special respect to certain people or certain

places, Friends — who believed that all people were equally worthy of respect as children of one

Father, and that all places were equally holy because God’s presence was everywhere—

expressed this belief by refusing to take off their hats for anyone or in any place, except when

comfort required it. Not even when entering a place of worship could the rule be relaxed,

because taking off the hat would imply that God was more present inside that building than

outside in the open air. This idea was completely opposed to fundamental Quaker beliefs.

Prof. William James, in his valuable book The Varieties of Religious Experience, discussing

early Quakers and their peculiarities, writes:

“Many of these peculiarities arose from their determination to have nothing to do with shams or

pretenses, but to be true and sincere in all their dealings with God and with their fellow- men.”

George Fox believed the Lord showed him that many conventional social customs were false and

hypocritical. He wrote:

“When the Lord sent me into the world, He forbade me to put off my hat to any, high or low; and

I was required to ‘thee’ and ‘thou’ all men and women, without any respect to rich or poor, great

or small. And as I traveled up and down, I was not to bid people ‘Good morning’ or ‘Good

evening’; neither might I bow or scrape with my leg to anyone... Oh, the scorn, heat, and fury

that arose! Oh, the blows, punchings, beatings, and imprisonments that we underwent for not

P

putting off our hats to men! But blessed be the Lord, many came to see the vanity of that custom

of putting off hats to men, and felt the weight of Truth’s testimony against it.”

All the followers of George Fox accepted these revelations as guidance for themselves as well as

for him. They abandoned the worldly customs he condemned, viewing this as a sacrifice to Truth

and as a way to make their actions better reflect the spirit they professed. This renunciation

continued up to my own time, although I suspect many who practiced it no longer fully

understood the reasons behind these peculiarities.

Some Friends in my youth went so far as to treat wearing the hat at all possible times — even

during meals — as a kind of religious duty. On one occasion, a young man I knew was walking

with an Elder along the streets of Wilmington, Delaware. The Elder was advising him about the

importance of supporting Friends’ testimonies in every situation, and sa id:

“I have noticed, my dear young friend, with great satisfaction, that thou art careful not to take off

thy hat when meeting thy acquaintances in the street, nor to remove it upon entering the

meetinghouse until thou hast taken thy seat. But I see room for even greater faithfulness in this

matter, and I feel free to tell thee that I believe it is right for me to wear my hat at all times

except when I am in bed. I put it on the moment I rise in the morning, and I do not feel at liberty

to remove it until I have put on my night clothes, just before getting into bed at night.”

This practice of keeping the hat on was often a source of conflict and testing for Quakers who,

because of social obligations or business, were required to appear before people who expected

this gesture of respect. In the old Friends’ Journals , there are many accounts of the suffering

caused by this “hat testimony.” In the Journal of Thomas Ellwood, the friend of Milton, who

became convinced of Friends’ views, he describes his father’s v iolent hatred of this testimony.

He writes:

“The sight of my hat upon my head when entering his presence made him so angry that, rushing

at me with both hands, he violently snatched off my hat and threw it away; and then, giving me

some blows on the head, he said, ‘Sirrah, get you up to your chamber.’”

On another day, he tells how he went to the dinner table wearing his hat:

“As soon as I came in, I could see by my father’s expression that my hat was still an offence to

him. But when I was seated, and before I had eaten anything, he made this even clearer by saying

to me, ‘If you cannot content yourself to come to dinner without your Hise upon your head (so

he called my hat), pray rise and go take your dinner somewhere else.’ After hearing this, I got up

from the table and went into the kitchen, where I stayed until the servants sat down to dinner, and

then I sat contentedly with them.”

Many years after Ellwood’s experience, a wealthy English Friend, Joseph John Gurney,

described his own trial in 1810:

“I was engaged long beforehand to a dinner party. For three weeks before, I was in agitation

knowing that I must enter the drawing-room with my hat on. From this sacrifice, strange and

unaccountable as it may seem, I could not escape. Wearing the attire of a Friend, and with my

hat on, I entered the drawing-room at the dreaded moment, shook hands with the mistress of the

house, then returned to the hall, deposited my hat, and came back. I went home with some degree

of peace. Afterward, I had to do the same thing at the bishop’s. The result was that I found

myself a decided Quaker, fully understood to have taken that position, and to dinner parties —

except within the family circle —I was asked no more.”

Later still, our own dear father had a similar challenge. On one occasion, he hoped to be

appointed captain of an important ship, and while preparing to apply to the owners, he struggled

greatly because he believed it was his duty to enter their presence with his hat on. He feared this

would prejudice them against him, but he remained steadfast in what he believed to be his

religious duty and trusted that the Lord would prosper him. In his diary, he writes:

“Some of my friends thought my plain dress and language would stand in my way, but I told

them to wait and see whether I would not secure the position by the blessing of God, to whom I

refer all my success in life. The ship New Jersey was launched on the first of Twelfth Month,

1824, and on the third, Whitton Evans, the owner, conferred on me the command.”

While reading a very interesting book recently, The Testament of Ignatius Loyola, I was struck to

find that this old saint of the sixteenth century shared many of these early Quaker scruples. He

writes that his custom in addressing people was to omit all titles such as “Your Lordship” or

“Your Reverence,” believing that simplicity to be the practice of Christ and His Apostles. He

also tells how he was tempted, out of fear of consequences, to relax this practice in the case of a

certain captain, and that as soon as he recognized this as temptation, he determined:

“Since so it is, I will not call him your Lordship, nor show him reverence, nor will I pull off the

cap from my head.”

In fact, throughout Christian history, one of the ways devoted believers have expressed their

commitment has been through peculiarities of dress or speech, and aside from the particular form

it took, the early Friends were not unusual in this. But unlike many other Christian groups, they

also held a particular testimony against all bright colors, which, for reasons not entirely clear,

were considered worldly. Browns and drabs were considered unworldly, and most of our clothes

were some variation of these colors. Occasionally a little green was allowed, and curiously, a

dark purple was sometimes permitted, but red, blue, pink, or yellow were entirely forbidden as

“too gay.” I even knew some conscientious Friends who did not feel free to grow scarlet

geraniums in their gardens or to keep a vase of scarlet flowers in their parlors.

After I became a recognized religious teacher, people in spiritual difficulty often came to me for

help. Among them was a young Friend with a very sensitive conscience, who came one day

greatly troubled about scarlet geraniums. She lived in one half of a semi-detached house in the

suburbs of Philadelphia. In front of both houses was a small shared garden with an oval

flowerbed, which she and her neighbor took turns filling each spring. That year, it was her turn,

and wishing to please her neighbor, she asked her what flowers they should plant. The neighbor

preferred scarlet geraniums, and my friend was about to order them when a sudden scruple

seized her against allowing such bright flowers to adorn the garden in front of her house. She

struggled and prayed about it, and the more she prayed, the louder the inward voice seemed to

tell her that it would not be right to plant scarlet geraniums. But how to explain this to her

neighbor — who knew nothing about Friends — she could not imagine, and she came to me in

great distress for help.

I have always found that nothing is more difficult to combat than scruples. Although I tried very

hard to convince my poor, perplexed friend that there were matters in the Christian life far more

important than the color of the flowers in our gardens — and that the Lord might well be more

pleased by courtesy and kindness toward her neighbor than by any rigid rule about flower colors,

which, after all, He Himself created and could not therefore find displeasing — it was all in vain.

At last, I was forced to give her a piece of advice to which I rather objected: I told her to “ask

Josiah.”

Josiah was her husband, and I knew he possessed a good measure of common sense. Although I

did not generally approve of letting husbands decide such matters for their wives, in this case, it

seemed almost a necessity. My confidence was justified, for Josiah said — very sensibly — that he

would take the responsibility for the scarlet geraniums upon his own shoulders, and that he felt

sure the Lord would not be displeased to see, in front of their house, flowers which He Himself

had made.

Naturally, over time, modifications of these extreme views began to appear, and in my lifetime I

have seen gradual changes that, as a child, I would have thought blasphemous even to imagine.

As the young people of my generation — who regarded these old testimonies merely as

“traditions of the elders” rather than personal convictions— grew to maturity, they gradually let

them go. One Yearly Meeting after another became accustomed to changes that would once have

bowed them to the earth with shame and sorrow.

English Friends, as far as I recall, were the first to yield; but the American Yearly Meetings,

except our own in Philadelphia, were not far behind. We in Philadelphia held fast to our old

customs as long as we possibly could, but even we had to yield in the end.

One of my sisters married and settled within Baltimore Yearly Meeting — a Meeting that

embraced these changes far more rapidly than we did, and which we in Philadelphia regarded as

lamentably “gay.” My sister, however, carried the Philadelphia spirit with her, and as her large

family of daughters grew up, she tried earnestly to keep them to the Philadelphia standard of

plainness. But it was all in vain; one innovation after another crept in, and she found herself

powerless to prevent it.

Fortunately, she was blessed with a delightful sense of humor, and even in the midst of her

struggles for plainness, she could still see the absurdity of the situation. She came to me one day

to describe her difficulties and to ask my advice. When she had laid everything before me, she

suddenly sprang up with a mischievous twinkle in her eye, lifted one foot into the air, and said:

“Now, Hannah, please tell me where it will be safe for me to put my foot down. Once I put it

down at the overskirts, but soon had to lift it again. Then I put it down among artificial flowers in

the children’s hats, and once m ore had to lift it. Next, I put it down at rings on their fingers, and

again it had to be lifted. Now I do not want to put it down again until I can be quite sure I will

not have to take it up. Do thee think, Hannah, ”— and here she assumed an amusingly solemn

expression —“that I might safely venture to put it down at nose rings?”

This was too much for my gravity. I burst into laughter, and my sister joined me. Somehow, the

air was cleared, and she decided she could no longer carry on the fruitless effort to impose

Philadelphia ideas upon Baltimore. She would accept the inevitable changes that were bound to

come, even among such a conservative body as Friends.

The simple truth, as I have shown, was that the aim of the Quakers had always been to avoid

following the “vain fashions of the world.” They only adopted a new style once it had become

old and was passing away. Baltimore Friends were simply ready to do this a little sooner than

Philadelphia Friends. One of my Baltimore nieces told me she remembered coming once to

Philadelphia to attend a party given by her Philadelphia cousins, and feeling horribly worldly and

wicked because her dress was made more in the fashion than theirs.

How little all this can be understood by the young Quakers of the present day! But how

tremendously real it all was to us.

fields.title: Chapter 11. Plainness Of Speech
fields.body_html:
he “plainness of speech” referred to in the Third Query primarily meant using thee and

thou when addressing a single person, instead of the customary you . This testimony, along

with the testimony of plain apparel, was one of the chief marks that set us apart as a peculiar

people. To say you to one person — whether Friend or outsider — was considered the height of

worldliness and insincerity. Never once, until I was married, did I dare to transgress this rule.

Naturally, it made mingling with the outside world rather difficult, since our quaint way of

speaking was sure to provoke curious stares or suppressed laughter.

The roots of this testimony lay in the absolute sincerity of the early Friends. They felt it was

dishonest to use a plural pronoun for a single individual. Furthermore, in their day, it was

customary to address a superior as you , reserving thee and thou for inferiors. But Friends, who

believed all people were equal before God — and who believed this in a very practical way —

could not tolerate such distinctions. They therefore addressed everyone alike.

Those early Friends were democrats in every fiber of their being, not from political theory but

from their unwavering conviction that God had made all the nations of the earth from one blood,

and that all were equally His children. It was a noble foundation upon which to build their moral

structure, and it helps explain many practices that might otherwise seem quaint or even foolish.

Thomas Ellwood, in his autobiography, recounts the various things he felt called to give up after

becoming convinced of Quaker principles. Concerning plain language, he wrote that using you to

a single person was a “corrupt and unsound form of speaking,” adopted in “later and corrupt

times” as a means of flattering worldly vanity. Since God had always addressed men with thou ,

and men had always addressed God with thou , Ellwood considered it a moral obligation to

follow that example. Under the illumination of what he called “a pure ray of divine light,” he felt

required to abandon many such “evil customs” that had sprung up during the long night of

spiritual darkness.

T

So insistent was this testimony in my childhood that it would have seemed shockingly worldly to

say you to a single person, almost as “gay” as wearing silk or scarlet. Even after I grew older and

went more into the world, meeting good and earnest Christians who used the forbidden word

without the slightest qualm, it took great effort to shape my Quaker lips to utter it. Gradually, the

difficulty faded. Now, after more than seventy years, thee and thou have become for me simply

the language of intimate affection, slipping out naturally whenever someone has truly found their

way into my heart. I often judge my own feelings toward a person by this test: when I hear

myself saying thee , I know I have begun to love them. Many of my friends — some with no

Quaker connection at all — have caught the habit from me, and use those dear old words in our

private companionship. My beloved friend Frances Willard was one of them; we thee’d , and

thou’d each other for many years.

The writer I quoted earlier, in A Boy’s Religion , describes how he felt as a child about plain

speech.

“I said ‘thee’ and ‘thy’ to everybody,” he wrote, “and I would just as soon have used profane

language as said ‘you’ or ‘yours’ to any person. I thought only Friends went to Heaven, and so I

supposed that using ‘thee’ and ‘thy’ was one of the main tests of admission. Nobody ever told

me such a thing, and if I had asked, I’d have been set straight— but for years that was my settled

belief.”

He goes on to describe pitying his neighbors who would never, as he imagined, be “let in,” and

wondering why they didn’t simply join the Meeting and learn to speak properly. He even taught

one little “Gentile” friend the plain language, and the boy used it faithfully with him until the

pressure of the outside world, as he put it, “got too heavy” around the age of twelve.

Another testimony related to plainness of speech was the prohibition against calling anyone Mr. ,

Mrs. , or Miss . These titles were believed to violate the spirit of Christ’s words, “Neither be ye

called masters, for one is yo ur Master, even Christ.” No sincere Friend could give a title to a

wealthy man while refusing it to a poor one; thus, Christian names were used for all — Thomas,

Samuel, Abigail, Elizabeth, and so forth. (We had no Reginalds, Bertrands, Ethels, or Evelyns in

those days!)

Where age demanded a touch more respect, young people were expected to use the full name —

Thomas Wistar, Abigail Evans, Samuel Bettle, Elizabeth Pitfield. This practice created no end of

difficulty when dealing with “the world’s people,” and b rought about many an awkward

dilemma.

Our dear father was very strict on this matter, and could never be persuaded — no matter how

inconvenient it might be —to use the “gay’’ titles Mr. or Mrs. I remember well the amusement

we had, once we were grown, watching his ingenious methods of escaping difficulty whenever

he did not know someone’s first name. In place of Mr. or Mrs. , he invented the substitute word

Cummishilamus , and would say, for example, “Cummishilamus Coleman said…” or

“Cummishilamus Coleman did…”

When, however, he had to address a letter, he could not, of course, write such a word, and then

he would turn to one of us, a merry twinkle in his dear eyes, and say, “Come, Han, thee has no

scruples — thee may write the Mr. or Mrs. on this letter.”

Plainness of speech also forbade us from greeting our friends with good morning , good evening ,

or from saying good-bye when parting from them. Good-bye was believed to be a corruption of

God be with you , and since God was always with you, it seemed a kind of unbelief to express the

wish. And to say good morning or good evening — a wish that you might have a good morning or

evening — implied doubt of the fact, known to every Friend, that your mornings and evenings

must, in the order of Divine Providence, always be good.

I grew up with the distinct feeling that these expressions were very gay and worldly, and that the

right — or, as we said, the plain — course was to greet friends with How art thou? Or how does

thee do? , and to part from them with the simple word Farewell.

Why Farewell was considered more truthful than good-bye , even if good-bye did mean God be

with you , I have never been able to understand.

In perfect consistency with the Quaker ideal of the absolute equality of all human beings in the

sight of God, plainness of speech also forbade us to give the title Saint to any departed Christian.

We were never allowed to use it, even as a prefix. For example, we never spoke of the Gospels

as the Gospel according to St. Matthew or St. Mark , but always as the Gospel according to

Matthew , or Mark, Luke, or John.

I recently saw, in an old diary from the seventeenth century, an account of one very

conscientious Friend who felt a “stop” against using the prefix saint even in place-names. She

once had great difficulty locating St. Mary Axe because, having dropped the Saint , she asked

only for “Mary Axe Street,” which no one understood.

As a testimony against idolatry, we were also forbidden to call the months of the year or the days

of the week by their “heathen” names. We were taught to adhere to the “simplicity of truth” by

using numbers: First Month , Second Month ; or First Day , Second Day , and so forth. This

practice was so universal in my circle that it never even occurred to me to use the heathen names.

I remember being greatly shocked when I came to England in 1873 and discovered that English

Friends had abandoned the practice and had returned to the old “heathen” names. For a time, I

could hardly persuade myself they were truly Friends at all. And even now, when I date my

letters with those names, I still feel as though I am making a forbidden little excursion into the

“gay world.”

fields.title: Chapter 12. Friends' "Testimonies" Against Fiction, Music, And Art
fields.body_html:
nother point raised in this same Third Query caused us no small amount of trouble: the

question of whether Friends were careful to bring up the ir children in “frequently reading

the Holy Scriptures, and to restrain them from reading pernicious books.” All fiction of every

kind was considered “pernicious” by the Friends of those days. On this point , our mother was

very strict, and we were not allowed to read even the most innocent and carefully chosen

Sunday-school stories. As for novels, the very word was considered wicked, and to this day I

never use it without a fleeting, instinctive sense of lawlessness, as if I were deliberately doing

something wrong.

As we grew older, the line was naturally drawn less tightly, and when we became old enough to

take a little more guidance of our lives into our own hands, we would sometimes snatch a fearful

joy from a storybook borrowed from one of our school friends. One of my most vivid memories

is of such an occasion, made all the more vivid because it was the first time I had dared to

partake openly and boldly of the forbidden fruit.

It was a First-day afternoon, when nothing much seemed to be happening. I had borrowed a book

from one of my schoolmates, who had told me it was “lovely,” and I took the book— with a plate

of apples and gingerbread — and stretched myself across the outside of my bed to read and eat at

my leisure.

The story I read that day, under such delightful circumstances, seemed to give me the nearest

approach to perfect bliss I had ever experienced, and it remains in my memory as one of the

happiest days of my life. The book was The Earl’s Daughter by Grace Aguilar. To my young

American Quaker mind, an Earl was something like an archangel rather than an ordinary man,

and to be an Earl’s daughter was almost akin to being a daughter of heaven. And to this day—

despite all the disillusionment life has brought me regarding earls and their daughters — the old

A

sense of grandeur that filled my soul with awe on that First-day afternoon long ago always

returns for a moment whenever earls or countesses are mentioned in my presence.

But although I enjoyed this and other stories intensely, it was always with an uneasy conscience,

and it took me fifty years to rid myself of the feeling that reading anything fictitious was a sin.

My diary is full of the struggles I endured because of this, and when I read them over now, I

cannot help feeling deep pity for the hungry, ignorant young soul so tormented by the constant

tendency to turn a perfectly innocent recreation into a moral offense.

What finally brought me deliverance was a sudden recognition that our Lord Himself constantly

used parables — which are simply stories — to illustrate and enforce His teaching. Fiction,

therefore, was not in itself, as I had always supposed, a synonym for sin. Its moral quality

depended entirely on the kind of fiction it was, and often, fiction could be found to be an

invaluable aid to virtue.

But I have known many Friends who have been tormented by scruples on this subject well into

old age.

Music was another matter against which the Friends of my day had a very strong testimony. In a

Philadelphia Discipline of 1873, I found the following passage concerning it, which clearly

expresses the Quaker view:

“We would renewedly caution to all our members against indulging in music, or having

instruments of music in their houses, believing that the practice tends to promote a light and vain

mind, and to disqualify for the serious thoughtfulness which becomes an accountable being,

hastening to his final reckoning.… The spirit and language of the Discipline forbid the use of

music by Friends, without any exception in favor of that called sacred.… Those m embers who

indulge in the use of music, or who have musical instruments in their houses, bring themselves

within the application of this second clause of the Discipline.… And if they be not reclaimed by

further labor, so as to condemn their misconduct to the satisfaction of the meeting, it should

proceed to testify our disunity with them.”

So strictly was the Discipline observed in this respect that I do not remember, in my young days,

a single individual in our select circle who owned any sort of musical instrument, above all a

piano, which was considered the gayest of the gay. Whenever I found myself in a room

containing a piano, I felt as though I were treading the very borders of hell.

For many years after I became a woman, I never heard music anywhere without a secret, half-

delicious sensation of tasting forbidden fruit. Even singing or whistling was frowned upon. I

remember once, when a party of young Friends were spending a summer holiday together in

Newport, a dear old Friend called us into his room and told us solemnly that he had been greatly

grieved to hear some of us whistling in the garden the day before, and he hoped we would never

again so transgress Friends’ testimonies.

That the Discipline on this matter was no dead letter is proved by the fact that, when I was older,

and this testimony was beginning to lose its power over the less “concerned” members, I knew

several instances in which Friends — though otherwise exemplary — were actually disowned

simply for having a piano in their homes.

And as late as 1865, when we presented our son Frank with a cottage organ (we did not dare give

him a piano, feeling that organs were somehow “plainer”), we were obliged to hide it in one of

the top rooms of the house in order to spare the feelings of our Quaker relatives.

I shall never forget my astonishment when I first realized that musical instruments were not only

permitted in the Bible, but that we were actually commanded to use them. One day, reading the

Psalms, I could hardly believe my eyes when I came to Psalm 150: “Praise ye the Lord. Praise

Him with the sound of the trumpet; praise Him with the psaltery and harp. Praise Him with the

timbrel and dance; praise Him with stringed instruments and organs.” I never heard a Friend

explain how they justified ignoring this.

“Plainness,” in my day, also excluded pictures everywhere except in books. No respectable

Quaker would hang pictures on the walls, nor did they feel free to have their likeness taken. Even

daguerreotypes, when they first appeared, were consider ed “gay” by all the truly “sound”

Friends. I believe the idea was that having one’s picture might encourage vanity. And for some

obscure reason, pictures or statuary were felt to be spiritually dangerous — temptations to

idolatry. I grew up firmly believing it was wicked to visit an art gallery or to look at a statue.

I remember clearly, at about seventeen, breaking loose from all the traditions of my upbringing

and going — my heart pounding as if on some perilously wicked adventure — into the Academy of

Fine Arts in Philadelphia. There stood a marble group of Hero and Leander, and Leander was not

very fully clothed. I still see myself standing before it, heart in my throat, saying inwardly, “I

suppose I shall go straight to hell for this, but I cannot help it. If I must go, I must — , but I will

look at this statue.” No words can express how daring a sinner I felt myself to be. And I

remember my astonishment distinctly to find myself afterward standing safely in Broad Street,

quite unharmed, without having experienced the swift judgment of an offended Creator.

I can still see that marble group vividly, far more vividly than any sculpture I have seen since.

Though I doubt it would now be considered great art, it has lived in my memory as the acme of

all art, for it marked my emancipation into an entirely unknown world. Nothing dreadful

happened to me, and I gradually gained courage for more, until I learned that a gift for art is as

truly a divine bestowal as a gift for mathematics, and therefore cannot be wrong to cultivate. And

gradually Friends also learned this; the old scruples against art and music have almost entirely

disappeared.

Another testimony included under “plainness of apparel” in my youth was one against beards.

When Friends’ customs first crystallize d, smooth faces were the universal fashion. Consequently,

in keeping with the principle of not following changing worldly fashions, when beards became

popular, Quakers clung to the clean-shaven face. As the fashion for beards became more

insistent, the Quaker resistance grew firmer, until — gradually, and without any real reason I ever

heard —it became a “religious testimony.” By the time I was born, it was one of the strictest.

I vividly recall the first time I saw a “preacher” wearing a beard. He was a visit ing Friend from

England, where they were less strict. Yet despite my great reverence for English Friends, his

beard seemed to me so plainly the mark of the Evil One that I felt it almost sinful to listen to his

preaching. In several “strict” Meetings, he w as refused entrance to the gallery because of his

beard, and I remember well the grave concern expressed by the Philadelphia Elders over this sad

evidence of “the gradual encroachments of a worldly spirit in London Yearly Meeting.”

This testimony against beards, I believe, is shared — though probably for different reasons — by

Roman Catholic priests and by High Church clergymen of the Church of England. But Friends

have long since abandoned it, along with many other strict testimonies of my childhood. They

still practice moderation in dress and speech, and in the furnishing of their homes and the

ordering of their lives; but they have mostly given up any idea that a special cut of clothing or

the suppression of natural gifts in literature, art, or music is necessary for divine favor.

Yet one cannot help admiring the sturdy adherence to what they sincerely believed was a

religious duty, even though it now seems to us a mistaken one, that characterized those dear old

saints.

fields.title: Chapter 13. Quaker "Scruples'~
fields.body_html:
he personal “scruples” born of Quaker testimonies seemed endless, for each individual

interpreted them according to their own sense of duty. Those with particularly sensitive

consciences often multiplied restrictions until life itself became a torment. One friend, burdened

with such a conscience, confessed to me later in life that her mornings as a young woman were

nearly unbearable. She could scarcely dress herself without being beset by doubts over every

article of clothing. At times, the only way she could silence the inner voice demanding fresh

sacrifices was to stuff her ears with cotton and recite poetry as quickly as possible, drowning out

the relentless admonitions.

An old diary kept by my great-grandmother between 1760 and 1762 offers a vivid glimpse into

the scruples of her day. She wrote with solemn conviction that laughter was madness, mirth a

vanity, and that she longed to be so fixed as never to smile again. Elsewhere, she lamented the

creeping fashions among Friends — the young men tying their hair with ribbons, the girls

adorning their necks with black bands. To her, these were sorrowful sights, evidence that the

elders had failed in their duty. She bewailed the indulgence in tobacco, tea, and calico, declaring

them all equally corrupting, “as bad as the negroes,” she wrote, grouping worldly habits together

as one abomination. Her words reveal how each generation found new points of conscience, yet

always in the same spirit of self-denial.

Closer to my own time, another grandmother refused to wear false teeth. Though toothless and

struggling to eat, she felt a “stop” in her spirit, believing them to be a vain fashion. They were

placed away in a drawer beside her best silk shawl, never to be worn. We, children, admired her

saintliness, even as we watched her struggle with food. A preacher friend of ours, after laying

down a new carpet, feared she had yielded to pride. To humble herself, she ordered

wheelbarrows of rough stones dumped upon it, stripping away its freshness. We, children, heard

the tale with awe, and her preaching thereafter seemed to us like the voice of an angel.

T

Years later, I faced my own trial over a new Brussels carpet, patterned with delicate flowers. My

husband arranged for rough working men to gather in that very room each Sunday for Bible

class. I resented their heavy boots on my prized carpet, though I knew I ought not to feel so.

While praying over the matter, a v erse came to me: “Take the spoiling of your goods joyfully .” I

seized upon it as a weapon of the Spirit, and from that moment I welcomed those men upon my

carpet. Strangely enough, it seemed never to wear out, lasting until I grew weary of its sight. I

cannot help but think my way was better than the rough stones of my dear old Friend.

After I had discovered the way of faith, a friend who had long suffered under Quaker “scruples”

gave me a striking picture of the different methods of living the Christian li fe. She said, “I have

noticed three ways of getting to the other side of a spiritual mountain. Some tunnel through by

the sweat of their brows — that is the Quaker way, and for a long time it was mine. Others wander

around the base, meandering this way and that, but because they keep their faces turned toward

the goal, they gradually draw nearer. That was my way when I grew weary of tunneling. But now

you tell me there is a third way — the way of faith. You say that some Christians have learned to

flap the wings of faith and fly right over the mountain. I must admit, those who take your way

seem to reach the other side far more quickly and easily than either the tunnellers or the

wanderers. I have decided to give up tunneling and meandering, and to flap my wings too.”

Yet the dear saints of my childhood and youth did not know how to fly. For the most part, they

spent their lives in steadfast, weary tunneling. Their faithfulness and self-sacrifice, even if

sometimes misdirected, seemed to me then — and still seems now — worthy of all honor. The one

overwhelming impression left upon my young heart was simply this: by hook or by crook, I must

be good. Whatever else was lacking in Quaker teaching, there was no lack of emphasis on

goodness. The necessity of being thoroughly, honestly, genuinely good was in the very air we

breathed.

At times, I chafed under this atmosphere. My adventurous nature longed for a chance to be

naughty, to defy expectations, but the boundaries of my life allowed only the most innocent

mischief. Looking back, I cannot help but admire the remarkable shield of goodness that

surrounded me, protecting me from temptations that might otherwise have enticed my free spirit.

For if ever a soul was born free, it was mine. The cry of my heart has always been for freedom.

Rules and conventions that enslave or fetter have been my lifelong abhorrence. Had my parents

made many rules, I would have rebelled. But the pervasive atmosphere of goodness in which

they lived constrained me with such unconscious power that I hardly knew I was being guided. I

felt blissfully as though I nearly always had my own way.

No one who did not live in it could imagine the narrow range of life I knew up to the age of

eighteen. I never met anyone from what was called “the gay world.” My c ompanions were only

the sober Friends of our circle, and their carefully guarded children. Novels were forbidden, and

I had no chance to learn what life meant outside our Quaker fold. As for the sins of the world, I

had not the faintest inkling. Even at school, if anything was hinted at, I was too innocent to

understand. I dare say it would be impossible today for a girl of eighteen to live in such an unreal

world of ignorance, or to enter life’s responsibilities so utterly unprepared.

My inner life until sixteen was simple. I believed what little I was told and troubled myself not at

all about the mysteries of the universe. My only religious thoughts were occasional fears of

hellfire, which flared up during epidemics or times of danger. How I came by this fear I cannot

recall, for Quakers rarely spoke of heaven or hell. Their concern was the life of God in the soul

now, trusting the future to divine care. Yet sometimes I was seized with sudden dread, made

great resolutions to “be good,” and tried for a few h ours to correct my faults — only to relapse

into my old ways. Still, the atmosphere of goodness around me made it difficult even to think of

wrongdoing, much less to act upon it. On the whole, I was as good as a lively, healthy creature

could be. But up to sixteen, I was simply a good animal. My spiritual nature was unawakened; I

had never consciously realized my soul.

A change was near, though I did not know it. My soul was stirring from its torpor, struggling like

a butterfly in its cocoon to break free from the bonds that held it. My long search after God was

about to begin.

fields.title: Chapter 14. The First Epoch In My Religious Life (The Awakening)
fields.body_html:
n the story of my religious life, four epochs stand out clearly before me. The first dawned, as I

have said, when I was sixteen. In a dim, mysterious way, I began to feel vague longings for

something that would satisfy my inward nature. In my diary from the autumn of 1848, I find

record of these longings — a blind reaching out for something to fill what I called, in the tragic

language of youth, “the aching void in my heart.”

In the midst of this, I fell head over heels in love with one of the young teachers at the school I

was attending, and her influence changed my life. I recorded in my diary every step of our

acquaintance — my longing to speak to her, to beg for her love, and my hesitation from fear of

troubling her. I wrote as follows:

“1848. Sixteen years old. This is an important time for me. Now is the time for forming my

character. I feel as I never felt before. The great and solemn duties of life have, for the first time,

come before me. I was not born to be an idler; for I feel something within me which tells me:

Life has more inspiring imports

Than the fancies of thy youth;

It has hopes as high as heaven,

It has labour, it has truth.

It has wrongs that may be righted,

Noble deeds that may be done.

Its great battles are unfought,

Its great triumphs are unwon.

Something which points onward — far onward — into the future, beyond this life into a brighter,

happier world, and tells me of the glorious reward of those who fulfill their duties.

I

I have not felt this long. Three months ago, I was a careless, happy child. I am still a child, but an

earnest, reflective one — no longer careless or indifferent. How can I be so, when there is so

much, so very much, to think about and so much to be done? What has caused this change?

There was an aching void in my heart. I felt a want of something — something I knew not what —

something indefinable that would make me sit dreamily for hours and look into the sky, watching

the pale stars or the moon, until my very being seemed merged into theirs. I almost forgot I was

on earth while my thoughts wandered into the pathless regions over which they presided, and I

strove in vain to pierce the mysteries of their existence.

Study, I thought, would fill that void, but I was mistaken. In this state of mind, at the beginning

of the Ninth Month, we left our darling little cottage home and returned to the city. If at that time

I had met someone I could love whose principles were bad, I shudder to think what might have

happened, for I am easily influenced by those I love.

But my Heavenly Father was willing to extend a little mercy toward me. He sent across my path

one in whom I found a true friend. She was a young girl employed by Miss Maryanna as a

composition teacher, named Anna S — . I was prepared to love her even before I saw her, for

someone dear to me had told me of her loveliness. For two weeks after she first came to school, I

believe I spoke to her only once; and that was when I saw her looking for a book and handed her

one, asking if it was the right one.

I thought we would never become acquainted. I would sit and watch her and wish I dared speak

to her and kiss her, and this very longing made me painfully shy. I would see her put her arms

around other girls, and I would turn away in sorrow to think she would not do the same to me. At

last, one day — how well I remember it — I was standing at my desk when she came up and spoke

to me about A. S. F. How happy I felt! How I longed to throw my arms around her neck and beg

her to let me love her! My heart was in a tumult, yet I answered calmly and without emotion, and

she soon left me. But the ice was broken. We began to speak more often, and one morning she

kissed me. That kiss was engraved on my heart. I felt that she loved me, and the thought brought

me happiness.

From that moment, I have loved — nay, almost idolized — her. The aching void in my heart is now

partly filled, for I have listened to her thoughts, seen the nobility of her actions, and learned that

“life is real, life is earnest,” and not to be passed in idle dreaming or wasted in frivolous

amusements. She has taught me — not in so many words, but quietly through her influence — that

I have a mission to fulfill on earth, and that I must straightway begin to perform it. Henceforth, I

must struggle earnestly to become pure and holy and noble-hearted, so that I may be great in the

world and faithfully play my part in the great battle of life. Her influence has awakened me from

my dream of childhood. In one short month, I have become a woman. Oh, how blessed her

friendship has been to me! I hope — earnestly hope —that I may not abuse the privilege.”

A day or two later, I wrote:

“Every day , I feel grateful to my Heavenly Father for blessing me with such a friend as Anna.

This is such an important period of my life. I tremble when I think of the awful responsibility

resting upon me. My character is forming, and I have the power to become what I choose. Oh,

may I choose to be a good and noble woman! Today, as I walked along the street and thought of

what my future destiny might be, it made me almost shrink. I may be destined for some great

work. I feel something within me that tells me I could accomplish it. At any rate, I shall do a

great deal of good or evil. I will choose the former.

Oh, my Father who art in Heaven, wilt Thou not help me advance in the path of self-conquest,

which must be my first great battle? What a glorious triumph it will be if I succeed!”

According to my diary, each day now seemed to awaken my spiritual nature more and more,

until at last a kind of climax arrived. On 11th Month 28th, 1848, I wrote:

“An eventful day! Eventful, I mean, in my spiritual life. Today I have felt and thought enough

for a year. My friend Anna read to us in class a book called Other Worlds , and also Future

Existence from the School Boy by Abbott. It was all intensely interesting and had an almost

overpowering effect on me.

As I listened to the accounts of those mighty worlds scattered everywhere around us — some so

distant that the rays of light which enter our eyes had left those stars six thousand years ago! —

and as I reflected that these worlds are all moving regularly, never disturbing one another, but all

obedient to one mighty Creator, the grandeur of the thought was overwhelming. For a few

minutes, I felt as though the very happiness of being born into a universe so limitless, so

magnificent, so glorious, was almost too great to bear.

And as I heard of our future existence, of the glorious and unimaginable happiness in store for

us, of the perfect bliss reserved for the good and the holy, I inwardly thanked my Creator for

placing me among beings whose expectations were so blessed. But then came the awful,

overwhelming thought that this eternity of endless bliss was only for the good — and the

realization that I could have no share in it unless my heart was changed. Oh, I cannot describe

the misery of that moment! It was almost more than I could bear. And these thoughts linger with

me. Why is i t?”

The impression made upon me by this glimpse into the magnificence of the universe has never

left me to this day. At the bottom of all my questionings about God, there has always been a

conviction of His illimitable power — something nothing could ever withstand. But for a long

time, as will be seen, I thought of this power as a selfish one, engaged not on my side but against

me. And my one question for many years was how I could win the God who possessed such

power over to my side.

fields.title: Chapter 15. My Search
fields.body_html:
y awakening had come in earnest. I was then about sixteen and a half, and from that time

onward, my soul thirsted to make myself worthy of the glorious destiny of which I felt I

had caught a glimpse. Even deeper than this was the longing to become acquainted with the God

who had created the unimaginable wonders I had been reading about. I have no recollection of

feeling any particular trouble about my sins; it was the magnificence of God that had enthralled

me. I felt that the grandest thing in life would be to come to know Him. And so, then and there,

my search began. But alas — what a blind, ignorant search it was at first.

My only confidante was my friend Anna. Not for the world would I have said anything on the

subject to my parents. Their Quaker habits of reserve on all matters of religion made it seem

impossible. But to my friend, after that day of awakening, I poured out my heart in a long letter

full of aspirations and yearnings. In my diary, I have a copy of her reply, with these comments:

“Anna wrote me a little note in reply to my letter. Never have I received one that thrilled me

more deeply than that! She begged me to give up all to my Saviour, to pray for strength, and to

strive earnestly after holiness, no matter what it cost me. ‘Oh , dearest Hannah,’ she said, ‘do let

us try. Let us seek to journey together toward His glorious kingdom! Let us struggle for a portion

of Hi s spirit.’

“Oh, that I could follow her advice! I sat here alone in my study and tried to feel as if I could

give up all. But I could not. I could not even feel repentance for the many, many sins I have

committed, and far worse than all, I could not feel as though I truly loved God. It is dreadful.

What shall I do? I must repent; I must love my Heavenly Father, or I shall be eternally ruined.

But I cannot do it on my own. God alone can help me, and I know not how to pray. Oh, what

shall I do? Where shall I go? It is said, ‘Ask, and ye shall receive.’ But I cannot become really

righteous until I repent, and I cannot repent.”

M

From this time onward, my religious diary is one long record of wrestlings and agonies, with

scarcely a ray of light. My friend did her best to help me, but she, like myself, supposed that the

only way to find God was to search for Him within. Our Quaker education had taught us always

to turn to “the light within” for teaching and guidance, and we believed that only when God

revealed Himself there could we truly come to know Him. In an old Quaker tract among my

papers called What Shall We Do to Be Saved? , there is a passage that clearly sets forth the kind

of teaching with which we had grown up. It reads:

“I cannot direct the searcher after truth who is pensively enquiring what he shall do to be saved,

to the ministry of any man; but would rather recommend him to the immediate teaching of the

word nigh in the heart, even the Spirit of God. This is the only infallible teacher and the primary

adequate rule of faith and practice. It will lead those who attend to its dictates into the peaceable

paths of safety and truth. ‘Ye need not,’ said the Apostle to the Church formerly, ‘that any man

teach you, save as this anointing teacheth, which is trut h and no lie.’”

The natural result of this teaching was to turn our minds inward, upon our feelings and emotions,

and to make us judge our relationship with God entirely by what we found within ourselves.

What God had said in the Bible seemed to us far less authoritative than what He might say to us

in our own hearts. I have no recollection of ever, even for a moment, turning to the Scriptures for

instruction. The “inward voice” was to be our sole teacher— and for me at that time, the inward

voice meant only my own feelings and emotions. As there is absolutely nothing more unreliable

or unmanageable than one’s inward feelings, it is no wonder that I was plunged into a hopeless

struggle.

In vain I tried to work myself up into what I supposed would be feelings acceptable to God. No

thought of salvation in any other way ever crossed my mind. I talked about “my Saviour,” as I

called Him, but I never imagined for a moment that He could — or would — save me unless I

made myself worthy to be saved. And as this worthiness consisted mostly, I believed, of inward

pious emotions, I thought only of trying somehow to force these emotions into being. Anyone

who has ever tried to do this will know what a weary, hopeless task it is. The records in the diary

of my religious life from the age of sixteen onward are a sad illustration of the false methods of

religion that were all I knew. As I read them now, I cannot help pitying the eager, hungry soul

reaching out so vainly after light but finding only confusion and darkness.

One thing, however, consoles me in this retrospect: none of these religious struggles seems, as

far as I remember, to have darkened the skies of my outward happiness. My times for attending

to my religious life were in our Quaker meetings, or when I was alone in my study during

twilight, or at night after everyone else had gone to bed — and all the tragic records in my diary

were written then. Throughout the day, I was generally too happy and too full of outward

interests to be troubled by what had taken place in my religious hours. I feel this was a great

cause for thankfulness, for if the struggles I endured in our silent meetings or in my hours of

meditation had extended into the daytime as well, I do not like to imagine what the consequences

might have been.

I believe my diary was my safety valve, for I remember well that after writing there the most

tragic and despairing entries, I would somehow feel as though my religious exercises were

finished, and would go off to bed quite happily, sleeping the sleep of the ju st without a moment’s

wakeful anxiety or worry, and waking the next morning full of the joys of a new day, having

forgotten all the miseries I had so despairingly recorded the night before. I recall being

occasionally surprised by this easy transition, and I find the following in my diary from this time:

“I cannot understand my feelings. Such a hungering and thirsting after righteousness, and yet,

except in a few moments of retirement (when I write in my diary), such lightness, gaiety, and

indifference. It seems almost wrong to laugh, and yet I indulge in it continually… I know not

how God can look upon me, even in pity; I am so wicked. So often have I entered into a

covenant to serve Him wholly and entirely, with fervour of spirit; but when the impression of my

hours of retirement has faded, and the temptations of the world have assailed me, I have yielded,

and have forgotten my high and holy calling through fear of the world’s dread laugh, and

through the love of sin. Oh that I could do otherwise! The mercy of God will some day be

exhausted —and where shall I be then? I dare not think.”

I can see now that it was, as I have said, my salvation from an utterly morbid and false sort of

religion that my naturally happy and joyous temperament continually delivered me out of its

snares — even though at the time this seemed wicked to me. How morbid and false all my ideas

of religion were during this period a few further extracts from my diary will reveal.

Diary:

“Oh, it is a sorrowful thought that upon myself depends th e salvation of my soul, and yet I can

do absolutely nothing! Wherever I turn, all looks dark and gloomy. Oh, I must renew my

efforts… Oh, that I could repent! But I cannot. I know it is wrong; I dread the anger of God; but I

cannot feel what I know true repentance to be. Oh, that I could! I almost wish I could be as

indifferent as I once was — could forget all that I have felt — for it seems impossible for me ever

to be a Christian…

“This afternoon in meeting, I was favored to feel, more perhaps than ever before, the spirit of

supplication. My exercise was so great that I could scarcely sit still. My head throbbed painfully,

and my heart felt as though it would break with the agony. Oh, how awful to feel that I have no

power of myself even to think a holy thought, and yet I must gain the salvation of my soul! I

cannot repent; I cannot love my Savior; and I do not believe I ever will. What —what shall I do?”

Three months after my awakening I wrote:

Diary:

“It has been more than three months since I began in ea rnest to seek the salvation of my soul, and

I have not advanced one step. Could I have seen then all that was before me, I would have given

up in despair. I would have thought it impossible to wait, and pray, and struggle for three

months — and gain nothing. Now I look forward to many, many more months of prayer and

struggling and waiting, with a fear — almost a certainty — that all of that, too, will be in vain.

“If there were only some outward work, entirely distinct from the inward change that is

necessary — something to be done, not something merely to be prayed for — a cutting off of a

hand or a foot, or some self-inflicted austerity — then perhaps I might become a Christian, for

such things I could do. But the inward change I cannot effect, and yet I am accountable if it is not

effected. Accountable for not doing what I cannot do! It is a dreadful thought.

“I feel as if I were seated, sick and weary, at the base of a high and inaccessible mountain peak

whose summit I must reach — alone, and in the darkness of night. Oh, Heavenly Father, wilt

Thou not enable me to be faithful, to strive earnestly, and to endure to the end?…

“I am so ignorant and inexperienced that I am almost afraid to do anything. There are many,

many things I long to inquire about, but whom shall I ask? I cannot speak to my parents until I

know for certain that I am accepted; I love them too dearly to cause them the anguish of seeing

me give up in despair. My dear friend Anna says she is not a Christian, and she dares not counsel

or comfort me. And there is no one. Alone, I must bear all my burdens! Alone, I must seek the

entrance to the straight and narrow way! Alone, I must work out my soul’s salvation. And I can

of myself do nothing. Oh, what shall I do?”

As an illustration of the sort of teaching I was receiving at this time, the following entry is

valuable:

Diary:

“Went to Twelfth Street Meeting this morning, where I was favored to have a few moments of

real prayer. But my discouragement was very great, so that I could scarcely avoid crying aloud

for help; and in my despair, I besought my Father in Heaven, if it seemed good unto Him, to put

a few words of encouragement into the mouth of one of His servants.

“My prayer was answered. Almost immediately Samuel Bettle rose and spoke in a manner

remarkably applicable to me, bidding the poor and needy — though now they might seem to be in

the depths of tribulation, in darkness seeing no light, and thirsty yet finding no water — to put

their trust in the Lord Jesus and patiently abide His time; and they would be filled with the light

of His Holy Spirit, and fountains of living wate r would flow from them freely.”

Of what it meant to put one’s trust in Jesus, I had not the faintest conception, and I do not

remember giving it a moment’s thought. But to patiently abide God’s time seemed something I

could understand, and I went home from the meeting that day with a weary sense of an

interminable waiting for the light of the Holy Spirit to shine in my heart and give me the longed-

for joy and peace.

And so day after day went by in a hopeless watching of my feelings and emotions, which I could

never bring up to the right pitch of fervor; and my unrest and darkness of spirit only grew more

and more despairing.

One final extract from my diary will suffice:

Diary:

“Third Month 1, 1849. Very sad. The fear that this longing for salvation may be all a delusion

attends me always, and everything is so completely veiled in gloom that I can scarcely take a

single step. It seems to me that I cannot bear this state much longer. But oh Father! Thy will, not

mine, be done.”

fields.title: Chapter 16. Eclipse Of Faith
fields.body_html:
his morbid self-introspection lasted, with variable degrees of earnestness, until the time of

my marriage at nineteen. Nothing ever came of it, and in the nature of things, nothing ever

could. It was a self-involved religion that had no relation whatever to any Divine facts. And I see

now that it was a mercy my marriage, and the new life and wider interests into which I was

introduced, more or less turned my attention in other directions, and made my religious emotions

and feelings sink into the background for a time, so that my mind became free at a later period to

take an entirely different view of the religious life.

I believe, however, that my experiences during these years have been valuable in one way, and

that is in teaching me to avoid ever encouraging in the young people I have known any sort of a

self-absorbed interior life. Self-absorption is always a temptation to young people, and if their

religion is of a sort to add to this self-absorption, I feel that it is a serious mistake. If I had my

way, the whole subject of feelings and emotions in the religious life would be absolutely ignored.

Feelings there will be, doubtless, but they must not be in the least depended on, nor in any sense

be taken as the test or gauge of one’s religion. They ought to be left out of the calculation

entirely. You may feel good or you may feel bad, but neither the good feeling nor the bad feeling

affects the real thing. It may affect your comfort in the thing, but it has nothing to do with the

reality of the thing. If God loves you, it is of no account, as far as the fact goes, whether you feel

that He loves you or do not feel it; although, as I say, it materially affects your comfort. Of

course, if you really believe that He loves you, you cannot help being glad about it; but if you

make your belief dependent upon your f eelings of gladness, you are reversing God’s order in the

most hopeless kind of way.

I like so much that story of Luther when the devil said to him: “Luther, do you feel that you are a

child of God?” and Luther replied: “No, I do not feel it at all, but I know it. Get thee behind me,

Satan.”

T

During all the years when I was struggling over my feelings, I never succeeded in making them

what I thought they ought to be; and as a consequence the religious part of my life was a misery

to me. But after I had learned that the facts of religion were far more important than my feelings

about these facts, and had consequently given up looking at my feelings, and sought only to

discover the facts, I became always happy in my religious life, and had, without any effort, the

very feelings of love to God, and of rest and peace and joy in my soul that before I had so vainly

tried to work up. No words can express how vital I consider this point to be, nor how much, since

I have found it out for myself, I have longed to make everybody else see it.

Many years after it had all become clear to me, one of my children came to me evidently in great

perplexity and said: “Mother, how long does it take God to forgive you when you have been

naughty?”

“It does not take Him a minute,” I replied.

“Oh,” she said, “I can’t believe that. I think you have to feel sorry first for a good many days,

and then you have to ask Him in a very pretty and nice way, and then perhaps He can forgive

you.”

“But,” I said, “daughter, the Bible says that if we confess our sins He is faithful and just to

forgive us right straight off.”

“Well,” she said, “I wouldn’t believe that if fifty Bibles said it, because I know that you have got

to feel sorry for quite a good while, and then you have got to ask God in a very pretty way, and

then you have got to wait till He is ready to forgive you.”

I found the case was really serious, so, taking the child on my lap, I opened the Bible and made

her read out loud the verse I had quoted, and then explained to her that God loved us so much

that He sent His Son to die for us, and that, because of His love, He was always ready to forgive

us the minute we asked Him, just as mothers were always ready to forgive their children as soon

as the children wanted to be forgiven.

At last the child was convinced, and putting her little hands together she said in a reverent little

voice: “Dear Lord Jesus, I want you to forgive me this very minute for all my naughty, and I am

certain sure you will, because you love me.” And then she jumped down off my lap and ran

away shouting merrily in childish glee.

My little girl was happy because she had found out a happy fact and believed it. But in her first

way of looking at the matter she was only voicing the natural idea of the human heart. We all

feel, as she did, that we must come to God with great doubt and timidity, as to a Being of whom

we know but little, and whom we fear much; and that His favour depends altogether upon the

beauty and suitableness of our emotions, and the ceremonious order of our approach.

To come “boldly to the throne of grace to find mercy and obtain help in the time of need” is only

possible to the soul that has been brought into a real acquaintance with the goodness of God.

During all the years, however, of which I speak, from the age of sixteen to twenty-six, I knew

nothing of this. God was to me a far-off, unapproachable Being, whom, in spite of all my eager

and painful searching, I failed utterly to find. I had not the slightest conception of what the

expression “God is love” meant. My idea of Him was that He was a stern and selfish taskmaster,

who might perhaps, if one could only secure the sort of feelings and conduct that would please

Him, be induced to pay some little attention to the needs of His children, but who was for the

most part so absorbed in thoughts of His own glory, and of the consideration and reverence due

to Himself, that it was almost impossible, except by a superhuman degree of perfection, to win

His regards.

He seemed to me a supremely selfish Autocrat who held my fate in His hands, but who only

cared for me in proportion to my power of adding to His honour and His glory.

Of all His loving and beautiful unselfishness, which I was afterwards to discover, I had for all

these years not the faintest glimpse. Moreover, the only way I knew by which one could know

that this unapproachable Deity did condescend to turn even a slight ear to the cries of His

children was to have some sort of an interior feeling of it. Consequently, whenever I was

religious at all, the whole energy of my spirit was spent, as I have said, in the effort to acquire in

some occult way this necessary inward feeling.

The sort of introspection I had imbibed from my Quaker teaching was calculated to lead to

constant self-examination of the most difficult sort, because it was an examination not so much

into one’s actions as into one’s emotions. And, considering what ticklish things our emotions are,

and how much they depend upon the state of our health, or the state of the weather, or the

influence of other minds, no more fatal occupation, in my opinion, can be indulged in than this

sort of self- examination. No more unreliable gauge could possibly be found as to one’s spiritual

condition than that afforded by one’s own interior emotions.

But the religion of my years between sixteen and twenty-six was nothing but a religion of trying

to feel; and, as I was a very natural, healthy sort of being, my feelings were not likely to be very

sentimental or pious. The agonizing, futile efforts that I have described to bring them up to the

right religious pitch is something pitiful to consider.

My soul hungered after God, but I could not find Him. Even the comfort of prayer was denied

me, for I had, as I have said, imbibed the idea that you could not pray acceptably unless you felt

an inward sense of the Divine favour, and that any prayers offered without this sense were really

a mockery, and even perhaps a sin. And, since this inward sense of God’s favour was the very

thing I was seeking to secure, and yet might not pray for until I first possessed it, I seemed tossed

out helpless and forlorn into dreary darkness.

What the Bible said about God’s love was altogether a secondary consideration to what I might

feel about it; indeed, as far as I can recollect, I did not consider the Bible at all. “How do I feel?”

not “What does God say?” was my daily cry. I was like a criminal in the presence of a judge,

who, instead of being concerned as to how the judge felt about him, should spend all his efforts

in trying to see how he felt about the judge.

A more ridiculous as well as pitiful attitude of soul one can hardly conceive of. And yet no one

whom I approached on the subject seemed to know any better; and I floundered on in a

despairing sort of way, afraid to give up my spiritual struggles lest I should be eternally damned,

and yet realizing that they brought no help; and being continually tempted to upbraid God for

being deaf to my cries.

I was like a man kneeling in a dark room and praying despairingly for light, ignorant of the fact

that outside the sun was shining, and that it only needed to open the windows and light would

pour in. In the very nature of things, light, either in the physical world or the spiritual world,

cannot be self-evolved. I had gone to work in entirely the wrong way. I was trying to feel before

I knew, and, instead of basing my feelings upon my knowledge, I was seeking to base my

knowledge upon my feelings.

It was just as if a man, wanting to travel to a certain place, should enter the first railway station

he might come across, and, without making any enquiries, should take a seat in the first railway

carriage at hand, and should then shut his eyes and try to feel whether he was in the right train or

not. No man in his senses would do such an idiotic thing. And yet it was exactly this I was doing

in my religious life. It never entered my head to try and find out the facts of religion. I did not

even know there were any facts to find out. My relations with God seemed to me altogether a

matter of my own feelings towards Him, and not in the least of His feelings towards me; and

every religious energy I possessed was consequently directed towards getting up these necessary

feelings.

Of course, it was an impossible task, and, as time went on, and no right feelings would come for

all my striving, I became more and more discouraged. At last, when I was between twenty-three

and twenty-four, I found myself being driven into absolute unbelief. I argued that, if there really

was a God anywhere, some answer to all my long and earnest wrestling would surely have been

vouchsafed to me; and that, since He made no sign, therefore He could not be.

Moreover, as I grew older, I had begun to learn something more of the awful condition of things

in the world because of sin; and the manifest evidences I seemed to see of an imperfect creation

in my own life and in the lives of others, where failure was generally the rule and success only

the exception, appeared to me incompatible with the idea of a wise and sensible Creator, not to

say a good One, such as I had been told I must believe in. And gradually the creation came to

seem to me such a grievous failure that I felt driven to the conclusion that either it must have

been a wicked God who had created us, or else we had not been created by God at all, but by

some evil and malicious power opposed to Him.

In my diary under date of Eleventh month, 5th, 1855, I head my entry with the following

ominous words:

“The Eclipse of Faith.” *“This last year has witnessed a great change in me. Every faculty of

my nature has been thoroughly aroused. I have felt my mind expanding and have been cognizant

of an actual and rapid mental growth. I pass from one phase of experience to another, leave

behind me one standing place after another, and am now — where! Oh Christ, that I indeed knew

where!

An inevitable chain of reasoning on free will has loosened every foothold, and I know not where

to rest, if indeed there is any rest. Without any apprehension on my part of the result, thoughts

and reasonings have been slowly gathering around my faith, and dashing themselves against it,

until at last, with a sudden shock, it has fallen; and I am lost!

It has come to me like this. Benevolence certainly is a necessary attribute of the Almighty. His

love, we are told, surpasses the love of an earthly parent far more than we can imagine. But it is

utterly inconsistent with this to suppose that He can have any foreknowledge of the destiny of the

human beings He creates. For of course, did He know, His benevolence would not allow Him to

create any but beings destined to eternal happiness. Therefore He cannot be omniscient.

Further, if He were omnipotent, as we are told, He would have made such modifications in

man’s nature as would at least render the work of salvati on less difficult and of far more frequent

occurrence. Therefore He cannot be both all-loving and also all-powerful. Without either of these

He ceases to be a God. Either He has set in motion a creating force which He can neither control

nor end, and has performed His work in the first place so imperfectly and blindly that the results

are grievously disastrous; or He has nothing to do with creation, and we are created by another

and an evil Power.

A further conclusion is forced upon me. Justice is another necessary attribute of a good God. But

it were most utterly unjust that we now should be feeling the effects of Adam’s fall, supposing

there ever was such a thing. We are driven therefore from the possibility of a just Creator making

independent beings suff er eternally for each other’s sins. And on the other hand benevolence

could not allow of the creation of innately wicked natures, while justice could not share in

punishing them.

There is no escape! A thousand questions rush in on every side. I am a scepti c!”*

fields.title: Chapter 17. A Renewed Search
fields.body_html:
his skepticism continued for more than two years, and I had settled into it, regarding it as

the normal condition of any thoughtful, reasonable person. But the year 1858 was destined

to change everything.

Early that year I became acquainted with some very orthodox Christians who were full of the

doctrines and dogmas of Christianity. As I have mentioned before, I knew absolutely nothing of

doctrines; they had never entered into my conception of religion at all. I was, therefore,

immensely interested in hearing about them and began to wonder whether my unbelief might

have arisen from my complete ignorance of these very doctrines.

Under the date of April 25, 1858, I wrote in my diary:

Diary:

“The Bible talks of the necessity of being ‘born again.’ What does it mean? Is there really such a

thing to be experienced in practice? And is a belief in Jesus of Nazareth as the Savior of the

world necessary to it? Oh, how I long for settlement… It may be that all my failures to find and

walk in the right way arise from my rejection of Christ in the sense in which most Christians

seem to receive Him; but I really cannot receive Him so. And besides, if their way is the truth, I

must wait until my Divine Guide leads me into it; and certainly He is not leading me there now,

but, it seems to me, farther and farther away…

“My whole soul and intellect seem to shrink from the m aterial orthodox view of the Gospel. It

seems impossible for me to believe in the atoning merits of Christ’s death. My mind revolts from

anything so material as the idea that the outward death of His body (which, after all, must

necessarily have taken place in some way as a consequence of His humanity) could have had any

atoning merit. Far more likely, if atonement were needed at all, was it His life that was the

sacrifice. To put on humanity must indeed have been to Divinity a wonderful condescension and

bitter suffering; to put it off, no matter in what way, could have been none at all.

T

“But I may be wrong in my views. Only the Lord can teach me.”

Again, on May 18, 1858, I wrote:

Diary:

“I cannot help the feeling that I have attained a higher form of Truth than the apostles had, and

therefore I cannot pray, ‘Lord, I believe; help Thou my unbelief,’ since I have no conviction of

being in unbelief. I am not comfortable, however, in either my belief or unbelief — whichever it

may be — and yet I see no way of escape.

“Last night at our Bible class I introduced the subject, hoping my orthodox friends would argue

so conclusively on their side as to force me into conviction in the orthodox form of faith. But I

felt, at the end, that no argument could avail anything. If my belief is to be changed, it will have

to be by a Divine power, and it would indeed be a being ‘born again.’ But it seems impossible to

me.”

Again, on June 25, 1858, I wrote:

Diary:

“Cold and dead again, and full of pride! The day will certainly come at last when it will be said

of me, as of Ephraim of old, ‘She is wedded to her idols; let her alone!’ My ‘idol’ now, I fear, is

the pride of human reason, which will not submit to become as a little child before it can enter

the Kingdom of Heaven…

“At prese nt I am in great trouble because of my religious belief. I long to adopt the Orthodox

creed, but cannot; and while on one hand it seems wicked that I cannot, at the same time it seems

also wicked in me to try to do so when a clearer light appears to have been granted to me.

“If the truth is what the Unitarians profess, I am afraid to know it. I dread the consequences. I

shrink from the contempt and reproaches it would bring upon me. And yet at the same time,

there is perhaps something a little pleasing to natural human pride and heroism in the thought of

being called upon to take an independent stand for what I consider a higher form of truth. And

yet I do not want to be independent of those I love. I am in a state of sad perplexity.”

This perplexity increased and deepened, and at last I began to feel that it was dishonest not to

speak of it to my friends. I was just making up my mind to do so when, one day, an event

occurred that changed the whole current of my life.

And this brings me to the second e poch in my soul’s history.

fields.title: Chapter 18. Second Epoch In My Religious Life (Restoration Of Belief)
fields.body_html:
t was in the year 1858, and I was twenty-six years old. I had just lost a precious little

daughter, five years old, and my heart was aching with sorrow. I could not endure to think

that my darling had gone out alone into a Godless universe; and yet, no matter on which side I

turned, there seemed no ray of light.

It happened that just at this time the religious world was being greatly stirred by the inauguration

of daily noonday meetings, held from twelve to one, in the business part of the city, and crowded

with business men. I had heard of these noonday meetings with a very languid interest, as I

thought they were only another effort of a dying-out superstition to bolster up its cause.

However, one day I happened to be near a place where one of these meetings was being held,

and I thought I would go in and see what it was like.
