It was an impressive thing to see such crowds of busy men and women collected together at that

hour in one of the busiest parts of the city, and I remember wondering vaguely what it could all

be about. Then suddenly something happened to me. What it was or how it came I had no idea,

but somehow an inner eye seemed to be opened in my soul, and I seemed to see that after all God

was a fact — the bottom fact of all facts — and that the only thing to do was to find out all about

Him.

It was not a pious feeling, such as I had been looking for, but it was a conviction, just such a

conviction as comes to one when a mathematical problem is suddenly solved. One does not feel

it is solved, but one knows it, and there can be no further question. I do not remember anything

that was said. I do not even know that I heard anything. A tremendous revolution was going on

within me that was of far profounder interest than anything the most eloquent preacher could

have uttered. God was making Himself manifest as an actual existence, and my soul leaped up in

an irresistible cry to know Him.

I

It was not that I felt myself to be a sinner needing salvation, or that I was troubled about my

future destiny. It was not a personal question at all. It was simply and only that I had become

aware of God, and that I felt I could not rest until I should know Him. I might be good or I might

be bad; I might be going to Heaven or I might be going to hell — these things were outside the

question. All I wanted was to become acquainted with the God of whom I had suddenly become

aware. How to set about it was the one absorbing question. I had no one I cared to ask, and it

never occurred to me that prayer would help me.

It seemed to me like the study of some new and wonderful branch of knowledge to which I must

apply with all diligence, and I concluded that probably the Bible was the book I needed. “This

book,” I said to myself, “professes to teach us about God. I will see if it can teach me anything.”

I was going with my family to spend some weeks at the seashore, and I decided to take no books

but the Bible, and to try and find out what it said about God.

In my diary I wrote under date of July 16, 1858: “I have brought my Bible to Atlantic City this

summer with a determination to find out what its plan of salvation is. My own plans have failed

utterly, now I will try G od’s if possible. … I am trying to believe Him simply as a little child. I

have laid aside my preconceived notions of what He ought to do and say, and have come in

simplicity to the Bible to see what He has done and said; and I will believe Him.”

Someone had remarked once in my hearing that the book of Romans contained the clearest and

fullest statements of Christian doctrine to be found in the Bible, and I set myself to read it. What

I should have made out of it without any guidance I cannot say, but one day I mentioned to a

lady, who was visiting us, how interested I was in trying to understand the teaching of the Book

of Romans, but how difficult I found it, when she said she had a little book which had explained

it to her, and asked if she might give it to me.

I accepted it eagerly, and found it most enlightening. It set forth the plan of salvation as

described in the third, fourth, and fifth of Romans in a clear, businesslike way that appealed to

me strongly. It stated that mankind were all sinners, and all deserved punishment — that all had

sinned and come short of the glory of God, and that there was none righteous, no not one; and it

declared that therefore every mouth was stopped and all the world had become guilty before God

(Romans 3:1 – 19).

It went on to show that there was no escape from this except through the righteousness of Christ,

which was “unto all and upon all them that believe”; and that Christ was our propitiation,

through whom we obtained the “remission of sins that are past” (Romans 3:20– 26). And then it

pointed out that by this process all boasting on our part was shut out, and we were justified

before God, not by anything we had done or could do, but by what our Divine Saviour had done

for us (Romans 3:27 – 31).

It declared that Christ was the substitute for sinners — that He had in their place borne the

punishment they deserved, and that all we had to do in order to secure the full benefit of this

substitution was simply to believe in it, and accept the forgiveness so purchased.

Of course, this was a very legal and businesslike interpretation of these passages, and was not at

all the interpretation I should give to them now; but I want to tell, as truthfully as I can, the way

things impressed me then. The very crudeness and outwardness of the interpretation made it easy

for my ignorance to grasp it, and it struck me at the time as a most sensible and satisfactory

arrangement.

It was a “plan of salvation” that I could understand. There was nothing mystical or mysterious

about it — no straining after emotions, no looking out for experiences. It was all the work of

another done for me, and required nothing on my part but a simple, common-sense

understanding and belief. Baldly stated, it was as follows: We were all sinners, and therefore all

deserved punishment. But Christ had taken our sins upon Himself and had borne the punishment

in our stead, and therefore an angry God was propitiated, and was willing to forgive us and let us

go free. Nothing could be more plain and simple. Even a child could understand it.

It was all outside of oneself, and there need be no searchings within or rakings up of one’s

inward feelings to make things right with God. Christ had made them right, and we had nothing

to do but to accept it all as a free gift from Him. Moreover, a God who could arrange such a

simple plan as this was understandable and approachable, and I began to think it must be true.

This all sounds very outward and very crude, but, after all, crude as it seems, there was behind it

the great bottom fact that God was, somehow or other, in Christ reconciling the world unto

Himself; and it was this vital fact of the reconciliation between God and man that had laid hold

of me. And I believe it is this fact, however it may be expressed, that is the one essential thing in

the outset of every satisfactory religious life. The soul must know that all is right between itself

and God before it can try, with any heart, to worship and serve Him.

I had discovered this vital fact, and the religious life had begun for me with eager and

enthusiastic delight. In my diary, I find the following entries in 1858:

“August 20, 1858. Am I really coming to Christ? I ask myself this question with wonder and

amazement. A month ago it seemed so utterly impossible. But I believe I am. It seems as if these

truths in the New Testament have taken hold of my soul, and I cannot gainsay them. God only

knows what the end will be.”

“August 21, 1858. Many passages of Scripture have been impressed on my mind in my reading,

and, having made up my mind simply to believe and not to reason or question, I do find myself

inevitably brought to Christ as my Redeemer. My watchword for the last few weeks has been

‘Thus saith the Lord’ as a conclusive argument in every case.”

“August 30, 1858. I am resting now simply on God’s own record as the foundation of my hope.

He says Jesus Christ is His well-beloved Son, and I believe it. He says further that He gave His

Son to be the propitiation for our sins, and I believe this also. He is my Saviour, not only my

helper, and in His finished work I rest. Even my hard heart of unbelief can no longer refrain

from crying out, ‘Lord, I believe. Help Thou my unbelief.’”

“September 13, 1858. My heart is filled with the exceeding preciousness of Christ. And I am lost

in wonder at the realization of His infinite mercy to me, who am so utterly unworthy of the least

favour from His hands. How could He be so tender and so loving! I can write the words, ‘It is all

of free grace,’ but they only feebly convey the deep sense I have o f the infinite freeness of this

grace. ‘While we were yet sinners Christ died for us.’ Could anything be more free than this? I

have so long bewildered myself with trying to work out my own righteousness, and have found

such weariness in it, that I feel as if I could never appreciate deeply enough the blessed rest

there is for me in Christ. ‘He was made sin for us who knew no sin, that we might be made the

righteousness of God in Him.’ No wonder the Apostle cried out from a full heart, ‘Thanks be

unto God f or His unspeakable gift!’”

My diary is full of similar records, but these will suffice to tell of the wonderful discovery I had

made. I want it to be clearly understood that it all came to me as a discovery, and in no sense as

an attainment. I had been seeking after attainments in the past, but now I had lost all thought of

any attainment of my own in the blaze of my discoveries of the salvation through Christ.

It was no longer in the slightest degree a question of what I was or what I could do, but

altogether a question of what God was and of what He had done. I seemed to have left myself, as

myself, out of it entirely, and to care only to find out all I could about the work of Christ.

The thing that amazed me was how I could have lived so long in a world that contained the

Bible, and never have found all this before. Why had nobody ever told me? How could people

who had found it out, have kept such a marvellous piece of good news to themselves? Certainly,

I could not keep it to myself, and I was determined that no one whom I could reach should be left

a day longer in ignorance, as far as I could help it.

I began to buttonhole everybody, pulling them into corners and behind doors to tell them of the

wonderful and delightful things I had discovered in the Bible about salvation through the Lord

Jesus Christ. It seemed to me the most magnificent piece of good news that any human being had

ever had to tell, and I gloried in telling it.

So little, however, had I known of Christian ideas and Christian nomenclature, that I had not the

least conception that what I had discovered made any difference in me personally, or that my

belief in all this made me what they called a Christian. It only seemed to me that I had found out

something delightful about God, which had filled me with happiness, and which I wanted

everybody else to know. But that this discovery constituted what was called “conversion,” or that

I personally was different in any way from what I had been before, never entered my head.

One day, however, a “Plymouth Brother” friend, hearing me tell my story, exclaimed: “Thank

God, Mrs. Smith, that you have at last become a Christian.” So little did I understand him, that I

promptly replied: “Oh, no, I am not a Christian at all. I have only found out a wonderful pi ece of

good news that I never knew before.”

“But,” he persisted, “that very discovery makes you a Christian, for the Bible says that whoever

believes this good news has passed from death unto life, and is born of God. You have just said

that you believe it and rejoice in it, so of course you have passed from death unto life and are

born of God.”

I thought for a moment, and I saw the logic of what he said. There was no escaping it. And with

a sort of gasp I said: “Why, so I must be. Of course I believe this good news, and therefore of

course I must be born of God. Well, I am glad.”

From that moment the matter was settled, and not a doubt as to my being a child of God and the

possessor of eternal life has ever had the slightest power over me since. I rushed to my Bible to

make myself sure there was no mistake, and I found it brimming over with this teaching.

“He that believeth hath.” “He that believeth is.” There seemed to be nothing more to be said

about it. Three passages especially struck me:

x 1 John 5:1: “Whosoever believeth that Jesus is the Christ is born of God.”

x John 3:24: “Verily, verily I say unto you, He that heareth My word and believeth on Him

that sent Me, hath everlasting life, and shall not come into condemnation, but is passed

from death unto lif e.”

x John 20:30 – 31: “And many other signs truly did Jesus in the presence of His disciples,

which are not written in this book: but these are written, that ye might believe that Jesus

is the Christ, the Son of God; and that, believing, ye might have life th rough His name.”

There seemed nothing more to be said. There were the things about Christ, written in the Bible,

as clear as daylight, and I believed what was written with all my heart and soul, and therefore I

could not doubt that I was one of those who h ad “life through His name.” The question was

settled without any further argument. It had nothing to do with how I felt, but only with what

God had said. The logic seemed to me irresistible; and it not only convinced me then, but it has

carried me triumphantly through every form of doubt as to my relations with God which has ever

assailed me since. And I can recommend it as an infallible receipt to every doubter.

Of course, at once, on having made this further discovery of the fact that I was a Christian, I

began to add it to the story I had already been telling, always ending my recital with the words:

“And now, if you believe all this, you are a Christian, for the Bible says that he that believeth is

born of God, and has eternal life.”

I had got hold of that which is the necessary foundation of all religion — namely, reconciliation

with God — and had had my first glimpse of Him as He is revealed in the face of Jesus Christ. All

my fear of Him had vanished. He loved me, He forgave me, He was on my side, and all was right

between us.

I had learned, moreover, that it was from the life and words of Christ that my knowledge of God

was to come, and not, as I had always thought, from my own inward feelings; and my relief was

inexpressible.

I can see now, in looking back, that in many respects I had only touched the surface of the

spiritual realities hidden under the doctrines I had so eagerly embraced. I was as yet only in the

beginning of things. But it was a beginning in the right direction, and was the introduction to the

“life more abundant,” which, as my story will show, was to come later.

Meanwhile, I had got my first glimpse of the unselfishness of God. As yet it was only a glimpse,

but it was enough to make me radiantly happy.

fields.title: Chapter 19. The Assurance Of Faith
fields.body_html:
was so filled with enthusiasm over my discovery that nothing else seemed to me of the

slightest importance; and, as I have said, I attacked every friend I had on the subject, and

insisted on knowing whether they too had found out the transcendent fact that their sins were all

forgiven, and that they were the children of God. I simply compelled them to listen, whether they

wanted to or not, for it seemed to me the most pitiful thing conceivable that anybody should fail

to know it, while I was alive to tell it.

And I must say that nearly everyone I spoke to — partly perhaps because of their surprise at being

attacked so vigorously — listened with eager interest, and sooner or later embraced the views I so

enthusiastically declared. Very many of my friends, of course, really were already Christians, but

had hardly dared to think themselves so; and to them my teaching brought the assurance of faith

they so sorely needed.

In fact, it seemed to me such a wonderful bit of good news that I thought if I would go into the

street and stand at the corners, and begin to tell it, everybody would open the doors and windows

to listen to my story. I felt like a herald marching through the corridors of a prison, with a

proclamation from the King of free pardon to every prisoner. Paul’s message in the synagogue of

the Jews at Antioch, when he spoke to them about Jesus and said: “Be it known unto you

therefore, men and brethren, that through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins;

and by Him all that believe are justified from all things from which ye could not be justified by

the law of Moses,” was my message. And the marvel to me was that every prisoner did not at

once, on hearing it, open the door of his cell and walk out a free man.

It seemed to me superlatively silly for anyone, in the face of such a proclamation, to hesitate a

single moment. Why should they worry about their sins, when God had so plainly declared that

Christ had borne their sins in “His own body on the tree,” and had taken them away forever?

Why should they fear God’s anger, when the Bible had assured us that “God was in Christ

reconciling the world unto Himself, not imputin g their trespasses unto them”? All these

I

wretched doubts and fears seemed then, and have always seemed since, not only irreligious and a

libel against the trustworthiness of God, but also as an evidence of a great lack of good sense.

Either God is true, or He is a liar. If I believe He is true, then good sense demands that I should

accept His statements as the statements of facts, and should rest in them as facts.

One of the most helpful things to me at this time was a tract called “The Fox Hunter” by César

Malan. It was the clearest and most logical presentation of justification by faith that I have ever

come across, and it proved to me beyond the possibility of question that the “assurance of faith”

was at once the only biblical ground anyone could take, and also the only common-sense ground

as well. The foxes in this tract were doubts, and the hunter was the preacher who caught and

killed them. And its whole teaching was that if God said Christ had taken away our sins, then He

certainly had done so, and they were of course gone, and it was not only folly but also

presumption in us not to believe it.

I continually asked myself why every preacher did not tell out these facts clearly and fully so that

no one could fail to understand them. And I felt this so strongly that, whenever I heard sermons

that seemed to leave the matter uncertain or confused, I thought nothing of going up to the

preachers afterwards and expostulating with them, because they had not clearly preached the

Gospel of Christ.

I am convinced, in looking back now, that I must have made myself a general nuisance to our

dear Quaker preachers, whose preaching I confess was not often in those days of this definite

sort. But the truth was that what I had discovered seemed to me of such paramount and

overwhelming importance that no other consideration was worth a moment’s notice. To be in a

world full of sinners, who did not know that their sins were forgiven, and that they were the

children of God, and who might know it if only someone would tell them, seemed to me such a

tremendous responsibility that I felt compelled to tell it to everyone I could reach.

The dear quiet Friends could not understand such excessive, and I dare say unwise, zeal, and my

visits at any of their houses were fairly dreaded. Even my brothers-in-law were almost afraid to

have me visit my own sisters, and in many ways I went through a sort of persecution, which no

doubt I largely brought upon myself by my unadvised zeal, but which at the time seemed to me a

martyrdom for the truth.

It is not often, I think, that the story of the Gospel comes so vividly to anyone as it did to me. But

from the fact that, as a Quaker, I had had no doctrinal teaching, all that I was learning about the

salvation in Christ came in a perfect blaze of illumination. The Bible seemed fairly radiant with

the “glad tidings of great joy,” and I wondered that everyone did not see it.

As I knew literally nothing of theology, and had never heard any theological terms, I took the

whole Gospel story in the most common-sense way possible, and believed it without any

reservations. I often said I was like a prisoner who had come out of a dark underground cell into

the light of ten thousand suns. And in spite of all the disapproval and opposition of the Elders

and Overseers among the Quakers, and of my own family as well, my enthusiasm gained me a

hearing, and nearly every friend I had came, sooner or later, into a knowledge of the truths I

advocated, and more or less shared my rejoicing.

So that gradually the opposition died down, and in the end, while the “solid Friends” could not

fully endorse me, they at least left me free to continue my course unmolested.

No doubt the crudeness of my views was very patent to the more advanced spiritual Christians

around me, and I feel sure now that a large part of the opposition I met with arose from this fact.

But while I might wish my views had been more mature, I can never regret the enthusiasm that

made me so eager to tell out to everyone the best I knew.

And even the opposition was blessed to me, for it taught me some most invaluable lessons. I

came across a book in those days, the name of which I regret to say I have forgotten, which

helped me enormously. Its central thought was that one of the richest gifts a Christian could have

was the gift of persecution, and that to be like the Master in being rejected of men was the

highest dignity to which a Christian could attain. It taught that he was the greatest Christian who

was willing to take the lowest place, and that to become the chief of all could only be attained by

becoming the servant of all.

I was so impressed by this teaching that I tried to put it in practice; and, whenever I expected in

any interview to meet with reproof or opposition, I would always beforehand pray fervently that

I might receive it in a true Christian spirit. I was much helped, too, by a saying of Madame

Guyon’s, that she had learned to be thankful for every snub and mortification, because she had

found that they helped to advance her in the spiritual life; and in time I learned something of the

same lesson.

The special advantage I gained from the disapproval I met with was that it took a great deal of

the conceit out of me. I had it so rubbed into me that I was altogether wrong and foolish, and was

only tolerated because of the kindness of my friends, that I really came at last to have a sort of

instinctive feeling that I deserved nothing but snubs and reproaches, and that any unkindness that

might be shown me was only my just desert. In fact, I got into the habit of never expecting

anything else, and ceased to think I had any rights that others ought not to trample on.

This habit of mind has given me the greatest liberty of spirit through all my life since, as I have

never been obliged, as so many people seem to be, to stand up for my rights, and have in fact

scarcely ever had the sense to see when I have been slighted. If one has no rights, their rights

cannot be trampled on; and if one has no feelings, their feelings cannot be hurt. So deeply was

this lesson engraved upon my soul by what I went through at the time of which I am speaking,

that to this day I am always surprised at any kindness that is shown me, as at something entirely

unexpected and undeserved.

I do not know any lesson I have ever learned that has been so practically helpful as this lesson,

learned from the opposition I met with in the early years of my Christian experience; although I

have no doubt, as I have said, that I brought my trials largely upon myself by my crudeness and

my ignorance.

Crude and ignorant as I was, I had, however, as I have said, got a firm grip on one magnificent

foundation truth that nothing has ever been able to shake, and this was that God was in Christ

reconciling the world unto Himself, not imputing their trespasses unto them. All was right

between my soul and God. He was my Father, and I was His child, and I had nothing to fear. It

was no matter that I had got hold of it in a crude sort of way. The thing was that I had got hold of

it. There it was — the grand central fact of God’s love and God’s forgiveness— and my soul was

at rest about this forever.

fields.title: Chapter 20. The Romance Of The Religious Life
fields.body_html:
he disapproval of my own religious society, in these early stages of my new life, threw me

very much under the influence of the Plymouth Brethren, who were at that time making

quite a stir in Philadelphia, and whose clear teaching of doctrines — especially the doctrine of

“justification by faith”— was particularly congenial to my new way of looking at things. They

were great Bible students, and I soon found, under their teaching, a fascinating interest in Bible

study.

It was all new ground to me, and I went into it with the greatest avidity. So delighted was I with

the treasures I found in its pages that, at first, my one fear was that, as the Bible was such a short

book, I should soon exhaust it and come to the end of its delights. I used to stint myself to small

portions in order to spin it out longer. But I soon found that this was not at all necessary, as the

more I studied, the more I found there was to study, and each passage seemed to have a thousand

continually unfolding meanings.

The book was no larger than I thought, but it was infinitely deeper. It seemed to me as if the

truths in the Bible were covered with a multitude of skins, and as if, as I studied, one skin after

another were peeled off, leaving the words the same but the meaning of those words deeper and

higher. I can never be thankful enough to the Plymouth Brethren for introducing me to the

fascinations of Bible study.

It was a wonderful and delightful life I had now begun to live. I had begun to know God, and I

was finding Him to be lovely and lovable beyond my fondest imaginings. The romance of my

life had dawned. I cannot say how religion may have affected other people, but to me my

religion has been, all through, a fascinating and ever-unfolding romance.

If for nothing else, I pity the poor unfortunate Agnostics of the present day for missing this most

delightful of all romances. They can have nothing, I am sure, in all their lives to equal it. The

nearest approach that I can think of to a like experience is the delight of exploring an unknown

T

science or a new field of mental research; but even that cannot equal, I am sure, the delights of

exploring the Science of God.

Imagine it for a moment: to have got on the track of a real acquaintance with the ways and

character of God, the Creator of heaven and earth, and to be making continually fresh discoveries

of new and delightful things about Him — what scientific research could be as entrancing?

All that I had longed for and agonized over in my first awakening was coming to me in clearest

vision, day by day, and the ever-recurring delight of new revelations and new ideas was more

delicious than words could express. Then too, the joy of telling it all to others, and the enormous

satisfaction of seeing their faces lighten, and their hearts expand, as their souls made the same

discoveries as my own. Ah, no one who has not experienced it can know the fascination of it all!

I do not mean to say that I discovered everything at once, nor even that all I thought I had

discovered proved to be permanent truth. My story, as I continue, will show that this was not the

case. Like all novices in scientific research, I grasped many half-truths, and came to many false

conclusions. But the search of itself was delicious, and the finding out of one’s mistakes far

surpassed the mortification at having made them.

My soul had started on its voyage of discovery, and to become acquainted with God was its

unalterable and unceasing aim. I was as yet only at the beginning, but what a magnificent

beginning it was. God was a reality, and He was my God. He had created me, and He loved me,

and all was right between us.

All care about my own future destiny had been removed from my shoulders. I could say with

Paul: “I know whom I have believed, and am persuaded that He is able to keep that which I have

committed unto Him against that day.” I needed no longer to work for my soul’s salvation, but

only to work out the salvation that had been bestowed upon me.

All the years of my self-introversion and self-examination were ended. Instead of my old

fruitless searchings into my feelings and emotions for some tangible evidence of God’s favour,

the glorious news declared in the Bible — that He so loved the world as to have sent His only

begotten Son to save the world — absorbed every faculty.

It was no longer “How do I feel?” but always “What does God say?” And He said such

delightful things, that to find them out became my supreme delight. I do not mean what He said

to me personally in my heart, but what He had said to every human being in the Bible — the good

news of salvation in the Lord Jesus Christ.

Anything said to myself alone might be open to doubt, as to whether it was really myself who

was meant; but anything said to the whole world could not help including me, and I greedily

appropriated it all.

This went on for several years, during which I had a really glorious time. Between the joys of

discovery on the one hand, and the joys of telling others about my discoveries on the other, my

cup of the wine of life was full and overflowing.

I had plenty of earthly trials, but somehow they were in the background compared to the

fascinations of my religious life. Nothing that belonged only to the earthly life could really

matter, when one’s soul was daily tasting the blissful joy of reconciliation with God, and of

being made a partaker of the glorious salvation of the Lord Jesus Christ.

And yet how little I knew, even of this, compared with what was to come!

fields.title: Chapter 21. Questionings
fields.body_html:
uring all the years of which I speak, the Plymouth Brethren were, as I have said, among

my principal teachers. But I began gradually to find some things in their teaching that I

could not accept; and this was especially the case with their extreme Calvinism.

There have always been, I believe, differences of opinion among them in regard to this view; but

those with whom I was thrown held very rigidly the belief that some people were “elected” to

salvation, and some were elected to “reprobation,” and that nothing the individual could do could

change these eternal decrees. We, of course, were among those elected to salvation, and for this

we were taught to be profoundly thankful.

I tried hard to fall in with this. It seemed difficult to believe that those who had taught me so

much could possibly be mistaken on such a vital point. But my soul revolted from it more and

more. How could I be content in knowing that I myself was sure of Heaven, when other poor

souls, equally deserving, but who had not had my chances, were “elected,” for no fault of their

own, but in the eternal decrees of God, to “reprobation”? Such a doctrine seemed to me utterly

inconsistent with the proclamation of forgiveness that had so entranced me. I could not find any

limitations in this proclamation, and I could not believe there were any secret limitations in the

mind of the God who had made it.

Neither could I see how a Creator could be just, even if He were not loving, in consigning some

of the creatures He Himself, and no other, had created, to the eternal torment of hell, let them be

as great sinners as they might be. I felt that if this doctrine were true, I should be woefully

disappointed in the God whom I had, with so much rapture, discovered.

I could not fail to see, moreover, that, after all, each one of us was largely a creature of

circumstance — that what we were, and what we did, was more or less the result of our

temperaments, of our inherited characteristics, of our social surroundings, and of our education;

and that, as these were all providentially arranged for us, with often no power on our part to alter

D

them, it would not be just in the God who had placed us in their midst to let them determine our

eternal destiny.

As an escape from the doctrine of eternal torment, I at first embraced the doctrine of annihilation

for the wicked, and for a little while tried to comfort myself with the belief that this life ended all

for them. But the more I thought of it, the more it seemed to me that it would be a confession of

serious failure on the part of the Creator, if He could find no way out of the problem of His

creation but to annihilate the creatures whom He had created.

Unconsciously, one of my children gave me an illustration of this. She waked me up one

morning to tell me that she had been lying in bed having great fun in pretending that she had

made a man. She described the colour of his hair and his eyes, his figure, his height, his power,

his wisdom, and all the grand things he was going to do, and was very enthusiastic in her evident

delight in the joy of creation. When she had finished enumerating all the magnificent qualities of

her man, I said to her: “But, darling, suppose he should turn out badly; suppose he should do

mischief and hurt people, and make things go wrong, what would thee do then?”

“Oh,” she said, “I would not have any trouble; I’d just make him l ie down and chop his head

off.”

I saw at once what a splendid illustration this was of the responsibility of a Creator, and it

brought to my mind Mrs. Shelley’s weird story of the artist Frankenstein, who made the

monstrous image of a man, which, when it was finished, suddenly, to his horror, became alive,

and went out into the world, working havoc wherever it went. The horrified maker felt obliged to

follow his handiwork everywhere, in order to try and undo a little of the mischief that had been

done, and to remedy as far as possible the evils it had caused.

The awful sense of responsibility that rested upon him, because of the things done by the

creature he had created, opened my eyes to see the responsibility God must necessarily feel, if

the creatures He had created were to turn out badly. I could not believe He would torment them

forever; and neither could I rest in the thought of annihilation as His best remedy for sin.

I felt hopeless of reconciling the love and the justice of the Creator with the fate of His creatures,

and I knew not which way to turn. But deliverance was at hand, and the third epoch in my

Christian experience was about to dawn.

fields.title: Chapter 22. The Third Epoch In My Religious Life (The Restitution Of All Things)
fields.body_html:
s I stated in the last chapter, after a few years of exuberant joy in the good news of

salvation through Christ — for myself and for those who believed as I did — my heart began

reaching outward toward those who believed differently, and especially toward those who,

through the providential circumstances of their birth and surroundings, had never had a fair

chance in life. I could not help seeing that ignorance of God, and therefore lives of sin, seemed

the almost inevitable fate of vast numbers of my fellow human beings. And I could not reconcile

it with the justice of God that such unfortunate souls should be doomed to eternal torment for

circumstances for which they were not responsible and from which, in the great majority of

cases, they could not escape.

The fact that I, who no more deserved it than they, had been brought to the knowledge of the

truth while they were left out in the cold became so burdensome to me that I often felt I would

gladly give up my own salvation if, by that means, I could bestow it upon those placed in less

fortunate conditions than my own.

I began to feel that the salvation in which I had rejoiced was, after all, a narrow and selfish

salvation —unworthy of the Creator who has so emphatically declared that His “tender mercies

are over all His works,” and even more unworthy of the Lord Jesus Christ, who came into the

world for the single purpose of saving the world. I could not believe that His life and death for us

were intended to fall so far short of remedying the very evil He came expressly to remedy. I felt

it must be impossible that there could be any shortcoming in the salvation He had provided.

I became convi nced that my difficulties had arisen simply from misunderstanding God’s plans,

and I set myself earnestly to discover my mistake. As I have said, my first refuge had been the

annihilation of the wicked. But this soon seemed unworthy of a wise and good Creator — indeed,

A

a sad confession of failure on His part — and I could not reconcile it with His omnipotence or His

omniscience. I began to fear I was going to be disappointed in God.

But one day a revelation came that vindicated Him and settled the whole question forever.

We often had revivalist preachers staying in our home, as we sought every opportunity to help

forward what we called “gospel work.” Among them came one who was very much taken up

with the idea that it was the privilege and duty of Christians to share, in a special manner, in the

sufferings of Christ as well as in His joys. He seemed to think that doing so would somehow help

those who knew nothing of salvation in Christ; and he had adopted the practice of making strong

appeals on this subject in his meetings. He would ask Christians who were willing, for the sake

of others, to take a share of Christ’s sufferings upon themselves, to “come forward” to a front

bench in the meeting and pray that such a privilege might be granted them.

Somehow it all sounded very grand and heroic, and it fit so exactly with my own longings to

help my less fortunate fellow human beings that, although I did not go forward for prayer at any

of his meetings, I did begin privately to pray — blindly and ignorantly — that I might come into

the experience, whatever it was.

The result was very different from what I had expected, and far more tremendous.

I had expected to enter into a sense of Christ’s personal sufferings in the life and death He bore

for our sakes. Instead, I seemed to receive a revelation, not of His sufferings because of sin, but

of ours . I seemed to see the misery and anguish brought upon humanity by the entrance of sin

into the world, and Christ’s sorrow— not over His own suffering because of it, but over the

suffering of the poor human beings who had been cursed by it.

I seemed to understand something of what His anguish must be at the sight of the awful fate

permitted to befall the human race, and of His joy that He could do something to alleviate it. I

saw that ours was the suffering, and His was the joy of sacrificing Himself to save us. I felt that

if I had been a Divine Creator and had allowed such a dreadful fate to overtake the creatures I

had made, I would have been filled with anguish and would have realized that simple justice —

even if not love — required that I find some remedy for it. And I knew I could not be more just

than God.

Over and over, I found myself repeating in my heart the lines that George MacDonald places on

a tombstone in one of his stories:

“O h Thou who didst the serpent make,

Our pardon give, and pardon take.”

I had heard a great deal about the awfulness of our sins against God; but now I found myself

asking: What about the awfulness of our fate in having been made sinners? Would I not

infinitely rather that someone commit a sin against me than that I commit a sin against anyone

else? Was it not far more dreadful to be made a sinner than to be sinned against?

And I began to see that, since God had permitted sin to enter the world, it must necessarily

follow that, in common fairness, He would be compelled to provide a remedy equal to the

disease. I remembered mothers I had known whose children suffered from inherited diseases,

and who were only too thankful to lay down their lives in self-sacrifice if, in any way, they could

undo the harm they had caused by bringing these children into the world under such disastrous

conditions. And I asked myself: Could God do less?

I saw that when weighed on the balance of wrong endured, we , who had been created sinners,

had infinitely more to forgive than anyone against whom we ourselves may have sinned.

The vividness with which all this came to me can never be expressed. I did not think it, or

imagine it, or suppose it. I saw it. It was a revelation of the real nature of things — not according

to surface, conventional ideas, but according to the actual underlying facts — and it could not be

denied. In every human face I saw, there seemed to be unveiled before me the story of the misery

and anguish that had entered the world through sin. I knew that God must see this with far

clearer eyes than mine, and therefore His suffering from the sight must be infinitely greater —

even though mine already felt nearly unbearable. And I began to understand how the least He

could do would be to embrace with untold gladness anything that would help to deliver the

beings He had created from such awful misery.

It was an unforgettable insight into the world’s anguish because of sin.

How long it lasted I cannot remember, but while it did, it nearly crushed me. And because it

always returned at the sight of a stranger’s face, I found myself forced to wear a thick veil

whenever I went out into the streets, so that I might spare myself the terrible impact of that

realization.

One day I was riding on a tram-car along Market Street in Philadelphia when two men came in

and sat opposite me. I saw them dimly through my veil and felt relieved — dimness meant

protection. When the conductor came for my fare, I had to lift the veil to count out the coins. As

I raised it, I caught a full view of those two faces, and an overwhelming flood of anguish swept

through me. I seemed to receive yet another revelation — clearer and deeper — of the misery sin

had brought upon humanity. It was more than I could bear. I clenched my hands and cried out

inwardly, “Oh God, how can You endure it? You might have prevented it, but did not. You

might even now change it, but You do not. I do not see how You can continue to live and endure

such a sight.”

I upbraided God. And I felt justified in doing so.

Then, suddenly, God seemed to answer me. An inward voice spoke in tones of infinite love and

tenderness:

“He shall see of the travail of His soul, and be satisfied.”

“Satisfied!” I cried within myself. “Christ is to be satisfied! He will look upon the world’s

misery, and then upon the travail He has endured because of it, and He will be satisfied with the

result! If I were Christ, nothing could satisfy me unless every human being were ultimately

saved. Therefore, nothing less can satis fy Him.”

With that, a veil seemed to be lifted from the plans of the universe. I saw that it was true, as the

Bible declares, that “As in Adam all die, even so in Christ shall all be made alive.” As was the

first, so was the second. The “all” in one case could not fairly mean anything less than the “all”

in the other. I saw, therefore, that the remedy must be equal to the disease — that salvation must

be as universal as the fall.

I saw all this that day on the tram-car on Market Street — not merely thought it, or hoped it, or

believed it, but knew it. It was a Divine fact. And from that moment, I have never had a doubt

about the final destiny of the human race. God is the Creator of every human being; therefore He

is the Father of each one, and they are all His children. And Christ died for every one, declared to

be the “propitiation not for our sins only, but also for the sins of the whole world” (1 John 2:2).

However great the ignorance, however grievous the sin, the promise of salvation is absolute and

without limitation.

If it is true that “by the offense of one judgment came upon all men to condemnation,” then it is

equally true that “by the righteousness of one the free gift came upon all men unto justification

of life.” To limit the latter “all men” is also to limit the former. The salvation is exactly equal to

the fall. There is to be a final “restitution of all things,” when “at the name of Jesus every knee

shall bow — of things in heaven, and things on earth, and things under the earth — and every

tongue shal l confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.” Every knee, every

tongue — nothing could be more all-embracing.

The how and the when I could not see. But the essential fact was all I needed: somewhere,

somehow, God was going to make everything right for all the creatures He had made. My heart

rested in this forever.

I hurried home eager to reach my Bible, to see whether this magnificent truth I had discovered

could possibly have been there all along without my noticing it. The moment I entered the house,

I did not even remove my bonnet, but rushed to the table where my Bible and Concordance

always lay ready. I began to search — and instantly the whole Book seemed illuminated. On every

page the truth about the “times of restitution of all things,” of which the Apostle Peter says “God

hath spoken by the mouth of all His holy prophets since the world began,” shone forth, leaving

no room for doubt.

I turned eagerly from page to page, laughing aloud for joy at the blaze of light that filled it. It

became a new book. It was as though another skin had been peeled off every text, and each verse

shone with new meaning — not a different meaning, for the new did not contradict the old, but a

deeper meaning, the true meaning hidden within the outward form of words. Nothing in the text

needed changing; only my understanding needed to be opened. And now, at last, it was.

I remember soon afterward, in the course of my daily Bible reading, coming to the Psalms and

being astonished at the new light thrown upon their most severe — even seemingly bloodthirsty —

denunciations. I saw that, when read in the spirit rather than the letter, they were full of the

promised and final triumph of good over evil, and were a magnificent vindication of the

goodness and justice of God, who will not — and ought not, and cannot — rest until all His

enemies, and ours, are placed beneath His feet.

I saw that His kingdom must be inward before it can be outward; that it is a kingdom of ideas,

not of brute force; that His rule is over hearts, not over territories; that His victories must occur

within before they are visible without. He seeks to rule spirits rather than bodies. No victory

could satisfy Him except the victory that wins the heart — the surrender of the free and convinced

soul, not the mere capitulation of the conquered slave. As Milton says, “Who overcomes by force

hath overcome but half his foe,” and I saw this was true.

Read in this light, the very words that had once filled me with horror now thrilled my soul with

praise:

“Let God a rise, let His enemies be scattered;

let them also that hate Him flee before Him.

As smoke is driven away, so drive them away;

as wax melts before the fire,

so let the wicked perish at the presence of God.”

God’s wrath is against sin , not the sinner; and when His enemies are scattered, ours are scattered

with them. His sword is righteousness, which puts sin to death so that the sinner may live. The

fire of His anger is the refiner’s fire ; He sits not as the destroyer of the soul but as its purifier, to

cleanse it as gold and silver are purified.

“Implacable is love.

Foes may be bought or teased

From their malign intent;

But He goes unappeased

Who is on kindness bent.”

The Psalmist says, “Thou wast a God that forgavest them, though thou tookest vengeance of

th eir inventions”; and with this key in hand, all the denunciations of God’s wrath— once so cruel

and unjust to my ears — were transformed into declarations of His loving determination to make

us good enough to live with Him in Heaven forever.

I could multiply examples endlessly of this new illumination that shone in entrancing beauty

across every page of Scripture, but these are enough. At last I began to understand what the

Apostle Paul meant when he said he had been made a minister of the new covenant, “not o f the

letter, but of the spirit; for the letter kills, but the spirit gives life.” The things I had once read in

the letter and shuddered at, now — read in the spirit — filled me with joy

fields.title: Chapter 23. The Unselfishness Of God
fields.body_html:
have always felt that this was the moment when I truly discovered the unselfishness of God .

Until then, although I rejoiced in the salvation I had found for myself, I still suffered from a

secret, torturing suspicion that, in the end, it was a rather selfish salvation —both on God’s part

and on mine.

How could a good God enjoy Himself in Heaven while knowing that a large proportion of the

beings He Himself had created were doomed to eternal misery — unless He were, in some way, a

selfish God? I knew the Bible said He was a God of love, and I supposed it must be true. But

deep down there remained that hidden feeling that His love could not stand comparison with the

ideal of love I felt in my own heart.

I knew that, imperfect as my love was, I could never enjoy Heaven while even one of my

children — no matter how disobedient — was shut out. And the thought that God could , and did ,

enjoy Heaven while countless thousands of His children were shut out seemed to reveal a failure

in the most essential element of love. So even while I was grateful for forgiveness and the sure

hope of Heaven for myself, I often felt that the God I worshipped must be a selfish God, caring

more for His own comfort and His glory than for the suffering beings He had made.

But now I began to see that the wideness of God’s love was far beyond anything I had ever

imagined. If I gathered together all the unselfish love of every mother’s heart in the whole world,

multiplied it by millions, and pressed it into one place, I would still have nothing more than a

faint shadow of the unselfishness of God.

I had always thought of Him as loving. But now I discovered something far deeper: He did not

merely possess love — He was love itself , love embodied and woven into the very essence of His

being.

I saw that God was, as it were, made of love, so that in the very nature of things He could not act

cont rary to love. It wasn’t that He chose not to — it was that He could not , because love was the

I

very essence of His nature. The law of love, like the law of gravity, is inevitable in its operation.

God, if I may say so, is under this law and cannot help obeying it. And once I understood this,

trusting the God of love became as natural as breathing. Every doubt evaporated, and I was filled

with boundless delight at the thought of having been created by such an unselfish God.

I saw that His role as Creator was, in itself, an absolute guarantee that He would care for us and

make all things work together for our good. The responsibilities of ownership blazed with

breathtaking clarity. Not the rights of ownership — as I had always thought — but its duties , the

obligations that ownership imposes.

Just as, in a civilized society, people are held responsible — by public opinion or even by law — to

care properly for the things they own, so our Creator is necessarily bound, by the moral law of

His own nature, to take proper care of the beings He has made. He must be held responsible for

our well-being.

It was all so glorious that it often seemed almost too good to be true — that we truly belonged to

such an unselfish God. Many a time, when some new insight into His goodness overwhelmed

me, I would take my Bible, open it to the passages declaring that we belong to Him, and put my

fingers on the verses, reading them aloud just to reassure myself that they really did say — freely

and without limitation — that He was indeed my Owner.

The phrase, “Remember thy Creator,” suddenly took on a wholly different character. I had

always thought of it as a warning meant to frighten us into good behavior. Now it shone with

comfort — a delightful assurance that everything must be well with the creatures of such an

unselfish Creator.

I saw that God was good not merely in a religious sense, but in the truest, most practical sense of

the word. And a good Creator was, of course, bound to make everything go right with His

creation. The fact that nothing was hidden from His eyes — once so terrifying — became the most

comforting truth in the universe, because it meant He knew all about us and could therefore do

His best for us.

My own experience as a mother — once a source of conflict with my beliefs about God — now

came into perfect harmony. My children have been the joy of my life. I cannot imagine bliss

more exquisite than the moments when my arms have been around them. Those moments have

seemed nearer to the joy of Heaven than anything else on earth. And I think this joy has taught

me more about God’s feelings toward His children than anything else.

If I, a finite human being with limited capacity, could find such joy in my children, what must

God — with His infinite heart — feel for His? Most of my understanding of the love of God has

come from this very experience. I could not believe that God had created me with a greater

capacity for unselfish love and self-sacrifice than He possessed Himself. Since discovering the

mother-heart of God, I have answered every doubt about God ’s love simply by looking into my

own heart as a mother.

To me, it is impossible that a true mother could be selfish toward her children. A mother who

puts her own comfort and welfare before her children is, in my mind, an unnatural mother, one

who has failed in her highest calling. And if one looks at what we call the lower creation, even

the animals teach us the supreme duty of maternal self-giving. The mother tiger will die before

she lets harm come to her young. She will starve so they may eat. Could God do less?

I speak of self-sacrifice, but in truth I cannot really call it sacrifice. No true mother — one who

knows the reality of motherhood — would ever regard her care for her children as a sacrifice. It

may involve exhaustion or hardship, but not sacrifice in the ordinary sense. The real sacrifice

would be if she were not allowed to care for them.

For this reason, I believe that many disappointed mothers — who do not receive the gratitude they

desire — have only themselves to blame, because they demanded gratitude rather than inspired it.

This understanding has revealed to me God’s feelings toward us: that what we call Christ’s “self -

sacrifice” was simply the natural and necessary expression of His love; and that the astonishing

thing is not that He did it, but that He could not have done otherwise .

Since discovering the mother-heart of God, I have never been able to feel the slightest anxiety

for any of His children — and by His children, I do not mean only the good ones, but the bad ones

equally. Did not Jesus tell us that the Good Shepherd leaves the ninety-nine safe sheep to search

for the one that is lost, and does not rest until He finds it?

Viewed in the light of motherhood, the word “lost” becomes profoundly comforting. Nothing

can be “lost” unless it is owned by someone. To be lost means only, “not yet found.” The lost

coin is still gold, bearing the king’s image. The lost sheep is still a sheep, not a wolf. The lost son

is still a son, with his father’s blood in his veins.

So if a person is a “lost sinner,” it simply means he is owned by the Good Shepherd, and that the

Shepherd, by the very duties of ownership, must go after that which is lost — and keep going until

He finds it.

To me, the word “lost” contains the strongest possible proof of ownership.

Who can imagine a mother with a lost child having one moment of rest until the child is found?

And who could imagine God being less concerned than a mother?

I believe that all the problems of the spiritual life , which so often distress conscientious souls,

would disappear like morning mist before the rising sun if only the full blaze of the mother-heart

of God were allowed to shine upon them.

I came to see that, since Scripture declares we were created in the image of God, we are obliged

to believe that the best in us — not the worst — is what reflects that image. Anything that, in our

highest and most unselfish moments, appears selfish, unkind, unjust, or self-seeking must never

be attributed to God, no matter how things may “seem.” If God is unselfish, then He must be at

least as unselfish as the noblest ideal we can conceive — and of course infinitely more.

All the biblical texts about God’s goodness suddenly shone with new meaning. I realized that His

goodness is not a condescending benevolence but a genuine, wholehearted goodness — one that

includes true unselfishness, deep consideration, and above all, justice. Justice has always seemed

to me one of the first essentials of goodness; I cannot imagine calling anyone “good” who is

unjust, no matter how impressive their outward appearance of virtue may be. In short, I had, such

an overwhelming revelation of God’s intrinsic and inherent goodness and unselfishness that

nothing since has been able to shake it. Many aspects of His dealings with the world have been,,

and still are, mysterious to me; but I am convinced that every one of them could be explained

through the lens of His love and justice, if only I could see deeply enough. And I believe that one

day I will see clearly what I now hold by faith: that His loving kindness truly reaches over all His

works.

I do not mean that all this understanding came to me at once. But I do mean that on that day,

riding a tramcar in Philadelphia, a light broke across the character of God — a light that has never

dimmed in the slightest and has only grown brighter with each passing year.

For me, it is enough to say, “God is,” and the answer to every difficulty is already present. What

amazes me is that I, along with so many other Christians, had failed to see this, even with the

open Bible before us —and that all sorts of distortions of God’s character, even outright slanders

against His goodness, can find a ready welcome in Christian hearts. To me, such

misrepresentations became almost unbearable. I could listen patiently — even with interest — to

almost any strange or unorthodox idea that did not malign God’s character. But the one thing I

could not endure, the one thing I could not sit quietly through, was anything that — even under a

cloak of piety —suggested the faintest insult to God’s love or His unselfishness.

I will never forget a memorable incident in our home when a distinguished preacher from Boston

was visiting us. At breakfast, the conversation turned to God’s love. He insisted that you must

not rely on it too much, for there were limits to what God could endure — just as, he said, there

were limits to a mother’s love. He claimed that a daughter might commit certain sins a mother

could never forgive, sins that would forever close her heart and her home, and he argued that

God was the same. To believe otherwise, he said, was to hold a “grandmotherly religion.”

I have no doubt he meant to undermine my views on Restitution, though we were not discussing

that topic. He simply wished to convince me that God was not as “foolishly loving” as I

believed. But to hear mothers, and the God who created mothers, so misrepresented was more

than I could bear. Though he was my guest, I burst out in fierce indignation, declared that I

would not sit at the table with anyone who held such slanderous ideas of God, and left the room

in tears. I refused to see him again. I do not claim that this reaction was courteous or even Christ-

like, but it shows how overwhelmingly I felt about the matter. To me, the honor of God

outweighed every rule of social etiquette.

I see now that I might have defended that honor just as strongly, but in a far more Christ-like

way. Still, to this day, the one thing I find extremely hard to tolerate is anything that maligns the

character of God. Nothing else compares to this in importance, for our entire salvation depends

absolutely on who God is. Unless he can be shown to be wholly good, wholly unselfish, and

wholly just, then our case is utterly hopeless. God alone is our salvation, and if He fails us — even

in the smallest degree — we have nowhere else to turn.

fields.title: Chapter 24. Effect Of My Views On My Public Work
fields.body_html:
s could be expected in those days, my views on Restitution — views I announced rather

quickly — met with considerable disapproval from the Plymouth Brethren and many of my

other orthodox friends. I had to endure a fair amount of what might be called persecution, though

in truth I took a certain satisfaction in it, for I felt it was a grand thing to know so much more of

God than those who opposed me.

I often compared my feelings to those of a civilized traveler trying to explain the marvels of his

world to people in a remote, “savage” country— people who could neither understand nor believe

what he described. His sense of superior knowledge would make their disapproval and

opposition only a reason to pity their ignorance and to bear with it patiently. On that same

principle, I almost enjoyed being regarded as a heretic, and I never wanted anyone’s

endorsement. To be endorsed felt, to me, like being bound; and I preferred to be a free lance,

unhindered in my absolute mental and spiritual freedom.

At that time the discovery I had made was not as widely known as it is now, and it seemed likely

that holding what many considered a grave heresy might hinder my Christian work. And perhaps

it did in some circles. But as I always had far more invitations to speak than I could possibly

accept, I never truly suffered any difficulty. I tried to be courteous enough not to place on

others — especially those who found my views abhorrent — the burden of endorsing me. Still, the

revelation I had received was too glorious to withhold whenever a door opened. And since I

refused to sail under false colors, and insisted that any place I spoke should know beforehand

exactl y what a “heretic” I was, I generally enjoyed all the freedom I desired.

In fact, these very views — and my open confession of them under rather trying circumstances —

opened the way for some of our most important and fruitful work. It happened in this way.

In 1873, my husband came to England to hold meetings in the interests of the Higher Life, or

what I prefer to call the Life of Faith. I followed soon after, and upon my arrival in London I was

A

invited to meet a gathering of leading Evangelical ladies who were to decide whether it would be

safe for them to support me and lend their influence to the work.

Lady Mount Temple, one of the women present, later described the meeting in her life of Lord

Mount Temple:

“I think it was in 1873 that Mr. Pearsall Smith cam e to England from America, followed a few

months later by his dear, beautiful wife. It was a time long to be remembered. They came, one

may say, full of the new wine of the Spirit, longing to help others onward in the Divine life. A

friend invited us to lunch to meet them. I shall never forget my first sight of Hannah Smith. We

called her the ‘angel of the Churches,’ and she looked like one, with her golden hair and clear,

beautifully cut face, in a dress all her own, yet as simple as that of the Friends among whom she

had been raised.

“What especially drew me to her that day was this. I must confess that I was only a seeker after

truth. Hannah was sitting in a small circle of excellent orthodox friends, gathered to hear the

good things she had to share, and she was, in fact, on trial. She had seen a funeral procession in

the street, and when she mentioned it, we all adopted the conventional expression of sorrow.

‘Oh,’ she said, ‘when I see a funeral I always give thanks for a brother or sister delivered from

the trials and pains of this mortal state.’ I thought, How wonderful! And I could not help asking,

‘Is that possible? Do you feel this about everyone?’ I was indeed an enfant terrible.

“She paused for a moment and glanced around. She was among evangelical s, at a time when the

universal hope was considered a heresy, and this was her examination. She later said she

experienced a brief inner struggle. But truth prevailed, and with her bright, fearless look she said,

‘Yes— about everyone. For I trust in the lov e of God.’ I surrendered my heart immediately to this

trust, love, and candor.”

I remember the occasion perfectly, and the thoughts running through my mind. I knew I was

being tested, and I suspected that my answer might shock the entire company. But I felt that

loyalty to God required me to say what honored Him, and to leave the consequences in His

hands.

The moment I finished speaking, Lady Mount Temple — then Mrs. Cowper Temple — rose from

her seat, came straight to me, and, though I was a stranger, gave me a warm, affectionate kiss.

“You must come and hold some meetings at Broadlands,” she said at once. I don’t know what

the others felt, but not a word of disapproval was spoken, and they later became some of my

dearest friends.

The result was that, within a few weeks, Broadlands — the country home of Lord and Lady

Mount Temple in Hampshire — was opened to us for our first conference. It was a time of

extraordinary blessing, and it became the doorway to all the later conferences and to our entire

subsequent work in England and beyond.

When a conference was planned at Brighton in 1874, some members of the organizing

committee became anxious about my “heresies,” fearing they might hinder the work. They

persuaded my husband — who had arrived in England before I did — to write to me in America

and tell me that unless I promised to keep my views quiet, they would strongly oppose my

participation in the meetings. Recently, while looking through an old bundle of letters, I found

my reply, which reveals precisely how I felt at the time:

“Philadelphia, April 6, 1874.

Thy letters from London have arrived. Thee need not think I would be troubled at not being

allowed to speak in the meetings, for nothing would suit me better. I am not in the least anxious

to preach. Indeed, I consider it quite a favor on my part to be willing to do it at all, and just as

much of a favor on others’ part to listen to me. If your committee should say, ‘We do not want to

hear you speak at Brighton,’ I would have thanked them heartily. No one need feel any delicacy

about this. But it must be thoroughly understood that I will make no compromises for anyone,

and that I believe in Restitution more firmly than ever. I do not think I could bear the misery I

see in this poor, sad, sin-stricken world without it. Our temperance work brings us face to face

with such helpless suffering that my heart would break if I did not know that God loves all His

creatures and has something gracious in store for everyone.”

Since I would not compromise — and since it was still considered important to have me at the

meetings — the committee dropped the matter and decided to take me as I was, heresies and all.

When my husband wrote to tell me this, I replied:

“Philadelphia.

I am very glad thee has escaped thy difficulty about thy heretical preaching wife with so little

trouble. But the idea of B — , with his shaky views, undertaking to excommunicate me! I do not

think it honest. I will not sail under false colors, and my conviction about Restitution grows

stronger every single day. If they leave me alone in England, I will probably say little about it;

but if there is even the slightest hint of compromise or secrecy on my part, I will blaze out into a

perfect conflagration. I cannot endure anything of that sort. So please remember this, ye Lords of

Creation.

Seriously, though, I do not feel drawn to preach or teach Restitution over there, and if the dear,

frightened orthodox friends make no fuss about it, I am unlikely to do so. Their worries about me

do not annoy me in the least. I believe I actually enjoy being the target of the odium theologicum.

I suppose there is som ething of the war horse in my constitution.”

Whether the committee’s fears were well founded or not, I cannot say; I only know that not once,

during all my work in England, did I ever feel that my views on Restitution hindered the

reception of my message or closed even a single door. In fact, I believe they opened doors that

might otherwise have remained shut. The deeper truth was that my underlying belief in the

absolutely unlimited justice and love of God enabled me to speak with a far more courageous

faith than I could ever have managed without it. I am convinced that without this conviction I

would have been deprived of half my power.

Whatever others may think, the revolution this discovery worked in my own experience was

immense — beyond words. The spiritual romance of my life became more captivating than ever.

Every day brought some deeper and more radiant insight into the unimaginable goodness and

unselfishness of God. I felt at last that I was beginning to enter into the meaning of the Apostle’s

prayer for the Ephesians: that we might comprehend, with all the saints, the breadth and length

and depth and height of Christ’s love, and know— even if only faintly — the love that surpasses

knowledge.

Such love truly does surpass knowledge; it could arise only from the heart of a wholly unselfish

God. I stood in awe before its breadth and length and depth and height, and I marveled —

endlessly — that I could ever have imagined a Divine love with boundaries.

For a long time the joy of it all was so wonderful that I thought there could be nothing more to

discover about God — that I had reached the final revelation.

But a further unveiling awaited me, and the fourth epoch of my soul’s life— its most entrancing

fields.title: Chapter 25. The Fourth Epoch In My Religious Life (The Life Of Faith)
fields.body_html:
t was in 1865 that the fourth, and by far the most captivating, epoch of my spiritual journey

dawned upon my soul. I had been a Christian for nine years — years filled with delight and

enchantment — but what now came to me was so far beyond all that preceded it that it felt as

though an entirely new and magical world had opened before me.

During those earlier years, my faith had been thoroughly satisfying in everything relating to God.

Every discovery I made about His character and His ways brought me only joy. But when it

came to my own part in the Christian life, the satisfaction was far less complete. I was happy,

yes, but I was not the person I longed to be.

I had found a religion that promised perfect deliverance for the future, but it did not seem to offer

deliverance now . I had found an unselfish and just God whom I could worship without fear of

disappointment — but I was continually disappointed in myself. I knew I was not what I ought to

be. My life felt full of failure — not so much outward sin, but inward sins: coldness, spiritual

deadness, lack of Christian love, roots of bitterness, all those hidden failings over which God’s

children so often grieve. When I wanted to do good, evil was present. The good I desired, I did

not do; and the evil I despised, I still did. I found myself constantly sinning and repenting,

making resolutions and breaking them, hating what was wrong yet yielding to it, longing for

victory but more often failing than overcoming.

Yet Scripture seemed to teach that Christ came to bring a real and present victory to His

followers. It implied that Christians were meant to be free from anxious cares and fears, and to

enjoy even now a peace that surpasses understanding. But I knew painfully little of that. My

heart was at rest about my future , but my present was torn by a thousand daily worries and

anxieties. The very fruits of the Spirit — which I believed I had received — were love, joy, peace,

I

patience, gentleness, meekness, goodness; yet these were the very qualities in which I felt most

deficient.

This was not what I had expected when I first became a Christian. Raised among the Quakers —

whose lives radiated peace — and taught from childhood that goodness was essential, I had

assumed that becoming a Christian necessarily meant becoming peaceful and good. I expected

victory over sin and over worry as naturally as I expected the sun to rise. But in the secret depths

of my soul, I had to admit that I was disappointed.

At first, the joy of my newfound salvation had swept everything else aside. I thought temptation

and fear and sin were gone forever. But when the initial glow faded, the old temptations returned

with their old power. It became as easy as ever to be anxious, worried, burdened, irritable,

unkind, critical, and severe — to do and be all the things from which I believed religion would

deliver me. None of this ever shook my conviction that I was God’s child and an heir of heaven,

but it often made me feel miserably ashamed. To be a child of God and yet unable to live like

one made me wonder whether I had missed something in the Christian life — something that

could have brought me victory.

Determined to discover what that missing element was, I questioned several older Christians. But

they all gave me the same answer: No, you have not missed anything. The life of sinning and

repenting is all we can expect in this world, because of the weakness of the flesh. They explained

that the old Adam, inherited at birth, and the new Adam, received at conversion, constantly

warred against each other — sometimes one prevailing, sometimes the other — and that only in

death would we find true deliverance from the old nature.

N othing could have described my condition better than Paul’s own lament in Romans 7:14– 23. It

seemed written for me. Again and again I cried out with him, “O wretched man that I am! Who

shall deliver me from the body of this death?” But I could not understa nd why Paul even asked

that question if, as everyone said, there was no deliverance in this life. Surely he knew the old

nature was destined to remain until death. Yet he not only asked the question — he answered it

triumphantly: “I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord.”

What could he have meant? I had entered into salvation through Jesus Christ, yet I knew nothing

of such triumphant deliverance. I was still bound by the “body of death” within me.

Why? Where lay the difficulty?

These questions grew even more pressing after I discovered the unlimited love of God. It felt so

ungenerous — almost ungrateful — to respond to His boundless unselfishness with such lack of

spiritual fruit. Since He had shown Himself so mighty to save in the future, how could He be

powerless in the present?

The Quaker lives around me also suggested there must be deliverance, for they claimed to have

experienced it — even though they could never explain clearly what it was or how it worked.

Another influence strengthened this conviction. I owned a book that taught not only that God’s

children were commanded to bear the fruits of the Spirit, but that they could do so — and that also

offered hints of the mystical pathway toward it. The book was Spiritual Progress , a collection

of selections from Fenelon and Madame Guyon. It was especially precious because it had been a

gift from my adored father and always lay on my desk beside my Bible.

My father had discovered it when he was only eighteen. As he walked through Philadelphia on

his way to board a ship for a long voyage to China, he passed a second-hand bookstall. Though

he had only recently begun the spiritual life, he was drawn to the title Spiritual Progress .

Knowing nothing of its contents, he bought it on impulse — guided unconsciously, no doubt, by

the Lord in whom he had begun to trust. He wrote in his Reminiscences:

“This book proved to be of the greatest comfort to me. I carried it in my pocket and read it in

spare moments, to my everlasting profit, I trust. I cannot but thank a kind Providence for placing

this blessed book in my hands.”

My father valued that book so highly that as soon as each of us children was old enough, he gave

us our own copy and asked us to study it carefully. Because we loved him so dearly, we always

wanted to please him, and during the years of my first hungry and despairing search for God, the

book became my constant companion.

But since it was written more to guide souls who were already progressing in the spiritual life

than to help seekers enter that life in the first place, it wasn’t of much definite help to me during

those early, blind years of searching. And when, in 1858, I came to believe I had discovered “the

plan of salvation”— settled, as I imagined, in the councils of Heaven, revealed in the life and

death of Christ, and neatly formulated by the Apostle Paul — I filled the margins of my copy with

what I thought were decisive critiques proving the book’s unsoundness.

Still, without my realizing it, its teachings made a profound impression on me. Even while I

criticized it, I felt an underlying hunger for the mystical side of religion that the book expressed.

Throughout the years that followed, I was pulled back and forth between the claims of Plymouth

Brethren doctrine on one side and the claims of mysticism on the other.

The practical, businesslike part of my nature leaned toward the Brethren; my Quaker upbringing

and the influence of my cherished book pulled me toward the mystical.

At times, doctrines seemed supr emely important and one’s actual life almost insignificant; at

other times, doctrines felt worthless unless they resulted in a righteous life. Sometimes Paul held

sway in my thinking — teaching salvation by faith — and sometimes James, insisting that faith

without works is dead. My Plymouth Brethren friends exalted Paul and justification by faith; my

Quaker friends and the Catholic saints in my book exalted James and justification by works. The

practical part of me leaned to the first; the mystical side leaned to the second. The result was an

ongoing restlessness of soul which, combined with my distress over my continual spiritual

failures, often made me question whether what I had learned about the salvation of Christ could

really be the whole story.

With no be tter remedy, I turned increasingly to “sound doctrine” to quiet my unrest. Under

Plymouth Brethren influence, these doctrines had become very clearly defined, each one neatly

labeled and stored away in the mental pigeonholes of my mind. Nothing could have been more

orderly — at least as far as doctrines were concerned. I had become quite a successful teacher of

these doctrines, and I looked down pityingly on anyone who was not as clear and definite as I

was.

I often wished I could seat all the religious teachers I knew in a row of baby high chairs before

me, so that I could explain to them the doctrines they seemed so confused about — especially

justification by faith and the judicial standing of the believer . I regularly declared that if one

simply understood these two points and believed them fully, then everything was all right and

nothing else mattered much.

I remember saying something like this to a cousin who came to me distressed about her

shortcomings in the Christian life. She said, “But Hannah, according to what you’re saying, all
