our sins — past, present, and future — are forgiven if we simply believe. It makes very little

difference what we do.”

“Yes,” I answered in my ignorance, “and that is exactly the beauty of it! We wear the robe of

Christ’s righteous ness, and that robe covers all the vileness underneath. When God looks at us,

He sees not our unrighteousness but Christ’s righteousness, and He accepts us because of that.”

Another time, a Quaker preacher who had heard me expound these crude ideas said, “ It seems to

me, Hannah Smith, that you talk as if you could walk into a ready-made clothing shop, buy

garments of salvation, put them on immediately, and come out fully clothed in righteousness and

ready for heaven.”

“Yes!” I replied. “That is exactly how it is —except I don’t have to buy the garments; Christ

gives them to me! Thank you for such a beautiful illustration; I shall certainly use it in my

preaching.”

I have no doubt I interpreted Plymouth Brethren teaching in a far more literal and external way

than they ever intended. But I liked to have everything defined with absolute clarity, and this

seemed the logical outcome of their views. Strangely, I failed to see how inconsistent it was to

believe in a righteous God who supposedly covered up our unrighteousness with the robe of His

own righteousness, and then pretended to Himself that we were fit for heaven — when He

certainly knew that beneath the robe our “filthy garments” were still there.

Whenever my Quaker friends hinted at this inconsistency, I silenced my uneasiness by telling

myself that although they were dear, good people, they were not doctrinal at all and knew very

little about the “plan of salvation,” “justification by faith,” or the “judicial standing of the

believer.” Their objections, there fore, were not worth considering.

However, after the discovery I had made of the vastness of God’s love , as described in my

previous chapters, I began to feel increasingly uneasy. It seemed a most ungrateful response to

such boundless love that we — its recipients — should fail so miserably in living the kind of life

God clearly intended for us. The more I thought, the more inconsistent it seemed that salvation,

which was ultimately to be so magnificent and complete, should fail so obviously now , in this

present life, to provide the victory over sin and over worry that the gospel so plainly promises as

its immediate result.

Why was it, I asked myself again and again, that the God who had planned such a glorious

deliverance for us in the future had not also planned a better deliverance for us in the present?

fields.title: Chapter 26. The Way Of Escape
fields.body_html:
his unrest and questioning came to a head in 1865. Because of family circumstances, we

had to leave our delightful home in Germantown — along with all our wide circle of

interests — and move to a remote village in New Jersey, where we were almost completely cut off

from any congenial society. Financially, it was an advantage, but in every other respect it was a

tremendous trial, especially for me. I confess that my spirit rebelled bitterly against the change.

Little did I imagine that in this very place, which felt so desolate and isolated, a glorious new

light would dawn, ushering in the fourth and crowning epoch of my spiritual life.

It happened this way. As I’ve said, I was deeply rebellious about the move. Yet I had enough

spiritual insight to know that this rebellion was wrong. Since the move was clearly a providential

arrangement beyond my control, the only right response was to accept it cheerfully and

genuinely say, “Thy will be done.” But although I scolded myself constantly, I couldn’t bring

myself to accept God’s will—and in truth, I didn’t want to acc ept it. I felt it was harsh treatment

to be forced to leave my happy Germantown home and my sphere of usefulness to live in such a

lonely, remote place as Millville. It seemed to me that God ought not to have allowed it, and that

I had every right to grumble and fret.

As a result, I fell into a deeply uncomfortable state of mind. Even my clear doctrines could no

longer help me, and I began to fear that I was going to lose whatever spirituality I had left.

In the face of a need so real, it was no comfort to know I was forgiven. I wanted more than

forgiveness — I wanted deliverance. But I had no idea how to obtain it.

Because we frequently had Mission preachers visit us, I explained my case to several of them

and asked for help, but no one could tell me anything useful. At last, a very successful religious

teacher came for a few days, and to him I poured out my trouble fully, begging him to suggest

some path to deliverance. He considered my situation seriously and finally said he believed what

I needed was to engage in some Christian work. If I would go out the next morning to visit the

T

poor in our neighborhood and see how I could help them, he thought my spiritual life would be

renewed and everything would come right.

So the next day, I tried his suggested remedy. But I quickly discovered how futile it was. Almost

in the first house I entered I found a woman struggling with the very same spiritual difficulty as

my own, and she desperately needed help — and I had none to give. I felt like someone trying to

feed the hungry out of an empty bowl. It was a silly and impossible task. I returned home more

discouraged than ever, convinced that before I could help anyone else, I would have to find

deliverance for myself.

There was a local dressmaker who often came to sew for me, and since I had so little

companionship in the village, I would sometimes sit and talk with her while we worked. She

seemed unusually spiritually minded, and I was fascinated by her experiences. I discovered that

she believed in an actual victory over temptation — that it was not necessary, as I had thought, to

go through life sinning and repenting, sinning and repenting, but that a Christian could truly be

delivered. She told me that among the Methodists there was a doctrine called “Holiness,” and an

acc ompanying experience called “sanctification,” or “the second blessing,” which brought

people into a place of victory. I was intensely interested in everything she said, and began to

hope that perhaps here might be the solution to my struggles.

She also told me that a small meeting was held in the village on Saturday evenings where this

doctrine was taught and where people shared their experiences. She urged me to attend. I thought

I might go someday, but allowed other things to interfere. I was convinced that poor, uneducated

factory workers could not possibly have anything to teach me. I had studied and taught the Bible

extensively and had a high opinion of my own religious attainments. I felt that if I did go to the

meeting, I would likely have far more to teach them than they would have to teach me.

Eventually, however, one evening I decided to grant them the favor of my presence — and I

confess, I did feel it was a great favor. I went to the meeting full of my own importance and

superiority, expecting to astonish them with my biblical knowledge.

When I entered, a factory woman with a shawl over her head —she likely didn’t own a bonnet—

was speaking. I heard her say:

“My whole horizon used to be filled with this great big Me of mine, but when I got a glimpse of

Christ as my perfect Savior, that great big Me shriveled down to nothing.”

Those words were a revelation to me. I realized I knew nothing whatsoever of such an

experience. My own “Me” was very large and very self - assertive, and I couldn’t imagine how it

c ould possibly “shrink to nothing.” But a deep conviction came over me that this must be real

Christianity — and perhaps the very thing I had been longing for.

Needless to say, I did not attempt any teaching that night. I sat instead as a learner at the feet of

these humble Christians, who knew little of book learning but whose souls were clearly taught by

the Holy Spirit in depths of spiritual truth I had never touched. I began attending the meeting

regularly as a learner, and took every opportunity I could to talk with those who understood this

way of life. I found that its essence was exactly what Paul meant when he wrote, “Not I, but

Christ”— that the victory I sought would come through ceasing to live my own life and allowing

God’s power to “work in me to will and to do His good pleasure.”

In my diary, dated October 18, 1866, I wrote:

“The Lord has been teaching me in many ways lately my utter weakness in the face of

temptation. I have grown much in knowledge, but not in grace, and I find that I have no more

real power over sin than I did when I was first converted. This has not led me to doubt that I am

a child of God — justified, forgiven, possessing eternal life, and heir to a heavenly inheritance.

But even with this assurance, I cannot be happy while my heart condemns me. I long for more

holiness, more power over sin, more unbroken communion with God. But I do not know how to

attain it. Resolutions are useless; my efforts in vain. My prayers go unanswered. A thousand

times I have been ready to give up in des pair and conclude that it is not God’s will for me ever to

gain victory over sin. And yet the Bible presents such a different picture —‘blameless, harmless,

without rebuke’; with every temptation a ‘way of escape’; ‘purified’; ‘conformed to the image of

Chr ist’; ‘holy as He is holy.’”

Then I wrote:

“I find there are Christians who say that by receiving Christ by faith for our sanctification, just as

we received Him by faith for our justification, all this work I long for is accomplished — that is,

the method of accomplishing it is discovered. They claim that the Bible teaches that the Lord can

deliver from the power of sin as well as from its guilt, and that the soul learns to trust Him to do

this, ceasing to rely on its own resolutions or efforts at holiness, and committing the entire work

of being kept from evil to the Lord alone.”

And finally:

“I am beginning to see more clearly that the Lord is worthy of the most unlimited and boundless

confidence; and perhaps this is the first dawning of the light I have been seeking. It is a

Methodist doctrine, and I have long been accustomed to hearing Methodists criticized for it, but

it seems to be the only thing that meets my need, and I feel compelled to try it.”

On February 11, 1867, I recorded my early efforts to grasp this conquering faith, and wrote:

“My soul’s present posture is one of trusting the Lord. And I’ve discovered that this is a practical

reality — He actually does deliver. When temptation comes, if I turn to Him at once with the

prayer, ‘Lord, save me. I cannot save myself from this sin, but You can and will,’ He never fails.

Either He completely changes my feelings or He makes me forget the whole matter — and the

victory, or rather His victory, is complete. This is a secret of the Christian life I never knew

before.

But why did I not know it? Why has my path been so halting and miserable when I might have

lived in victory? I am a striking example of the inherent legalism and unbelief of the human

heart. While trusting the Lord entirely for my justification, I have always trusted myself for my

sanctification.

I have relied on my own efforts, resolutions, watchfulness, fervor, and striving to accomplish

holy living. This was legalism — just as truly legalism as if I had trusted these things to save my

soul in the first place. I was ‘frustrating’ the grace of God as fully in sanctification as those

whom I had condemned as legalists were frustrating it in justification. I could easily see how

they nullified Christ’s death by their legal efforts, but I was blind to th e fact that I was doing the

same thing. Their striving and mine differed in the goal, but in both cases it was self and not

Christ. For ‘if righteousness comes by the law, then Christ died in vain.’

But now how different everything is! Now I entrust my daily life to Him just as I entrust my

eternal destiny. I trust Him just as nakedly in one as in the other. I am equally powerless in both.

I can do nothing —not even I, the ‘new man’— and if the Lord does not do everything, nothing

will be done.

And oh, glorious truth — He does do it! When I trust Him, He gives deliverance from the power

of sin as well as from its guilt. I can place everything in His care — my troubles, my temptations,

my growth, my service, my daily life, moment by moment. Oh, the rest and calm of living this

way!

And this is the Methodist ‘blessing of holiness.’ Expressed by them in terms I do not fully

endorse, and surrounded by what seems to me a mixture of error — but still genuinely

experienced and enjoyed by them. I am truly grateful for their testimony to its reality. And I now

see that it is far better to have the experience — even if mixed with error — than to live without it

and be doctrinally correct, as I formerly was.”

My diary from this period is full of the astonishing discoveries I was making, but these extracts

are enough. From then on, the possibilities of faith opened before me in ways I had never

dreamed. I saw that faith was truly the victory that overcomes the world, and I marveled at my

blindness in never having understood it.

Once again, it felt as if a veil had been stripped from the Bible, and it became a new book to me:

“The truth that was mine yesterday

Is larger truth today;

Its face has grown more divine,

Its kingship fuller sway.

For truth must grow as ages roll,

And God loom larger in the soul.”

One day I was at a meeting where the speaker read John 15, and the words “Without Me you can

do nothing” struck me with breathtaking force. I had read and quoted these words hundreds of

times — even preached on them. But now they blazed with such meaning that it seemed as though

they must have been newly added to the Bible. Here was the Lord saying plainly, “Without Me

you can do nothing,” and yet all the while I had been thinking I could— and must — do so much.

What meaning ha d I previously given the word “nothing”? I tried to recall, but there was only a

blank. I had never truly noticed it.

Another day I read the passage in Matthew 6 where Jesus tells us to “take no thought for your

life,” because our Heavenly Father cares for us — citing the birds of the air and the lilies of the

field, and reminding us that we are of far greater value. I read the passage repeatedly in utter

astonishment. Could it possibly be true? Had it really been in the Bible all these years? If so, how

had I never seen it? And yet not only had I seen it — I had memorized it and recited it often. But

in the only sense that matters, I had never seen it before.

Now I saw — and at that sight, my cares, worries, fears, and anxieties vanished like mist before

the sun.

The same happened with all the familiar Scriptures — they were illuminated with entirely new

meaning. Every page proclaimed, as if with a trumpet, the reality of a victorious Christian life

lived by faith in Jesus Christ. My whole soul burned with the discovery. I could think and speak

of little else. I had found something about the salvation of Christ I had never imagined —

something that proved Him a far more complete Savior than I had ever conceived.

I saw that He was not only my Savior for the future but my all-sufficient Savior for the present.

My Captain to fight my battles so I need not fight them myself. My Burden-Bearer so I could roll

my burdens off my weak shoulders. My Fortress from my enemies. My Shield, my Guide, my

Comforter, my Shepherd. No longer did I need to protect, defend, or fight for myself. Everything

was in the hands of One mighty to save — and what else could I do but trust Him?

No words can express the fullness and sufficiency I found stored up in the Lord. I could not keep

such glorious news to myself. Everyone who came near me was obliged to hear my story.

One of the first I told was the cousin I had mentioned earlier — the one who had once been

puzzled by my teaching that although our sins were forgiven, we must remain lifelong slaves to

sin’s power. I seized the earliest opportunity to invite her for a visit, and as soon as she arrived, I

exclaimed:

“Oh, Carrie, I have something wonderful to tell you. We mustn’t lose a minute!”

As soon as we were alone, I poured out my discovery — that in Christ there is not only

forgiveness for sin but deliverance from its power , and that we need no longer live as slaves to

sin but may be more than conquerors through Him.

She listened with astonished, perplexed interest, her expression growing more amazed at every

sentence. Finally she burst out:

“But Hannah, what do you mean? You always told me that even though you were a child of God,

you couldn’t expect deliverance from sin or from worry— that the old Adam was too strong and

the new nature too weak. When I was converted, I fully expected to be delivered from sin and

unrest, but when I asked you about it, you said it was impossible in this life. And I believed you!

And now you say the opposite. It’s terribly confusing—I don’t know what to think!”

I agreed it was confusing, but it had been ignorance, not malice, that had enabled me to teach

such a distorted view. Now that I had discovered something far better in the gospel, all we

needed to do was abandon the old error and embrace the new truth shown us.

My cousin — who all along had instinctively felt the old view could not possibly represent the

best Christ had to offer — embraced the new teaching with eagerness and lived it out far more

faithfully than I did.

The practical working of my discovery amazed me. I surrendered my entire rebellious spirit to

the Lord and told Him I could not conquer it but believed He could conquer it for me. Then I

stepped aside, so to speak, and left the battle to Him. To my indescribable joy, He removed all

my rebellion and replaced it with such peaceful acceptance of His will that the life which had

seemed so distasteful now appeared pleasant —even desirable. I could say “Thy will be done”

with genuine gratitude.

My discovery proved itself a practical success, and I was delighted. I tested it in countless

ways — and it never once failed. One instance in particular remains vivid in my mind.

There came a time when I was treated in a way I felt was utterly unfair — unjustifiable then, and

still unjustifiable now when I look back on it. I felt deeply wronged and was strongly tempted to

retreat into a long, simmering sulk, letting my silence and coldness express the indignation I felt

so keenly.

But the moment the temptation came, I saw at once the way of escape. I hurried off to be alone,

prac tically running to my bedroom because I was so full of provocation that I couldn’t even walk

calmly. I slammed the doors behind me, desperate for privacy to fight the battle out.

Once alone, I knelt down and prayed:

“Lord, I am provoked. I want to be provo ked. And honestly, I think I have good reason.

But I know I shouldn’t give in to this, and I want victory. I give this whole matter to You. I

cannot fight this battle —You must fight it for me. Jesus saves me now.”

I said those words while my heart still felt completely rebellious. Outwardly, it probably looked

as though I was declaring a lie. I didn’t feel saved from my anger, and it didn’t seem at all likely

that I could be. But by faith I clung to the truth, insisting — even in the midst of turmoil — that the

Lord could and did save me now.

And then it happened.

Instantly, a calm as bright as a summer morning settled over me. All my resentment vanished.

My anger dissolved. I felt as carefree and joyful as a bird in the sunshine, delighting in the very

situation that only moments before had enraged me. My faith had seized hold of a divine reality:

God was able to deliver, and He did deliver the soul that trusted Him.

I realized what a remarkable truth it was that I did not need to fight my own battles at all. The

Lord would fight for me, and I could simply be still. Since that day, hundreds of such battles

have been fought — and won — for me by the Captain of my Salvation. The secret I learned then,

of placing the battle entirely in His hands and stepping aside to let Him fight, has never once

failed when I have practiced it. It has proven again and again to be a living demonstration of

Christ’s words: “Be of good cheer—I have overcome the world.”

He has overcome it — not we — and He always will, if only we will surrender the matter into His

hands.

Never once, when I have done this, have I been disappointed. It is gloriously true — though so

few seem to realize it — that He is able to save completely those who come to God through

Him , because He lives forever to intercede for them. He was able when the Epistle to the

Hebrews was written, and He is just as able now, for He is not dead — He still lives to intercede

for us.

I had discovered that faith is the governing law of the universe . God spoke, and it was done;

and when we rely on Him, we too may speak, and it shall be done. A brilliant new light shone on

the words in 1 John 5:14 – 15:

“This is the confidence we have in Him: that if we ask anything according to His will, He hears

us. And if we know He hears us, whatever we ask, we know we have what we asked of Him.”

I had always thought such words were merely beautiful ideals — bright dreams of the Christian

life that no sensible person would expect to experience on earth. But now I saw they were not

dreams at all, but straightforward statements of a divine law : the law of faith, as real and as

dependable as the law of gravity, if only one understands it.

Christ tells us again and again that it will be to us according to our faith, and He declares without

limitation that all things are possible to the one who believes . I had assumed this was poetic

exaggeration. Now I understood: He was simply describing the laws of the spiritual kingdom —

laws that anyone may test and prove. Faith connects us to the almighty power of God, making it

possible for our weakness to draw freely on His strength. Its possibilities seemed endless.

“Faith, mighty faith, the promise sees

And looks to that alone;

Laughs at impossibilities,

And cries, ‘It shall be done.’”

I wish I could say that from that moment forward I continually lived in the power of this divine

law. I have not. But I can say this: every time I have deliberately chosen to lay hold of God’s

strength by faith, His strength has been made perfect in my weakness, and I have been

victorious. Again and again I have been able to echo the ap ostle’s triumphant words:

“In all these things we are more than conquerors through Him who loved us.”

fields.title: Chapter 27. A Discovery, Not An Attainment
fields.body_html:
gain I want once more to make this absolutely clear: what came to me was a discovery ,

not an attainment . I did not suddenly become a better woman. I simply realized that

Christ was a far better Savior than I had ever imagined. I was no more capable of conquering my

temptations than before — but I had discovered that He was able, and that He was willing, to

conquer them for me. I had no more wisdom or righteousness of my own, but I had finally

learned that He could truly become for me — just as the Apostle declared — wisdom,

righteousness, sanctification, and redemption .

I will never forget the first time I discovered that this was not merely a beautiful saying, but an

actual, practical fact.

Not long after I first began to grasp the fullness of Christ’s salvation, I learned that someone

particularly antagonistic toward me was coming to stay at our house for two weeks. She had

always been provoking and difficult. As the time drew near, I felt certain that if I were to treat

her in a Christlike manner, I would need far more patience than I normally possessed.

Still being new in the life of faith, I assumed the only way to obtain enough patience was to

wrestle for it in prayer . My days were too busy, so I decided to devote an entire night to this

spiritual struggle. After the family went to bed, I shut myself in my room, brought along a plate

of biscuits in case I grew hungry, and knelt by my bed prepared for an all-night battle. I felt

almost heroic, for long hours in prayer had always exhausted me; but since I desperately needed

a storehouse of patience, I thought this was the only way to secure it. I expected something like a

large “lump” of patience to be deposited into my heart— a reserve from which I could break off

pieces whenever needed.

But no sooner had my knees touched the floor than the familiar Scripture flashed into my mind:

“But of Him are ye in Christ Jesus , who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and

sanctification, and redemption… that he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord.”

A

“Yes!” I cried inwardly. “And that must surely include patience as well!”

Immediately I rose from my knees with absolute confidence that I did not need to acquire a

stockpile of patience ahead of time. Instead, I could simply look to the Lord for a present supply

whenever the need arose. I saw Christ as a vast, inexhaustible storehouse, always open, always

full — offering exactly the grace required at exactly the moment it was required. And suddenly it

seemed absurd for me to carry about packages of grace in my spiritual pockets, which — even if I

could gather them — would be misplaced the very moment I needed them most.

Naturally, that faith was fully answered. My visitor proved even more aggravating than usual,

yet patience came to me moment by moment — always exactly enough for the moment at hand.

Even more wonderful than the patience itself was the discovery I had made: the storehouse of

God’s grace is always open , and His supplies are always available to His children.

Some people might call my patience an “attainment.” But I had not attained anything. I had

simply discovered God’s supply and taken hold of it by faith, hour by hour, as each hour

required.

When reduced to its simplest form, my discovery was this: In Christ there is a perfect supply

for every need, and faith alone is the channel through which that supply flows. Struggling

cannot bring it. Wrestling cannot bring it. Worrying and agonizing cannot bring it. Faith always

will. Faith always does.

It seems such a simple realization — one would think that any believer who reads the Bible would

immediately know it. But I did not know it, not even after nine years of careful study and earnest

striving. And when at last I discovered it, it revolutionized my life.

There was nothing mysterious about it. It wasn’t something added to the gospel— it was the true

meaning of the gospel. Christ came, according to Scripture, to accomplish certain things; my

discovery was simply that He could actually be depended on to accomplish them . And if that

is true, then surely those who desire these things accomplished should hand them over to the One

who has undertaken the work.

To me, this seemed — and still seems — not some extraordinary spiritual attainment, but simple,

practical common sense . When I hire a builder to construct a house, it is because he knows how

to build and I do not. I don’t consider handing the job to him to be some great “attainment” on

my part — it is merely sensible. If I come to a roaring river and find a bridge, I do not consider

crossing it an accomplishment — I merely take advantage of what has been provided.

For this reason, I much prefer the word gifts to attainments . Attainments imply my own work

and effort; but Christian graces are free gifts from God. Those who “reign in life” are not those

who rise to great heights by their own efforts, but those who receive abundance of grace and the

gift of righteousness. If God did not spare His own Son, but gave Him up for us all, how shall He

not with Him freely give us all things?

To discover that all things are truly ours is not an attainment — it is a magnificent discovery. And

any soul that discovers such riches would be profoundly lacking in common sense not to take

possession of whatever it needs.

No angel could fully describe what this discovery meant to me. But it is enough to say that life

was transformed. Where defeat and failure once ruled, victory and triumph became my daily and

hourly experience — whenever I chose to take hold of them by faith. I was no longer a slave to

sin, forced to obey it even when I hated it, but had entered into the liberty Christ gives, no longer

bound by the old chains.

I had thought myself happy before, but now my joy was beyond words. At times it seemed to me

that even Heaven itself could scarcely offer more. Yet this joy was not rooted in myself, nor in

any achievement of my own — for I had none. It was joy in the Lord.

I understood, at last, t he prophet’s words:

“Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the mighty man in his might, nor the rich man in

his riches; but let him who glories, glory in this: that he understands and knows Me.”

I had no wisdom, no strength, no riches in myself — but I was learning to know the Lord, and in

Him I could glory with all my heart.

“Where, then, is boasting?” asks the Apostle.

“It is excluded… by the law of faith.”

A soul that has no attainments cannot boast in itself; and a soul that receives everything freely

from the Lord cannot help but boast in Him.

“For by grace you are saved through faith… not of yourselves… not of works, lest any man

should boast.”

“They did not gain the land by their own sword, nor did their own arm save them; but Your right

hand, O Lord, and the light of Your countenance.”

This was my experience. And with all my heart I could echo the Psalmist:

“In God we boast all day long, and praise His Name forever.”

fields.title: Chapter 28. The Secret Of A Happy Life
fields.body_html:
his new spiritual life I had entered had been given many different names. The Methodists

called it “the Second Blessing” or “the Blessing of Sanctification.” The Presbyteri ans

preferred “the Higher Life” or “the Life of Faith.” The Friends spoke of it as “the life hidden

with Christ in God.” Whatever the terminology, the truth behind each phrase was exactly the

same, and it could be reduced to four simple words: “Not I, but Christ.”

In every case, the heart of the matter was surrender — turning ourselves over to the Lord so that

He might work within us, shaping both our desires and our actions according to His will. It

meant taking Him at His word: trusting Him not only to save us from sin’s punishment but also

from sin’s power, and believing His promise to give us grace and help in every moment of need.

Personally, I prefer to call this simply “the life of faith,” because that is the plainest description.

But in the book where I explained it most fully, I called it The Secret of a Happy Life , because

for so long it truly had been a secret to me — and because I fear it is still a secret to hundreds of

God’s children who are staggering under the same heavy burdens I once carried. It was not a

secret because God hid it, but because I had not yet discovered it. It has always been an open

secret — spread clearly across the pages of Scripture — if only I had possessed the spiritual

perception to see it.

“The secrets of the gods are from of old,

Guarded forever, and forever told;

Blabbed in all ears, but published in a tongue

Whose purport the gods only can unfold.”

An ox and a philosopher may look at the same field, yet see entirely different things. In the same

way, before and after this glorious discovery, I looked at the same Bible and even read the same

verses — but I saw them with entirely different eyes. Scripture, like nature, lies open to all, but

not all truly see it. The law of gravitation operated plainly before humankind for ages, but only

T

Newton recognized it. Likewise, the law of faith had been written plainly in the Bible, though I

had failed to discern it. The forces we harness in nature were not created by us, only discovered;

they existed just as truly before discovery as afterward. And I am certain that no scientific

discoverer ever felt gre ater delight in uncovering nature’s secrets than I felt when I uncovered

the “secrets of God.”

My joy was so great that I felt compelled to speak of it to everyone — to insist upon their

listening. At first, my husband — an earnest and successful Christian worker — was somewhat

alarmed. He feared I might be rejoicing in some error that would harm me and perhaps others.

He frequently returned to the argument that the “old man” within us could never be completely

conquered in this life, and must always hold us in some degree of bondage.

One morning, as we were discussing this, I said, “Well, impossible or not, the Bible certainly

says it. What does thee make of this passage in Romans 6: ‘Knowing this, that our old man is

crucified with Him, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve

sin.’ What else can that mean but that sin’s power is truly to be conquered, so that we need no

longer serve it?”

Startled by the sudden light that seemed to flash from those words, he said, “There is no such

passage in the Bible.”

“Oh yes, there is,” I replied. I opened my Bible and showed it to him. It was a verse he had, of

course, known for years, yet in that moment it appeared to him with such a new and striking

meaning that he felt as if he had never seen it before. It brought with it a deep conviction, and

from that moment he did not rest until he had discovered the truth for himself.

His own account of this discovery, published in 1868, was as follows. After describing the lack

he had been feeling in his Christian life, he continued:

“I knew that the Bible seemed to promise a better life for the Christian than the one I knew, and

for years the conviction had grown in me that there was some part of God’s truth that I had yet to

discover. I felt that something essential was missing in the way I understood Scripture —

something that would supply that spirit of love which the Bible declares is greater than all

knowledge and all faith. I had often expressed my growing sense that some truth was waiting to

bre ak forth from God’s Word— something that would fill our hearts with a love that could bear

all things. My feeling was so strong that I arranged a meeting with several brethren well-versed

in Scripture so that we might examine, carefully and in detail, what part of God’s Word we had

failed to understand and to teach.

Circumstances delayed that meeting, but in the meantime — through a completely unexpected

channel — I received the secret that taught me the joy of Christian liberty and the power of true

service. That secret was faith . How strange that I, who had constantly taught faith as the channel

for the forgiveness of sins, had failed to see that faith alone is also the means of deliverance from

the inward power of sin. Not only the sinner, but the Christian also, must receive everything by

faith.

“At this time, I met some Christians whose inner life, as they described it, seemed utterly

different from mine. They declared that practical sanctification was obtained, just like

justification, by simple faith; that it could be realized at any moment when one’s faith could fully

grasp it; and they insisted that they themselves had experienced it. The subject continued to

confront me, and again and again passages of Scripture were presented to me — passages to

which I sincerely believed myself completely submissive. Yet I regarded the entire matter with

profound unease, for it seemed to me that what they sought and claimed to possess was nothing

less than perfection in the flesh —and that, I knew, was impossible.”

I can hardly describe the depth of prejudice I felt against this teaching. Few ideas had ever stirred

such instinctive resistance in me, and I spent many anxious hours worrying over what I believed

were the dangerous consequences of this “heresy” creeping in among us. My opposition was so

determined that even familiar passages of Scripture — texts I had known for years — seemed

strange and almost unrecognizable when someone quoted them to prove that sanctification was

by faith, and that it was possible to “walk worthy of the Lord unto all pleasing.”

One morning, Romans 6:6 was read to me: “Knowing this, that our old man is crucified with

Christ, that the body of sin might be destroyed, that henceforth we should not serve sin.” My

friend added, “Surely these words must m ean something — and something that makes it possible

for a believer to cease being a slave to sin.”

I was so startled by the force of the verse that I blurted out emphatically, “That passage is not in

the Bible!”— even though, in truth, it was one of the most familiar passages in all of Scripture to

me. When I was forced to admit that it really was there, I took refuge in the explanation that it

was merely judicial truth: something true “in God’s sight,” but never actually true in a

Christian’s experience.

But from that moment, I began to wonder whether there might be some truth in what these

people were teaching. Slowly it dawned on me that I had misunderstood them. They were not

talking about perfection in the flesh, but about the death of the flesh — and a life hidden in Christ.

A life of abiding in Him, walking in Him, living through His power — a life of victory and joy

that was truly pleasing to God.

“So that is all you mean?” I asked once, when this truth had been pressed upon me with unusual

force. “That is nothing new. I have always known that.”

“But have you lived it?” came the reply.

“Yes,” I answered, “I have lived so at times. Often I have given myself wholly into the Lord’s

care and realized that I was dead, and that He alone lived in me.”

“You have kno wn this as an occasional experience,” my friend said gently. “But have you ever

known it as a life ? You say you sometimes take refuge in the Lord — but have you ever made

your home in Him?”

I saw at once that I had not. My faith in this matter had been intermittent. In moments of unusual

difficulty, or whenever I felt especially weak, I had turned exclusively to the Lord and had

always found Him sufficient for my need. But that this occasional experience might become —

and ought to become — the experience of my whole life had never occurred to me.

“What would you think,” my friend continued, “of people who trusted Christ in such an

intermittent way for the salvation of their souls? Suppose one week they felt powerless and cast

themselves entirely on Him, only to spend the next week trying to earn salvation partly

themselves, merely asking Him to make up what they lacked. Would you not think such a course

inconsistent and foolish? And yet is it not just as inconsistent — and just as dishonoring to

Christ — to trust Him in this on-again, off-again way for your daily life? Sometimes walking by

faith, sometimes relying on your own strength?”

I could not deny the truth of this, and the possibility — and beauty — of a life of continuous faith

began to open before me.

Such was my husband’s account of his discovery. To my great joy, from that time forward we

were entirely united in the matter. It was not that either of us believed we had become sinless, or

that we never failed again. Rather, we had discovered the secret of victory — that we were no

longer slaves to sin, compelled to yield to its power, but could, if we chose, become “more than

conquerors through Him who loved us.”

This did not mean temptations ever ceased. But we had learned that the Lord is both able and

willing to deliver us out of every temptation — if only we would trust Him. We saw that our old

belief —that we were doomed to be lifelong “servants of sin”— was contrary to Scripture and a

slander upon the completeness of Christ’s salvation, for He died precisely to free us from sin’s

bondage. “For sin shall not have dominion over you, for you are not under the law, but under

grace.”

We learned further that faith — faith alone — was the road to victory, and that effort and self-

struggle accomplished nothing in this battle. Our part was surrender and trust; God’s part was

everything else.

For the third time, as I have said, a veil seemed to lift from the pages of Scripture, and

everywhere we saw the “secret of victory” shining in letters of light. Old texts blossomed with

new fullness. Take, for instance: “For whatsoever is born of God overcomes the world; and this

is the victory that overcomes the world, even our faith. Who is he that overcomes the world, but

he that believes that Jesus is the Son of God?” Formerly we thought this referred only to a future

victory, after death. Now we saw it spoke of a present victory, by a present faith, while still

living in the world.

Or this: “Behold the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world.” We had always taken it

to mean the rem oval of sin’s penalty . Now we saw it meant the removal of its power — that we

need no longer serve it or be enslaved by it.

I could give countless examples of this unveiling of Scripture, but these must suffice. We had

made a transforming discovery, and it filled our every thought. Whenever I met a friend, my first

question was, “How much time do you have? I have something wonderful to tell you.” And I

would pour out my story of the great salvation I had discovered.

To most, it was as new and delightful as it had been to me, and many immediately embraced it as

an experiential reality. But one friend — the same who had awakened me to religious things at

sixteen, and who had been my closest spiritual confidante ever since — listened and then said,

“But Hannah, that is nothing new. I have always known that.”

“Then why,” I cried indignantly, “did you never tell me? You knew how I have struggled all

these years — winning a few battles, losing far more — and all the while you had this secret of

victory and never told me! How could you be so unkind?”

“But I thought everyone knew it,” she said. “It is what the Quakers have always taught. Their

preaching is almost entirely about it.”

“Well,” I said, “everyone does not know it. Very few know it. Most Christians believe they must

remain ‘servants of sin’ all their lives because of the weakness of the flesh. And most think that

if they are ever to gain victory, they must fight for it themselves, and only if defeat seems

imminent may they call the Lord to help. They do not understand that the battle is to be handed

over to Him from the beginning — just as the Israelites stood still at the Red Sea and saw the

salvation of the Lord.”

“And,” I added with conviction, “I intend to tell this to everyone I can.”

And I did. Young or old, whether mature Christians or beginners — no one escaped hearing the

story if I dared speak. Nearly all who heard it embraced it and began to live in its power.

One of them was my little daughter, about seven or eight years old. She had begun to develop a

strong willfulness that I found almost impossible to manage. She herself recognized it as wrong

and tried hard to conquer it, but she seemed almost possessed by it. One day she came to me,

puzzled, and said, “Mother, why am I so naughty? I know I’m a little C hristian girl, and I

thought Christian children were always good. But no matter how hard I try to make myself good,

I just can’t help being naughty.”

From my own experience, I understood her perfectly. I said, “I think, darling, the reason is that

you are trying to make yourself good. We never can make ourselves good, try as we may. Only

our Heavenly Father can do that. Whenever you feel tempted to be naughty, tell Him all about it,

ask Him to make you good, and then trust Him to do it. He will surely take the naughtiness

away.”

She thought a moment and said, “Oh, I didn’t know that. I thought you had to use your will and

just do it yourself.”

She walked away quietly, clearly considering this new idea. Soon I noticed a great change. Her

willfulness seemed entirely gone; she was gentle and obedient as a lamb. I said nothing, wanting

to respect the delicacy of the moment. A few days later, I heard her playing softly with her dolls

and murmuring with quiet delight, “Oh, I am so glad Heavenly Father is making me so good. It

feels so nice to be good.”

Still I said nothing. But a few nights afterward, as I tucked her into bed, she burst out, “Oh,

Mother, aren’t you glad Heavenly Father is making me so good? He’s going to make me a great

deal gooder, but aren’t you glad He has made me as good as I am now?”

As I hugged and kissed her, rejoicing with her, she added earnestly, “Mother, do you tell

everybody about this?”

I said I tried to, but she insisted, “You mustn’t only try— you must really do it every time you

preach. I think lots of people are like I was — wanting to be good but not knowing how. You must

tell every single person you meet.”

I have always taken that as a kind of divine call to my work.

In truth, our hearts were so full that we hardly needed encouragement. Everyone we knew heard

the story eventually, and soon a great stir arose — not only in our own community, but throughout

the American church and even in England. Letters poured in from all directions asking what this

“new doctrine taught by the Pearsall Smiths of Millville, New Jersey” might be. Meetings and

conferences sprang up that continue even to this day, many known as “meetings for the

deepening of the spiritual life.”

This discovery was the beginning of a great revival in the spiritual life of the Church

everywhere. It reached its height in the meetings of 1873 and 1874 on the Continent, and later at

Oxford and Brighton, where thousands came to hear the message. Its effects are still felt in

countless lives. Wherever I go, people tell me their whole lives were changed by what they

learned there.

It was not a new religion they discovered, but the vitality of the old one. Truths they had long

professed became living realities. They had called Christ their Savior; now they learned that He

truly saves , and trusting Him, they found Him faithful.

There was nothing sectarian in the teaching. No one had to change creed or denomination.

Across all churches — Methodist, Quaker, Catholic, and more — there have always been those

who truly understood and lived the life of faith. It lies, I believe, at the heart of every Christian

creed. All that is needed is for believers to stop merely professing their faith and begin actually

believing it — and they will always find it true.

The life of faith fits every creed and every denomination. The story is the same everywhere.

fields.title: Chapter 29. The Life Of Faith Quaker Doctrine
fields.body_html:
mong those especially interested in these new spiritual discoveries were the Friends. As I

mentioned in the last chapter, one of them — after hearing my story — expressed surprise

that any of it was new to me. She insisted it was exactly what the Quakers had always taught.

Her comment suddenly cast a new light on Quakerism, one I had never imagined.

My mother said something similar after he aring me speak one day. “But Hannah,” she asked,

“why do you call this doctrine new? You’re only preaching what the old Friends always

preached.”

“Yes,” I replied, “I’m beginning to see that. But they have never preached it in a way that

ordinary people could grasp. Unless one already knew the secret, their words could hardly give

it. Certainly I never understood it, though I listened to their preaching all my life. For my part,” I

added, “I am determined to speak plainly enough that no one can fail to understand.”

But I eventually concluded that my mother and my friend were right: what we had discovered

really was genuine Quaker doctrine. With my eyes newly opened, I reread their writings and

listened again to their sermons. I realized that the heart of true Quakerism is this “life hid with

Christ in God,” and that their central teaching was that Christ is a present and complete Savior —

One who keeps His people’s feet, as He promised, and makes them more than conquerors

through His strength.

I saw that a life of absolute consecration, full obedience, and simple trust was the life they had

always urged upon us. I had not understood them before because they were preaching about the

building of the Christian life, while I was still searching for the foundations of that life.

Alexander Knox says that the Christian faith has “foundation truths” and “superstructure truths,”

both necessary to form a complete whole. The foundation and the building are different, yet

perfectly harmonious. Foundation truths introduce us to the Christian life; superstructure truths

A

teach us how to live once we are in it. Without superstructure, the foundation remains bare and

unfinished; without foundations, the superstructure is unstable.

The early Friends were, from the beginning, a society devoted to building the superstructure.

Their message was directed chiefly to Christians. Their early history shows that most of them

had already been serious believers within the denominations of their day, yet had not found there

what fully satisfied their spiritual hunger.

One writer describes them this way: for years they had sought the Lord with deep longing, trying

every teacher, every practice, every form of devotion, yet still craving something more. They

wanted the inward presence and power of the Spirit — something beyond what they could gather

merely from Scripture’s letter. They longed for life, for communion with Christ, for an entrance

into His kingdom and His reign within. When the light of the Spirit finally broke upon them, it

came with such joy and power that they never forgot it — a sense of life poured into their hearts,

drawing them into divine rest and setting them apart for God’s service.

My own dear father, a genuine and wonderfully delightful Friend, lived this early Quaker

experience. We had long known that he lived a life of steady trust and simple obedience. But in

our more evangelical days, we thought him unclear on doctrines such as justification by faith or

the believer’s legal standing before God. We often tease d him that although he was certainly

good, he was also rather “unsound.”

After discovering the life of faith for ourselves, however, we became convinced that this was the

secret of his steadiness. At the first opportunity I asked him, “Now, Father, isn’t t his the secret of

your life and the source of your strength? Haven’t you always lived this way?”

I will never forget his answer.

“Why, of course it is, daughter,” he said with a joyful triumph in his voice. “I know no other way

to live. And I certainly know what it is, when the enemy comes in like a flood, for the Lord to

raise His standard against him and drive him off.”

It now seems clear to me that Friends were meant to be workers on the interior life — not

primarily to convert sinners, but to lead believers into a deeper walk with God and a life of

abiding trust. Yet in recent days it seems to me they have drifted from this calling, striving more

to do foundational work than to build the superstructure. Their traditions and methods, suited for

the latter, are less suited for the former. The results, unsurprisingly, do not compare with

denominations whose chief aim has long been the foundation work of evangelism.

A thoughtful Friend recently said to me that they were meant to be a strong mystical society, but

feared they were becoming a weak evangelical one. I could not deny the truth in his words.

If only the Friends would again proclaim with the old clarity and power that glorious message of

a full and present salvation in Christ — available here and now — the blessing to thousands of

hungry souls would be immeasurable.

One of their early preachers once said: “I bring you good news. Not that the day of your

redemption is near, but that it has already come. Many are already blessing God that they are

redeemed and delivered from corruption’s bondage, and have more joy in His service than they

ever had in the world’s. Oh, the conquering faith, the overcoming life and power of the Spirit!

We cannot help but speak of these things, and exalt the perfect gift and power of Him who not

only can complete His work in the heart, but delights to do so — yes, even to tread down Satan

under the feet of those who trust Him.”

No matter how vague Quaker preaching had become in my time, the early Friends spoke plainly

enough. Small wo nder their message spread so widely. And if today’s Friends were to sound that

same clear trumpet again, I believe multitudes would respond — for the children of God are as

hungry now as ever to know the fullness of Christ’s salvation.

fields.title: Chapter 30. Holiness Camp Meetings
fields.body_html:
s may be imagined, we eagerly seized every opportunity to learn more about the truths we

had discovered. And though the Friends did indeed teach them, it was among the

Methodists that we found the clearest light. The Methodists spoke with great certainty: they

taught that the Christian life involved two distinct experiences — the first, justification; the

second, sanctification. They urged believers not to rest content with justification (that is,

forgiveness), but to press on to sanctification, the “second blessing,” as they called it. I would not

now express the truth in quite that way, but at the time it was profoundly helpful.

Not all Methodists embraced this teaching; many considered it too extreme. Those who did were

known as “Holiness Methodists,” and it was from them that we received the greatest help. They

held special “Holiness Meetings” devoted to the subject, and we delighted in attending whenever

possible. Most of all, we cherished their “Holiness Camp Meetings,” held in summer in secluded

forests or by the sea. These gatherings —“Meetings for the Promotion of Holiness”— were in fact

great open-air conferences, drawing Christians of many denominations from across the country,

all intent on seeking deeper communion with God. Living in tents beneath the trees, we spent a

week or more waiting upon God and sharing together the profound things of the Kingdom.

No words can capture the extraordinary power, solemnity, and yet overwhelming joy of those

meetings. We were cut off from our ordinary occupations and cares, with nothing to do but yield

ourselves to the spiritual influences around us and open our hearts to what we believed to be the

teaching of the Holy Spirit. Such a company of earnest Christians, all intent on drawing nearer to

God, created an atmosphere of spiritual intensity that was unforgettable. Testimonies of joy

resounded in every meeting, songs of praise echoed through the forest, and the radiant faces of

those we met made it seem as though we stood on the very threshold of Heaven. I cannot help

but pity any Christian who has never known such seasons of pure delight. For me, they were the

culmination of the grand spiritual romance that religion has always been, and I count them

among the most entrancing experiences of my life. Even now, the sight of a camp chair or a tent

A

beneath the trees brings back something of that supreme happiness that filled every hour of those

blessed gatherings.

On one occasion, a friend of ours — unaware of the true purpose of the meetings — came to see

what they were like. Arriving early in the morning, he met worshippers returning from prayer.

Struck by their radiant expressions, he asked us, “What is the matter with all these people, that

their faces shine so? Nearly everyone I have seen here has a shining face; but I met a few whose

faces did not shine, and I want to know the difference.” We explained that the shining faces

reflected hearts at rest in the Lord, while those without such radiance had not yet discovered the

blessed secret. He listened intently, then declared , “I am determined that I too will get a shining

face, and I will stay here until I do.” And indeed, within days his face shone with the joy of

God’s salvation.

I shall never forget my first Camp Meeting, nor the first prayer gathering I attended there. It was

an early morning meeting in a tent. Having known only the small Methodist meetings at

Millville, I had no conception of the emotional atmosphere into which I had stepped. I realized,

too late, that I had forgotten my handkerchief — but having never shed tears in a meeting before, I

thought little of it. Yet in that gathering the fountains of my being were broken open, and floods

of sweet tears poured from my eyes. In desperation I lifted my dress and used the white

underskirt to dry them. Ever since, I have carried at least two handkerchiefs to every meeting,

though I have never again been so overwhelmed with emotion as I was then.

That morning was my first taste of the entrancing joys of spiritual emotion, and I reveled in it. As

I left the tent, a Metho dist “Holiness Sister,” seeing my tears, put her arm around me, shared her

own experience of sanctification, and began to guide me. Under her care, I soon learned how to

receive the full benefit of the meetings. Much was said about the “blessing of sanctification,” and

at every gathering we were urged to come forward to the “altar”— a simple bench set apart — to

seek it. I did not fully understand what this “blessing” was, but it seemed something tangible,

born of complete consecration and simple faith, and it filled people with rapturous joy. My

Holiness Sister soon had me going forward to the altar myself, determined to receive whatever

God had to give. The thrilling testimonies I heard continually fired my enthusiasm, and I

embraced every opportunity to seek the blessing. I enjoyed it immensely, for it seemed to bring

me to the very edge of unknown spiritual possibilities ready at any moment to unfold.

Apart from those moments of standing, as it were, on the threshold, no special “blessing” ever

came to me from my visits to the altar. I am not naturally emotional, and the overpowering

feelings others described as the essence of the blessing never fell to my share. What I did receive

was the grand truth taught at those meetings — that the Lord Jesus Christ is a Savior not only

from the guilt of sin but also from its power. That truth became increasingly real and effective to

me. But as for any blessing apart from the truth itself, I experienced nothing. In time, I came to

see that the knowledge of the truth was al l the blessing I needed. Much of what was called “the

blessing” seemed to me simply the emotional response of emotional natures to the discovery of a

magnificent truth. For me, it came with intellectual conviction and delight; for others, with

emotional conviction and delight. But in both cases the truth was the same, and it was the truth —

not the emotion — that set the soul free.

My husband, however, being of a more emotional nature, did at one of these Camp Meetings

receive the blessing in true Methodist fashion. He returned home radiant, filled with a divine

glow that touched everyone he met. He could not speak of the meeting without moving us to

tears, and it was clear he had undergone a remarkable spiritual experience. He told us of a special

gathering devoted to prayer for the Baptism of the Spirit. Afterwards, he withdrew alone into the

woods to continue in prayer. Suddenly, from head to foot, he was shaken by what felt like a

magnetic thrill of heavenly delight. Floods of glory poured through him, body and soul, with the

inward assurance that this was indeed the longed-for Baptism of the Holy Spirit. The whole

world seemed transformed: every leaf and blade of grass shimmered with exquisite color, heaven

opened before him as a present possession, and everyone he saw appeared beautiful, for he

seemed to perceive the Divine Spirit within them. This ecstasy lasted for weeks and marked the

beginning of a life of extraordinary spiritual power and blessing.

I confess I was jealous that I did not receive a similar blessing, for I felt I needed it as much as he

did. I renewed my efforts to obtain it, but all in vain. I never passed from the realm of conviction

into the realm of emotion. My experiences remained intellectual rather than emotional. At last I

became con vinced that the difference lay not in God’s favor but in the differing natures of the

recipients. Emotional natures received the truth with floods of delight; I received it calmly, with

intellectual joy. The truth was the same, only the manner of reception differed.

Over time I observed that emotional experiences were often less solid and permanent than

intellectual ones. Emotions, by their nature, fluctuate, while true convictions remain. Once a

person is convinced that two and two make four, no amount of ill health or adverse weather can

shake that conviction. Feelings, however, are at the mercy of countless influences. I learned,

therefore, not to seek emotions but convictions. To my surprise and delight, convictions brought

me a more stable and lasting joy than many of my emotional friends seemed to know. In times of

stress, their emotions flagged or vanished, and they struggled to avoid despair. Some were

grateful at last to return to the stable ground of conviction, which in their emotional days had

seemed barren.

This lesson took me years to learn. Meanwhile, the joy and power of the glorious secret we had

discovered grew ever more practical. My soul learned to rest in absolute confidence in the

keeping and saving power of the Lord. Temptations did not cease, nor d id we attain “sinless

perfection.” Temptations arose, failures occurred. But we had discovered a way of escape— the

way of faith. We learned that Christ is a Deliverer not only from the future punishment of sin but

from its present power. We realized we need no longer be slaves to sin. As far as we laid hold of

this deliverance by faith, so far we were delivered. We had not pocketed holiness as a permanent

possession, but we had discovered the highway of holiness and learned the secret of walking in

it. When we walked there, we had victory; when we strayed, we met failure. After years of

wilderness wandering, we had entered the promised land, and found it true, as God said to Israel

of old: “Every place the sole of your foot shall tread upon, that have I given you.” The whole

land was ours; we need only go up and possess it.

We discovered that the Bible’s words were fact: “God is able to make all grace abound toward

you; that you, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work.” And

we proved in experience that God truly was able — if only we were willing. Christ was revealed

to us not merely as our future Savior, but as our present and complete Savior, able to keep us

from falling and to deliver us from all our enemies.

For me, this was the beginning of a romance before which all others paled. It was like exploring

the courts of heaven itself. Each day brought fresh revelation. Words fail me. I often called it the

“bird life,” for I felt like a bird set free, soaring upward into the bl ue of an unfathomable sky.

Once I had been a caged bird, content because I knew nothing of the freedom beyond. Now all

barriers were gone, and my soul was free to comprehend with all saints the breadth, length,

depth, and height of the love of Christ, which surpasses knowledge. What once seemed

unfathomable now opened into an abyss of delight.

I found that God Himself was enough. Even His promises paled beside the comfort of His

presence. What did it matter if I could not find a promise to fit my case? I had found the

Promiser, and He was infinitely more than all His promises. As a child, when in trouble, the

mere presence of my father or mother brought instant relief. They did not need to explain or

promise; their presence was assurance enough. How much more true is this of our Heavenly

Father, whose very name is Love. His presence is all we need. Over and over in Scripture He

settles His people’s fears with the simple words, “I will be with thee.” That means all His

wisdom, love, and power are engaged on our behalf.

I learned that God’s character is our resting place. His ways or promises we may misunderstand,

but His goodness cannot be mistaken. If He is good, loving, wise, just, omnipotent, and

omnipresent, then all must be ordered rightly for us. Appearances may deceive, but the deeper

reality is secure. As George MacDonald said, we need “eyes that can see below surfaces.” Once

we discover God’s utter unselfishness, those eyes are opened, and all mysteries of His dealings

are answered forever.

No wonder th e Psalmist rejoiced again and again in God’s goodness: “Oh, give thanks unto the

Lord, for He is good.” “Oh, trust in the Lord, for He is good.” “Oh, taste and see that the Lord is

good.” Surrounded by nations whose gods were cruel, selfish, and indifferent, Israel’s triumph

was to declare without fear that their God was good. And I feel it is no less a triumph today, in a

world that misunderstands and maligns Him, to be able to say with absolute conviction: “Come,

taste and see that the Lord is good!”

fields.title: Chapter 31. The Lovely Will Of God
fields.body_html:
ith my eyes newly opened to the absolute goodness and selflessness of God, my entire

attitude toward His will was transformed. In the past, I had viewed God’s will as

something set against me; now I discovered it was wholly for me. I had feared it as something

harsh; now I saw it as something to embrace with joy. I once thought His will was the terrible

weapon of His severity, descending upon me to punish. Now I saw it as the tender instrument of

His love, bringing into my life only what was kindest and best.

I realized that the will of perfect, unselfish love could only be good, and that since God possesses

all knowledge and all wisdom, His will must — by its very nature — be the best thing the universe

could offer. No greater bliss could come to any of us than to have that beautiful, selfless will

perfectly done both in us and for us.

Sometimes hiding myself in God’s will felt like retreating into an impregnable fortress of love

and protection, where no harm could reach me. At other times it felt like sinking into the softest

bed of down, resting in perfect peace. I can never fully put into words all that I began to see of

the loveliness, tenderness, generosity, and infinite goodness of the will of God. I truly reveled in

its sweetness.

This did not mean life would be free of trials; a wise and loving will might see trials as necessary

gifts of love. Nor was it essential that I perceive the divine hand in every difficulty. My common

sense told me that if God is omnipresent, He must be present in my trials as well — and, being

there, He must be there to help and bless.

We are not wise enough to judge whether our experiences are truly joys or sorrows, but the Lord

knows. And because He loves us with limitless, unselfish love, He cannot fail — literally cannot

fail — to make even the things that appear hard, or cruel, or wicked, work together for our

greatest good. I say “cannot fail” because it is unimaginable that such a God could act otherwise.

W

It does not matter who begins the trial — whether human malice, spiritual evil, or our own

foolishness. If God allows it to reach us, then by that very permission He makes the trial His

own, transforming it into a chariot of love that carries our souls to blessings we never could have

reached otherwise. For the Christian who dwells in the fortress of God’s will, there are no

“second causes”; nothing can enter that fortress unless th e Divine Keeper of it opens the door.

And when He does, it means He has adopted that thing for our eternal good.

Joseph was sold into Egypt through the wickedness of his brothers, yet God made their cruelty

the very chariot that carried him to triumph. So we may be more certain of this than we are that

the sun will rise tomorrow: God’s will is the loveliest thing in the universe for us— not because it

always looks best, but because it cannot be anything but best, being the will of infinite love.

I found myse lf continually singing Faber’s beautiful hymn:

“I worship Thee, sweet will of God,

And all Thy ways adore;

And every day I live it seems

I love Thee more and more.”

One verse delighted me especially because I so often found it true in experience:

“I know n ot what it is to doubt,

My heart is always gay;

I run no risks, for, come what will,

Thou always hast Thy way.”

The first time I realized this in a deeply practical way was three days after the birth of my

beloved baby girl — a child I had longed for with unspeakable yearning, who felt to me like the

most exquisite treasure ever entrusted to human care.

My nurse had suddenly fallen ill and was forced to leave, so we had to bring in a stranger whose

looks I mistrusted and whose ignorance seemed obvious. At that time trained nurses were far less

common, and I felt this one was wholly unqualified. I could hardly bear to have her touch my

precious child, yet I was not allowed to care for my baby myself.

It was winter, and a bright wood fire burned on the hearth of my room. On the nurse’s first

evening, after settling me in bed, she sat close to the fire with my baby on her lap. Soon she fell

into a deep sleep, snoring loudly, and I awoke to see my infant lying perilously near the blaze on

her slanting knees, while the nurse’s head drooped dangerously above her.

My voice was weak, and I could not rouse her. I expected at any moment to see my little one roll

into the fire. I could make no one hear me, and to rise from bed and cross the cold floor might

have seriously harmed my health. Yet my anxiety drove me upright, and I was struggling to

stand when suddenly these words flashed through my mind: “I run no risks, for, come what will,

Thou always hast Thy way.”

With those words came a deep conviction that my child was u tterly safe in God’s care. A

profound peace settled over me. My head sank back onto my pillow and my soul sank back into

the sweetness of God’s will. I saw that my baby was cradled in the arms of almighty love. I fell

asleep without a trace of fear and woke to find her being tucked beside me for her feeding.

It was beyond words beautiful to have experienced such a practical revelation of the loveliness

and blessedness of the will of God.

Since that first awakening, I have had many similar insights, and I have come to know — beyond

even the faintest shadow of doubt — that the will of God is the most delicious, delightful reality in

the universe. This is not because life always unfolds according to my preferences, nor because of

any special piety in me, but simply because plain common sense tells me that the will of perfect,

unselfish love could only be delightful. Heaven is heaven precisely because God’s will is done

perfectly there; and earth would inevitably resemble heaven if His will were perfectly done here.

For years I had heard Christians describe consecration to God’s will as a spiritual achievement so

lofty that only a few exceptionally devout souls could hope to reach it. But once I discovered the

infinite unselfishness of God, I realized that consecration is not an attainment at all — it is a

priceless privilege. I am convinced that if people truly understood the beauty of His will, not

only the particularly devout but every soul in existence would rush to choose it gladly for every

moment of their lives.

This is not a higher degree of piety; it is simply a higher degree of good common sense. If I were

lost in a trackless wilderness, unable to see any way out, and an experienced guide offered to

lead me to safety, would it feel difficult or sacrificial to pl ace myself in his hands and say, “Your

will be done”? And if not, how could it feel burdensome to entrust myself to my heavenly Guide

and say, “Thy will be done”? It cannot— it is impossible. Surrender to God, or consecration as

many call it, is the greates t privilege offered to any soul in this life. To say “Thy will be done” is

one of the most delightful sentences a human being is permitted to utter.

An old writer once said that God’s will is not a burden to carry, as so many imagine, but a pillow

on which to rest. I found this profoundly true. My soul sank into His will with an indescribable

sweetness of peaceful content. At other times, saying “Thy will be done” felt like a magnificent

cry of victory — like raising a triumphant banner before the entire universe and daring it to

oppose me. So vivid was this feeling that I found myself repeating, day and night, as a victorious

soldier might sing after battle:

“Thy wonderful, grand Will, my God,

With triumph now I make it mine;

And Love shall cry a joyous Yes

T o every dear command of Thine.”

But I could never fully tell all that my soul discovered when I discovered the goodness and

unselfishness of God. To say that He is enough is to give a complete and unshakeable answer to

every doubt and question that can ever arise. My feelings may not always confirm that prayers

are answered or promises fulfilled — but what of that? Behind every prayer and every promise

stands God Himself — the sheer God, if I may put it so — and if He exists at all, then He must be

enough.

For years I had sung the familiar words:

“Thou, O Christ, art all I want;

More than all in Thee I find.”

But until now, I had never understood what they truly meant. They had sounded beautiful, but

only as a poetic sentiment. Now I saw that they state a fact. I had begun to discover that He

really was everything I needed — and that infinitely more than all I could ask or imagine was

stored up for me in Him.

In a certain sense, my search for God ended there, for I had found that He was enough. I have

discovered many other beautiful and precious truths about Him since, but at that moment I had

reached Himself — the real God behind all appearances — and my heart entered into its rest. I saw

that nothing else ultimately mattered: not creeds, nor ceremonies, nor doctrines, nor dogmas.

fields.title: Chapter 32. Old Age And Death
fields.body_html:
ow that I am seventy years old and life is swiftly moving toward its close, I can say

without hesitation that discovering the unselfishness of God has transformed the way I

feel about both old age and death. Knowing — utterly and securely — that God is , and that God is

enough , makes old age a joy in the present and death a delicious prospect for the future.

Without Him, old age — with its diminishing strength and frequent infirmities — could only be

dreary and exhausting. But with God, our beautiful, unselfish God, behind it all, old age becomes

a gentle resting place. Reaching seventy gives me permission to step aside from the pressures of

life, to put down the burden of keeping the world running, and I gladly accept that release.

I did my part to carry the responsibilities of my own generation, and now that it has nearly

passed away, I rejoice that the weight of today’s world rests, not on me, but on younger and

stronger shoulders — those whom God has called to their own appointed work. I laugh to myself

with real pleasure at the thought, and I even enjoy the infirmities of age as they arrive. Each one

frees me from some task or duty and allows me the peaceful leisure to watch the younger

wrestlers in the world’s arena. I may not always think they wrestle in the best way, judging with

my old eyes, but I admire the divine order that assigns to each generation its own work, to be

done in its own way. Whether it seems wise or foolish to us, the passing generation must make

room for the rising one, and must refrain from interfering.

We older people may offer advice and share the fruits of our experience, but we must hold

ourselves completely content when our advice is ignored. If we did this — truly did it — I am

convinced the young would gladly seek our counsel far more often. But they hesitate because

they fear that asking for advice obliges them to follow it, and that we will feel wounded if they

do not. True freedom in seeking guidance can only exist alongside true freedom not to take it.

I am not speaking of children, but of adults in two different generations. And in general, when

the older insist that their advice must be followed, they put themselves in the unfortunate

N

position of obstructing the world’s progress. In almost every field today, businesses employ

younger and younger workers because older ones tend to settle into ruts and resist being urged

out of them. It is striking, in this regard, that by divine command the Israelites retired from

public service at the age of fifty —whether in the Tabernacle or the army. “From the age of fifty

years they shall cease their service… and serve no more.” If they step ped back at fifty, then at

seventy I am surely free to withdraw from the world’s work and enjoy the blissful sense of

release from responsibility that belongs to old age.

We often hear about the duty the young owe to the old. But I believe it is far more important for

us to consider the duty the old owe to the young. I do not mean that the young owe us nothing;

but at seventy, I see clearly that the greater burden lies on our side. We brought the younger

generation into the world without consulting them. Therefore we are obligated to pour ourselves

out for their good — just as God, who created us, has poured Himself out for ours through the

sacrifice of Christ. I cannot see how God could have done less, and I cannot see how we should

do less either.

Having discovered the unselfishness of God — as everyone who reaches seventy ought to have

done — our attitude toward others should reflect, in our measure, the same unselfishness. Surely

this is what Jesus meant when He urged us to love our enemies, bless those who curse us, and do

good to those who hate us, so that we might be “children of our Father in Heaven,” who does

exactly these things. And Jesus ends with, “Be perfect, therefore, as your Father in Heaven is

perfect.” Our perfection is the perfection of unselfish love. The older we are, the more deeply we

should understand this and live it.

Everything is safe when guided and controlled by unselfish love. And so my old heart rests

quietly. I can lay down my arms with joyful confidence. Since God is in His Heaven, all must

ultimately be right with His world, whatever appearances may suggest. I can peacefully wait to

understand what now seems mysterious until that glorious day of revelation that draws closer

with every hour.

One of my most comforting discoveries is that God can manage His universe by Himself, even

without my assistance. Whenever I look at the sun, the moon, or the stars —“the work of His

fingers”— I feel the deep satisfaction of knowing they are His responsibility, not mine. Because

of this, I can gladly die and leave the whole universe in His care, without the slightest fear that

things will fall apart when I depart. God is the housekeeper of His own creation. Just as it would

be foolish for me to trouble myself about the housekeeping of my neighbors in Grosvenor Road,
