such ‘waste’ and withheld their monthly contributions. They

felt themselves to be justly indignant; however, within one

year, the proceeds from the showing of that film, exceeded

five times the cost of making it! I believe we should rather be

on the cautious side when we come to spend the Lord’s

money, but taking offense could be a greater source of

embarrassment!

Judas was offended, so he went out to betray his master. The

potential for betrayal was already there, but the offense stirred

that potential into action. The result of his offense was that he

no longer trusted the Lord to do what He said He would. Judas

would goad Him into action. If He were the promised

Messiah who would establish His kingdom in place of the

Roman empire, now was the time to prove it! But only one

thing was proved - that he, Judas, was a poor politician and

an even poorer friend!

Judas had lost confidence in the Lord! Where is your

confidence placed? What do you place your trust and your

hope in? Christian ‘hope’ is an eager expectation that what

He has promised, He will complete! The hymnist declares

“My hope is built on nothing less than Jesus’ blood and

righteousness!” (My Hope is Built On Nothing Less, Robert

Critchley).

The writer of Hebrews encourages us to “not throw away

[our] confidence, which has a great reward” (Hebrews 10:35).

When we are offended, a lack of hope will be the result, and

therefore, we will have no confidence !

Peter’s Denial → Matthew 26:31-35, 69-75

Jesus had just come to the Mount of Olives, having instituted

the communion covenant with His disciples. He now teaches

them that He is about to be taken away from them.

Jesus tells His disciples, that “You shall all be offended

because of Me tonight.” But Peter, being brave and foolish,

says, “I will never be offended in You, even if everyone else

is!” (Matthew 26:31-33). How he must have regretted those

words just a few hours later! I feel for Peter because he is so

much like me! How wonderful a Savior we have who, feeling

his pain, would appear first to Peter after His resurrection, and

before the others saw Him (Luke 24: 34). I can only imagine

that scene as the two of them were reconciled through the

Saviour’s love.

John and Peter entered the house of the High Priest where

Jesus was being tried. As Peter passed through the doorway a

slave girl said to him, “Aren’t you one of His disciples?” He

responded, “I am not!” Then two more times he denies his

Lord, adding some choice oaths before the roosters crow.

I like to imagine that young slave girl and her question. Could

it have been possible that she was interested in the Lord and

wanted to know more about Him? If Peter had acknowledged

his discipleship, would she have asked him to tell her about

his friend since she wanted to love Him also? However, Peter

was offended , and the result of his offense was no testimony !

Many Turn Away → John 6:53-61

In this passage, Jesus is speaking some hard things to His

followers. He is calling them to “eat of My flesh and drink of

My blood” (John 6:53). Today, in retrospect, we understand

this in terms of the communion cup and the new covenant He

has called us into, but to them it was a hard saying which was

difficult to understand.

Jesus asked them, “Are you offended?”

Are you offended by His call to the discipleship demanded in

the communion covenant? The discipleship which is the core

challenge of this book? The result of their offense was that

many of His disciples went back and walked no more with

Him (John 6:66). The result of their offense was no

community.

So we have five Biblical examples of those who were

offended, with the result that they lost their fruit , confidence ,

and testimony . Within them there was disunity, and God

didn’t do any miracles among them! Therefore we can be sure

Satan must have gloated.

fields.title: The Rock of Offense
fields.body_html:
Jesus was the cause of much offense! Both Peter and Paul

quote the Old Testament in calling Him “a rock of offense”

(Romans 9:33 and 1 Peter 2:8).

The Pharisees were offended by Him, demons were offended

by Him, and even His family was offended by Him!

But to some He deliberately avoided offending such as the

despised tax gatherers. He told Peter to go to the sea where

he would find the required tax in the mouth of a fish, “so that

we do not give them any offense” (Matthew 17: 24)

But to others He seems to deliberately offend!

John the Baptist - Jesus’ Cousin

John the Baptist was second cousin to Jesus and had been

born just a few months before Him. He was full of the Holy

Spirit even while in his mother’s womb and was the first to

show any response to the promised Messiah. He had leapt in

Elizabeth’s womb when Mary, the mother of Jesus, had first

come to tell the remarkable story of her baby’s conception.

I’m sure the two boys must have spent many hours together

during childhood. They had probably played and worked

together, run and fought together, and talked and argued

together. Perhaps they even talked together about the burden

that was growing in each of their hearts.

Finally, John leaves home to answer a strange compulsion. It

could have been possible that Jesus was the only one who

understood when he announced that he must “prepare the way

of the Lord” (Matthew 3:3), and then he left for the desert.

There, John began to preach to all who would listen to him.

“The Messiah is coming soon” he would proclaim, “and we

are not ready! Repent and be baptized. Return to your God!”

(Matthew 3:2-12) The people responded, seeking to be

reconciled to Jehovah and indicating their new resolve by

being baptized in the local stream, the River Jordan. Theirs

was a baptism of repentance and a return to orthodoxy.

One day Jesus came to the Jordan River and John cried out to

the people, “Behold the lamb of God who takes away the sin

of the World!” (John 1:29). John gave witness that he saw a

dove descending upon Jesus and remaining upon him.

Moreover, the Holy Spirit had already told John that this

would be the sign of the coming Messiah in John 1:34 where

it’s written “I have seen and have borne witness that this is

the Son of God.”

John was not a popular preacher who ‘tickled men’s ears.’

Most of those who came to hear and see him were looking for

a curiosity, hoping that they would be there to hear his

condemnation of the self-righteous leaders of the synagogue.

He had some choice things to say to such leaders and the

people loved it; however, Herod did not. He was the ruler of

the Roman Empire at the time, and was a wicked man who

was having an affair with his sister-in-law - an affair that John

openly condemned. To silence his voice Herod had John sent

to prison.

I can imagine the thoughts of John while in those dungeons.

“Herod, you old fool! You think you are in control and that

putting me in prison will silence my voice. But my cousin is

the Messiah and He has come to overthrow your little empire

and to establish His own kingdom! He’ll get me out of this

prison soon, and you will be the one locked away! He has

declared that He has come to set the captive free. I can hardly

wait to see your face when He does it!” And with that, John

sits back in his cell and waits… and waits… and waits…

Meanwhile, Jesus continues with His ministry in the nearby

villages, not even finding the time to visit John in prison!

Surely, He would at least come to visit him! But because He

doesn’t come, John gets offended and subsequently was

beheaded! John’s disciples are sent to Jesus to ask a pointed

question. “Are you truly the Messiah or should we wait for

another?” (Matthew 11:3). “You do not meet our criteria

since You are not doing what we expected You to do!”

Jesus replies, “And he answered them, “Go and tell John what

you have seen and heard: the blind receive their sight, the

lame walk, lepers are cleansed, and the deaf hear, the dead are

raised up, the poor have good news preached to them. And

blessed is the one who is not offended by me” (Luke 7:22-

23).

Jesus’ Dear Friend Mary

Jesus had some very special friends who lived in the small

town of Bethany. He was just a few miles away when He

received news that His friend Lazarus was dying and that his

sisters Mary and Martha were grieving for him. “Now Jesus

loved Martha and her sister and Lazarus. So, when he heard

that Lazarus was ill, he stayed two days longer in the place

where he was” (John 11:5-6).

We do not read of any miracles, any teaching, or anything that

He did during those two days! And Lazarus died! When Jesus

finally came to Bethany, Lazarus had been in the tomb for

four days and his sisters were in deep sorrow. It is Martha

who comes out to greet Him. That is noteworthy, for she was

the one we often think of as ‘the drudge’ - the one who was

kitchen-bound - while her sister Mary would leave everything

to sit at Jesus’ feet, washing them with precious perfume and

wiping them with her hair while absorbing everything He

said. Today, Mary would be prominent in Christian activity -

president of the local Women’s Adoration Group while her

sister would be in the background making coffee and serving

cookies.

Martha said to Jesus, “Lord, if you had been here my brother

would not have died” (John 11:21). Jesus assures her that her

brother will live again, for He is the resurrection and the life.

I do not hear any condemnation in Martha's comment, just

sadness. She then goes to Mary, to ask her to come to Jesus.

But why isn’t Mary already there? Surely, she knows that He

is coming? Everyone would be aware of that, but Mary sat

still in the house. Why? May I suggest that she was pouting!

She was offended ! When she comes to Jesus, she falls before

Him weeping and says the same words as Martha had. “Lord,

if you had been here, my brother would not have died” (John

11:32).

Note that Jesus does not say the same comforting words to

Mary that He expressed to her sister. Could this have been

because of the tone of her voice? Accusing? Judgemental?

Instead of comforting Mary, “Jesus wept” (John 11:35), but

not because Lazarus was dead - He had known that for some

time and also that, in a short while, all would be rejoicing at

his resurrection. He didn’t weep because Mary, Martha, and

their friends were in sorrow - He had known that they would

be for that was natural at the death of a loved one.

He wept because Mary was offended.

Jesus would die for our “offenses,” but He still grieves when

we take offense.

On the journey to Bethany, Jesus had told His disciples that

people are often offended when they cannot understand. They

are walking in the dark (John 11:10). Had He known how

Mary would react?

Why Offenses Come

Why does the Lord allow offenses to come? Could it be that

His purpose is to reveal to us something about ourselves? Did

John have to realize that, though he had declared that, “He

must increase, and I must decrease” (John 3:30), that the

timetable has to be the Lord’s not his.

It’s easy for us to fall into the trap of trying to manipulate God

into doing things our way. It’s too easy to cross the line

between accomplishing His will, versus our will. We must not

get offended when He doesn’t do things ‘our way’ because

only He knows what is best for us, even when we cannot see

the reasons for the valleys we experience.

Did Mary need to learn that obedience and trust is far better

than prominence and popularity, even in the Lord’s ‘service?’

Greatness in the Kingdom comes to those who would be least,

even as servants (Luke 9:48).

What to Do With Offenses

First, you must own it ! The offense is yours! Another has not

sinned against you - you ‘took the monkey’ on your own

shoulders, so throw it off - or carry it!

Next, examine it ! The Lord allowed it to come that it may

teach you something about yourself.

I have had to learn some hard things this way, and I have

given you some of the reasons for offenses in the previous

chapter. You must study your personality types and learn to

major on your strengths. For example, most pastors tend to be

melancholics. One gift of the melancholic is the ability to see

problems long before others do. This can cause them to be

critical of others, offended by their inability to see ‘the

obvious,’ and to do something about it. Thank God you are

not all like me!

Everybody’s giftings are different. For many years I was

offended by others’ failure to recognize my teaching as a

‘gift.’ Everyone thinks they can teach, and I have had to learn

to be ‘thick skinned’ when people ignore my giftings and

calling as a pastor.

Once you have owned it and examined it , discard it !

By choice, pray about it and bury it! Bless those who have

offended you and seek the empowering of the Holy Spirit if

the offense seems too heavy - He has promised to be

sufficient for all your trials.

“Strive for peace with everyone, and for the holiness without

which no one will see the Lord. See to it that no one fails to

obtain the grace of God; that no ‘root of bitterness’ springs up

and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled” (Hebrews

12:14-15).

Then, the last step to take when the monkeys are on your

shoulders, is to forget it ! Do not let the offense dwell in your

heart any longer. Hand it off to the Lord, and let it off of your

mind and heart.

Finally, do not be the one who causes offense , for, “woe to

him through whom they come!” (Luke 17:1)!

fields.title: The Wounded Soul
fields.body_html:
The Bible clearly presents to us the devices of Satan as seen

in:

● The roaring lion affecting our emotions.

● The arrows of lies affecting our thoughts.

● The ‘monkeys’ of offense affecting our peace.

However, his most effective device is not so clearly

understood. He has targeted you from before your birth. He

is not omniscient, so he doesn’t know if you will become a

believer and an opponent in the battle, so he has tried to

wound you before you were aware of any battle. This is

evident in the large number of ‘dysfunctional’ people in our

churches, but it is my belief that there are many more who

struggle, but are unaware of their wound.

A New Creation

When I became a believer I was taught that “if anyone is in

Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold,

the new has come” (2 Corinthians 5:17). This verse was used

to challenge me concerning the little things of the old nature

that still were present in my life. Naturally, I was made to feel

guilty. I eased my guilt by reasoning that my old habits

weren’t as bad as some of those I saw in others. We were very

quick to condemn those who were not so able as we were to

overcome their old habits, particularly those obvious “sins”

such as smoking and drinking, not to mention dancing and

keeping company with those who do such things! I’m glad I

have come to understand this verse better, and to understand

something more of the grace of God.

Thank God that in Christ we are fully accepted and reconciled

to the Father - that we are justified, forgiven, and made new

creatures. However, my teeth did not shed their fillings and

return to the undecayed brightness of my youth when I was

converted. Indeed, my body has not been made a new

creation, rather, it continues to die day by day.

The ‘new creation’ refers to that part of me which once was

dead - my spirit. I am aware that there is much confusion

about the difference between the soul and the spirit but, for

the purpose of this book, I shall call the spirit that part of me

which, now being alive to God, differentiates me from an

unconverted person, whose spirit is dead however noble or

religious they may be. They, like me, have a body with

varying degrees of health, but which will surely die one day,

unless the Lord comes before.

We also have souls - our minds, our wills, and our emotions.

Even the non-Christian man has a living soul. At conversion,

these are not made a new creation; they carry many wounds

from the past and provide a fertile battlefield for Satan. He

knows the wounds - after all, his hosts were very active in

causing them! For too long we have made many new (and

some older) believers feel incompetent in the battle by

charging them to be more mature than their wounded souls

have allowed them to be. We have urged them to run when

their soul is crippled - to fight when their muscles have

atrophied! Instead, we should have been ministering to their

hurts and wounds, bringing healing through Biblical teaching

since the Lord has committed unto us the ministry of

reconciliation (2 Corinthians 5:18-19).

Bruises of the Soul

Many people have been subject for most of their lives to

continuous criticism and verbal abuse perhaps from a parent

or siblings. Their retiring personality invites others to

continue this abuse at school or at work, then they enter

adulthood with great ‘bruises’ on their soul. They are often

accused of being too sensitive, and indeed they are, as a result

of the abuse. They function well enough until criticized again

when they find themselves unable to handle the pain. New

bruises are formed and each new criticism, real or imagined,

is like a punch on the bruise.

Peter had been raised in a somber, though Christian home. He

was an only child and had few friends. He was not allowed to

bring friends home from school because they were ‘worldly’

and there were no other youth his age that attended the small

church his family went to. He could never quite meet his

father’s expectations or demands and was unable to hold a job

for very long. He was never made to feel good enough to be

accepted. In his mid-thirties he left home and went to work

for a Christian mission where he was befriended by three

other men. He began to enjoy his work and friends and

became a well-accepted part of that ministry until, just over a

year of working there, each of his three friends announced

that they would soon be leaving to work elsewhere.

Instead of the usual sorrow one would expect, Peter began to

act in a strange way. He deliberately set out to make himself

disliked by his departing friends. For example, he would

borrow something from one of them, and deliberately break

it, claiming that it was an accident. Each of the friends left the

mission offended by Peter.

Just why did he act like this? He told me that it had started

just after he had returned from holidays - at home. That had

not been a good time and he had been glad to return to the

mission. When I suggested that his experience of more

criticism at home had produced renewed bruising on his soul,

and that the departure of his friends had been like punches on

the bruising, Peter broke down and cried. “That’s exactly how

I feel,” he declared, “their leaving just added to my feelings

of being unworthy of love and acceptance.” Today, Peter is

walking in a new freedom, knowing his worthiness in Christ.

Stab Wounds

For others, the wound may have been created by a single act

- a wound similar to being stabbed. A classic example, of

course, is the child who is sexually abused by a trusted, loved

one. In this example, the child does not understand that they

are the victim and not the guilty one. They are afraid to speak

about the incident, choosing rather, to bury it in their memory.

Sometime afterwards, the wound is covered over and not

easily brought to the surface to be faced, even in adulthood.

The ‘bandage’ with which the wound was covered has

become a bondage affecting other areas of the adult’s

personality. Such a soul needs healing!

When I asked Alec why he couldn’t read or write, he told me

a sad story. For four years his mother had doted on him, her

only child, after his father had walked out on them. Then

another father came on the scene - one who did not like or

want Alec around him. He soon knew the deep pain of

rejection.

At the age of five, Alec started primary school where he

would sit in the back of the room, daydreaming. He

remembers well the occasion when an unthinking teacher

shouted at him. “Alec, you’re nothing but a dumbo!” The

hurting, little soul said to himself, “If that’s what you think I

am, that’s what I’ll be!” He resolved, as a young child, never

to study to please that teacher… and therefore grew into a

teenage illiterate!

Was Alec bright enough to have learned? Just one month after

we talked, Alec was reading all the sports news in the daily

newspaper! He had an interest in a young lady and was

motivated to walk out healing. I used his knowledge of sports

personalities and their photographs in the newspapers, to

encourage him in reading the words explaining the pictures.

Soon, he needed no pictures and I watched his self-esteem

grow as he began to read with understanding. So many

teachers, parents, and others will never know the negative

significance of the stabbing wounds their unthinking words

have had on so many young souls. Many adults today are still

carrying the scabs and scars from those wounds on their

souls!

Grazes

Then there’s the grazing kinds of wounds. They usually leave

no scar or permanent bondage, but can bleed profusely at the

time of injury. If not treated correctly, however, they can

fester and then produce far worse injury. I see such wounds

of the soul occurring when one experiences discouragement

or a great disappointment. It is accompanied by feelings of

inadequacy and loneliness, and spiritual defenses are down.

This is the time when we need to come around in tender

support for the hurting one. It is the time for empathy and

understanding.

Mary had become ill with “Epstein Barr” or “Yuppie Flu”

which was widely known as the disease of the nineties. It was

hard not knowing how long she was likely to be ill, for the

doctors had no ready cure. The members of her church were

praying for her, but she wished someone would come to visit

her. No one came, giving their reason that they were unsure

if such a disease was contagious. That was hard to accept, but

Mary did so with grace. Then one day, she received a

telephone call which caused much ‘bleeding’ of her soul. Her

closest friend called to tell her that the church had stopped

praying for Mary since it was obvious she was not exercising

faith. Her reasoning being, that if she had been so doing, she

would have been well by then.

Fractures

Let us continue with our metaphors. Are there such wounds

as fractures in the soul? Yes, and there are many believers

who are limping through life because of some traumatic

experience. It may be the death of a loved one, a broken

engagement, or some accident of life. They were crippled by

the experience and have never learned to walk again.

Melinda had an argument with her mother during which she

had pushed her away with some force. Some months later,

mother was diagnosed as having developed breast cancer, and

within a year, had died. No amount of argument could

convince Melinda that her push had not created the cancer in

her mother. She would not forgive herself and could not

accept the Lord’s forgiveness. She was a broken woman

when I met her, and to this day, remains crippled.

“He Restores My Soul”

I am convinced that many believers today have wounded

souls. I am also convinced that the Lord wants to heal those

wounds - to restore the soul. The psalmist David was guilty

of adultery and murder; he carried terrible soul wounds, but

he could still say, “The Lord is my shepherd… He restores

my soul” (Psalm 23:3).

There are also wounds created by our own doings. It seems to

me that when we deliberately act contrary to the explicit

Word of God, we create our own wounds. Sex outside of

marriage and divorce will always create wounded souls that

need healing through the grace of God. Be very sure that it is

His desire to bring such healing. Indeed, I see this as the true

work of sanctification - the second part of salvation.

Justification is when one has been set free from the penalty

of sin: salvation for one’s spirit. The Holy Spirit has already

completed this work.

Sanctification is when one has been set free from the power

of sin: salvation for one’s soul. This is the present work of the

Holy Spirit.

Glorification is when one has been set free from the presence

of sin: salvation for the body. This is the work that the Holy

Spirit has yet to do.

For these reasons we call Him Savior!

The Angler

We have likened Satan to a roaring lion and an archer;

however, it seems to me that his most effective warring

device is like an angler’s hook and rod -he knows exactly

where our soul wounds are. After all, he was instrumental in

creating them. When we get ready to enter the battle in the

heavenlies, he then casts his line, hooks it into the wound, and

manipulates the soul into ineffectiveness.

A Personal Story

Early in 1990 I became closely involved in a new work of

God among the native peoples of western Canada. The

spiritual battle was intense. I also stopped sleeping at the

same time. My doctor tried many different medications to get

me to sleep, but it was several weeks before a way was found

for me not to lie awake all night. Many thought I was under

an Indian curse and I would receive letters and telephone calls

of encouragement from throughout the north-west of America

and Canada. I asked Charles and Claudia, another pastor and

his wife, to pray for me, at which time she told me that she

was aware of a “terrible spirit of abandonment” upon me. I

had no understanding of what she meant.

Shortly afterwards, I was invited to spend a week at an

Anglican Retreat for clergymen and wives. There I was told

that there was an area of my emotions missing and it had

much to do with my mother’s death. My mother had died

when I was a teenager, and though I had not cried at the time

in a normal mourning, I thought I had dealt with her death

very well. Now I was being told that this had something to do

with my sleeplessness? I still did not understand.

After four months I offered to resign my position at the

church, but the elders and members would not let me. Instead,

much love was shown to me by them and the greater church

body of our city.

After eight months, I entered Vancouver University Hospital

as a patient in the sleep clinic where it was diagnosed that

there had been a physical breakdown in my body’s production

of the sleep-inducing neurochemicals. The specialist put this

down to stress. The next week, I was able to resign from the

church, which had now decreased to sixty percent the

attendance rate it had been at the beginning of the year.

The following Tuesday I was with a group of my closest

friends, other pastors who met together weekly for prayer. As

we finished our breakfast, one of them said to me, “Gareth, I

sense an awful spirit of abandonment upon you!” These were

the same words I had heard almost nine months earlier. When

I got back home, I called Claudia to ask her to explain to me

just what she had meant by her comment. She told me to sit

down that evening and to go back over my life, looking for

the times when the little boy in me might have felt abandoned.

My wife Anne and I were amazed as we considered the

different periods of my life - there were so many times when

I had felt the pain of abandonment, not least of which was my

mother’s death when I was just fourteen. I had not cried then,

but for some time afterwards, I had grieved. Later that same

evening I relaxed to read a novel about the Crusades of the

thirteenth century.

Two knights were leading their men into battle on the fields

of France. Suddenly, they were face to face; however, Sir

Rufus had been wounded and was slumped over in his saddle,

his sword hanging by his side. His enemy, Sir Nigel, quickly

rode toward him, raising his mighty sword to slay his

opponent. Just as he would strike the fatal blow, nine arrows

from Sir Rufus’ bowmen flew through the air to find their

target in Sir Nigel’s armpit. They were ineffective against his

armor, but very effective at his weak spot, where no armor

could be worn. I sensed that the Spirit of the Lord was

speaking to me.

“Gareth, you might be putting on the armor of God, but when

you go into battle against the enemy, be aware that he knows

exactly where your weakest spots are - and yours is that of

abandonment. They must be healed if you would be effective

in the battle!”

I now began to understand why people had been drifting away

from our church over the past two years. Three elders had left

because of job relocation and had been replaced by three other

good men; however, the new elders’ board did not have the

gifts necessary to maintain the programs initiated by the

former men and soon there began a slow exodus from the

church. I would meet people on the street who would rush up

to me to tell me that they loved me, but had started to go to

another church “because our children enjoy their youth work

so much.” There were many reasons, but few had displayed

the grace to come and tell me of their intentions. I would have

gladly given them letters of introduction if I had known they

wanted to transfer.

Then, as I grew more weary, I was not feeding and leading

my flock as they were used to, so more began to leave. Instead

of the fulfillment I was used to, I had the pain, almost every

week, of seeing another vacant pew. Since I was very

committed to my people, each departure was like a mini

divorce. I’m sure that none of those people would have

deliberately hurt me, but their actions were used by the enemy

as hooks in my wounds of abandonment. No wonder the

doctor called it stress, even though I would boast that I never

took my church problems home with me!

A personal note for readers potentially planning on leaving

your local church: do it the right and ethical way. Let your

pastor know of your intentions, because you’d be surprised if

you knew exactly how easily we wound one another.

fields.title: Our Response
fields.body_html:
God’s Priority is Satan’s Priority!

We can be certain of this! Whatever God’s purposes are for

mankind, Satan will do his utmost to hinder that work. If it is

the Lord’s desire that believers live in unity, the enemy works

very hard to hinder such unity.

As we study the Bible it is very evident that relationships are

high on God’s priority list. He created us for Himself, and for

one another. From cover to cover, the Bible emphasizes

relationship: man with God, and man with man.

In Genesis, God created man in His own image - that they

might have fellowship together (1 John 1:3). Then for the

man, He created a woman, because “it is not good for man to

be alone” (Genesis 2:18).

Later, He chose one man from whom would come a special

nation. He called Himself, “The God of Abraham, Isaac, and

Jacob,” becoming a Father and husband to their descendants.

Satan did all he could to break these relationships with a lot

of help from men themselves! Know that today he is still

working frantically to draw men from God, to break up

families, and to destroy the Jews.

The Old Testament ends with a wonderful promise

concerning relationships, “He will turn the hearts of fathers

to their children and the hearts of children to their fathers, lest

I come and strike the land with a decree of utter destruction”

(Malachi 4:6).

The emphasis of the New Testament is the same as the old

with the added responsibility for the believers of being in

unity as a foundation for their witness.

Major sections of the New Testament emphasize this truth,

ending with the invitation of the last chapter, “The Spirit and

the bride say, ‘Come!’” (Revelation 22:17). “Bride,” like

“Body” is a relationship word!

Dysfunctional Wounds

If the Lord would mature a man or woman to become a

mighty warrior who is effective in the battle against evil, the

enemy will try to ‘cripple’ that soldier even before he enters

the army as a cadet.

Satan is not omniscient, and therefore, does not know your

future. He is neither omnipresent, to wrestle with you every

moment, so he must use ‘guerrilla’ tactics in the warfare, with

his soldiers (demons) using a ‘hit or miss’ policy. Clear ‘hits’

are seen in the high proportion of people classified as coming

from ‘dysfunctional’ families.

Counselors, both secular and Christian, spend many hours

trying to teach people how to deal with their wounds - their

dysfunction. They hope to bring their patients to a place of

‘maintenance’ where they learn to effectively use the

‘crutches’ the counselors offer them. For example, the goal of

Alcoholics Anonymous is to enable their members to

maintain their sobriety rather than bringing them to healing.

Sadly, many Christian counselors have adopted worldly

methods and tools in dealing with these wounds, seldom

bringing their people to the place of healing that Jesus

obtained on the cross. “With His wounds, we are healed”

(Isaiah 53:5).

Satan’s devices wound many who will never even enter the

army against him, since they will never avail themselves of

the salvation offered to them in Christ. However, when one is

recognized as being in the Body of Christ, then Satan

concentrates his efforts on that person, especially if they

begin to come on the offensive against him.

The Ministry of Reconciliation

Jesus came to defeat Satan’s power in the life of men. In Him,

our new relationship should be manifested in our unity as

believers: as one Body. Satan has no power to destroy this

unity or these relationships, but through ignorance, carnality,

and the unhealthy wounds of our souls, we have given him

strongholds.

What can we do to correct this situation? Of course, we can

pray! After all, without the help and guidance of the Holy

Spirit, we can do nothing! However, we must realize that the

Father will seldom answer prayer in those areas where He has

already given the authority and responsibility to us. The

responsibility for reconciliation between people, is no longer

His, it is ours. “All this is from God, who through Christ

reconciled us to himself and gave us the ministry of

reconciliation; that is, in Christ God was reconciling the

world to himself, not counting their trespasses against them,

and entrusting to us the message of reconciliation” (2

Corinthians 5:18-19).

We need to deal with our offenses, seek to understand our

‘wounds,’ and use Biblical principles to obtain healing,

restoration, and reconciliation. If you are wounded, I trust that

this section of the book will give you some assistance in

bringing you to a place of wholeness in Christ, knowing as

David did, that “He restores the soul” (Psalm 23:3) and that

those, “whom the Son sets free, are free indeed” (John 8:36).

The Offended Sheep

For those who are counselors, elders, or pastors, I would

charge you that this is your ministry. A passage of Scripture

that greatly challenges me as a pastor and counselor is found

in Matthew 18. The entire context of this chapter is dealing

with offense, restoration, reconciliation, and forgiveness.

I am particularly challenged by Matthew’s account of the

parable of the shepherd and the hundred sheep where it is

written, “If a man has a hundred sheep, and one of them has

gone astray, does he not leave the ninety-nine on the

mountains and go in search of the one that went astray? And

if he finds it, truly, I say to you, he rejoices over it more than

over the ninety-nine that never went astray” (Matthew 18:12-

14).

It is a sheep that has left the fold, not a goat. In the New

Testament, believers are usually referred to as “sheep”

whereas the word “goat” is used for non-believers.

This picture is of the believer who has been offended, and has

walked out of the church, possibly with a little poison ready

to spread to whomever will listen. All of us have had this

happen in our congregations and very often we are tempted

to rub our hands together saying, “Good riddance! He was

such a miserable man!” Instead, we are urged to go after that

sheep, seeking to understand him and to minister to him

without condemnation, trusting that the Lord will bring about

a reconciliation and restoration. If we did, maybe we would

have far fewer ‘miserable men’ in our church!

Sometimes the sheep leaves feeling deeply wounded. I

remember a young lady who came to me, deeply hurt because

the leaders of her ‘ministry’ had disciplined her, having

received some bad reports concerning her; however, no one

would tell her what the reports said. I went to see her leaders

and was told by her chief judge that they were “letting her

stew in her own juice to teach her a lesson.” I told that leader,

who considered himself a pastor, that we have no permission

to treat the sheep that way.

“If a sheep is caught in a bramble bush, I must crawl in to set

it free, even though I may get scratched with thorns and

possibly bitten by the hurting sheep. Then I pour in oil and

wine and bind up the wounds, before releasing the sheep with

the admonition not to go into a bramble bush again. If I hear

the bleating again and see the sheep in another bush a little

while later, I repeat the process. This continues with more

admonition and possible use of a leash, but I can never stand

outside the bush, wag my finger and say, ‘Serve you right!

Stew in your own juice!’ The Great Shepherd gave me no

such permission when He called me to serve as an under-

shepherd!”

That young lady was dismissed from that ministry, though I

had clearly shown her leaders that the reports against her were

based on a lie! No wonder she was so badly wounded and

needed lengthy professional counseling!

fields.title: The Key to Release
fields.body_html:
Much of the counseling I do is to help people deal with their

offenses. How many hours would be saved if they knew their

personal responsibility and acted according to Biblical

principles!

I am of the opinion that one of the major ploys used by the

enemy to hinder us in the battle, is the large number of hours

spent by pastors (especially in North America), dealing with

counseling matters that believers could handle themselves if

they were more active in studying the Word.

The role of a pastor should be to do away with most

counseling needs of his people, by teaching them Biblical

principles. It’s his role, as a shepherds, to lead them to ‘green

pastures’ where the sheep feed themselves; however, we have

come to the place where the sheep still need to be bottle fed

(counseled), every time there is a ‘crisis!’ Satan has robbed

the church of many of its shepherds by overloading them with

counseling ‘needs.’

A natural analogy is that, if we eat and exercise properly, we

will stay in good health; however, one recognizes that there

will come times whether through an accident or chronic

sickness, that one needs the assistance of another. When there

are terrible wounds and the patient is handicapped in some

way, the empathy, comfort, and help of another is

appreciated. This is the same with spiritual wounds.

There are many Christian books on the market dealing with

wounds to the soul. They speak of ‘healing the memories’ of

dysfunctional families and codependency. Many of them are

very good and have given a lot of help to people seeking a

new perspective of life and themselves. The ‘12-step’

program by Alcoholics Anonymous has become the basis for

much of this teaching, with the goal of bringing the wounded

person to a place of ‘maintenance.’ They are then able to deal

with their problem in a practical way, with the use of support

groups, ongoing counseling, and prescribed plans or a

‘formula’ of action. Each day, they have a prescription to

‘walk out’ their healing. I have used these books and continue

to do so in part. What bothers me about most of them is that

few of them mention the releasing effect of forgiveness .

I do not believe that the Lord’s intention is to bring His

wounded people to ‘maintenance,’ but that He wishes to

restore their souls, and bring them healing. The main purpose

of this book is to teach how we can be set free from the

bondage of our wounds, so that we can be most effective in

the warfare against our enemy, Satan. The key of healing is

found in forgiveness.

The Keys to the Kingdom → Matthew 16:19

For three years the disciples had walked with the Lord

through the regions of Judea, Samaria, and Galilee. They had

watched Him perform many miracles and had heard Him

teaching the multitudes, but He had seldom sat down just to

talk with them. Now, after a very busy time, He leads them to

the far north of the country, to the regions around Caesarea

Philippi, on the lower slopes of Mount Hermon. As they walk,

the master turns to His disciples and asks them two questions.

The first question is concerning men’s opinions of Jesus,

whereas the next question is concerning the disciples opinion

of Jesus.

After the disciples answer the first question, He again turns

to them, and asks, “But who do you say I am?” (Matthew

16:15). Had they come to understand that Jesus was more

than just a good man or a miracle worker?

“Simon Peter replied, “You are the Christ, the Son of the

living God.” And Jesus answered him, “Blessed are you,

Simon Bar-Jonah! For flesh and blood has not revealed this

to you, but my Father who is in Heaven. And I tell you, you

are Peter, and on this rock I will build my church, and the

gates of hell shall not prevail against it. I will give you the

keys of the kingdom of Heaven, and whatever you bind on

earth shall be bound in Heaven, and whatever you loose on

earth shall be loosed in Heaven” (Matthew 16:16-19).

For centuries, the Roman Catholic Church taught that this is

the mandate given to all popes, as successors of Peter, the

head of the church, to excommunicate kings, countries, and

peoples who do not support their edicts, or grant indulgences.

Wouldn’t it be wonderful if you had the key to the kingdom

for your loved ones? For your spouse? For your unsaved

child? For your parents? If only you could open up the way

to eternal life for them! Well, I believe we have that

possibility!

It is certain that many are being kept away from the joys of

seeing and entering the kingdom by our failure to be the

witnesses we ought to be. Much of that failure is in our

attitudes of unforgiveness. There are many parents today who

pray, with weeping, for their wayward child, not realizing that

the unforgiveness they bear against that child is the greatest

hindrance to God answering the prayer!

What did Jesus mean by the latter part of the verse above? I

have been given many explanations, from the popes

‘authority,’ to ‘deliverance from the demonic,’ but I see

neither here.

It is good exegesis when considering an obscure verse, to look

for parallel verses, particularly from the same author. In this

case, we do not have to go very far, for just two chapters later,

Matthew writes it again.

“Truly, I say to you, whatever you bind on earth shall be

bound in Heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be

loosed in Heaven” (Matthew 18:18).

This time the Lord is speaking to all the disciples, not just to

Peter. If the keys were given to loose and to bind (a common

use of keys!), then they were given to all the disciples -

including you and me!

A second principle of good exegesis is to study the context,

so we will consider what the Lord was teaching in the rest of

Matthew 18. We soon see that the entire chapter is dealing

with restoration, reconciliation, and forgiveness. The small

scenarios speak of being like children, having no guile and

holding no bitterness - such believers do not offend or wound,

and we should be careful not to cause them offense or

wounds.

The second thing I notice is that if one is wounded or hurt,

and as a result, goes away, a good shepherd will leave the

others to restore that ‘sheep’ to the fold. Note again, that the

story is about ‘sheep’ not ‘goats.’ It is about believers, not the

‘lost.’ How often, when a ‘problem person’ leaves the church,

we wipe our hands saying, “good riddance!” God’s demand

of servant shepherds, and the rest of the sheep, is that we seek

their restoration, not their dis-fellowship.

“If a brother sins against you, you are to go to him, privately

at first, with the one purpose of seeking understanding and

reconciliation” (Matthew 18:15). Note the word “sin . ” Too

often we leave when we are offended, which in turn, creates

an even greater offense. We have no such injunction to go to

them when we are offended - only when we are sinned

against. The only exception would be, when the church pastor

or elders feel it necessary to approach someone who they

believe to consistently be a cause of offense, or who has

sinned against others. In that case, the purpose of approaching

them is always for reconciliation.

When Jesus is giving the teaching of Matthew 18:18-20, a

question comes to Peter asking the Lord how many times he

should forgive. “Up to seven times?” (Matthew 18:22). Peter

probably thought his question was going to be good, but the

Lord used it to emphasize that forgiveness is to be unlimited.

Love demands that we always forgive.

The entire context of chapter 18 is to do with restoration,

reconciliation, and forgiveness, all without causing offense

yourself… the theme of this book!

John 20:23

This verse is another parallel verse to the two above, though

it is written by John in John 20:23.

In this verse, the disciples are all in a locked room because

they are afraid that the Jewish leaders would soon come to

take them, just as they had taken their Lord. Their emotions

are running high, and some there claimed that they had seen

the Lord, risen from the dead! The story was going around

that Jesus had appeared to Peter and Mary Magdalene as well

as two others on the Emmaus Road. Others would not believe

unless they also saw the risen Lord.

Suddenly, even though the doors were locked, Jesus stood in

their midst! He said, “Peace be with you! As the Father has

sent Me, I also send you… receive the Holy Spirit” (John

20:21-22).

The Greek tense of “receive,” is the aorist imperative which

always demands an immediate response. At that moment, the

disciples received their new life in the Spirit. Then later, on

the day of Pentecost, they would receive His fullness to

empower them for service. They had been given a new

authority! “If you forgive the sins of any, they are forgiven

them; if you withhold forgiveness from any, it is withheld”

(John 20:23). Allow me to paraphrase, “Those you loose (set

free) are loosed; those you bind, are bound.”

“Who can forgive sins but God alone?” (Mark 2:7) asked the

Pharisees. In a sense, they were correct because the Lord’s

mandate to us does not ‘forgive’ sins to the same measure as

His forgiveness. When He forgives it is “as far as the east is

from the west to the depths of the sea, never to be

remembered anymore” (Psalm 103: 12) . You and I cannot do

that - for our own sins, let alone anyone else’s. The only sins

we can ‘forgive’ are those committed against ourselves - sins

that have likely caused the soul-wounds we bear, by which

Satan has hindered us.

Removing the Barrier of Sin

Should I sin against you, I also sin against God. Immediately,

a barrier comes between me and my Lord. I find it more

difficult to pray, the Word loses its interest, and fellowship is

not so sweet -my sin has become a cloud above my head!

There are two ways in which that ‘cloud’ can be removed.

First, is to “confess my sin, [because] He is faithful and just

to forgive me my sin and to cleanse me from all

unrighteousness!” (1 John 1:9). Hallelujah! I have found that

promise to be true.

However, I have also discovered that the Lord has this little

‘habit’ of talking to me about the sin. Having forgiven me, He

then whispers to my soul, “Now, go to your brother and for

him to forgive you. I don’t just desire to cleanse you from the

sin, but I want to see you reconciled.” His priority is not

forgiveness - it is reconciliation! The confession is not

complete unless it brings about reconciliation. That is not His

responsibility - it is mine, for “Christ reconciled us to himself

and gave us the ministry of reconciliation” (2 Corinthians 5:

18-19).

The second way that my ‘cloud’ can be removed, so that

Heaven is once more opened to me, is if you remove it by

your forgiveness. The King James Version of the Bible uses

a special word in its translation of John 20:23, which writes,

“Whosoever’s sins you remit…” The word “remit” speaks of

‘setting aside.’ You can remit my sin, which was committed

against you, and in doing so, open Heaven up to me. As you

‘set aside’ my sin, you move the ‘cloud’ away, and the way

is open for the Father to speak to me just as when I sought His

forgiveness for myself. He again will move upon my heart, in

order to bring about our reconciliation!

You might choose to forgive me because you know the

Scripture demands that, but it is essential if we are to be

reconciled, that you also loose me from God’s judgment upon

me by seeking to set aside the ‘cloud’ of sin above me.

I always speak of “forgiveness and release” - they must be

preached together! A good example would be Stephen, the

first martyr. He had just been appointed as a leader in the

early church when the Jewish leaders took him and stoned

him to death. Saul of Tarsus stood by, in hearty agreement

with their actions, for he had a great hatred for these followers

of Jesus.

As Stephen died, he cried out in a loud voice, “Lord, do not

lay this sin to their charge!” (Acts 7: 60) . He did not pray on

behalf of himself for courage, strength, or even to be released,

but rather, he released them of their guilt.

I wonder, would Saul have ever become the great apostle

Paul, if Stephen had not prayed that prayer? It is my

conviction that he ‘opened Heaven’ for Saul! Jesus also

prayed a similar prayer where He cried out, “Father, forgive

them for they do not know what they do” (Luke 23:34) as He

died for you and me.

One wonderful result of releasing others is that we are also

released! It’s like having a horse on the end of a rope - we

might say that the horse is bound as it runs around us in the

paddock; however, should the horse decide to gallop off

across the muddy field, we are going to get dragged along

through the mud unless we let go of the rope!

That knot you feel in your stomach after someone has sinned

against you, is just like that rope. You are emotionally bound

to those who hurt you . That pain is part of the wound they

caused. Though you have forgiven them, the knot is there

whenever you meet them or hear someone talk about them.

You, and they, need to be released!

Jesus in the Midst

It is sad how often Matthew 18:18-20 is quoted out of

context! These verses are referring to forgiveness, release,

and reconciliation, not God’s presence when multiple people

come together! The promises of Jesus given there, are for

those who actively seek to be reconciled.

“Again I say to you, if two of you agree on earth about

anything they ask, it will be done for them by my Father in

Heaven. For where two or three are gathered in my name,

there am I among them” (Matthew 18:19-10). The emphasis

here is not His presence, for He is always with each of us who

are believers, but instead His blessing for reconciliation - His

priority!

We have been given a key that will open Heaven for others

and that will set us free from the wounds, the bondages they

have caused in our soul! Let us learn how to use that key!

fields.title: Heaven is Opened
fields.body_html:
I have seen several miracles in my time - including a number

of physical healings. I was present when a 12 year old deaf-

mute girl received hearing and could talk for the first time. I

saw a woman, crippled from birth, walk after prayer. I have

seen a large goiter disappear from a woman’s neck as she was

being prayed for.

However, as much as these miracles thrilled and encouraged

me, they were no more spectacular than the miracles of soul-

healing I have witnessed in recent years as wounded believers

have used the “key to the kingdom of heaven” to release those

who have wounded them, and to release themselves.

The following stories are based on true experiences with the

exception of altered names and locations to maintain

confidentiality; however, I have not exaggerated the outcome

in any way, and have tried to be faithful in reporting the

miraculous work of the Lord.

Marie

I first met Marie when she was 28. Her counselors were trying

to place her under psychiatric care, and she was deeply

depressed and withdrawn. She told me of her sad childhood,

having been brought up in a strict Jehovah’s Witness home in

Canada where they never celebrated any birthdays or

Christmas. There were no memories of affection from either

parent, and she had never heard her father tell her that he

loved her, nor had she ever felt his embrace or received his

kisses.

At the age of 16, Marie ran away from home. Several years

later, she heard the wonderful news of the Gospel and

immediately yielded her life to Christ, desiring to serve Him.

A small local church nurtured her in those early years as she

wrestled with her identity and emotions. On one occasion an

attempt was made to be reconciled with her family, but the

experience was very painful since arguments arose about

their differing understandings of Scripture. The parting was

acrimonious, and Marie decided that she would never see her

parents again. “I hate them,” she told me at our first meeting.

Over the next months, I spent many hours with Marie. She

looked to me as her father, and I saw in her the little girl who

had never grown up. Many of her actions were those of the

adolescent, though she was well educated and even bilingual.

She was a hard worker and very competent at her designated

task, but her emotions and attitudes were those of an insecure

teenager. We talked about many things, but whenever her

parents were mentioned, a barrier grew between us.

Finally, I was able to explain that God had created her as a

‘heart-shaped’ vessel, designed to receive love from her mum

and dad. Such love is demonstrated, not so much in the giving

of sweets and presents, but in nurturing security, self-worth,

identity, comfort, and acceptance by encouraging ambitions

and goals, and so much more - things that she never received.

Marie was eager to agree that her parents had sinned against

her in failing to pour this love into her, but it was much harder

to explain to her that her parents were no different to the great

majority of us. They are walking in darkness, bearing their

own wounds - their own dysfunction - as victims of Satan’s

attacks. They had no desire to hurt Marie and were probably

ignorant of the wounds she was carrying.

“I want you to write a letter to your parents,” I said. “Don’t

worry! You won’t have to send it, but I do want you to think

about what you’d say in such a letter. Tell them specifically,

just how they have hurt you, with examples. Also tell them

how much you long for their love.”

This is a practice I often use in my counseling since it enables

the patient to bring the subconscious to the conscious surface.

The letter will not be sent, but it enables them to have

something concrete on which to concentrate. It took Marie

three tear-filled weeks to complete the letter. As we prayed

for the Lord to direct her thinking, she was amazed at the

memories He brought back to her.

When the letter was finished, I was invited to read it. This is

not essential for the counselor, and I make it quite clear to all

I counsel that they do not have to show me what they have

written. There was obviously a great deal of pain in this letter,

and my heart ached for this lost, little girl hidden inside a

woman’s body.

I folded the paper and returned it to its envelope. “Marie, will

you choose now to forgive your parents and to release them?”

I asked. “I cannot!” she cried through her tears. I told her I

could do no more, the remedy for her hurts was now in her

hands, the “key to the kingdom” was hers should she choose

to use it.

Three more weeks passed before Marie knelt in my office,

and with much weeping, told the Lord that she was forgiving

her parents and wanted Him “not to lay their sin to their

charge.” She then promised me that she would pray a blessing

upon her parents each day.

A few weeks later, as I saw Marie grow in confidence, I told

her that I wanted her to go home to visit her parents for a few

days. She protested strongly, but finally agreed to write to see

if they would receive her.

It was two weeks later that she rushed into my office, full of

excitement. She had received an envelope containing two

letters, a brief one from mum saying that she was welcome,

and a longer one from dad. The latter was quite clinical and

cold, telling her that they had changed homes and that, should

she come, it would now be a long journey. She would need to

catch an early train in Toronto, change at Montreal, and

would then arrive at their home quite late at night. He wasn’t

sure if he would see her since he had so much work to do;

however, what excited Marie the most was that he ended his

letter with, “Hugs and kisses, Dad!”

As I saw Marie onto the train at Toronto, I told her I would

be praying for her and encouraged her not to get into any

religious arguments. “Before you leave” I said, “make sure

you ask your dad for those ‘hugs and kisses.’” She doubted

that she would have the courage, but I assured her of my

prayers toward that end.

Late that evening I received a telephone call. “Gareth, it’s me,

Marie.” She sounded so excited and could hardly contain

herself as she told me what had happened. As she was

changing platforms in Montreal, she suddenly noticed her

mother and father standing there! They had journeyed some

distance to meet her. Marie was walking toward them when

suddenly, her father stepped forward, threw his arms around

her and kissed her! O how the angels of Heaven must have

rejoiced!

But what had happened? I believe that Marie had opened

heaven for her father by her prayer of release. That morning,

her Heavenly father had spoken down through that ‘opened

door’ to her earthly father, prompting him to take a day off

work and take his wife on a trip to meet their daughter. Then,

He had moved upon his heart, causing him to reach out in

love to kiss Marie for the very first time. Of course, dad was

unaware that his plans and actions were being directed by

God.

After two years, Marie had grown into a wholesome,

beautiful young lady. She fully reconciled to her family and

even moved to their city. She became active in her

evangelical church and was even appointed a deaconess. It

didn’t take long for Marie to find a husband in the church with

the plan to serve the Lord as missionaries. God is so good!

Angela

“What’s wrong with me, Gareth?” Angela cried, when she

had settled into my office chair. “I wake up each morning so

full of fear that I will be making a mistake if I marry John.”

She went on to explain that each morning she was determined

to finish the relationship, but, as the day progressed, she knew

that she could not, since John was a fine young man whom

any girl would be proud to marry. He was a committed

Christian and he treated her with courtesy and love. Their

interests were similar and both had a desire to serve the Lord

in missionary work.

Angela knew that the problem was hers since this was not the

first relationship in which she had felt such fear. Twice, she

had ended good relationships and then cried for weeks

afterwards wondering why she had been ‘so foolish.’

In our counseling, she told me of a father who was an elder in

a healthy evangelical church. She respected him greatly, but

felt she could never satisfy him. He had made it known that,

for his first child, he had wanted a boy instead of a girl. As

she grew up, Angela would play cricket with her father and

her younger brothers. She was good, but never quite as good

as her brothers were so she never received the plaudits that

they did. When she received an A grade at school, she was

asked why it wasn’t an A+. When she took her first job in a

bank, she was told that she should have applied to another,

better, bank. She had never heard her father’s commendation

or affirmation though she had tried so hard to please him.

I suggested to her that her dad had failed to give her identity

and worth, that her self-confidence was low because she

constantly saw herself as unable to satisfy the men in her life.

Satan was using the wounds produced by her father’s lack of

acceptance of her, to hinder her in developing a Godly

relationship with John. Angela saw the pattern and

understood how she could break the bondage by healing the

wounds through release of her father. We prayed together as

she asked the Lord “not to lay this sin to my father’s charge.”

Some weeks later, Angela developed some kidney stones.

She left the area where we were working together to return to

her home state, where she would enter a hospital for surgery.

Two months later, when I met her for the first time since the

operation, she ran up to me, threw her arms around me, and

with great excitement, told me an amazing story.

When she had arrived home, her father announced that he was

taking five weeks off work so that he could spend it with his

daughter! He took her out to meals and to visit local places of

interest. They talked together and discovered so many things

about one another that neither had known before. There were

many visits to the places where her father worked, and at

each, she was embarrassed because he would boast about his

daughter and the wonderful things she was doing. He was so

proud of her!

“Gareth,” she said, “I’ve fallen in love with my father!” Then

she added, “and I could hardly wait to get back to see John.”

John and Angela happily got married and together, served the

Lord with joy.

What had prompted her dad to take five weeks off work to

spend with his daughter? Could it have been the Lord

speaking to him through the door opened by Angela’s prayer

of release? I certainly believe so.

Tony

It took quite an effort for Tony to pluck up courage to visit

me. He did not relate very well to any man, having been

brought up by his mother after an angry divorce.

Since leaving school, there had been a succession of jobs, but

he had failed to keep any of them. I listened as he gave me his

excuses and soon saw a pattern that it was always “my

supervisor’s fault.”

We talked together about his childhood, loneliness, and

dislike of school. It soon emerged that he had a great fear of

one of his teachers. He had not been a brilliant student and

this particular teacher had been quite cruel in some of the

things he had done and said. His teacher seemed to delight in

making his students uncomfortable in class and would

embarrass the more sensitive ones by mocking them in front

of the class. Tony was often the target of his barbs.

Then there were the threats. Hardly a week went by without

Tony being threatened with a trip to see the headmaster

because his work was not “up to standard.” Even though he

worked harder, he could never satisfy this teacher, and was

often given extra work to do. He was so glad when he was old

enough to leave school and to start earning money; however,

it soon became evident that wounds remained since Tony was

unable to relate to any dominant man in a position of

authority. Whenever he was given an unpleasant task to do,

he took it as punishment meted out by a supervisor who must

have disliked him. He could not see that it was a task normally

expected of any young employee of that company.

I explained how we often get wounded by the actions or

words of others and how those wounds hinder us in walking

out a life in the freedom Jesus bought for us on the cross.

Tony understood how his teacher had been used by Satan to

wound his soul. Together we prayed as he chose to forgive

and to ask the Lord to forgive that teacher. He committed

himself to prayer for his family, and in particular, for his sons

who were quite rebellious which had been causing much

heartache to their parents.

Soon another work opportunity was opened, and Tony

applied. He was given the job and started within a few days.

A year later he was promoted to foreman because he had

developed such a good relationship with his colleagues. Also,

as the company owner declared, “You can give him any task

to do and you know it will be done well. He’s a man I can

trust!” God had done a good work.

fields.title: Jesus - The Healer
fields.body_html:
Generational Sins

Through my years of counseling, I have learned that wounds

hindering my patients in their walk with the Lord, often go

back to causes many years earlier. Sometimes, there is

evidence of a line of similar wounds through several previous

generations. It is a Biblical truth that, “the sins of the father

may come upon the children to the third and fourth

generation” (Exodus 20:5) .

Further, there was a barrier to the children of illegitimacy

coming into full fellowship with the congregation of the Lord

“even to the tenth generation” (Deuteronomy 23:2)! These

are Old Testament judgements showing how sin can affect,

not just the sinner, but many of his descendants. Thankfully,

Jesus came to remove the curse of sin and to set us free from

its effects, therefore, we do not have to continue in bondage

to the wounds of our parents’ sin.

The Lord wants us to walk free, but how can we release those

who caused the wounds if they have already died? If we

cannot release them, can we be released ourselves? These are

the types of questions I am often asked as the counselees

recognize the wounds of the past and the patterns of the

present. We do not believe that praying for the dead will

change in any way, their standing before God, the Great

Judge, therefore, we unfortunately cannot open the kingdom

of heaven for them.

Even though we cannot use the key to the kingdom that has

been given to us, the Lord still will set us free by the healing

He purchased on Calvary, because it was “by His wounds we

are healed” (Isaiah 53:5).

Hidden Memories

Whenever I counsel someone, we always start by asking the

Holy Spirit to direct our thoughts. We want Him to reveal to

us the areas of the soul where wounds may be found.

It constantly amazes me (though it shouldn’t) how often

memories of long-forgotten events come flooding back! On

one occasion, I was counseling a middle-aged lady who was

having some relational problems. She started to quietly sob

for no apparent reason.

My assistant, Debbie, moved over and put her arms around

her, at which the counselee began to weep uncontrollably.

Debbie took her onto her lap and hugged her as a mother

would a small child. After a few moments of deeply

emotional tears, the patient began to beat upon Debbie with

her fists, crying out “Why did you do it? Why did you do it?”

As she calmed down, she told us that she had thought she was

beating her mother for throwing out her favorite rag doll when

she was just four years old! The little girl had carried that

wound for over 40 years even though she had not remembered

it! It had been buried in the subconscious.

Many times patients have returned to tell me of a sudden

recall of memory of some traumatic event of the past. I do not

automatically assume that these recalls are all accurate. There

is a great danger today because many people want to blame

others for imagined sins of the past, and they want to excuse

themselves from blame for present weaknesses and attitudes.

That is not my purpose in writing this book. I want to see

people take responsibility for their own actions, to exercise

the key to the kingdom of Heaven, to set themselves free, and

to release those who may have wounded them. Both are

victims of Satan - both need to be set free. Recrimination

never produces freedom, only forgiveness does!

The Same Yesterday, Today and Forever

As the Holy Spirit reveals wounds, we must take time to

present that wound before the Lord, for His touch of healing.

He is the “alpha and omega, the beginning and the end”

(Revelation 1:8). He is “the same yesterday, today and

forever” (Hebrews 13:8) . He knows your wound - He was

there when it happened - and He wept for you. As we present

the wound to Him, with forgiveness for the one who caused

it, He begins to heal and to restore the soul. Even though we

cannot release the one who wounded us, the Lord is faithful

to heal and to release us.

The Letter

When the patient and I have talked, and they have recognized

the hurts, wounds, and patterns, I invite them to write a letter

to the person who wounded them outlining the perceived

wound and the pain it caused. I encourage them to express

their feelings and longings.

“If only you understood how much you hurt me when you…

Oh how much I longed to hear you tell me you loved me!”

The letter can be very detailed because it will not be sent. Its

purpose is to bring to the surface all the subconscious feelings

and pain. When the time for forgiveness and release (if

possible) comes, this letter becomes the ‘contract’ of

forgiveness. “Are you willing to forgive for all that you have

written down here?” I ask them. Then when I am confident

that they have fully understood what I have taught, and that

they have truly forgiven (and released) the offender, I invite

them to destroy the letter making note of the location and date

of their action. They are then encouraged to pray blessings

upon their offender, if they are still alive.

In order to complete their release, I have known of people

who took the letter to a local cemetery, where they have

sprinkled its ashes and placed flowers upon the grave of the

departed. For some, this has been the first time they have truly

mourned over the death of a family member, even a parent,

and have known the healing touch that follows true mourning.

Our conscious act of forgiveness breaks the power of Satan.

As the Lord does His work of healing in our lives, we learn

to walk in the power of His Spirit.

As we take upon ourselves the whole armor of God, the

enemy finds that we have no area of weakness in our lives by

which he can hinder us in the battle.

Of course, forgiveness is not a one-time event or even a

seven-time commitment. As Jesus taught Peter, it is a

“seventy-times-seven” (Matthew 18:22) requirement. In

other words, we are to have a continuous forgiving attitude.

We must always be quick to be reconciled with those whose

actions or words may cause a division between us. One must

recognize that there could very well be a need to ‘cool-off,’

but there can be no excuse for ongoing animosity.

May we become so committed to exercising the key in our

hands that we will be known as ‘peacemakers,’ those who are

known as the children of God (Matthew 5:9).

fields.title: Walking Out Your Healing
fields.body_html:
In many ways, this is the most difficult chapter to write. I have

taught the principles outlined in the earlier chapters, to many

different groups of people. There have been youth groups and

seniors, to liturgical congregations and non-conformist, to

Bible colleges and home groups. In almost all of them, there

has been an emotional response, with many weeping people

coming to me seeking counsel.

I am saddened that I am usually just passing through, and am

unable to commit myself to the long process of walking out

the healing so many of them require. I am aware that I have

often ‘opened a wound’ - a memory long suppressed - that

now needs healing.

Sometimes their response is quite unexpected. I remember

one Episcopalian congregation made up of mature adults,

who broke into applause as the pastor and I embraced as we

acted out the reconciliation that follows release. They were

very conscious of their need to forgive and release a former

pastor of that church, and excitement at their new

understanding of how they could be relieved of the pain they

bore, caused them to break out into spontaneous applause. We

immediately lifted that applause as a praise offering to the

Lord.

I hope that this book will awaken many pastors and

counselors to the tremendous responsibility we have to bring

reconciliation and healing to the broken relationships and

wounded souls that are so prevalent in our churches. I further

hope that many believers will learn how to operate the keys

that open the kingdom of Heaven for their loved ones, and

bring release to themselves from the wounds that they have

carried for too long.

It’s about time Satan was put in his place and the people of

God were able to walk in wholeness and power, rather than

limping along as so many do!

For those who may have recognized themselves as wounded

as they have read this book, I am closing with some guidelines

that will enable them to ‘walk out’ their own healing. If it is

possible to find a good counselor who will walk through this

with you, such a companion would be of utmost value. I

would encourage you to urge them to become familiar with

this book before you start.

Ask the Lord to Direct Your Thoughts

Be assured that the Lord wants to heal your soul wounds. He

is aware of them, but has given you the key to being healed,

and wants you to use it! He will not answer prayer in the areas

of our lives where He has already won the victory on the

cross, and where He has given the authority or mandate to us.

Take Your Time

Healing rarely comes quickly. Most of the stories I can tell

relate to many months of counseling. It takes time to walk

again after a bad wound.

Just as physiotherapy is essential if we are to walk again after

a bad accident-causing leg injuries, so spiritual therapy is

essential to walk out our healing after long-standing soul-

wounds.

Talk About Your Past

I usually encourage the counselee to break their past down

into short time periods. For example, preschool, junior

school, teenage years, young adult, etc. I prompt them with

questions about their home, school, friends, things they love,

and things they hate, meanwhile assessing for patterns of

attitudes or hurts. “How did the little child inside you feel?”

Ask the Lord to touch each wound as it is revealed.

Write Down Anything You Feel Is Relevant

I always have a pen and paper handy to note any patterns that

may be emerging or any thoughts that strike me. During the

days when no counselor or friend is with you, you will

become surprised as memories come of things long forgotten,

but why should you be surprised when you have already

asked the Lord to be actively involved in your healing

process? Make a note of these memories.

Recognize if You Have Been Wounded by Another’s Sin

Do not blame another if the sin is your own. If you have taken

offense, you must deal with it as described in chapter nine.

Do not go into denial if the one who has wronged you is

someone you love, and certainly do not make excuses for

them. God sees they as a sinner, just like you and me - and

sinner’s sin! There’s no need to beat around the bush - just

call it as it is - sin! He may be a redeemed sinner, but he is

still capable of wounding you.

Most often, the wounds were created unintentionally, but they

are real wounds, and if the offender were not a sinner, they

would not have been so injurious to you.

As I came to understand this principle, I saw how I had

probably wounded my own daughter through ignorance.

Anne was in hospital for a few weeks before the birth of our

first daughter, Corinne, so when she began labor, I was at

home, unaware of what was happening. Two friends were the

first to tell me of her labor since they had called the hospital

just before departing on vacation. The nursing staff told them

that the baby was born, but would not be specific about the

birth details, especially the sex of the child - the father would

be the first to be so informed. They urged me to phone the

hospital so that they could know the details before beginning

their vacation. I told them that I would do so after finishing

the Agatha Christie novel I was reading! Of course, I was

joking, just to keep them in suspense, and we quickly went

together to the public call-box to hear the exciting news that

I was now the father of a lovely baby girl.

However, that story was repeated many times to visiting

friends over the years, and sometimes, in the presence of my

daughter. I never thought about how she was hearing the story

- that daddy didn’t really care when she was born. Perhaps he

did not want her?

Just two years after first publishing this book, I wrote to

Corinne asking her forgiveness for the wounds caused by my

thoughtlessness.

Write a Letter, Being Specific About Your Hurts

You do not have to show this letter to anyone, though you

may choose to confide in your counselor. However, this

should only be if they can be trusted with confidentiality, and

you know that he will not allow your information to affect his

attitude toward you or the one who wounded you. Try to be

comprehensive and objective in the letter, writing down how

you felt when wounded: rejected, belittled, embarrassed, etc.

Try to also add any positive things you can say.

Being objective may be very difficult as this letter can raise

strong emotions and pain. Its purpose is to enable you to bring

emotions you have suppressed for years to the surface.

Bandages that have become bondages have to come off! Take

your time!

Choose to Forgive

Recognize that the one who wounded you is a sinner walking

in darkness. They are blind to what they have done to your

soul. Your real adversary is Satan whose army has targeted

you from birth, and your offender is but an agent, ignorant of

Satan’s devices. Get angry at Satan, and forgive the blind

man. Make sure you are prepared to forgive for every item

mentioned in the letter you wrote.

Do not expect the Lord to heal where you are not prepared to

forgive.

Choose to Release

Why not use the prayer of St. Stephen? “Father, do not lay

these sins to their charge! Today, I choose to release them

from all guilt.”

After praying that prayer, I suggest you make a note of the

date, recording it in your memory just as you would a

birthday.

Burn the Letter!

The matter has been dealt with - why keep it hanging around?

This should be recorded in your memory only as the day on

which you started to walk out your healing - a day for

celebrating!

Pray for the One Who Wounded You

Commit yourself to pray each day for God to bless the one

who wounded you. Are his children far from the Lord? Pray

for them. Is his business in difficulty? Pray for its success. As

you continue to pray in this way, God will work through the

channel between Himself and them - a channel that you

opened by your forgiveness and release. In doing this, you

will be delivering yourself from slavery to the emotional

bondage of your wounds and becoming the servant Jesus

called you to be.

If one wrongs you by taking your shirt, he makes you his
