me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself to him.” (John 14:21) This verse tells us that if we love the Lord we will keep His commandments. Who can say today that he has kept all the commandments God has given them? Putting aside those which you do not know, have you kept all the commandments which you know? The phrase “Whoever has my commandments” means he must find out what those commandments are. Many believers are afraid of God’s commandments. Many appear to have their ears closed out from hearing. We should know, that besides keeping the commandments we know are from God, we must seek out those other commandments of His and keep them too. Seeking out God’s commandments is minding the things of God which in turn is the true expression of loving God.

(b) “And he who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him and manifest myself

to him” (John 4:21b). This shows us the benefit we receive by loving God. I have met many renowned persons in Christianity, but I am afraid only a relatively few of them really know God. Many people know how to study the Bible, but they do not know God. They may know the Scriptures, yet they do not know the power of God. Some of them even preach what they do not understand. Why is this so? It is because the Lord has not been revealed to them, which means they have not loved the Lord and kept His commandments. There is only one class of people in the world who truly love the Lord, and they are the faithful, obedient ones.

If you want to find people who truly know the Lord, don't look in famous places. Often, you'll find them in quiet spots or small homes, serving God. When you meet them, you witness God’s presence. These are the people whom I admire the moment I see them. However, several others have zeal, ability, and good deeds, yet they don’t have the presence of God with them. I was asked what I considered to be the overriding characteristic of a certain missionary. I replied that each time I saw her, I sensed the presence of God. Such is the revelation of God. Do you remember the great woman in Shunem and how she told her husband about Elisha? “And she said to her husband,

“Behold now, I know that this is a holy man of God who is continually passing our way.” (2 Kings 4:9) What did Elisha do that left this woman with such an impression? He had not performed any miracle yet; each time he passed by her house, the woman had a sense of God. Let me ask, do we love the manifestation of God? If we really do, then let us seek out the commandments of God and keep them.

(c) “Jesus answered him, 'If anyone loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love

him, and we will come to him and make our home with him.” (John 14:23) God and Christ will be with those who believe, but God and Christ will abide in those who love. He won't just be present, but dwell in us. Sometimes we may not sense His presence, yet we have the Lord dwelling fully in us if we faithfully seek the commandments of God. “As the Father has loved me, so have I loved you. Abide in my love.

If you keep my commandments, you will abide in my love, just as I have kept my Father’s commandments and abide in his love” (John 15:9-10) what does it mean by abiding in the Lord’s love? When we were first saved, we truly felt how much the Lord loved us. Yet now, we sense nothing. Though we may still say that the love of the Lord is deep, we do not feel anything. If we abide in the Lord’s love, we shall always sense His love. To abide in His love is to give chance to the Lord. In other words, we are surrounded by His love. When we are opposed and rejected by people, we know how deeply the Lord loves us. (d) We stick to seeking out the commandments of God and keeping them, so we abide in His

love. Was there any moment on earth when our Lord did not sense the love of the Father? He lived continually in His Father’s love. This is because He always kept the commandments of God. In order to abide in the love of the Lord, we must always keep His commandments. With God’s love in us, even the most difficult commandment we can keep.

4. “And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose.” (Romans 8:28) Many are quite familiar with this verse. Yet only one class of people will benefit from it, and they are those who love God. If anyone does not love God, nothing will work for him for good. For God does not change the “all things,” He changes our hearts instead. Though all things remain the same, we will be benefited only if we love God. How easy it is for us to blame this or that for what happens to us. Yet if we love God we will not mind it when under unsatisfactory circumstances because we know that all things will work together for good to those who love God.

5. “But, as it is written, “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love him” These things God has revealed to us through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God.” (1 Corinthians 2:9-10) What do we learn from these two verses? That what God has prepared for those who believe in Him is eternal life, but that what things He has prepared specifically for those who love Him is yet in the future. Such future blessing is known only to those who love God.

This is far better than any good thing men have ever seen because it is something which no eye has seen before. This is more excellent than anything men have heard of or even thought of, because it is something which has never entered into the heart of man. Yet now it is revealed to us by the Holy Spirit. In other words, one who loves the Lord may enjoy even in this lifetime the good things which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, and heart has not thought of. When God reveals His glory to you, you will exclaim, how delightful this is! Heavenly glory is so abundant that you feel as though you cannot bear it any more.

6. “Blessed is the man who remains steadfast under trial, for when he has stood the test he will receive the crown of life, which God has promised to those who love him.” (James 1:12) Often when we think of the crown of life, we contemplate how much work we have to do. Yet here we are told that there is but one condition for gaining the crown of life which is, to love the Lord.

How we lack love towards our God! It seems as if we have lost our first love! How truly sad.

7. “Jesus said to Simon Peter, “Simon, son of John, do you love me more than these?” He said to him, “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.” He said to him, “Feed my lambs.” (John 21:15) The Lord had asked Peter, “Do you love Me? Feed My lambs.” If anyone really loves the Lord, he will be concerned about souls. It is impossible to love the Lord and be totally uninterested in people’s souls. You cannot help but love the souls of those who are near to you.

8. “If you loved me, you would have rejoiced, because I go unto the Father: for the Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). In loving the Lord, we not only love the brethren and keep God’s commandments but also rejoice over the fact that our Lord Jesus has gone to the Father. In other words, we are glad that our Lord Jesus has gone to the Father and has received the glory. Is this too deep for us to understand? Many do not understand what glory was bestowed on the Lord as He ascended back to the Father who is greater than He. Lack of understanding this glory hinders people from worshiping God. Without a doubt we greatly desire to see those whom we love receive glory. And so, those who love Jesus will rejoice over the return of our Lord back to the Father.

9. “Whoever loves father or mother more than me is not worthy of me, and whoever loves son or daughter more than me is not worthy of me. And whoever does not take his cross and follow me is not worthy of me.” (Matthew 10:37:38) From these two verses we realize that unless we forsake all we cannot love the Lord more. For the sake of loving the Lord people will forsake their parents, wives, children, positions and fame. They can forsake all because they have the love of God. A believer once commented that during worship we ought to sense the loveliness of God as well as the majesty of God. This is indeed well spoken. We draw near to God because of His loveliness.

How does God love us? There are many passages in the Scriptures which tell us of the Lord’s love towards us. Such as, personally: “I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me. And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me.” (Galatians 2:20) or, corporately: “Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her,” (Ephesians 5:25). In (Romans 5:8) we read: “but God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” In (1 John 4:10) it declares: “In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.”

Where can we find love apart from the cross? And why does the Lord command us to break the bread often? It is because He does not want us to drift away from Him. We seem so likely to forget, so He draws us back. How can we fail to love Him as we remember how miserable we were as sinners and how great His grace was in saving us! The children of Israel recalled in the wilderness the cucumbers and the leeks and the garlic of Egypt, but they forgot how they had suffered as slaves under the oppression of Pharaoh as well as how the Lord had delivered them out of their great afflictions. It appears like their hearts still lingered back in Egypt. If we forget the cross, we will also forget the love of God. If we forget the love of God, we will undoubtedly be drown back to the world.

How can we love the Lord? “Therefore I tell you, her sins, which are many, are forgiven—for she loved much. But he who is forgiven little, loves little.” (Luke 7:47) If we remember how our sins were forgiven, we cannot help but love the Lord. The day the cross ever fails to move us, that very day we are fallen. Evan Roberts wept greatly when he realized that he was not moved by the cross; and this went on for several months until God moved him again but then there followed the great Welsh Revival, the greatest spiritual renewal the world has ever seen. How did it come to be that the woman washed the Lord's feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, and kissed them with her lips? It was because she remembered how all her sins had been forgiven.

Let us continually stand at the foot of the cross. And even if later we should become spiritually stronger a hundred times more than what we are today, let us always remember how our sins were forgiven by the Lord. “If anyone has no love for the Lord, let him be accursed. Our Lord, come!” (1 Corinthians 16:22) How serious this word is! Truly, anyone who does not love the Lord is to be cursed. “Grace be with all who love our Lord Jesus Christ with love incorruptible.” (Ephesians 6:24). To whom will God give grace? To all those who love the Lord with a true heart. If anyone asks you if you believe in the Lord, your answer, 'I love the Lord,' will amaze the whole world.

“Though you have not seen him, you love him. Though you do not now see him, you believe in him and rejoice with joy that is inexpressible and filled with glory” (I Peter 1:8) Here we are told that we love Him because we have believed in Him. What comes out of such love as a result of faith? There is an unspeakable joy and glory. In closing I would like to quote the last words of an elderly man to a young man: May you always be a passionate lover of the Lord Jesus!

fields.title: Chapter 9
fields.body_html:
Mary Magdalene

Mary Magdalene should be our perfect inspiration as we seek God because she sought our Lord

Jesus Christ until she got a personal revelation of Him. There were a lot going obstacles that she

could have just given up but she kept searching everywhere and this is the kind of heart we all

need if we are to encounter the Lord.

ow on the first day of the week, Mary Magdalene came to the tomb early, while it was still dark, and saw that the stone had been taken away from the tomb. So she ran and went to Simon Peter and the other disciple, the one whom Jesus loved, and said to them, “They have taken the Lord out of the tomb, and we do not know where they have laid him.” So Peter went out with the other disciples, and they were going toward the tomb. Both of them were running together, but the other disciple outran Peter and reached the tomb first. And stooping to look in, he saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not go in. Then Simon Peter came, following him, and went into the tomb. He saw the linen cloths lying there, and the face cloth, which had been on Jesus’s head, not lying with the linen cloths but folded up in a place by itself. Then the other disciple, who had reached the tomb first, also went in, and he saw and believed; for as yet they did not understand the Scripture, that he must rise from the dead. Then the disciples went back to their homes. (John 20:1-10)

Jesus Appears to Mary Magdalene

But Mary stood weeping outside the tomb, and as she wept she stooped to look into the tomb. She saw two angels in white, sitting where the body of Jesus had lain, one at the head and one at the feet. They said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them, “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.” Having said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus. Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.” Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to him in Aramaic, “Rabboni!” Which means Teacher. (John 20:11-16)

N

Jesus said to her, “Do not cling to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father; but go to my brothers and say to them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.’’ Mary Magdalene went and announced to the disciples, “I have seen the Lord,”—and that he had said these things to her. (John 20:17-18)

After He had been raised from the dead, the Lord Jesus appeared to many people, but to whom did He appear first? To Mary Magdalene. The Lord was anxious to appear to Peter, for he was in great weakness. He was more anxious, however, to appear to Mary Magdalene. He was eager to appear to the two disciples on their way to Emmaus because they had gone the wrong way. Yet he was more eager to appear to Mary Magdalene. He was keen to appear to John, for John was the one whom He loved; but He was keener still to appear to Mary Magdalene. He also was desirous to appear to Thomas due to his unbelief; He was even more desirous to appear to Mary Magdalene. The Lord did, in fact, appear to many other disciples; nonetheless, He appeared to Mary Magdalene first. Why did He set aside Peter, John, Thomas, and all the other disciples and appear first to Mary Magdalene?

1. Please note that Mary Magdalene was the last to leave Calvary’s cross and was the first to arrive at the tomb. She was not the only one saved, nor was it from her alone that demons were cast out; yet early in the morning, she came to the tomb to find the Lord. True, there were many things she did not understand (some have even though she did not have a very good brain), but she had a very excellent spiritual portion one that perhaps many of us lack, which was, that she had a desire for the Lord. This is what every Christian ought to desire after. It is recorded in “The true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world.” (John 1:29) that when John the Baptist saw Jesus coming to him, he cried out, “The next day he saw Jesus coming toward him, and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God, who takes away the sin of the world!”(John1:29) This is the word which John the Baptist declared when he saw the Lord on that first occasion. Then in verse 36 we read that he saw the Lord Jesus again and declared: “And he looked at Jesus as he walked by and said, “Behold, the Lamb of God!” (John 1:36). Did he forget to finish his sentence with the other words previously uttered (“that takes away the sin of the world”)? No, this explains the experience of a saved person. When a person first sees the Lord, he always thinks of the Lord and himself, of the Lord as the Lamb of God who takes away his sins.

However, at the second encounter with the Lord, he forgets all about himself and thinks only of the Lord. On the first occasion, he thanks the Lord for the grace given to him; on the second, he draws near to the Lord because of what He is. In baptism, we are joined to the Lord, but in breaking bread, we remember the Lord himself. At our first encounter, we become believers in the Lord; at our second encounter, we become His “sweethearts.” The first step is to believe in the work of the Lord; the second step is to draw near to the person of the Lord.

Many are there who only know the preciousness of the Lord’s work but do not know the preciousness of the Lord himself. They know the grace they receive, but they do not know the loveliness of the Lord. What makes Mary Magdalene different from other people is that she treasures the Savior himself, not just the salvation she receives. Many people were there from whom demons were cast out, but one alone sought after the Lord, Mary Magdalene. Though other women also came to find the Lord, the first one who arrived at the tomb was Mary Magdalene. She came early on the first day of the week, while it was still dark. She only cared about finding the Lord. As one brother said, after the Lord Jesus died, the whole world seemed like a vacuum in Mary's eyes. The whole world could not captivate her heart, for one person alone had already won it. Her heart belonged entirely to the Lord.

2. When Mary came to the tomb, what did she see? And what did she intend to do? She thought that since her beloved Lord was now dead, it would be good if she could see His body once more. Yet unexpectedly, even the body was gone! So she ran to tell Peter and John, saying, “They have taken away the Lord out of the tomb, and we know not where they have laid him.” Immediately, the two took off and ran to the tomb. John ran faster than Peter, so he arrived at the tomb first. He looked into it and saw the linen cloths lying there, but he did not enter in. Simon Peter arrived afterwards and entered the tomb and saw the linen cloths lying, also the napkin that had been upon Jesus’ head now rolled up in a place by itself.

Then John also went in. He saw and believed. Yet what did they do after they had seen the situation? These two “went away again unto their own home.” They still had a sweet home on earth to which they could go. Although they realized the absence of the Lord, they felt strongly that they should return to their own house. Apart from the Lord, they still had a place to call their home.

How about Mary? “But Mary was standing at the tomb weeping.” She had no place to go! She could not go! How profound is this word “but”! Mary pondered in her heart: “You may have a home to go to, but I cannot go because the Lord is gone. You may not miss the Lord’s presence, but I do. Who has taken Him away? How can I leave?” So she stood by the tomb and wept. To her, the whole world was all emptiness. The Lord was gone; what else, then, could one do but weep. Oh, Mary’s heart is the heart of a widow! The disciples who had followed the Lord could go away. Those with deep knowledge of the Lord could go away. John who loved the Lord went away; the “courageous” Peter also went away. Only a simple woman out of whom the Lord had cast seven demons was captivated by the Lord. She had neither rest nor consolation. She could not go away. Without the Lord all was finished. She could only weep, because thereafter her heart was nothing but a great void.

3.“So, as she wept, she stooped and looked into the tomb; and she saw two angels in white sitting, one at the head, and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had lain. And they said unto her, Woman, why are you weeping? She said unto them, because they have taken away my Lord, and I don’t know where they have laid him.” When Mary saw the angels, she was neither surprised nor frightened. Why? Because her heart was completely occupied with “they have taken away my Lord.” With this one thing in mind, she cared for nothing else. Such a heart was so fixed on her Lord that even the appearance of the angels could not attract her attention. She was not concerned about the angels; her whole heart was focused on the Lord.

Some may feel how good it would be if they could travel along for a while with John who so loved the Lord, or how exciting it might be if they could hear just once the preaching of Peter who was so deeply disciplined by the Lord. But the heart of Mary does not care for such things. To her, the presence of Peter and John is not sufficient for her. For her heart is like the heart of a widow. People may imagine how joyous Mary must have become in having the angels speak to her; but the fact of the matter is she did not feel anything special at all. How very different from men these angels must have appeared; they must have been very attractive, and their garments were white and shining; nevertheless, Mary could only think of one thing: how her Lord had been taken away. Even the glorious angels could not fill the void of her heart. There was only one thing she could do, and that was to weep. Without the Lord, nothing could satisfy her, not Peter, not John, not even the angels!

4. “They said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping?” She said to them, “They have taken away my Lord, and I do not know where they have laid him.” (John 20:13) In her thinking, though the Lord had died, His body was still precious. She had not thought of the Lord’s resurrection. Four times as recorded in the Gospel according to Matthew, the Lord had told His disciples that after He died He would be raised from among the dead “From that time Jesus began to show his disciples that he must go to Jerusalem and suffer many things from the elders and chief priests and scribes, and be killed, and on the third day be raised.”(Matthew 16:21) “And they will kill him, and he will be raised on the third day.” And they were greatly distressed.” (Matthew 17:23) “And deliver him over to the Gentiles to be mocked and flogged and crucified, and he will be raised on the third day.” (Matthew 20:19) “But after I am raised up, I will go before you to Galilee.” 33Peter answered him, “Though they all fall away because of you, I will never fall away. Matthew 26:32). Yet Mary knew nothing of it. So on that day all her hope had been shattered; and then she only desired after the Lord’s body.

Yet in spite of her ignorance, the Lord revealed himself to her because of her singular desire for

Him. The Lord appeared to Mary so as to satisfy a heart that was hungering and thirsting after Him. Peter and John went home, and the Lord did not seek them out. But here was a heart wholly occupied with the Lord, and He sought her out. It’s not so harmful if we lack some knowledge, but having a heart that can stir up the Lord is truly precious.

5. “ Having said this, she turned around and saw Jesus standing, but she did not know that it was Jesus. Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.” (John 20:14-15). She saw the Lord Jesus, but she thought He was the gardener. “ Sir, if you have carried him away .” Here she forgot to state that she was seeking the Lord—Jesus of Nazareth. She merely said “him.” To her, there was only “him” in the whole world. She thought everybody ought to know who the “him” was to her. She assumed that everyone should know who this “him” was! And such was the heart of Mary.

“Let him kiss me with the kisses of his mouth! For your love is better than wine” (Song of Solomon1:2). This was spoken by the Shulammite as an expression of her desire for Solomon. In a similar way, whom Mary desired in her heart was this “Him” and whom she spoke about was also this “Him.” How we also need to have this “Him” in our hearts. It is not so important to have spiritual knowledge; having “Him” is all that really matters. We do not need more knowledge; we need such a perfect heart before Him as Mary Magdalene had.

6. “Jesus said to her, “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom are you seeking?” Supposing him to be the gardener, she said to him, “Sir, if you have carried him away, tell me where you have laid him, and I will take him away.”(John 20:15) What kind of person was Mary? She was a woman. We do not know whether she was physically strong or weak, but we do know that her heart intended to take the Lord away herself. At this moment, she didn’t even think about how strong she was or how long the road was. She only thought of taking Him. Love knows no difficulty.

One quite amazing thing in the world is that where there is love, there is no problem. She was not mindful of anything other than to take Him. And such was the heart of Mary Magdalene. On witnessing this, the Lord could not help but reveal himself to her. He could not let her weep on. He determined to satisfy this longing heart and appeared to Mary before He could then seek out Peter, John, and the two disciples on the road to Emmaus.

7. How did the Lord appear to her? Jesus said to her, “Mary.” She turned and said to him in Aramaic, “Rabboni!” (which means Teacher) (John 20:16) Have we ever heard the voice that

Mary heard? If we ever hear this voice “Mary” as we pray in our closet, we shall be satisfied. As soon as the Lord said “Mary,” she recognized Him right away. This is a revelation. It is enough if the Lord would say just one word. As the shepherd calls his sheep, the eyes of the sheep open immediately. When Mary heard the Lord’s voice, she knew instantly that this was not the gardener, but the Teacher. She therefore had no need to weep any more. Whenever the Lord reveals himself to a person, no further words need to be said. Do we, like Mary, recognize the voice of our Lord?

There lived a family which was composed of only two people, a mother and her son. Every evening when the son came home on his bicycle, he whistled as he approached the house. His mother knew immediately that her son was coming home. One day a brother in the Lord was talking with her at her home, and just as he was leaving, the mother stopped him and asked him to wait for a while, for her son was coming home. Upon inquiring how she knew this, she replied that she had already heard her son’s whistle. To other people, the whistle didn’t mean anything, but to the mother’s ears it had a special meaning. When the Lord said “Mary,” it might have sounded meaningless, but Mary recognized this voice and knew it was the Lord.

8. “Jesus said to her, “Do not cling to me, for I have not yet ascended to the Father; but go to my brothers and say to them, ‘I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God.” (John 20:17) In Matthew 28 it is recorded that some women touched the Lord. He allowed them to do so because it was worship. However why did He forbid Mary to touch Him here? It’s because the Lord knew that Mary wanted to keep the Lord on earth by clinging to Him and would refuse to let Him go. Yet what had the Lord gotten while on earth? Nothing except a thorny crown, a cross, and a tomb. Now He was to ascend to heaven to God his father.

Jesus told Mary not to touch Him, that is to say, not to retain Him on earth. For the Lord has not only been resurrected, He has also ascended to heaven to be the Head of a new race as well as the representative of men. There had not been any man in heaven before Jesus. In His ascension, the Lord Jesus became the first man in heaven, and after Him there will be those others who believe in Him. “But we see him who for a little while was made lower than the angels, namely Jesus, crowned with glory and honour because of the suffering of death, so that by the grace of God he might taste death for everyone. For it was fitting that he, for whom and by whom all things exist, in bringing many sons to glory, should make the founder of their salvation perfect through suffering” (Hebrews 2:9-10)

Due to the suffering of death, the Lord is now crowned with glory and honor, and He will lead many other sons into glory too. The Lord has gone ahead, and thereafter the disciples will follow. After His resurrection, He will begin to call the disciples brethren. In other words, the Lord is now the firstborn Son and we become the many sons. By His resurrection and ascension, His Father becomes our Father, and His God becomes our God.

9. What more could Mary say? Nothing, for she was truly satisfied. Hence, she went back, because now she could go back. Can we ever blame the Lord if we are lacking in such revelation as Mary experienced in seeing and hearing Him? Absolutely not, because it can only be due to our lack of hunger and thirst for the Lord that Mary had. Let us ask ourselves if we really long for the Lord? Do we desire the Son of God with all our heart? Are we ignorant of the fact that our position or fame cannot at all touch the Lord’s heart, but that He will be touched if we really yearn after Him? May God create such a desire in us so that we may desire after the Son of God and love Him whole heartedly.

THE END

B

ACK COV

E

R

.

fields.title: Chapter 1
fields.body_html:
THE SLUGGARD'S FARM Introduction From a neglected field and a broken vineyard comes a searching lesson on spiritual laziness—

look carefully, consider wisely, and learn the value of diligence in serving God faithfully.

“I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the vineyard of a man lacking sense, and behold, it was all

overgrown with thorns; the ground was covered with nettles, and its stone wall was broken down.

Then I saw and considered it; I looked and received instruction.” — Proverbs 24:30–32 (ESV)

No doubt Solomon was sometimes glad to set aside his royal robes, escape the formalities of court,

and travel through the countryside unnoticed. On one such occasion, he looked over the broken

wall of a small estate belonging to one of his countrymen. This property consisted of a piece of

ploughed land and a vineyard. One glance showed him that it belonged to a sluggard who had

neglected it. The weeds had grown thickly and covered the entire ground. From this sight, Solomon

received instruction. People generally learn wisdom if they already possess wisdom. The artist’s

eye sees beauty in a landscape because he has beauty in his mind. “To him who has will more be

given,” and he shall have abundance, for he will reap a harvest even from a field covered with

thorns and nettles.

There is a great difference between one person and another in how they use the mind’s eye. I have

a book entitled The Harvest of a Quiet Eye, and it is a good one. The harvest of a quiet eye can be

gathered from a sluggard’s land just as much as from a well-managed farm. When we were

children, we were taught a small poem called Eyes and No Eyes. It contained much truth. Some

people have eyes but do not see, which is much the same as having no eyes at all. Others, however,

have sharp eyes for discovering instruction. Some look only at the surface, while others see not

only the outer shell but the living kernel of truth hidden within outward things.

We may find instruction everywhere. To a spiritual mind, nettles have their purpose and weeds

have their lesson. Are not thorns and thistles meant to teach sinful people?

Do they not grow from the earth to show us what sin has done, and the kind of produce that results

when we sow seeds of rebellion against God? “I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the vineyard

of a man lacking sense,” says Solomon. “I saw and considered it; I looked and received

instruction.” Whatever you see, take care to consider it carefully, and you will not see it in vain.

You will find books and sermons everywhere — in the land and in the sea, in the earth and in the

skies. You may learn from every living beast, bird, fish, and insect, and from every useful or

useless plant that springs from the ground. We may also gather valuable lessons from things we

do not like. Solomon certainly did not admire the thorns and nettles that covered the vineyard, yet

he still found instruction in them. Many are stung by nettles, but few are taught by them. Some are

hurt by briars, yet here was one who was improved by them. Wisdom has a way of gathering grapes

from thorns and figs from nettles. She draws good from plants that seem unpleasant and harmful.

Do not complain about thorns; instead, gain good from them. Do not sting yourself on nettles;

grasp them firmly and use them for the health of your soul.

Trials and troubles, worries and disturbances, small irritations and disappointments, may all help

you if you allow them. Like Solomon, see and consider them carefully — look at them and receive

instruction. As for us, we will now first consider Solomon’s description of a sluggard: he is “a man

lacking sense.” Secondly, we will notice his description of the sluggard’s land: “it was all

overgrown with thorns; the ground was covered with nettles.” When we have considered these two

matters, we will conclude by gathering the instruction this neglected land may provide.

First, think of Solomon’s description of a slothful man. Solomon was not someone we would

contradict, for he possessed great wisdom, and he wrote under divine inspiration in the Book of

Proverbs. Solomon says a sluggard is “a man lacking sense.” The slothful man does not think so.

He places his hands in his pockets, and from his confident manner you would think he owned the

Bank of England. He appears very wise in his own estimation and carries himself in a way meant

to impress others with his supposed ability. How he gained this wisdom is difficult to say. He has

never taken the trouble to think. I cannot say he leaps to conclusions, for he never leaps at all; he

simply settles lazily into them. Yet he believes he knows everything and has resolved every issue.

Meditation is too much effort for him. Learning is something he has never been willing to endure.

Yet he delights in thinking himself naturally clever. He does not wish to know more than he already

knows, for in his own mind he knows enough — though in truth he knows nothing.

The proverb is not flattering, but Solomon was correct in calling him “a man lacking sense.”

According to modern polite society, this may sound blunt, especially since the man owned a field

and a vineyard. As the saying goes, “When I have a horse and a cow, every man bids me good

morning.”

How can a man be said to lack understanding if he owns land and property? Is it not commonly

assumed that a person’s intelligence is measured by his wealth? Wealth often brings praise for

supposed ability. Such is the way of the world.

But it is not the way of Scripture. Whether he owns a field and a vineyard or not, Solomon says

that if he is a sluggard, he is foolish — or to put it plainly, he is empty of understanding.

Not only does he fail to understand, but he also lacks the capacity to understand. If he is slothful,

he is empty-headed. He may be called a gentleman. He may be a landowner. He may possess a

vineyard and a field.

Yet these possessions make him no better. Indeed, they make him worse, for he is a man lacking

sense and therefore unable to make proper use of what he has.

I am glad that Solomon tells us so plainly that a slothful man is lacking sense, for that is useful

information. I have met people who believed they fully understood the doctrines of grace. They

could clearly explain the election of the saints, the predestination of God, the certainty of the divine

decree, the necessity of the Spirit’s work, and all the glorious doctrines that build the structure of

our faith.

Yet from these truths they concluded that they had nothing to do, and so they became sluggards.

Doing nothing became their creed. They would not even encourage others to labour for the Lord

because, they said, “God will do his own work. Salvation is all of grace.”

Their idea was that a man should simply wait and do nothing — sit still and let the grass grow to

his ankles while hoping for heavenly help. To stir himself, in their view, would interfere with

God’s eternal purpose.

I have known such a man look sour, shake his aged head, and speak harshly against earnest

believers who were trying to win souls. I have seen him discourage young people and, like a heavy

steam hammer, crush them by calling them unsound and ignorant.

How are we to endure the criticism of such a dogmatic person? How are we to escape this

supposedly knowledgeable and fault-finding sluggard? Solomon comes to our aid and silences him

by declaring that he is lacking sense. He may consider himself the standard of orthodoxy and judge

everyone else, yet Solomon applies a different standard and says he lacks understanding. He may

know the doctrine, but he does not truly understand it. If he did, he would know that the doctrines

of grace lead us to seek the grace those doctrines proclaim.

When we see God at work, we learn that he works in us, not to make us idle, but “to will and to

work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13, ESV). God’s predestination of a people means he

has ordained them “for good works” (Ephesians 2:10, ESV), that they may display his praise. If

you or I draw from any doctrine — however true — the conclusion that we may be idle and

indifferent about the things of God, then we lack understanding. We misuse the gospel. We take

what was meant as nourishment and turn it into poison. The sluggard, whether lazy in business or

careless about his soul, is a man lacking sense.

As a general rule, we may measure a person’s understanding by his useful activity. Some call

themselves “cultured,” yet they cultivate nothing. Much modern thought, from what I have

observed, is like a bottle of smoke — impressive in appearance, but producing nothing solid. There

are people who can analyse, debate, refine, and refute, yet meanwhile the hemlock grows in the

furrow and the plough rusts unused. If your knowledge, culture, or education does not lead you to

serve God practically in your own generation, then you have not learned what Solomon calls

wisdom. You are not like the Blessed One — incarnate Wisdom — of whom it is written, “He

went about doing good” (Acts 10:38, ESV).

A lazy person is not like our Saviour, who said, “My Father is working until now, and I am

working” (John 5:17, ESV). True wisdom is practical. Empty culture only speaks and theorises.

Wisdom ploughs its field. Wisdom hoes its vineyard. Wisdom watches its crops. Wisdom makes

the best of everything. Whoever does not do so, whatever knowledge he may claim, is a man

lacking sense. Why does he lack understanding? Is it not because he has opportunities he does not

use? His day has come and is passing, yet he lets the hours slip away without purpose. Let each of

us examine ourselves seriously. Am I using the minutes as they pass? This man had a vineyard but

did not cultivate it. He had a field but did not till it. Do we use our opportunities? Each of us has

some ability to serve God. Do we employ it?

If we are his children, he has not placed us where we must be useless. He has given us somewhere

we may shine with the light he has given us, even if it is only a small candle. Are we shining? Do

we “sow beside all waters”? Do we sow our seed in the morning and not withhold our hand in the

evening? (Ecclesiastes 11:6, ESV) If not, Solomon’s verdict stands: the slothful is a man lacking

sense; a man void of understanding. This man had opportunities he did not use. He also had duties

he did not fulfil. When God gave each Israelite a portion of land, he did not intend it to lie waste,

but to be cultivated.

When God placed Adam in the garden of Eden, it was not merely to admire its beauty, but “to

work it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15, ESV). Likewise, each Israelite’s land was meant to reach its

full fruitfulness through faithful labour. Ownership brought responsibility. The sluggard failed in

that responsibility, and so he lacked understanding.

What is your role? A father? A master? A servant? A minister? A teacher? In these roles you have

your fields and vineyards. If you fail to use them rightly, you neglect the purpose of your existence

and fall short of the calling God has given you. The slothful farmer also had abilities he did not

use. He could have worked his land if he had chosen to do so. He was not ill; he was simply lazy

by choice.

God does not require from us what we do not have. “It is required according to what a person has,

not according to what he does not have” (2 Corinthians 8:12, ESV). The man with two talents is

not expected to produce five, but he is expected to use his two. This sluggard refused to attempt

what was clearly within his power. Many have abilities lying dormant. Others use their gifts for

themselves rather than for the One who gave them. If God has granted us any power to do good,

let us use it. This world is weary and wicked. We should not hide even a glow-worm’s light in

such darkness. We should not withhold even a single word of truth in a world filled with error.

However weak our voice, let us raise it for truth and righteousness. Let us not lack understanding

by neglecting opportunities, ignoring duties, and failing to use our abilities. In matters of the soul,

the sluggard is especially lacking in sense, for he trifles with matters that require utmost

seriousness.

Have you never cultivated your heart? Has the plough never broken the hard soil of your soul? Has

the seed of the Word never been sown — or has it taken no root?

Have you never watered the young shoots of desire? Never tried to pull up the weeds of sin? You

care for your body by spending time in front of the mirror, yet neglect your soul. You adorn the

flesh, which will soon return to dust, while your soul remains unwashed and uncared for. This is

folly of the highest order. He who is lazy regarding the vineyard of his heart is truly lacking sense.

And if you are a Christian, truly saved, yet negligent in the Lord’s work, then you show little

understanding. If you know the danger of lost souls, how can you not strive to rescue them? Time

does not delay. Death does not delay. Hell does not delay. Satan is not idle. The powers of darkness

are active. How then can we be sluggish if the Master has placed us in his vineyard? If we have

been saved by God’s infinite love, should we not spend and be spent in his service? The very order

of things demands that a saved person be earnest.

The Christian who is lazy in service does not realise what he loses. The richest part of fellowship

with God is wholehearted consecration to God. Some possess just enough religion to make it

doubtful whether they have any at all. They display a little godliness, yet little evidence of the

Spirit’s work. We are meant to reflect Christ. Instead, some bring reproach upon him. When we

see lazy servants, we assume their master must also be indifferent.

Let the world never think that Christ is indifferent to suffering or lacking in zeal. Yet they may

think so if those who claim to serve him are mere sluggards. The slothful person loses honour and

joy in service. He dishonours the cause he claims to love and prepares thorns for his dying pillow.

Let it stand settled: the slothful, whether minister, deacon, or private Christian, is a man lacking

sense.

Now, secondly, let us consider the sluggard’s land: “I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the

vineyard of a man lacking sense, and behold, it was all overgrown with thorns; the ground was

covered with nettles, and its stone wall was broken down.” (Proverbs 24:30–31, ESV) Land will

always produce something. Soil fit for a field or vineyard will yield fruit of some kind. Likewise,

our hearts and our spheres of influence will produce something. We cannot live as blanks. We will

do good or evil.

If you are idle in Christ’s work, you are active in the devil’s. By sleeping, the sluggard cultivated

thorns more effectively than by any effort. If we do not produce wheat for Christ, we will grow

weeds fit only for burning. If the soul is not cultivated for God, it will produce its natural fruit.

And what is that natural fruit? Sin and misery. If children are left untrained, what will they

produce? If a city is left without the Gospel, what will grow there? Crime and corruption. There

will always be a harvest. If we are slothful, that harvest will be painful even to ourselves. No one

rests comfortably on thorns. While you sleep, Satan sows. If you withhold good seed, he will

scatter evil seed freely. From that will come regret, perhaps for eternity.

“Thorns and thistles it shall bring forth for you” (Genesis 3:18, ESV). Often the evil growth will

be abundant. Good land yields abundant weeds if neglected. The person who might have done

much for God will do much harm if left idle. The best, when neglected, becomes the worst. If you

want salvation, effort must be made to show you the way. But if you want to be lost, it requires

only neglect: “How shall we escape if we neglect such a great salvation?” (Hebrews 2:3, ESV)

The sluggard says, “A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest” (Proverbs

24:33, ESV), and the thorns multiply beyond number and prepare many a sting for him.

As we look at the lazy man’s vineyard, let us also look into the heart of the ungodly sluggard. He

does not care about repentance and faith. To think seriously about his soul or eternity is too much

effort for him. He prefers to take life easily, with “a little folding of the hands to rest.” What is

growing in his mind and character? In some of these spiritual sluggards, you see drunkenness,

impurity, greed, anger, pride, and many other thistles and nettles. In others, where such obvious

sins are restrained by respectable surroundings, you find different varieties of evil. The heart

cannot remain empty. Either Christ or the devil will occupy it. My friend, if you are not decided

for God, you cannot remain neutral. In this conflict, each person stands either with God or against

him.

You cannot remain like a blank sheet of paper. The clear handwriting of Satan is upon you; can

you not see the marks? Unless Christ has written his own gracious name across the page, the

signature of Satan remains. You may say, “I do not live in open sin; I am moral.” Yet if you would

examine your heart carefully, you would see hostility towards God and his ways. You do not love

his law, nor his Son, nor his gospel. You are estranged in heart, filled with vain thoughts and wrong

desires.

These will grow and increase as long as you remain a spiritual sluggard and leave your heart

uncultivated. May the Spirit of God awaken you. May he stir you to serious and earnest reflection.

Then you will see that these harmful growths must be uprooted, that your heart must be broken up

by conviction, and sown with the good seed of the gospel until it yields a harvest for the great

Husbandman. Friend, if you believe in Christ, allow me also to look into your heart, especially if

you are a sluggish Christian. I fear that nettles and thistles may be growing there as well. Did I not

hear you sing recently, “‘Tis a point I long to know”? That question will often trouble you, for

doubt readily grows in idle minds.

I do not recall reading in John Wesley’s diary that he questioned his salvation. He was so busy in

his Master’s harvest that it did not occur to him to distrust his God.

Some Christians have little faith because they have never sown the mustard seed they were given.

If you do not use your faith, how can it grow? When faith is actively exercised in Christ’s service,

it takes root, grows strong, and eventually chokes out doubt. Others suffer from gloomy

forebodings. They become discontented, irritable, selfish, and complaining — often because they

are idle. These are the weeds that grow in a sluggard’s garden.

I have known lazy believers become so peevish that nothing pleased them. The most earnest

Christian could not satisfy them. The most loving believers were never affectionate enough. The

most active church was never energetic enough. They found fault everywhere, even where God

was clearly at work. This spirit of criticism, contention, and constant complaint is one of the nettles

that surely grow where there is spiritual laziness.

If your heart does not bear fruit for God, it will certainly produce what harms you and others.

Thorns often choke good seed, but it is a blessed thing when good seed grows so abundantly that

it chokes the thorns. God enables some believers to become so fruitful that when Satan sows tares,

they cannot grow. The Holy Spirit weakens evil in the heart so that it no longer dominates. If you

are slothful, examine the field of your heart and grieve over what you see.

Now consider your home. It is a serious matter when a person fails to cultivate their own family.

In my early days, I knew a man who often accompanied me into villages where I preached. I

appreciated his company until I learned more about him. He spent every evening attending

meetings, yet neglected his many children. They grew into ungodly young people because their

father never sought to lead them to Christ. What is the use of zeal abroad if there is neglect at

home? How sad to say, “My own vineyard I have not kept” (Song of Solomon 1:6, ESV).

I once heard of a man who refused to teach his children about God because he did not wish to

prejudice them. He preferred to let them choose their religion later. One of his sons broke his arm,

and while the doctor was setting it, the boy was swearing. The doctor remarked, “You feared to

prejudice your son towards good, but the devil had no such hesitation.” It is our duty to cultivate

the field in favour of good crops, or it will soon be overrun with weeds. Train a child towards good,

or he will naturally drift towards evil. As it is with homes, so it is with schools. A man who later

joined this church had once been an atheist. He traced his unbelief partly to his school experience.

On Sundays, the boys were confined to a distant gallery in church where they could scarcely hear

a word. They endured endless prayers, but nothing touched their hearts. Eventually, he became so

weary of religion that he resolved to abandon it once free. Sunday-school teachers must take care.

Classes can be made so dull that children come to dislike Sunday itself. Time can be wasted

without bringing young hearts to Christ.

Some Christian parents, through harshness and lack of tenderness, have sown seeds of resentment

instead of love. May we live among our children in such a way that they love not only us but our

Father in heaven. Let parents show cheerful and genuine faith, so that children may desire to follow

their example. If faith does not rule in the home, we will see disorder, pride, folly, and the

beginnings of vice. Let not your home become a sluggard’s field. Let every deacon, class leader,

and minister examine the field entrusted to him. If we neglect our responsibilities, we become like

barren trees occupying space that fruitful trees could have used. We will hinder rather than help

unless we render real service. Consider this seriously. You cannot remain neutral. If you produce

no gain, you create loss. May God grant that we become profitable servants.

Now look at the vast field of the world. See how it is overgrown with thorns. Vast regions are

covered with error, unbelief, and false religion. The world abounds in cruelty, oppression,

impurity, and misery. To what extent is this due to a negligent church? Nearly two thousand years

have passed, yet much of the vineyard remains overgrown. Wherever the church has ceased

missionary labour, she has declined. When she stops reclaiming the wilderness, she becomes

barren herself. Rather than asking what the church has done in past centuries, let us ask what we

will do now.

Will we continue cultivating the same ground repeatedly while vast fields remain untouched? May

God awaken us from our sluggishness. If not, the report may be: “I passed by the field of the

sluggish church, and it was all overgrown with thorns.” There is a lesson here. Left to itself, human

nature produces only thorns and nettles. Apart from grace, this is all we would have yielded. If we

now produce good fruit, it is entirely due to grace. Let us then display the fruit of grace in our

lives. Shall we serve Christ less earnestly than we once served sin? Shall we sacrifice less for him

than we did for our former desires? May the Holy Spirit produce abundant fruit in us.

We also learn the emptiness of good intentions without action. This man always meant to work

hard one day. He said, “A little sleep, a little slumber, a little folding of the hands to rest” (Proverbs

24:33, ESV). Only a little delay — then he would begin. But that day never came. Many hear

serious sermons and intend to respond. They mean to turn to God “one day.” Some have delayed

for forty years. When will you turn? “Before I die,” you say. Will you postpone it to your final

hour? Is that wise? You may die suddenly. Life is uncertain. Take heed of small delays. You have

wasted enough time already. Decide now. May the Holy Spirit bring you to decide.

“Surely you do not object to my having a little more sleep?” says the sluggard. “You have waked

me so soon. I only ask another little nap.” “My dear man, it is far into the morning.” He answers,

“It is rather late, I know; but it will not be much later if I take just another doze.” You wake him

again, and tell him it is noon. He says, “It is the hottest part of the day: I daresay if I had been up

I should have gone to the sofa and taken a little rest from the hot sun.” You knock at his door when

it is almost evening, and then he cries, “It is of no use to get up now, for the day is almost over.”

You remind him of his overgrown field and weedy vineyard, and he answers, “Yes, I must get up,

I know.” He shakes himself and says, “I do not think it will matter much if I wait till the clock

strikes. I will rest another minute or two.”

He is glued to his bed, dead while he lives, buried in his laziness. If he could sleep forever he

would, but he cannot, for the judgment day will rouse him. It is written, “And in Hades, being in

torment, he lifted up his eyes” (Luke 16:23, ESV). God grant that you spiritual sluggards may

wake before that; but you will not unless you bestir yourselves in time, for “now is the favorable

time; behold, now is the day of salvation” (2 Corinthians 6:2, ESV). And it may be now or never.

Tomorrow is only to be found in the calendar of fools; today is the time of the wise man, the chosen

season of our gracious God. Oh that the Holy Spirit may lead you to seize the present hour, that

you may at once give yourselves to the Lord by faith in Christ Jesus, and then from his vineyard—

“Quick uproot The noisome weeds, that without profit suck The soil’s fertility from wholesome plants.”

fields.title: Chapter 2
fields.body_html:
THE BROKEN FENCE Introduction

From the sluggard’s neglected vineyard and its broken stone wall comes a solemn lesson—

consider carefully how spiritual neglect, weakened principles, and delayed repentance leave

the soul exposed to creeping ruin.

“I passed by the field of a sluggard, by the vineyard of a man lacking sense, and behold, it was all overgrown with thorns;

the ground was covered with nettles,

and its stone wall was broken down.

Then I saw and considered it;

I looked and received instruction.” Proverbs 24:30–32 (ESV) This slothful man did no harm to his fellow men: he was not a thief, nor a ruffian, nor a meddler

in other men’s business. He did not trouble himself about other men’s concerns, for he did not

even attend to his own—it required too much effort. He was not openly vicious; he had not have

enough energy for that. He liked to take things easily. He always let well enough alone, and, for

that matter, he let ill alone too, as the nettles and thistles in his garden plainly proved.

What was the use of disturbing himself? It would all be the same a hundred years from now; and

so he took things as they came. He was not a bad man, so some said of him; and yet, perhaps, it

will be found at last that there is no worse man in the world than the man who is not good. In some

respects he is not good enough to be bad; he has not enough strength of character to serve either

God or Baal. He simply serves himself, worshiping his own ease and adoring his own comfort.

Yet he always meant to be right. Dear me! he was not going to sleep much longer; he would only

have forty winks more, and then he would be at his work and show you what he could do. One of

these days he meant to be thoroughly earnest and make up for lost time. The time never actually

came for him to begin, but it was always coming. He always meant to repent, but he went on in

his sin. He meant to believe, but he died an unbeliever. He meant to be a Christian, but he lived

without Christ. He halted between two opinions because he would not trouble himself to decide;

and so he perished through delay.

This picture of the slothful man and his garden and field overgrown with nettles and weeds

represents many a man who has professed to be a Christian, but who has become slothful in the

things of God. Spiritual life has withered in him. He has backslidden. He has come down from

healthy spiritual energy into listlessness and indifference to the things of God. While things have

gone wrong within his heart, and all sorts of mischiefs have entered him, grown up, and taken root

in him, mischief is also taking place outwardly in his daily conduct. The stone wall that guarded

his character is broken down, and he lies open to every evil. Upon this point we will now meditate:

“the stone wall thereof was broken down.”

Come, then, let us walk with Solomon, and stand with him, and consider, and receive instruction

while we look at this broken-down fence. When we have examined it, let us consider the

consequences of broken-down walls; and then, in the last place, let us try to rouse up this sluggard

so that his wall may yet be repaired. If this slothful person should be one of ourselves, may God’s

infinite mercy rouse us before this ruined wall has let in a herd of prowling vices.

I. Let Us Look at This Broken Fence In the beginning it was a very good fence, for it was a stone wall. Fields are often surrounded with

wooden fences that soon decay, or with hedges that may easily have gaps made in them; but this

was a stone wall. Such walls are very common in the East, and also in some of our own counties

where stone is plentiful. It was solid protection to begin with, and it securely enclosed the little

estate that had fallen into such bad hands. The man had a field for farming, and another strip of

land for a vineyard or garden. It was fertile soil, for it produced thorns and nettles in abundance;

and where these grow, better things can grow as well. Yet the idler took no care of his property,

but allowed the wall to fall into disrepair, and in many places to be completely broken down.

Let me mention some of the stone walls that men allow to crumble when they backslide. In many cases, sound principles were instilled in youth, but these are forgotten. What a blessing

Christian education is. Our parents, both by instruction and example, taught many of us what is

pure, honorable, and of good repute. We saw in their lives how to live. They opened the Word of

God before us, and taught us what is right toward God and toward men. They prayed for us, and

they prayed with us, until the things of God surrounded us and enclosed us like a stone wall.

We have never been able to rid ourselves of those early impressions. Even in times of wandering,

before we knew the Lord savingly, those truths had a healthy influence over us. We were restrained

when we would have done evil. We were helped when we were struggling toward Christ. It is very

sad when people allow these first principles to be shaken and removed like stones falling from a

boundary wall. Young people begin by speaking lightly of the old-fashioned ways of their parents.

Soon it is not merely the old-fashioned aspect they despise, but the ways themselves. They seek

other company, and from that company they learn nothing but evil. They seek pleasure in places

that would horrify their parents. This leads to worse. If they do not bring their father’s gray hairs

down with sorrow to the grave, it is no credit to them.

I have known young men, who truly were Christians, sadly backslide because they were persuaded

to modify, conceal, or alter those holy principles in which they were trained from their mother’s

knee. It is a great calamity when professing believers become unstable and are carried about with

every wind of doctrine. It shows weakness of mind and unsoundness of heart when we can trifle

with those serious and sacred truths that were watered with a mother’s tears and upheld by a

father’s faithful life.

“I am your servant, the son of your maidservant” (Psalm 116:16, ESV). David felt it to be both an

honor and a sacred bond that he was the son of one who was called God’s servant.

Take care, you who have received Christian training, that you do not trifle with it. “My son, keep your father’s commandment,

and forsake not your mother’s teaching.

Bind them on your heart always;

tie them around your neck.” (Proverbs 6:20–21, ESV) Protection of character is also found in solid doctrine. This too is a strong stone wall. Many among

us have been taught the gospel of the grace of God and have learned it well, so that they are able

to contend earnestly for the faith once delivered to the saints. Happy are those whose religion rests

upon clear knowledge of eternal truth.

A religion that is all excitement and little instruction may serve for a time; but for lifelong strength

there must be knowledge of those great doctrines that are foundational to the gospel. I tremble

when I hear of a man giving up, one by one, the vital truths of the gospel and boasting of his

liberality. I hear him say, “These are my views, but others have a right to theirs.” That is proper

when speaking of mere opinions; but we may not speak so of truth revealed by God. That truth is

one and unchanging, and all are bound to receive it. It is not your personal view of truth that saves

you, but truth itself as God has revealed it, embraced by faith.

I will gladly give up my way of stating a doctrine, but not the doctrine itself. One man may express

it this way, another in a different way; but the truth itself must never be surrendered. The spirit of

the Broad School robs us of certainty. I would ask some of its leaders whether they believe that

anything taught in Scripture is worth dying for, and whether the martyrs were fools for giving their

lives for what might be merely opinions. This broad-church spirit breaks down stone walls. It lets

in the devil and all his company, and it will do immeasurable harm to the church of God if it is not

resisted. A loose state of belief damages any man’s soul.

We are not bigots; yet we would be none the worse if we lived so faithfully that men called us

such. I met a man recently who was accused of bigotry, and I said, “Give me your hand. I like to

meet with bigots now and then. They are becoming rare, and the material they are made of is so

strong that if there were more of it we might see more men among us and fewer creatures without

backbone.”

Lately we have seen few men with backbone; most have been like jellyfish. There was a time when

I would have said, “Be liberal and cast-off narrowness.” Now I must say, “Be steadfast in the

truth.” The faith once delivered to the saints is more precious to me now that it is called narrow,

for I am tired of that breadth which comes from broken hedges.

There are fixed truths and definite certainties of faith, and woe to you if you allow these stone

walls to crumble. I fear that the slothful are many, and that future generations may lament the

carelessness applauded in this negligent age.

Another fence often neglected is that of godly habits already formed. The sluggard lets this wall

fall into ruin. Let me mention some important safeguards of life and character.

One is the habit of secret prayer. Private prayer should be regularly offered, at least morning and

evening. We cannot do without set times of drawing near to God. To look into the face of man

without first looking into the face of God is dangerous. To go into the world without committing

your heart to God is to leave it open to every spiritual intruder. At night, to go to bed like animals

into their stall, without thanking God for the mercies of the day, is shameful. The evening sacrifice

should be offered as surely as we enjoy the evening fire. We should place ourselves beneath the

wings of the Preserver of men.

It is said, “We can pray at all times.” That is true; but I fear those who do not pray at stated times

seldom pray at all. Those who pray regularly are most likely to pray continually. Spiritual life does

not thrive on rigid formalism, but since life always takes some outward form, we should care for

its outward habits as well as its inward power. Never allow large gaps in the wall of habitual private

prayer.

I go further. There is great protective power in family prayer, and I am deeply grieved that many

Christian families neglect it. There was a time when Romanism could make little progress in

England because it offered only a shadow of what Christian homes already possessed in substance.

“Do you hear that bell in the morning?”

“What is it for?”

“To go to church to pray.” The Puritan replied, “I have no need to go there. I have gathered my children. We have read

Scripture, prayed, and sung God’s praise. We have a church in our house.” The evening bell rang

again. It was for vespers. But he had already held his evening worship around his own table, with

the large Bible as its chief ornament. They said there could be no service without a priest. He

answered that every godly man should be a priest in his own home.

Thus the saints resisted priest craft and preserved the faith from generation to generation.

Household devotion and the pulpit are, under God, the stone walls of Protestantism. My prayer is

that these walls may not be broken down.

Another protective fence is the weeknight service. When people abandon weeknight meetings, the

power of their religion declines. I do not speak of those providentially hindered by sickness, work,

or duty. Exceptions exist. I speak of those who could attend but choose not to. When someone

says, “Sunday sermons are enough for me. I do not want prayer meetings or lectures,” it shows a

lack of appetite for the Word, and that is a bad sign. If you build a fence around Sunday and leave

the rest of the week exposed, Satan’s cattle will enter and cause great destruction.

Take care also to maintain the wall of Bible reading and of Christian conversation. Associate with

the godly. Commune with God. By the Spirit’s blessing, you will maintain a strong fence against

temptation. Otherwise, temptations will enter the fields of your soul and consume all the good

fruit. Many have found great protection for the field of daily life in the stone wall of a public

profession of faith. I am speaking to you who are true believers, and you know that it has often

been a strong safeguard to be openly known and recognized as a follower of Jesus.

I have never regretted—and I never shall regret—the day when I walked to the little River Lark in

Cambridgeshire and was there buried with Christ in baptism. In doing so, I acted contrary to the

opinions of all my respected friends; but having read the Greek Testament for myself, I felt bound

to be immersed upon a profession of my faith, and so I was. By that act I declared to the world, “I

am dead to you, and buried to you in Christ, and I hope from this time forward to walk in newness

of life.”

That day, by God’s grace, I followed the strategy of a general who intended to fight until he

conquered, and therefore burned his boats so there could be no retreat. I believe that a solemn

confession of Christ before men is like a thorn hedge, keeping a man within bounds and keeping

away those who would draw him aside. Of course, it is only a hedge, and it is useless if it surrounds

a field of weeds; but when wheat is growing, a hedge is of great importance.

You who imagine that you can belong to the Lord and yet lie open like common ground are greatly

mistaken. You ought to be distinct from the world and obey the voice that says, “Come out from

among them, and be separate” (2 Corinthians 6:17, ESV).

The promise of salvation is to the one who believes in the heart and confesses with the mouth

(Romans 10:9–10). Say boldly, “As for me and my house, we will serve the Lord” (Joshua 24:15,

ESV). By such a confession you step onto the King’s highway and place yourself under the

protection of the Lord of pilgrims, and he will care for you.

Often, when you might otherwise hesitate, you will say, “The vows of the Lord are upon me; how

can I draw back?” Therefore I urge you: set up the stone wall and maintain it. If at any point it has

been thrown down, build it up again. Let it be evident by your conduct and conversation that you

are a follower of Jesus and not ashamed to be known as such.

Hold firmly to your religious principles like true men and women. Do not turn aside for the sake

of gain or social respectability. Do not allow wealth to break down your wall. I have known some

who made a wide gap to let their carriage pass through, and to welcome wealthy worldlings into

their company for the sake of their status. Those who forsake principle to please men will

eventually be lightly esteemed; but the one who is faithful will receive honor from God. Guard

this hedge of steadfast adherence to the faith, and you will find great blessing in it.

There is yet another stone wall to mention: firmness of character. Our holy faith teaches a person

to be decisive for Christ and resolute in removing sinful habits. “If your right eye causes you to

sin, tear it out and throw it away” (Matthew 5:29, ESV). It does not say to cover it with a patch.

“If your right hand causes you to sin, cut it off and throw it away” (Matthew 5:30, ESV). It does

not say to put it in a sling. True religion is thorough. It says, “Touch no unclean thing” (2

Corinthians 6:17, ESV).

But many are so idle in the ways of God that they have no firmness of their own. Evil companions

tempt them, and they cannot say, “No.” They need a stone wall made of repeated refusals. Here

are the stones: “No. No. No.” Dare to be different. Resolve to cling closely to Christ. Make a firm

determination to allow nothing in your life—however profitable or pleasurable—if it would

dishonor the name of Jesus. Be unwavering in truth, unyielding in holiness, immovable in honesty,

steadfast in kindness, and fixed in uprightness. If God’s grace builds such a hedge around you,

even Satan will recognize it and say, “Have you not put a hedge around him?” (Job 1:10, ESV).

I have kept you long enough looking over the wall. Let me now invite you inside and consider the

consequences of a broken-down fence.

First, the boundary disappears. The lines of separation once maintained by sound principles, godly

habits, open confession, and firm resolve are gone. Now the question arises: is this man a Christian

or not? The fence has fallen so far that he no longer knows what belongs to the Lord and what lies

open as common ground. He does not know whether he himself is part of the King’s domain or

merely wasteland under the world’s rule.

This happens when fences are not maintained. If that man had lived near to God, walked in

integrity, and enjoyed the rich presence of the Spirit in holy living and patient waiting, he would

know exactly where the boundary lies. He would know whether his land belonged to the parish of

All-Saints, to No-Man’s-Land, or to the territory where Satan rules.

I heard of a dear elderly saint who, near death, was assaulted by Satan. She gently waved her finger

and said, “Chosen! Chosen! Chosen!” She knew she was chosen, and she remembered the words,

“The Lord who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you” (Zechariah 3:2, ESV). When the wall stands

firm around the field, we can resist the devil and say, “Leave the Lord’s property alone. I belong

to Christ, not to you.” To speak like this, you must mend the fences carefully, so that the boundary

is clear and you can declare, “Trespassers, beware.” Yield not an inch to the enemy. Raise the wall

higher when he attempts to climb it. May he never find a gap through which to enter.

Second, when the wall falls, protection is lost. When a man’s heart is unfenced, his thoughts

wander across the mountains of vanity. Like sheep, thoughts must be enclosed, or they will stray.

David said, “I hate vain thoughts” (Psalm 119:113, ESV). Slothful men have plenty of them, for

unless every gap is stopped and every gate secured, vain thoughts will rush in. Holy reflections,

comforting meditations, devout longings, and gracious fellowship with God will disappear if we

lazily allow the wall to crumble.

As good things depart, bad things enter. When the wall is down, every passerby sees an invitation.

The gate is open, and in they come. Are there fruits? They pluck them. They roam as if in a public

park and pry into every corner. Is there a private place in your heart for Jesus alone? Satan and the

world will invade it. Why should we be surprised? Every stray animal tramples and spoils more

than it consumes when gaps are wide open. So too, every kind of evil desire and imagination feeds

upon an unguarded soul.

It is useless to pray, “Lead us not into temptation” (Matthew 6:13, ESV), if you deliberately walk

toward it. God will not lead you into temptation, but you may lead yourself. If you expose yourself

to evil influences, you grieve the Spirit of God, and he may leave you to reap the results of your

folly. Would it not be wiser to repair the fence at once?

There is yet another consequence: the land itself may be lost. In England, a broken wall does not

remove ownership; but in Palestine, fields on hillsides were held in place by terraced walls. When

those walls collapsed, the soil slipped away, terrace by terrace, and vines and trees went with it.

Then rains washed the soil away entirely, leaving only barren rock.

So it is spiritually. A man may neglect himself and the things of God—becoming careless about

doctrine and holy living—until his power for good is gone. His mind, heart, and strength seem to

disappear. The prophet said, “Ephraim is like a dove, silly and without sense” (Hosea 7:11, ESV).

Many are such silly doves. The man who trifles with religion trifles with his soul and soon becomes

incapable of serious thought or useful service.

Therefore, stand firm in this evil day. When religious thought slides like mud into the Dead Sea of

unbelief, build solid walls around your life, faith, and character. “Stand therefore” (Ephesians 6:14,

ESV), and having done all, still stand. May the Holy Spirit root and establish you, so that you do

not cast away your confidence, “which has a great reward” (Hebrews 10:35, ESV).

Lastly, let me try to wake the sluggard. It is time to rise. The sun has already dried the dew. You

ask for “a little more sleep.” If you sleep a little longer, you may not wake until you lift up your

eyes in another world. Rise now. Leap from your bed before it becomes your grave.

Look at your heart. Neglect has allowed sins to grow like weeds. You have neglected God and

Christ until you have become worldly, careless, indifferent. Some of you once bore the sacred

name; now you resemble the world. Examine the results of your neglected walls. Compare yourself

with diligent believers—poor and uneducated perhaps—who serve Christ faithfully. With all your

gifts and opportunities, you have become an unprofitable servant. Is it not time to stir yourself?

Consider others who once intended to wake later. Some have fallen into open sin and dishonored

Christ. They only went a little farther than you. Your heart is much the same. Under similar

temptation, you might fall as they did. A slothful professor is ready for anything. A lazy heart is

tinder for the devil’s sparks.

Remember the coming of the Lord Jesus Christ. Will he find you sleeping? Remember the

judgment. What excuse will you offer for wasted time and unused talents, when the Master returns?

And you, my unconverted friend, if you drift through life without concern for your soul, you will

surely be lost. “If the righteous is scarcely saved, what will become of the ungodly and the sinner?”

(1 Peter 4:18, ESV). Salvation is entirely of grace; but grace does not produce laziness or

indifference. It produces energy, zeal, fervency, persistence, and self-denial.

May God grant us the indwelling of his Holy Spirit, that all may be set in order, sins uprooted from

the heart, and the whole person guarded by sanctifying grace from the destroyers that lurk near

every low wall. O Lord, in mercy remember us. Fence us by your power. Keep us from sloth that

would expose us to evil, for Jesus’ sake. Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 3. Frost And Thaw
fields.body_html:
Introduction

Snow blankets the earth, frost glitters, and ice forms—all under God’s command. Witness His

power and wisdom in nature’s swift transformations, revealing lessons of providence, care,

and divine order.

“He gives snow like wool; he scatters the frost like ashes. He hurls down his crystals of ice like

crumbs; who can stand before his cold? He sends out his word, and melts them; he makes his wind

blow and the waters flow.” — Psalm 147:16–18 (ESV)

Looking out of our window one morning, we saw the earth clothed in a white covering; for in only

a few short hours the ground had been covered to a considerable depth with snow. We looked out

again a few hours later and saw the fields as green as ever, and the ploughed land as bare as if not

a single flake had fallen.

It is not uncommon for a heavy fall of snow to be followed by a rapid thaw. These interesting changes are brought about by God, not only with a purpose toward the outward

world, but with some design toward the spiritual realm. God is always a teacher. In every action

he performs he is instructing his own children and opening to them the way into deeper mysteries.

Happy are those who find food for their heaven-born spirits, as well as for their minds, in the works

of the Lord’s hands.
