believe. It is a wonder that my Lord has not said, “You have done your duty with them; never

present Christ to them again; My Son shall not be insulted.” If you offer a beggar a coin and he

refuses it, you simply put it back in your pocket and walk away. You do not plead with him to

accept relief. Yet our God, in mercy, pleads with sinners to come to Him and implores them to

receive His Son. In gracious condescension He stands, as it were, like a merchant in the

marketplace, crying, “Ho, everyone who thirsts, come to the waters; and he who has no money,

come, buy and eat!” And elsewhere He says, “All day long I have held out My hands to a

disobedient and contrary people.”

When the Lord of mercy has been refused for so long, does not some righteous indignation mingle

with your pity? While you long for sinners to be saved, do you not feel there must be an end to

such insult? I ask even the careless to consider this. If they do not respect the ploughman, let them

at least consider his Master.

Moreover, there are so many others who need the gospel and would receive it, that wisdom seems

to suggest leaving those who despise it. Did not our Lord say that if the mighty works done in

Bethsaida and Chorazin had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented? Even more

astonishing, He said that if the same works had been done in Sodom and Gomorrah as were done

in Capernaum, they would have repented in sackcloth and ashes. Should we not then take the word

to those who will receive it and leave the despisers to their willfulness? Does not reason say, “Send

the medicine where there are sick people who value it”?

Thousands are willing to hear the gospel. See how they gather wherever the preacher goes — how

they press upon one another in their eagerness. If those who hear daily will not receive the message,

“then in God’s name,” says the preacher, “let me go where there is hope of soil that can be

ploughed.” “Shall horses run upon the rock? Will one plough there with oxen?” Must I always

labor where nothing results? Does not reason say, let the word go to China, to India, to the farthest

ends of the earth — where people will receive it — rather than remain where it is despised in the

streets?

I will not extend the argument further, but I ask the question again solemnly: Would any of you

continue pursuing an object once it proved hopeless? When the Lord has sent His servants with

kind, gracious, tender words and people refuse to hear, do you marvel that He says, “They are

joined to their idols; let them alone”? There is a limit to human patience, and we reach it quickly.

Surely there is also a limit — though we reach it slowly — to the patience of God. At last He says,

“It is enough. My Spirit shall no longer strive with them.” If the Lord declares this, can we

complain? Is this not wisdom? Does not prudence itself affirm it? Any thoughtful mind will agree:

a rock cannot be ploughed forever.

There must, then, be a change — and that soon. The oxen will be taken away from such labor. This

can be done easily and quickly, and in three ways.

First, the unresponsive hearer may be removed so that he no longer hears the gospel from the lips

of the minister most fitted to reach him. There may be a preacher who has some measure of

influence over him; but since he rejects the message and remains unrepentant, he may be relocated

to another place where he hears monotonous discourses that do not touch his conscience. He will

go where he is no longer urged and pleaded with, and there he will sleep himself into hell. That

can be done easily enough. Some of you may even now be arranging your own removal from the

field of hope.

Another possibility is this: the plowman may be taken away. He has done his work as faithfully as

he could, and he will be released from his difficult task. He is weary. Let him go home. The soil

would not break up, but that was not his fault. Let him receive his wages. His plow has been

damaged in the effort; let him go home and hear his Lord say, “Well done.” He was willing to

continue the discouraging labor as long as his Master commanded him, but if it is clearly fruitless,

then let him go home, for his work is finished. He has been seriously ill—let him die and enter into

his rest. This is not unlikely.

Or something else may happen. The Lord may say, “That field will trouble the plowman no more.

I will remove it.” And he may remove it in this way: the man who has heard the gospel but rejected

it may die. I pray that my Master will not allow any of you to die in your sins, for then we can no

longer reach you or hold even the faintest hope for you. No prayer of ours can follow you into

eternity.

There is one name by which you must be saved, and that name has been proclaimed to you—the

name of Jesus. But if you reject him now, even that name will not save you. If you refuse to receive

Jesus as your Savior, he will appear as your Judge. I plead with you: do not destroy your own soul

by stubbornly resisting almighty love.

God grant that something better may happen. Is there nothing else that can be done? This soil is

rock—can we sow it without breaking it up? No. Without repentance there is no forgiveness of

sins. Is there some way of saving people without the grace of God? The Lord Jesus never suggested

such a thing. Instead, he said, “Whoever believes and is baptized will be saved, but whoever does

not believe will be condemned” (Mark 16:16, ESV). He did not hint at a middle path or suggest a

“larger hope.” He plainly declared, “Whoever does not believe will be condemned.” Do not

imagine there is a hidden back door into heaven. The Lord has provided none.

What then? Should the preacher continue his seemingly fruitless labor? If even half a hope remains,

he is willing to go on and cry, “Hear, you deaf, and see, you blind, and live, you dead.” He will

speak that way today, because his Master commands him to preach the gospel to every creature.

But it is heavy work to repeat words of appeal for years to those who refuse to listen.

Yet there is still one more possibility. There is a God in heaven—let us pray that he would stretch

out his power. Jesus is at his right hand—let us ask for his intervention. The Holy Spirit is

almighty—let us call on him for help. Brothers who plow and sisters who pray, cry out to the

Master for aid. The horse and the ox may fail, but there is One above who can accomplish mighty

wonders. Did he not once speak to the rock and turn flint into a flowing stream? Let us ask him to

do the same now.

And if there is someone who feels and grieves that his heart is like a rock, I am glad he feels it.

The very awareness that your heart is hard is a sign that the stone may already be softening. O hard

heart, instead of striking you—as Moses struck the rock in the wilderness and sinned in doing so—

I would speak to you. Would you become like wax? Would you melt into streams of repentance?

Listen to God’s voice. Break with holy desire. Melt with longing for Christ, for God may even

now be at work within you. Who knows? At this very moment you may begin to crumble. Do you

feel the power of the Word? Does the sharp blade of truth pierce you now?

Break and break again, until through true sorrow you are softened. Then the good seed of the

gospel will enter your heart, and you will receive it, and we will see its fruit.

So I will cast one more handful of good seed before I finish. If you desire eternal life, trust in Jesus

Christ, and you are saved at once. “Turn to me and be saved, all the ends of the earth! For I am

God, and there is no other” (Isaiah 45:22). Whoever believes in him has eternal life. And as Jesus

said, “As Moses lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up, that

whoever believes in him may have eternal life” (John 3:14–15).

O Lord, break up the rock. Let the seed fall into the broken ground and bring a harvest even from

hardened stone, for the sake of Jesus Christ. Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 7
fields.body_html:
THE PARABLE OF THE SOWER Introduction

The sower scatters seed freely, yet not all soil receives it. Hearts may be hardened, distracted,

or entangled, preventing growth. God’s Word calls for receptive ground, patience, and

perseverance, reminding us that fruit depends on divine grace, not human effort.

“And when a great crowd was gathering and people from town after town came to him, he said in

a parable: ‘A sower went out to sow his seed. And as he sowed, some fell along the path and was

trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it. And some fell on the rock, and as it grew

up, it withered away, because it had no moisture. And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew

up with it and choked it. And some fell into good soil and grew and yielded a hundredfold.’ As he

said these things, he called out, ‘He who has ears to hear, let him hear.’” Luke 8:4–8.

In our country, when a farmer goes out to sow, he usually works in an enclosed field, scattering

seed from his basket along every ridge and furrow. But in the East, near small towns, farmland

was often an open stretch of ground. It was divided into different properties, but there were no

visible fences—only ancient boundary markers or perhaps small ridges of stones.

Footpaths ran through these open fields. The most traveled paths were called highways, though

they were nothing like our paved roads—just well-worn tracks, hardened by constant use. There

were also smaller side paths, made by travelers seeking safer routes or shortcuts. Over time, these

too became worn and firm.

When the sower went out to sow, he worked soil that had been scratched by a simple, primitive

plow. He aimed to scatter most of his seed there. But since a path ran through the middle of the

field, unless he left a wide strip unused, some seed would fall on the path. In another place, a rock

might rise close to the surface, covered only by a thin layer of soil. Seed would fall there as well.

In yet another corner, the ground might be tangled with the roots of nettles and thistles.

The farmer would scatter seed there too, and both the grain and the weeds would grow together—

until the stronger thorns choked the young plants so that they produced no mature fruit.

Remembering that the Bible was written in the East, and that its images come from that setting,

often helps us understand its meaning more clearly than if we picture only English farming

customs. The preacher of the Gospel is like that sower. He does not create the seed; it is given to

him by his divine Master. No one can create even the smallest grain that grows in the earth, much

less the heavenly seed that gives eternal life. The minister goes to his Master in private prayer and

asks to be taught the gospel. In that way, he fills his basket with the good seed of the kingdom.

Then he goes out in his Master’s name and scatters the precious truth. If he knew exactly where

the best soil was—where hearts had already been prepared by conviction—he might focus only

there. But since he cannot see into human hearts, he must preach the gospel to every creature. He

must scatter seed on hardened hearts, on distracted minds, and on those entangled in the cares and

pleasures of this world.

He must leave the results to the Lord who gave him the seed. He is not responsible for the harvest;

he is responsible only for faithfully and diligently doing his work. Even if not a single ear of grain

should ever make the reaper glad, the sower will still be rewarded by his Master if he has planted

the right seed with careful hands. Without this assurance, how could we avoid crying out with the

prophet, “Lord, who has believed what he has heard from us? And to whom has the arm of the

Lord been revealed?” (Isaiah 53:1, ESV).

Our duty is not determined by the character of our hearers but by the command of our God. We

must preach the gospel whether people listen or refuse. We must sow beside all waters. Whatever

condition hearts may be in, the minister must preach—to the rock as well as the furrow, to the path

as well as the plowed field.

Now I will speak about the four kinds of hearers described in our Lord’s parable. First, those like the path—hearers only. Second, those like rocky ground—briefly moved, but without lasting fruit. Third, those among thorns—where the word begins to grow, but is choked by life’s cares, the

deceitfulness of riches, and worldly pleasures.

And lastly, that small group—may God greatly increase it—the good soil, in whom the Word

produces abundant fruit.

I. The Path “Some fell along the path and was trampled underfoot, and the birds of the air devoured it.” Many of you do not come to worship seeking a blessing. You do not intend to worship God or to

be changed by what you hear. You are like the path, never meant to be a field of grain. If even one

seed of truth were to grow in you, it would be as surprising as wheat growing in the middle of a

busy street.

If the seed is skillfully scattered, some may rest briefly on your thoughts. You may not understand

it fully, but if it is presented attractively, you might discuss it for a time—until something more

entertaining captures your attention. Even that small benefit is short-lived. Soon you forget

everything you heard.

We wish we could hope that the Word would remain with you, but your heart is so hardened by

constant traffic that there is no place for the seed to take root. Satan continually passes over it with

blasphemies, lusts, lies, and empty distractions. Pride rolls across it like heavy wheels. Greed

tramples it down until it becomes hard as stone.

The seed finds no resting place. Thoughts rush back and forth constantly. Your soul has become a

marketplace where everything is traded. You are busy buying and selling, yet you do not realize

that you are selling the truth and buying your own destruction.

You say you have no time to think about spiritual things. The road of your heart is so crowded that

there is no room for the seed to grow. If it ever begins to sprout, some new amusement or

distraction crushes it before it matures. Just as grain could never grow in the busiest streets of a

city, so truth cannot grow in a heart filled with constant noise, pride, worry, and rebellion against

God.

We have looked at this hardened roadside; now let us consider what becomes of the good word

when it falls on such a heart.

The seed would have grown if it had fallen on proper soil. But it has landed in the wrong place,

and it remains as dry as when it first left the sower’s hand. The word of the gospel lies on the

surface of that heart but never enters it. It is like snow falling on a busy street: it touches the wet

pavement, melts, and disappears at once. The word has no time to awaken life in the soul. It rests

there briefly, but it never takes root or produces any lasting effect.

Why do people come to hear if the word never enters their hearts? That question has often puzzled

us. Some would not miss a Sunday for anything. They enjoy gathering for worship. Yet no tear

falls from their eyes. Their souls never rise to heaven in praise. They do not truly join in confession

of sin. They do not think seriously about coming judgment or the future state of their souls. Their

hearts are like iron; the minister might as well preach to a heap of stones.

What brings such unfeeling sinners here? At times it seems we would have as much hope of

converting wild beasts as these untamed, unresponsive hearts. Has all feeling vanished? Do people

attend worship merely because it is respectable? Or does coming help them feel more comfortable

in their sins? If they stayed away, conscience might trouble them; but by attending, they persuade

themselves that they are religious.

Oh, my hearers, your condition could make an angel weep. The sun of the gospel shines on your

face, yet your eyes remain blind. The music of heaven sounds in your ears, yet you do not truly

hear it. You can appreciate a turn of phrase. You can admire an illustration. But the spiritual

meaning—the living power within the message—you do not grasp. You sit at the wedding feast,

but you do not taste the food. Heaven rejoices over redeemed souls, yet you remain unredeemed,

without God and without Christ. Though we plead with you, pray for you, and weep over you, you

remain as hardened and careless as ever. May God have mercy on you and break up your hard

heart so that his word may dwell within you.

The picture is not yet complete. The passage tells us that the birds of the air devoured the seed. Is

there a wayside hearer here? Perhaps he did not intend to listen carefully today. When the sermon

ends, someone invites him into questionable company. He goes along, and the good seed is quickly

devoured.

There are many influences ready to snatch the gospel from a heart. The devil himself—whom

Scripture calls the “prince of the power of the air”—is always eager to steal away a good thought.

And he does not work alone. He has countless helpers. A spouse, children, friends, enemies,

customers, creditors—any of these may become instruments to consume the seed, and they often

succeed. What a tragedy that heavenly seed should become food for the devil—that God’s grain

should feed unclean birds.

If you have heard the gospel since childhood, how many wagonloads of sermons have been wasted

on you? In your younger days, you may have heard a faithful preacher who prayed for his

congregation until his eyes were red with tears. Do you remember the Sundays when you said to

yourself, “I will go to my room and pray”? But you did not. The birds devoured the seed, and you

continued in sin.

Even now, you are rarely absent from church. Yet the gospel falls on your soul as if it dropped

onto iron. The law may be preached with thunder—you do not mock it, but neither are you moved.

Christ may be lifted up before you. His wounds may be described. His blood may be set before

your eyes. You may be urged earnestly to look to him and live. But it is like sowing seed along the

seashore.

What shall I do for you? Shall I stand here and weep over this hardened path? My tears cannot

soften it; it has been trampled too long. Shall I bring the plow of the gospel? The blade cannot

penetrate soil so compacted. What then? O God, you alone know how to melt the hardest heart

through the precious blood of Jesus. Do it now, we pray. Glorify your grace by causing the good

seed to live and produce a heavenly harvest.

Now consider the second kind of hearer. Some seed fell upon rock, and as it grew up, it withered

away because it lacked moisture. You can picture that rock in the middle of the field, covered only

by a thin layer of soil. The seed falls there as it does everywhere else. It sprouts quickly. It grows

rapidly. Then it withers and dies.

Only those who deeply love souls can understand the hopes, joys, and bitter disappointments that

these rocky places have caused. There are hearers whose hearts seem soft and responsive. While

others feel nothing, these are visibly moved. Whether the message speaks of judgment or of

Christ’s love at the cross, they are stirred. Strong impressions are made.

They resolve to change, yet they delay. They are not hardened opponents of God. They appear

open and eager. Rejoicing, we direct the message toward them, and it seems to penetrate. But there

is hidden armor beneath the surface. No lasting wound is made.

Scripture describes them this way: “And these are the ones sown on rocky ground: the ones who,

when they hear the word, immediately receive it with joy. And they have no root in themselves,

but endure for a while; then, when tribulation or persecution arises on account of the word,

immediately they fall away” (Mark 4:16–17, ESV).

Have we not seen many who receive the word with joy? They have no deep conviction of sin, yet

they quickly profess faith in Christ. Their belief appears genuine. The seed has sprouted. There is

a green blade. We thank God, thinking a soul has been saved. But our joy is premature. The same

lack of depth that made them respond quickly also causes them to wither when difficulty comes.

We see this often. Someone asks to join the church and tells us how deeply a sermon moved them.

They say they believed at once and have never felt such happiness. We ask about conviction of

sin. They believe they were convicted. What they know for certain is that religion brings them

great pleasure.

We ask if they will continue, and they are confident that they will. Everything seems new. They

claim to hate what they once loved. And all of this has happened suddenly, without deep plowing

of the heart. It is as if a field were instantly covered with wheat by magic. Perhaps they are received

into fellowship. Within weeks they are less regular. When gently corrected, they explain that

opposition has made things difficult. Soon they disappear entirely. A little ridicule or

inconvenience has driven them back. The minister feels like a farmer who saw his field green and

flourishing, only to wake and find every shoot destroyed by frost.

If it is tragic to be a wayside hearer, it is hardly better to be like the rock. This second group gives

more initial hope. They gather eagerly, especially around a new minister. They seem devoted. But

time tests everything. What appeared strong proves shallow. When trials come, they fade away.

Some of you may belong to this group. You have felt deeply. You have resolved often. Yet years

pass, and nothing changes. There is no depth, no steady work of the Spirit. Must it remain so?

Shall one day your life be remembered as a plant that sprouted but never ripened? God forbid.

May the Spirit work deeply and effectively in you, so that you may yet bear fruit for God and bring

honor to Christ.

III. I shall briefly treat of the third class, and may the Spirit of God help me to deal faithfully with you.

“And some fell among thorns; and the thorns sprang up with it, and choked it.” Now, this was

good soil. The first two characters were bad; the wayside was not the proper place, the rock was

not a suitable situation for the growth of any plant; but this is good soil, for it grows thorns.

Wherever a thistle will spring up and flourish, there wheat would flourish too. This was rich, fertile

soil; it was no wonder therefore that the farmer dealt generously there, and threw handful after

handful upon that corner of the field. See how happy he is when in a month or two he visits the

spot. The seed has sprung up. True, there is a suspicious little plant down there of about the same

size as the wheat. “Oh!” he thinks, “that is not much, the corn will outgrow that. When it is stronger

it will choke these few thistles that have unfortunately mixed with it.” Ah, Mr. Farmer, you do not

understand the power of evil, or you would not dream like this! He comes again, and the seed has

grown, there is even corn in the ear; but the thistles, the thorns, and the briers have become

intertwined with one another, and the poor wheat can hardly get a ray of sunshine. It is so choked

with thorns on every side, that it looks quite yellow; the plant is starved. Still it keeps on growing,

and it does seem as if it would bring forth a little fruit. Alas, it never comes to anything. With it

the reaper never fills his arm.

We have this class very largely among us. These hear the word and understand what they hear.

They take the truth home; they think it over; they even go so far as to make a profession of religion.

The wheat seems to spring up and form an ear; it will soon come to perfection. Do not be in a

hurry; these men and women have a great deal to look after; they have the cares of a large business;

their establishment employs so many hundreds; do not be mistaken about their godliness—they

have no time for it. They will tell you that they must live; that they cannot neglect this world; that

they must somehow look after the present, and as for the future, they will give it proper attention

by and by. They continue to attend gospel preaching, and the poor little stunted blade of religion

keeps on growing in a fashion.

Meanwhile they have grown rich; they come to the place of worship in a carriage; they have all

that heart can wish. Ah! now the seed will grow, will it not? No, no.

They have no cares now; the shop is given up, they live in the country; they no longer have to ask,

“Where shall the money come from to meet the next bill?” or “How shall we provide for an

increasing family?” Now they have too much instead of too little, for they have riches, and they

are too wealthy to be gracious. “But,” says one, “they might spend their riches for God.” Certainly

they might, but they do not, for riches are deceitful. They have to entertain much company, and go

along with the world, and so Christ and his church are left behind.

Yes, but they begin to spend their riches, and they have surely overcome that difficulty, for they

give generously to the cause of Christ, and they are liberal in charity; the little blade will grow,

will it not? No, for now look at the thorns of pleasure. Their generosity to others involves

generosity to themselves; their pleasures, amusements, and vanities choke the wheat of true

religion; the good grains of gospel truth cannot grow because they must attend that musical party,

that ball, and that soirée, and so they cannot think about the things of God. I know several examples

of this class. I knew one, high in court circles, who confessed to me that he wished he were poor,

for then he might enter the kingdom of heaven. He said to me, “Ah, sir, these politics, these politics,

I wish I were rid of them, they are eating the life out of my heart. I cannot serve God as I would.”

I know of another, burdened with riches, who said to me, “Ah, sir, it is an awful thing to be rich;

one cannot keep close to the Saviour with all this earth around him.”

Ah, my dear readers, I will not ask that God lay you on a bed of sickness, that he strip you of all

your wealth, and bring you to poverty; but, oh, if he were to do it, and you were to save your souls,

it would be the best bargain you could ever make. If those mighty ones who now complain that the

thorns choke the seed could give up all their riches and pleasures, if those who live in luxury every

day could take the place of Lazarus at the gate, it would be a happy change for them if their souls

might be saved. A man may be honorable and rich, and yet go to heaven; but it will be hard work,

for “It is easier for a camel to go through the eye of a needle than for a rich person to enter the

kingdom of God.” God does cause some rich people to enter the kingdom of heaven, but hard is

their struggle. Steady, young man, steady! Do not hurry to climb to wealth! It is a place where

many heads are turned. Do not ask God to make you popular; those who have popularity are

wearied by it. Cry with Agur, “Give me neither poverty nor riches.” God grant that I may walk in

the golden mean, and may I always have in my heart that good seed, which shall bring forth fruit

a hundredfold to his own glory.

IV. I now close with the last character, namely, the good ground. Of the good soil, as you will notice,

we have but one in four. Will one in four of our hearers, with a well-prepared heart, receive the

Word?

The ground is described as “good”; not that it was good by nature, but it had been made good by

grace. God had ploughed it; he had stirred it up with the plough of conviction, and there it lay in

ridge and furrow as it should lie. When the gospel was preached, the heart received it, for the man

said, “That is exactly the blessing I want. Mercy is what a needy sinner requires.” So the preaching

of the gospel brought comfort to this disturbed and ploughed soil. Down fell the seed to take good

root. In some cases it produced fervent love, largeness of heart, and devotedness of purpose of a

noble kind, like seed which produces a hundredfold. The man became a mighty servant for God;

he spent himself and was spent. He took his place in the front ranks of Christ’s army, stood in the

hottest part of the battle, and did deeds of courage which few could accomplish—the seed produced

a hundredfold. It fell into another heart of the same kind; the man could not do the most, but still

he did much. He gave himself to God, and in his business he had a word to say for his Lord; in his

daily walk he quietly adorned the doctrine of God his Saviour—he brought forth sixtyfold. Then

it fell on another, whose abilities and talents were small; he could not be a star, but he would be a

glow-worm; he could not do as the greatest, but he was content to do something, however humble.

The seed had brought forth in him tenfold, perhaps twentyfold. How many are there of this sort

here? Is there one who prays within himself, “God be merciful to me, a sinner”? The seed has

fallen in the right place. Soul, your prayer shall be heard. God never sets a person longing for

mercy without intending to give it. Does another whisper, “Oh that I might be saved”? Believe in

the Lord Jesus Christ, and you, even you, will be saved. Have you been the chief of sinners? Trust

Christ, and your great sins shall vanish as a millstone sinks beneath the flood. Is there no one here

who will trust the Saviour? Can it be possible that the Spirit is entirely absent? that he is not moving

in one soul? not giving life in one spirit? We will pray that he may now descend, that the word

may not be in vain.

fields.title: Chapter 8
fields.body_html:
THE PRINCIPAL WHEAT Introduction

The farmer sows the principal wheat, giving chief care to what matters most. So must we in life:

identify the greatest good—salvation, holiness, and Christ—and devote our minds, hearts, and

actions to cultivating it above all else.

“The principal wheat.” Isaiah 28:25 The prophet mentions it as a matter of wisdom on the part of the farmer, that he knows what is the

principal thing to cultivate, and makes it his chief care. The text, with the connection, runs thus:

“Does not the farmer sow the principal wheat?” He does not go to the granary and take out wheat,

and cummin, and barley, and rye, and scatter these about carelessly, but he estimates the value of

each grain, and arranges them in his mind accordingly. He does not think that cummin and

caraway, which he grows merely to flavor his meal, are of half such importance as his bread-corn;

and, though rye and barley have their value, yet he does not consider even these equal to what he

calls “the principal wheat.” He is a man of judgment; he arranges things; he places the most

important crop in the front rank, and spends upon it the most care.

Here let us learn a lesson. Do keep things clear in your minds—not mixed and muddled by careless

thought. Do not live a confused life, without care and discretion, running everything together; but

sort things out, and divide and distinguish between the precious and the worthless. See what this

is worth, and what the other is worth, and set your matters in rank and order, making some of them

principal, and others of them secondary. I suggest to you young people especially that, in starting

life, you say to yourselves, “What shall we live for? There is a principal thing for which we ought

to live; what shall it be?” Have you really considered that question, or have you gone at it at

random? What are you living for? What is your principal aim? Is it to be that of the old gentleman

in Horace who said to his boy, “Get money; get it honestly, if you can; but, by all means, get

money”? Will you be a money-maker? Shall money be your principal corn?

Or will you choose a life of pleasure—“a short life and a merry one,” as so many fools have said

to their deep regret? Is it in dissipation that your life is to be spent? Are thistles to be your principal

crop? Because there is a certain pleasure in looking at a Scotch thistle, do you intend to grow acres

of pleasurable vice? And will you make your bed upon them when you come to die? Search and

see what is worthy to be the principal object in life; and, when you have found it, then ask the Holy

Spirit to help you to choose that one thing, and to give all your powers and faculties to cultivating

it. The farmer, who finds that wheat ought to be his principal crop, makes it so, and directs his

efforts with that end in view; learn from this to have a main object, and to give your whole mind

to it.

This farmer was wise, because he counted that to be principal which was most necessary. His

family could do without cummin, which was only a flavoring. Perhaps the mistress might

complain, or the cook might grumble, but that did not matter so much as it would if the children

cried for bread. They certainly must have wheat, for bread is the staff of life. It is bread that

strengthens man’s heart, and therefore the farmer must grow wheat if he grows nothing else. What

is necessary he regarded as the principal thing. Is not this simple common sense? If we were wisely

to sit down and consider, should we not say, “To have my sins forgiven, to be right with God, to

be holy, to be fit to live eternally in heaven, is the greatest and most necessary thing for me, and

therefore I will make it the principal object of my pursuit”? A creature cannot be satisfied unless

he is fulfilling the purpose for which he was created; and the purpose of every intelligent creature

is first, to glorify God, and next, to enjoy God. What a joy it must be to enjoy God himself for ever

and ever! Other things may be desirable, but this one thing is necessary. A sufficient income, a

measure of respect among men, a degree of health—all these are the flavoring of life; but to be

saved in the Lord with an everlasting salvation is life itself. Jesus Christ is the bread by which our

soul’s best life is sustained. Oh, that we were all wise enough to feel that to be one with Christ is

the one thing necessary; that to be at peace with God is the principal thing; that to be brought into

harmony with the Most High is the true music of our being. Other herbs may take their place in

proper order, but grace is the principal wheat, and we must cultivate it.

This farmer was wise, because he made that the principal thing which was most fit to be so. Of

course, barley is useful as food, for nations have lived on barley bread, and lived healthily too; and

rye has been the nourishment of millions; neither have they starved on oats and other grains.

Still, give me a piece of wheaten bread, for it is the best support for life’s journey. This farmer

knew that wheat was the most suitable food for man, and so he did not put the inferior grain, which

might serve as a substitute, into the prominent place; but he gave his wheat the preference. He did

not say, “the principal barley,” or “the principal rye,” much less “the principal cummin,” or “the

principal fitches,” but “the principal wheat.”

And what is there, brethren, that is so fit for the heart, the mind, the soul of man, as to know God

and his Christ? Other mental foods, such as the fruits of knowledge and the delights of science,

excellent though they may be, are inferior nourishment and unsuitable to build up the inner man.

In my God and my Saviour, I find my heaven and my all. My soul feeds on a crumb of truth about

Jesus, and finds deep satisfaction in living upon it. The more we know God, and enjoy God, and

become like God, and the more Christ is our daily bread, the more we perceive the fitness of all

this for our new-born natures. O beloved, make that your principal object which is the fittest pursuit

of an immortal mind.

“Religion is the chief concern Of mortals here below; May I its great importance learn, Its sovereign virtue know!” “More needful this than glittering wealth, Or aught the world bestows;

Not reputation, food, or health,

Can give us such repose.”

Moreover, this farmer was wise, because he made that the principal thing which was most

profitable. Under certain circumstances, in our own country, wheat is not the most profitable crop

a man can grow; but ordinarily, it is the best crop the earth yields, and therefore the text speaks of

“the principal wheat.” Our grandfathers used to rely upon the wheat stack to pay their rent. They

looked to their corn as the source of their strength; and though it may not be so now, it was so of

old, and perhaps it may yet be so again.

In any case, the illustration holds true with regard to true religion. That is the most profitable thing.

I am told that rich men find it very hard to secure anything that yields five percent nowadays; but

this blessed fear of the Lord is an extraordinarily profitable investment, for it does not yield a

hundred percent, or a thousand percent, but a man begins with nothing and all things become his

by faith.

Being freely forgiven of our sins, we are by overflowing grace greatly enriched, so that we count

among our possessions heaven itself, Christ himself, God himself. All things are ours. Oh, what a

blessed crop to sow! What a harvest comes from it! Godliness is profitable for the present life, and

for the life to come. Godliness is a blessing to a man’s body—it keeps him from drunkenness and

vice; and it is a blessing to his soul—it makes him gentle and pure. It is a blessing to him in every

way. If I had to die like a dog, I would prefer to live like a Christian. If there were no hereafter,

still, for comfort and joy, give me the life of one who strives to live like Christ. There is a practical

everyday truth in the verse—

“’It is religion that can give

Sweetest pleasures while we live;

’It is religion must supply

Solid comfort when we die.” Only that religion must not be of the common sort; it must have as its root a sincere faith in Jesus

Christ. See to it. Our religion must be either everything or nothing, either first or nowhere. Make

it “the principal wheat,” and it will richly repay you.

II. Secondly, the husbandman is a lesson to us because he gives this principal thing the principal

place. I find that the Hebrew is rendered by some eminent scholars, "He puts the wheat into the

principal place." That little handful of cummin for the wife to flavor the cakes with he grows in a

corner; and the various herbs he places in their proper borders. The barley he sets in its plot, and

the rye in its acre; but if there is a good bit of rich soil—the best he has—he appropriates it to the

principal wheat. He gives his choicest fields to that which is to be the main means of his living.

Now, here is a lesson for you and for me. Let us give to true godliness our principal powers and

abilities. Let us give to the things of God our best and most intense thought.

I pray you, do not take religion at second hand from what I tell you, or from what somebody else

tells you; but think it over. Read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest the word of God. The thoughtful

Christian is the growing Christian. Remember, the service of God deserves our first consideration

and endeavor. We are poor things at our prime, but we ought to give the Lord nothing short of our

best. God would not have us serve him heedlessly, but he would have us use all the brain and

intellect and mind that we have in studying and practicing his word. "Acquaint now yourself with

him, and be at peace" (Job 22:21). "Meditate on these things; give yourself wholly to them" (1

Timothy 4:15). If your mind is more clear and active at one time than at another, then sow the

principal wheat. If you feel more fresh and more inclined to think at one time of the day than at

another, let your mind then go towards the best things.

Be sure, also, to yield to this subject your most earnest love. The best field in the little estate of

manhood is not the head, but the heart; sow the principal wheat there. Oh, to have true religion in

the heart; to love what we know—intensely to love it; to hold it fast as with the grip of life and

death—never to let it go! The Lord says, "My son, give me your heart" (Proverbs 23:26, ESV),

and he will not be contented with anything less than our heart. Oh, when your zeal is most burning,

and your love is most fervent, let the warmth and the fervency all go towards the Lord your God,

and to the service of him who has redeemed you with his precious blood. Let the principal wheat

have the principal part of your nature. Towards God and his Christ also turn your most fervent

desires. When you enlarge your desire, desire Christ; when you become ambitious let your

ambition be all for God. Let your hunger and your thirst be after righteousness. Let your aspirations

and your longings be all towards holiness, and the things that shall make you like to Christ. Give

to this principal wheat your principal desires.

Then let the Lord have the attentive respect of your life. Let the principal wheat be sown in every

action. If we are truly Christians we must be as much Christians outside the church as in it. We

shall try to make our eating and our drinking, and everything we do, tend to the glory of God.

Draw no line between the secular and the religious part of your conduct, but let the secular be made

religious by a devout desire to glorify God in the one as much as in the other (1 Corinthians 10:31).

Let us worship God in the commonest duties of life, even as they do who stand before his throne.

So it ought to be. Let us sow the principal wheat in all the fields of our conversation, in business,

in the family, among our friends, and with our children.

May we each one feel, "For me to live is Christ. I cannot live without Christ, or for anything but

Christ" (Philippians 1:21, ESV). Let your whole nature yield itself to Jesus, and to none else.

We should give to this principal wheat our most earnest labors. We should spend ourselves for the

spread of the gospel. A Christian man ought to lay himself out to serve Jesus. I hate to see a

professing man zealous in politics and lukewarm in devotion; all on fire at a parish vestry, and

chill as winter when he comes to a prayer-meeting. Some fly like eagles when they are serving the

world, but they have a broken wing in the service of God. This should not be. If anything could

rouse us up, and make the lion within us roar in his strength, it should be when we confront the

foes of Jesus or fight in his cause. Our Lord's service is the principal wheat; let us labor most in

connection with it.

This, I think, should also take possession of us so as to lead to our greatest sacrifices. The love of

Christ ought to be so strong as to swallow up self, and make sacrifice our daily joy. For Christ's

name's sake we should be willing to endure poverty, reproach, slander, exile, death. Nothing should

be dear to a Christian in comparison with Christ. Now, I will put it to you whether it is so or no. Is

the love of Jesus the principal wheat with us? Are we giving our religion the chief place or not? I

am afraid some people treat religion as certain gentlemen treat an off-hand farm; they put a bailiff

into it, and only give an eye to it now and then. Their minister is the bailiff, and they expect him

to see to it for them. These off-hand farms are losing concerns.

Look at these half-and-half brethren. They have religion? Certainly. But they are like the man of

whom the child spoke at the Sunday-school. "Is your father a Christian?" said the teacher. "Yes,"

said the child, "but he has not worked much at it lately." I could point out several of this sort, who

are sowing their wheat very sparingly, and choosing the most barren patch to sow it in. They

profess to be Christians, but religion is a tenth-rate article on their farm. Some have a large acreage

for the world, and a poor little plot for Christ. They are growers of worldly pleasure and self-

indulgence, and they sow a little religion by the roadside for appearance’s sake. This will not do.

God will not thus be mocked (Galatians 6:7). If we despise him and his truth we shall be lightly

esteemed. O come, let us give our principal time, talent, thought, effort to that which is the chief

concern of immortal spirits. May we imitate the husbandman who gives the principal wheat the

principal place in his farm.

III. Let us learn a third lesson. The husbandman selects the principal seed-corn when he is sowing

his wheat. When a farmer is setting aside wheat for sowing, he does not choose the tail corn and

the worst of his produce, but if he is a sensible man he likes to sow the best wheat in the world.

Many farmers search the country round for a good sample of wheat for sowing, for they do not

expect to get a good harvest out of bad seed. The husbandman is taught of God to put into the

ground "the principal wheat." Let me learn that if I am going to sow to the Lord and be a Christian,

I should sow the best kind of Christianity.

I should try to do this, first, by believing the weightiest doctrines. I would believe not this "ism,"

nor that, but the unadulterated truth which Jesus taught; for a holy character will only grow by the

Spirit of God out of true doctrine. Falsehood breeds sin; truth begets and fosters holiness. You and

I therefore ought to select our seed carefully, and cast out all error. If we are wise we shall think

most of the most important truths, for I have known people attach the greatest importance to the

smallest things. They fight over the fitches, and leave the wheat to the crows. As for me, those

who will may dispute over vials and trumpets; I shall mainly preach the doctrine of the precious

blood and the glorious truths of substitution and atonement. These doctrines are the principal

wheat, and therefore these shall have my choice.

Next to that, we ought to sow the noblest examples. Many men are dwarfed because they choose

a bad model to start with. They imitate dear old Mr. So-and-so till they grow wonderfully like him

with the best of him left out. A minister happens to be of a gloomy turn of mind, and he preaches

the deep experience of the children of God, and in consequence a band of good people think it their

duty to be melancholy. Why need they fall into a ditch because their leader has splashed himself?

We should never copy any man's infirmities. To be like Paul there is no need to have weak eyes;

to be like Thomas there is no necessity to doubt. If you copy any good man, there is a point at

which you ought to stop short. If I must have a human model, I would prefer one of the bravest of

the saints of God; but oh how much better to follow that perfect pattern which you have in Christ

Jesus!

We should sow the best wheat by seeing that we have the purest spirit. Alas! how soon do spirits

become soiled by self or pride, or despondency or sloth, or some earthly taint. But what a grand

thing it is to live in the spirit of Christ! May we be humble, lowly, bold, self-sacrificing, pure,

chaste, and holy.

And then, there is one more mode of sowing selected seed. We should endeavor to live in the

closest communion with God. A dear brother prayed just now that we might have as much grace

as we were capable of receiving, and that God would bring us into such a state that we might not

hinder him in anything which he willed to do by us. This is a good prayer. It should be our desire

to rise to the highest form of spiritual life. If you sow this principal wheat, get the best sort of it.

There is a spirit and a spirit; and there are doctrines and doctrines; the best is the best for you. O

young men, if you mean to have piety, go in for it thoroughly. Do not sneak through the world as

if you were ashamed of your Lord. If you are Christ's, show your colors. Rally to his banner, gather

to his trumpet call, and then stand up, stand up for Jesus. If there is any manhood in you, this great

cause calls for it all; exhibit it, and may the Spirit of God help you so to do.

IV. Fourthly, the husbandman grows the principal wheat with the principal care. Some critics say

that the proper translation is that the husbandman plants his wheat in rows. It is said that the large

crops in Palestine in olden times were due to the fact that they planted the wheat. They set it in

lines so that it was not checked or suffocated by being too thick in one place, neither was there any

fear of its being too thin in another. The wheat was planted, and then streams of water were turned

by the foot to each particular plant. No wonder, therefore, that the land brought forth abundantly.

This is a lesson for us. We must not give a careless, half-hearted attention to the things of God.

The principal wheat requires careful cultivation—our hearts, minds, and lives must be deliberately

trained for holiness. As it is written, “And some fell among thorns, and the thorns grew up and

choked it” (Matthew 13:7). Let us avoid sowing the best of our hearts in a distracted, worldly

manner, or we shall find our fruitfulness choked.

Just as the husbandman waters each row, so must we nurture every part of our spiritual life. “But

the seed falling on good soil refers to someone who hears the word and understands it. This is the

one who produces a crop, yielding a hundred, sixty, or thirty times what was sown” (Matthew

13:23). The care we give to our principal wheat—our devotion to Christ, our love for God, our

obedience—determines the abundance of the harvest. Do not neglect the principal; give your best

thought, your deepest love, your strongest efforts, to the cultivation of your soul in Christ.

Let the principal wheat have the principal care in your life. Let your heart, mind, and conduct all

be devoted to God. Sow diligently, water faithfully, guard carefully. Then you will see the blessing

of a fruitful harvest, and your life will yield abundantly to God’s glory.

We should give our main attention to the most important thing. Our godliness should be carried

out with care and thoughtfulness. Brothers, are we careful enough in our spiritual walk? Have you

examined the depth of your profession? Why are you a member of a particular church? Because

your mother was? That is some reason, but it is not enough to justify you before God. I urge you

to honestly assess your standing. If any Christian minister is afraid to call you to this duty, I

question him. I am not afraid. I ask you to examine everything I teach, for I do not want to be

responsible for another man’s beliefs. Like the Bereans, check and see whether these things are

true according to Scripture (Acts 17:11).

One of the greatest blessings for the church would be a spirit of inquiry that tests everything against

the Word of God. If people speak contrary to Scripture, it is because there is no light in them. Serve

God as carefully as an Eastern farmer planted his wheat, placing it in orderly rows with care and

precision. You serve a precise God, so serve Him precisely. He is a jealous God, so be careful to

avoid even the smallest error or form of self-worship (Exodus 20:5).

Also, water every part of your spiritual life as the farmer waters each plant. Pray for grace from

above, so that no part of your faith, hope, or love ever dries up. Serve each part of your soul as a

farmer serves his wheat. Make grace your main concern, for it deserves it.

With this I conclude: focus on this, because from it you can expect your main harvest. If religion

is the most important thing, you can expect your main reward from it. The harvest will come in

various ways. You will achieve the greatest success in life if you live wholly for God’s glory.

Success or failure depends largely on the focus of our efforts. It is useless for me to try to conduct

a choir—I am not made for that—but I may succeed in preaching, because that is my calling.

Christian, if you live for the world, you will not prosper, for you are not made for it. Grace has

made you unsuitable for sin. If you live for God with all your heart, you will succeed, because God

made you for this purpose. Just as He made the fish for water and the birds for air, He made the

believer for holiness and for serving Him. You will be out of your element, like a fish out of water

or a bird in the stream, if you abandon God’s service. The Eastern farmer’s success depends on his

wheat; yours depends on your devotion to God. Look to godliness for your joy. Is there any

happiness like knowing you are in Christ and loved by the Lord? It is in your faith that you will

find comfort on a sick and dying bed, and that time may come soon.

In the life to come, what a harvest will result from serving the Lord! What does the world give?

Only smoke. A man may make a million dollars and die—what has he gained? A man’s fame may

spread across the earth, yet he dies—what remains? Living for the world is like children playing

in the street for coins or shells. Life for God is real and lasting; everything else is waste. Let us

remember this and dedicate ourselves to serving the Lord. May the Spirit help us to sow the

“principal wheat” and live in joyful expectation of reaping a harvest, as promised: “Those who

sow in tears shall reap with shouts of joy” (Psalm 126:5).

fields.title: Chapter 9
fields.body_html:
SPRING IN THE HEART Introduction

God blesses the springtime of the soul, preparing hearts for growth. As He waters the earth, so

His Spirit nurtures new faith, tender desires, prayer, and hope, laying the foundation for a

fruitful and enduring spiritual harvest.

"You visit the earth and water it; you greatly enrich it; the river of God is full of water; you provide

their grain, for so you prepare the land." Psalm 65:9-10

Though other seasons may excel in fullness, spring stands out for freshness and beauty. We thank

God when harvest time comes and golden grain is ready, but we should also thank Him for spring,

which prepares the harvest. April showers bring May flowers, and winter’s cold and wet bring the

beauty of summer. God blesses the spring, just as He provides for summer; therefore, we should

praise Him all year.

Spiritual spring is a blessed time in a church. Young faith is developing, and we hear joyfully, “We

have found the Lord.” Our children spring up like grass and willows by the water. We marvel and

ask, “Who are these that come like clouds, like doves to their windows?” During revival, when

God brings many to Himself, the church rejoices and can say, “You bless the springing of it”

(Psalm 65:9-10, ESV).

I will focus on individual cases. There is a time when grace begins to spring, just as a bud breaks

through the cold, hard earth. I want to speak about the blessing given to the green blade of new

godliness, to those beginning to hope in the Lord.

1. Work Before the Spring The text shows that God alone must do some work before springing comes, and He works through

us too. There is work for us. Before new life appears in a soul, there must be plowing, harrowing,

and sowing. The ground must be prepared, but we do not expect to reap immediately.

Blessed be God, sometimes the reaper overtakes the plowman, but not always. In some hearts, God

convicts long and deeply; the law digs deeply until every part of the soul is plowed. Conviction

reaches the core of the spirit, wounding it. When God works, the soil of the heart is broken by His

presence.

Then comes sowing. For springing to occur, something must be sown. After the preacher uses the

plow of the law, he applies for the gospel’s seed. Promises of the gospel, doctrines, and clear

teaching on free grace and the atonement are scattered like handfuls of seed. Some fall on the path

and are lost, but others fall on prepared soil and remain.

Next is the harrowing. We cannot leave the seed after sowing; it must be prayed over. The prayers

of the preacher and the church cover the seed, hiding it in the heart of the listener.

I emphasise this to encourage those who have not seen immediate results—not to give up—but

also as a warning against expecting a harvest without preparation. Sudden revivals without

prayerful labor rarely last. A lasting revival grows from much effort, longing, pleading, and

watching. The servant of God preaches whether the people are ready or not, but for great success,

hearts must be prepared.

2. Work Beyond Our Power After plowing, sowing, and harrowing, there must come the rain from heaven. “You visit the earth

and water it” (Psalm 65:9). Our efforts are in vain without God’s blessing through the Spirit. O

Holy Spirit, only You work wonders in the human heart, coming from the Father and Son to fulfill

God’s purposes.

Three effects are described: Watering the ridges: Just as rain saturates the ridges, the Spirit moves and influences every part of

the heart. Understanding is enlightened, conscience quickened, will controlled, and affections

inflamed. We present gospel truth, but only God’s Spirit can truly affect the heart.

Settling the furrows: Heavy rain compacts the soil. Similarly, the Spirit humbles and steadies the

soul. A proud, unsettled heart becomes solid and serious. Lofty thoughts and carnal pride are

leveled. Genuine humility is a gracious fruit of the Spirit. “A broken and contrite heart, O God,

you will not despise” (Psalm 51:17).

Softening with showers: Man’s heart is naturally hard, like dry soil. The Spirit softens it

completely. The once-hard heart feels and responds; tears flow, tenderness grows.

All this is God’s work. God works through us, but He alone sends the rain of grace. Perhaps He is

at work in some of you now, though spiritual life has not yet appeared. Your condition may seem

sad, but we hope that soon the seed of grace will sprout, and may the Lord bless the springing

thereof.

II. In the second place, let us give a brief description of the springing thereof. After the work of

the Holy Spirit has been quietly going on for a certain time, as pleases the great Master and

Farmer, there begin to appear signs of grace. Remember the apostle’s words: “First the blade,

then the ear, then the full grain in the ear” (Mark 4:28). Some are greatly disturbed because they

do not see the full grain in the ear in themselves. They suppose that if they were the subjects of

divine work, they would be just like certain mature Christians with whom they commune, or

about whom they may have read in biographies. Beloved, this is a great mistake. When grace

first enters the heart, it is not like a great tree covering acres with its shadow, but like the smallest

of seeds, like a mustard seed. When it first rises in the soul, it is not the sun shining at high noon,

but the first faint ray of dawn. Are you so simple as to expect the harvest before you have passed

through the springing-time? I hope that by describing the earliest stage of Christian experience,

you may be able to say, “I have gone as far as that,” and then take comfort from the text: “You

bless the springing thereof” (Psalm 65:9-10).

What then is the springing up of piety in the heart? We think it first appears in sincere, earnest

desires after salvation. The person is not yet saved in their own view, but longs to be. What was

once indifferent is now a matter of intense concern. Once they despised Christians and thought

them needlessly earnest, thought religion trivial, and regarded the things of this world as the only

substantial matters; but now they are changed. They envy the humblest Christian, and would gladly

exchange places with even the poorest believer if they could be assured of a home in heaven.

Worldly things have lost dominion, and spiritual things are uppermost. Once, like many, they cried,

“Who will show us any good?” but now they cry, “Lift up the light of your face upon me, O Lord”

(Psalm 4:6). Once it was grain and wine that brought comfort, but now it is God alone. Their rock

of refuge must be God, for they find no comfort elsewhere. Their holy desires, once fleeting like

smoke from a chimney, are now enduring, though not always equally strong.

At times, these desires become a hungering and thirsting after righteousness, yet they are not

satisfied and long for a still deeper yearning after heavenly things. These desires are among the

first springings of divine life in the soul.

“The springing thereof” next shows itself in prayer. It is now true prayer. Once, the words were a

mockery of God, sounds without the heart; but now, though the prayer is such that no human ear

might hear it, God approves it, for it is the communication of a spirit to God, not the muttering of

lips to an unknown God. The prayers may be short: “Oh!” “Ah!” “Would to God!” “Lord, have

mercy on me, a sinner!” and similar brief cries; yet they are prayers. “Behold, he prays” does not

refer to length, but even a sigh or tear proves spiritual life. These “groanings that cannot be uttered”

are part of “the springing thereof” (Romans 8:26).

There will also appear a love for the means of grace and for God’s house. The Bible, long unread

and considered of little more value than an old almanac, is now treated with respect. Even if it

brings little immediate comfort and much alarm, it is still the book for the soul, and the reader

turns to its pages with hope. In attending God’s house, the believer listens eagerly, hoping for a

message from the Lord. Previously, worship was attended as a social duty; now it is for the purpose

of finding the Savior. Once there was no more religion in the soul than in a door swinging on its

hinges; now the heart enters the house praying, “Lord, meet with my soul,” and if no blessing

comes, it leaves sighing, “O that I knew where I might find Him, that I might come even to His

seat.” This is one of the blessed signs of “the springing thereof.”

Yet another sign is that the soul begins to have faith in Jesus Christ, at least to some degree. It may

not yet bring great joy or peace, but it keeps the heart from despair and prevents it from sinking

under the weight of sin. I have known times when no one could perceive faith in me, and I could

scarcely perceive it in myself, yet I was bold to say with Peter, “Lord, you know all things; you

know that I love you” (John 21:17). What man cannot see, Christ sees. Many are so focused on

their small faith that they fail to recognize it; but if they look to Christ and not to their faith, they

will see both Christ and their own faith. They may compare themselves to mature believers and

feel their faith is too small, but even the tiniest faith to receive Christ is enough. Remember: “To

all who received him, he gave the right to become children of God” (John 1:12). Weak faith is still

faith, and God blesses “the springing thereof.”

The difficulty often comes from misunderstanding or lack of trust in God. Misunderstanding is

like seeing green wheat for the first time and thinking it is just grass. Yet as one becomes familiar

with it, it is not strange to see wheat go through stages: first the blade, then the ear, and finally the

full grain in the ear. Many newly converted believers feel they are nothing like mature Christians,

but they are simply at an earlier stage. One must go through the blade stage before the ear stage,

and in the ear stage, there may be doubts about ever reaching the full grain; but in due time,

maturity will come. Thank God that you are in Christ at all. Whether faith is large or small, whether

you can do much or little for Christ, salvation depends not on what you are but on what Jesus

Christ is. Trusting in Him, however small your faith, keeps you as safe as the strongest of the

saints.

Yet alongside misunderstanding, there is often unbelief. Not all is excusable ignorance; there is

sinful unbelief as well. O sinner, why do you not trust Christ? God gives you His word that those

who trust Him are not condemned, yet you may fear that you are. This doubts God’s truth. Be

ashamed that you have doubted His promise. All other sins grieve Christ less than the sin of

suspecting that He will not forgive, or that He will cast away one who trusts Him. Do not slander

His gracious character. “Whoever comes to me I will never cast out” (John 6:37, ESV). Come in

faith, and He will receive you immediately.

I have thus described “the springing thereof.” III. Thirdly, according to the text, there is one who sees this springing: Thou, Lord—“You bless

the springing thereof” (Psalm 65:9).

I wish we had keener eyes to see the beginnings of grace in others; through our lack of

attentiveness, we let slip many opportunities to help the weak. If a mother tends her own children,

she notices the first signs of illness immediately; how much more should we watch tenderly over

precious souls. Many young believers may endure weeks or months of unnecessary distress if we

who know the Lord are not attentive. Shepherds stay up all night at lambing time to catch and

nurse newborn lambs; we, as shepherds for God, should watch over all the newborn in His fold,

especially when many are coming to Him, for tender care is needed in the first stages of new life.

Even when we miss it, God sees “the springing thereof.”

Silent, withdrawn souls who dare not speak to anyone, take comfort: God sees your new life. Even

if you only think, “I will arise and go to my Father,” He hears you. Even if it is only a desire, He

registers it. “You have collected my tears in your bottle; are they not in your book?” (Psalm 56:8).

He watches your return, embraces you, and welcomes you with tender love. Be encouraged that

wherever you are—in your room or in secret—God is there. “You God see me” (Genesis 16:13).

“The Lord takes pleasure in those who fear him, in those who hope in his steadfast love” (Psalm

147:11).

Even a small beginning of fear or hope delights Him. “You will perfect the thing that concerns

me” (Psalm 138:8). If your soul is concerned about reconciliation with God and having an interest

in Christ’s blood, it is only “the springing thereof,” yet He blesses it. “A bruised reed he will not

break, and a smoldering wick he will not quench, until he brings justice to victory” (Matthew

12:20). Victory comes even before the soul is fully mature; even the weakest beginnings are under

God’s care, and He sees the first springing of grace.

IV. A few words on a fourth point: what a misery it would be, if it were possible, to have this

springing without God’s blessing! The text says, “You bless the springing thereof” (Psalm 65:9-

10). Let us for a moment consider what the springing would be like without that blessing.

Suppose there were a revival among us without God’s blessing. I am convinced that some

revivals are not from God at all, but are produced by mere excitement. If there is no blessing

from the Lord, it will be only a delusion, a bubble blown into the air for a moment and then gone

to nothing. People may be stirred, only to become duller and deadlier afterwards, and this is a

serious harm to the church.

In the individual heart, if there were a springing without God’s blessing, it would bring no real

good. Suppose you have good desires, but no blessing on them—they would only tantalize and

torment you. Over time, they would vanish, and you might become even harder than before to

religious convictions. If religious desires are not from God but caused by excitement, they may

prevent you from taking God’s Word seriously in the future. Convictions that do not soften the

heart will harden it. Think of those who have experienced a certain kind of springing without being

led to Christ—some have been crushed by despair.

People sometimes say religion drives the insane—it is not true in general, but there is no doubt

that a certain type of religious fervor has led many to madness.

These poor souls have felt their wounds but have not found the balm. They have not known Jesus.

They have sensed their sin but have not fled to the refuge God provides. Do not be surprised if

men go mad when they refuse the Savior. It may be God’s judicial visitation upon those who, even

in deep distress, will not run to Christ. For some, this is the case—you must either fly to Jesus, or

your burden will grow heavier until your spirit breaks. This is not the fault of religion, but of those

who reject the remedy it offers. A springing of desires without God’s blessing would be terrible,

but we thank Him that we are not left in such a state.

V. And now I dwell on the comforting thought that God does bless “the springing thereof.” I want

to speak to those who are tender and troubled, to show that God blesses your springing, often in

many ways. Frequently He does it through small consolations. You have a few very sweet

moments: you cannot yet say you belong to Christ, but at times the bells of your heart ring at

His name. The means of grace are precious to you. When you attend worship, you feel a holy

calm and leave wishing there were seven Sundays in the week instead of one. By God’s blessing,

the Word may seem spoken for your case alone: you set aside your crutches for a moment and

begin to run. Though these comforts may be brief, they are tokens of good.

On the other hand, if you have experienced few or no comforts, if the means of grace have brought

little consolation, consider that a blessing. Sometimes the greatest blessing is that God removes

comforts in order to quicken your running toward the end. When a man flees to a City of Refuge

from a pursuer, it may be wise to let him rest briefly to regain strength, but if danger is immediate,

the kindest act may be to give him nothing, so he runs with undiminished speed. The Lord may be

blessing you through your unease. If you cannot yet say you are in Christ, it may be the greatest

blessing to remove other comforts so that you are compelled to run to Him. Perhaps a bit of self-

righteousness remains in you, and until it is gone, you cannot find true joy and peace in Christ.

The royal robe He gives will never shine until every rag of our own goodness is removed. Fear

often drives people to faith. Have you not seen a timid bird fly into a man’s bosom because a hawk

pursues it? It would not have ventured without fear compelling it. So it may be with you; your

fears may drive you more swiftly to the Savior, and if so, even these present sorrows are signs that

God is blessing “the springing thereof.”

Looking back at my own springing, I sometimes think God blessed me then in a way even more

lovely than now. Though I would not wish to return to that early stage, it had many joys.

An apple tree laden with fruit is beautiful, but an apple tree in bloom is even lovelier. A mature

Christian full of fruit is a comely sight, but a young believer has a special beauty. You likely now

feel a greater horror of sin than many mature believers, and your tenderness of conscience may

surpass theirs. You have a deeper sense of duty, a more solemn fear of neglect, and greater zeal.

You are performing your first works for God, burning with first love; nothing seems too difficult

or heavy. I pray that you never decline, but always advance.

And now to close. I see three lessons for us. First, older saints must be gentle and kind to young

believers. God blesses the springing thereof—let us do the same. Do not dampen young desires or

quench new believers with hard questions. While they are babes needing the milk of the Word, do

not overwhelm them with strong meat; they will grow into it. Remember Jacob did not overdrive

the lambs—be equally prudent. Teach and guide with gentleness and tenderness, not as superiors,

but as nurturing fathers for Christ’s sake. God blesses the springing thereof—may He bless it

through you!

The second lesson is to fulfill the duty of gratitude. If God blesses the springing thereof, we should

be thankful for even a little grace. If you have seen only the first shoot break through the soil, be

thankful, and you shall see the green blade waving in the breeze; be thankful for ankle-deep

verdure, and you shall see the ear begin to form; be thankful for the first green ears, and you shall

see the wheat flower and ripen for the harvest.

The third lesson is encouragement. If God blesses “the springing thereof,” what will He not do in

later days? If He gives such a meal when you first break your fast, what feasts will He prepare

when He says, “Come, eat”? What a banquet awaits at the supper of the Lamb! O troubled soul,

let storms, snow, and wintry blasts that nip your springing be forgotten in this one comforting

thought: God blesses your springing, and whom God blesses none can curse. Over your head, dear

desiring and pleading soul, the Lord of heaven and earth pronounces the blessing of the Father, the

Son, and the Holy Spirit. Take that blessing and rejoice in it forever. Amen.

FARM LABORERS Introduction

The church is God’s field, tenderly cultivated by His hand. We are called to labor faithfully,

sowing and watering His Word, yet only He gives growth. Let us commit ourselves wholly to His

work, bearing fruit for His glory.

“I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth. So neither he who plants nor he who waters

is anything, but only God who gives the growth. He who plants and he who waters are one, and

each will receive his wages according to his labor. For we are God’s fellow workers. You are

God’s field.” 1 Corinthians 3:6–9

I will begin at the end of my text, because I find it to be the easiest way of mapping out what I

want to say. We shall first notice that the church is God’s farm: “You are God’s field.” In the

margin of the Revised Version we read, “You are God’s tilled ground,” and that is the expression

I want to use. “You are God’s tilled ground,” or farm. After speaking about the farm, we will then

say a little about the fact that the Lord employs laborers on His estate. And when we have looked

at the laborers—poor fellows as they are—we will remember that God Himself is the great worker:

“We are God’s fellow workers.”

I. We begin by considering that the church is God’s farm. The Lord has made the church His own by His sovereign choice. He has also secured it for Himself

by purchase, having paid an immense price for it. “But the Lord’s portion is his people, Jacob his

allotted heritage.” Every acre of God’s farm cost the Savior a bloody sweat—yes, the blood of His

own heart. He loved us and gave Himself for us; that is the price He paid. From now on, the church

is God’s rightful possession, and He holds the title to it. It is our joy to know that we are not our

own; we were bought with a price. The church is God’s farm by choice and by purchase.

And now He has made it His by enclosure. It once lay open like common land, bare and barren,

covered with thorns and thistles, and the home of every wild beast; for we were “by nature children

of wrath, like the rest of mankind.” Divine foreknowledge looked over the wasteland, and electing

love marked out its portion with a full measure of grace, setting us apart to be the Lord’s own

estate forever. In due time, effectual grace came with power and separated us from the rest of

mankind, just as fields are hedged and ditched to separate them from open land. Has not the Lord

declared that He has chosen His vineyard and fenced it?

“We are a garden walled around,

Chosen and made peculiar ground;

A little spot, enclosed by grace

Out of the world’s wide wilderness.” The Lord has also made this farm clearly His own by cultivating it. What more could He have

done for His farm? He has completely changed the nature of the soil. From being barren, He has

made it fruitful. He has plowed it, dug it, enriched it, watered it, and planted it with all kinds of

flowers and fruits. It has already brought forth many pleasant clusters for Him, and brighter times

are coming, when angels will shout at the harvest, and Christ “shall see the fruit of the travail of

his soul and be satisfied.”

This farm is preserved by the Lord’s continual protection. Not only did He enclose it and cultivate

it by His miraculous power to make it His own farm, but He continually keeps it in His possession.

“I, the Lord, am its keeper; every moment I water it. Lest anyone punish it, I keep it night and

day.” If it were not for God’s constant power, its hedges would soon be broken down and wild

beasts would devour its fields. Wicked hands are always trying to tear down its walls and lay it

waste again so that there would be no true church in the world. But the Lord is jealous for His land

and will not allow it to be destroyed. A church would not remain a church for long if God did not

preserve it for Himself.

What if God were to say, “And now I will tell you what I will do to my vineyard. I will remove its

hedge, and it shall be devoured; I will break down its wall, and it shall be trampled down”? What

a wilderness it would become. What does He say?

“Go now to my place that was in Shiloh, where I made my name dwell at first, and see what I did

to it because of the evil of my people Israel.” Go to Jerusalem, where once stood the city of His

glory and the place of His dwelling—what is left there today? Go to Rome, where Paul once

preached the gospel with power—what is it now but the center of idolatry? The Lord can remove

the lampstand and leave a place that was bright as day to become dark as night. So God’s farm

remains a farm because He is always present in it, preventing it from returning to its former wild

state. Almighty power is just as necessary to keep the church under cultivation as it was to reclaim

it in the beginning.

Since the church is God’s own farm, He expects to receive a harvest from it. The world is

wasteland, and He looks for nothing from it; but we are tilled land, and therefore a harvest is

expected from us. Barrenness may suit open moorland, but on a farm it would be a disgrace. Love

looks for a return of love; grace given calls for gracious fruit. Watered with the drops of the

Savior’s bloody sweat, shall we not bring forth a hundredfold for His praise? Kept by the eternal

Spirit of God, shall there not be fruit produced in us for His glory? The Lord’s care for us has

involved great cost, labor, and thought. Should there not be a matching return? Should not the Lord

have a harvest of obedience, a harvest of holiness, a harvest of usefulness, a harvest of praise?

Should it not be so?

I think some churches forget that increase is expected from every field of the Lord’s farm, because

they never have a harvest or even look for one. Farmers do not plow their land or sow their fields

for amusement; they mean business. They plow and sow because they want a harvest. If this truth

could enter the minds of some believers, surely they would see things differently. But lately it

seems as if we think God’s church is not expected to produce anything and exists only for its own

comfort and personal benefit. Brothers and sisters, it must not be so. The great Farmer must have

some reward for His work. Every field must yield its increase, and the whole estate must bring

forth praise to Him.

We join with the bride in the Song in saying, “My vineyard, my very own, is before me; you, O

Solomon, may have the thousand, and the keepers of the fruit two hundred.”

But I return to where I started. This farm is, by choice, by purchase, by enclosure, by cultivation,

and by preservation, completely the Lord’s. See then how wrong it would be for any of the laborers
