to call even part of the estate their own.

If a wealthy man owns a large farm, what would he think if the plowman said, “I plow this farm,

so it is mine. I will call this field my own”? Or if another said, “I harvested that land last year, so

it belongs to me”? What if all the other workers divided the farm among themselves and named

the fields after themselves? The owner would quickly remove them all. The farm belongs to its

owner, and it should be called by his name. It makes no sense to call it by the names of the workers.

Should insignificant people rob God of His glory? Remember how Paul put it: “What then is

Apollos? What is Paul? Servants through whom you believed, as the Lord assigned to each.” “Is

Christ divided? Was Paul crucified for you? Or were you baptized in the name of Paul?”

The whole church belongs to the One who chose it in His sovereignty, bought it with His blood,

fenced it by His grace, cultivated it by His wisdom, and preserved it by His power. There is only

one church on earth, and those who love the Lord should remember this. Paul is a worker, Apollos

is a worker, Cephas is a worker—but the farm is not Paul’s, not even a small portion of it. No part

belongs to Apollos or Cephas, for “you are Christ’s.”

The truth is that in this case the workers belong to the field, not the field to the workers: “For all

things are yours, whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas.” “For what we proclaim is not ourselves, but

Jesus Christ as Lord, with ourselves as your servants for Jesus’ sake.”

II. We now move to our second point: the great Farmer employs laborers. By human agency God ordinarily carries out His plans. He can, if He chooses, by His Holy Spirit

work directly in the hearts of men, but that is His work and not ours. We are given instructions

like this: “For since, in the wisdom of God, the world did not know God through wisdom, it pleased

God through the folly of what we preach to save those who believe.” The Master’s command is

not, “Sit still and watch the Spirit of God convert the nations,” but, “Go into all the world and

proclaim the gospel to the whole creation.”

Look at God’s method in providing food for the world. In answer to the prayer, “Give us this day

our daily bread,” He could command the clouds to drop manna every morning at each person’s

door. But He knows it is good for us to work, so He uses the hands of the plowman and the sower

to supply our needs. God could cultivate His chosen farm, the church, by miracles or by angels,

but in great kindness He blesses her through her own sons and daughters. He uses us for our own

good, because we who labor in His fields receive far more benefit ourselves than we give. Labor

strengthens our spiritual muscles and keeps us spiritually healthy. “To me, though I am the very

least of all the saints, this grace was given, to preach to the Gentiles the unsearchable riches of

Christ.”

Our great Master intends that every laborer on His farm should receive some benefit from it, for it

is written, “You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the grain.” The laborer’s daily bread

comes from the soil. Though he works not for himself but for his Master, he still receives his share

of food. In the Lord’s storehouse there is seed for the sower and bread for the eater. However

selflessly we may serve God in the care of His church, we ourselves share in the fruit. It is great

kindness on God’s part that He uses us at all, for we are poor tools at best, and often more of a

hindrance than a help.

The laborers employed by God are all engaged in necessary work. Notice: “I planted, Apollos

watered.” Who beat a big drum or blew his own trumpet? No one. On God’s farm, no one is kept

just for decoration. I have read sermons that seemed meant only for display, because there was not

a single grain of the gospel in them. They were like plows without blades, seed drills with no wheat

in them, or tools made of butter. I do not believe that God pays wages to people who only walk

around His fields to show themselves off. Speakers who display their eloquence in the pulpit are

more like wanderers picking up chickens than faithful laborers producing a crop for their Master.

Many church members live as if their only job on the farm were to pick blackberries or gather

wildflowers. They are quick to criticize how others plow and mow, but they will not lift a hand to

work themselves. Come now, my friends. Why do you stand idle all day? “The harvest is plentiful,

but the laborers are few.” Those who think themselves more refined than others, if you are truly

Christians, must not walk around proudly and look down on those who are working hard. If you

do, I will say that you have mistaken your master. Perhaps you think you serve someone who

values appearance over results, but our great Lord is practical, and on His estate His laborers do

necessary work.

When you and I preach or teach, we should ask ourselves, “What good will this do? I am about to

teach a difficult subject—will it truly help anyone? I have chosen a complex theological point—

will it serve a useful purpose?” A laborer may work very hard on his own idea and yet accomplish

nothing useful. Some sermons only show minor differences in arguments, and what good does that

do? Suppose we sow fields with sawdust or sprinkle them with perfume—what would that

accomplish? Will God bless our moral essays, polished speeches, and elegant phrases? We must

aim at usefulness. As workers together with God, we must focus on work that truly matters. “I

planted,” says one—and that is good, for planting must be done. “I watered,” says another—and

that also is good and necessary. Let each of you be able to give a solid report, but let no one be

satisfied with mere performance, public speaking, or organizing entertainments.

On the Lord’s farm there is a division of labor. Even Paul did not say, “I planted and watered.”

No—Paul planted. And Apollos did not say, “I planted as well as watered.” It was enough for him

to water. No one has every gift. How foolish it is when people say, “I enjoy this preacher because

he builds up believers in doctrine, but when he was away I could not benefit from the other

preacher because he focused on converting sinners.” Yes, he was planting. You have already been

planted; you do not need to be planted again. You should be thankful that others are receiving the

benefit. “For here the saying holds true, ‘One sows and another reaps.’” Instead of complaining

that the plowman did not bring a sickle, you should pray that he has strength to plow deeply and

break up hard hearts.

On God’s farm there is unity of purpose among the workers. “He who plants and he who waters

are one.” One Master employs them. Though He sends them at different times and to different

parts of the field, they are united in one purpose—to work toward one harvest.

In England we do not fully understand watering, because farmers there cannot water all their land.

But in the East, farmers water almost every part of their fields. Without irrigation there would be

no crop. In places like Italy, Egypt, or Palestine, there are wells, pumps, wheels, buckets, channels,

small streams, and pipes that carry water to every plant. Without this, the intense heat would dry

everything up. Planting requires wisdom; watering requires just as much. To bring these two

together, workers must be united in mind. It is harmful when workers are at cross purposes and

work against each other. This is especially harmful in the church. How can I plant successfully if

my helper will not water what I have planted? Or what good is watering if nothing has been

planted? Farming fails when foolish people argue over it, because from sowing to reaping it is one

continuous work. Let us work together all our days, for division leads to barrenness.

We are told in our text that all the laborers together are nothing. “So neither he who plants nor he

who waters is anything.” Workers are nothing without their Master. All the laborers on a farm

could not manage it without someone in charge, and all the preachers and Christian workers in the

world can accomplish nothing unless God is with them.

Every laborer on God’s farm has received his abilities from God. No one knows how to plant or

water souls unless the Lord teaches him daily. These holy gifts are acts of free grace. All laborers

must work under God’s direction, or they work in vain. Without the Spirit’s guidance, they would

not know when or how to work, and without His help they cannot even think a good thought. All

workers must receive their seed from God, or they will sow weeds instead of wheat. All good seed

comes from God’s storehouse. If we preach, it must be the true Word of God, or nothing lasting

will result.

Even the strength to sow comes from the Master. We cannot preach unless God is with us. A

sermon is empty talk unless the Holy Spirit gives it life. “The preparation of the heart belongs to

man, but the answer of the tongue is from the Lord.” When the good seed is sown, the entire

outcome depends on God. If He withholds dew and rain, the seed will not grow. If He does not

shine upon it, the green ear will not ripen. The human heart will remain barren—even if Paul

himself were preaching—unless the Holy Spirit works with him and blesses the Word. Since the

growth comes from God alone, keep the workers in their proper place. Do not think too highly of

us, for after we have done everything, we are unworthy servants.

Yet, though Scripture says the workers are nothing, it also says they will be rewarded. God works

our good works in us and then rewards us for them. “Each will receive his wages according to his

labor.” The reward is based not on success, but on effort. Many discouraged workers can find

comfort in this. You are not paid by results but by faithful labor. You may have hard soil to plow

or difficult ground to sow, with stones, birds, thorns, travelers, and scorching sun working against

you—but you are not responsible for those things. Your reward is according to your work.

“One sows and another reaps,” but the one who reaps does not receive all the reward; the one who

sowed will share in the joy. Workers may be considered nothing, but they will enter into the joy

of their Lord.

Together, according to the text, the workers have been successful, and that is part of their reward.

“I planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.” Often in prayer we say, “A Paul may plant,

an Apollos may water, but it is all in vain unless God gives the growth.” That is true. But another

truth is often overlooked: when Paul plants and Apollos waters, God does give the growth. We do

not labor in vain. There would be no growth without God, but we are not without God. When

faithful workers labor in the right spirit, God blesses them. That blessing is a great part of the

reward.

III. Now we return to the main point: God Himself is the great Worker. He may use whatever laborers He chooses, but the growth comes from Him alone. You know this

is true in natural farming. The most skilled farmer cannot make wheat germinate, grow, and ripen.

He cannot even protect a field until harvest, because many dangers threaten it. Just when a farmer

expects a harvest, blight or disease may destroy it. God must give the growth. If anyone depends

on God, it is the farmer. Through him, we all depend on God year by year for our food. “Even the

king himself is served by the field.” God gives the increase in the barn and the haystack, and it is

even more so in the spiritual field.

If you think it is easy to win a soul, try it. Without divine help, you might as well try to create a

world. You cannot create a fly—how can you create a new heart and a right spirit? Regeneration

is a great mystery beyond your power. “The wind blows where it wishes, and you hear its sound,

but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone who is born of

the Spirit.” What can you or I do in this matter? It is beyond us. We can declare the truth of God,

but applying that truth to the heart and conscience is another matter entirely.

I have preached Jesus Christ with all my heart, yet I know I have never produced saving results in

an unregenerate person unless the Spirit of God opened the heart and planted the living seed of

truth within it. Experience teaches us this. It is also the Lord’s work to keep the seed alive once it

grows. We think we have converts, but often we are disappointed. Many are like blossoms on

apple trees—beautiful but fruitless. Others are like small apples that fall before they mature.

Anyone who leads a large church and cares deeply for souls will soon be convinced that unless

God works, nothing will be accomplished—no conversion, no sanctification, no perseverance, no

glory to God, no satisfaction for the suffering of the Savior—unless the Lord is with us. “Apart

from me you can do nothing.”

From this truth, I draw several practical lessons. First, if the entire farm of the church belongs to the great Master and workers are nothing without

Him, this should promote unity among all He employs. If we serve one Master, let us not quarrel.

It is sad when we cannot rejoice at good being done by those from other denominations who work

differently from us. If a new worker arrives and uses different tools, should I become his enemy?

If he does his work better than I do mine, should I be jealous?

Do you remember that on one occasion the disciples could not cast out a demon? That should have

humbled them. Yet soon after, they saw someone casting out demons in Christ’s name, and they

tried to stop him because he was not part of their group. They could not cast out the demon

themselves, yet they tried to stop someone who could. Some groups are winning souls, but because

they do not do it in our style, we disapprove. They may have unusual methods, but they truly bring

souls to Christ—and that is what matters most. Instead of criticizing, let us encourage everyone

who stands with Christ. “Yet wisdom is justified by her deeds.” Workers should be satisfied with

a new plowman if their Master approves of him. If the great Lord has employed you, it is not my

place to question His choice. Can I help you? Can I show you how to improve? Or can you help

me improve? That is how workers should treat each other.

This truth should also make all workers deeply dependent on God. Are you about to preach, young

man? “Yes, I am going to accomplish great things.” Are you? Have you forgotten that you are

nothing? “So neither he who plants nor he who waters is anything.” A teacher may come filled

with gospel truth to comfort believers, but if he does not come in full dependence on God, he too

is nothing. Power belongs to God. Man is empty and his words are wind; power and wisdom belong

to God alone. If we remain humble, our Lord will use us. But if we exalt ourselves, He will leave

us to our nothingness. This truth also gives dignity to everyone who works in God’s field. My

heart is lifted up with joy at these words: “For we are God’s fellow workers.” We are simple

workers on His farm, yet we work with Him. Does the Lord truly work with us?

We know He does by the results that follow. “My Father is working until now, and I am working.”

That is true for all God’s children. When you serve Him with all your heart, God is with you. When

you speak to your class about Jesus, God speaks through you. When you stop a stranger and tell

him about salvation by faith, Christ speaks through you just as He spoke to the woman at the well.

When you preach forgiveness through the atoning blood in the open air, it is the God of Peter

testifying about His Son, just as He did on the day of Pentecost.

Finally, this truth should drive us to our knees. Since we are nothing without God, let us cry out to

Him for help in this holy work. Let both sower and reaper pray together, or they will never rejoice

together. If blessing is withheld, it is because we have not asked and expected it. Fellow workers,

let us come to the throne of grace, and we shall see the reapers return with their sheaves, though

they may have gone out weeping when they sowed.

To our Father, who is the Farmer, be all glory, forever and ever. Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 11. What The Farm Laborers Can Do And What They Cannot Do
fields.body_html:
Introduction

This chapter of Mark shows us the mystery of God’s kingdom, where seed grows beyond human

understanding. Let us embrace our role as sowers, faithfully spreading the Word, trusting God

for growth, and rejoicing in every soul He brings to the harvest.

“And he said, ‘The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground. He sleeps

and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how. The earth produces

by itself, first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear. But when the grain is ripe, at

once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest has come.’” Mark 4:26–29 (ESV)

There is a lesson here for those who are laborers together with God. It is a parable for all who are

involved in the kingdom of God. It will be of little value to those who remain in the kingdom of

darkness, because they are not called to sow good seed. “But to the wicked God says: ‘What right

have you to recite my statutes or take my covenant on your lips?’” But all who are commissioned

to scatter seed for the Royal Farmer will be glad to understand how the harvest is being prepared

for the One they serve. Listen, then, you who sow beside all waters; you who diligently seek to fill

the storehouses of heaven—listen, and may the Spirit of God speak to you as much as you are able

to receive it.

We shall first learn from our text what we can do and what we cannot do. “The kingdom of God is as if a man should scatter seed on the ground.” This is what the gracious

worker can do. “He sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not

how.” This is what he cannot do. Once the seed is sown, it is beyond human control, and a person

can neither make it sprout nor grow. Yet before long the worker appears again: “But when the

grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle.” We can reap in due season, and it is both our duty and

our privilege to do so. You see, then, that there is a place for the worker at the beginning; though

there is no place for him in the middle process, another opportunity is given to him later when

what he sowed has produced fruit.

Notice, then, that we can sow. Anyone who has received the knowledge of the grace of God in

their heart can teach others. I use the word “man” to include all who know the Lord, whether male

or female. We cannot all teach in the same way, for we do not all have the same gifts; to one is

given one talent and to another ten. Neither do we all have the same opportunities, for one lives in

obscurity and another has far-reaching influence. Yet there is not within the family of God a single

small hand that cannot drop its own little seed into the ground. There is not a person among us

who needs to stand idle, for work suited to their strength is waiting for them. There is not a saved

woman who is left without a holy task; let her do it and receive the approving word, “She has done

what she could.”

We should never complain that we cannot do everything if God allows us to do this one thing; for

sowing the good seed is work that requires all our wisdom, strength, love, and care. Holy seed-

sowing should be embraced as our highest calling, and it is not an unworthy pursuit for the noblest

life. You will need heavenly teaching so that you may carefully choose good wheat and keep it

free from the weeds of error. You will need guidance to remove from it your own thoughts and

opinions, for these may not align with the mind of God. People are not saved by our words but by

God’s Word. We need grace to understand the gospel correctly and to teach all of it. To different

people we must wisely bring forward that part of God’s Word that best speaks to their conscience,

for much may depend on a word spoken at the right time.

Having selected the seed, we will have plenty of work if we go out and sow it everywhere, for

every day brings opportunity and every gathering presents an opening. “In the morning sow your

seed, and at evening withhold not your hand.” “Blessed are you who sow beside all waters.” Wise

sowers recognise favourable opportunities and gladly seize them. There are times when sowing

would clearly be wasted because the soil is not ready. After a shower, or before one, or at whatever

time the experienced farmer knows is best, that is when we must be active. While we are to serve

God at all times, there are seasons when speaking would be like throwing pearls before pigs, and

there are other times when silence would be a serious sin. Those who are lazy during plowing and

sowing season are truly lazy, because they not only waste the day but lose the year.

If you watch for souls and make use of favorable hours and softened moments, you will not

complain about a lack of opportunity. Even if you are never called to water or to reap, your role is

large enough if you faithfully fulfill the work of the sower.

Though it may seem small to teach the simple truth of the gospel, it is essential. How are people

to hear without someone teaching them? Servants of God, the seed of the Word is not like thistle-

down carried by every wind. The wheat of the kingdom requires a human hand to sow it, and

without such action it will not enter people’s hearts or bring forth fruit to the glory of God. The

preaching of the gospel is necessary in every age. God grant that our country may never be

deprived of it. Even if the Lord were to send a famine of bread and water, may He never send a

famine of His Word. “So faith comes from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ.”

Scatter the seed of the kingdom, then, for this is essential to the harvest.

This seed must be sown often, for many enemies oppose the wheat, and if you do not repeat your

sowing you may never see a harvest. The seed must be sown everywhere, for there are no parts of

the world you can afford to leave untouched, hoping they will produce fruit on their own. You

must not leave the rich and educated thinking the gospel will surely reach them without effort, for

pride often keeps them from God. You must not leave the poor and uneducated thinking they will

naturally sense their need for Christ. They may sink lower and lower unless you lift them with the

gospel. No group of people, no type of mind, may be neglected. Everywhere we must preach the

Word, in season and out of season. I have heard that Captain Cook, the well-known explorer,

carried a small packet of English seeds wherever he traveled and scattered them wherever he

landed, leaving flowers and herbs from his homeland across the world. Imitate him wherever you

go; sow spiritual seed in every place your foot steps.

Now let us consider what you cannot do. After the seed has left your hand, you cannot cause it to

produce life. You cannot make it grow, because you do not know how it grows. The text says, “He

sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows not how.” What is beyond

our understanding is certainly beyond our power. Can you make a seed germinate? You may place

it in warmth and moisture so that it swells and breaks open, but the act of germination itself is

beyond you. How does it happen? We do not know. After it begins to grow, can you make it

develop into leaf and stem? No. When the blade becomes the ear, can you ripen it? It will ripen,

but not by your power.

You cannot participate in the inner process, though you may create favorable conditions. Life is a

mystery. Growth is a mystery. Ripening is a mystery. These are sealed fountains beyond human

control. This is equally true of the life of God in the heart. The Word enters the soul and takes

root—we do not know how. Naturally, people resist the Word, yet it enters and transforms them

so that they come to love it. Their nature is renewed so that instead of producing sin, it produces

repentance, faith, and love. We do not know how. How the Spirit of God works on the human

mind, how He creates a new heart and right spirit, how we are born again to a living hope—we

cannot explain. The Holy Spirit enters us; we do not see Him, hear Him, or feel His touch

physically, yet He accomplishes a powerful work within us that becomes evident over time. We

know His work is described as a new creation, a resurrection, a making alive from the dead; but

these words only cover our ignorance of the method. Since we do not understand how He works,

we certainly cannot take over His work. We cannot create, we cannot give life, we cannot

transform, we cannot regenerate, we cannot save.

When God has carried out this hidden work in the growth of the seed, what follows? We can reap

the ripe grain. After a time, God the Holy Spirit uses His servants again. When the living seed has

produced first the blade of thought, then the green ear of conviction, and finally faith—like full

grain in the ear—the Christian worker returns to service, for he can reap. “But when the grain is

ripe, at once he puts in the sickle.” This does not refer to the final day of judgment, which is not

within the scope of this parable. It clearly refers to a human sower and reaper. The reaping Jesus

speaks of here is the kind He mentioned when He said to His disciples, “Lift up your eyes, and see

that the fields are white for harvest.” After sowing in the hearts of the Samaritans and seeing faith

begin to appear, the Lord Jesus declared, “The fields are white for harvest.” The apostle says, “I

planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the growth.” Our Lord said to His disciples, “I sent you to

reap that for which you did not labor.” Is there not also this promise: “And let us not grow weary

of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up”?

Christian workers begin their harvest work by watching for signs of faith in Christ. They are eager

to see the first blade and glad to see the ripening ear. They may hope that people believe, but they

long to be sure. When they are persuaded that faith is truly present, they begin to encourage,

congratulate, and comfort. They know the new believer needs to be gathered into the barn of

Christian fellowship to protect them from many dangers.

No wise farmer leaves ripe grain exposed to hail, mildew, or birds. Likewise, no true believer

should remain outside the fellowship of the church. They should be welcomed into the church with

the joy that accompanies bringing in sheaves. The worker watches carefully, and when the right

time comes, he gathers in the converts so they may be cared for by the church, separated from the

world, shielded from temptation, and kept for the Lord. He does this promptly, because the text

says, “at once he puts in the sickle.” He does not delay in cold suspicion. When faith is evident, he

encourages open confession and says to the new believer, “Have you confessed your faith? Is it

not time to do so openly? Has not Jesus commanded the believer to be baptized? If you love Him,

keep His commandments.” He does not rest until the convert is brought into fellowship with the

faithful. For our work is only half complete when people are made disciples and baptized. We must

then encourage, instruct, strengthen, comfort, and help them in every difficulty. What does the

Savior say? “Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptising them in the name of the

Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded

you.”

Notice, then, the scope and limit of our work. We can bring the truth to people, but the Lord alone

can bless it. The living and growing of the Word within the soul belongs to God alone. When that

hidden work of growth is complete, we can gather the saved into the church. For Christ to be

formed in a person—the hope of glory—is not our work; that remains God’s. But when Christ has

indeed been formed in them, to recognize His image and say, “Come in, you who are blessed by

my Father. Inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world,” is our duty

and joy. Creating divine life belongs to God; nurturing it belongs to us. Causing hidden life to

grow belongs to the Lord; recognizing its development and gathering it in belongs to the faithful,

just as it is written, “But when the grain is ripe, at once he puts in the sickle, because the harvest

has come.”

This, then, is our first lesson: we see what we can do and what we cannot do. II. Our second heading is similar to the first and concerns what we can know and what we cannot

know.

First, what we can know. We can know that when we have sown the good seed of the Word, it will

grow, because God has promised it. Not every grain in every place—for some will be taken by

birds, some destroyed by worms, and some scorched by the sun—but as a general rule, God’s

Word will not fail. As it is written, “so shall my word be that goes out from my mouth; it shall not

return to me empty, but it shall accomplish that which I purpose, and shall succeed in the thing for

which I sent it.” This we can know. We can also know that once the seed takes root it will continue

to grow. It is not a dream or a passing image that disappears, but a living force that moves from

the blade to the ear, and under God’s blessing develops into true salvation, becoming like “the full

grain in the ear.” With God’s help and blessing, our work of teaching will lead not only to thought

and conviction but to conversion and eternal life.

We also know, because we are told, that the reason for this growth is chiefly that there is life in

the Word itself. In the Word of God there is life, for it is written, “For the word of God is living

and active, sharper than any two-edged sword.” It is also called “the living and abiding word of

God.” Living seeds naturally grow, and the reason the Word of God grows in people’s hearts is

that it is the living Word of the living God. Where the word of a king is, there is power. We know

this because Scripture teaches it. Is it not written, “Of his own will he brought us forth by the word

of truth”?

Moreover, the earth, which in this parable represents the person, “produces by itself.” We must be

careful in explaining this, for human hearts do not produce faith on their own; they are like hard

rock where seed would perish. What it means is this: just as the earth, under the blessing of dew

and rain and by God’s hidden working upon it, becomes ready to receive and hold the seed, so the

human heart is made ready to receive and embrace the gospel of Jesus Christ. An awakened heart

desires exactly what the Word of God provides. Moved by divine influence, the soul embraces the

truth, and the truth embraces the soul, so that it lives within the heart and is energized there. A

person’s love receives the love of God; a person’s faith, worked in them by the Spirit of God,

believes the truth of God; a person’s hope, produced in them by the Holy Spirit, takes hold of the

promises revealed. In this way, the heavenly seed grows in the soil of the soul. The life does not

come from the one who preaches the Word; it is placed within the Word by the Holy Spirit. The

life is not in your hand, but in the heart that is led by the Spirit to receive the truth. Salvation does

not come from the preacher’s authority, but through the hearer’s personal conviction, personal

faith, and personal love. This much we can know, and is it not enough for practical purposes?

Still, there is something we cannot know—a secret into which we cannot look. As I have said

before, you cannot look inside a person and see exactly how the truth takes hold of the heart, or

how the heart takes hold of the truth. Some people have examined their own feelings so closely

that they have become discouraged and spiritually blind. Others have examined the feelings of

young believers so strictly that they have harmed them rather than helped them. In God’s work

there is more room for faith than for sight. The heavenly seed grows in secret. It must be buried

out of sight, or there will be no harvest. Even if you kept the seed above ground and it sprouted,

you still could not see the inner life force that moves it. “The wind blows where it wishes, and you

hear its sound, but you do not know where it comes from or where it goes. So it is with everyone

who is born of the Spirit.” Explain the new birth? Experience it, and you will know what it is.

There are secrets into which we cannot enter, because their light is too bright for human eyes. You

cannot become all-knowing, for you are a creature, not the Creator. There will always be a realm

that is not only unknown but unknowable to you. Your knowledge goes so far and no further. You

may thank God for this, because it leaves room for faith and gives reason for prayer. Cry out to the

Great Worker to do what you cannot do, so that when you see people saved you may give the Lord

all the glory.

III. Thirdly, our text tells us what we may expect if we work for God, and what we may not expect.

According to this parable, we may expect to see fruit. The farmer scatters his seed, the seed sprouts

and grows, and he naturally expects a harvest. I wish I could stir up the expectations of Christian

workers, for I fear many work without faith. If you planted a garden or field and sowed seed, you

would be greatly surprised and grieved if nothing came up. Yet many Christians seem content to

work without expecting results. This is a miserable way to work—drawing up empty buckets year

after year. Surely, either I must see some result of my labor and rejoice, or, if I see none, I must be

deeply grieved if I am truly serving my Master. We ought to expect results. If we expected more,

we would see more. Lack of expectation has been a great cause of failure among God’s workers.

But we must not expect every seed we sow to spring up immediately. Sometimes—glory be to

God—the moment the Word is spoken people are converted, and the reaper overtakes the sower.

But it is not always so. Some have labored faithfully for years and seen little visible result, yet at

last the harvest has come—a harvest that would never have been gathered if they had not

persevered.

I believe this world will be converted to Christ—but not today, nor tomorrow, perhaps not for

many generations. The sowing of centuries is not lost; it is moving toward its great conclusion.

Mushrooms may appear quickly, but an oak forest requires generations. It is ours to sow and to

hope for quick reaping, yet we must remember that “Be patient, therefore, brothers, until the

coming of the Lord. See how the farmer waits for the precious fruit of the earth, being patient

about it, until it receives the early and the late rains.” So we must expect results, but not lose heart

if we must wait.

We should expect to see the good seed grow, but not always in our preferred way. Like children,

we are often impatient. A boy plants seeds one day and digs them up the next to see if they are

growing. Nothing will come of that, because he will not leave them alone long enough. So it is

with impatient workers. They want immediate visible results, or they begin to distrust the Word.

Some preachers are so hurried that they allow no time for reflection, no space to count the cost, no

opportunity for people to consider their ways and turn to the Lord with full commitment. Every

other seed is allowed time to grow, but the seed of the Word must grow instantly before their eyes

or they think nothing has happened. In their eagerness, they overheat the seed with fanaticism and

destroy it. They convince people they are converted when they are not, and so prevent them from

coming to a true saving knowledge of the truth. Some are kept from salvation because they are

told they are already saved and are filled with pride before their hearts are truly broken. Perhaps if

they had been taught to look for something deeper, they would not have been satisfied with shallow

soil. Their growth appears rapid, but so is their decline. Let us confidently expect growth, but let

us expect it in order: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.

We may also expect the seed to ripen. By God’s grace our work will lead to genuine faith in those

upon whom He works by His Word and Spirit. But we must not expect perfection at the beginning.

Many mistakes have been made here. A young person comes under conviction, and a well-

meaning, experienced believer questions them deeply and severely. He looks for full maturity at

once. He enters the field early in the season and complains that he sees no grain, only grass. Of

course he sees no grain yet. He refuses to accept the blade as evidence of life and insists on full

maturity immediately. If he had looked for the blade, he would have found it and been encouraged.

For my part, I am thankful to see even a faint desire, a weak longing, a sense of uneasiness about

sin, or a craving for mercy. Should we not allow things to begin small?

Notice the blade of desire, then watch for more. Soon conviction and resolve will follow, and then

a small faith—like a mustard seed—but certain to grow. “For who has despised the day of small

things?” Do not examine a newborn believer to see if they are fully sound in doctrine according to

your standards. They are far from that, and difficult questions will only trouble them. Speak to

them about their sin and Christ as Savior, and in doing so you will water the growing ear until it

becomes full grain. It may not look like wheat yet, but later you will say, “That is wheat indeed. I

recognize it. This is a true ear of grain, and I gladly gather it among my Master’s sheaves.” If you

cut down the blade, how will the ear grow? Expect grace in your converts, but do not expect glory

yet.

IV. Finally, we consider what kind of sleep workers may take and what kind they may not take.

The man in the parable “sleeps and rises night and day, and the seed sprouts and grows; he knows

not how.” Farming is said to be a good trade because it continues while the farmer sleeps. Our

work is similar. When we serve our Master by sowing good seed, it grows even while we sleep.

How may a faithful worker for Christ rightly sleep? First, he may sleep with restful confidence.

Are you afraid that Christ’s kingdom will fail? Who asked you to worry for the ark of the Lord?

Are you anxious that the Almighty’s purposes will collapse? Such anxiety dishonors God. Will

omnipotence be defeated? You would do better to sleep than to interfere like Uzzah. Rest patiently.

God’s purposes will stand. His kingdom will come. His chosen people will be saved. Christ “shall

see of the travail of his soul and be satisfied.” Take the sweet sleep God gives to His beloved—the

sleep of full confidence—like Jesus sleeping in the stern of the boat during the storm. God’s cause

has never been in danger and never will be. The seed is secured by omnipotence and will produce

a harvest. “In returning and rest you shall be saved; in quietness and in trust shall be your strength.”

Wait for the harvest, for the pleasure of the Lord shall prosper in the hand of Jesus.

Take also the sleep of joyful expectation that leads to a hopeful waking. Rise each morning

believing that the Lord rules over all things for His purposes and for the good of those who trust

Him. Expect blessing during the day, and go to bed calmly trusting Him for tomorrow. If you never

rest, you will not rise refreshed and ready to work. If you spent all night anxiously worrying, you

would be unfit for service in the morning. So rest and be at peace, and work steadily and calmly,

because the matter is safe in the Lord’s hands. “It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to

rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep.”

Rest also because you have consciously committed your work into God’s hands. After speaking

the Word, go to God in prayer, entrust the matter to Him, and do not fret. It cannot be in better

hands. Leave it with Him who “works all things according to the counsel of his will.”

But do not sleep in carelessness. The farmer sows seed, but he does not forget it. He repairs fences,

drives away birds, removes weeds, and guards against flooding. He does not watch the seed grow,

but he has plenty else to do. He sleeps in proper measure and season, not like a lazy person. He

never sleeps in indifference or inactivity, for every season demands work. One field is sown, but

another waits. One crop is reaped, but another must be threshed and winnowed. A farmer’s work

is never finished. His sleep is only a pause to give strength for continued labor. The parable teaches

us to do all that lies within our responsibility, but not to intrude into God’s work. In teaching, we

must labor diligently; but regarding the secret working of truth in the human heart, we must pray

and rest, looking to the Lord for inward power.

fields.title: Chapter 12. The Sheep Before The Shearers Introduction
fields.body_html:
This chapter shows Christ’s perfect patience and submission as He bore our sins silently, like a

sheep before its shearers. Let us examine His example and ask ourselves: will we, too, surrender

our comforts and pride, yielding fully to God’s refining hand?

“Like a sheep before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth.” — Isaiah 53:7 (ESV) Our Lord Jesus took our place so completely that, in this chapter, we are compared to sheep: “All

we like sheep have gone astray” (Isaiah 53:6, ESV), and he also is compared to a sheep “As a

sheep before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth.” It is remarkable how complete the

exchange of positions was between Christ and his people. He became what they were so that they

might become what he is. We can easily understand how we are the sheep and he the Shepherd;

but to compare the Son of the Most High to a sheep would have been unacceptable presumption if

his own Spirit had not chosen this humble picture.

Although this image is gracious, its use here is not unusual. Long before Isaiah’s day, our Lord

was foreshadowed in the lamb of the Passover. Later he was proclaimed as “the Lamb of God,

who takes away the sin of the world!” (John 1:29, ESV), and even in his glory he is described as

the Lamb in the midst of the throne.

In unfolding this divine picture, I invite you first to consider our Saviour’s patience, shown in the

image of a sheep silent before its shearers.

Our Lord was brought before the shearers to be stripped of his comfort, stripped of his honour,

stripped even of his good name, and at last stripped of his very life; yet under the shearers he was

silent like a sheep. Think of how patient he was before Pilate, Herod, and Caiaphas, and upon the

cross. There is no record of him crying out in impatience at the pain and shame he suffered at the

hands of those wicked men. Not one bitter word escaped him.

Pilate said, “Have you no answer to make? See how many charges they bring against you” (Mark

15:4, ESV). Herod was deeply disappointed because he hoped to see some miracle performed by

him. The few words our Lord did speak were gentle and submissive, like the quiet sound of a

sheep, yet infinitely full of meaning. He said, “For this purpose I was born and for this purpose I

have come into the world—to bear witness to the truth” (John 18:37, ESV), and, “Father, forgive

them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34, ESV). Apart from this, he remained patient

and silent.

Notice first that our Lord was silent and did not open his mouth against his enemies. He did not

accuse a single one of cruelty or injustice. They slandered him, but he did not reply. False witnesses

rose up, but he did not answer them. You might think he would have spoken when they spat in his

face. Could he not have said, “Friend, why are you doing this? For which of my works do you

insult me?” But the time for such questions had passed. When they struck him on the face with

their hands, it would not have been surprising if he had asked, “Why do you strike me?” But no—

he acted as though he did not hear their insults. He brought no accusation before his Father. He

needed only to lift his eyes to heaven, and legions of angels would have driven away the mocking

soldiers. One flash of a seraph’s wing, and Herod would have perished; Pilate could have fallen

under the judgement he deserved as an unjust judge. The hill of the cross could have become like

the mouth of a volcano to swallow up the crowd that stood there mocking and jeering at him. But

there was no such display of power. Rather, there was a far greater display of power over himself.

He restrained omnipotence itself with a strength beyond measure.

Again, as he spoke no word against his enemies, so he spoke no word against any of us. You

remember how Zipporah said to Moses, “Surely you are a bridegroom of blood to me!” (Exodus

4:25, ESV), as she saw her child bleeding. Surely Jesus could have said to his church, “You are a

costly bride to me, bringing me all this shame and bloodshed.” But “God gives generously to all

without reproach” (James 1:5, ESV). He opened the very fountain of his heart and did not rebuke

us. He had counted the full cost beforehand. Therefore he endured the cross, despising the shame.

“This was compassion like a God, That when the Saviour knew, The price of pardon was his blood,

His pity never withdrew.” Without doubt he looked across the ages, for his eyes were not dim, even when filled with blood

upon the tree. He must have foreseen your indifference and mine, our cold hearts and our

unfaithfulness. He could have left behind words such as these: “I am suffering for those who are

unworthy of my love. Their love will be a poor return for mine. Though I give my whole heart to

them, how lukewarm their love will be towards me. I am weary of them; it grieves me to lay down

my life for such a people.” But there is no trace of such a thought. No. “Having loved his own who

were in the world, he loved them to the end” (John 13:1, ESV). He did not speak a single word

that sounded like regret or complaint for suffering on their behalf, nor any sorrow that he had

begun the work.

And as there was no word against his enemies, and no word against you or me, so there was no

word against his Father, nor a syllable of complaint about the severity of the punishment laid upon

him for our sake. You and I have complained under far lighter troubles, feeling that we have been

treated unfairly. We have even dared to cry out to God, “My face is red with weeping, and on my

eyelids is deep darkness, although there is no violence in my hands, and my prayer is pure” (Job

16:16–17, ESV). But not so the Saviour. No complaint was found in his mouth. We cannot begin

to understand how deeply the Father pressed and crushed him, yet there was no rebellion. “My

God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Matthew 27:46, ESV) was a cry of astonished sorrow,

not a complaint. It showed true humanity in weakness, but not humanity in revolt. Jeremiah wrote

many laments, but Jesus spoke few. Jesus wept, and Jesus sweat great drops of blood, yet he never

murmured or rebelled in his heart.

Look at your Lord and Saviour lying in quiet surrender beneath the shearers, as they take away

everything dear to him, yet he does not open his mouth. Here we see his complete submission. He

gave himself fully; there was no holding back. The sacrifice did not need to be tied with ropes to

the horns of the altar. How different from you and me. He stood willing to suffer, to be spat upon,

to be shamefully treated, and to die, for he was fully surrendered. He was entirely given to do the

Father’s will and to accomplish our redemption. There was complete self-control as well. No part

of him rose up to demand freedom or to escape the suffering. No part of his body, no thought of

his mind, no power of his spirit resisted.

All submitted to the will of God. The whole Christ gave his whole being to God so that he might

offer himself perfectly, without blemish, for our redemption. There was not only self-control, but

complete focus on his mission. The sheep lying there does not think of the pastures; it yields itself

to the shearer. The zeal for God’s house consumed our Lord in Pilate’s hall as much as anywhere

else, for there he made the good confession. His only concern was to uphold the honour of God

and to save his chosen people. Brothers and sisters, I wish we could reach this point: to surrender

our whole spirit to God, to learn self-control, and to give our conquered selves entirely to him.

The calmness and submission of our Lord are illustrated even more clearly if it is true that sheep

in the East are more docile than ours. Those who have seen the noise and rough handling at many

of our sheep shearings may struggle to believe the testimony of the ancient writer Philo Judaeus,

who said that sheep came willingly to be shorn. He wrote that wool-covered rams, heavy with

thick fleeces, place themselves into the shepherd’s hands to have their wool cut, as if paying their

yearly tribute to man, their natural ruler. The sheep stands in a quiet, bowed posture, unconstrained

under the hand of the shearer. This may sound strange to those unfamiliar with the gentle nature

of sheep, but he insists it is true. How wonderful was such submission in our Lord’s case. Let us

admire it and seek to follow his example.

I have tried, however imperfectly, to describe the patience of our beloved Master. Now, secondly,

let us consider our own situation under the same image used of our Lord.

Did I not say at the beginning that because we are sheep, he was willing to compare himself to a

sheep? Let us look at it from another angle. Our Lord was a sheep before the shearers, and as he

is, so are we in this world. Though we will never be offered like lambs in the temple as an atoning

sacrifice, yet for ages the saints have been treated as a flock for slaughter. As it is written, “For

your sake we are being killed all the day long; we are regarded as sheep to be slaughtered” (Romans

8:36, ESV). Jesus sends us out as sheep in the midst of wolves (Matthew 10:16, ESV), and we are

to see ourselves as living sacrifices, ready to be offered. But I want to focus especially on this

second image: we are brought like sheep under the shearer’s hand.

Just as a sheep is taken by the shearer and its wool is cut off, so the Lord sometimes takes his

people and shears them, removing their earthly comforts and leaving them stripped.

I wish that when our time comes to go through this shearing, it could be said of us as it was of our

Lord, “As a sheep before its shearers is silent, so he opened not his mouth.” I fear we speak far too

much and complain endlessly, often without real cause, or for very small reasons. But now let us

consider the image itself.

First, remember that a sheep repays its owner for all his care and effort by allowing itself to be

shorn. As far as I know, there is nothing else a sheep can do in return. It provides food when it is

killed, but while it is alive the one payment it can make to the shepherd is to give its fleece at the

proper time. Some of God’s people can offer Christ the tribute of gratitude through active service,

and they should do so gladly every day of their lives. But many others cannot do much in active

service, and almost the only return they can give to their Lord is to surrender their fleece through

suffering when he calls them to suffer, quietly yielding to be stripped of personal comfort when

the time comes for patient endurance.

Here comes the shearer. He takes the sheep and begins to cut, cut, cut, cutting away the wool in

great handfuls. Affliction is often the large pair of shears. A husband, or perhaps a wife, is taken

away. Little children are removed. Property is cut off, and health is gone. Sometimes the shears

remove a person’s good name; slander arises and comforts disappear. Well, this is your shearing

time, and it may be that you cannot glorify God in any great outward way except by going through

this process. If that is so, should we not, like good sheep belonging to Christ, surrender ourselves

willingly, saying, “I lay myself down with this intention: that you may take from me anything and

everything, and do what you will with me; for I am not my own, for I was bought with a price” (1

Corinthians 6:19–20, ESV)?

Notice that the sheep itself benefits from the act of shearing. Before the sheep are shorn, the wool

is long and old, and every bush and briar tears at it until the sheep looks ragged and miserable.

If the wool were left on when the heat of summer came, the sheep would hardly be able to bear it.

It would be so overloaded with fleece that it would be as uncomfortable as we are when we keep

on our heavy winter clothes far too late in the season. So, brothers and sisters, when the Lord shears

us, we do not enjoy the process any more than the sheep do; but first, it is for his glory, and second,

it is for our good. Therefore we are bound to submit willingly. There are many things we would

have liked to keep which, if we had kept them, would not have been blessings but curses.

A blessing that has gone stale becomes a curse. The manna, though it came from heaven, was good

only as long as God commanded it to be kept for the proper time. When it was kept beyond that

time, it “bred worms and stank” (Exodus 16:20, ESV), and then it was no blessing at all. Many

people would keep their mercies until they rot, but God will not allow it. Up to a certain point,

your wealth was a blessing; beyond that point it would not have been, and so the Lord took it away.

Up to that point, your child was a gift; beyond that, it would not have been so, and therefore

sickness came and the child died. You may not be able to see it, but it is true: when God removes

a blessing from his people, he takes it away because it would not have remained a blessing.

Before sheep are shorn, they are always washed. Have you ever seen the scene when they are

driven down to the brook? Men stand in rows leading to the shepherd who waits in the water. The

sheep are driven down; the men seize them, throw them into the pool, keep their heads above

water, and swirl them round and round to wash the wool before cutting it off. Then you see them

come out on the other side trembling, poor creatures, wondering what will happen next. I want to

suggest to you, brothers and sisters, that whenever a trial threatens to come upon you, you should

ask the Lord to sanctify it to you. If the good Shepherd is about to cut off your wool, ask him to

wash it before he removes it. Ask to be cleansed in spirit, soul, and body. Christian people have

the good habit of asking a blessing on their meals before eating bread. Is it not even more necessary

to ask a blessing on our troubles before we enter them? Your dear child may be near death; will

you not, dear parents, come together and ask God to bless even the death of that child, if it must

happen? The harvest fails; would it not be right to say, “Lord, sanctify this poverty, this loss, this

bad harvest. Make it a means of grace to us”? Why not ask a blessing on the cup of bitterness as

well as on the cup of thanksgiving? Ask to be washed before you are shorn, and if the shearing

must come, let it be your chief concern to offer clean wool.

After the washing, when the sheep has dried, it loses what was its comfort. It is thrown down, and

the shearers begin their work. The poor creature loses its warm fleece. You too will have to part

with your comforts. Remember this: the next time you receive a fresh blessing, call it a loan. Poor

sheep, there is no wool on your back that will not one day be cut off. Child of God, there is no

earthly comfort in your possession that will not either leave you, or you will leave it. Nothing truly

belongs to us except our God. “Why,” someone says, “not our sin?” Sin was ours, but Jesus took

it upon himself, and it is gone.

Nothing is truly ours but our God, for all his gifts are held on loan and can be recalled at his

sovereign will. We foolishly think our mercies belong to us, and when the Lord takes them away,

we begin to complain. A loan, it is said, should go home laughing, and so should we rejoice when

the Lord takes back what he lent us. All our possessions are brief favours borrowed for a time. As

the sheep yields its wool and loses its comfort, so must we give up all our earthly possessions. Or

if they remain with us until death, we shall leave them then. We shall not carry a single one of

them across the river of death.

The shearers take care not to harm the sheep. They cut as close as possible, but they do not cut the

skin. If they can help it, they do not draw blood, not even the smallest amount. When a cut does

happen, it is usually because the sheep does not lie still. A careful shearer keeps his shears free

from blood. Of this Thomson wrote in his poem The Seasons, and the lines beautifully illustrate

the whole subject:

“How meek, how patient, the mild creature lies! What softness in its melancholy face,

What silent, suffering innocence appears!

Fear not, you gentle flocks! It is not the knife

Of dreadful slaughter raised above you;

No, it is the shepherd’s careful, guided shears, Who, having borrowed your fleece

As payment for his yearly care,

Will send you back to the hills light and free.” It is the kicking and struggling that make the shearing difficult. If we are silent before the shearers,

no harm will come. The Lord may cut very close. I have known him strip some so completely that

they seemed to have nothing left, like Job when he said, “Naked I came from my mother’s womb,

and naked shall I return” (Job 1:21, ESV). Yet they have also said with Job, “The Lord gave, and

the Lord has taken away; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1:21, ESV).

Notice that shearers always choose the right time. It would be cruel and foolish to begin shearing

in winter. There is a saying about God “tempering the wind to the shorn lamb.” Whether or not

that is accurate, it would indeed be cruel to shear lambs when bitter winds are blowing. Sheep are

shorn in warm, pleasant weather, when they can afford to lose their fleece and are better without

it. As summer approaches, shearing time comes. Have you not noticed that when the Lord afflicts

us, he chooses the best possible time? He taught his disciples to pray, “Pray that your flight may

not be in winter” (Matthew 24:20, ESV). The spirit of that prayer can be seen in the timing of our

sorrows. He does not send our heaviest trials at our weakest moments. If your soul is already deeply

depressed, the Lord does not add the heaviest burden then. He keeps such loads for times when

“the joy of the Lord” is your strength. We often feel that when joy increases, a trial may be near;

and when sorrow deepens, deliverance may be approaching. The Lord does not send two burdens

at once, or if he does, he gives double strength. His shearing time is chosen with gentle wisdom.

There is something else to remember. As with the sheep, new wool grows. Whenever the Lord

removes earthly comforts with one hand—one, two, three—he restores with the other hand six,

twenty, a hundred. We cry and complain about the small loss, yet that loss is necessary so that we

may receive a greater gain. Yes, it will be so. We shall have reason to rejoice, for “weeping may

tarry for the night, but joy comes with the morning” (Psalm 30:5, ESV). If we lose one position,

another awaits us. If we are driven from one place, a better refuge is prepared. Providence opens

a second door when it closes the first. If the Lord took away the manna from Israel, it was because

they ate the produce of the land of Canaan. If the water from the rock did not follow them any

longer, it was because they drank from the Jordan and from the streams. O sheep of the Lord’s

fold, new wool is coming. Therefore do not be anxious about the shearing. I have said these things

briefly so that we may come to the final point.

Let us try to follow the example of our blessed Lord when our time comes to be shorn. Let us be

silent before the shearers, submissive and still, as he was.

Everything I have said gives a reason for doing so. Our shearing through affliction glorifies God,

honours the Shepherd, and benefits ourselves. The Lord measures and tempers our trials and sends

them at the right time. In many ways I have shown that it is wise to submit as the sheep does, and

that the more completely we do so, the better.

We struggle far too much, and we often excuse ourselves for doing so. Sometimes we say, “This

is too painful; I cannot be patient. I could have borne anything but this.” When a father disciplines

his child, does he choose something pleasant? No. The pain is part of the discipline. In the same

way, the bitterness of sorrow is part of our correction. “By the wounds a heart is healed” (see

Proverbs 20:30, ESV). Do not complain because your trial feels sharp and unusual. That would be

like saying, “If everything goes my way, I will submit; but if it does not, I will rebel.” That is not

the spirit of a child of God.

Sometimes we complain about our weakness. “Lord, if I were stronger I would not mind this heavy

loss; but I am frail, like a dry leaf blown by the storm.” But who decides what trial suits you—God

or you? Since the Lord judges this trial suitable for your weakness, you can be sure it is so. Lie

still. Lie still. “But my grief comes from a cruel source,” you say. “This trouble did not come

directly from God. It came through my cousin or my brother, who should have treated me better.

If it had been an enemy, I could have borne it.” My brother, trial does not truly come from an

enemy. God stands behind all your trouble. Look past secondary causes to the great First Cause. It

is a serious mistake to focus on the human instrument that strikes us and forget the hand that holds

the rod. If I strike a dog, he bites the stick. Poor creature, he knows no better. If he could think

more clearly, he would either bite me or quietly accept the blow. You must not start biting the

stick. It is your heavenly Father who uses it. Whether the rod is made of ebony or thorn, it is in his

hand. It is best to stop trying to choose our trials and to leave everything in the hands of infinite

wisdom.

The heart of my message is this: believer, yield yourself. Lie quietly in God’s hands. Do not

struggle. There is no point in struggling. If the great Shearer intends to shear, he will do so. As I

said before, when the sheep struggles, it may be cut by the shears. If we struggle against God, we

may receive two blows instead of one. In truth, there is not half as much pain in a trial as there is

in fighting against it. The Eastern farmer uses a goad to guide the ox. The gentle prod does little

harm, but if the ox kicks, it drives the goad into itself and bleeds. So it is with us. It is hard “to

kick against the goads” (Acts 26:14, ESV). We suffer more through rebellion than we would if we

submitted to the will of God.

What good comes from worrying? We cannot make “one hair white or black” (Matthew 5:36,

ESV). You who are troubled cannot change the weather by your sighing.

Have you ever earned a penny by fretting, or put bread on the table by complaining? Complaining

wastes breath, and worrying wastes time. To lie quietly in God’s hand brings blessing to the soul.

I wish I were more calm and self-controlled. I long to say continually, “Lord, do what you will,

when you will, as you will, with me your servant. Give me honour or dishonour, wealth or poverty,

sickness or health, joy or sorrow, and I will gladly receive it from your hand.” A person is not far

from the gates of heaven when he is fully submissive to the Lord’s will.

You who have been shorn have, I trust, received comfort through the blessed Spirit of God. May

God bless you. And may the sinner also humble himself under the mighty hand of God. “Humble

yourselves, therefore, under the mighty hand of God” (1 Peter 5:6, ESV). Submit yourselves to

God (James 4:7, ESV). Let every thought be brought captive to him (2 Corinthians 10:5, ESV),

and may the Lord send his blessing, for Christ’s sake. Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 13. In The Hay - Field
fields.body_html:
Introduction

Observe how God “causes the grass to grow for the cattle” (Psalm 104:14, ESV). In every

blade of grass, He works, sustains, and provides. Let us open our eyes to His care, and respond

by trusting Him fully, knowing He nourishes all who depend on Him.

“He causes the grass to grow for the cattle.” — Psalm 104:14 (ESV) At the appointed season all the world is busy with gathering the grass crop, and you can scarcely

ride a mile in the country without breathing the delicious fragrance of the new-mown hay and

hearing the mower's scythe being sharpened. There is a gospel in the hay-field, and that gospel we

intend to bring out as we may be enabled by the Holy Spirit.

Our text brings us immediately to the place, and so we need no preface. “He causes the grass to

grow for the cattle” — three things we shall notice: first, that grass is in itself instructive; secondly,

that grass is far more so when God is seen in it; and thirdly, that by the growth of grass for the

cattle, the ways of grace may be illustrated.

First, then, “He causes the grass to grow for the cattle.” Here we have something that is in itself

instructive. Hardly any symbol, apart from water and light, is used more often in Scripture than

the grass of the field.

In the first place, the grass may be looked at instructively as a symbol of our mortality. “All flesh

is grass.” The whole history of man can be seen in a meadow. He springs up green and tender,

subject to the frosts of infancy that threaten his young life; he grows, he comes to maturity, he puts

on beauty just as the grass is adorned with flowers; but after a while his strength goes and his

beauty becomes wrinkled, just as the grass withers and is followed by a fresh generation that

withers in its turn. Like ourselves, the grass ripens only to decay. The sons of men come to maturity

in due time, and then decline and wither like the green herb.

Some grass is not left to come to ripeness at all, but the mower’s scythe removes it, just as swift-

footed death overtakes the careless children of Adam. “For all flesh is as grass, and all its beauty

is like the flower of the field. The grass withers, the flower fades, when the breath of the LORD

blows on it; surely the people are grass.” — Isaiah 40:6-7 (ESV)

This is very humbling, and we often need to be reminded of it, lest we begin to dream of

immortality under the stars. We should never walk on the grass without remembering that while

the green sod covers our graves, it also reminds us of them, preaching with every blade a sermon

about our mortality, of which the text is, “All flesh is grass, and all its beauty is like the flower of

the field.”

Second, grass is often used in Scripture as a picture of the wicked. David tells us from his own

experience that the righteous man is prone to grow jealous of the wicked when he sees the

prosperity of the ungodly. We have seen them spread themselves out like green trees, seemingly

fixed and rooted in their places; and when we have smarted under our own troubles, feeling that

all day long we have been beaten and disciplined every morning, we have been inclined to ask,

“How can this be consistent with the righteous government of God?” We are reminded by the

Psalmist that in a short time we shall pass by the place of the wicked, and see that he is not there;

we shall carefully look for his place, and see that it is no longer known; for he is soon cut down

like grass, and withers like the green herb.

“But the wicked are like the tossing sea; for it cannot be quiet, and its waters toss up mire and dirt.

‘There is no peace,’ says my God, ‘for the wicked.’” — Isaiah 57:20-21 (ESV) The grass withers, the flower fades away, and in the same way the glory of those who place their

confidence in temporal things and dig for comfort in the treasures of the earth will pass away

forever. As the Eastern farmer gathers up the green herb and, despite its former beauty, throws it

into the furnace, such shall be your lot, O boastful sinners! Thus the Judge will command his

angels, “Bind them in bundles to burn.”

“So these will I destroy with the people, and they will be included in the nethermost parts of the

pit, and your name will be forgotten in the grave…” — Psalm 9:17 (ESV)

Where now is your merriment? Where now is your confidence? Where now is your pride and your

pomp? Where now are your boastings and your loud-mouthed blasphemies?

They are silent forever; for, just as thorns crackle under a pot but are quickly consumed and leave

nothing but a handful of ashes, so it will be with the wicked in this life; the fire of God’s wrath

shall devour them.

It is more pleasing to remember that grass in Scripture also pictures the elect of God. The wicked

are compared to dragons of the wilderness, but God’s own people shall spring up in their place,

for it is written, “In the habitation of jackals, where each lay, shall be grass with reeds and rushes.”

The elect are compared to grass because of their number in the latter days and because of the

rapidity of their growth. You remember the passage, “A handful of this [grain] shall become a

large cluster, and the large cluster shall become a young plant in the nation.” O that the long-

expected day might soon come, when God's people shall no longer be like a lone tuft of grass, but

when they shall spring up among the grass, like willows by the watercourses. Grass and willows

are two of the fastest growing things we know; so shall a nation be born in a day, and crowds be

converted at once. When the Spirit of God is mightily at work in the church, men shall turn to

Christ as doves fly to their dove-cotes, so that the astonished church shall exclaim, “Where did

these come from?” O that we might live to see the age of gold, the time prophets have foretold,

when the company of God’s people shall be countless as blades of grass in the meadows, and grace

and truth shall flourish.

How like grass are God’s people for this reason: they are utterly dependent on the influences of

heaven. Our fields become dry if spring showers and gentle dew are withheld; and what are our

souls without the gracious visitations of the Spirit? Sometimes through severe trials our wounded

hearts are like mown grass, and then we have the promise, “He will come down like rain upon the

mown grass, like showers that water the earth.” Our sharp troubles have taken away our beauty,

and then the Lord visits us and we revive again. Thank God for the old saying, which teaches a

gracious truth as well as a true proverb, “Each blade of grass has its own drop of dew.” God is

pleased to give his own special mercies to each one of his servants: “The blessing of the LORD

makes rich, and he adds no sorrow with it.”

Once again, grass is like the food with which the Lord supplies the needs of his chosen ones. Take

the twenty-third Psalm, and you have the image worked out in the sweetest form of pastoral song:

“He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters.”

Just as the sheep has nourishment suited to its nature, and this nourishment is provided in

abundance by its shepherd so that it not only feeds but lies down in the midst of the fodder, satisfied

with plenty and perfectly at ease, so are the people of God when Jesus Christ leads them into the

pastures of the covenant and reveals to them the precious truths upon which their souls are fed.

Beloved, have we not found that promise true, “On this mountain the LORD of hosts will make

for all peoples a feast of rich food, a feast of well-aged wine, of rich food full of marrow, of aged

wine well refined”? My soul has sometimes fed on Christ until I felt I could receive no more, and

then I have lain down in the abundance of my God to take my rest, satisfied with his favour and

full of the goodness of the Lord.

Thus you see that the grass itself is not without instruction for those who will incline their ear. In the second place, God is seen in the growing of the grass. He is seen first as a worker — “He

causes the grass to grow”. He is seen secondly as a caretaker — “He causes the grass to grow for

the cattle”.

First, as a worker, God can be seen in every blade of grass if we have eyes to perceive him. The

world is blind when it talks about ‘natural laws’ and ‘natural causes’ and forgets that laws cannot

operate by themselves, and that so-called natural causes are not causes at all unless the First Cause

sets them in motion. The old Romans used to say, God thundered; God rained. We say, it thunders;

it rains. What “it”? All such expressions are attempts to avoid the thought of God. We commonly

say, “How wonderful are the works of nature!” But what is “nature”? I remember an unbeliever in

the street, speaking about nature, being asked by a Christian whether he could define what nature

was. He gave no answer. The production of grass is not the result of natural law apart from the

actual work of God; mere law would be powerless unless the great Master himself sent the force

through the matter that is governed by the law — much like a steam engine that supplies power to

all the wheels of a cotton mill. I find rest on the grass as on a royal couch now that I know my God

is there at work for his creatures.

Having asked you to see God as a worker, I want you to make use of this — therefore I urge you

to see God in everyday things. He makes the grass grow — grass is common. You see it

everywhere, yet God is in it. Study it, break it apart; the attributes of God are shown in every single

flower of the field and in every green leaf.

In the same way, see God in your everyday experiences — in your daily troubles, your common

joys, your regular mercies. Do not say, “I must see a miracle before I see God.” In truth, everything

is full of wonder. See God in the bread on your table and the water in your cup. It will be the

happiest way to live if in every event you can say, “My Father has done all this.” See God also in

small things. The little things of life are often the greatest troubles. A man will hear that his house

has burned down more quietly than he will complain when he sees an ill-cooked joint of meat on

his table when he expected it to be perfect. It is the little stone in the shoe that makes the pilgrim

limp. To see God in small things as well as in the great — to believe that the guidance of every

drop of spray when a wave breaks on the rock is under God’s hand, as much as the movement of

the mightiest planet in its orbit — all this is true wisdom.

Think also of God working among solitary things; for grass does not grow only where people tend

it, but even on the side of the lonely mountain where no traveller has ever been. Where only the

eye of a wild bird has seen the green grass and moss, God’s works show their beauty; for God’s

works are fair even to eyes other than those of humans. And you, solitary child of God, living

unseen and unknown in a remote village — you are not forgotten by the love of heaven. He makes

grass grow all alone; shall he not make you flourish despite loneliness? He can develop your graces

and prepare you for heaven in solitude and neglect. Grass lies beneath our feet, and nobody thinks

of the fact that it is crushed by the foot, yet God makes it grow. Perhaps you are oppressed and

worn down, but do not let that depress you, for God executes righteousness for all those who are

oppressed: he causes the grass to grow, and he can make your heart flourish under all the pressures

and afflictions of life, so that you will still be joyful and holy even if all the world tramples over

you, living in the immortal life that God himself gives you, even if hell itself set its heel upon you.

Poor and needy one, unnoticed, oppressed, and trodden down, God makes the grass grow, and he

will care for you.

But I said we should see in the text God also as a great caretaker. “He causes the grass to grow for

the cattle.” Does God take care of oxen? Or is this only for our sake? “You shall not muzzle an ox

while it is treading out the grain.” That shows that God cares for the beasts of the field; but it shows

even more: that he wants those who work for him to be fed as they work. God cares for the cattle

and makes grass grow for them. Then, my soul, though sometimes you have said with David, “I

was senseless and ignorant; I was like a beast before you,” yet God cares for you.

“He gives to the beast its food, and to the young ravens when they cry.” There you have an example

of God’s care for birds, and here we have his care for cattle; and though you, my listener, may see

yourself as black and defiled as a raven and as far from anything spiritually good as beasts are, yet

take comfort from this text: he gives grass to cattle, and he will give grace to you, though you think

yourself to be like a beast before him.

Notice that he cares for these beasts who are helpless in caring for themselves. The cattle cannot

plant the grass or cause it to grow. Though they can do nothing in the matter, yet he does it all for

them: he causes the grass to grow. You who are as helpless as cattle to help yourselves, who can

only stand and groan in misery yet do not know what to do, God can support you with his loving-

kindness and favour you with his tenderness. Let the bleating of your prayers go up to heaven; let

the meaning of your desires go up to him, and help will come to you though you cannot help

yourselves. Beasts are dumb, speechless creatures, yet God makes the grass grow for them. Will

he hear those who cannot speak and not hear those who can? Since our God gives careful attention

even to the cattle in the field, he will surely have compassion on his own sons and daughters when

they desire to seek his face.

There is this also to be said: God not only cares for cattle, but the food he provides for them is

suitable—he causes grass to grow for the cattle, exactly the kind of food ruminants need. In the

same way, the Lord God provides appropriate sustenance for his people. Depend on him by faith

and wait upon him in prayer, and you will receive food suitable for you. You will find in God’s

mercy exactly what your nature requires—provisions matched to your unique needs.

This “suitable” food the Lord ensures for the cattle, for no one else eats the cattle’s food. There is

grass for them, and nobody else takes it; it is kept for them. In the same way, God has a special

provision for his own people: “The secret of the LORD is with those who fear him, and he will

show them his covenant” — Psalm 25:14 (ESV). Though the grass is technically free for anyone
