to eat, no creature cares for it except the cattle for which it was prepared. Similarly, though God’s

grace is freely offered to all, only the elect pay attention and are prepared to receive it. There is as

much reserve of the grass for the cattle as if walls enclosed it; likewise, though God’s grace is free,

it is effectively reserved for those he has chosen.

God is seen in the grass as both worker and caretaker. Let us then observe his hand in providence

at all times. See it not only when we enjoy abundance, but even when our supplies are scant; for

grass is preparing for the cattle even in the depth of winter. And you, sons of sorrow, in your trials

and troubles, are still under God’s care; he will accomplish his gracious purposes in you. Be still

and witness the salvation of God. Every winter’s night connects directly to the joyous days of

mowing and reaping; every season of grief is linked to future joy.

Our third point is most interesting: God’s work in providing grass for the cattle gives us

illustrations of his grace.

I reflect on the text and say to myself, “He causes the grass to grow for the cattle. Here I see a full

provision for that creature. I am also a creature, but nobler than cattle. Surely God will provide for

me as well as for them. Yet naturally I feel uneasy: I cannot find what I want in this world. Even

if I obtained all its riches, I would still feel discontented; even if I had all my heart could wish of

temporal treasures, my soul would remain empty. There must be something somewhere that can

satisfy me as a man with an immortal soul. God fully satisfies the ox; he must have something that

will fully satisfy me if I receive it. There is the grass; the cattle eat it and then lie down content; all

I have found on earth never satisfied me enough to rest fully. Therefore, there must be something

that would satisfy me if I could reach it.” Is not this sound reasoning? I ask both Christians and

unbelievers to follow me this far.

Let us proceed another step: the cattle not only have the grass provided, but they actually receive

it. Why should I not also obtain what I want? My soul hungers and thirsts after something beyond

what I can see or hear; there must be something to satisfy my soul. The cattle feed on what satisfies

them; why should I not find satisfaction too? I begin to pray, “O Lord, satisfy my soul with good

things, and renew my youth like the eagle’s” — Psalm 103:5 (ESV).

While I pray, I reflect: God has provided for cattle what fits their nature—they are flesh, and flesh

eats grass. I too am flesh, but also spirit; to satisfy me I need spiritual nourishment. Where is it?

When I turn to God’s Word, I find, “The grass withers, the flower fades, but the word of our God

will stand forever” — Isaiah 40:8 (ESV), and the words Jesus speaks are “spirit and life” — John

6:63 (ESV).

“Here is spiritual food for my soul,” I say; “I will rejoice in it.” O may God help me understand

what that spiritual food is and enable me to receive it; for though God provides grass for cattle,

they must eat it themselves. If they refuse, they are not nourished. I must imitate the cattle and

receive what God provides for me. What is provided in Scripture? I am told that the Lord Jesus

came to suffer, bleed, and die in my place, and if I trust him I shall be saved. Being saved, the

thoughts of his love will give me solace and joy, strengthening me. What else have I to do but feed

on these truths? The cattle bring nothing to the pasture except their hunger; they enter it and

partake. Likewise, by faith I must live upon Christ. Lord, give me grace to feed on him; make me

hungry and thirsty for him; give me the faith to receive him, so that I may be satisfied with favour

and full of the goodness of the Lord.

Though the text seems small, it grows under meditation. Let me give further illustrations of divine

grace. Preventive grace is symbolised here: grass grew before cattle were created. In Genesis we

see that God provided grass before he made the cattle. What a mercy that God’s covenant

provisions for his people were prepared before they were born! God gave his Son, Jesus Christ, as

Saviour for his chosen before Adam fell; long before sin entered the world, God’s everlasting

mercy foresaw it and provided a refuge for every elect soul. What comfort to know that before I

hunger, God has prepared the manna; before I thirst, God has caused the rock in the wilderness to

produce crystal streams to satisfy my soul’s thirst! See what sovereign grace can do! Before the

cattle come to pasture, the grass is ready; before I experience my need for mercy, mercy is already

prepared for me.

Here is an illustration of free grace: when the ox enters the field, it brings no money. Similarly, I,

a poor, needy sinner, bring nothing but receive Christ without money and without cost. “The Lord

makes the grass grow for the cattle, and so he provides grace for my needy soul, though I have no

money, no merit, no excellence of my own.”

Why does God give grass to the cattle? Because they belong to him. Scripture affirms, “The silver

is mine, and the gold is mine, declares the LORD of hosts, and the cattle on a thousand hills” —

Haggai 2:8 (ESV). God provides grass for his cattle; likewise, grace is provided for God’s people.

Every herd of cattle is God’s: long before the farmer brands a bullock, God has marked it; so, long

before the fall of Adam, the stamp of electing love was set on our brow: “Your eyes saw my

unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for

me, when none of them as yet existed” — Psalm 139:16 (ESV).

God also feeds cattle because he has entered a covenant with them. “A covenant with cattle?”

someone asks. Indeed: when God spoke to Noah, after the flood, he said, “I establish my covenant

with you, and with your offspring after you, and with every living creature that is with you, of the

birds, of the livestock, and of every beast of the earth with you” — Genesis 9:9-10 (ESV). Thus a

covenant was made with the cattle: seedtime and harvest would not fail; therefore the earth

produces for them, and for them the Lord causes the grass to grow. If God keeps his covenant with

cattle, will he not keep it with his beloved? Yes, his chosen are covenanted in Christ, and he

provides for all their needs in time and eternity, satisfying them out of the fullness of his everlasting

love.

God feeds the cattle, and then the cattle praise him. David writes, “Praise the LORD from the earth,

you great sea creatures and all deeps, fire and hail, snow and frost, stormy wind fulfilling his

command! Mountains and all hills, fruit trees and all cedars! Beasts and all livestock, creeping

things and flying birds!” — Psalm 148:7-10 (ESV). The Lord feeds his people so that their glory

may praise him, and not be silent. While other creatures give him glory, let the redeemed of the

Lord especially proclaim it, those he has delivered from the hand of the enemy.

Yet even now, our text is not exhausted. Consider the grass itself: “He causes the grass to grow”.

Here is a doctrinal lesson: if grass cannot grow without God, how could grace arise in the human

heart apart from divine action? Grace is a far more wonderful product of God’s wisdom than grass.

If grass cannot grow without a divine cause, any growth of grace must be traced to God, and all

glory must be given to him.

Furthermore, if God deems it worthwhile to make grass and care for it, much more will he

honourably cause his grace to grow in our hearts. If the great invisible Spirit, whose thoughts are

high and lofty, condescends to watch over that humble growth by the hedge, surely he will oversee

his own seed in us, “the incorruptible seed that lives and endures forever” — 1 Peter 1:23 (ESV).

Mungo Park, exploring the deserts of Africa, took comfort from a small piece of moss, seeing

God’s wisdom and power even in that lonely patch of green.

Likewise, when you see fields ripe for mowing, your heart should leap with joy at how God has

produced the grass, tending it through the winter cold and spring frost until rain and sunshine bring

it to perfection. So, my soul, though you endure many frosts of sorrow and long winters of trial,

the Lord will cause you to grow in grace and in the knowledge of our Lord and Saviour Jesus

Christ, to whom be glory forever. Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 14
fields.body_html:
THE JOY OF HARVEST Introduction

Harvest reminds us of God’s faithfulness, provision, and the joy of reaping what He has sown in

our lives. Let us open our hearts, rejoice in His blessings, and share the gospel, bearing fruit for

His glory.

"They rejoice before you as with joy at the harvest" — Isaiah 9:3 (ESV) The other day I kept the feast with a company who shouted "Harvest Home." I was glad to see the

rich and poor rejoicing together; and when the cheerful meal was ended, I was glad to turn one of

the tables into a pulpit, and in the large barn to preach the gospel of the ever-blessed God to an

earnest audience. My heart was merry in harmony with the occasion, and I shall now keep in the

same key, and talk to you a little upon the joy of harvest. Londoners forget that it is harvest time;

living in this great desert of dingy bricks we hardly know what a wheat-ear is like, except as we

see it dry and white in the window of a corn dealer's shop; yet let us all remember that there is such

a season as harvest, when by God's goodness the fruits of the earth are gathered in.

What is the joy of harvest which is here taken as the simile of the joy of the saints before God? I

am afraid that to the mere selfish order of spirits the joy of harvest is simply that of personal

gratification at the increase of wealth. Sometimes the farmer only rejoices because he sees the

reward of his toils, and is so much the richer man. I hope that with many there mingles the second

cause of joy; namely, gratitude to God that an abundant harvest will give bread to the poor, and

remove complaining from our streets. There is a lawful joy in harvest, no doubt, to the man who

is enriched by it; for any man who works hard has a right to rejoice when at last he gains his desire.

It would be well if men would always recollect that their last and greatest harvest will be to them

according to their labor. He who sows to his flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but he who

sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.

A young man commences life by sowing what he calls his wild oats, which he had better never

have sown, for they will bring him a terrible harvest. He expects that from these wild oats he will

gather a harvest of true pleasure, but it cannot be; the truest pleasures of life spring from the good

seed of righteousness, and not from the hemlock of sin. As a man who sows thistles in his furrows

must not expect to reap the golden wheatsheaf, so he who follows the ways of vice must not expect

happiness.

On the contrary, they sow the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind. When a sinner feels the

pangs of conscience he may well say, "This is what I sowed." When he shall at last receive the

punishment of his evil deeds he will blame no one but himself; he sowed tares and he must reap

tares. On the other hand, the Christian man, though his salvation is not of works, but of grace, will

have a gracious reward given to him by his Master. He who goes out weeping, bearing the seed

for sowing, shall come home with shouts of joy, bringing his sheaves with him. The joy of harvest

in part consists of the reward of labor; may such be our joy in serving the Lord.

The joy of harvest has another element in it, namely, that of gratitude to God for favors bestowed.

We are singularly dependent on God; far more so than most of us imagine. When the children of

Israel were in the wilderness they went forth every morning and gathered the manna. Our manna

does not come to us every morning, but it comes once a year. It is as much a heavenly supply as if

it lay like a hoarfrost round about the camp. If we went out into the field and gathered food which

dropped from the clouds we should think it a great miracle; and is it not as great a marvel that our

bread should come up from the earth as that it should come down from the sky? The same God

who bade the heavens drop with angels' food bids the dull earth in its due season yield corn for

mankind. Therefore whenever we find that harvest comes, let us be grateful to God, and let us not

suffer the season to pass over without psalms of thanksgiving. I believe I shall be correct if I say

that there is never in the world, as a rule, more than sixteen months' supply of food; that is to say,

when the harvest is gathered in, there may be sixteen months' supply; but at the time of harvest

there is not usually enough wheat in the whole world to last the population more than four or five

months; so that if the harvest did not come we should be on the verge of famine. We live still from

hand to mouth. Let us pause and bless God, and let the joy of harvest be the joy of gratitude.

To the Christian it should be great joy, by means of the harvest, to receive an assurance of God's

faithfulness. The Lord has promised that while the earth remains, seedtime and harvest, cold and

heat, summer and winter, shall not cease. and when you see the loaded wain carrying in the crop

you may say to yourself, "God is true to his promise.

Despite the dreary winter and the damp spring, autumn has come with its golden grain." Depend

upon it, that as the Lord keeps this promise he will keep all the rest. All his promises are yea and

amen in Christ Jesus; if he keeps his covenant to the earth, much more will he keep his covenant

with his own people, whom he hath loved with an everlasting love. Go, Christian, to the mercy-

seat with the promise on your lip and plead it. Be assured it is not a dead letter. Let not unbelief

cause you to stammer when you mention the promise before the throne, but say it boldly—"Fulfil

this word unto thy servant on which thou hast caused me to hope." Shame upon us that we so little

believe our God. The world is full of proofs of his goodness. Every rising sun, every falling shower,

every revolving season certifies his faithfulness. Wherefore do we doubt him? If we never doubt

him till we have cause for it we shall never know distrust again. Encouraged by the return of

harvest, let us resolve in the strength of the Spirit of God that we will not waver, but will believe

in the divine word and rejoice in it.

Once more. To the Christian, in the joy of harvest there will always be the joy of expectation. As

there is a harvest to the husbandman for which he waits patiently, so there is a harvest for all

faithful waiters who are looking for the coming and the appearing of our Lord and Saviour Jesus

Christ. The mature Christian, like the ripe ear of corn, hangs down his head with holy humility.

When he was but green in the things of God he stood erect and was somewhat boastful, but now

that he has become full of the blessing of the Lord he is humbled thereby, and bows himself down;

he is waiting for the sickle, and he dreads it not, for no common reaper shall come to gather Christ's

people—he himself shall reap the harvest of the world.

The Lord leaves the destroying angel to reap the vintage and to cast it into the wine-vat to be

trodden with vengeance; but as for the grain which he himself has sown, he will gather it himself

with his own golden sickle. We are looking for this. We are growing among the tares, and

sometimes we are half afraid lest the tares should be stronger than ourselves and choke the wheat;

but we shall be separated by-and-by, and when the corn is well winnowed and stored in the garner,

we shall be there. It is this expectation which even now makes our hearts throb with joy. We have

gone to the grave with precious sheaves that belonged to our Master, and when we were there we

thought we could almost say, "Lord, if they sleep they shall do well. Let us die with them." Our

joy of harvest is the hope of being at rest with all the saints, and forever with the Lord.

A view of these shadowy harvests upon earth should make us exceedingly glad, because they are

the image and foreshadowing of the eternal harvest above.

So much about the joy of harvest; but I hasten onward. What joys are those which to the believer

are as the joy of harvest? It is a common notion that Christians are an unhappy people. It is true

that we are tried, but it is false that we are miserable. With all their trials, believers have such a

compensation in the love of Christ that they are still a blessed generation, and it may be said of

them, "Happy art thou, O Israel."

One of the first seasons in which we knew a joy equal to the joy of harvest—a season which has

continued with us ever since it commenced—was when we found the Saviour, and so obtained

salvation. You recollect for yourselves, brethren and sisters, the time of the ploughing of your

souls. My heart was fallow, and covered with weeds; but on a certain day the great Husbandman

came and began to plough my soul. Ten black horses were his team, and it was a sharp ploughshare

that he used, and the ploughers made deep furrows. The ten commandments were those black

horses, and the justice of God, like a ploughshare, tore my spirit. I was condemned, undone,

destroyed, lost, helpless, hopeless—I thought hell was before me. Then there came a cross

ploughing, for when I went to hear the gospel it did not comfort me; it made me wish I had a part

in it, but I feared that such a boon was out of the question.

The choicest promises of God frowned at me, and his threatenings thundered at me. I prayed, but

found no answer of peace. It was long with me thus. After the ploughing came the sowing. God

who ploughed the heart made it conscious that it needed the gospel, and the gospel seed was

joyfully received. Do you recollect that auspicious day when at last you began to have some little

hope? It was very little—like a green blade that peeps up from the soil; you scarce knew whether

it was grass or corn, whether it was presumption or true faith. It was a little hope, but it grew very

pleasantly. Alas, a frost of doubt came; snow of fear fell; cold winds of despondency blew on you,

and you said, "There can be no hope for me." But what a glorious day was that when at last the

wheat which God had sown ripened, and you could say, "I have looked to him and have been

lightened; I have laid my sins on Jesus, where God laid them of old, and they are taken away, and

I am saved." I remember well that day, and so no doubt do many of you. O sirs! no husbandman

ever shouted for joy as our heart shouted when a precious Christ was ours, and we could grasp him

with full assurance of salvation in him.

Many days have passed since then, but the joy of it is still fresh with us. And, blessed be God, it is

not the joy of the first day only that we look back upon; it is the joy of every day since then, more

or less; for our joy no man taketh from us; still we are walking in Christ, even as we received him.

Even now all our hope on him is stayed, all our help from him we bring; and our joy and peace

continue with us because they are based upon an immovable foundation. We rejoice in the Lord,

yea, and we will rejoice.

The joy of harvest generally shows itself by the farmer giving a feast to his friends and neighbors;

and, usually, those who find Christ express their joy by telling their friends and their neighbors

how great things the Lord hath done for them. The grace of God is communicative. A man cannot

be saved, and always hold his tongue about it; as well look for dumb choirs in heaven as for a

silent church on earth. If a man has been thirsty, and has come to the living stream, his first impulse

will be to cry, "Ho! everyone that thirsts!" Do you feel the joy of harvest, the joy that makes you

wish that others should share with you? If so, do not repress the impulse to proclaim your

happiness. Speak of Christ to brothers and sisters, to friends and kinsfolk; and, if the language be

stammering, the message in itself is so important that the words in which you couch it will be a

secondary consideration. Tell it, tell it out far and wide—that there is a Saviour, that you have

found him, and that his blood can wash away transgression. Tell it everywhere; and so the joy of

harvest shall spread o'er land and sea, and God shall be glorified.

We have another joy which is like the joy of harvest. We frequently have it, too. It is the joy of

answered prayer. I hope you know what it is to pray in faith. Some prayer is not worth the words

used in presenting it, because there is no faith mixed with it. “With all your sacrifices you shall

offer salt”, and the salt of faith is needful if we would have our sacrifices accepted. Those who are

familiar with the mercy-seat know that prayer is a reality, and that the doctrine of divine answers

to prayer is no fiction. Sometimes God will delay to answer for wise reasons; then his children

must cry, and cry, and cry again. They are in the condition of the husbandman who must wait for

the precious fruits of the earth; and when at last the answer to prayer comes, they are then in the

husbandman's position when he receives the harvest. Remember Hannah's wail and Hannah's

word. In the bitterness of her soul she cried to God, and when her child was given to her she called

him "Samuel," meaning, "Asked of God;" “For this child I prayed, and the LORD has granted me

my petition that I made to him.” 1 Samuel 1:27.

He was a dear child to her, because he was a child of prayer. Any mercy that comes to you in

answer to prayer will be your Samuel mercy, your darling mercy. You will say of it, "For this

mercy I prayed," and it will bring the joy of harvest to your spirit.

We have another joy of harvest in ourselves when we conquer a temptation. We know what it is

to get under a cloud sometimes; sin within us rises with a darkening force, or an external adversity

beclouds us, and we miss the plain path we were accustomed to walk in. A child of God at such

times will cry mightily for help; for he is fearful of himself and fearful of his surroundings. Some

of God's people have been by the week and month together exposed to the double temptation, from

without and from within, and have cried to God in bitter anguish. It is a very hard struggle; the

sinful action has been painted in very fascinating colors, and the siren voice of temptation has

almost enchanted them. But when at last they have got through the valley of the shadow of death

without having slipped with their feet; when, after all, they have not been destroyed by Apollyon,

but have come forth again into the daylight, they feel a joy unspeakable, compared with which the

joy of harvest is mere childish merriment. Those know deep joy who have felt bitter sorrow. As

the man feels that he is the stronger for the conflict, as he feels that he has gathered experience and

stronger faith from having passed through the trial, he lifts up his heart, and rejoices, not in himself,

but before his God, with the joy of harvest. Brethren beloved, you know what that means.

Again, there is such a thing as the joy of harvest when we have been rendered useful. The master

passion of every Christian is to be useful. There should be a burning zeal within us for the glory

of God. When the man who desires to be useful has laid his plans and set about his work, he begins

to look out for the results; but perhaps it will be weeks, or years, before results will come. The

worker is not to be blamed that there are no fruits as yet, but he is to be blamed if he is content to

be without fruits.

A preacher may preach without conversions, and who shall blame him? but if he be happy, who

shall excuse him? It is ours to break our own hearts if we cannot by God's grace break other men's

hearts, if others will not weep for their sins it should be our constant habit to weep for them. When

the heart becomes earnest, warm, zealous, God usually gives a measure of success, some fiftyfold,

some a hundredfold. When the success comes it is the joy of harvest indeed. I cannot help being

egotistical enough to mention the joy I felt when first I heard that a soul had found peace through

my youthful ministry.

I had been preaching in a village some few Sabbaths with an increasing congregation, but I had

not heard of a conversion, and I thought, "Perhaps I am not called of God. He does not mean me

to preach, for if he did he would give me spiritual children." One Sabbath my good deacon said,

"Don't be discouraged. A poor woman was savingly impressed last Sabbath." How long do you

suppose it was before I saw that woman? It was just as long as it took me to reach her cottage. I

was eager to hear from her own lips whether it was a work of God's grace or not. I always looked

upon her with interest, though only a poor laborer's wife, till she was taken away to heaven, after

having lived a holy life.

Since then have I rejoiced over in the Lord, but that first seal to my ministry was peculiarly dear

to me. It gave me a sip of the joy of harvest. If somebody had left me a fortune it would not have

caused me one-hundredth part of the delight I had in discovering that a soul had been led to the

Saviour. I am sure Christian people who have not this joy have missed one of the choicest delights

that a believer can know this side heaven. In fact, when I see souls saved, I do not envy Gabriel

his throne nor the angels their harps. It shall be our heaven to be out of heaven for a season if we

can but bring others to know the Saviour and so add fresh jewels to the Redeemer's crown.

I will mention another delight which is like the joy of harvest, and that is fellowship with the Lord

Jesus Christ. This is not so much something to talk about as something to experience and enjoy. If

we try to describe what communion with Christ is, we fail. Solomon, the wisest of men, when

inspired to write about the fellowship of the church with her Lord, had to use allegories and

symbolic language, and though to a spiritual mind the Song of Solomon is always delightful, to a

worldly mind it seems just like a love poem. The natural person does not accept the things of God,

because they are spiritually discerned. 1 Corinthians 2:14

But oh, the happiness of knowing that Christ is yours, and of being close to him. To touch his side

and put your finger in the mark of the nails; these are not everyday joys. But when such close and

personal communion comes to us on our special days, it lifts our souls like the chariots of

Amminadab, or, if you like, it allows us to walk over the world and all that it calls great or valuable.

Our circumstances mean nothing if Christ is with us—he is our God, our comfort, and our

everything, and we rejoice before him like we rejoice at harvest.

I do not have time to go into more detail, because I want to end with one practical word. Many of

us are eagerly longing for a harvest that would bring us intense joy. Lately, several people have

shared with me how deeply they feel compassion for the souls of people. Others of us have felt a

mysterious push to pray more than we ever have, and to care more than we ever did that Christ

would save those who are perishing. We will not be satisfied until there is a thorough spiritual

awakening in this land. We did not create this feeling ourselves, and we do not want to suppress

it. We do not believe it can be suppressed; and others will feel the same heavenly concern, and

will sigh and cry to God day and night until the blessing comes. This is the sowing, this is the

ploughing, this is the harrowing—may it continue until the harvest. I long to hear my brothers and

sisters everywhere saying, "We are full of anguish; we are in agony until souls are saved." The cry

of Rachel, "Give me children, or I die," is the cry of your minister today, and the longing of

thousands more. As that desire grows stronger, a revival approaches. We must have spiritual

children for Christ, or our hearts will break because of our longing for their salvation. Oh, for more

of these longings, yearnings, cravings, and efforts! If we pray until the harvest of revival comes,

we will share in its joy.

Who will have the most joy? Those who have been most concerned about it. Those of you who do

not pray in private, and who do not come to prayer meetings, will not have joy when the blessing

comes and the church grows. You had no part in the sowing, so you will have little part in the

harvest. Those who never speak to others about their souls, who do not participate in Sunday school

or mission work, but just enjoy the blessings—they will have none of the joy of harvest, because

they do not work for the Lord. And who would want lazy people to be happy? Instead, in our zeal

and care, we feel like saying, "Curse Meroz; curse its inhabitants bitterly, because they did not

come to help the LORD, to help the LORD against the mighty." — Judges 5:23 (ESV)

If you come to help the Lord by his Spirit, you will share the joy of harvest. Perhaps no one will

have more joy than those who see their loved ones brought to God. Some of you have children

who are a trial to you whenever you think of them; let them be a trial that drives you to constant

prayer for them, and if the blessing comes, why should it not come to them? If a revival happens,

why should your daughter not be converted, why should your wild son not be saved, or even your

grey-headed father, who has been sceptical and unbelieving—why should God’s grace not reach

him? And oh, what joy you will have then!

What happiness will fill your spirit when you see those related to you united with Christ your Lord!

Pray earnestly for them, and you will yet experience the joy of harvest in your own home, a shout

of harvest home in your own family.

Perhaps, my listener, you have little to do with this joy because you are unsaved. Yet it is a

wonderful thing for an unconverted person to be under a ministry blessed by God, and among

people who pray for conversions. It is a blessing for you, young man, to have a Christian mother.

It is a great blessing for you, O unconverted woman, to have a godly sister. These give us hope for

you. While your relatives are praying, we are hopeful for you. May the Lord Jesus be yours yet.

But, oh, if you remain unbelieving, however rich a blessing comes to others, it will not benefit

you. "If you are willing and obedient, you shall eat the good of the land." — Isaiah 1:19 (ESV)

But some may cry in sorrow, "The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved." —

Jeremiah 8:20 (ESV) It has been observed that those who pass through a revival and remain

unconverted often become more hardened than before. I believe it, and I therefore pray that the

Spirit of God comes with such power that none escape his influence.

May you pray: "Pass me not, O mighty Spirit!

You can make the blind to see;

Witness of Jesus’ merit,

Speak the word of power to me,

Even me."

"Have I long been sleeping in sin,

Long been ignoring and grieving you?

Has the world kept my heart?

Oh forgive and rescue me,

Even me."

Oh, for earnest, persistent prayer from all believers around the world! If our churches were stirred

to continuous, intense prayer, giving God no rest until he makes Zion a praise on earth, we might

see God’s kingdom come and the power of Satan broken.

As many of you love Christ, I urge you by his name to pray earnestly; as many of you love the

Church and desire her growth, I beg you not to hold back in this time of prayer. May the Lord lead

you to pray until the joy of harvest is granted. Do you remember me saying one Sabbath, "The

Lord will treat you as you treat his work during this next month"? I feel it will be true for many—

that the Lord will treat you as you treat his Church. If you sow little, you will reap little; if you

pray little, you will receive little favour. But if you act with zeal and faith, and pray and work much

for the Lord, good measure, pressed down and overflowing, will be returned to you. If you water

others with drops, you will receive drops; but if the Spirit helps you to pour rivers of living water

from your soul, floods of heavenly grace will flow into your spirit. May God bring in the

unconverted, and lead them to simple trust in Jesus; then they too will know the joy of harvest. We

ask it in his name. Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 15
fields.body_html:
SPIRITUAL GLEANING Introduction

Ruth’s gleaning teaches us God’s grace and provision for the humble. Just as she gathered

freely among the sheaves, we too are invited to partake of heavenly blessings. Step into His

fields, receive His Word, and grow rich in spiritual harvest today.

"Let her glean even among the sheaves, and do not reproach her." — Ruth 2:15 People from the country understand gleaning. I hope this custom never disappears, so the poor

always get their share of the harvest. But many who see gleaning in their parish fields every year

are not yet wise enough to understand the spiritual meaning of gleaning. That is the subject today,

and my text comes from the story of Ruth, known to all of you. I will use it to illustrate our case

in a simple but instructive way. First, there is a great Husbandman; in Ruth’s story it was Boaz, in

ours it is our heavenly Father. Second, there is a humble gleaner; Ruth was the gleaner, but she

represents every believer. Third, there is a gracious permission given to Ruth: "Let her glean even

among the sheaves, and do not reproach her." The same permission is given to us spiritually.

In the first place, the God of the whole earth is a great Husbandman. This is true in natural things.

All farm operations happen by his power and wisdom. Man may plough the soil and sow the seed,

but as Jesus said, "My Father is the farmer." — John 15:1 (ESV) He controls the clouds and the

sunshine; he directs the winds and distributes dew and rain; he gives frost and heat; and through

all these natural processes, he provides food for humans and animals. All this farming is for the

benefit of others, never for himself. He has no need of our work. "The cattle on a thousand hills

are mine," — Psalm 50:10 (ESV). The purest kindness and generosity are in God’s heart. Though

all things belong to God, his works in creation and providence are not for himself, but for his

creatures. This encourages us to trust him.

In spiritual matters, God is also a great Husbandman, and all his work is done for his children, so

they may be nourished with the finest spiritual food. Consider the wide gospel fields our heavenly

Father tends for his children. These fields are very productive. "The people of Israel shall dwell in

safety; Jacob shall dwell securely in a land of grain and wine; his heavens shall drop down dew."

— Deuteronomy 33:28 (ESV) Every field God tends yields a plentiful harvest; there are no failures

or famines with him.

One part of his farm is called the Doctrine field. What full sheaves of fine wheat are there! Those

allowed to glean here will gather more than enough, for the land yields abundantly. Look at the

sheaf of election, full of heavy, strong ears of wheat, like Pharaoh saw in his dream. There is the

sheaf of perseverance, where each ear represents the promise that God will finish what he started.

If we do not have faith to partake of these, we may glean from the sheaves of redemption by the

blood of Christ. Many who cannot feed on election or perseverance can feed on the atonement and

rejoice in substitution. These rich sheaves, when meditated on, provide royal food for the Lord’s

family.

I wonder why some of God’s stewards lock the gate of this field, as if they think it dangerous. I

want my people not just to glean here, but to carry home wagon-loads, for they cannot be too well

fed when truth is the food. Are my fellow workers afraid that God’s people will become arrogant

if they get too much food? I fear they may starve if the bread of sound doctrine is withheld. If we

love the commandments and warnings of God, we need not fear the doctrines; we should study

and feed on them with joy. The doctrines of God’s distinguishing grace must be presented

alongside the rest of the Word, and those pulpits that exclude these truths are incomplete. Do not

keep God’s people out of this field. Open the gate and come in, all of you children of God! In my

Master’s field nothing grows that will harm you. Gospel doctrine is always safe. You can feast

until you are full with no harm. Fear no revealed truth. Fear ignorance, not holy knowledge. Grow

in grace and in the knowledge of Jesus Christ. Everything taught in God’s Word is meant for study;

neglect nothing. Visit the Doctrine field daily and glean with the utmost diligence.

2. The great Husbandman has another field called the Promise field; I need not speak much of it,

for I hope you often enter it and gather from it. Let us just take an ear or two from one of the

sheaves and show them to you so that you may be encouraged to stay there all day and carry home

a rich harvest at night. Here is an ear: "The mountains may depart and the hills be removed, but

my steadfast love shall not depart from you, and my covenant of peace shall not be removed,"

(Isaiah 54:10).

Here is another: "When you pass through the waters, I will be with you; and through the rivers,

they shall not overwhelm you; when you walk through fire you shall not be burned, and the flame

shall not consume you," (Isaiah 43:2). Here is another; it is small in stalk but heavy with grain:

"My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness," (2 Corinthians 12:9).

Another is long in the stalk but very rich in corn: "Do not let your hearts be troubled. Believe in

God; believe also in me. In my Father’s house are many rooms. If it were not so, would I have told

you that I go to prepare a place for you? And if I go and prepare a place for you, I will come again

and will take you to myself, that where I am you may be also," (John 14:1–3). What a promise that

is—"I will come again." Truly, beloved, we can say of the Promise field what cannot be said of

any field in all England: it is so rich that it could not be richer, and it has so many ears of grain that

you could not fit another in. As the poet sings:

"What more can he say, than to you he hath said,—

You who unto Jesus for refuge have fled?"

Glean in that field, you poor and needy ones, and never think you are intruding. The whole field

is yours; every ear is yours. You may gather from the sheaves themselves, and the more you take,

the more you may.

Then there is the Ordinance field; a great deal of good wheat grows here. The field of Baptism has

been especially fruitful to some of us, for it has shown us our death, burial, and resurrection in

Christ, and so has encouraged and instructed us. It has been good for us to declare ourselves on

the Lord’s side, and we have found that keeping our Lord’s commandments brings great reward.

But I will not delay you long in this field, for some think the soil is damp; I wish them more light

and more grace. We will move on to the field of the Lord’s Supper, where the best of the Lord’s

grain grows. What rich things we have tasted in this choice spot! Have we not there enjoyed the

sweetest and most sustaining spiritual food? Across the whole estate no field rivals this central and

crown jewel; this is the King’s Acre. Gospel gleaner, remain in this field; glean in it on the first

day of each week, and expect to see your Lord there; for it is written, "And he was recognised by

them in the breaking of the bread," (Luke 24:35). The heavenly Husbandman has a field on a hill,

which is equal to the best of the others, though it may not surpass them.

You cannot truly enter any of the other fields unless you pass through this one; the road to the

other fields lies through this hill farm, called Fellowship and Communion with Christ. This is the

field for the Lord’s choicest ones to glean in. Some of you have only passed through it quickly,

not staying long enough; but those who know how to dwell here, truly to live here, will spend their

hours most profitably and pleasantly.

Only as we have fellowship and communion with Christ do ordinances, doctrines, and promises

profit us. All else is dry and barren unless we enjoy Christ’s love, bear his likeness, dwell

continually with him, and rejoice in his love. I regret that few Christians value this field; it is

enough for them to be sound in doctrine and fairly correct in practice. They care far less than they

should about intimate interaction with Christ by the Holy Spirit. If we gleaned in this field, we

would have far fewer tempers, far less pride, and far less sloth. This is a sheltered, protected field,

and in it you will find food better than even angels eat; indeed, you will find Jesus himself as the

bread from heaven. Blessed field, may we visit it every day. The Master leaves the gate wide open

for all believers; let us enter and gather the golden ears until we can carry no more. Thus we have

seen the great Husbandman in his fields; let us rejoice that we have such a Husbandman near and

such fields to glean in.

II. And now, secondly, we have a humble gleaner. Ruth was a gleaner, and may serve as an

example of what every believer should be in the fields of God.

1. The believer is a favoured gleaner, for they may take home as much as they can carry;

everything is freely given by the Lord. I use the metaphor of a gleaner because few

Christians go beyond it, though they are free to do so if they are able. Some may ask, why

does the believer not reap the entire field? I answer, they are welcome to do so if they can;

no good thing will the Lord withhold from those who walk uprightly. If your faith is like a

large wagon and can carry the whole field, you have full permission to take it. Alas, our

faith is small; we glean rather than reap. We are limited, not God. May you all grow beyond

the metaphor and return home with your sheaves.

2. Again, a gleaner must endure toil and fatigue. She rises early and goes to a field; if it is

closed, she moves to another; if that one is gone over, she hurries further still. All day she

bends down, gathering ears one by one, seldom sitting to rest. She returns home at night,

heavily laden if the field was good. Beloved, let us do the same in seeking spiritual food.

Let us not fear a little fatigue in the Master’s fields; if the gleaning is rich, we must not

weary in gathering the precious grain, for the reward is great. I know of a friend who walks

five miles every Sunday to hear the gospel, and the same distance back. Another considers

ten miles a small matter; they are wise, for no effort is too great to hear the pure Word of

God. A gleaner does not expect the ears to come to her; she knows gleaning is hard work.

We may not always find the best field nearby; we may need to journey to the far end of the

parish. But gleaners must not be choosy; wherever the Lord sends the gospel, there we

must go.

3. Every ear the gleaner gathers requires stooping. Proud people rarely profit from the Word

because they expect the corn to be lifted for them. They admire the preacher who holds

truth high, out of reach, but this is no great feat. A preacher’s job is to place truth within

reach of all, children and adults. Handfuls may be deliberately given to poor gleaners, and

they do not mind stooping to gather them. If we only preach to the educated, the wise

understand, but the illiterate do not. Preach simply to the poor, and others can understand

if they choose. Those who will not stoop for plain truth should give up gleaning. I would

learn from a child if it helped me understand the gospel. The gleaning in the Lord’s field

is rich enough to make hard labour worthwhile. Hungry souls know this; they must not be

hindered. We stoop through prayer, humility, and confession, and gather daily bread for

our souls.

4. The gleaner gathers ear by ear; occasionally handfuls fall, but usually it is straw by straw.

Ruth was favoured with handfuls, but normally one stoops, gathers, and stoops again.

Where abundance is found, go there; if not, rejoice in gathering one ear at a time. Some

only attend their favourite minister and refuse to hear others; remember, "not forsaking the

assembling of yourselves together," (Hebrews 10:25). Do not deprive your soul of food. If

you cannot gather much at once, gather little by little. Be content to learn here a little and

there a little; otherwise, you will be half-starved and then return to the despised minister to

pick up what his field yields.

5. The gleaner keeps what she gathers in her hand; she does not drop it. Some hear a good

thought but rush for the next, losing all before. At the end, a handful falls, and they forget

all prior. A sermon is like a field; gather, tie up, and carry home, but do not lose it to idle

talk. I knew a man who rushed home after a sermon, but deacons discussing it destroyed

all he remembered. Avoid such losses; walk home quietly and keep your gleanings. Be like

a miser who keeps all he gathers; do not lose your eternal riches through frivolous

conversation.

6. Then the gleaner threshes the wheat. Threshing a sermon is wise, whoever preached it, for

there is always some straw. Many "thresh" by criticising the preacher, but better is to

separate truth from straw through meditation and prayer. Lay the sermon on the floor of

reflection, beat it with prayer, and the wheat is yours. Do not neglect this; if a gleaner stores

corn without threshing, mice will consume it. Satan, sin, and the world may waste an

unprocessed sermon. He who threshes carefully and separates truth from straw becomes a

wise hearer, feeding on what he hears.

7. Finally, the gleaner winnows the corn. Ruth did this in the field; we may need to do it at

home. She left the chaff behind; we should separate precious from worthless, leaving the

chaff. Do not take home trivialities or odd remarks from ministers. Ask, "What did the

preacher say that was truly worth hearing?" Often the answer is, "I do not recall." They

have sifted the wheat and brought home chaff. Follow the opposite rule: drop the straw,

retain the good grain. Judge carefully, reject false teaching, and keep true doctrine. This is

the art of heavenly gleaning. May the Lord grant us wisdom so we may be "rich for all the

purposes of happiness," and our mouths be satisfied with good things, our youth renewed

like the eagle’s (Psalm 103:5).

III. And now, finally, here is a gracious permission given: "Let her glean among the sheaves and

reproach her not" (Ruth 2:15). Ruth had no right to go among the sheaves until Boaz gave her

permission by saying, "Let her do it." Being allowed to gather in the part of the field where the

wheat was freshly cut, and none yet collected, was a great favour. But Boaz also whispered that

handfuls would be deliberately dropped for her—an even greater favour. Boaz had a secret

affection for Ruth, and in the same way, beloved, it is because of our Lord's eternal love that he

lets us enter his best fields and glean among the sheaves. His grace allows us to receive blessings

of doctrine, promises, and experience. All heavenly blessings are given freely by God; we have no

right to them of ourselves—our portion is from his sovereign grace.

Let us notice that, while these meal-times come without warning, there are certain seasons when

we may expect them.

Eastern reapers generally sit under the shelter of a tree or a booth to take refreshment during the

heat of the day. Likewise, when trouble, hardship, persecution, and loss press most heavily upon

us, it is often then that the Lord gives us the sweetest comforts. We must labour until the hot sun

causes sweat to fall from our faces before we can expect rest; we must bear the burden and heat of

the day before we are invited to the special meals which the Lord prepares for his true workers.

When your day of trouble is hottest, then the love of Jesus will feel the sweetest.

These meal-times sometimes occur before a trial. Elijah was fed under a broom tree because he

was to travel forty days and forty nights in the strength of that food. (“And as he lay and slept

under a broom tree, suddenly an angel touched him and said to him, ‘Arise and eat.’ And he looked,

and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on hot stones and a jar of water. And he ate and

drank and lay down again. And the angel of the LORD came again a second time and touched him

and said, ‘Arise and eat, for the journey is too great for you.’ And he arose and ate and drank, and

went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb the mount of God.” — 1

Kings 19:5–8 ESV) If you receive extraordinary seasons of communion with Jesus, be ready: you

may be entering a long trial ahead. Just as a ship taking on abundant provisions is preparing for a

distant journey, so these rich spiritual seasons prepare you for more difficult times. Sweet

nourishment readies the soul for stern conflict.

Times of refreshing can also come after service or hardship. Christ was tempted by the devil, and

afterward angels came and ministered to him. (“Then the devil left him, and behold, angels came

and ministered to him.” — Matthew 4:11 ESV) Jacob wrestled with God, and afterward hosts of

angels met him. (“So Jacob called the name of the place Peniel, saying, ‘For I have seen God face

to face, and yet my life has been delivered.’ … And Jacob called the name of the place Mahanaim.”

— Genesis 32:30–31 ESV) Abraham defeated the kings and returned from battle, and then

Melchizedek met him with bread and wine. (“And Melchizedek king of Salem brought out bread

and wine. (He was priest of God Most High.) And he blessed him and said, ‘Blessed be Abram by

God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth; and blessed be God Most High, who has delivered

your enemies into your hand!’ And Abram gave him a tenth of everything.” — Genesis 14:18–20

ESV) After conflict there is contentment, after battle there is a banquet. When you have served

your Lord faithfully, you may sit down, and your Master will attend you.

Let worldly people say what they will about religion being hard, we do not find it so. Reaping for

Christ has its difficulties, but the bread we eat is heavenly sweet, and the wine we drink comes

from the choicest vineyards.

“I would not change my bless’d estate

For all the world calls good or great;

And while my faith can keep her hold,

I envy not the sinner’s gold.”

Now we turn to another point: the gleaner is affectionately invited to these meals. That is, the poor,

trembling stranger who is too weak to reap, who has no right in the field except by mercy — the

poor sinner aware of their faults, with little hope and little joy — is invited to the feast of love.

In our text the gleaner is invited to come: “At meal-time come thou hither.” (Ruth 2:14 ESV) Do

not let shame about your clothes, character, poverty, or physical weakness keep you from the place

of sacred feasting. “At meal-time come thou hither.” I knew a deaf woman who could never hear

a sound, yet she was always in God’s house. When asked why, she said that a friend had given her

the text, and God gave her many sweet thoughts of it as she sat with his people. She felt that, as a

believer, she should honour God by being present with his people. She enjoyed the best company

— the presence of God, holy angels, and the saints. If she found pleasure in coming, then those

who can hear should never stay away. Although we feel our unworthiness, we should desire to be

in God’s house, like the sick waiting at the pool of Bethesda, hoping to be healed. (“Now there is

in Jerusalem by the Sheep Gate a pool, in Aramaic called Bethesda, which has five roofed

colonnades… a multitude of invalids… waiting for the water to be stirred.” — John 5:2-3 ESV)

Trembling soul, never let the devil’s temptations keep you from the assembly of worshippers: “At

meal-time come thou hither.”

Moreover, she was invited not only to come but to eat. Whatever is sweet and comforting in the

Word of God, those who are broken in spirit are invited to share it. “For Christ Jesus came into the

world to save sinners…” (“…Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the

foremost.” — 1 Timothy 1:15) …and “…Christ died for the ungodly.” (“But God shows his love

for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” — Romans 5:8)

You may be saying in your heart, “O that I could eat the children’s bread!” — and you may. You

have no right except the Lord’s invitation.

“Let not conscience make you linger,

Nor of fitness fondly dream.”

Since he bids you come, take him at his word. If there is a promise, believe it. If there is

encouragement, accept it, and let its sweetness be yours.

Further, she was urged not only to eat but to dip her morsel in the vinegar. This is not sourness,

but a mild refreshing drink used with bread in the fields — something like watered wine or fruit

juice that adds flavour. Beloved, the Lord’s workers have sauce with their bread: not merely

doctrines, but the holy joy that accompanies them. For example, the doctrine of election is like

bread; the joy of knowing “…he chose us in him before the foundation of the world.” (“…even as

he chose us in him before the foundation of the world…” — Ephesians 1:4 ESV) is the sauce to

dip the bread in. You, poor gleaner, are invited to dip your morsel too.

I used to hear people sing Toplady’s hymn: “A debtor to mercy alone,

Of covenant mercy I sing…

Yes, I to the end shall endure,

As sure as the earnest is given;

More happy, but not more secure, The glorified spirits in heaven.” At first I could not sing it — it was too sweet. But I thank God I have ventured to dip my morsel

in it, and now I hardly like my bread without it. I want every trembling sinner to partake of the

comforting truths of God’s Word, even those called “high doctrine.” Believe the simple truths first,

then enjoy the richer truths.

Perhaps the gleaner hesitates, saying, “I have no right; I am not a reaper.” But Jesus invites you.

Come! Take his invitation and draw near. You may say, “I am weak; I hardly get any grain.” Still,

Jesus invites you. You may say, “I am a stranger, a sinner.” But Jesus knows your sin and invites

you anyway. You may say, “I feel I do not deserve it.” Jesus bids you come. Your doubt is more

presumptuous than your faith.

There is enough grace for you. Jesus’ mercy is not like the sea being drained; it never runs out.

Come now. Jesus loves you and takes delight in seeing you feast at his table. Here is a secret: he

intends to be married to you. If you become his spouse, the fields will be yours, for a wife shares

all her husband’s inheritance. All the promises that are “yes and amen in Christ” (“For all the

promises of God find their Yes in him…” — 2 Corinthians 1:20 ESV) belong to you in Christ

now. Though a stranger, Jesus loves you: “…he came eating and drinking, and they say, ‘Look at

him! A glutton and a drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!’” (Matthew 11:19 ESV —

showing Jesus' heart for sinners). The Good Shepherd leaves the ninety-nine to seek the lost sheep.

(“…which one of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them…” — Luke 15:4 ESV)

The prodigal’s return is celebrated in heaven. (“…for this my son was dead, and is alive again; he

was lost, and is found.” — Luke 15:24 ESV) Come, trembling gleaner! Jesus invites you:

“At meal-time come thou hither, and eat of the bread, and dip thy morsel in the vinegar.” — Ruth

2:14 ESV

The main reason Boaz allowed Ruth to glean among the sheaves was love. He wanted her there

because he had a deep affection for her, which he later revealed more fully. Similarly, the Lord

lets his people glean because he loves them. Did you enjoy a soul-enriching time in the fields the

last Sabbath? Did you return home with your sack full, like Joseph's brothers returning from Egypt?

Were you satisfied with the abundance? That was your Master’s goodness. Look at all your

spiritual blessings as proof of his eternal love. When you remember that each sweet experience,

each high enjoyment of the Spirit, comes from his love, your spiritual “corn” will grind more easily

and taste all the sweeter. Your joys, your moments of deep spiritual delight, are all evidence of

divine affection—be doubly glad for them.

Another reason Boaz let Ruth glean was that he was her relative. In the same way, our Lord gives

us special blessings because he is our kinsman.

Jesus, our Redeemer, is our closest relative, bone of our bone and flesh of our flesh. It is a

wonderful mystery that Christ is the Husband of his Church. He may rightly let his bride glean

among the sheaves because all that he owns is already hers. Her interests and his are one. He can

say, “Beloved, take all you please; I am not poorer because you share my fullness. You are mine,

and all I have is yours.”

So, my friends, enrich yourselves from what is your Lord’s. Go gleaning spiritually as often as

you can. Never miss an opportunity to gather a blessing. Glean at the mercy seat, in private

meditation, in reading godly books, or in company with faithful Christians. Even if you can only

take a small handful, it is better than nothing. Those of you busy with work and cares, if you can

spend just five minutes in the Lord’s field, do it. If you cannot carry a sheaf, carry an ear; if you

cannot find an ear, pick up even a single grain. Gather as much as you can.

One more point: never be afraid to glean. Have faith and claim God’s promises for yourself. Jesus

delights to see you using his gifts freely. His invitation is, "Eat abundantly, and drink, yes, drink

abundantly, O beloved" (Isaiah 55:1). When you find a rich promise, live upon it. Draw the honey

from Scripture and enjoy its sweetness. If you discover a remarkable blessing, carry it away

joyfully. You cannot believe too much about the Lord; do not be satisfied with a meagre portion

when all heaven’s granaries are open to you. Glean with diligence and confidence, knowing that

he who owns the fields and the sheaves watches over you in love and will one day unite you with

himself in eternal glory. Happy is the gleaner who finds eternal love and eternal life in the fields

she enters!

Meal-time in the Cornfields "And Boaz said to her, 'Come here, and eat of the bread, and dip your morsel in the vinegar.' So

she sat beside the reapers, and he passed her roasted grain, and she ate and was satisfied, and left"

(Ruth 2:14). We go to the cornfields not just to glean, but to rest with the reapers, sitting under a

wide-spreading tree to refresh ourselves. May timid gleaners accept this invitation and have the

confidence to enjoy the meal fully, and to carry some home to share with needy friends.

First, God’s reapers have their meal-times. Those who work for God will find him a good Master.

He cares for oxen, and he commanded Israel, "You shall not muzzle an ox when it treads out the

grain" (Deuteronomy 25:4).

How much more does he care for his servants! "He gives food to those who fear him; he will ever

be mindful of his covenant" (Psalm 111:5). Reapers in Jesus’ fields receive not only a final reward,

but also comforts along the way. God rewards his servants twice: first in the work itself, and second

in the joy it produces. He gives such joy in serving him that they can say, "We delight to do your

will, O Lord" (Psalm 40:8). Heaven is serving God day and night, and we get a taste of that by

serving him earnestly on earth.

God also ordains special meal-times when his servants gather to hear the Word. When the Lord

blesses ministers, they act like the disciples of old: receiving loaves and fish from Jesus and

distributing them to the people. We cannot feed a soul by ourselves, but with the Lord, even

thousands are provided for. You know what it is to sit under the Word with delight, finding the

teaching sweet to your soul. When doctrines of grace are explained clearly, when Christ is lifted

up, when the Spirit’s work is remembered, and the Father’s purpose honoured, the table is rich and

all God’s children are satisfied.

Often, too, God appoints private meal-times in reading and meditation. "His paths drop fatness"

(Psalm 65:11). Nothing nourishes the believer more than meditating on the Word. Men grow

slowly in the faith because they chew the truth too little. Cattle must chew the cud; it is not what

they crop that nourishes, but what they digest. We must turn the truth over and over in our hearts

to draw nourishment. Private devotion is a land of milk and honey, a paradise yielding spiritual

fruits and delights. No earthly feast can compare. Meditation on the Word offers green pastures,

still waters, and joy exceeding honey. These private times of prayer and reflection are refreshing,

like reapers sitting at midday with their Master. Many have found the Bible to be food, drink, and

company when all else failed.

One specially ordained meal-time occurs at least weekly—the Lord’s Supper. There we have a

literal and spiritual meal. Bread and wine symbolise Christ’s body and blood, which give

everlasting life: "Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him

up on the last day" (John 6:54). Oh, the sweet experiences we have had at the Lord’s Supper! If

some realised the blessing of feeding on Christ in this ordinance, they would not neglect fellowship

with the Church. There is great reward in keeping the Master’s commandments, and loss in

neglecting them. Christ is not bound to the sacramental table, yet "if you love me, keep my

commandments" (John 14:15) reminds us that he meets us there.

At the table, our soul ascends from symbol to reality; we eat spiritual bread and lean our head on

Jesus’ bosom: "He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me was love" (Song

of Solomon 2:4).

Besides these regular meal-times, God also gives surprise seasons of grace. While walking, we

feel a sudden outpouring of love; in business, our hearts are lifted and dance like spring streams.

Even on sick beds, tender grace can make our trials sweet. In the morning, Christ drops thoughts

into our minds like dew; in the evening, meditation refreshes us; in the night watches, he becomes

our song.

God’s reapers work hard, but they find comfort when they rest and eat of their Master’s rich

provision. Then, strengthened, they rise again to reap in the heat of the day.

Now, thirdly—and here is a very sweet point in the story—Boaz reached her the parched corn. She

did “come and eat” (Ruth 2:14 ESV). Where did she sit? Note carefully that she “sat beside the

reapers” (Ruth 2:14 ESV). She did not feel that she was one of them. Like some of you who do

not approach the Lord’s Supper but sit and watch, you are sitting “beside the reapers”. You fear

that you are not God’s people, yet you love them, and so you sit beside them. If there is a blessing

to be had and you cannot reach it fully, you will sit as close as possible to those who do receive it.

And while she was sitting there, what happened? Did she reach out and take the food herself? No,

it is written, “He reached her the parched corn” (Ruth 2:14 ESV). That is the point: only the Lord

of the harvest can give the choicest spiritual refreshment. I can give the invitation in my Master’s

name, sincerely and affectionately, yet none will come until the Spirit draws them. No trembling

heart accepts divine blessing at my bidding alone. Only if the King himself draws near and reaches

the parched corn will it be received. How does He do this? Through His gracious Spirit, He first

inspires your faith. You may fear that a sinner like you can never be “accepted in the Beloved”

(Ephesians 1:6 ESV), yet the Spirit breathes life into your hope, turning it into confident faith,

which says, “Yes, my beloved is mine, and His desire is toward me” (Song of Solomon 7:10 ESV).

Having done this, the Saviour does more: He pours the love of God into your heart. The love of

Christ is like sweet perfume in a box. Only He knows how to open the box and release the

fragrance. He personally sheds the love of God into the soul.

But Jesus does more still: He reaches the parched corn with His own hand when He gives us close

fellowship with Himself. Do not think this is a dream; there truly is such a thing as speaking with

Christ today. As certainly as you may converse with a close friend or find comfort with a beloved

companion, so surely can you commune with Jesus and delight in the presence of Immanuel. He

is not a far-off Saviour; He is near. His Word is in our mouths and hearts, and we walk with Him

today as the elect did of old, and commune with Him as His apostles did on earth—spiritually, yet

truly.

Yet again, the Lord Jesus reaches the parched corn when the Spirit gives the internal witness that

we are “born of God” (1 John 5:1 ESV). A believer may know their salvation beyond all doubt.

Just as Philip de Morny said in his day, the Spirit can make salvation as clear to us as a geometric

proof. Just as clearly as two and two make four, we may “know that we have passed from death to

life” (1 John 3:14 ESV). The sun in the sky is not more certain to the eye than salvation is to a

heart assured by the Spirit.

Now let poor Ruth’s trembling prayer rise: Lord, reach me the parched corn! “Show me a sign for

good; deal bountifully with your servant; draw me, that I may run after you” (Psalm 86:17 ESV;

Song of Solomon 1:4 ESV). Lord, pour Your love into my heart!

“Come, Holy Spirit, heavenly Dove, with all thy quickening powers, come, shed abroad a

Saviour’s love, and that shall kindle ours.”

There is no access to Christ except by Christ revealing Himself to us. After Boaz had reached the parched corn, we are told that “she ate and was satisfied, and she kept

some back” (Ruth 2:14 ESV). So shall it be with every Ruth. Every penitent shall become a

believer, every mourner a singer. There may be long periods of conviction and hesitation, but a

time will come when the soul decides for the Lord, saying, “If I perish, I perish” (Esther 4:16

ESV). “I will go as I am to Jesus. I will not play with my buts and ifs. Since He bids me believe

that He died for me, I will trust His cross for my salvation.” When this happens, you will be

satisfied. Your mind will be filled with the precious truths Christ reveals; your heart content in

Jesus as the altogether lovely one; your hope secure, for whom have you in heaven but Christ?

Your desires will be met, for what can satisfy more than “to know Christ and the power of His

resurrection, and the fellowship of His sufferings” (Philippians 3:10 ESV)?

“She ate and was satisfied” (Ruth 2:14 ESV). Some of us have had deep draughts of Christ’s love,

thinking we could drink Him all in, only to leave much behind. We have feasted with a ravenous

appetite at the table of the Lord’s love, saying, “Nothing but the infinite can satisfy me,” and yet

that infinite has been granted. Even as sinners, we find our sins forgiven and abundance of merit

in Jesus. Sweet portions of God’s Word remain for us to enjoy later. As Jesus said, “I still have

many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now” (John 16:12 ESV). There is a higher

fellowship, a deeper intimacy, a greater height of communion with Christ still to come.

A little later, we see what Ruth did with her leftovers. She took them home to Naomi (Ruth 2:14

ESV). Likewise, you who think you have no claim to the Lord’s blessings shall be allowed to eat,

be satisfied, and even share with those hungry at home. Young believers, cultivate this habit: when

you hear a sermon, think of someone you love who cannot attend, and carry home something for

them. Love as you have been loved. Remember “You shall love the Lord your God with all your

heart and your neighbour as yourself” (Matthew 22:37–39 ESV). You cannot truly love your

neighbour’s soul if you do not love God and receive His grace first. Take home your gleanings for

those who cannot gather for themselves.

I know no kinder invitation than this: “Come, and welcome to Jesus.” May the Lord reach a handful

of parched corn to you if you are a trembling sinner, and fill you until you are fully satisfied.

fields.title: Chapter 16
fields.body_html:
THE LOADED WAGON Introduction

“Behold, I am pressed under you” calls us to see the weight of sin upon God’s heart. Today, we

reflect on mercy, justice, and the cost of rebellion. Let us examine our lives, repent, and flee to

Christ, who lifts the heaviest burdens from our souls.

"Behold, I am pressed under you, as a cart is pressed that is full of sheaves."—Amos 2:13. We have been into the cornfields to glean with Boaz and Ruth, and I trust that the timid and faint-

hearted have been encouraged to take the handfuls that are purposely left for them by the generous

order of our Lord. Today, we go to the gate of the harvest-field with another purpose—to see the

wagon piled high with many sheaves, creaking as it moves along and leaving ruts in the field. We

come with gratitude to God, thanking him for the harvest, blessing him for favourable weather,

and praying that he continues it until the last sheaf of corn is brought in, and the farmers

everywhere celebrate the "Harvest Home."

What a picture a wagon loaded with corn gives of you and me, as if we were loaded with God’s

mercies! From our cradle until now, each day has added a sheaf of blessing. What more could the

Lord do for us than he has already done? He has daily filled our lives with benefits. Let us worship

his goodness and offer him our heartfelt gratitude.

Alas! that this same image could carry another meaning. Alas! that while God loads us with mercy,

we load him with sin. While he piles favour upon favour, we also pile iniquity upon iniquity, until

the weight of our sin becomes intolerable to the Most High, and he cries out because of the burden,

saying, "I am pressed under you, as a cart is pressed that is full of sheaves."

Our text begins with a "Behold!" and rightly so. "Behold" is used in Scripture like a sign outside

a shop to attract attention. Whenever we see "Behold" in the Bible, it signals something new,

important, or worthy of attention.

I see this "Behold!" standing, like a maiden on the steps of the house of wisdom, calling, "Come

in, you wise-hearted, and listen to the voice of God." Let us open our eyes to "behold," and may

the Spirit guide our hearts through our eyes and ears so that repentance and self-abhorrence may

take hold because of our wrongdoings toward our gracious God.

It must be understood before we go further that this text is figurative. God cannot literally be

oppressed by humans; all the sin that man commits cannot disturb the serenity of divine perfection

or even cause a ripple in his eternal calm. He speaks to us in human terms, bringing the mysteries

of heaven down to the limitations of earthly understanding. He talks to us as a loving father might

to a small child. Just as a cart creaks and bends under excessive weight, the Lord says that under

the load of human guilt, he is pressed down until he cries out, because he can bear no longer the

iniquity of those who offend against him.

The first and most obvious truth in the text is that sin is extremely grievous and burdensome to

God.

Be astonished, O heavens, and be amazed, O earth, that God should speak of being pressed and

weighed down! Nowhere in Scripture do we read that the weight of creation is any burden to the

Most High. "He takes up the isles like a very little thing" (Psalm 136:16). Neither the sun, nor the

moon, nor the stars, nor all the mighty orbs created by his power cost him any labour to sustain.

The heathen picture Atlas stooping under the globe, but the eternal God, who upholds the pillars

of the universe, "faints not, neither is weary" (Isaiah 40:28). Even distant providence does not tire

him. He watches both night and day; his power goes forth every moment. He brings forth the

constellations in their seasons and guides Arcturus with its sons. He upholds the foundations of

the earth and holds its cornerstone. He commands the morning to know its place and sets a limit

to darkness and the shadow of death. All things are sustained by his power, and nothing exists

without him. Just as a wave carries its foam and the foam disappears, so would the universe vanish

if God did not sustain it every day. This continual work has not weakened him, nor is there any

hint of weakness. He works all things, and when they are done, they are as nothing in his sight.

Yet strange, most extraordinary, miraculous among miracles—sin burdens God, though the world

cannot; iniquity presses the Most High, though the weight of all creation is like a tiny speck in the

balance. Ah, careless sons of Adam, you think sin is trivial; and you sons of Belial, you think it

sport, saying, "He does not notice, he sees not; how could God know? And if he knows, he does

not care for our sins." Learn from God’s Word that the truth is the opposite: your sins grieve him,

they are a burden and load to him, until, like a cart overloaded with sheaves, he is weighed down

with human guilt.

This becomes clearer if we consider what sin is and what it does. Sin is the great destroyer of all

God’s works. Sin turned an archangel into a fallen angel and angels of light into spirits of evil. Sin

looked on Eden and withered all its flowers. Before sin entered, the Creator said of the new earth,

"It is very good" (Genesis 1:31), but when sin entered, it grieved God at his very heart that he had

made humans. Nothing tarnishes beauty like sin, for it spoils God’s image and erases his imprint.

Moreover, sin makes God’s creatures unhappy. Can we imagine God tolerating this? God never

intended any of his creatures to be miserable. He made them to be glad; he gave birds their songs,

flowers their fragrance, the air its freshness; he gave the day the smiling sun and night its crown

of stars, intending joy to be worship and gladness to be the incense of praise. But sin has made

God’s favourite creature a wretch, bringing down the offspring of God, made in his image, to

nakedness, poverty, and misery. Therefore, God hates sin and is pressed down by it, because it

makes the objects of his love unhappy at their core.

Sin attacks God in all his attributes, assails him on his throne, and strikes at his very existence.

What is sin? Is it not an insult to God’s wisdom? O sinner, God commands you to do his will;

when you act against it, you are essentially saying, "I know what is good for me, and God does

not." You are declaring that infinite wisdom is mistaken and that you, a creature of a day, are the

best judge of happiness. Sin challenges God’s goodness by implying he withholds what would

make you happy, and this is not the action of a good, loving father. Sin attacks God’s wisdom with

one hand and his goodness with the other.

Sin also abuses God’s mercy. When you sin boldly because God has been patient with you, when

you indulge in wrongdoing because you face no immediate consequences, you turn the mercy that

was meant to guide you to repentance into an excuse for further rebellion. It grieves a loving father

to see his mercy turned against himself. Every sin is, in effect, a defiance of divine power. It is like

lifting your puny fists against the majesty of heaven and daring God to punish you. Each act of

disobedience defies the Lord to see whether he can enforce his law.

Is it a small matter that a tiny creature challenges the Lord of all ages, the God who sustains

everything by his word? Well may he be burdened by such provocations! Every attribute you may

mention has been affronted by sin; every aspect of God’s character is slurred by it. Sin is evil, and

it is continuously evil; in every perspective, it is offensive to the Most High.

Sinner, do you know that every act of disobedience to God’s law is virtually high treason? Each

time you swerve from his will, you put your will in his place; you make yourself a god and diminish

the Most High. Is this a small offence, to snatch from him his crown and sceptre? Such an act

cannot be ignored by heaven; if it were, the moral order would collapse. This treason against God

will be punished.

Finally, sin is an attack on God himself; sin is heart atheism. No matter the religious profession,

the sinner in their heart says, "There is no God." They wish there were no law and no Supreme

Ruler. Is this trivial? To be a Deicide! To desire to remove God from his world! Can this be

ignored? Can the Most High hear it and not be pressed down beneath its weight?

I do not exaggerate against sin and disobedience. It is beyond human imagination to fully convey

the evil of sin, and no mortal tongue, even if touched by God’s own fire, could speak the enormity

of the smallest sin against God. Think, friends: we are his creatures, and yet we will not obey him.

He feeds us, sustains our breath, yet we waste it in murmuring and rebellion.

We are always in the sight of our omniscient God, and yet his presence is not enough to compel

obedience. Surely if a man insulted the lawgiver in his presence, that would be intolerable; yet that

is exactly our situation. We must confess, "Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is

evil in your sight" (Psalm 51:4). We offend knowingly. We do not sin like the ignorant or the

savage. We in England sin against extraordinary light and understanding; is this a small matter?

Can we expect God to overlook wilful, deliberate offences? Oh, that these lips could speak, that

this heart could burn, for if I could declare the horror of sin, even Pharaoh or Nebuchadnezzar

would tremble. It is terrible to rebel against the Most High. May the Lord have mercy on his

servants and forgive them.

This is our first point, but God himself must teach it through his Spirit. May the Holy Ghost make

you feel that sin is exceedingly sinful, grievous, and burdensome to God.

Secondly, some sins are especially grievous to God. The context of our text helps to show the force

of this truth.

There is no such thing as a “little” sin, but still, there are degrees of guilt. It would be wrong to

claim that a sinful thought has the same degree of evil as a sinful act. A sinful imagination is indeed

wrong—completely sinful and serious—but a sinful action carries a greater degree of provocation.

Some sins particularly provoke God. In the context of our text, we see that licentiousness does

this. The Jewish people in the days of Amos appear to have reached a very high level of fornication

and lechery. This sin is still common today; our midnight streets and divorce courts bear witness.

I will say no more. Let each person keep their body pure; for lack of chastity is a grievous evil in

the sight of the Lord.

Oppression, too, according to the prophet, is another great provocation to God. The prophet speaks
