of selling the poor for a pair of shoes, and some would crush widows and orphans, making

labourers work without pay. Many businesspeople have no “compassion.” They form themselves

into societies, then demand excessive interest on loans from the unfortunate who fall into their

hands. Clever legal loopholes and evasions of rightful debts often amount to heavy oppression and

certainly bring down the anger of the Most High.

Idolatry and blasphemy are also highly offensive to God and extremely heinous. The text says the

people “drank the wine of false gods.” Anyone who sets up their appetite, their gold, or their wealth

as their god, and lives for these instead of the Most High, commits idolatry. Woe to such a person,

and equal woe to those who worship crosses, sacraments, or images.

Blasphemy, especially, is a God-provoking sin. For blasphemy, there is no excuse. As George

Herbert said, “Lust and wine plead a pleasure; there is gain to be pleaded for avarice; but the

profane swearer lets his soul run for nothing.” There is no benefit in profane speech; cursing brings

no pleasure—it offends for the sake of offending, and is therefore a high and crying sin that makes

the Lord weary of humanity. Some of you may find these words personally directed. Do I address

the lecherous, the oppressive, or the profane? Soul, what mercy God has shown you for so long!

The day will come when he will say, “I will ease myself of my adversaries,” and how easily he

could cast you off to a terrible destruction.

While some sins are grievous because of their particular heinousness, many people are especially

offensive to God because of the length of their sin. That grey-haired man—how many times has

he provoked the Most High? Even young men have reason to consider their years and apply

themselves to wisdom because of the time they have spent in rebellion. What can we say of those

who have been in open rebellion against God for fifty, sixty, seventy, even nearly eighty years?

Eighty years of mercy met with eighty years of neglect; for eighty years of patience, they have

returned eighty years of ingratitude. O God, how weary you must be of the length and number of

human sins!

Furthermore, God takes special note of sin mixed with obstinacy. Oh, how obstinate some people

are! They seem determined to be damned; nothing can stop them. They act as if they would climb

mountains to reach destruction and swim through seas of fire to ruin their souls. Some have

recovered from serious illness only to return to sin. Some have suffered business failures, lost

wealth, fallen into poverty, yet continue in sin. Another child dies; the wife is sick; starvation

threatens the family—but they persist with arrogance. This is true obstinacy. Sinner, God will let

you have your own way one day, and that way will be your eternal ruin. God is weary of those

who persist in wrongdoing despite warnings, invitations, and entreaties.

The text also suggests that ingratitude is especially burdensome to God. He reminds the people

how he brought them out of Egypt, defeated the Amorites, raised up prophets and Nazarites—yet

they still rebelled. This struck me deeply when I first came to God as a guilty sinner—not only the

visible wickedness of my life, but the particular mercies I had enjoyed. How generous God has

been to some of us who never lacked anything! He never let us fall into poverty, nor leave us to

infamy, nor abandon us to evil example. He preserved our morality, encouraged love for his house

even when we did not love him, year after year. And how poor have been our returns! What joy,

deliverance, love, and comfort we have received—and yet we have sinned openly! Well may he

be like a cart pressed under a heavy load of sheaves.

Notice also that the Lord’s burden is so great that he even cries out. Just as a heavily loaded cart

groans under its weight, so the Lord cries under the weight of sin. Have you heard these words?

"Hear, O heavens, and give ear, O earth: for the Lord has spoken: I have nourished and brought up

children, and they have rebelled against me!" (Jeremiah 7:28). Hear again: "Return, O faithless

people; I will heal your faithlessness" (Jeremiah 3:22).

Better still, hear the lament from Jesus, gentle as dew: "O Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the

prophets and stone those sent to you, how often would I have gathered your children together, as

a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you would not!" (Matthew 23:37). Sinner, God is

grieved by your sin; your Creator suffers over what you mock; your Saviour cries in his spirit over

what you deem trivial. "O do not this abominable thing which I hate!" For God’s sake, do it not.

Cease your evil ways; why will you die, O house of Israel?

While sin is grievous to the Lord, his mercy is magnified when we see that he bears the load. As

the cart does not break but is pressed, so he is pressed, yet he bears. If you and I were in God’s

place, would we have borne it? Within a week we would have destroyed the world. If the law of

heaven punished as swiftly as human law, where would we be? God could easily avenge his

honour; countless servants stand ready to do his bidding. A mere stone, a breath of wind, a grain

of dust, and all is over. Yet God restrains the servants of his anger. The heavens and the earth

would gladly punish, yet God restrains. The angels are astonished at his patience. Have you seen

a patient man insulted and bear it? So God bears with sinners, pressed under the weight of their

guilt yet unbroken.

This brings us to a profound point: some of you have never seen sin as grievous to God. Others

know how bitter evil is and wish to escape it. Not only does God bear with sin, but in the person

of his Son, he bore and removed it.

These words gain deeper meaning in the lips of Jesus: "I am pressed under you, as a cart is pressed

that is full of sheaves." God must punish sin yet desires mercy. Jesus comes as a substitute for all

who trust him. The burden of human guilt is laid upon his shoulders, sheaf after sheaf.

"The Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all" (Isaiah 53:6). He is despised and rejected, a man

of sorrows acquainted with grief (Isaiah 53:3). He sweats great drops of blood (Luke 22:44). Herod

mocks him; Pilate jeers; they strike him. "I gave my back to those who strike, and my cheeks to

those who pull out the beard; I did not hide my face from insult and spitting" (Isaiah 50:6). They

scourge him; "the chastisement for our peace was upon him, and by his stripes we are healed"

(Isaiah 53:5). Like a cart pressed under sheaves, he moves through the streets of Jerusalem.

Daughters of Jerusalem, weep, though he bids you dry your tears! Abjects insult him as he bears

the cross, the emblem of our sin. He is brought to Golgotha, laid upon the ground, his hands and

feet nailed, the iron piercing the tender parts of his body. The cross is raised. God forsakes him;

his enemies mock. The sun refuses to shine; tenfold darkness covers his soul. "My God, my God,

why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46). Never was sorrow like his. Shall we treat sin

lightly? Shall we toy with what made our Saviour groan? Sinner, will you give up your sins for

him who suffered for them?

"Yes," you say, "if I could believe he suffered for me." Trust your soul to him, and he died for you,

taking your guilt and sorrows; you may go free. Christ was burdened that you might be lightened;

pressed that you might be free. Believe in him.

Finally, God will bear the load of our sins only a little while. If you are not in Christ at the end,

that same load will crush you forever. Some translate the text differently: "I will press you as a

cart full of sheaves presses the way beneath it." Just as a heavily loaded cart presses the soft roads,

so will God crush you beneath your sin if you are out of Christ. You must apply this personally.

Do you believe in the Lord Jesus Christ? If yes, the threat is not yours. If no, listen carefully: a

Christless soul will soon be lost; they are already condemned by unbelief. How will you escape if

you neglect this great salvation? "Consider your ways" (Haggai 1:5). By time, eternity, life, death,

heaven, hell, I urge you to believe in Christ, who can save completely those who come to him. If

you do not believe, you will die in your sins.

After death comes judgment! The trumpet sounds, the multitudes, the books, the great white

throne, "Come, you blessed," and "Depart, you cursed" (Matthew 25:34, 41). After judgment, hell

awaits the Christless. Who among us shall endure the devouring flame? Who shall dwell with

everlasting burnings? None of us can, except we flee to Christ. Fly to Jesus! I may never see your

face again. My tears entreat you; let God’s long-suffering lead you to repentance. He does not wish

anyone to die but to turn to him and live. This turning comes through trusting Jesus with your soul.

Will you trust him? The Spirit may compel you; if not, it will not be for lack of pleading. Come

now, while mercy calls. Jesus with pierced hands invites you, though you have rejected him long.

His love defies your sin. Whosoever will, let them come and take of the water of life freely

(Revelation 22:17). May God help you come, for the Redeemer’s glory. Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 17
fields.body_html:
THRESHING Introduction

God’s wisdom in husbandry teaches us more than farming—it shows His careful discipline of

His people. Just as different seeds require distinct threshing, so does He correct each

believer according to need. Let us open our hearts to His refining hand, trusting His

guidance toward holiness and eternal usefulness.

“For the fitches are not threshed with a threshing instrument, neither is a cart wheel turned about

upon the cu mmin; but the fitches are beaten out with a staff, and the cummin with a rod. Bread

corn is bruised; because he will not ever be threshing it, nor break it with the wheel of his cart, nor

bruise it with his horsemen” (Isaiah 28:27–28).

The art of husbandry was taught to man by God. Without this instruction, he would have starved

while discovering it. Therefore, when the Lord sent him out of the Garden of Eden, he gave him a

measure of elementary instruction in agriculture. As the prophet says, “His God instructs him to

discretion, and teaches him” (Isaiah 28:26). God has taught man to plough, to break the clods, to

sow different kinds of grain, and to thresh the various sorts of seeds.

The Eastern husbandman could not thresh with machinery as we do today, but he was ingenious

and careful in his methods. Sometimes a heavy instrument was dragged over the corn to separate

the grain. This is what is intended in the first clause by the “threshing instrument,” as also in the

passage, “I have made you a sharp threshing instrument with teeth” (Jeremiah 51:20). When the

corn-drag was not used, they often turned the heavy solid wheel of a country cart over the straw.

This is alluded to in the next sentence: “Neither is a cart wheel turned about upon the cummin.”

They also had flails not unlike our own, and for still smaller seeds, such as dill and cummin, they

used a simple staff or a slender rod: “The fitches are beaten out with a staff, and the cummin with

a rod.”

This is not the time or place for a full dissertation on threshing. Proper books provide all the

information needed on the subject. The meaning of the illustration, however, is this: just as God

has taught husbandmen to distinguish between different kinds of grain in threshing, so does he, in

his infinite wisdom, deal discreetly with different kinds of people. He does not test us all in the

same way, as we are differently constituted. He does not put all through the same agony of

conviction; we are not all threshed with terrors to the same degree. He does not give all the same

family or bodily affliction; one may escape with only being beaten with a rod, while another

experiences, as it were, the feet of horses in severe tribulations.

Our subject is this: threshing—first, all kinds of seeds need it; second, it is done with discretion;

third, it will not last forever, for as the text says, “Bread corn is bruised; because he will not ever

be threshing it, nor break it with the wheel of his cart, nor bruise it with his horsemen” (Isaiah

28:28).

I. First, all of us need threshing. Some have the foolish conceit that they have no sin, but they deceive

themselves, and the truth is not in them. Even the best of men are only men at the best. Being men,

they are not perfect, but remain surrounded by infirmity. What is the purpose of threshing the

grain? Is it not to separate it from straw and chaff?

Even the best of men still have a measure of chaff. Not all is grain on the threshing-floor. Not all

is grain even in those golden sheaves joyfully brought into the garner. Even wheat is joined to

straw, which was once necessary to it. Around the kernel, the husk still clings even on the

threshing-floor. Even the holiest of men have something superfluous, something which must be

removed. We sin either by omission or commission—whether in spirit, motive, zeal, or discretion.

If we escape one error, we often fall into the opposite. If our actions are right before doing them,

we may err in the doing, or become proud afterwards. If sin is shut out at the front door, it tries the

back gate, climbs in the window, or comes down the chimney. Those who cannot perceive it in

themselves are frequently blinded by its smoke. They are so immersed in sin that they do not know

it is raining. In my observation, I have yet to find a person the old divines would call perfectly

perfect. The fully all-round man is a being I expect to see in heaven, not in this fallen world. We

all need the cleansing and purging the threshing-floor is designed to accomplish.

Threshing also loosens the connection between the good grain and the husk. Of course, if the grain

slipped easily from the husk, it would only need shaking. There would be no need for a staff, a

rod, much less the feet of horses or the wheel of a cart. But here is the difficulty: our souls do not

merely lie in the dust—they cleave to it. There is a fearful intimacy between fallen human nature

and the evil in the world, and this compact is not easily broken. In our hearts, we hate every false

way, yet sorrowfully confess, “For I do not do the good I want, but the evil I do not want is what

I keep on doing” (Romans 7:19). Sometimes our spirit cries ardently after God, a holy will is

present, yet we find not how to do the good. Flesh and blood have tendencies and weaknesses

which, though not sinful themselves, incline toward sin. Appetites need but slight excitement to

grow into lusts. It is not easy to forget our own kindred or our father’s house, even when the king

desires our beauty. Our alien nature remembers Egypt and the flesh-pots while manna is still in

our mouths. We were all born in a house of evil; some nursed on the lap of iniquity, our first

companions among heirs of wrath. What is bred in the bone is hard to remove from the flesh.

Threshing is used to loosen our hold on earthly things and to break us away from evil. This requires

a divine hand, and nothing but God’s grace can make threshing effective. Something is achieved

when the soul ceases to cling to sin, when sin no longer brings pleasure or satisfaction. Yet, as

threshing is never complete until the grain is entirely separated from the husk, so chastening and

discipline are never complete until God’s people abandon every form of evil and abhor all iniquity.

When we are fully separated from the straw and chaff, the flail rests. It has required much threshing

to bring some of us near that mark, and many more heavy blows will likely fall before total

separation is reached. Some sins are easily removed by God’s grace early in our spiritual life, but

once gone, another layer of evil appears, and the process repeats. Complete removal of our

attachment to sin demands the divine skill and power of the Holy Spirit alone.

Threshing is necessary for usefulness: the wheat must be freed from the husk to serve. We can

honour God and bless others only by being holy, harmless, undefiled, and separate from sinners.

O corn of the Lord’s threshing-floor, you must be beaten and bruised or perish as worthless!

Eminent usefulness usually comes with eminent affliction. Without such separation from sin, we

cannot be gathered into the garner. God’s pure wheat must not be defiled by chaff.

Nothing that defiles can enter heaven; therefore, every imperfection must be removed for eternal

blessedness and perfection. Even now, we cannot have true fellowship with the Father unless we

are delivered daily from sin.

Some of us may lie on the threshing-floor today, suffering chastisement. What then? Rejoice, for

this shows our value to God. If the wheat cried, “The great drag has gone over me, therefore the

husbandman cares not for me,” we would reply: the farmer only drags over the precious wheat,

not the weeds. Because he esteems the wheat, he deals sternly with it and spares it not. Do not

judge that God hates you because of affliction; see instead that he honours you through every

stroke. As the Lord says, “You only have I known of all the nations of the earth; therefore I will

punish you for all your iniquities” (Amos 3:2). Because Christ made full atonement for his people,

God does not punish us as a judge; but because we are his children, he corrects us as a father. In

love, he refines his children to perfect them in his image and make them partakers of his holiness.

“I will bring them under the rod of the covenant” (Psalm 89:32). “I have refined you, but not with

silver; I have chosen you in the furnace of affliction” (Isaiah 48:10).

Do not judge by what you see or feel, but by faith. Just as threshing shows the value of wheat, so

affliction shows God’s delight in his people. As threshing reveals impurity, so affliction indicates

the Christian’s current imperfection. If we were free from evil, correction would not be needed.

The sound of the flail is never heard in heaven, for there is no threshing there—only the garner of

the fully sanctified. The threshing instrument is a humbling sign, and so long as we feel it, we

should humble ourselves under God’s hand, recognising that we are not yet free from the straw

and chaff of fallen nature.

On the other hand, the instrument is a prophecy of our future perfection. We are undergoing a

discipline from the hand of God which will not fail: by his prudence and wisdom, we shall be

completely delivered from the husk of sin. We feel the blows of the staff, yet we are being

effectively separated from the evil that has so long surrounded us, and we shall one day be pure

and perfect. Every tendency to sin shall be removed. “Foolishness is bound in the heart of a child,

but the rod of discipline drives it far from him” (Proverbs 22:15). If, while we are imperfect, we

succeed with our children through our poor and limited correction, how much more shall the Father

of spirits bring us to live unto himself through his holy discipline? If the corn understood the

necessary use of the flail, it would welcome the thresher’s work.

Since we know to what tribulation tends, let us rejoice in it and yield ourselves cheerfully to its

processes. We need threshing; it proves our value in God’s sight, and while it marks our

imperfection, it secures our ultimate cleansing.

II. Secondly, God’s threshing is done with great discretion: “For the fitches are not threshed with a

threshing instrument.” The poor little fitches, a small seed used to flavour cakes, are not crushed

with a heavy drag, for such rough treatment would destroy them. “Neither is a cart wheel turned

about upon the cummin”; this little seed, perhaps caraway, would be crushed by such weight. The

fitches are removed from the stalks by being “beaten out with a staff,” and the cummin requires

only a touch of a rod. For tender seeds, the farmer uses gentle means; for the hardier grains, he

reserves the sterner processes. Consider the spiritual lesson here.

Reflect, my brother, that your threshing and mine are in God’s hands. Our chastening is not left to

servants, nor to enemies: “We are disciplined by the Lord!” (Hebrews 12:6). The Great

Husbandman himself directs the labourers, for they know neither the time nor the manner except

as wisdom dictates. They would turn the wheel upon the cummin or attempt to thresh wheat with

a staff. I have seen God’s servants try both these follies: crushing the weak and tender, and dealing

softly with those who needed stern rebuke. Some ministers, elders, and godly men and women are

rough with timid souls; yet we need not fear they will destroy the true-hearted, for the Lord

preserves his chosen from such mistaken severity. How comforting is this! Many today would

grind the tender to powder if they could.

As the Lord has not left us to man, neither has he left us to the devil. Satan may sift us as wheat,

but he cannot thresh us as fitches. He may blow away chaff with his foul breath, but he does not

manage the Lord’s corn: “The Lord preserves the righteous” (Psalm 37:17). Not a providential

stroke is left to chance. The Lord ordains the timing, the measure, and the place. The divine decree

leaves nothing uncertain; supreme love governs even the smallest events. Whether we endure the

teeth of the corn-drag, the trampling of horses, or gentler touches, all is appointed by infallible

wisdom. Let this comfort the afflicted.

Notice also that the instruments used for our threshing are chosen by the Great Husbandman. As

the Eastern farmer has several instruments, so has our God. No form of threshing is pleasant; each

seems objectionable to the one enduring it. We say, “I could bear anything but this trouble,” or

“If it were the enemy, I could endure it.” Perhaps the cummin foolishly thinks horse-hooves would

be gentler than the rod, or the fitches might prefer the wheel to the staff. Thankfully, the choice is

left to One who judges perfectly. What can we know? “Ah!” cries a mother, “I could bear poverty,

but to lose my child is too much!” Another laments, “I could lose all wealth, but to be slandered

cuts me to the heart.” We cannot please ourselves in chastisement. When I was at school under my

uncle, I had to find a cane for him; I never once chose a stick that pleased the one to be struck.

Either it was too thin or too thick, and I was threatened with punishment if I failed next time. I

learned never to expect God’s children to like the rod that corrects them. You may smile at my

simile, yet you may find yourself crying, “Any trial but this, Lord.” Trials are seldom pleasant;

indeed, almost every useful medicine is unpleasant, almost every effective surgery painful. No trial

is joyous in the present, yet it is right, and right despite its bitterness.

Notice also that God selects the place. Eastern farmers have large threshing-floors for corn or

barley, but near the house, I have seen smaller circles of hardened clay or cement where garden

seeds are carefully beaten. Some saints are not afflicted in common life but bear sorrow in the

innermost spirit; they are threshed on a smaller, private floor, yet the effect is no less real. How

foolish to rebel against the Lord’s appointment, as if we could choose our own afflictions! “Should

it be according to thy mind?” Should the grain appoint its thresher? Should a child choose the rod?

Leave these matters to higher wisdom. Some complain of timing: to be crippled in youth, poor in

age, or widowed with young children. Yet there is wisdom. Just as a physician arranges doses for

effectiveness, so the Lord knows when we should drink the cup he prepares. A dear saint endures

a trial in old age; though I would shield him, our heavenly Father knows best. The instrument, the

place, the measure, the time, and the purpose are appointed by infallible love.

The text also shows the limit of threshing. The farmer beats to separate the seed, but not to destroy

it. The wheel does not grind; the horse’s feet do not smash. He removes the cummin from its husk

without crushing it. Likewise, the Lord measures all chastening. Courage, tried friend: you shall

be afflicted as you need, but not as you deserve. Tribulation comes as you can bear it. The wheat

may feel the wheel, but the fitches bear nothing heavier than a staff. No saint is tempted beyond

measure; every stroke is bounded by tender wisdom.

It is easy to say this in calm reflection, harder under the flail. Yet I have experienced it in pain and

mental distress. I thank God for my afflictions; I never doubted his wisdom. The Great

Husbandman knows how to separate us from the husk, and his method deserves eternal praise.

It is comforting that God’s limit is absolute: “If trials six be fixed for men,

They shall not suffer seven.

If God appoint afflictions ten,

They shall not be eleven.”

The law allowed forty stripes save one; in all our scourging, the “save one” appears. When God

multiplies sorrows, it is because previous measures failed; no power can give us one blow above

the set number. The Lord never plays with his saints’ feelings. “He does not afflict willingly”

(Lam. 3:33). No unnecessary blow is given.

The wisdom of the farmer in limiting threshing is far exceeded by God’s wisdom in setting a limit

to grief. Some endure little, perhaps due to frailty. Delicate seeds must not be beaten; saints with

weak bodies shall not be roughly handled. Perhaps their minds are fragile, and what others bear

lightly would be fatal to them; they are kept as the apple of God’s eye.

If you are free from tribulation, do not ask for it. A brother recently worried because he had no

trouble; I said, “Rejoice while you may.” Only a foolish child would beg for flogging. Some gentle,

shining saints are spared harsh treatment; they neither need it nor could bear it. Why wish for it?

Others endure heavy pressure. Yet if they are superior grain, intended for greater use, let them not

regret it. The bread corn must go under horse’s feet and the cart wheel; the most useful must

undergo the sternest processes. None among us would say, “I wish I were Martin Luther or as

noble as him?” Yet besides outward perils, his inward trials were such none would wish to bear.

He faced Satanic temptations and despair, riding storms of conflict, then lay broken and trembling.

We only see public heroes, not their private suffering; the bread corn is bruised, and those

comforting others often suffer most. Envy no one; you do not know how they were threshed to

make them right.

God uses discretion in chastening; let us do likewise with others. Be gentle with children; rebuke

brothers tenderly. Do not drive horses over tender seed. Remember: cummin is beaten with a staff,

not crushed with a wheel. Perhaps leave the rod to wiser hands; sow and let elders thresh.

Let us trust in God’s discretion. Do not seek escape from affliction. When praying, say,

“Nevertheless, not my will.” Part freely with your chaff. To escape the flail, separate from the husk

quickly: “Come out from among them” (2 Cor. 6:17). Separate from sin and sinners; the process

completes sooner. God make us wise!

III. Thirdly, the threshing will not last forever. It will not occupy all our days: “Bread corn is

bruised, but he will not always thresh it” (Isaiah 28:28). “For a little while I have forsaken you,

but with great mercies I will gather you” (Isaiah 54:7). “He will not always rebuke, nor will he

keep his anger forever” (Psalm 103:9). “Weeping may stay for the night, but joy comes in the

morning” (Psalm 30:5). Rejoice, daughters of sorrow; be comforted, sons of grief; hope in God,

for you shall yet praise him. The rain does not always fall, clouds do not always return; sorrow

and sighing shall flee. Threshing is not needed year-round; mostly the flail rests. Bless the Lord,

O my soul! He will yet bring home the banished.

Above all, tribulation will not last forever. We shall soon be taken to a better world, where there

are no threshing-floors or corn-drags. I sometimes hear the herald’s call: “Up and away! Boot and

saddle! Leave the camp and the battle, and return in triumph!” The night is far spent, but morning

comes. The day breaks over the hills. The eternal day comes. Come, eat your bread with joy, and

march with a merry heart; the land flowing with milk and honey is near. Until the day breaks, abide

the Great Husbandman’s will, and may the Lord glorify himself in you. Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 18
fields.body_html:
WHEAT IN THE BARN Introduction

The Son of Man sows good seed with patience and purpose. Though weeds grow among the

wheat, Christ will separate and gather His own. This chapter unveils the harvest of grace, the

angels’ joyful work, and the eternal security of the righteous in the Lord’s barn.

"Gather the wheat into my barn."—Matthew 13:30 "Gather the wheat into my barn." Then the purpose of the Son of Man will be accomplished. He

sowed good seed, and he shall have his barn filled with it in the end. Do not be discouraged—

Christ will not be disappointed. "He shall see the fruit of his suffering and be satisfied." He went

forth weeping, carrying precious seed, but he will return rejoicing, bringing his sheaves with him.

"Gather the wheat into my barn;" then Satan's plan will fail. The enemy came and sowed weeds

among the wheat, hoping that the false wheat would destroy or seriously harm the true; but he

failed in the end, for the wheat matured and was ready to be harvested. Christ's storehouse will be

full; the weeds will not choke the wheat. The evil one will be humiliated.

In gathering the wheat, good angels will be used: "the angels are the reapers." This highlights the

defeat of the great evil angel. He sows the weeds, trying to ruin the harvest; and so the good angels

are sent to celebrate his failure and to rejoice with their Lord in the success of God's work. Satan

will gain very little from his interference; he will be thwarted in all his efforts, and so the threat

will be fulfilled: "You will crawl on your belly and eat dust."

By giving the angels work to do, all intelligent creatures, of whom we know, are drawn into the

work of grace; whether out of malice or awe, redemption excites them all. To everyone, God's

wonderful works are made visible; for these things are not done in secret.

We often forget the angels. Let us not overlook their tender concern for us; they watch the Lord

rejoicing over our repentance, and they rejoice with him.

They are our guardians and the Lord's messengers of mercy; they hold us so that we do not stumble,

and when we die, they carry us into the presence of our Lord. One of our joys is that we belong to

a countless company of angels; let us think of them with affection.

I will now stick closely to my text, preaching almost word by word. It begins with "but," and that

is a word of separation.

Note that the weeds and the wheat will grow together until the time of harvest comes. It is a great

sorrow to some of the wheat to grow side by side with weeds. The ungodly are like thorns and

briers to those who fear the Lord. How often does the godly heart sigh: "Woe is me that I sojourn

in Mesech, that I dwell among the tents of Kedar!" A man's enemies are often found within his

own household; those who should help him most may hinder him the most; their conversation

troubles and torments him. It is often futile to try to escape them, for the weeds are permitted in

God's providence to grow with the wheat, and they will do so until the end.

Godly people have emigrated to distant lands to build communities of saints, and yet sinners have

appeared even among them. Attempts to weed out ungodly and heretical members have led to

persecution and other troubles, and the plan has largely failed. Others have secluded themselves in

hermitages to avoid worldly temptations, hoping to achieve victory by fleeing; this is not the way

of wisdom. The word for now is, "Let both grow together," but a time will come when a final

separation will occur. Then, dear Christian woman, your husband will no longer persecute you.

Godly sister, your brother will cease mocking you. Pious worker, the ungodly will no longer taunt

you. That "but" will be an iron gate between the god-fearing and the godless; then the weeds will

be cast into the fire, but the Lord of the harvest will say, "Gather the wheat into my barn."

This separation must occur; for the wheat and the weeds growing together on earth cause much

pain and harm, and this will not continue in a better world. Godly men and women might wish

their unconverted children to be with them in heaven; but this cannot happen, for God will not

allow his purified to be defiled, nor his glorified to be tried by the presence of the unbelieving. The

weeds must be removed for the perfectness and usefulness of the wheat. Would you have weeds

and wheat heaped together in the barn? That would be terrible husbandry. They cannot be put to

proper use until thoroughly separated.

Likewise, the saved and unsaved may live together here, but not in the next world. The command

is clear: "Gather the weeds and bind them in bundles to burn them, but gather the wheat into my

barn."

Sinner, can you hope to enter heaven? You have never loved your mother's God, and will he allow

you in his heavenly courts? You have never trusted your father's Saviour, and yet you hope to see

his glory forever? Will you swagger through heaven, letting fall an oath, or singing loose songs?

You grow weary of worship on the Lord's Day; do you think the Lord will tolerate unwilling

worshippers in his temple above? You find the Sabbath tiresome; how can you hope to enter God's

eternal rest? You have no taste for heavenly pursuits, and they would be profaned if you were

allowed to partake; therefore, that "but" must come, and you must part from the Lord's people

forever. Can you bear to be separated from godly friends for eternity?

That separation involves a terrible difference of destiny: "Gather the weeds in bundles to burn

them." I cannot draw the full picture; but once the bundle is bound, its only place is the fire. May

you escape from all that anguish. It is no trivial matter that the Lord of love compares to being

consumed by fire. No words can fully convey its terror. We often speak of the wrath to come; yet

we surely understate it. What did the tender, loving, gracious Jesus mean by "Gather the weeds

and bind them in bundles to burn them"? Consider the vast distinction between the fate of the

Lord's people and Satan's followers. Burn the wheat? No—"Gather the wheat into my barn." There

they are safely and happily housed forever. Oh, the infinite gulf between heaven and hell—the

harps and angels, the wailing and gnashing of teeth! Who can measure the distance between the

glorified saint, white-robed and crowned with immortality, and the soul driven forever from God

and his glory? That "but" is dreadful. Remember, it divides brother from brother, mother from

child, husband from wife. "One will be taken and the other left." And once that sword descends,

there is no reunion. The separation is eternal.

But one might ask, "Why such a difference?" Because there has always been a difference. The

wheat was sown by the Son of Man; the false wheat by the enemy. There has always been a

difference in character—the wheat good, the weeds evil. At first this difference may not be visible,

but it becomes apparent as the wheat and the weeds mature. They are entirely different plants; so

too a regenerated and an unregenerated person are entirely different beings. I have heard an

unregenerate man claim he is as good as a godly man; in doing so, he reveals his pride.

Surely, in God's eyes, the difference between believer and unbeliever is as great as between light

and darkness, or life and death. One has life, the other does not; the difference is vital and radical.

Oh, may you never trifle with this matter, but truly be the Lord's wheat! It is not enough to bear

the name of wheat—we must have its nature. God cannot be mocked; he is not pleased by those

who call themselves Christians while they are not. Do not be satisfied with church membership;

seek membership with Christ. Do not speak of faith; exercise it. Do not boast of experience;

possess it. Be the wheat, not an imitation. The terrible "but" will roll like a sea of fire between the

true and false. Oh Holy Spirit, let each of us be transformed by your power.

The second word of our text is "gather"—a word of congregation. What a blessing this gathering

is! It is a pleasure to bring multitudes to hear the gospel; is it not a joy to see a house full of people,

on weekdays and Sabbaths, willing to travel to hear the gospel? That is great; but the gathering of

the wheat into the barn is far more wonderful. Gathering is inherently better than scattering, and I

pray that the Lord Jesus may always draw people here; for he is no Divider, but "to him shall all

the gathering of the people come." Has he not said, "And I, when I am lifted up from the earth,

will draw all people to myself"?

Observe that the congregation in our text is chosen and assembled by skilled gatherers: "The angels

are the reapers." Ministers could not do this alone, for they do not know all the Lord's wheat and

are prone to mistakes—some being too lenient, others too severe. Human judgment occasionally

excludes saints and admits sinners. Angels know their Master's property. They know each saint,

for they were present at their birth. Angels know when sinners repent and never forget the penitent.

They have witnessed the lives of believers and helped them in spiritual battles. Yes, angels, by a

holy instinct, discern the Father's children and are not deceived. They will gather all the wheat and

leave out every weed.

But they are gathered under very strict rules. According to the parable, the weeds—the false

wheat—are first removed, and then the angelic reapers gather only the wheat. The seed of the

serpent, fathered by Satan, is separated from the seed of the kingdom, belonging to Jesus, the

promised Deliverer. This is the one distinction; no other is considered. Even the most amiable

unconverted person, standing among the saints, would not be carried to heaven by the angels, for

the command is, "Gather the wheat." Even if the most honest man stood in the centre of the church,

surrounded by members and ministers pleading for his mercy, if he were not a believer he could

not enter the divine storehouse. There is no exception. The angels have no choice; the peremptory

command is, "Gather the wheat," and they must gather no one else.

The gathering will come from vast distances. Some wheat ripens in the South Sea Islands, in China,

and in Japan. Some flourishes in France, and broad fields grow in the United States. There is hardly

a land without some of God's good grain. Where all of God’s wheat grows, I cannot say. There is

a remnant, according to the election of grace, among every nation and people; but the angels will

gather all the good grain into one storehouse.

"Gather the wheat." The saints will be found in every rank of society. The angels will bring a few

ears from palaces, and great armfuls from cottages. Many will be collected from the humble homes

of our villages and hamlets, and others will be raised from the back streets of our great cities to the

metropolis of God. From the darkest corners, angels will bring those children of sweetness and

light who rarely saw the sun, yet were pure in heart and knew their God. The hidden and obscure

will be brought into the light, for the Lord knows those who belong to him, and his harvesters will

not miss them.

It is a wonderful thought that they will come from all ages. Let us hope that our first father, Adam,

will be there, and mother Eve, following in the footsteps of their dear son Abel, trusting in the

same sacrifice. We shall meet Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Moses, David, Daniel, and all the saints

made perfect. What a joy to see the apostles, martyrs, and reformers! I long to see Luther, Calvin,

Bunyan, and Whitefield. I love the rhyme of good old father Ryland:

"They all shall be there, the great and the small,

Poor I shall shake hands with the blessed St. Paul."

I do not know exactly how it will be, but I am confident we will have fellowship with all the saints

of every age in the general assembly and church of the firstborn, whose names are written in

heaven.

No matter when or where the wheat grew, it shall be gathered into the one barn—never to be

scattered again. They grew in different fields. Some flourished on hillsides where Episcopalians

prosper, and others in lower soil where Baptists multiply and Methodists thrive. But once the wheat

is in the barn, no one can tell which field the ears came from.

Then, indeed, shall the Master’s prayer have a glorious answer: "That they may all be one." All

errors removed, all mistakes corrected and forgiven, the one Lord, the one faith, and the one

baptism will be fully known, and there will be no more vexing or envy. What a blessed gathering!

What a meeting! The elect of God, the finest of all centuries, of whom the world was not worthy.

I would not want to be absent. Even if there were no hell, it would be hell to miss such heavenly

company. Even without wailing and gnashing of teeth, it would be dreadful to miss the presence

of the Lord, the joy of praising him forever, and the bliss of meeting the noblest beings who ever

lived. Amid the controversies of the age, I, who have seemed a man of strife, long for the blessed

rest where all spiritual minds shall blend in eternal accord before the throne of God and of the

Lamb. Oh, that we were all right, that we might all be united in one spirit!

In the text, the next word is one of designation. I have already touched on that. "Gather the wheat."

Nothing but "the wheat" may enter the Lord’s homestead. Lend me your hearts while I urge you

to a searching examination for a few minutes. The wheat was sown by the Lord. Are you sown by

the Lord? Friend, if you have any religion, how did you receive it? Was it self-sown? If so, it is of

no use. The true wheat was sown by the Son of Man. Are you sown by the Lord? Did the Spirit of

God plant eternal life in your heart? Did it come from that hand nailed to the cross? Is Jesus your

life? Does your life begin and end with him? If so, it is well.

The wheat sown by the Lord is also the object of his care. Wheat requires much attention. The

farmer gains nothing if he does not watch it carefully. Are you under the Lord’s care? Does he

preserve you? Is it true to your soul: "I, the Lord, keep it; I water it every moment: lest any harm

it, I guard it day and night"? Do you experience such keeping? Answer honestly, for the sake of

your soul.

Next, wheat is useful, a gift from God for the benefit of humanity. The false wheat was good for

nothing; it could only feed swine, making them stagger as if drunk. Are you one who is wholesome

in society—like bread to the world, so that if men receive your example, teaching, and life, they

are blessed? Judge whether you are good or harmful in life and influence.

"Gather the wheat." God must put the goodness, grace, strength, and usefulness into you, or you

will never be wheat fit for angelic gathering. Wheat is the most dependent of all plants. I have

never heard of a field of wheat that grew and ripened without a husbandman’s care.

Some ears may appear after harvest, but I have never heard of plains covered with unsown wheat.

There is no wheat without a man, and there is no grace without Christ. We owe our existence to

the Father, the husbandman. Yet, dependent as it is, wheat holds honour and esteem; likewise,

godly people are esteemed by those of understanding. We are nothing without Christ, but with him

we are full of honour. Oh, to be among those through whom the world is preserved, the excellent

of the earth, in whom the saints delight. God forbid we should be among base and worthless weeds!

Finally, a word of destination: "Gather the wheat into my barn." The process of gathering will be

completed at the day of judgment, but it is ongoing every day. Saints are gathered continually,

moving heavenward even now. I rejoice to hear that departed members of my own church find joy

in being harvested. Glory to God, our people die well. Living well is best, but dying well often

testifies most powerfully to vital godliness. The world senses the power of a triumphant death.

Every hour, the saints are gathered into the barn. That is where they wish to be. We feel no sorrow

at this ingathering, for we desire to be safely stored by our Lord. If the wheat in the field could

speak, each ear would say: "The goal for which we live and grow is the barn, the granary." For this

purpose the frost and sun, the dew and rain, all labour. Every process of the wheat moves toward

the granary. Likewise, everything in us works toward heaven—the gathering place, the

congregation of the righteous, the vision of our Redeemer's face. Our death causes no discord; it

completes our life’s symphony. For the wheat, the barn is a place of security. There is no mildew,

frost, heat, drought, or wet once inside. All perils are past. It has reached perfection, rewarded the

husbandman’s labour, and is safely housed. Oh, long-awaited day, begin! Oh, brethren, what a

blessing when we reach maturity, and Christ sees in us the fruit of his soul’s travail.

I delight to think of heaven as his barn—what a thought! Language is poor that we must call the

home of our Father, the dwelling of Jesus, a barn. Heaven is the King’s palace, yet to us a barn, a

place of security, rest, and safety. It is Christ’s homestead, and we are ripening for it. Think of it

with ecstatic joy; for gathering into the barn is a harvest home. Men do not weep at earthly harvests,

nor follow the sheaves with tears. They clap, dance, and shout for joy. Let us do similarly for those

already housed. With grave and sweet melodies, let us sing around their tombs.

The bitterness of death is past. Remember their glory, and rejoice like a woman whose child is

born, "who remembers no more the anguish, for joy that a man is born into the world." Another

soul begins singing in heaven—why do you weep, heirs of immortality? Is eternal happiness the

birth that follows death-pangs? Then blessed are those who die. Is glory the outcome of what fills

our homes with mourning? Thank God for bereavements, for sad separations. He has promoted

our dear ones to the skies! He has blessed them beyond all we could ask or imagine, taking them

from this weary world to lie in his bosom forever. Blessed be his name, if for nothing else but this.

Would you keep your old father here, full of pain and weakness? Your dear wife, enduring

suffering? Your husband from the immortal crown? Your child to return to earth from bliss? No.

We long to go home ourselves, but concerning the departed, we rejoice before the Lord as at

harvest. "Therefore comfort one another with these words."

THE END

fields.title: Chapter 1
fields.body_html:
Why This Book Has Been Written

“My heart overflows with a pleasing theme; I address my verses to the king.” Psalm 45:1

I was once talking on the subject of religion with an intelligent agnostic, whom I very much

wished to influence, and after listening to me politely for a little while, he said, “Well, madam,

all I have to say is this. If you Christians want to make us agnostics inclined to look into your

religion, you must try to be more comfortable in the possession of it yourselves. The Christians I

meet seem to me to be the most uncomfortable people anywhere around. They seem to carry

their religion as a man carries a headache. He does not want to get rid of his head, but at the

same time it is very uncomfortable to have it. And I, for one, do not care to have that sort of

religion.” This was a lesson I have never forgotten, and it is the primary reason for my writing

this book.

I was very young in the Christian life at the time of this conversation and was still in the first joy

of entering into it, so I could not believe that any of God’s children could be as uncomfortable in

their religious lives as my agnostic friend had claimed. But when the early glow of my

conversion had passed, and I had come down to the dullness of everyday duties and

responsibilities, I soon found from my own experience, and also from the similar experiences of

most of the Christians around me, that there was far too much truth in his statement, and that the

religious life of most of us was full of discomfort and unrest. In fact, it seemed, as one of my

Christian friends said to me one day when we were comparing our experiences, “as if we had just

enough religion to make us miserable.”

I confess that this was very disappointing, for I had expected something altogether different. It

seemed to me extremely inconsistent that a religion, whose fruits are declared in the Bible to be

love, joy, and peace, should so often work out in practice in exactly the opposite way, and should

produce doubt, fear, unrest, conflict, and discomfort of every kind; and I resolved, if possible, to

find out what was wrong. Why, I asked myself, should the children of God lead such completely

uncomfortable religious lives when He has led us to believe that His yoke is easy and His burden

is light? Why are we troubled with so many spiritual doubts, and such heavy spiritual anxieties?

Why do we find it so hard to be sure that God really loves us, and why is it that we never seem

able to believe for long in His kindness and His care? How is it that we can allow ourselves to

suspect Him of forgetting us and forsaking us in times of need? We can trust our earthly friends

and feel at ease in their companionship, so why is it that we cannot trust our heavenly Friend,

and that we seem unable to be at ease in His service?

I believe I have found the answer to these questions, and I would like to say frankly that my

purpose in writing this book is to try to bring a little real and genuine comfort into some troubled

Christian lives around me. My own understanding of the religion of the Lord Jesus Christ is that

it was meant to be full of comfort. I am sure that any unbiased reader of the New Testament

would say the same, and I believe that every newly converted person, in the first joy of their

conversion, fully expects it. And yet, as I have said, it seems that for a large number of

Christians, their religious lives are the most uncomfortable part of their existence. Does the fault

of this situation lie with the Lord? Has He promised more than He is able to give?

A writer has said, “We know what over-advertising is. It is a modern disease from which we all

suffer. There are posters on every billboard, exaggerations on every blank wall, representations

and misrepresentations without number. What visions we have seen of impossible fruits and

flowers grown from so-and-so’s seeds. Everything is over-advertised. Is it the same with the

kingdom of God? Do the fruits we produce from the good seed of the kingdom match the

description given by Him from whom we received that good seed? Has He misled us? There is a

feeling around that Christ has offered in His Gospel more than He has to give. People think that

they have not quite experienced what was promised as the portion of the children of God. But

why is this so? Has the kingdom of God been over-advertised, or has it simply been under-

believed? Has the Lord Jesus Christ been overestimated, or has He only been under-trusted?”

What I want to do in this book is to show, in my small way, what I firmly believe: that the

kingdom of God cannot possibly be over-advertised, nor can the Lord Jesus Christ be

overestimated, for “what no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what

God has prepared for those who love him”; and that all the difficulty arises from the fact that we

have under-believed and under-trusted.

I want, therefore, to show as clearly as I can the reasons there are in the religion of the Lord

Jesus Christ for that deep and lasting peace and comfort of soul, which nothing on earth can

disturb, and which is said to be the portion of those who embrace it. And I also want to explain,

if this is indeed our rightful portion, how we are to make use of it, and what things stand in the

way. There is God’s part in the matter, and there is man’s part, and we must look carefully at

both.

A wild young man, who was brought to the Lord at a mission meeting, and who afterwards

became a joyful Christian and lived a good life, was asked by someone what he did to be

converted. “Oh,” he said, “I did my part, and the Lord did His.”

“But what was your part,” asked the questioner, “and what was the Lord’s part?”

“My part,” was the quick reply, “was to run away, and the Lord’s part was to run after me until

He caught me.”

A very meaningful answer; but how few can truly understand it!

God’s part is always to run after us. Christ came to seek and to save that which is lost. “What

man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in

the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? And when he has found it, he

lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing.” This is always the divine part; but in our foolishness we do

not understand it, and instead think that the Lord is the one who is lost, and that our part is to

seek and find Him. The very expressions we use show this. We urge sinners to “seek the Lord,”

and we talk about having “found” Him. “Have you found the Saviour?” asked an overly zealous

mission worker of a happy, trusting little girl.

With a look of amazement, she replied in a tone of wonder, “Why, I did not know the Saviour

was lost!”

It is our ignorance of God that causes all this. Because we do not know Him, we naturally form

all sorts of wrong ideas about Him. We think He is an angry Judge watching for our slightest

faults, or a harsh Taskmaster determined to demand the utmost service from us, or a self-centred

Deity requiring His full measure of honour and glory, or a distant Sovereign concerned only with

His own affairs and indifferent to our welfare. Who can wonder that such a God can neither be

loved nor trusted? And who could expect Christians, with such ideas of Him, to be anything

other than full of discomfort and misery?

But I can say with confidence, and without fear of contradiction, that it is impossible for anyone

who truly knows God to have such uncomfortable thoughts about Him. There may be many

outward discomforts, and many earthly sorrows and trials, but through them all the soul that

knows God must dwell inwardly in a place of perfect peace. “Whoever listens to me will dwell

secure and will be at ease, without dread of disaster.” And this is a statement no one can

question. If we would truly listen to God—which means not only hearing Him but believing

what we hear—we could not fail to know that, because He is God, He cannot do anything other

than care for us as the apple of His eye, and that everything that tender love and divine wisdom

can do for our good will surely be done. Not a single opening for worry or fear is left to the soul

that knows God.

“Ah, yes,” you say, “but how am I to know Him? Other people seem to have some kind of

inward revelation that makes them know Him, but I never do; and no matter how much I pray,

everything seems dark to me. I want to know God, but I do not see how to manage it.”

Your difficulty is that you have a wrong idea of what knowing God is, or at least of the kind of

knowing I mean. For I do not mean any mystical inward revelations. Such experiences are

delightful when they occur, but they are not always under our control, and they can be uncertain

and inconsistent. The kind of knowing I mean is the simple, practical knowledge of God’s nature

and character that comes from believing what is revealed about Him in the Bible.

The apostle John, at the end of his Gospel, says concerning the things he had written: “Now

Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book;

but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by

believing you may have life in his name.” (John 20:30). It is believing what is written, not what

is inwardly revealed, that gives life; and the kind of knowing I mean is the knowing that comes

from believing what is written.

I mean, in practical terms, that when I read in the Bible that God is love, I am to believe it simply

because it is written, not because I have had any inward experience proving it to be true; and

when the Bible says that He cares for us as He cares for the lilies of the field and the birds of the

air, and that even the hairs of our head are all numbered, I am to believe it simply because it is

written, whether or not I have any inward sense of it.

It is very important for us to understand that the Bible is a statement, not of theories, but of

actual facts; and that things are not true because they are in the Bible, but they are in the Bible

because they are true. A little boy, who had been learning at school about the discovery of

America, said to his father one day, “Father, if I had been Columbus, I would not have taken all

that trouble to discover America.”

“Why, what would you have done?” asked his father.

“Oh,” replied the little boy, “I would have just gone to the map and found it.”

This little boy did not understand that maps are only representations of places already known,

and that America did not exist because it was on the map, but that it could only be on the map

because it already existed. And it is the same with the Bible. It is, like the map, a simple

statement of facts; so that when it tells us that God loves us, it is only telling us something that is

already true, and that would not be in the Bible if it were not a fact.

It was a great discovery to me when I understood this. It seemed to remove all uncertainty and

speculation from the revelation given to us in the Bible about the salvation of the Lord Jesus

Christ, and to make everything written about Him a simple statement of undeniable facts. And

facts are something we can believe—and indeed, we do believe them as soon as we recognise

them as facts. Inward revelations are not something we can control, but anyone in their right

mind can believe what is written. And although this may seem rather plain and simple at first, if

it is steadily followed, it will result in deeply blessed inward assurance, and will eventually lead

us into such a knowledge of God as will transform our lives.

This kind of knowing brings conviction; and in my view, conviction is far superior to inward

experiences, as delightful as those may be. An inward experience may be affected by one’s

health or by many other disturbances, but a conviction remains. Once a person is convinced that

two and two make four, no amount of illness, discomfort, or external influence can shake that

conviction. He knows it just as well when he is unwell as when he is in good health. Convictions

come from knowledge, and no change in feelings or physical condition can alter knowledge.

It is to help my readers come to this kind of practical knowledge of God, and to the convictions

that come from it, that this book is written. I will first try to show what God is—not in a

theological or doctrinal sense, but simply what He is in real, everyday life, as the God and Father

of each one of us. I will also point out some of the things that seem to me to be the main

obstacles to truly knowing Him.

I am completely certain that coming to know Him as He truly is will bring unfailing comfort and

peace to every troubled heart, and I deeply long to help everyone within my reach to come to this

knowledge. One of Job’s friends said, in response to Job’s distress, “Agree with God, and be at

peace; thereby good will come to you.” (Job 22:21) And our Lord, in His last recorded prayer,

said: “And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you

have sent.” (John 17:3). It is not a matter of knowing ourselves—what we are, what we do, or

what we feel—but simply a matter of becoming acquainted with God, and knowing what He is,

what He does, and what He feels. Comfort and peace never come from what we know about

ourselves, but always from what we know about Him.

We may spend our days performing what we call religious duties, and fill our devotions with

enthusiasm, and still be miserable. Nothing can truly bring rest to our hearts except a real

knowledge of God; for in the end, everything in our salvation depends on Him. Our comfort

depends entirely on whether He is worthy of our trust. If we were planning a dangerous voyage,

our first concern would be the kind of captain we would have. Common sense would tell us that

if the captain were untrustworthy, no amount of trustworthiness on our part could make the

voyage safe. It would be his character, not ours, that mattered most.

If I can only say this often enough, and in enough different ways, to bring conviction to some

troubled hearts, and lift them out of their unhappy and uncomfortable religious lives into the

kingdom of love, joy, and peace—which is their rightful inheritance—I will feel that my purpose

in writing this book has been fulfilled. And I will be able to say, “Lord, now you are letting your

servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation”; and my

pen has tried to describe it.

It must, however, be clearly understood that this book does not attempt to deal with the critical or

theological aspects of religion. It does not address questions about the authenticity of the Bible.

Others, far more capable, can deal with such matters. This book is written for people who, like

myself, profess to believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and who accept the Bible simply as His

revelation.

Setting aside all critical questions, therefore, I seek only to explain what seems to me to be the

natural result of such belief, and how believers can personally experience it.

There may be mistakes in how I express these things, and for that I ask the understanding of my

readers. But the truth I want to communicate—and to communicate in such a way that no one

can fail to understand—is not a mistake. And that truth is this: our religious lives ought to be full

of joy, peace, and comfort, and if we come to know God better, they will be.

fields.title: Chapter 2
fields.body_html:
What is His Name?

“And Moses said to God, ‘If I come to the people of Israel and say to them, “The God of your

fathers has sent me to you,” and they ask me, “What is his name?” what shall I say to them?’”

Exodus 3:14

The vital question of all ages and of every human heart is expressed here: “What is his name?”

The whole fate of humanity depends on the answer to this question. As we know, the condition

of a country depends upon the character of its rulers. The state of an army depends upon the

officers who command it. And the more absolute the government, the more this must be the case.

We can see, therefore, that everything in a universe depends upon the kind of creator and ruler

who has brought that universe into existence, and that the whole well-being of the human beings

placed in it is necessarily bound up with the character of their Creator. If the God who created us

is a good God, then everything must ultimately be right for us, since a good God cannot ordain

anything but what is good. But if He is a bad God, or a careless God, or an unkind God, then we

cannot be sure that anything is right, and we can have no real peace or comfort anywhere.

The true foundation for peace and comfort is found only in the kind of God we have. Therefore,

we must first find out what His name is—that is, what His character is—in short, what kind of

God He is.

In Bible language, a name always means character. Names there are not given arbitrarily, as they

often are with us, but are always given in relation to the character or work of the person named.

Creden, in his Concordance, says that the names of God signify what He truly is, and are used

throughout the Bible to express His attributes, His purposes, His glory, His grace, His mercy, His

love, His wisdom, His power, and His goodness. A careful study of His names makes this clear.

When, therefore, the children of Israel asked, “What is his name?” they meant, “Who and what is

this God of whom you speak? What is His character? What are His attributes? What does He do?

In short, what kind of being is He?”

The psalmist says, “Those who know your name put their trust in you, for you, O Lord, have not

forsaken those who seek you.” (Psalm 9:10) And again he says, “The name of the Lord is a

strong tower; the righteous man runs into it and is safe.” (Psalm 18:10) “Those who know your

name put their trust in you.” They cannot do otherwise, because in knowing His name they know

His character and His nature—that He is a God who is completely trustworthy.

There can be no doubt that a large part of the unrest and discomfort in many Christian hearts

comes simply from the fact that they do not yet know His name. “Some trust in chariots and

some in horses, but we trust in the name of the Lord our God. They collapse and fall, but we rise

and stand upright.” (Psalm 20:7-8) In all that we read about Israel in the past, we find this

constant truth: everything they were and everything they had depended on the fact that their God

was the Lord. “Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people whom he has chosen as

his heritage.” (Psalm 33:12) “Therefore you are great, O Lord God. For there is none like you,

and there is no God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears. And who is

like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem to be his people,

making himself a name and doing for themd great and awesome things by driving out before

your people,e whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt, a nation and its gods? And you

established for yourself your people Israel to be your people forever. And you, O Lord, became

their God.” (Psalm 7:22-24) “Happy are the people whose God is the Lord!” (Psalm 144:15)

Blessed is that nation; happy are those people whose God is the Lord. All the blessing and

happiness of Israel came from the fact that their God was the Lord. Nothing else was important

enough to mention when recounting their advantages. The fact that their God was the Lord was

enough to explain every good thing they possessed.

The question above all questions for each one of us, therefore, is this: “What is his name?”

To the Israelites, God Himself answered this question. God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM.”

(Exodus 3:14) And He said, “Say this to the people of Israel: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’” God

also said to Moses, “Say this to the people of Israel: ‘The Lord, the God of your fathers, the God

of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name

forever, and thus I am to be remembered throughout all generations.” (Exodus 3:15)

In the Gospel of John, Christ takes this name “I am” for Himself. When the Jews questioned Him

about His authority, He said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am.”

(John 8:58) And in the Book of Revelation He declares again: “I am the Alpha and the Omega…

who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty.” (Revelation 1:8)

These simple words, “I am,” express eternity and unchangeableness of existence, which is the

first essential quality of a God who can be relied upon. No one could place confidence in a

changeable God. He must be the same yesterday, today, and forever if we are to have any peace

or comfort. But is this all His name means—simply “I am”? I am what? we ask. What does this

“I am” include? I believe it includes everything the human heart longs for and needs. This

unfinished name of God seems like a blank cheque signed by a wealthy friend, given to us to fill

in with whatever amount we require. The whole Bible tells us what it means.

Every attribute of God, every revelation of His character, every proof of His unfailing love,

every declaration of His watchful care, every assurance of His tender mercy, every expression of

His loving kindness—all are the filling out of this unfinished “I am.”

God tells us throughout His Word what He is. “I am,” He says, “all that my people need. I am

their strength. I am their wisdom. I am their righteousness. I am their peace. I am their salvation.

I am their life. I am their all in all.”

This seemingly unfinished name is therefore the most comforting name the human heart could

imagine, because it allows us to add to it, without limit, whatever we need—even “far more

abundantly than all that we ask or think.”

But if our hearts are full of our own miserable “I ams,” we will have no ears to hear His glorious,

soul-satisfying “I am.” We say, “I am such a weak person,” or “I am so foolish,” or “I am so

useless,” or “I am so helpless,” and we give these poor “I ams” as the reason for the misery and

discomfort of our religious lives, and even feel that we deserve sympathy because things are so

difficult for us. Meanwhile, we completely ignore the blank cheque of God’s magnificent “I am,”

which gives us permission to draw from Him an abundant supply for every need.

If you are an uncomfortable Christian, then the only thing that can give you a truly comfortable

religious life is to know God. The psalmist says that those who know God’s name will trust in

Him, and I am convinced it is impossible to truly know Him and not trust Him. A trustworthy

person naturally inspires trust—not by demanding it, but by winning it through their character.

What our Lord declares is eternally true: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw

all people to myself.” Once you truly know Him, Christ is irresistible. You cannot help trusting

Him any more than you can help breathing. And if the whole world could know Him as He truly

is, the whole world—sinners and all—would fall at His feet in worship. They simply could not

help it. His surpassing beauty would overcome everything.

How then can we come to know God?

Two things are necessary: first, God must reveal Himself; and second, we must accept His

revelation and believe what He reveals.

The apostle John tells us that “no one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s

side, he has made him known.” (John 1:18) Christ, therefore, is the revelation of God. None of us

has seen God, nor can we see Him in our present state, because we do not have the ability to do

so. But He has revealed Himself in Christ, and we can see Christ, since He became a man like us.

A man who wanted to speak with ants might stand over an anthill and talk all day, yet not a

single word would reach them. They would move about, completely unaware of him. As far as

we know, ants have no ability to understand human speech. But if a man could become an ant,

live among them, and speak their language, he would immediately make himself understood.

When a higher form of life wants to communicate with a lower, incarnation is necessary.

Christ revealed God by what He was, by what He did, and by what He said. From the cradle to

the grave, every moment of His life revealed God. We must go to Him, then, to know God, and

we must refuse to believe anything about God that is not shown to us in Christ. All other

revelations are incomplete and therefore not fully reliable. Only in Christ do we see God as He

truly is, for Christ is “the exact imprint of his nature.”

Whatever God would have said or done in any situation, Christ said and did. “I do nothing on my

own authority… the Father who dwells in me does his works” (John 14:10) “I and the Father are

one” (John 10:30) “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” (John 14:9)

Nothing is stated more clearly in the New Testament than this truth: that we are to see “the light

of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ,” (2 Corinthians 4:6) and that we

cannot see it fully anywhere else.

If we want to know the full meaning of what God meant when He gave Moses that seemingly

unfinished name, “I am,” we will find it revealed in Christ. He alone explains God. He alone is

the image of the invisible God.

It is clear, therefore, that we must never accept any idea of God that contradicts what we see in

Christ, and we must completely reject any view of His character, His actions, or His relationship

with us—no matter how strongly it is taught—if it does not agree with what Christ has revealed.

We are all aware that the Old Testament revelation of God sometimes seems to differ from the

revelation given in Christ, and the question arises as to which we are to accept as the truest. In

view of the fact that God Himself tells us that in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son,

who is “the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature,” we cannot reject

Christ’s testimony. Instead, we must regard the Old Testament revelation, where it differs from

the revelation in Christ, as partial and incomplete, and accept as a true picture of God only what

we find in Christ.

Christ alone tells us the true and real name of God. In His final and wonderful prayer He says: “I

have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world… I have given

them the words that you gave me, and they have received them and have come to know in truth

that I came from you; and they have believed that you sent me.”

Could we ask for greater authority than this?

In the whole life of Christ, nothing is clearer or more emphatic than the fact that He continually

claimed to be a complete revelation of God. “The words that I say to you I do not speak on my

own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works.” (John 14:10) Again and again

He declares that He speaks only what the Father gives Him to speak. “I declare to the world what

I have heard from him.” (John 8:26) “I do nothing on my own authority, but speak just as the

Father taught me.” (John 12:49)

The apostle also declares most plainly that it pleased the Father that in Christ “all the fullness of

God was pleased to dwell.” (Colossians 1:19) And although we may not fully understand all that

this means in a theological sense, we cannot fail to see that if we want to know God, we only

need to become familiar with Christ’s ways and Christ’s character in order to know God’s ways

and God’s character. “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” And again He declares that

“no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.”

(Matthew 11:27) This settles the matter completely. We may have many thoughts about God; we

may imagine or speculate—but it is all in vain. We simply cannot know Him except through the

revelation given in Christ.

We may know many things about God, but that is very different from knowing Him as He truly

is in nature and character. Other witnesses may tell us about His outward acts, but from these we

often form very wrong impressions of His true character. No one but Christ can reveal the true

inner nature of God, for only of Him can it be said that “the only God, who is at the Father’s

side, he has made him known.” (John 1:18)

It makes all the difference in our Christian lives whether or not we believe this to be true. If we

do believe it, then the stern Judge and hard Taskmaster we have feared—even while trying to

follow Him—and whose service we have found so difficult and uncomfortable, will disappear. In

His place will come the God of love revealed to us in “the face of Jesus Christ,” the God who

cares for us as He cares for the sparrows and the flowers of the field, and who tells us that even

the hairs of our head are all numbered.

No one could be afraid of a God like this.

If we have been used to approaching God with any doubt about His kindness towards us; if our

religious life has been poisoned by fear; if unworthy thoughts of His character and will have

filled our hearts with suspicion of His goodness; if we have imagined Him as a harsh ruler or a

self-seeking tyrant; if, in short, we have thought of Him in any way other than what has been

revealed to us in “the face of Jesus Christ,” we must go back, in simplicity of heart, to the record

of that beautiful life lived among people, and bring our understanding of God into full agreement

with the character and ways of Him who declares that He came to make known the name of God.

In answer, then, to the question, “What is His name?” I have only this to say: ask Christ. We are

told that He was “God manifested in the flesh,” and that whoever sees Him sees the God who

sent Him. Therefore, it is perfectly clear that if we want to know the name, we must look at the

manifestation. This simply means that we must study the life, words, and actions of Christ, and

say to ourselves, “Whoever has seen Christ has seen God,” and that what Christ was on earth,

God is in heaven. All the confusion that surrounds the character of God will disappear if we

accept the light Christ has given and believe the “manifestation of His name” that Christ has

shown us, and refuse to believe anything else.

When Nicodemus came to Jesus by night to ask how these things could be true, Jesus told him

that whether he understood them or not, they were still true, and said very clearly: “Truly, truly, I

say to you, we speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen.” (John 3:11) No

one who believes in Christ can doubt that He knew God; and no one can question whether we

ought to accept His testimony. He repeatedly assured us that He knew what He was speaking

about, and that His words are to be accepted as absolute truth, because He came down from

heaven and therefore knows heavenly things.

None of us would openly question this; yet in practice many of God’s people ignore Christ’s

testimony and instead listen to their own doubting hearts, which tell them that it cannot be true

that God is as loving, as tender, or as ready to forgive as Christ has shown Him to be. Yet I must

repeat again and again, even at the risk of repetition, what so few seem to understand: if there is

one truth taught more clearly than any other in the Bible, it is that the name—that is, the

character—of the Father, as revealed by Christ, is His true character. Christ continually declares

that He is the living expression of the Father, and that in everything He said and did, He was

simply saying and doing what the Father would have said and done if He had acted directly from

heaven.

In the face of such clear statements from our Lord Himself, it becomes not only our privilege but

our responsibility to remove from our understanding of God anything that does not agree with

the life, character, and teaching of Christ. If we want to know the true name of God, we must
