wrong and what needs mending. This would of course be necessary if we were our own

workmanship, but since we are God's workmanship and not our own, he is the one to examine

us, for he is the only one who can tell what is wrong. The man who makes watches is the one to

examine a watch when it is out of order and to set it straight. We have too much good sense to

meddle with our watches; why is it that we have not enough good sense to give up meddling with

ourselves? Surely we must see that the examining of the Lord is the only kind of examination

that is of any use. His examination is like that of a physician, who examines in order to cure;

while our self-examination is like that of the patient, who only becomes more of a hypochondriac

the more he examines the symptoms of his disease.

But the question may be asked whether, when there has been actual sin, there ought not to be

self-examination and self-reproach, at least for a time. This is a fallacy which deceives a great

many. It seems too much to believe that we can be forgiven without first going through a season

of self-reproach. But what is the Bible teaching? John tells us that "If we confess our sins, he is

faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9).

All that God wants is that we should turn to him at once and acknowledge our sin and believe in

his forgiveness; and every minute that we delay doing this, in order to spend the time in self-

examination and self-reproach, is only adding further sin to that which we have already

committed. If ever we need to look away from self and to have our eyes turned to the Lord, it is

just when we become conscious of having sinned against him. The greater the multitude of our

enemies, the greater and more immediate our need of God.

All through the Bible, we are taught this lesson of death to self and life in Christ alone. "It is no

longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me" (Galatians 2:20) was not intended to be a unique

experience for St Paul, but was simply a declaration of what ought to be the experience of every

Christian. We sometimes sing, "Thou, O Christ, art all I want," but in reality, we actually want a

great many other things. We want good frames of mind and feelings; we want fervour and

earnestness; we want realisations and satisfying experiences; and we continually examine

ourselves to try and find out why we do not have these things.

We think if we could only discover our points of failure, we would be able to set them straight.

But there is no healing or transforming power in gazing at our failures. The only road to

Christlikeness is to behold, not our own hatefulness, but his goodness and beauty. We grow like

what we look at, and if we spend our lives looking at our hateful selves, we will become more

and more hateful.

Do we not find as a fact that self-examination, instead of making us better, always seems to

make us worse? By beholding self, we are more and more changed into the image of self. On the

contrary, if we spend our time beholding the glory of the Lord—that is, letting our minds dwell

upon his goodness and his love, and trying to drink in his spirit—the inevitable result will be that

we shall be, perhaps slowly but surely, changed into the image of the Lord upon whom we are

gazing.

Fénelon says that we should never indulge in any self-reflective acts, whether of mortification at

our failures or of congratulation at our successes. Instead, we should continually consign self and

all self's doings to oblivion and should keep our interior eyes upon the Lord only. It is very hard

during self-examination not to try to find excuses for our faults, and our self-reflective acts are

often in danger of being turned into self-glorying ones. The only way is to ignore self altogether

and to forget there is any such being in existence.

No one who does not understand this can possibly appreciate the comfort and relief it is to be

done with self and all self-reflective acts. I have known Christian workers whose lives have been

one long torment because of these acts; and I am convinced that the "Black Mondays," of which

so many clergymen complain, are nothing but the result of indulging in self-reflective acts

concerning their services in the church the day before.

The only way to treat all forms of self-reflective acts, of whatever kind, is simply to give them

up. They always do harm and never good. They are bound to result in one of two things: either

they fill us with self-praise and self-satisfaction, or they plunge us into the depths of

discouragement and despair. Whichever it may be, the soul is inevitably shut out from any sight

of God and his salvation.

One of the most effective ways of conquering the habit is to make a rule that, whenever we are

tempted to examine ourselves, we will always at once begin to examine the Lord instead. We

should let thoughts of his love and his all-sufficiency sweep out all thoughts of our own

unworthiness or our own helplessness.

I have been trying in this book to set the Lord before our eyes in all the beauty of his character

and his ways, in the hope that the sight will be so ravishing as to take our eyes off everything

else. But no revelation of God will be of any use if we will not look at it, but instead persist in

turning our backs on what has been revealed and gazing at our own inward experiences. For

again I must repeat that we cannot see self and see the Lord at the same time, and while we are

examining self, we cannot be looking at him.

Fénelon says concerning self-examination: "There is something very hidden and very deceptive

in the suffering it causes; for while you seem to yourself to be wholly occupied with the glory of

God, in your inmost soul it is self alone that occasions all your trouble. You are indeed desirous

that God should be glorified, but you wish it should take place by means of your perfection, and

you thus cherish the sentiments of self-love. It is simply a refined pretext for dwelling in self... It

is a sort of infidelity to simple faith when we desire to be continually assured that we are doing

well. It is, in fact, a desire to know what we are doing, which we shall never know, and of which

it is the will of God we should be ignorant. It is trifling by the way, in order to reason about the

way. The safest and shortest course is to renounce, forget, and abandon self, and, through

faithfulness to God, to think no more of it. This is the whole of religion—to get out of self and

self-love, in order to get into God."

What we must do, therefore, is to shut the door definitely and resolutely, once and for all, upon

self and all of self's experiences, whether they are good or bad. We should say with the Psalmist,

"I have set the Lord always before me; because he is at my right hand, I shall not be shaken.

Therefore my heart is glad, and my whole being rejoices; my flesh also dwells secure" (Psalm

16:8-9).

fields.title: Chapter 11
fields.body_html:
Things That Cannot Be Shaken

"This phrase, 'Yet once more,' indicates the removal of things that are shaken—that is, things

that have been made—in order that the things that cannot be shaken may remain" (Hebrews

12:27).

After all we have been considering regarding the unfathomable love and care of God, it might

seem to those who do not understand the deepest ways of love that no trials or hardness could

ever come into the lives of his children. But if we look deeply into the matter, we shall see that

often love itself must bring the hardness. "For the Lord disciplines the one he loves, and

chastises every son whom he receives. It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating

you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? If you are left without

discipline, in which all have participated, then you are illegitimate children and not sons"

(Hebrews 12:6-8).

If love sees those it loves going wrong, it must, because of its very love, do what it can to save

them; and the love that fails to do this is only selfishness. Therefore, just because of his

unfathomable love, the God of love—when he sees his children resting their souls on things that

can be shaken—must necessarily remove those things from their lives in order that they may be

driven to rest only on the things that cannot be shaken. This process of removing is sometimes

very hard.

We will all acknowledge, I think, that if our souls are to rest in peace and comfort, it can only be

on unshakable foundations. It is no more possible for the soul to be comfortable when it is trying

to rest on "things that can be shaken" than it is for the body. No one can rest comfortably in a

shaking bed or sit in comfort on a rickety chair.

Foundations, to be reliable, must always be unshakable. "Everyone then who hears these words

of mine and does them will be like a wise man who built his house on the rock. And the rain fell,

and the floods came, and the winds blew and beat on that house, but it did not fall, because it had

been founded on the rock. And everyone who hears these words of mine and does not do them

will be like a foolish man who built his house on the sand. And the rain fell, and the floods came,

and the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell, and great was the fall of it" (Matthew

7:24-27).

It is very possible in the Christian life to build one's spiritual house on such insecure foundations

that, when storms beat upon it, the ruin of that house is great. Many a religious experience that

has seemed fair enough when all was going well in life has tottered and fallen when trials have

come, because its foundations were insecure. It is therefore of vital importance to each one of us

to see to it that our religious life is built upon "things that cannot be shaken."

Of course, the immediate thought that will come to every mind is that it must be built upon the

Rock, Christ Jesus. This is true; but the great point is what is meant by that expression. It is one

of those religious phrases that is often used conventionally, with no definite or real meaning

attached to it. Conventionally, we believe that Christ is the only Rock upon which to build, but

practically—though perhaps unconsciously—we believe that in order to have a rock upon which

it will be really safe to build, many other things must be added to Christ. We think, for instance,

that the right frames of mind and feelings must be added, or the right doctrines or dogmas, or

whatever else may seem to each one of us to constitute the necessary degree of security. And if

we were only perfectly honest with ourselves, I suspect we would often find that our dependence

was almost wholly upon these additions of our own, and that Christ himself, as our rock of

dependence, was of altogether secondary importance.

What we ought to mean when we talk of building upon the Rock, Christ Jesus, is what I am

trying all through this book to make plain: that the Lord is enough for our salvation—just the

Lord only, without any additions of our own. It is the Lord himself, as he is in his own intrinsic

character, our Creator and Redeemer, and our all-sufficient portion.

"But God's firm foundation stands" (2 Timothy 2:19), and it is the only foundation that does.

Therefore, we need to be "shaken" off every other foundation so that we may be forced to rest on

the foundation of God alone. This explains the necessity for those "shakings" through which so

many Christians seem called to pass. The Lord sees that they are building their spiritual houses

on flimsy foundations which will not be able to withstand the "stream [that] broke against that

house" (Luke 6:48) during the storms of life. Not in anger, but in tenderest love, he shakes our

earth and our heaven until all that "can be shaken" is removed, and only those "things which

cannot be shaken" are left behind.

The Apostle tells us that the things that are shaken are the "things that have been made"

(Hebrews 12:27); that is, the things that are manufactured by our own efforts—feelings that we

stir up, doctrines that we elaborate, and good works that we perform. It is not that these are bad

things in themselves. It is only when the soul begins to rest on them instead of upon the Lord that

he is compelled to "shake" us off them. And this shaking applies, we are told, "not only the earth

but also the heavens" (Hebrews 12:26). This means, I am sure, that it is possible to have "things

that are made" even in religious matters. How much of the so-called religiousness of many

Christians consists of these "things that are made," I cannot say; but I sometimes think the great

overturnings and tossings in matters of faith, which so distress Christians in these times, may be

only the necessary shaking of the "things that are made," in order that only that which "cannot be

shaken" may remain.

There are times, perhaps, in our religious lives, when our experience seems as settled and

immovable as the roots of the everlasting mountains. But then comes an upheaval; all our

foundations are shaken and thrown down, and we are ready to despair and to question whether

we can be Christians at all. Sometimes it is an upheaval in our outward circumstances, and

sometimes it is in our inward experience. If people have rested on their good works and their

faithful service, the Lord is often obliged to take away all power for work or all opportunity, so

that the soul may be driven from its false resting place and forced to rest in the Lord alone.

Sometimes the dependence is upon good feelings or pious emotions, and the soul has to be

deprived of these before it can learn to depend only upon God. Sometimes dependence is placed

upon "sound doctrine," and a person feels they occupy an invulnerable position because their

"views" are so correct and their doctrines are so "orthodox." Then the Lord is obliged to "shake"

those doctrines and to plunge that person, perhaps, into confusion and darkness regarding their

"views." It was at just such a moment as this that my own soul caught its first real sight of God;

what had seemed like certain spiritual ruin and defeat was turned into the most triumphant

victory.

Or it may be that the upheaval comes in our outward circumstances. Everything has seemed so

firmly established in prosperity that no dream of disaster disturbs us. Our reputation is assured,

our work has prospered, our efforts have all been successful beyond our hopes, and our soul is at

ease; the need for God is in danger of becoming far off and vague. Then the Lord is obliged to

put an end to it all. Our prosperity crumbles around us like a house built on the sand, and we are

tempted to think he is angry with us. But in truth, it is not anger, but tenderest love. His very love

compels him to take away the outward prosperity that is keeping our souls from entering the

interior spiritual kingdom for which we long.

"Though the fig tree should not blossom, nor fruit be on the vines, the produce of the olive fail

and the fields yield no food, the flock be cut off from the fold and there be no herd in the stalls,

yet I will rejoice in the Lord; I will take joy in the God of my salvation" (Habakkuk 3:17-18).

Then, and often not until then, will our souls learn to rejoice in the Lord only.

Paul declared that he "count[ed] everything as loss because of the surpassing worth of knowing

Christ Jesus my Lord" (Philippians 3:8). When we learn to say the same, the peace and joy that

the gospel promises become our permanent possession.

"What wrong did your fathers find in me that they went far from me, and went after

worthlessness, and became worthless?" asks the Lord of the children of Israel (Jeremiah 2:5).

"For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the fountain of living waters,

and hewed out cisterns for themselves, broken cisterns that can hold no water" (Jeremiah 2:13).

Like the Israelites, we too forsake the fountain of living waters and try to dig out cisterns of our

own devising. We seek to quench our thirst with our own experiences or activities, and then

wonder why we still thirst. It is to save us from perishing for want of water that the Lord finds it

necessary to destroy our broken cisterns; only then can we be forced to drink from the fountain

of living waters.

We are told that if we "trust in emptiness," then "emptiness will be [our] payment" (Job 15:31),

and many times we have found this to be true. Have you ever crossed a dangerous swamp full of

quicksands, where every step was a risk? Firm-looking hillocks continually deceived you into a

false dependence, causing you to sink into the mire and water hidden beneath them. If you have,

you will understand what it means to "trust in vanity," and you will appreciate the blessing of

any situation that reveals the rottenness of your false dependencies and drives you to trust in

what is safe and permanent. When our feet are walking on "miry bog," we should welcome the

Divine Guide who brings us out of the mud and "set[s] my feet upon a rock, making my steps

secure" (Psalm 40:2), even though the paths he calls us to walk may seem narrow and hard.

The prophet Jeremiah, when lamenting the sins of his people, says, "we have made lies our

refuge, and in falsehood we have taken shelter" (Isaiah 28:15). He adds that the Lord declared,

"hail will sweep away the refuge of lies, and waters will overwhelm the shelter" (Isaiah 28:17). It

might look as though it were God's wrath doing this, and many frightened Christians think it is;

but his wrath is only against the refuges of lies, not against us. Love could do no less than

destroy these refuges so that we may be delivered.

A dear old friend of mine, who was very interested in my spiritual welfare, once gave me a little

book called The Seventeen False Rests of the Soul. He evidently felt I was in danger of settling

down upon one of these false rests. The book explained, in quaint old language, that the soul is

continually tempted to sit down upon something false as if it were a final resting place. God is

then continually obliged to "unbottom" all such false resting places, much like someone might

remove the seat of a chair and let the sitter fall through. All seventeen false rests were described,

showing how the soul—being "unbottomed" from each one in turn—settled down at last upon

the only true rest in God.

This "unbottoming" is just another word for the "shakings" and "emptyings" I have been writing

about. It is always a painful process and often a discouraging one. Everything seems unstable,

and rest seems utterly unattainable. No sooner do we find an experience or a doctrine in which

we think we may surely rest, than a great "shaking" comes and we are forced out again. This

process must continue until all that can be shaken is removed, and only "those things which

cannot be shaken" remain. Often the answer to our most fervent prayers for deliverance comes in

such a form that it seems as if "the foundations also of the mountains trembled and quaked"

(Psalm 18:7). We do not always see at first that it is through this very shaking that the

deliverance we prayed for is accomplished, bringing us into the "broad place" (Psalm 18:19) for

which we long.

The old mystics used to teach what they called "detachment," meaning the cutting loose of the

soul from all that could hold it back from God. This need for detachment is the secret of many of

our "shakings." We cannot follow the Lord fully as long as we are tied fast to anything else, any

more than a boat can sail into the boundless ocean while it is tied to the shore.

If we would reach the "city that has foundations, whose designer and builder is God" (Hebrews

11:10), we must go out like Abraham from all other cities and be detached from every earthly tie.

Everything in Abraham’s life that could be shaken was shaken. He was, as it were, emptied from

vessel to vessel—here today and gone tomorrow. All his resting places were disturbed, with no

settlement or comfort anywhere. We, like Abraham, are looking for a city with foundations, and

therefore we too will need to be emptied from vessel to vessel. We do not realise this, and when

the shakings come, we are in despair, thinking we shall never reach that city at all. But it is these

very shakings that make it possible for us to reach it.

The Psalmist had learned this, and after all the shakings of his eventful life, he cried, "For God

alone, O my soul, wait in silence, for my hope is from him. He only is my rock and my salvation,

my fortress; I shall not be shaken. On God rests my salvation and my glory; my mighty rock, my

refuge is God" (Psalm 62:5-7). At last, God was everything to him; and then he found that God

was enough.

It is the same with us. When everything in our lives and experience is shaken that can be shaken,

and only that which cannot be shaken remains, we are brought to see that God only is our rock

and our foundation. We learn to have our expectation from him alone. "Therefore we will not

fear though the earth gives way, though the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea, though

its waters roar and foam, though the mountains tremble at its swelling... God is in the midst of

her; she shall not be moved; God will help her when morning dawns" (Psalm 46:2-3, 5).

"Shall not be moved"—what an inspiring declaration! Can it be possible that we, who are so

easily moved by the things of earth, can arrive at a place where nothing can upset our temper or

disturb our calm? Yes, it is possible; and the Apostle Paul knew it. When he was on his way to

Jerusalem, where he foresaw that "imprisonment and afflictions" awaited him, he could say

triumphantly, "But I do not account my life of any value nor as precious to myself" (Acts 20:23-

24). In the older language, he said, "None of these things move me." Everything in Paul’s life

that could be shaken had been shaken. If we let God have his way with us, we may come to the

same place. Neither the small irritations of life nor its great trials will have the power to move us

from the "peace of God, which surpasses all understanding" (Philippians 4:7), which is the

portion of those who have learned to rest only on God.

In the Revelation made to John on the island of Patmos, the Spirit tells the churches what awaits

those who overcome: "The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God.

Never shall he go out of it" (Revelation 3:12). To be as immovable as a pillar in the house of our

God is an end for which one would gladly endure all the "shakings" and "unbottomings"

necessary to get there!

"Therefore let us be grateful for receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken, and thus let us offer

to God acceptable worship, with reverence and awe, for our God is a consuming fire" (Hebrews

12:28-29). A great many people are afraid of the consuming fire of God, but that is only because

they do not understand what it is. It is the fire of God’s love that must, by its very nature,

consume everything that can harm his people. If our hearts are set on being what the love of God

wants us to be, his fire is something we shall warmly welcome rather than fear.

"Implacable is love.

Foes may be bought or teased

From their malign intent;

But he goes unappeased,

Who is on kindness bent."

Let us thank God then that he is "on kindness bent" towards us, and that the consuming fire of

his love will not cease to burn until it has refined us as silver is refined. For the promise is that

"he will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them

like gold and silver, and they will bring offerings in righteousness to the Lord" (Malachi 3:3). He

gives us this inspiring assurance: if we will but submit to this purifying process, we shall become

"pleasing to the Lord" (Malachi 3:4). "Then all nations will call you blessed, for you will be a

land of delight, says the Lord of hosts" (Malachi 3:12).

To be "pleasing" and a "delight" to the Lord may seem impossible to us when we look at our

shortcomings and our unworthiness. But when we think of this lovely, consuming fire of God’s

love, we can take heart and be courageous. He will not fail or be discouraged until all our dross

and inferior silver is burned away, and we ourselves come forth in his likeness, conformed to his

image.

Our souls long for the "kingdom that cannot be shaken" (Hebrews 12:28). He who is "on

kindness bent" will, if we let him, shake everything in our lives that can be shaken. He will

"unbottom" us from every false rest until only that which cannot be shaken remains.

One of the most impressive sermons I ever heard was preached by a sweet-faced old Quaker

lady. She rose in the stillness and said, "Yesterday, sister Tabitha broke my best china teapot into

pieces. But the Lord, whom I trust, kept my soul in perfect peace and enabled me not to utter a

single word of reproach." That was all; the sermon was ended. But into every heart there entered

a sense of what it would mean to be kept in the immovable kingdom of the love of God. This

kingdom can be our home if we will only submit to the shakings of God and learn to rest only

and always on him.

May he hasten that day for each one of us!

fields.title: Chapter 12
fields.body_html:
A Word to the Wavering Ones

"But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is

driven and tossed by the wind. For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything

from the Lord" (James 1:6-7).

It would be difficult to find anything that produces more discomfort in the religious life than a

wavering faith. The image given to us by the Apostle James describes it exactly: "a wave of the

sea... driven and tossed". Just as it is impossible for a traveller to reach a destination by moving

forward one day and retracing their steps the next, it is equally impossible for the wavering soul

to reach a place of settled peace while it continues to waver.

In our last chapter, we considered the shakings of God. It might be thought that our wavering is

similar to his shaking, but they are very different. God’s shakings are caused by his love for our

blessing; they always lead to rest and peace. Our waverings are caused by our lack of faith; they

always lead to discomfort and turmoil.

A wavering Christian is someone who trusts in the love of God one day and doubts it the next,

and is alternately happy or miserable as a result. They climb to the hilltop of joy at one time,

only to descend into the valley of despair the next. They are driven back and forth by every

"wind of doctrine," always striving but never attaining. They are a victim of every changing

influence—whether it is their physical health, the people around them, or even the weather.

You would suppose that even the most inexperienced child of God would know that this sort of

experience is wrong. Wavering in one's faith in such a way is deeply dishonouring to the Lord, as

it questions his truth and faithfulness. Yet, many Christians are so blinded that they actually

think this tendency to waver is a sign of humility. They treat every new attack of doubt as if it

were a pious virtue.

A wavering Christian might say complacently, "Oh, but I know I am so unworthy that I'm sure

it's right for me to doubt." They often imply that if their listener were truly humble, they would

doubt as well. I once knew a devoted Christian whose religious life was a constant torment of

doubt. After I urged him to have more faith, he said in all seriousness, "My dear friend, if I were

ever so arrogant as to feel sure that God loved me, I would be certain I was on the direct road to

hell."

He clearly thought that such assurance could only come from feeling he was "good enough" to

deserve God’s love. He was right that thinking we are worthy of God’s love is arrogant.

However, the ground for our assurance does not come from our own goodness, but from the

goodness of God. While we should never be satisfied with our own goodness, there can be no

question—for anyone who believes the Bible—regarding the total sufficiency of his.

To see how absurd this position of doubt is, consider how it would work in human relationships.

Imagine a marriage, or the relationship between a child and a parent—both of which the Lord

uses as symbols for our relationship with him. If a wife or husband had a "wavering experience"

of confidence in their spouse—trusting one day and doubting the next—would that be seen as a

sign of humility or a virtue to be cherished? Similarly, if children wavered in their confidence

toward their parents the way Christians do with their heavenly Father, what word would be harsh

enough for such unfilial conduct? In human relationships, such wavering might be excused if one

person were actually untrustworthy. But with God, there is no such excuse. The wavering faith of

his children may even lead outsiders to conclude that he isn't worthy of much confidence.

We would shrink in horror from causing people to think poorly of God’s character. But if we are

honest, we must acknowledge that a wavering faith conveys exactly that impression. It is, in

essence, disloyalty to a trustworthy God and should be viewed as a serious sin.

The truth is that our wavering comes from a subtle, often unconscious form of pride rather than

humility. True humility accepts the love and gifts bestowed upon it with a meek and happy

thankfulness. Pride, on the other hand, shrinks from accepting kindness and is afraid to believe in

the selfless goodness of the giver. If we were truly humble, we would accept God’s love with

thankful meekness. While acknowledging our own unworthiness, we would see it only as

something that highlights his grace and goodness in choosing us.

A wavering faith is not only disloyal to God, but it is a source of great misery for us. It cannot

advance our spiritual interests; it can only hinder them. The Apostle tells us that "we have come

to share in Christ, if indeed we hold our original confidence firm to the end" (Hebrews 3:14). To

be steadfast is the exact opposite of wavering. Expecting the results of steadfastness while

wavering is as foolish as trying to reach a mountain peak by alternating short climbs with long,

disastrous slides back down.

Yet many people expect exactly that. They make a "beginning of confidence" and, while the

freshness lasts, they are full of joy. Then trials and temptations come, and doubts begin to

intrude. Instead of treating these doubts as enemies to be resisted, they welcome them as friends.

Before long, they begin to waver in their faith and allegiance, and their peace is gone. When life

is bright, their faith revives; when things go wrong, doubts win and they waver again.

I once spoke with an eminent clergyman about the possibility of a religious life of abiding peace.

He frankly told me he didn't think it was possible and that most Christian experiences were like

his own. "When I want to write my sermons," he said, "I get to the mountain-top through prayer

and effort. I put my foot on one promise and then another until I reach the summit and can begin.

It goes well for a while, but then an interruption comes—a problem with my children or a quarrel

with a neighbour—and I tumble down. I can only get back by another wearisome climb. I might

stay on the summit for a few days, or once in a great while, a few weeks. But as for 'abiding'

there continually, I cannot believe it."

This describes the experience of many of God’s children who hunger for the peace Christ

promised but only find it for moments at a time. They get a glimmer of faith, but then the old

doubts return. "Look at your heart," they say; "see how cold and indifferent it is. How can you

believe God loves a poor, unworthy creature like you?" It sounds so reasonable that they are

plunged back into darkness.

The whole trouble comes from a lack of faith. In the spiritual life, it is always according to our

faith. This is a spiritual law that cannot be ignored or avoided. It is inherent in the nature of

things and is therefore unalterable. Equally, if it is to be according to our faith, it will also be to

us according to our doubts.

The cause of our wavering is not our sins, but our doubts. Doubts create an impassable gap

between our souls and the Lord, just as they do between us and our friends. No amount of

earnestness can bridge that gap. "For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything

from the Lord" (James 1:7). This isn't because God is angry; it is because the nature of things

makes it impossible for doubt and confidence to exist together. "And to whom did he swear that

they would not enter his rest, but to those who were disobedient? So we see that they were

unable to enter because of unbelief" (Hebrews 3:18-19). It wasn't that God wouldn't let them in

as a punishment; they simply could not enter. It was an impossibility. Faith is the only door

into the Kingdom of Heaven, and there is no other. If we will not go in by that door, we cannot

get in at all, for there is no other way.

God's salvation is not a purchase to be made, nor wages to be earned, nor a summit to be

climbed, nor a task to be accomplished; but it is simply and only a gift to be accepted, and it can

only be accepted by faith. Faith is a necessary element in the acceptance of any gift, whether

earthly or heavenly. My friends may put their gifts upon my table, or even place them in my lap,

but unless I believe in their friendliness and honesty of purpose enough to accept these gifts, they

can never truly become mine.

It is therefore plain that the Bible is simply announcing the nature of things, as it always does,

when it declares, "Be it done to you according to your faith" (Matthew 9:29). The sooner we

settle down to this, the better. All our wavering comes from the fact that we do not believe in this

law. We acknowledge, of course, that it is in the Bible, but we think it cannot really mean what it

says. We think there must be some additions made to it, such as "according to our fervency it

shall be unto us," or "according to our persistence," or "according to our worthiness."

If the whole truth were told, we are inclined to think that these additions of ours are, if anything,

by far the most important part of the matter. As a consequence, our attention is mostly directed to

getting these matters settled. We watch our own states of mind and feelings, and search into our

own worthiness or unworthiness with so much diligence that we almost entirely overlook the one

fundamental principle of faith, without which nothing can be done. Moreover, as our moods and

feelings are the most variable things in the universe, and our sense of worthiness changes with

those feelings, our experience cannot help but waver. The possibility of a steadfast faith recedes

further into the background. In short, we make the faithfulness of God and the truth of his word

depend upon the state of our feelings.

I am certain that if any of our friends treated us in this doubting fashion, we would be wounded

and indignant beyond measure. No feeling of unworthiness on their part could excuse them in

our eyes for such a wavering of their confidence in us. In fact, we would far rather our friends

even sinned against us than doubted us. No form of sinfulness ever hindered the Lord Jesus

while on earth from doing his mighty works. The only thing that hindered him was unbelief. In

his own town, among his own neighbours and friends where he would have liked to perform

miracles, we are told that "he did not do many mighty works there, because of their unbelief"

(Matthew 13:58). It was not that he would not, but simply that he could not. And he cannot in

our case, any more than in theirs.

But I am afraid some of you may think I am making a mistake. You might think that, in spite of

what God has said, the person whose faith wavers can still receive something from the Lord if

they are only fervent and earnest enough. That would mean you do not believe God understands

the laws of his kingdom as well as you do, and that it is safer to follow your own ideas rather

than his word. Yet you must know that, up until now, your doubts have brought you nothing but

darkness and misery. Recall the days, weeks, or even years of a halting, stumbling,

uncomfortable religious life, and ask yourself honestly whether the cause of it all has not been

your wavering faith.

If you believe one day that God loves you and is favourable to you, and the next day doubt his

love and fear he is angry with you, does it not stand to reason that your experience must waver

from joy to misery? Only a steadfast faith in his love and care could give you an unwavering

experience.

The one question, therefore, for all whose faith wavers, is how to put an end to that wavering

once and for all. Here, I am thankful to say, I know of a perfect remedy. The only thing you have

to do is to GIVE IT UP. Your wavering is caused by your doubting, and by nothing else. Give up

your doubting, and your wavering will stop. Keep on with your doubting, and your wavering will

continue. The whole matter is as clear as daylight, and the choice is in your own hands.

Perhaps you think this is an extreme statement, for it has probably never entered your head that

you could give up doubting altogether. But I assert that you can. You can simply refuse to doubt.

You can shut the door against every suggestion of doubt that comes and, by faith, declare exactly

the opposite. Your doubt says, "God does not forgive my sins." Your faith must say, "He does

forgive me; he says he does, and I choose to believe him. I am his forgiven child." You must

assert this steadfastly until all your doubts vanish. You have no more right to say that you are of

such a "doubting nature" that you cannot help doubting than to say you are of such a "thieving

nature" that you cannot help stealing. One is as easily controlled as the other. You must give up

your doubting just as you would give up thieving. You must treat the temptation to doubt exactly

as a person struggling with alcohol must treat the temptation to drink; you must take a pledge

against it.

The process I believe to be most effective is to lay our doubts—just as we lay our other sins—

upon God's altar and make a total surrender of them. We must give up all liberty to doubt and

must consecrate our power of believing to him, trusting him to keep us trusting. We must make

our faith in his word as inevitable and necessary a thing as is our obedience to his will. We must

be as loyal to our heavenly Friend as we are to our earthly friends. We must refuse to recognise

the possibility of any questioning or doubting of his love or his faithfulness.

Of course, temptations to waver will come. It will sometimes seem impossible that the Lord can

love such disagreeable, unworthy beings as we feel ourselves to be. But we must turn as deaf an

ear to these insinuations against the love of God as we would to any gossip against our dearest

friend. The fight to do this may sometimes be very severe and may even seem unendurable. But

our unchanging declaration must continually be: "Though he slay me, I will hope in him" (Job

13:15). Our steadfast faith will unfailingly bring us a glorious victory.

It will often seem as if it would be a "righteous" thing—given our many shortcomings—to waver

in our faith and question whether salvation is meant for us. But if we understand what the

salvation of the Lord Jesus Christ is, we must recognise that all this is only temptation. We must

persistently lift up the "shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the

evil one" (Ephesians 6:16).

The Spirit of God never, under any circumstance, suggests a doubt of the love of God. Wherever

doubts come from, one thing is certain: they do not come from heaven. All doubts are from an

evil source and must be treated as the suggestions of an enemy. We cannot, it is true, prevent the

suggestions of doubt from making themselves heard in our hearts, any more than we can prevent

our ears from hearing swearing in the streets. But just as we can refuse to approve of or join in

with that language, so can we refuse to pay any attention to these suggestions of doubt. The cases

are exactly similar. While we know it would be wrong to join in with swearing, we often have a

lingering feeling that doubts might be "pious" and should be encouraged. I believe one is as

displeasing to God as the other.

Again, I would repeat: the only way to treat the doubts that make you waver is to give them up.

An absolute surrender is the only remedy. Like the person struggling with drink, half measures

are of no use. Total abstinence is the only hope.

The most practical way of doing this is to meet each doubt with a flat denial and to carry the war

into the enemy's country by an emphatic assertion of faith. For instance, if the doubt arises as to

whether God can love someone as sinful and unfaithful as you feel yourself to be, you must at

once assert in your own heart—and if possible, aloud to someone else—that God does love you.

He says he does, and his word is worth a million times more trust than any of your feelings. If

you cannot find anyone to whom to say this, then write it in a letter or say it aloud to yourself

and to God. Be very definite about it.

If in anything you have had a "beginning of confidence," if you have ever laid hold of any

promise of the Lord's, hold on steadfastly to that promise without wavering, let come what may.

There can be no middle ground. If it was true once, it is true still, for God is unchangeable. The

only thing that can deprive you of it is your unbelief. While you believe, you have it. "Therefore

I tell you, whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours"

(Mark 11:24).

Let nothing shake your faith. Should even sin unhappily overtake you, you must not let it make

you doubt. At once, upon discovering any sin, act on the truth that "If we confess our sins, he is

faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9).

Confess your sin immediately and believe at once that God does forgive it, as he declares, and

does again cleanse you. No sin, however grievous, can separate us from God for one moment

after it has been treated in this fashion. To allow sin to cause your faith to waver is only to add a

new sin to the one already committed. Return at once to God in the way the Bible teaches and let

your faith hold steadfastly to his word. Believe it, not because you feel it or see it, but because he

says it. Believe it actively and steadfastly, through dark and light, through ups and downs,

through times of comfort and times of despair, and I can promise you that your wavering

experience will be ended.

"Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the work of the

Lord, knowing that in the Lord your labour is not in vain" (1 Corinthians 15:58). To be

"immovable" in one's religious life is the exact opposite of wavering. In the Forty-sixth Psalm,

we can see what it is. The earth may give way and the mountains may be moved into the heart of

the sea; our whole universe may seem to be in ruins; but while we trust in the Lord, we "shall not

be moved" (Psalm 46:5).

The person who wavers in their faith is upset by the smallest trifles; the person who is steadfast

in their faith can look on calmly even at the ruin of their universe. To be thus immovable is a

blessing most ardently to be desired, and it may be ours if we will only hold the beginning of our

confidence steadfast to the end.

"Faith is sweetest of worships to him who so loves

His unbearable splendours in darkness to hide;

And to trust in Thy word, dearest Lord, is true love,

For those prayers are most granted which seem most denied.

And faith throws her arms around all Thou hast told her,

And able to hold as much more, can but grieve;

She could hold Thy grand self, Lord! if Thou wouldst reveal it,

And love makes her long to have more to believe."

fields.title: Chapter 13
fields.body_html:
Discouragement

"The soul of the people was much discouraged because of the way" (Numbers 21:4).

The Church of Christ abounds in people who are "discouraged because of the way." Whether

inwardly or outwardly—and often both—things look wrong, there seems to be no hope of

escape, and their religious lives are full of discomfort. There is nothing that paralyses effort like

discouragement, and nothing that more successfully invites defeat. The secret of failure or

success lies far more in the soul's interior attitude than in any other cause. It is a law of our being

that the "inward man" counts for far more in every conflict than anything the outward man may

do or possess.

Nowhere is this truer than in the spiritual life. The Bible declares from beginning to end that faith

is the law of the spiritual life, and "according to your faith be it done to you" (Matthew 9:29).

Since faith and discouragement cannot exist together, discouragement is an absolute barrier to

faith. Where discouragement rules, it shall be to us not according to our faith, but according to

our discouragement.

In fact, just as courage is a faith in good, discouragement is a faith in evil. While courage opens

the door to good, discouragement opens it to evil. An allegory I heard early in my Christian life

has always remained in my memory as a warning, like those signs for cyclists at the top of a hill:

"This hill is dangerous."

The allegory tells of a council Satan called to decide how to entrap a devoted Christian worker.

One imp offered to paint the pleasures of sin in glowing colours. Satan shook his head: "The man

has tried sin and knows it leads to ruin." Another offered to picture the trials and self-denials of a

righteous life to make him eager to escape them. "No," said Satan, "he knows that the paths of

righteousness are paths of peace." Then a third imp started up: "I will discourage his soul." "That

will do!" exclaimed Satan. "You will be successful."

An old Quaker once said, "All discouragement is from the devil." I believe this is a deep truth.

Discouragement cannot have its source in God. The religion of Jesus is one of faith, good cheer,

and hope. "Be discouraged," says our lower nature, "for the world is a place of temptation." "In

the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world" (John 16:33).

There is no room for discouragement in a world Christ has overcome.

We must settle it, then: discouragement always comes from an evil source. We often persuade

ourselves that being discouraged is a "pious" state of mind or evidence of humility, but the

causes we think are legitimate are often just short-sightedness.

The most common cause is our own incapacity. We think it is right to be cast down because we

are "good-for-nothing" creatures. Moses is a perfect illustration of this. When God called him to

lead Israel out of Egypt, Moses looked at his own infirmities: "Oh, my Lord, I am not eloquent...

but I am slow of speech and of tongue" (Exodus 4:10). Naturally, we think Moses had cause for

discouragement. But notice God's answer. He did not try to convince Moses that he was actually

eloquent. He simply said: "Who has made man's mouth? Who makes him mute, or deaf, or

seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the Lord? Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth and teach

you what you shall speak" (Exodus 4:11-12).

When the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, he felt unequal to the work: "Ah, Lord God!

Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am only a youth" (Jeremiah 1:6). But the Lord

answered: "Do not say, 'I am only a youth'; for to all to whom I send you, you shall go... Do not

be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you" (Jeremiah 1:7-8).

Gideon is another example. Called to deliver Israel from the Midianites, the Lord told him: "Go

in this might of yours and save Israel... Do not I send you?" (Judges 6:14). Gideon looked at his

lack of status: "Please, Lord, how can I save Israel? Behold, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh,

and I am the least in my father's house" (Judges 6:15). How familiar this sounds to victims of

discouragement! But the Lord simply said: "But I will be with you, and you shall strike the

Midianites as one man" (Judges 6:16).

God never gives us "encouragement" regarding our own capacities. He gives us the bare

statement: "I will be with you." This answer precludes all argument. I, your Creator, your

strength, and your wisdom, will be with you.

Even so, discouragement is subtle. We think our "temperament" makes it right for us to be

discouraged. We think we are too weak to grapple with enemies. And we would be right—if we

were fighting the battles ourselves. But if the Lord is to fight them for us, our lack of ability

becomes an advantage. "For when I am weak, then I am strong" (2 Corinthians 12:10).

The children of Israel provide a warning here. At the borders of the promised land, Moses urged

them: "Do not fear or be dismayed" (Deuteronomy 1:21). But they felt helpless and murmured

that God must hate them. They said: "Where are we going up? Our brothers have made our

hearts melt, saying, 'The people are greater and taller than we. The cities are great and fortified

up to heaven'" (Deuteronomy 1:28). This is the voice of discouragement—looking at the "giants"

instead of the God who is with us. When we read the report of the spies, we cannot be surprised

at their discouragement. In fact, we might even feel that courage under such circumstances

would have been foolhardiness. "The land, through which we have gone to spy it out, is a land

that devours its inhabitants," the spies declared, "and all the people that we saw in it are of great

height. And there we saw the Nephilim... and we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers, and so

we seemed to them" (Numbers 13:32-33).

Nothing could have seemed more humble than for them to look upon themselves as poor, good-

for-nothing grasshoppers; true humility would have seemed to teach that it would be the height

of presumption for grasshoppers to try to conquer giants. We also often feel ourselves to be but

grasshoppers in the face of the giants of temptation and trouble that assail us, and we think

ourselves justified in being discouraged. But the question is not whether we are grasshoppers, but

whether God is; for it is not we who have to fight these giants, but God.

In vain Moses reminded the Israelites of this. In vain he assured them that they had no need to be

afraid of even the sons of the Anakim, for "The Lord your God who goes before you will himself

fight for you" (Deuteronomy 1:30). He even reminded them of past deliverances, asking if they

did not remember how "in the wilderness... the Lord your God carried you, as a man carries his

son, all the way that you went" (Deuteronomy 1:31). But they were still too discouraged to

believe. The result was that not one of that "evil generation" was allowed to see the promised

land, except for Caleb and Joshua, who had steadfastly believed that God could and would lead

them in.

Such are the fruits of giving way to discouragement, and such is the reward of a steadfast faith.

The Apostle, in commenting on this story, asks: "And to whom did he swear that they would not

enter his rest, but to those who were disobedient? So we see that they were unable to enter

because of unbelief" (Hebrews 3:18-19).

Is there no parallel here to our own case? Do we not look at our weakness instead of looking at

the Lord's strength? Have we not sometimes become so discouraged as to sink into such "anguish

of spirit" (Exodus 6:9) that we cannot even hearken to the Lord's own declarations that he will

fight for us and give us the victory? Our souls long to enter into the rest the Lord has promised,

but giants and cities "fortified up to heaven" seem to stand in our pathway, and we are afraid to

believe. So we too, like the Israelites, cannot enter in because of unbelief.

How different it would be if we only had faith enough to say with the Psalmist: "Though an army

encamp against me, my heart shall not fear; though war arise against me, yet I will be confident...

For he will hide me in his shelter in the day of trouble; he will conceal me under the cover of his

tent; he will lift me high upon a rock" (Psalm 27:3, 5). How joyfully and triumphantly would we

be able to enter into rest if this were our language.

Another very subtle cause for discouragement is found in the "fear of man." There seems to exist

in this world a company of beings called "they" who lord it over life with an iron hand of control.

What will "they" say? What will "they" think? These are among the most frequent questions that

assail the timid soul. At every turn, this ubiquitous "they" stands in our way to discourage us.

This form of discouragement often wears the disguise of "due consideration for others," but it is

especially dangerous because it exalts "they" into the place of God. The only remedy is the

constant reminder that God is with us. "Be not afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you,

declares the Lord" (Jeremiah 1:8). "The Lord is my helper; I will not fear; what can man do to

me?" (Hebrews 13:6).

There is, however, one sort of discouragement that is very common and seems as if it must be

right: the discouragement arising from our own failures. This is what the children of Israel

suffered after their defeat at Ai. They had "broken the covenant" and "therefore the people of

Israel cannot stand before their enemies" (Joshua 7:11-12). Their discouragement was so great

that "the hearts of the people melted and became as water," and Joshua "fell on his face to the

earth before the ark of the Lord until the evening" (Joshua 7:5-6).

When God's people "turn their backs before their enemies," one might think they ought to lie on

their faces in despair. But the Lord thought otherwise, for he said to Joshua, "Get up! Why have

you fallen on your face?" (Joshua 7:10). The proper thing to do after a failure is not to abandon

ourselves to discouragement, humble as that may appear, but to face the evil, get rid of it, and

immediately reconsecrate ourselves to the Lord. "Up, consecrate the people" (Joshua 7:13) is

always God's command. "Lie down and be discouraged" is always our temptation.

You may ask whether a sense of sin produced by the Holy Spirit ought not to cause

discouragement. If I see myself as a sinner, how can I help it? To this I answer that the Holy

Spirit does not convict us of sin to discourage us, but to encourage us. He shows us our sin not so

we may lie down in despair, but so we may get rid of it. A good mother points out her children's

faults to help them correct them. Conviction is a privilege; it means deliverance is coming.

A good housewife discovers stains on her linen not to throw it away, but to have it cleansed. If

she has a good laundress, she won't be discouraged by the worst of stains. Surely then, when God

says, "though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow" (Isaiah 1:18), it is pure

unbelief to be discouraged by our failures. God's "washing of regeneration" is more effective

than any human effort.

Fénelon says:

"It is of great importance to guard against discouragement on account of our faults.

Discouragement is not a fruit of humility, but of pride... It springs from a secret love of our own

excellence. We are hurt at feeling what we are... Poor nature longs from self-love to behold itself

perfect; it is vexed that it is not so; it is impatient, haughty, and out of temper with itself and

everybody else."

Discouragement leads people to "murmur" and "speak against God." When the Israelites were

"discouraged because of the way," they "spoke against God" (Numbers 21:4-5). Discouragement

is, in its essence, a claim that God has failed to keep his promises. The Psalmist says: "They

spoke against God, saying, 'Can God spread a table in the wilderness?'" (Psalm 78:19). Even our

"reasonable" questions about God's willingness to help are a "speaking against God" because

they reveal that we "did not believe in God and did not trust his saving power" (Psalm 78:22).

Another grievous quality of discouragement is its contagiousness. Nothing is more catching.

When the spies sent out by Moses brought back an "evil report" of the promised land and spoke

of the giants there, they so "made the heart of the people melt" (Joshua 14:8) that the people

"lifted up their voices and cried" (Numbers 14:1) and utterly refused to enter the land the Lord

had given them. The "evil report" that so many Christians bring of their failures and

disappointments is one of the most discouraging things in our fellowship. The hearts of young

Christians are far too often discouraged by older believers who have little idea of the harm they

do with their doleful accounts of the trials of the way.

I can never look back without shame to a time when I "discouraged the heart" of a young friend

by the "evil report" I gave of the "giants" of doubt I had met. Later, when a stronger faith

delivered me from those fears, I found my former report had so effectively discouraged her that

it took a long time before she would listen to the good report I then had to bring.

So important did the Lord feel it to be that no one should discourage another, that he gave this

law for warfare: "What man is there who is fearful and fainthearted? Let him go back to his

house, lest he make the heart of his fellows melt like his own" (Deuteronomy 20:8). Discouraged

people, if they must be discouraged, should at least keep it to themselves, hidden in the privacy

of their own bosoms.

We know that courage is contagious; one brave soul can save a crowd from panic. But we forget

that one fainthearted person can infect a crowd with fear. We even, strange to say, sing our

discouragements in our hymns:

"Where is the blessedness I knew

When first I saw the Lord?

...But now I find an aching void,

The world can never fill."

Or this:

"And shall we then for ever live

At this poor dying rate...

Hosannas languish on our tongues,

And our devotion dies."

To sing such hymns seems a travesty of worship. If there are "aching voids" in our experience,

let us keep it to ourselves. Surely it cannot please God to hear complainings exalted into the

place of hosannas. What would we think of wives who met together to sing such things about

their husbands? They would not be tolerated for a single day.

If the Church would expurgate all hymns of discouragement and allow only songs of courage

and good cheer, the faith of Christians would go up with a mighty bound. "Take heart," is the

Lord's command, founded on the fact that "I have overcome the world" (John 16:33).

Which would you rather have been? The spies who brought an evil report, or Caleb and Joshua,

who "stilled the people before Moses and said, 'Let us go up at once and occupy it, for we are

well able to overcome it'" (Numbers 13:30)? Moses spoke of Caleb as one who "wholly followed

the Lord" (Deuteronomy 1:36). This "wholly following" consisted simply in the fact that Caleb

gave a good report.

How different it would be if discouragement were seen in its true light—as a "speaking against

God." In Isaiah’s prophecy, he describes God’s people: "Everyone helps his neighbor and says to

his brother, 'Be strong!' The craftsman strengthens the goldsmith, and he who smooths with the

hammer him who strikes the anvil" (Isaiah 41:6-7). Shall we follow their example?

If asked how to get rid of discouragement, I can only say: give it up. It is never worth while to

argue with it. When David found his city burned and his men spoke of stoning him, "David

strengthened himself in the Lord his God" (1 Samuel 30:6). The result was a magnificent victory.

The Psalmist asked himself: "Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil

within me?" (Psalm 42:11). He answered with the argument of God: "Hope in God; for I shall

again praise him, my salvation and my God." He did not analyse his disquietude; he turned to the

Lord and began to praise. Faith flies when discouragement appears, and discouragement flies

where faith appears. You must choose between them.

fields.title: Chapter 14
fields.body_html:
The Shout of Faith

"And as soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, then all the people shall shout with a great

shout, and the wall of the city will fall down flat" (Joshua 6:5).

The shout of a steadfast faith is in direct contrast to the moans of a wavering faith or the wails of

a discouraged heart. In the history of Israel, they often indulged in wailing to their own undoing;

but on one occasion, they gave a magnificent shout that brought a glorious victory.

This took place after they had crossed the Jordan. God had said to Joshua: "Every place that the

sole of your foot will tread upon I have given to you" (Joshua 1:3). They entered the land

expecting possession, but were immediately brought face to face with Jericho—a city "great and

walled up to heaven." To the eye of sense, there was no possibility of conquering it.

But the Lord said: "See, I have given Jericho into your hand" (Joshua 6:2). He did not say "I will

give," but "I have given." It belonged to them already; they were simply called to take

possession. God’s plan was strange: after marching and blowing trumpets, "all the people shall

shout with a great shout; and the wall of the city shall fall down flat."

It came to pass just as the Lord said. Joshua told the people, "Shout, for the Lord has given you

the city" (Joshua 6:16). When they shouted, the walls fell down flat. No one supposes the noise

of the shout caused the walls to fall. The secret lay in the fact that it was the shout of a faith

which dared, on the authority of God's word alone, to claim a victory while as yet there were no

signs of it.

Faith reckoned God's word to be true. Unbelief might have said, "Wait to shout until the walls

actually fall, lest we look foolish." But faith laughed at such "prudence" and gave a shout of

victory while the walls were still standing. "By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had

been encircled for seven days" (Hebrews 11:30).

"Faith, mighty faith, the promise sees

And looks at that alone;

Laughs at impossibilities,

And cries, It shall be done."

Jehoshaphat is another example. A great multitude came against him, and he realized he had "no

might" and did not know "what to do." He did not waste time on engines of warfare; he "set his

face to seek the Lord" (2 Chronicles 20:3). He stood before the people and prayed: "We are

powerless against this great horde... we do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you" (2

Chronicles 20:12).

The Lord answered: "Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed at this great horde, for the battle is

not yours but God's... You will not need to fight in this battle. Stand firm, hold your position, and

see the salvation of the Lord" (2 Chronicles 20:15, 17).

Without a thought of doubt, Jehoshaphat and the children of Israel believed the word of the Lord

and began at once to praise him beforehand for the victory they were sure was coming. The next

morning they rose early and went out to meet their enemy. Jehoshaphat, instead of exhorting

them to look to their arms and be brave in battle as an ordinary General would have done, simply

called upon them to have a courageous faith. "Hear me, Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem!

Believe in the Lord your God, and you will be established; believe his prophets, and you will

succeed" (2 Chronicles 20:20).

Jehoshaphat then consulted with the people; and their faith proving equal to his own, they

appointed singers to go out before the army to sing praises as they went forward to meet the

enemy. And it came to pass that when they began to sing and to praise, the Lord set an ambush

against the enemy, so that they struck one another down. When the children of Israel came to a

watchtower in the wilderness, from which they could see the great multitude that had come up

against them, "behold, there were dead bodies lying on the ground; none had escaped" (2

Chronicles 20:24).

By this wonderful method of warfare they were made even "more than conquerors"; for they

were "three days in taking away the spoil, for it was so much" (2 Chronicles 20:25).

David’s fight with Goliath is another example of this method of victory. To the eye of sense,

David had no chance whatever of conquering the mighty giant who had been defying the armies

of Israel. But David, looking with the eye of faith, could see the unseen divine forces fighting on

his side. When Saul said to him, "You are not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him,

for you are but a youth, and he has been a man of war from his youth," David stood firm in his

faith. After recounting his past deliverances, he said calmly, "The Lord who delivered me from

the paw of the lion and from the paw of the bear will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine"

(1 Samuel 17:33, 37).

Saul, partly convinced by this strong faith, said, "Go, and the Lord be with you!" He could not,

however, quite give up all trust in his own accustomed armour; he armed David with a bronze

helmet, a coat of mail, and his own powerful sword. David "tried in vain to go," for he was not

used to them. He put them off and took instead the simple weapons the Lord had blessed before:

his staff, his sling, and five smooth stones from the brook. Thus equipped, he drew near to the

giant.

When the giant saw the youth who had come to fight him, he disdained him and said

contemptuously, "Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the air and to the beasts

of the field" (1 Samuel 17:44). To the eye of sense, it looked as though this must necessarily be

the end of such an unequal battle. But David’s faith triumphed, and he shouted a shout of victory

before the battle had even begun. "You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a

javelin," he said, "but I come to you in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of the armies of

Israel, whom you have defied. This day the Lord will deliver you into my hand... that all the

earth may know that there is a God in Israel, and that all this assembly may know that the Lord

saves not with sword and spear. For the battle is the Lord's, and he will give you into our hand"

(1 Samuel 17:45-47).

In the face of such faith, what could even a giant do? Every word of that triumphant shout of

victory was fulfilled, and the mighty enemy was delivered into the hands of the youth he had

disdained. And so it will always be. Nothing can withstand the triumphant faith that links itself to

omnipotence. For "this is the victory that has overcome the world—our faith" (1 John 5:4).

The secret of all successful warfare lies in this shout of faith. It is a secret incomprehensible to

those who know nothing of the unseen divine power that waits on the demands of faith; a secret

that must always seem the height of folly to those who do not understand it.

We are all called to be "a good soldier of Christ Jesus" (2 Timothy 2:3) and to "fight the good

fight of the faith" (1 Timothy 6:12) against worse enemies than those which attacked the

Israelites. Our enemies are interior, and the giant that defies us is the strength of our temptations

and the powerlessness of our own strength to resist. It is a hard and often discouraging fight.

Many of God's children have sinned, repented, and resolved so often that they see no hope of

victory. They hate sin and love righteousness, but "the good I want to do, I do not do, but the evil

I do not want to do—this I keep on doing" (Romans 7:19). In the language of the Apostle, they

find a law in their members warring against the law of their mind. They know they ought to

conquer, but they do not know how. It is for these people that this chapter is written. If they can

discover the secret of this shout of faith, they will know how, for it never fails to bring victory.

In John 16:33, our Lord reveals the ground of this triumphant shout: "Take heart; I have

overcome the world." Not "I will overcome," but "I have overcome." It is already done; we only

need to enter into the power of it. Joshua did not say, "Shout, for the Lord will give you the city,"

but "Shout, for the Lord has given you the city" (Joshua 6:16). It must have required all of

Joshua's will to make such a statement while the walls of the city were still standing as massive

as ever. But God was a reality to Joshua, and he was not afraid to proclaim the victory before it

was visible.

There is a great difference between saying "The Lord will give" and "The Lord has given." A

victory promised in the future may be hindered by a thousand things, but a victory already

accomplished cannot be undone. When our Lord assures us that he has already overcome the

world, he gives an assured foundation for a triumphant shout. Henceforward, the forces of sin are

a defeated foe. If we believe the words of Christ, we can meet them without fear, since we have

been made "more than conquerors through him who loved us" (Romans 8:37).

It is a well-known fact that as long as a defeated army can keep its defeat a secret, it can still

show some resistance. But the moment it finds out that its defeat is known, it loses all heart and

has no resource left but to retreat. The secret lies in this: we must meet sin not as a foe yet to be

conquered, but as one that has already been conquered. When Rahab helped the spies escape, she

confessed: "I know that the Lord has given you the land... and that all the inhabitants of the land

melt away before you" (Joshua 2:9). If we had eyes to see the unseen kingdom of evil, I believe

we would find that a terror has fallen upon all the forces of that region, and that they see in every

person of faith a triumphant conqueror.

A Christian I know, who had been fearfully beset by temptation, was told this secret. It brought

conviction at once, and she went forth to a fresh battle with the assurance of an already

accomplished victory. She said afterwards it seemed as if she could hear the tempter saying as he

slunk away, "Alas! She has found out the secret. She knows that I am an already conquered foe!"

We are told that "The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil" (1

John 3:8); and again, "he appeared in order to take away sins" (1 John 3:5); and "he has appeared

once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself" (Hebrews 9:26).

We must accept it as a fact that sin is for us a conquered foe. If our faith will lay hold of this and

"consider yourselves dead to sin" (Romans 6:11), and will dare to raise the shout of victory when

temptation comes, we shall find that every wall will fall down flat!

Our enemies are "giants" now just as they were in Israel's day, and cities as great as Jericho

confront us. Like the Israelites, we have no human weapons with which to conquer. Our armour

must be the "armor of God" (Ephesians 6:11). Our shield is the same invisible shield of faith, and

our sword is the "sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God" (Ephesians 6:17). But how

different is our usual method of warfare! Instead of a triumphant shout, we meet temptations

with feeble resolutions, futile arguments, or despairing prayers. "O Lord, save me!" we cry.

When no deliverance seems to come and we are defeated, we cry out that God has failed us. But

what we ought to do is recognise sin as a conquered foe and meet it with a shout of victory.

Where we prayed before that the Lord would save us, we must now make the assertion that he

does save us, and that he saves us now. We must add the letter "s" to the word "save" and make it

the present tense.

The walls may look as high as ever, and prudence may say it is not safe to shout until the victory

is won. But the faith that can shout in the midst of temptation, "Jesus saves me; he saves me

now!" is a faith that will win a glorious and speedy victory.

Many of God's children have tried this plan and found it to work far beyond their expectations.

Temptations have come in like a flood—temptations to irritability, wicked thoughts, bitterness of

spirit, or a thousand other things. They have seen the danger, and their feelings declared there

was no hope of escape.

But their faith laid hold of the grand fact that Christ has conquered. They fixed their gaze on the

unseen power of God's salvation and gave their shout of victory: "The Lord saves! He saves me

now! I am more than a conqueror through him who loved us" (Romans 8:37). The result is

always a glorious victory.

It may sometimes seem so impossible that the Lord can save that the words will not "say

themselves" inside. They have to be said aloud, forcing one's lips to utter them over and over,

shutting one's eyes and ears against every suggestion of doubt. These declarations of faith often

seem "untrue" at first because the reasons for discouragement appear so real. But the unseen

facts are truer than the seen. If faith is steadfastly persisted in, these facts never fail to prove

themselves. "According to your faith be it done to you" (Matthew 9:29). When we shout the

shout of faith, the Lord invariably gives the victory of faith.

I once knew a Christian carman (a driver) who had a naturally violent temper. In his daily work

among ungodly companions, he was sorely tempted to give way to it. He struggled valiantly but

in vain. One morning, he told his minister in despair, "Can you tell me of any short road to

victory—something I can lay hold of at the needed moment?"

"Yes," the minister replied. "When the temptation comes, at once lift up your heart and claim the

promised victory. Shout the shout of faith, and the temptation will flee."

The carman understood that sin is an already conquered foe. That day at the station, his fellow-

drivers taunted him and jostled him out of his rightful place. The temptation to anger was

overwhelming. But, folding his arms, he said inwardly over and over, "Jesus saves me; he saves

me now!" At once his heart was filled with peace. Later, a heavy box fell on his foot, causing

great pain. Again he folded his arms and repeated his shout of victory, and all was calm. Night

found him more than a conqueror, and even his companions were forced to own the reality of a

religion that could so triumph over their assaults.

The Psalmist, after telling of the enemies who tried to swallow him up, declared: "Then my

enemies will turn back in the day when I call. This I know, that God is for me" (Psalm 56:9).

Do you know what the Psalmist knew? Do you know that God is for you? If you do, then go out

to meet your temptations singing a song of triumph. At the first approach of temptation, begin to

give thanks for the victory. Claim that you are more than a conqueror. Shout the shout of faith

with Joshua, Jehoshaphat, David, and Paul. When you shout, the Lord will "set ambushments,"

and your enemies shall fall.

fields.title: Chapter 15
fields.body_html:
Thanksgiving Versus Complaining

"Give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you" (1

Thessalonians 5:18).

Thanksgiving and complaining are two contrastive attitudes. The soul that gives thanks can find

comfort in everything; the soul that complains can find comfort in nothing.

God’s command is, "In everything give thanks." It is a positive command. If we want to obey

God, we simply must give thanks in everything. There is no getting around it. Yet many

Christians look upon this as a "counsel of perfection" that mere flesh and blood could never

reach. Unconsciously, they change the wording to "be resigned" instead of "give thanks," and "in

a few things" instead of "in everything."

They argue, "If everything came direct from God, I might do it, but most things come through

human sources or sin." To this I answer: we cannot always give thanks for the things themselves,

but we can always give thanks for God’s love in the things. He is in them somewhere,

compelling even the most grievous to work together for our good. Faith never sees "second

causes" (the people or mistakes that hurt us); it sees only the hand of God behind them. By the

time the effects of a trial reach us, they have become God's will for us and must be accepted from

his hands.

The story of Joseph is an illustration. Nothing could have seemed more contrary to God’s will

than being sold into slavery by his brothers. Yet, if he had known the end from the beginning, he

would have been filled with thanksgiving. His slavery was the direct doorway to the greatest

blessings of his life. At the end, Joseph could say, "As for you, you meant evil against me, but

God meant it for good" (Genesis 50:20). To the eye of sense, his brothers sent him to Egypt; to

the eye of faith, "God sent me" (Genesis 45:7).

I remember a trial in my own life brought upon me by another person. I was filled with bitter

rebellion and saw nothing to be thankful for. But that very trial worked out the richest blessings

of my life. If only I had had faith enough to give thanks at first, how much sorrow I would have

been spared.

I am afraid the highest many Christians reach is "striving after resignation" to things they cannot

alter. Thanksgiving is almost an unknown exercise. In the world, it is considered discourteous to

receive a benefit and fail to say thank you; I cannot see why it is not just as discourteous toward

God. We wouldn't dream of omitting a thank-you note to a human friend for a trifling gift, yet

we fail to thank God for the innumerable benefits he showers on us.

Worse still, many allow themselves to complain and murmur. We are told that "the people

complained in the hearing of the Lord about their misfortunes, and when the Lord heard it, his

anger was kindled" (Numbers 11:1). We are tempted to think our "spiritual" complaining doesn't

displease him—that it is a sign of zeal or deep insight. But complaining is the opposite of the

faith that pleases God.

But complaining is always alike, whether it is on the temporal or the spiritual plane. It always

contains the element of fault-finding. Webster says to complain means "to make a charge or an

accusation." It is not merely disliking the thing we have to bear; it is finding fault with the

agency that lies behind it. If we carefully examine the inwardness of our complainings, we shall

generally find they are founded on a subtle fault-finding with God. We secretly feel as if He were

to blame, and we make mental charges against Him.

On the other hand, thanksgiving always involves praise of the Giver. Have you ever noticed how

much we are urged in the Bible to "praise the Lord"? It was the principal part of Israel's worship:

"Praise the Lord, for the Lord is good; sing to his name, for it is pleasant!" (Psalm 135:3). I

believe if we counted them, we would find more commands to give thanks "always for all

things" than for any other act. It is evident that the Lord loves to be thanked and praised just as
