This is NOT uniformity nor ecumenicism (Promotion of cooperation and unity among Christians).

The body’s characteristic is that Jesus is its head and it is His fullness (1:23). It exists to do the

will of its head and master. Paul might have been aware of the prayer of Jesus recorded for us in

John 17 – “that they may be One as You ( the Father ) and I ( the Son ) are one”. The last prayer of

Jesus for all who would come to believe Him, is that we may be ONE. Further, that we might be

‘one’ as He and the Father are ‘one’. There is no tension here – no conflict of differing goals, ideas,

etc., but a unity molded in love. The outcome of such unity will be that “the world will know that

You sent Me and loved them, even as You loved Me” (John 17:23).

The body is a good example of many differi ng parts functioning as ‘one’. In a healthy body, all

parts coordinate well even though some may be ‘in opposition’ to one another. E.g. for progress,

one leg pu shes backward as the other reaches forward! The foot cannot say to the hand ‘I have no

need of you’ nor can the ear say to the eye ‘I have no need of you’. (1 Cor 12:15). Might one say,

“the Baptist cannot say to the Pentecostal ‘I have no need of you’; no r vice versa. The evangelist

cannot say to the teacher ‘I have no need of you,’ etc. ?” Where there are parts of the body which

do not do what they are designed to do, the body is sick or dysfunctional.

G

Paul teaches much about the body and its ministry in three places: Romans 12, 1 Corinthians 12,

and here in Ephesians. It is striking that these are the same three references where he writes

concerning the operation of the Holy Spirit in gifting individuals for service. Some are gifted to

‘equip the saints’ (4:12) while others are gifted to minister to a lost world wit h the hands and heart

of Jesus. None is gifted for their own, individual enjoyment. How sad it is when we envy others’

giftings and ministry and fail to exercise/those which the Holy Spirit has given to us! Every one

of us has been given a Holy Spirit gift for ministering to the common good (1 Cor 12:7). Are you

using yours? Do not know what it is? Ask your pastor or some godly people in your fellowship –

you might be surprised what they can see that you do not see!

“The whole body, being fitted and held together by what each joint supplies, according to the

proper working of each part, causes the growth of the body for the building up of itself in love.”

Eph 4:16).

Consider the unity that exists between the Father and the Son.

How do I contribute my part of the functioning body – “so that the world may believe”? (John

17:21)

Whenever I am asked semi- seriously, “So, what part of the Body are you?” I usually reply, with

an appropriate grin, “Why, I’m a big toe!” I then add in explanation, “I often find myself in the

dark, smelly places of the lives of those I am counselling. However, as a teacher/encourager, I

count it my responsibility, and privilege, to bring balance to the body.”

The building – a holy temple – a dwelling place of God

Paul joins Peter in presenting the church as a building, made of living stones (1 Pet 2:5). It is built

on the foundation of both the apostles and prophets (new covenant and old covenant) and is being

‘built together’ to be a dwelling place for God, the Holy Spirit. Jesus is the ‘chief cornerstone (Eph

2:20) that establishes the lines. As in the body, all the parts are bound together in unity and each

have a particular function. One does not use door jambs for rafters, nor glass windows for flooring!

How ridiculous such a building would be! Paul calls himself a wise master builder who wishes to

lay a foundation upon which others can build carefully (1 Cor 3:10).

We are all to be builders, just as we are also the building. “Do you not know that you are a tem ple

of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?”

As we consider these two metaphors for the church, we must come to the conclusion that the

church is meant to be a functioning entity, in which each member has a particular and important

role to play. Jesus said that He would build His church and the gates of Hell would not prevail

against it (Matt 16:18). Such a church is bonded together in love and ministering in the power of

an indwelling Holy Spirit. Naturally, Satan will do his utmost to divide this church, sadly with the

aid of many of its members!

If we would know ‘the riches of the glory of His inheritance in the saints’ or ‘the exceeding

greatness of His power to us who believe’ (1:18 , 19), it is incumbent upon us that we fulfill our

roles as members of the body and as a building fitly framed together as a habitation of the Holy

Spirit.

So, what part of the Body are you? Are you functioning in your Holy Spirit giftings, or are you

weak because you are envious of another’s giftings?

I was once the guest speaker at a Full Gospel Business Men’s dinner. I arrived early at the hotel

and was warmly greeted by two men. A short time later, another brother joined us, but it was soon

obvious that he wasn’t in a good place emotionally. As I listened to the conversation that followed,

I gathered that his wife was not in harmony with him concerning his coming out that evening.

“Let’s pray together , ” suggested one of my new friends, so in typical FGBM fashion, we joined

arms in the hotel lobby and they began to pray for the newcomer. After we finished, I said to him,

“I don’t know if this means anything to you, but as we prayed, I saw a house in a rainstorm. The

rain was beating down into the house.” He fell to the floor weeping. Finally, getting to his feet, he

said, “Brothers, I must go home!” then turning to me, said “Thank you! On my way here this

evening, I was complaining to the Lord about my wife when He said, “You are a leaky roof! When

you get yourself in order, I will do something about your wif e!” God had given me a word of

knowledge for that brother. (1 Cor 12:9)

John Donne, a sixteenth-century Anglican priest, wrote: No man is an island, entire of itself; every

man is a piece of the continent, a part of the main. If a clod be washed away by the sea, Europe is

the less, as well as if a promontory were, as well as if a manor of thy friend’s or thine own were:

any man’s death diminishes me, because I am involved in mankind, and therefore never send to

know for whom the bell tolls; it tolls for thee. These sentiments should be true of all believers

recognizing themselves as members of one body, built together as one building, a habitation of the

Holy Spirit.

The church does not exist for man’s blessing but for the glory of God – we are created ‘fo r good

works’ (Ephesians 2:10). As we function together as a living body, as a building indwelt by the

Holy Spirit, the Lord will do His work in calling men and women to Himself, counteracting the

humanistic philosophies of this world’s systems and bringin g glory to Himself. In the words of the

old Moravian missionaries, “May the Lamb that was slain receive the reward of His suffering”.

fields.title: Chapter 5. A C
fields.body_html:
Ephesians 2:11-22

aul writes a lot about ‘us’ and ‘you’. He is referring to the Jews (us) and the Gentiles (you).

He knew what a privilege it was to be a Jew. They were the chosen people of God, called

out from the world to occupy a land God had chosen for them. They were r ecipients of God’s love

and faithfulness and had a history full of His deliverance and blessing. They had the Law by which

they alone could find righteousness. They had a priesthood and sacrifices by which they could

approach a holy God. And they were the people from whom the Messiah would come that would

rule the world – and Paul knew who that was!

The Jews had a very low opinion of the Gentiles – ‘dogs’ they were called (note the words of Jesus

in Matt 15:26!).

However, Paul has been the recipient of a ‘mystery’ – that he is to be the apostle to the Gentiles

(3:1-7).

See how he describes ‘you’ – Gentiles.

2: 1 dead in trespasses and sins – as we also were, children of wrath (v3)

2:11 ‘uncircumcision’. This means they were not in covenant relationship with God.

2:12 separate from God; excluded from the commonwealth of Israel; strangers to the covenants

of promise, having no hope and without God in the world. What a sad situation!

But note that he does not write about this in terms of their being sinners needing forgiveness, but

rather, as aliens needing to be ‘brought near’. His thoughts do not center around salvation but on

relationship and reconciliation.

v13: “ But now …” Brought near, made one with the Jew.

2:18 having access to the Father

2:19 no longer strangers and aliens; fellow citizens with the saints; of God’s household.

2:20 built upon the same foundation of apostles and prophets.

P

Paul continues this theme into Chapter 3:

3:6: ‘You have become fellow heirs and fellow members of the ‘body’; fellow partakers of the

promise in Christ Jesus.

3:8 recipients of unfathomable riches in Christ.

We have become a covenant people. I want in this chapter to speak about COVENANT.

The Jews understood covenant. They were well taught that God had made a covenant with

Abraham, their ‘father’ , and repeated it to Moses in the establishment of the Law . “I will be your

God and you will be My people” (Ex 6:7).

What is a covenant ? It is an agreement between two parties. In OT times, God was the party

that dictated the covenant terms. He called Abram from Ur (Babylonia) and promised him a great

heritage and a land (Gen 12). God repeated these promises several times in Genesis. In Gen 17,

it is to be through Isaac (the son of Sarah) that the covenant will continue, not through Ishmael

(the son of the bond woman). In Gen 26, the covenant promise is repeated to Isaac; in Gen 28, it

is repeated to Jacob after his vision of a ladder reaching into heaven.

It seemed that the promise was in vain after Jacob immigrated to Egypt at a time of great famine.

His descendants gradually became slaves in that land after being out of the “Promised Land” for

400 years. Then Moses is raised to deliver them.

Ex 2:24: God ‘remembered’ His covenant with Abraham, Isaac , and Jacob. Ex 3:6: God declared

(from a ‘burning’ bush) “I am the God of Abraham, Isaac , and Jacob”. Ex 3:15: “ Tell the people,

the Lord God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob has sent you”.

Ex 6:2-4: God declares Himself to Moses as Jehovah (Lord) – a name NOT known before by

Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who only knew Him as El Shaddai – Almighty God (impersonal).

Ex 19:5: A new promise is made to the Children of Israel, now out of Egypt. “If you keep My

covenant, you shall be a peculiar treasure unto Me above al l other peoples.”

Then in Ex 20 the “terms” of the (old) covenant are laid out – the 10 commandments (followed by

various civil laws). These were established to teach the high demands of the life God required if

His people would be accepted by Him as ‘righteous’. All history attests to the fact that they were

unable (and unwilling) to meet their side of the covenant agreement.

The following chapters outline the ceremonies and their laws, by which man could “draw near” to

God. The highlight of those ceremoni es was on the “Day of Atonement” (Yom Kippur) when the

High Priest would take the blood of a (perfect) lamb and sprinkle it upon the ‘mercy seat’ in the

Holy of Holies in the tabernacle. If the High Priest returned safely to his people, it was a sign that

God had accepted the shed blood as a covering for their sins for another year, and the people would

greatly celebrate! That was the OLD COVENANT , in which we Gentiles had no part (see above).

What is the NEW COVENANT into which we have entered? What are its benefits, and what are

its terms (requirements)? Where/when did you agree to the terms?

A New Covenant was established by Jesus the night before He died. (John 13-17). He invited His

disciples to share the Feast of Passover with Him. That annual feast was to celebrate the time when

God had brought His people out of the bondage of Egypt by ‘passing over’ every house where the

blood of a lamb had been placed upon the doorpost. (Ex 12). He had a room prepared and sent

Peter and John to check that everything was ready (Luke 22). I can only imagine what each one

was thinking as they entered that room.

Surely Peter must have been thinking, “Wow, what a week this has been! The crowds gathered to

greet us as we came, throwing their clothes down on the street and waving palm branches! I wonder

if this is the time when Jesus will reveal Himsel f as Messiah!” James and John, “Sons of Thunder , ”

must have been more impressed as they watched Him cast the money changers out of the temple.

Surely, they must have thought, “He is about to reveal Himself as the Messiah!”

Similar thoughts must have crossed each of the disciple’s minds as they entered that room, but

Jesus knew something that they did not know – tomorrow He would die!

If I knew I had only a short time to live, I would prioritise my actions. I would want to make sure

that my wife and daughters knew how much I loved them. I would want to make sure I was leaving

no work undone that I should have done, no debts unpaid, no promises unfulfilled.

I would not spend my time as I often do, watching sport on TV or reading a novel - I would want

to deal with priorities.

This was to be a night when He would deal with PRIORITIES !

He made many wonderful promises! He promised them (and us) a place in heaven and that He

will come again (John 14:3); power to do ‘greater works’ (14:12) ; the Comforter (14:16); peace,

unlike the world’s peace (14:27); fruit (15:4); fullness of joy (15:11); guidance (16:13); answered

prayer (16:24). I believe He meant to fulfill these promises as I have experienced His faithfulness

in so many of them. This is His side of the Covenant.

He asked of them (and us) three things: to serve one another (as He demonstrated by washing their

feet, 13:14); to love one another (a commandment, 13:34); to obey His word (14:15). This is our

side of the Covenant.

He has promised peace, power, the Holy Spirit, etc., if we will serve one another, love one another,

and obey His word. This is the New Covenant.

At the end of supper, He took the bread and said, “This is My body for you – take and eat”. Then

He took the cup, saying, “This is the cup of the new covenant in My blood. Drink it.” Every time

you and I take the bread and cup, we are declaring our agreement to the covenant. In other words,

we are say ing, “I will serve Your people, I will love Your people, and I will obey Your word!”

What then are the ‘laws’ of this new covenant? They are written upon our hearts (Jer 31:33) , and

we become aware of them by the teaching and convicting word of the Holy Spirit, who alone gives

us the power to live according to them. They are contained in ‘the Sermon on the Mount’ and other

teachings of Jesus, expanded by the teachings of the epistles. They can never earn us salvation, but

they are the expectation God has of every one of His children.

In acknowledgment that they were in a covenant relationship, all male Jews were circumcised –

lit: ‘a cutting away’ of the flesh. If circumcision was the symbol or token of a covenant relationship

with God, what is the ‘symbol’ by which we also enter a covenant relationship? See Colossians

2:11-15, recognising the very close relationship between these two books. Baptism is the act by

which our hearts are circumcised – a ‘cutting away’ of the flesh of the old nature. Without

circumcision, the Jew could not inherit the promises of God. He could live according to the Law,

even live as a ‘stranger’ in the land, but could not enjoy the riches of his inheritance.

In Col 2:14 we read that He has cancelled the ‘certificate of death, consisting of decrees against

us, which was hostile to us’. This aligns with Eph 2:15 where we read of the ‘enmity, which is the

Law of commandments contained in ordinances’. To us , the Law was a decree of death, for we are

unable to meet its awful requirements – but Jesus has cancelled that debt.

We are now being built on the double foundation of the prophets (OT) and apostles (NT). Jehovah

has become our God – we have been brought nigh because of the shed blood of the perfect lamb,

Jesus – blood that covers our sin, not for a year but for all eternity!

We have become a new people, people of a New Covenant, the terms of which were given at the

last Supper, the Laws of which are written upon our hearts, and the commitment to such is

expressed every time we take the communion elements.

Whenever I take the bread – “His body, broken for us” - I look around me and say, “Thank you,

Father, that I am a part of this body, both local and global.” Whenever I take the cup , I say, “Lord,

I will serve your people, I will love your people, I will obey your Wo rd.”

I am very aware that should I take the elements ‘unworthily , i.e. I am not serving or loving His

people, not obeying His word, I risk bringing judgment and sickness upon myself. (1 Cor 11:27-

30).

fields.title: Chapter 6
fields.body_html:
Ephesians Chapter 3:1-13

different perspective: Paul is in prison in Rome but he recognises himself foremost, as a

prisoner of Jesus Christ. Here we see again the dual nature of the believer – in this world but

not of it. One’s perspective can make all the difference!

Note that v2- 13 are another parenthesis in Paul’s teaching. “For this reason…” is repeated when

he gets ‘back on track’ with his prayer in v14. This parenthesis is triggered by his consideration

of his being ‘a prisoner of Christ Jesus’. He revels in it!

He refers again to the great ‘mystery’ he has received by revelation from God . The Gentiles also

are to receive blessings from God! That is radically different to current thought among the Jews

who considered all Gentiles as “dogs” not worthy of God’s attention. As Peter became the apostle

to the Jews, Paul has become the apostle to the Gentiles.

Paul has received stewardship of God’s grace to Gentile people. This involves a new revelation :

(v3). It is not something he has discovered – but something God has revealed. It was not thought

out, developed, argued through – but revealed. God has taken the initiative in choosing Paul for

this great work.

Paul has received a ‘ grace- gift’ : (v7), this was a gift to preach. Paul teaches elsewhere that there

are many ‘grace - gifts’ (charismata) by which we all can be ministers for Christ Jes us. Indeed, we

have all been given ‘grace - gifts’ for the building up of the church (see again 1 Cor 12:11).

Paul has received a ministry : (v7), he considered this to be an awesome privilege, as all Christian

service is. It has the greatest dignity and should never be despised. For this work he has received

power ( dunamis) – the same power that came upon the disciples at Pentecost – a mighty baptism

with the Holy Spirit. He knew how impossible this work would be without that power. How sad it

A

is to see the weakness of the church when (good) men try to do God ’s work without the enabling

of His Spirit with power! If Jesus needed the fullness of the Spirit to come upon him at His baptism,

before He began His ministry, how much more so do we.

Paul will glory in his suffering for this great cause: (v13), he did not expect his service to be an

easy one. To suffer for Christ is not a penalty; it is our glory for it is to share in the sufferings of

Christ himself and an opportunity to demonstrate our loyalty to him.

The privilege of ministry : The angels in heaven did not understand this - (v10). The mystery has

been revealed and God’s wisdom is now being made known to all creation through the church .

So, Paul has a double privilege – a) he has received this revelation, b) he can proclaim this message,

i.e. he has received so that he might proclaim. Such an awesome privilege does not make him

proud – rather, it makes him humble (v8). He realizes that his greatness does not lie in himself but

in his message. True ministry (e.g. preaching) will never cause one to glory in the preacher but in

the Christ who is preached.

The plan and wisdom of God : Gentiles and Jews are fellow heirs of the riches of God. They are

fellow partakers of His promise in Christ (v6). This is not an afterthought of God – it was His

intention from the beginning – a mystery now revealed to Paul and to all the angelic beings (rulers

and authorities in heavenly places). What is the ‘promise’ of the Father? – see again Chapter 3.

We together with Paul, can have boldness and access to God through faith. But like all riches that

are ours in Christ, they must be appropriated – taken in. What ‘riches’ have you appropriated for

yourself?

We have all been given grace-gifts (charismata) to build up the c hurch but they are of the Spirit’s

choosing, not ours. One should be very careful not to step into a ministry that God has not called

you to, nor equipped you for.

A personal story: I was a highly-paid schoolteacher in 1979 when I was invited to become a

pastor by my denomination’s District Superintendent. I said that would be a great privilege but I

would want to know for certain that God was calling me. “What are you looking for – a flash of

light from Heaven?” he asked. “Yes!” I replied. “All I’d look for is the witness of the brethren,”

he said. I then added that I could not afford to go to seminary, as we had struggled financially for

many years before taking on my present teaching position, just two years earlier. To my surprise,

he then said that he would not want me to go to seminary but would welcome me as I was! He

saw something in me that I was not aware of! A few weeks later, my pastor was leaving the pulpit

to go into an itinerant singing ministry. As the only elder with some preaching experience, I spoke

at his farewell, following which two men came to me, both retired pastors who knew nothing of

my conversation with the District Superintendent, saying, “Brother, you shouldn’t be teaching!

You should be in the ministry!” – the “witness of the brethren”. The next several months, I wrestled

with God, afraid to tell my wife of the growing witness within me. Six months later, I told Anne.

To her surprise and contrary to all her feelings about life as a pastor’s wife, my godly wife released

me with t he words, “If God is calling you, and you’d better obey!” Read my book Stepping Stones

to see something of the amazing journey the Lord has led me on since that day.

I believe our seminaries have done a disservice to the church when they release men/women into

the pastoral ministry simply because they graduate top of their class. Going to seminary, passing

exams with good marks does not make one a pastor. Such are given to the church by the Lord

Himself. Ephesians 4:11 declares, “He gave some as apostles, some as prophets and some as

evangelists and some as pastors and teachers”. They are Christ’s gift to His precious bride, the

church. One should be very careful before assuming a position the Lord may not have called you

to.

V 14 : “For this reason…” – Paul continues his prayer of chapter 1: 15-20 and as he had intended

at 3:1. He wants them to receive what is theirs by ‘right’ through the atoning work of the cross –

and according to God’s riches in glory (v16).

✔ ‘power through His Spirit in the inner man’ .

✔ Christ dwelling in our hearts by faith.

✔ Being rooted and grounded in love.

✔ Comprehension of God’s vast love for us .

✔ Fullness of God.

Wow! Now read again Paul’s prayer in 1:15 -20 and on to 3:14-19. What is your response?

No wonder Paul is again forced to worship!

Note also that Paul ‘bows his knees’ whereas the normal posture for prayer to a Jew is standing –

this emphasizes Paul’s earnestness in prayer.

fields.title: Chapter 7
fields.body_html:
trust we have lea rned to “sit” in Christ as in chapter 3. (Eph 2:6) – knowing what it is that has

thrilled Paul, causing him to pray such a wonderful prayer for us. Now he exhorts us to walk.

We are to “walk in a manner worthy of our calling”. (4:1)

We are to “walk no longer as the Gentiles in the futility of our mind.” (4:17)

We are to “walk in love, just as Christ also loved you.” (5:2)

We are to “walk as children of light.” (5:8)

We are to “walk as wise men not as unwise.” (5:15)

“I’m not interested in your talk - show me your walk!” Your walk is determined by the ground on

which you stand; in this world (system) or in ‘heavenly places’?

Rise with thy risen Lord, ascend with Christ above, and in the heavenlies walk with Him, Whom

seeing not, you love.

Walk as a heavenly race, Princes of royal blood; walk as the children of the light, the sons and

heirs of God. A B Simpson

4:1: WALK in a manner worthy of your calling : with humility, gentleness, patience, tolerance –

in love. Elsewhere these may be seen among the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22, 23). They take

time to grow! A fruit tree does not produce its fruit by striving; as it takes in the sunshine and the

rain, feeds upon the nourishment of the ground, it brings forth its fruit. Similarly, we cannot

produce the fruit of the Spirit by our own efforts. We are to be “like a tree planted by rivers of

water that brings forth fruit in its season.” Ps 1:3).

When we arrived in Canada, we bought an old house where there were four fruit trees in the garden.

They had been left alone and bore no fruit so I decided to prune them. My friends thought I had

cut away too much and that the trees would now die. Imagine our delight the following spring

when they bore a vast quantity of luscious fruit, apples, plums and cherries!

I

One evening, Anne and I were sitting on our garden chairs when I heard a very strange sound – a

groaning fo llowed by an ‘ahhh’ of relief. I could not determine the source of the sound until I

noticed one of the branches on the apple tree swelling with a sound of pain before it suddenly

burst, and a beautiful apple appeared! Then another branch began to swell with the same result.

Anne and I were amazed as we watched cherries, plums, and apples suddenly appear after straining

and groaning.

Now I hope you realise that I am making this story up! Fruit doesn’t grow that way. The story is

very foolish – just like believers who think they can produce the Fruit of the Spirit by their effort!

No amount of striving will produce joy or peace or gentleness, etc., in your life – only abiding in

Him can produce such fruit.

In passing: as we consider those fruits , we see that they grow more ‘exotic’ (rare) as we read along.

Further, the first three (love, joy, peace) are ‘inward’; the second three (longsuffering, gentl eness,

goodness) relate mostly to my response to others, while the last three (faith, meekness, and

temperance) speak of my response to God. (Words as in KJV)

Humility is knowing myself as I am. Nothing more and nothing less! “I am a leader in the church

of Christ” may be said with pride, boastfully or with humility as Paul is doing here. False humility

(“Oh, I’m nothing but a worm!”) is a sickness akin to pride.

Gentleness is elsewhere translated as ‘meekness’ – teachability or pliability. It has been described

as ‘controlled strength’ – like the stallion with the bit in its mouth.

Long-suffering (patience) – endures to the end, patience with men.

Tolerance with love – bearing with one another. This ‘love’ is ‘agape’ – which seeks nothing but

the highest good.

4:17-24: Walk, no longer as the Gentiles walk. A contrast between the old nature and the new

n ature (‘Gentile’ and New Man). The old man walked in darkness, lacking understanding,

ignorant, and excluded from the life of God because of his hardness of heart, given to sensuality

and impurity with greediness. These are all in contrast to what is demanded by the truth you have

found in Christ.

Paul uses three very strong words to depict the heathen mind.

“hardness of heart” – porosis – petrified rock – calloused to lose all feeling.

“abandoned to sensuality” – aselgeia – does not care how he appears to others in his sensuality.

“impurity with greediness” – pleonexia – accursed love of possessing – lust for that which one has

no right to.

We are to “lay aside” the old self;

We are to be renewed in the spirit of our mind;

We are to “put on” the new self.

These are actions we are accountable for – it is a continual attitude. Consider here, Romans 12:1,

2.

5: 1-6: Walk in love just as Chris t also loved you… These verses show us the lifestyle of a lover.

It is the ‘engagement’ covenant between two. There is no room for impurity in thought or living.

We are betrothed to our bridegroom, Christ, and are not to play the harlot with the world, as Israel

did, though betrothed to God. Our best example is Jesus. His sacrificial life was as a fragrant aroma

rising to God – acceptable. His was a perfect obedience and a perfect love.

It has been said that chastity is the one new virtue that Christianity brought to the world. The

ancient world regarded sexual immorality so lightly that it was no sin at all.

Paul gives us two warnings:

i) We are not even allowed to talk about such things lightly.

ii) We must not be deceived by empty words – voices that speak lightly of such things as

the Gnostics did.

5:8-14: Walk as children of light. You were once children of darkness, but now the light has

come to guide you and to shine in this darkened world. We are not to keep company with darkness

but rather, to walk in the light (of our groom). We are to walk carefully, with discretion, knowing

that we belong to another and not to the world.

Verse 14 would appear to be part of an ancient hymn – possibly used in baptism?

5:15-21: Walk as wise men, not as unwise. Know what the will of God is; study the Word,

spend time alone with Him to allow His Spirit to teach you. Further, do not be drunk with wine

but be filled with the Spirit.

Verse 17-21 : show us what we should become as we walk these ways. We must be a “Spirit -

filled” people.

The follow three pieces of evidence of a Spirit-filled life:

i) a praising spirit (v19)

ii) a thankful spirit (v20)

iii) a submitted spirit (v21).

Don’t tell me you are filled with t he Spirit if you are not a worshipper, nor if you grumble about

the church or others in the fellowship. You are called to be a servant of all – submitted to serve.

There are many today who claim to be “Spirit - filled”. I believe we can question the reality of one

who claims to be ‘Spirit - filled’ if these three ‘evidences’ are missing – more evident are

grumbling, politicking, and pride. This is why Paul puts chapter 13 between chapters 12, 14 in 1

Corinthians. The latter teaches much about the charismata, gifts of the Spirit, and their operation

in the local church, but such manifestations are such as a ‘noisy gong or a clanging symbol –

nothing of value. Chapter 12 speaks of the excellence of love, which should be evident whenever

the charismata are exercised.

“I’m not interested in your talk – I’m more concerned about your walk.”

fields.title: Chapter 5
fields.body_html:
In v22, we too often put the emphasis on the word ‘submit’ (or ‘subject’) when that word is not

found in the original! It is a carry-over from the previous verse where it applies to all of us – men

and women. Both parties are called to submit in v 21, just as both are called to ‘love one another’

in the great command of Jesus the night He died. By the way, this word we translate ‘submit’ has

the meaning of honour rather than obey . (See also v 33). I must confess that my chest swells just

a little when other men tell me how their wives comment on how wonderful a husband I am -

according to my wife! She doesn’t join in their negative gossip about their own husbands.

I bel ieve the emphasis here should be on the phrase “to your own husband”. In Bible days, women

had little or no rights – they were treated at chattel – the possession of their husbands who could

do as they liked. It would be easy for women, hearing the gospel message for the first time, hearing

that they were precious to a loving God, to honour the young man preaching this good news in the

market square. Paul reminds them that their first ‘honour’ is to their own husbands – not the

preacher.

In v23, the man is the ‘head’ over the woman in the sense of her ‘covering’ or protection. It carries

with it great responsibility before it can exercise any authority. He is responsible for the spiritual

nurturing and testimony of his family. Many will stand before the Lord one day, hoping that He

will commend them for all the work they have done for the kingdom; instead He will ask why they

neglected the spiritual growth and nurture of their own family members, their #1 priority!

In the same way Jesus is our ‘covering’ and thereby, the ‘Saviour of the body’.

In v25, men are to love their own wives as Christ loved the church … a love without conditions.

H

History has proven over and over that the happiest marriages are those in which there is mutual

love and submission (honour). I believe that when a man loves his wife (as Christ loves His bride,

the church) and when women honour their husbands above all other men, their marriage will grow

in sweetness and Christlikeness – a “delicious circle” in contrast to the vicious c ircle so common

in worldly marriages today.

fields.title: Chapter 5
fields.body_html:
In chapter 1:9, we read of this mystery, revealed in v10, that at the end of time, all things will be

drawn together in Christ. i.e., He will be over ALL things. Government, nature, organisations, etc.,

will be under His control. At this moment, man is free to do ‘his own thing’ , but that will end when

ALL things are put under His feet.

In chapter 3:9, Paul rejoices that he has been called to reveal this mystery to the intent that “all in

heavenly places’ (the external world of the spirit) might know the purposes of God revealed

through His church.

As we consider the ‘end of time’ in the book of Revela tion, we see the exalted Jesus upon the

throne, accompanied by The BRIDE, formerly the church. It is God’s good purpose that she should

be exalted with Him as joint heir of all God’s riches! This is what He has willed to do and what

will be revealed to “all in heavenly places”. This is the mystery! (God’s secret now revealed).

This is why Paul writes here of a mystery in connection with his teaching on the bride and the

relationship of a marriage.

In chapter 6, Paul continues with his examples of lives “filled with the Spirit” - how children and

parents should interact, how employers and their employees should relate. A Christian home

should be an example to all other homes around. Parents have a responsibility to pour love into

their children. This does not only mean hugs, cuddles and kisses but also esteem, value, safety,

goals, Godly character.

A Christian employer should run his business with grace and encouragement – his employees

should be the happiest workers around. They, in turn, should do their work with diligence and be

known as trustworthy, willing to go beyond what their employer expects of them. Both are called

to show integrity in all their actions.

Let us go back to chapter 4:25-32, where Paul gives us four principles which should govern us

in all our relationships: (I have had many occasions to use these in marriage counselling).

i) Do not tell lies – even half-truths are lies. Consider the cover-ups we do almost daily.

“What’s wrong?” “O, nothing!” when we are hurting inside. Always keep open

communication between you and your wife/husband/children/ colleagues.

ii) Be current – do not let the sun set on your squabble. Deal with it today. It will produce

a ‘root of bitterness’ otherwise (Heb 12:15).

iii) Attack the problem, not the other person . Speak only that which edifies. Remember,

the battle is with the enemy, not fellow members of the Body.

iv) PROact, not REact! Look for ways to turn enmity into unity.

Consider: i) What are lies? – Speech, silence, actions, etc.

ii) What is the right kind of ‘anger’? Righteous anger that changes situations –

e.g., Wilberforce and slavery.

iii) How do we “give the devil an opportunity’? He will sow distrust and turmoil.

iv) Why does Paul write here about stealing? A demand for honesty/integrity in

action as well as in words.

v) What are some unwholesome words we might say?

Paul ends the chapter with a list of things which should go from life:

a) bitterness – long-standing resentment.

b) wrath and anger – short-term (temper) and long-term anger.

c) clamour and slander – loud talking (raised voices) and insulting language.

d) malice – bitterness of spirit to another.

Instead, we are to be kind, as defined by tender-hearted, forgiving. Such a life would be

impossible if it were not for the Holy Spirit, who makes us “more than conquerors” by His

fullness (Rom 8:37).

Greater is He that is in you than he that is in the world – 1 John 4:4.

fields.title: Chapter 9
fields.body_html:
hen we have learned to be seated in heavenly places (2:6) and to walk in love and in the

light (5:2, 8), we are called to be strong and to stand firm (6:10,11). The bride of Chapter

8 must become an overcomer if she is to wear the crown and reign with Jesus. As such, she is

called to be a soldier.

We saw in the first part of chapter 6 that Paul continues the theme of the Spirit-filled life as it

applies to the relationship between children and parents; workers and masters. One major thought

here is concerning ‘fathers’ who “provoke their children to anger.” It could well be mothers but is

most commonly fathers. It is interesting that many psychologists consider “anger” as the fruit of

inward wounds – wounds of the soul produced by fathers (and mothers) who do not fill their love-

tank child with love (hugs, kisses, identity, morals, self-esteem, security, goals, etc.). It is my sad

reflection that such wounds of the soul are the most effective weapons Satan uses in defeating

many believers.

An interesting study is to consider what it means to be an ‘overcomer’ and to see the rewards of

such overcoming. Let us take ‘time out” to consider 3 verses in 1 John that speak about

overcoming. 1 John 2:12-14 .

Here John places all believers in one of three categories which he calls, little children, fathers and

young men.

Little children are those whose sins have been forgiven for His name’s sake (v12) and they can

call God ‘Father’ (13). This is true of all who have been born again by the Spirit. They may know

nothing of theology or church history but they ca n say two things: “My sins are forgiven and I can

call Him ‘Father’.” Note that this has nothing to do with chronological age. I know many believers,

well on in age, who have sadly never progressed beyond this stage – they have remained childish!

W

Fathers are those who have come to know Him who is from the beginning. This is not just a head

knowledge but an intimacy as God has made Himself known to them. This is the goal of Paul’s

prayer in Eph 1:17.

This is Christian maturity – knowing Him. Note that this is not chronological age either, nor is it

gender based. Happily, I know many young men and women who have come to know God in a

deep personal way – they are spiritual ‘fathers’.

There is only one way we may progress from those early days of being ‘little children’ to a place

where God makes Himself known to us as we progress in maturity – it is by being “young men”.

Again, this is not a chronological age nor a gender term.

Young men are those who have overcome the evil one (v13); they are strong because the word of

God abides in them (v14). To every weapon of Satan they have an answer in the Word of God.

They counteract his lies with Biblical truth. e.g., the enemy might gloat over your failure and say,

“God doesn’t love you any more as you have disappointed Him!” This lie is counteracted by the

truth that “nothing can separate me from the love of God in Christ Jesus (Rom 8:39).

Whenever we are tried by o ur circumstances, by Satan’s lies, by temptations from the world, God

is watching to see how we react. He is on the sidelines cheering us on. As we overcome, He rejoices

and reveals more of His character to us.

Now let us look at the overcomers of Rev 2, 3 – where John sees the glorified Christ and is

instructed to write to the sever churches of Asia Minor. To end each letter, Jesus speaks of rewards

given to “those who overcome”.

Rev 2 : the overcomer shall eat of the tree of life (v7); shall not be hurt by the second death (v11);

shall feed on hidden ‘manna’ and shall be given a white stone and a new name (v17); shall be

given authority over nations and the morning star (v26-8).

Rev 3 : the overcomer shall be clothed in white and have his name confessed before the Father and

angels (v5); will be made a pillar in the eternal temple and shall receive the three-fold mark of God

(v12); shall sit down with Jesus on His throne – reign with Him (v21).

This is why the Lord allows believers to go through some hard tests with suffering and opposition,

and why He often seems to stay out of the difficulty even when we cry to Him in prayer. He wants

us to become overcomers in the difficulty rather than Him delivering us from it. He has given us

the Holy Spirit to be our helper in the battle and has given us armour to wear. Greater is He that is

in us than he that is in the world.

Further, we should become adept in the “word” to understand th e tactics of the enemy, Satan. Paul

was quick to forgive, so he wouldn’t give Satan an advantage ‘for we are not ignorant of his tactics’

(2 Cor 2:11). Earlier in Ephesians, he exhorted us not to ‘let the sun go down on our wrath lest we

give the devil a foothold’ (4:27).

Again, the devil will fire his ‘flaming arrows’ (6:16) – lies we so easily allow into our minds and

believe. Peter describes him as a ‘roaring lion’ seeking whom he may devour (1 Peter 5:8) – those

roars that affect our emotions and frighten us into cowardice in the battle. Remember that the roar

is all he can do, for he has lost his teeth and claws!! Jesus disarmed him at the cross – Colossians

2:15.

The battle truly is the Lord’s , but we are to be armed to overcome.

Now let us return to Ephesians chapter 6:

V 11: Put on the full armour of God.

V12 – 13: Note where our focus should be in this battle – it is not other people, believers or

otherwise. This is where our energies should be directed. We are, of course, to oppose the flesh

(our old self nature) but even that is a battle of the spirit rather than a battle of the material. We

must see the enemy beyond the personality.

‘Principalities’ are spiritual overseers of governments, nations, etc.

‘Powers’ are demonic ‘pirates’ who carry out the devil’s work in smaller areas.

‘Rulers of darkness’ influence those who influence others – politicians, educators, philosophers,

etc.

‘Spiritual wickedness’ refers to overseers of religion, etc.

These are approximate divisions of the various ranks of angels (fallen) and were a common

understanding in Paul’s day.

V14: Truth is the key garment to which all others are tied or joined. We desperately need truth or

integrity in all our actions. The breastplate of righteousness guards our hearts; our feet are shod

with the preparation of the gospel of peace – we are always on mission!

Note that there is no armour for the back! One cannot turn and run away!

V17, 18: The offensive weapons are a sword (the Word of God) and prayer in the Spirit. By these

we shall be overcomers, so we had better learn how to use them! I am amazed at how many

believers go into battle without being “prayed up”!

Finally, in 1 Thess 5:8, Paul adds to this armour, “Put on the breastplate of faith and love and for

a helmet, the hope of salvation.” Again , we see Paul’s three jewels – he puts them together at least

7 times in his letters, most notably in that great chapter on love – 1 Cor 13 13 – “Now, faith, hope,

love abide these three, but the greatest of these is love” .

We so seldom recognise the greatness of (Christian) hope, associating it with its weak English

meaning. “I hope it doesn’t rain today” , – but it might!

To Paul, hope was something far greater. Before King Agrippa, he would declare, “These Jews

accuse me of insurrection, but I stand before you today for the hope of the resurrection! (Acts 26:1-

8 paraphrased). He is not saying, “I hope there’s a resurrection and that I have not given up my

gr eat career to follow this way!” He is saying, “I know that I know that I know there is a

resurrecti on for me!” He has a certainty within him.

I define hope as “an attribute of the mind and is evidenced in confidence”. This is why the helmet

is called the hope of salvation .

Similarly, “faith is an attribute of the heart and is evidenced in obedience.”

I trust these short chapters have been a blessing to you as you seek to draw close to Him - learning

to be seated in Him and to walk in love and the light. May you be an overcomer to whom the Lord

is happy to reveal more of His character.

Let me close with Paul’s prayer: (1:15 -20; 3:16-19)

I pray that the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of Glory, may give to you a

spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of Him. I pray that the eyes of your heart may be

enlightened, so that you will know what is the hope of His calling, what are the riches of the glory

of His inheritance in the saints, and what is the surpassing greatness of His power toward us who

believe … that He would grant to you, according to the riches of His glory, t o be strengthened with

power through His Spirit in the inner man, so that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith,

and that you, being rooted and grounded in love, may be able to comprehend with all the saints

what is the breadth and length and height and depth, and to know the love of Christ which

surpasses knowledge, that you may be filled up to all the fullness of God.

To Him be glory in the church!!

THE END

fields.title: Chapter 1. God’S Side And Man’S Side
fields.body_html:
Faith involves two essential parts, which include God’s role in transforming us and

man’s role in trusting Him. While we must surrender and trust God, it is He who does

the actual work of sanctification, shaping and purifying us. This process is similar to

clay being molded by a potter, where the clay’s job is to yield, and the potter does the

shaping. Trusting God is not passive; it allows Him to work in us, leading to real

spiritual transformation, as we rely on His power to make us more like Christ.

n discussing the life and walk of faith, I want to address a common misunderstanding that often

hinders a clear understanding of the subject. This misunderstanding arises from the tendency to focus

on only one aspect of the topic without considering the other. As a result, people often see a well-

presented perspective on one side but overlook the balance that comes from viewing both sides

together. Unsurprisingly, this can lead to a distorted view of the whole matter.

There are two strong, distinct sides to this subject and, like all other subjects, it cannot be fully

understood unless both of these sides are kept constantly in view. I refer, of course, to God’s side and

man’s side; or, in other words, to God’s part in the work of sanctification, and man’s part. These are

very distinct and even contrasting. They are not contradictory. But, to a casual observer, they

sometimes appear so.

This was illustrated to me in a striking manner not long ago. Two teachers of this higher Christian life

held meetings in the same place, at alternate hours. One s poke only of God’s part in the work, and the

other dwelt only upon man’s part. They were in perfect sympathy with one another. They knew they

were each teaching different sides of the same great truth. A large part of their hearers also understood

this. But, it was different with some of the hearers. One lady said, in great perplexity, "I cannot

understand it at all." Two preachers are trying to teach the same truth. Yet, they seem to contradict each

other.”

I

I felt her puzzlement. It troubles many honest seekers of truth. Suppose two friends visit a famous

building, then return home to describe it. One has seen only the north side, and the other only the south.

The first says, “They built the building in such a manner, and it has such and such stories and

ornaments.” “Oh, no!” says the other, interrupting him. "You are quite mistaken. I saw the building.

They built it distinctly.

Its ornaments and stories were so and so." A lively dispute would likely arise over their descriptions.

Then, the two friends would find they had described different sides of the building. Everyone would

reconcile at once.

I want to be clear about the two sides in this matter. Focusing on one side, without seeing the other,

will create false views of the truth. In brief, I would say that man's part is to trust and God's part is to

work. These two roles are distinct, but they do not have to conflict with each other.

I mean this. Someone needs to do a certain work. God will deliver us from the power of sin and will

make us perfect in every good work to do His will. “And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the

glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another’s For

this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit.”2 Corinthians 3:18. We must transform ourselves by

renewing our minds. Then, we can prove God's good, acceptable, and perfect will. A real work is to be

wrought in us and upon us. We must conquer besetting sins. We must overcome evil habits. We must

root out wrong dispositions and feelings. We must develop holy tempers and emotions.

A positive transformation is to take place. So at least the Bible teaches. Now somebody must do this.

Either we must do it for ourselves, or another must do it for us. Most of us tried to do it ourselves at

first, and failed. Then, we learned from the Scriptures and our own experience that we cannot do it.

But, the Lord Jesus Christ came to do it. He will do it for all who trust Him completely.

Now under these circumstances, what is the part of the believer, and what is the part of the Lord? The

believer can only trust. The Lord, in whom he trusts, does the work entrusted to Him. Trusting and

doing are opposite, and often contradictory. But, are they contradictory in this case? Manifestly not,

because two different parties are concerned. It is a contradiction to say one party in a transaction trusted

his case to another, but attended to it himself. But, when we say one party trusts the other in a

transaction, and the other does it, we make a simple, harmonious statement.

We do not present a difficult problem. In this higher life, man's part is to trust, and God's is to do the

thing entrusted to Him. The preacher, speaking for man, can only talk of surrender and trust. That is all

a man can do. We all agree about this. Yet, such preachers are often criticized. Their words imply there

is no other part. So, we only trust. And the cry goes out that this doctrine of faith does away with all

realities. Souls are told to trust, and that's it. They then sit in a sort of religious easy-chair, dreaming

away a life that has no real results.

This misapprehension arises, of course, from a failure to communicate. Either the preacher neglected

to state, or the hearer failed to hear, the other side of the matter. It is, that when we trust, the Lord

works. He does a great deal, not us. Our trust brings results. Our Lord undertakes what we trust to Him

and accomplishes it. We do not act, but He does. This makes His work more effective.

The puzzle about the preaching of faith vanishes when this is clear. But critics target the preacher who

favors God's view for a different reason. He does not speak of trust, for the Lord’s part is not to trust,

but to work. The Lord does the thing entrusted to Him. He disciplines and trains the soul by inward

exercises and outward providences.

He brings to bear all the resources of His wisdom and love upon the refining and purifying of that soul.

He makes all of a person's life and circumstances serve one purpose: to grow him in grace and to make

him like Christ, hour by hour.

He carries him through a process of transformation, as his case requires. He makes actual and

experimental the results for which the soul has trusted. We have dared, for instance, according to the

c ommand in Romans. 6:11 “So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ

Jesus.” by faith to reckon ourselves dead unto sin. The Lord makes this real. He leads us to victory over

self by His daily, providential discipline. Our reckoning is available only because God makes it real.

Yet, the preacher who focuses on this practical side is accused of having no faith. He is said to promote

a gradual sanctification by works and to present an impossible task.

Now, sanctification is both a sudden step of faith and a gradual process of works. We consider it a step;

God sees it as a process. By a step of faith, we get into Christ; by a process, we are made to grow up

unto Him in all things.

By a step of faith, we trust the Divine Potter. By a gradual process, He makes us a vessel for His honor,

fit for His use, and ready for every good work. To illustrate: I will describe, to a beginner, how to turn

a lump of clay into a beautiful vessel. I first tell him the clay's role in the matter. All I can say is this:

the potter puts the clay into his hands. It then lies passive, submitting to all his turning and overturning

of it.

There is really nothing else to be said about the clay’s part. But could my hearer argue from this that

nothing else is done, because I say that this is all the clay can do? If he is an intelligent hearer, he will

not dream of doing so, but will say, “I understand. This is what the clay must do; but what must the

potter do?” “Ah,” I answer, “now we come to the importan t part. The potter takes the abandoned clay

and begins to work it. He molds it to his own will. He kneads and works it, he tears it apart and presses

it together again, and he wets it and then suffers it to dry.

Sometimes he works at it for hours. Sometimes, he lays it aside for days and does not touch it. Then,

when he has made it perfectly soft, he proceeds to make it into the vessel he has planned. He turns it

on the wheel, planes, and smooths it. Then, he dries it in the sun. Next, he bakes it in the oven. Finally,

he turns it out of his workshop, a vessel to his honor and fit for his use.” Will my hearer now say I am

contradicting myself?

I had said the clay could do nothing but lie passive in the potter's hands. Now, I am demanding it to

perform great work. To make itself into such a vessel is an impossible task. Surely not.

He will see that, while I spoke of the clay's part, I am now speaking of the potter's. These two are

contrastive, but not contradictory. The clay must not do the potter's work, but yield to it. The harmony

between these two teachings, which seem contradictory, is unmistakable. What can be said about man's

role in this great work? He must surrender and trust without hesitation.

But, on God's side of the question, what can be said about the many, wondrous ways He accomplishes

His work entrusted to Him? It is here that the growing comes in. The lump of clay would never grow

into a beautiful vessel if it stayed in the clay-pit for thousands of years. But once is put into the hands

of a skillful potter, and, under his fashioning, it grows rapidly into a vessel to his honor. So, the

Heavenly Potter changes the abandoned soul. The Spirit changes it from glory to glory into the Lord's

image.

You have taken a step of faith. You have put yourself completely in His hands. Now, you must expect

Him to begin to work. His way of accomplishing what you entrusted to Him may differ from yours.

But he knows, and you must satisfy yourself. I knew a lady. She had entered this life of faith with a

great outpouring of the Spirit and a wonderful flood of light and joy. She supposed, of course, this was

a prep for some great service. She expected to be sent into the Lord's harvest field. Instead of this, her

husband soon lost all his money. She shut herself in her house to do endless chores. This left her no

time or strength for any gospel work.

She accepted the discipline. She then devoted herself to sweeping, dust, baking, and sewing. She would

have done the same to preach, pray, or write for the Lord. Through this training, He made her a vessel

"meet for the Master's use, and prepared unto every good work." Another lady, who had come to faith

under similar circumstances, expected to be sent to do some great work. Instead, she was shut up with

two peevish invalid nieces to nurse, humor, and amuse them all day long.

Unlike the first lady, this one did not accept the training. She grew restless and angry. In the end, she

rebelled. She lost all her blessings and fell into a state of cold misery. She had understood her part in

trusting, at first. But, not knowing the divine way to do that, she took herself from the hands of the

Heavenly Potter. The wheel marred the vessel.

I believe many a vessel has been similarly damaged due to a lack of understanding these things.

Christian experience matures over time. It is the work of God’s Holy Spirit. His power transforms us

and helps us grow into Christ in all things. We can only reach this maturity by yielding ourselves to

His mighty work. But, the Scriptures urge all believers to seek a present sanctification. It does not

consist in the maturity of growth, but in the purity of heart. This may be as complete in the babe in

Christ as in the veteran believer.

The lump of clay, once it comes under the potter's hand, is, at every hour of the process, just what the

potter wants it to be. Therefore, it pleases him. But it is very far from maturing into the vessel he intends

to make in the future. The baby may be perfect. It may please its mother. But, it is not what she wishes

it to be when it matures.

The apple in June is a perfect apple for June. It is the best apple that June can produce. But, it is very

different from the apple in October. That is a perfected apple. God's works are perfect at every stage of

their growth. Man’s works are never perfect until they are in every respect complete. In this life of

sanctification, we claim only this: By a step of faith, we put ourselves in the Lord's hands. We trust

Him to work in us all His goodwill. By faith, we must keep ourselves there.

This is our part 8 in the matter. In doing so, we are, in the Scriptural sense, pleasing to God. It may

require years of training to mature us into a vessel, fit for His honor and every good work. Our part is

to trust; it is His to achieve the results. When we do our part, He never fails to do His, for no one ever

trusted in the Lord and felt confounded.

Do not fear that if you trust or tell others to, it will end there. Trust is only the beginning and the

foundation. When we trust, the Lord works. His work is an important part. And this explains that

apparent paradox which puzzles so many. They say, “In one breath you tell us to do nothing but trust,

and in the next you tell us to do impossible things. How can you reconcile such contradictory

statements?”

We must reconcile them. It's like reconciling statements about a saw in a carpenter's shop. We say, at

one moment, that the saw has cut a log. Then, we declare that the carpenter did it. The saw is the

instrument used, the power that uses it is the carpenter’s. So, we yield ourselves to God. We also give

our bodies to Him as instruments of righteousness. We find that He works in us to will and to do of His

good pleasure. We can say with Paul, “I labored; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.”

For we are to be His workmanship, not our own. For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus

for good works, which God prepared beforehand, that we should walk in them . (Eph. 2:10.) Only God,

who created us, can re-create us. He alone understands the "work of His own hands." All attempts at

self-creation mark the vessel. No soul can find its highest fulfillment except through His work. He

"works all things after the counsel of His own will."

I will, of course, focus on man's side in this matter. I am writing for men. I hope to teach believers how

to fulfill their part of the great work. But I want it clearly understood. Unless I believed in God's work,

I would not have written a word of this book.

fields.title: Chapter 2. The Scripturalness Of This Life
fields.body_html:
The true Christian life offers complete deliverance from sin, not just partial freedom.

Believers are urged to recognize that Christ’s sacrifice on the cross provides total

victory over sin’s power, calling them to trust in God’s promises for a life of holiness

and triumph. The chapter challenges Christians to experience the fullness of this

redemption, which is not only a future hope but a present reality.

hen I approach this subject of the true Christian life, that life which is hid with Christ in God,

so many thoughts struggle for utterance that I am almost speechless. Where will I begin? What

is the most important thing to say? How will I make people read and believe? The subject is so glorious,

and human words seem so powerless! But something I am impelled to say. Someone must tell the

secret.

For it is one of that victory which overcomes the world, that promised deliverance from all our enemies,

for which every child of God longs and prays, but which seems so often and so generally to elude their

grasp.

May God grant me to tell it so. I hope every believer who reads this book will see the truth in Jesus.

May they gain this glorious life for themselves. I am sure that every converted soul longs for victory

and rest. Most feel, at times, that they are their birthright. Can you not remember, some of you, the

shout of triumph your souls gave when you first became acquainted with the Lord Jesus, and had a

glimpse of His mighty saving power? How sure you were of victory then! How easy it seemed, to be

more than conquerors, through Him that loved you. Under the leadership of a Captain who had never

been foiled in battle, how could you dream of defeat?

W

And yet, to many of you, how different has been your real experience. The victories have happened,

but few and fleeting, the defeats many and disastrous. You have not lived as you feel children of God

ought to live. There has been a resting in a clear understanding of truth, without pressing. After the

power and life thereof. There has been a rejoicing in the knowledge of things testified of in the

Scriptures, without a living realization of the things themselves, experienced in the soul. People believe

in Christ, talk about Him, and serve Him, but they do not know him as the soul’s actual and very life,

abiding there forever, and revealing Himself there continually in His beauty.

You have found Jesus as your Saviour and your Master, and you have tried to serve Him and advance

the cause of His kingdom. You have studied the Holy Scriptures with great attention and have gathered

much precious truth here from, which you have endeavored faithfully to practice, but despite all your

knowledge and all your activities in the service of the Lord, your souls are starving in silence, and you

cry out repeatedly for that bread and water of life which you saw promised in the Scriptures to all

believers.

In the very depths of your hearts, you know that your experience is not a Scriptural experience; that, as

an old writer says, your religion is “but a talk to what the early Christians enjoyed, possessed, and lived

in.” And your souls have sunk within you, as day after day, and year after year, your early visions of

triumph have seemed to grow more and more dim, and you have forced yourself to settle down to the

conviction that the best you can expect from your religion is a life of alternate failure and victory; one

hour sinning, and the next repenting; and beginning again, only to fail again, and again to repent.

Is this all? Had the Lord Jesus only this in His mind when He laid down His precious life to deliver

you from your sore and cruel bondage to sin? Did he propose to himself only this partial deliverance?

Did he intend to leave you thus struggling along under a weary consciousness of defeat and

discouragement? Did He fear that a continuous victory would dishonor Him and bring reproach on His

name?

When He made those declarations about His coming and the work He was to do. Did they mean only

what you have experienced? Was there a hidden reserve in each promise that was meant to deprive it

of its complete fulfillment? Did each promise contain a reserve that aimed to deprive it of its complete

fulfillment? Did “delivering us out of the hands of our enemies” mean only a few of them? Did

“enabling us always to triumph” mean only sometimes , or did being “more than conquerors through

Him that love us” mean constant defeat and failure?

No, no, a thousand times no! God can save unto the uttermost, and He means to do it. His promise,

confirmed by His oath, was that “He would grant unto us, that we, being delivered out of the hand of

our enemies, might serve Him without fear, in holiness and righteousness before Him, all the days of

our life.” It is a mighty work to do, but our Deliverer can do it. He came to destroy the works of the

devil, and dare we dream for a moment that He is not able or not willing to do His own purposes?

In the very outset, then, settle down on this one thing, that the Lord can save you completely, now, in

this life, from the power and dominion of sin, and to deliver you altogether out of the hands of your

enemies. If you do not think He is, search your Bible, and collect together every announcement or

declaration about the purposes and object of His death on the cross. You will be astonished to see how

full they look.

Everywhere and always, His work is said to be to deliver us from our sins, from our bondage, from our

defilement; and not a hint is given anywhere that this deliverance was to be only the limited and partial

one with which the Church so continually tries to be satisfied.

Let me give you a few texts on this subject. When the angel of the Lord appeared unto Joseph in a

dream, and announced the coming birth of the Saviour, he said, “And you shall call His name Jesus,

for He will save His people from their sins. “When Zacharias was “filled with the Holy Ghost” at the

birth of his son, and “prophesied,” he declared that God had visited His people to fulfil the pr omise and

the oath He had made them, which promise was, “That He would grant unto us, that serve Him without

fear after He delivered us from the hands of our enemies, in holiness and righteousness before Him, all

the days of our life.”

When Peter was pr eaching in the porch of the Temple to the wondering Jews, he said, “Unto you first,

God, having raised up His Son Jesus, sent Him to bless you in turning away every one of you from his

iniquities. “When Paul was telling the Ephesian church the wondrous tru th that Christ had loved them

so much as to give Himself for them, he went on to declare, that His purpose in thus doing was, “that

He might sanctify and cleanse it by the washing of water by the word, that He might present it to

Himself a glorious church, not having spot or wrinkle, or any such thing; but that it should be holy and

without blemish.”

When Paul was seeking to instruct Titus, his own son after the common faith, about the grace of God,

he declared that the object of that grace was to teach us Godliness in this present world”; and adds, as

the reason of this, that Christ “gave Himself for us that He might redeem us from all iniquity, and purify

us unto Himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works.” When Peter was urging upon the Christian ,

to whom he was writing, a holy and Christ- like walk, he tells them that “even hereunto were you called

because Christ also suffered for us, leaving us an example that you should follow His steps: who did

no sin, neither was deceite found in His mouth”; and adds, “who His own self bare our sins in His own

body on the tree, that we, being dead to sins, should live unto righteousness; by whose stripes you were

healed.”

When Paul was contrasting in the Ephesians the walk suitable for a Christian, with the walk of an

unbeliever, he sets before them the truth in Jesus as being this, “that you put off, concerning the former

conversation.

The corrupt old man, according to, and renew your mind in the spirit by putting off the deceitful lusts.

The new man, c reated by God, embodies righteousness and true holiness. “And when, in Romans 6, he

was answering forever the question about continuing in sin, and showing how utterly foreign it was to

the whole spirit and aim of the salvation of Jesus.

He brings up the fact of our judicial death and resurrection with Christ as an unanswerable argument

for our practical deliverance from it, and says, “ By no means! How can we who died to sin still live in

it? Do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his

death? We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from

the dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.”(Romans 6:2 -3)

We were buried therefore with him by baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the

dead by the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life. For if we have been united with

him in a death like his, we shall certainly be united with him in a resurrection like his. We know that

our old self was crucified with him so that the body of sin might be brought to nothing, so that we would

no longer be enslaved to sin. (Romans 6:4-6)

Dear Christians, will you receive the testimony of Scripture on this matter? The same questions that

troubled the Church in Paul’s day are troubling it now: first, “Must we continue in sin that grace may

abound?” And second, “Do we then make void the law through faith?” Will not our answer to these be

Paul’s emphatic “God forbid”; and his triumphant assertions that instead of making it void “we

establish the law”; and that “what the law could not do, in that it was weak through the flesh, God

sending His own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh, and for sin, condemned sin in the flesh: that the we

who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit might fulfill the righteousness of the law.

Can we suppose for a moment that the holy God, who hates sin in the sinner, is willing to tolerate it in

the Christian, and that He has even arranged the plan of salvation in such a way that makes it impossible

for those who are saved to feel guilt of sin to find deliverance from its power.

Dr. Chalmers makes a precise statement, “We must root out that scandal called sin. “The great spiritual

household over which the Divinity rejoices, Strange administration, indeed, for sin to be so hateful to

God as to lay all who had incurred it under death, and yet when readmitted, life acknowledges that one

should permit sin even under death.

What was before the object of destroying vengeance should now become the object of an upheld and

protected toleration.

Now that they have taken off the penalty, do you think that the unchangeable God may have so given

up His antipathy to sin, as that man, ruined and redeemed man, may now perseveringly indulge under

the new arrangement in that which under the old destroyed him? Does not the God who loved

righteousness and hated iniquity six thousand years ago, bear the same love to righteousness and hatred

to iniquity still?

I now breathe the air of loving-kindness from Heaven, and can walk before God in peace and

graciousness; will I again attempt the incompatible alliance of two principles as adverse as that of an

approving God and a persevering sinner? How must we, recovered from so awful a catastrophe,

continue that which first involved us in it? The cross of Christ, by the same mighty and decisive stroke

wherewith it moved the curse of sin away from us, also surely moves away the power and the love of

it f rom over us.”

And not Dr. Chalmers only, but many other holy men of his generation and of our own, as well as of

generations long past, have united in declaring that the redemption accomplished for us by our Lord

Jesus Christ on the cross at Calvary is a redemption from the power of sin as well as from its guilt, and

that He can save to the uttermost all who come unto God by Him. A quaint old divine of the seventeenth

century says: “There is nothing so contrary to God as sin, and God will not suffer sin always to rule his

masterpiece, man.

When we consider the infiniteness of God’s power for destroying that which is contrary to Him, who

can believe that the devil must always stand and prevail? It is inconsistent and disagreeable with true

faith for people to be Christians, and yet to believe that Christ, the eternal Son of God, to whom all

power in heaven and earth is given, will suffer sin and the devil to have dominion over them. “But you

will say no man by all the power he has can redeem himself, and no man can live without sin. We will

say, Amen, to it. But if men tell us that when God’s Power helps us and redeems us from sin , if we

cannot effect this, then this doctrine we cannot do away with; nor I hope you neither.

“Would you approve of it if I tell you that God puts forth His power to do such a thing, but the devil

hinders Him? That God can't do it because the devil does not like it? That no one may be free from sin

because the devil has such a power in them that God cannot cast him out? This doctrine is lamentable,

yet who has not preached it? It does, in plain terms say that, though God doth interpose His power, it

is impossible, because the devil has so rooted sin like man. Isn't man God’s creature, and cannot He

make him new, and cast sin out of him? If you say that man roots sin, I agree, but not to the same

extent.

Christ Jesus has entered profoundly into the root of the nature of man that He has received power to

destroy the devil and his works, and to recover and redeem man into righteousness and holiness. Or

else it is false that ‘He can save to the uttermost all that come unto God by Him.’ We must throw away

the Bible if we say that God can't deliver man out of sin.

“We know,” he continues, “when our friends are in captivity, as in T urkey, or elsewhere, we pay our

money for their redemption; but we will not pay our money if they still keep them in their fetters.

Would not anyone think himself cheated to pay so? He will be said to have made the bargain for their

redemption with much money.

Will he redeem himself and be called a redeemed captive, but still wear his fetters? How long? As long

as he has a day to live. “This is for bodies, but now I am speaking of souls. I must make Christ to me .

.redemption, and rescue me from captivity. Am I a prisoner anywhere? Yes, he that committed sin, said

Christ, he is a servant of sin, he is a slave of sin. If you have sinned, you are a slave, a captive who

must be redeemed from captivity.

Who will pay the price for me? I am poor; I have nothing; I cannot redeem myself; who will pay a price

for me? There is one who has paid a price for me. That is well; that is good news, then I hope I will

come out of my captivity. What is His name? Is He called a Redeemer? So, then, I do expect the benefit

of my redemption, and that I will go out of my captivity. No, say they, you must abide in sin as long as

you live.

What! Must we never deliver ourselves? Must this crooked heart and perverse will always remain?

Must I be a believer, and yet have no faith that reaches to sanctification and holy living? Is there no

mastery to be had, no getting victory over sin? Must it prevail over me as long as I live? What sort of

a Redeemer, then, is this, or what benefit have I in this life, of my redemption?”

You could quote similar extracts from Marshall, Romaine, and many others show that this doctrine is

no new one in the Church, yet much it may have been lost sight of by the present generation of believers.

It is the same old story that has filled with songs of triumph the daily lives of many saints of God

throughout all ages; and is now, we sound forth afresh to the unspeakable joy of weary and burdened

souls. Do not reject it, then, dear reader, until you have conducted a thorough search through prayer.

Examine the Scriptures to see whether these things are indeed so. Ask God to open the eyes of your

understanding by His Spirit that you may know “ And what is the immeasurable greatness of his power

toward us who believe, according to the working of his great might. That he worked in Christ when he

raised him from the dead and seated him at his right hand in the heavenly places, ”(Ephesians 1:19 -20),

And when you have begun to have some faint glimpses of this power, learn to look away utterly from

your own weakness, and, putting your case into His hands, trust Him to deliver you.

In Psalms 8:6, the text tells us that God made man to “ have dominion over the works of your hands;

you have put all things under his feet, .” The fulfillment of this is in 2 Cor. 2:14, wh ere the apostle cries,

“ But thanks be to God, who in Christ always leads us in triumphal procession, and through us spreads

the fragrance of the knowledge of him everywhere .”

If the maker of a machine should declare that he had made it to perform a certain purpose, and if upon

trial it should be incapable of accomplishing that purpose, we would all say of that maker that he was

a fraud.

Then we will not dare to think that it is impossible for the creature whom God has made, to fulfill the

declared object for which he was made. Especially when the Scriptures are so full of the assertions that

Christ has made it possible. The only thing that can hinder is the creature’s own failure to work in

harmony with the plans of his Creator, and if this want of harmony is removable, then God can work.

Christ came to bring about an atonement between God and man, which should make it possible for

God to work in man to will and to do of His good pleasure.

Therefore we may be of good courage; for the work Christ has undertaken He is able and willing to

perform. Let us then “walk in the steps of that faith of our father Abraham,” who “staggered not at the

promise of God through unbelief; but was strong in faith, giving glory to God; being totally persuaded

that what He had promised, He was able also to perform.”

fields.title: Chapter 3. The Life Defined
fields.body_html:
The Higher Christian Life is portrayed as a life of complete surrender and trust in

God's care. It emphasizes the importance of letting go of personal burdens — whether

spiritual, emotional, or temporal — and allowing God to take control. By living with a

childlike faith, Christians are encouraged to abandon their worries and rely fully on
