truth shall be thy shield and buckler. Do not be afraid of the terror by night, or the arrow that flies by

day. Do not fear the pestilence that walks in darkness, or the destruction that wastes at noon.

“A thousand may fall at your side, ten thousand at your right hand, but it will not c ome near you. You

will only look with your eyes and see the recompense of the wicked. Because you have made the Lord

your dwelling place, the Most High, who is my refuge, no evil shall be allowed to befall you, no plague

come near your tent. For he will co mmand his angels concerning you to guard you in all your ways.”

Psalms 91:7-11 These Scriptures, and others like them, settle, once and for all, the question of second

causes in the lives of God's children. They are all under the control of our Father. Nothing can touch

us except with His knowledge and by His permission. Man's sin may cause the action. So, it can't be

called God's will. But by the time it reaches us, it is God's will. We must accept it as directly from His

hands.

No man or group, no power on earth or in heaven, can touch the soul that abides in Christ. They must

first pass through Him and get His permission. If God be for us, it matters not who may be against us;

nothing can disturb or harm us, except He shall see that it is best for us, and shall stand aside to let it

pass. An earthly parent’s care for his helpless child is a feeble illustration of this. If the child is in its

father’s arms, nothing can touch it without that father’s consent, unless he is too weak to prevent it.

And even if this should be the case, he suffers the harm first in his own person, before he allows it to

reach his child. If an earthly parent would thus care for his helpless child, how much more will our

Heavenly Father! His love is infinite. His strength and wisdom are unfailing.

Some, even of God's children, doubt His love and care. They secretly blame Him for neglect they would

not tolerate. But His care is far beyond human care. He counts the hairs on our heads and knows when

a sparrow falls. He watches every small thing that affects His children's lives. He controls them all

according to His will, no matter their origin.

The instances of this are numberless. Take Joseph. What could seem more a result of sin than his being

sold into slavery? It was u tterly against God's will. And yet Joseph, in speaking of it, said, “ As for you,

you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring it about that many people should be kept

alive, as they are today. ”

Genesis 50:20.Now, do not be grieved or angry with yourselves for selling me. “ God sent me here to

preserve life." To the eye of sense, it was surely Joseph's wicked brethren who had sent him into Egypt.

Yet, with faith, Joseph could say, "God sent me." His brothers had sinned. But by the time it reached

Joseph, it was God's will. It was, though it didn't seem so at first, the greatest blessing of his life. So

we see how the Lord can turn even man's anger to praise Him. And, how all things, even others' sins,

shall work for good to those who love Him.

I learned this lesson, practically and experimentally, long before I knew the scripture. I was at a prayer

meeting for scriptural holiness. A strange lady rose to speak. I wondered who she was, not knowing

she would teach me a grand lesson. She said she had great difficulty in living a life of faith. The second

cause that seemed to control everything about her caused it. Her confusion grew. She began to ask God

to teach her the truth. Was he really in everything, or not?

After praying this for a few days, she had what she described as a vision. She thought she was in a dark

place. Then, a body of light advanced towards her from a distance. It gradually surrounded and

enveloped her and everything around her. As it approached, a voice seemed to say, “This is the presence

of God; this is the presence of God.” This presence showed her all the great and awful things in life.

She saw fighting armies, wicked men, raging beasts, storms, and plagues. She saw every kind of sin

and suffering. At first, she shrank back in terror. But, she soon saw that God's presence surrounded and

enveloped each one of these. Not a lion could reach out its paw, nor a bullet fly through the air, except

as His presence moved to permit it.

She knew that, if there were the thinnest of sheets of this glorious presence between her and the terrible

violence, nothing could touch her. Not a hair on her head could be ruffled.

But, the presence must divide to let the evil through. Then, all the small annoyances of life flashed

before her. She saw they were so wrapped in God's presence that nothing could touch her. Not a cross

look, harsh word, or petty trial could reach her unless He let them through.

Her difficulty vanished. Her question was answered forever. God was in everything, and to her

henceforth there were no second causes. She saw that her life came to her, day by day, and hour by

hour, from His hand. It did not matter what seemed to control it. And, she never again found it hard to

trust in His care. But if we focus on the seen things, we won't understand this secret. The children of

God must "not look at the things which are seen: for the things which are seen are temporal, but the

things which are not seen are eternal." If we could see His unseen forces around us, we'd feel safe. We

would walk through this world in an unbreakable fortress. For "the angel of the Lord encamped round

about them that fear Him, and delivered them."

We have a striking illustration of this in the history of Elisha. The king of Syria was at war with Israel.

His evil plans were foiled by a prophet. So, he sent his army to the prophet's city to capture him. We

read, “He sent their horses and chariots and a great host; and they came by night and compassed the

city about.” This was the seen thing. A nd the servant of the prophet, whose eyes had not yet been

opened to see the unseen things, was alarmed. We read, "And when the man, God's servant, rose early

and went forth, a host encompassed the city, with horses and chariots." His servant said, "Alas, my

master, how shall we do?” But his master could see the unseen things, and he replied, “Fear not; for

they that be with us are more than they that be with them.” And then he prayed, saying, “Lord, I pray

thee, open his eyes that he may see.

The Lord opened the young man's eyes, and he saw. The mountain was full of horses and chariots of

fire around Elisha. The presence of God is the fortress of His people. Nothing can withstand it. At His

presence, the wicked perish. The earth trembles. The hills melt like wax. The cities crumble. "The

heavens also dropped, and Sinai itself was moved at the presence of God." In this secret, He has

promised to hide His people from man's pride and from the strife of tongues. "My presence shall go

with thee," He says, "and I will give you rest." I wish every Christian could see this truth as plainly as

I do. It is the only clue to a completely restful life. Nothing else will let a soul live only in the present,

as we are commanded to do. We must not think of tomorrow.

Nothing else will remove all the risks from a Christian's heart. It won't let him say, "Surely goodness

and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life." Abiding in God’s presence, we run no risks. A soul

like that can say: "I know not what it is to doubt. My heart is always gay. "I run no risks, for, come

what will, God always has His way." I once heard of a colored woman. She earned a precarious living

by daily labor. But, she was a joyous, triumphant Christian.

“Ah!”Nancy," said a gloomy Christian lady one day. She almost disapproved of her constant

cheerfulness, yet envied it.

"Ah!" Nancy, it is all well enough to be happy now, but I should think the thoughts of your future

would sober you. Only suppose, for instance, that you fell sick and couldn't work. Or, suppose your

employers moved away, and no one else hired you. Or suppose -- "Stop!” cried Nancy, “I never

supposes.

The Lord is my shepherd, and I know I shall not want. And, honey,” she added to her gloomy friend,

“I know it’s all those things they’re suggesting that are making you so miserable . You should give them

all up and just trust in the Lord. ”

One text can end a believer's "suppose." If only it is received and acted on with childlike faith. It is in

Heb. 3:5- 6 “ Now Moses was f aithful in all God’s house as a servant, to testify to the things that were

to be spoken later, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son. And we are his house, if indeed we

hold fast our confidence and our boasting in our hope . ”

Be content with what you have. For He said, “Keep your life free from love of money, and be content

with what you have, for he has said, ' I will never leave you nor forsake you.” So we can confidently

say, the Lord is my Helper, I will not fear. What can man do to me?” Hebrews 13:5-6 What if dangers

threaten you from every side? What if men's malice, foolishness, or ignorance combine to harm you?

You may face every contingency with these words: "The Lord is my helper, and I will not fear what

man shall do unto me.”

If the Lord is your helper, how can you fear what man may do unto you? No man, nor any company of

men, can touch you. Unless, of course, your God, in whom you trust, allows it. “He will not let your

foot be moved; he who keeps you will not slumber. Behold, he who keeps Israel will neither slumber

nor sleep. The Lord is your keeper; the Lord is your shade on your right hand. The sun shall not strike

you by day, nor the moon by night. The Lord will keep you from all evil; he will keep your life. The

Lord will keep you going out and your coming in from this time forth and forevermore.” (Psalm 121:3 -

8) Only seeing God in everything will make us loving and patient with those who annoy us.

They will be only instruments for His wise, tender purposes. We'll end up thanking them for the

blessings they bring. Nothing else will completely put an end to all murmuring or rebellious thoughts.

Christians often feel a liberty to murmur against man when they would not dare to murmur against

God. But this way of receiving things would make it impossible ever to murmur. If our Father allows

a trial, it must be the best thing for us. We must accept it with thanks from His dear hand.

The trial itself may be hard to flesh out and blood, and I do not mean that we can like or enjoy the

suffering of it. But we can and must love the will of God in the trial, for His will is always sweet,

whether it be in joy or in sorrow. Our trials may be our chariots. We long for some victory over sin and

self, and we ask God to grant it to us.

His answer comes in the form of a trial, which He means shall be the chariot to bear us to the longed

for triumph. We may either let it roll over us and crush us like an unstoppable force. Or we may mount

into it and ride triumphantly onward. Joseph's chariots, which raised him to glory, were his trials. They

were being sold into slavery and unjustly imprisoned.

Our chariots may be less than these. They may be just annoying people or tough situations. But

whatever they are, God means them to be our forces of triumph.

They shall bear us to the victories we have prayed for. If we are impatient and long to be patient, our

chariot will probably be a trying person. Their ways or words will test our very souls. If we accept the

trial as from God and submit, it will be the best discipline. It will give us the patience we seek.

God does not order the wrong thing. But, He uses it for our blessing. He did this with the cruelty of

Joseph's wicked brethren. And, with Pharaoh's wife's false accusations. It makes life a long

thanksgiving. It gives us a deep peace and a joy beyond words. Someone says, “God’s will on earth is

always joy, always tranquility.” He must have His own way with His children. The soul that learns this

secret finds green pastures and still waters. They offer rest and refreshment.

If the will of God is our will, and if He always has His way, then we always have our way also, and we

reign in a perpetual kingdom. He who sides with God will win every time. Whatever the outcome, we

can join the ap ostle's victory shout: “ But their minds were hardened. For to this day, when they read

the old covenant, that same veil remains uplifted , because only through Christ is it taken away.”

(2Corinthians 2:14)

fields.title: Chapter 9. Growth
fields.body_html:
Believers' spiritual journey begins with surrender and trust, but true growth in grace

continues beyond that. Scripture calls for ongoing development, as seen in 2 Peter

3:18, which encourages growth in grace and knowledge. Growth happens when

believers are rooted in God's grace, allowing the Divine Husbandman to nurture them.

By abiding in God's presence and trusting His guidance, without relying on self-effort,

believers will mature spiritually, becoming fruitful and strong, just like a tree planted

by waters.

fter a believer fully surrenders and trusts, they find a life of happy communion and peace. This

raises the question, "Is this the end? “I answer emphatically “No, it is only the beginning.” But,

this is so little understood that many oppose the faith advocates. They claim the advocates do not

believe in growth in grace. They are to teach that the soul can reach a perfect state. There is no

further advance beyond it. This teaching voids all the Scriptural calls for growth and development.

Since the opposite is true, I must, next, consider this subject. I want to, if possible, fully answer such

objections. I also want to show the scriptural place and way for the soul to grow. The most quoted text

is 2 Pet 3:18. It says, " But grow in the grace and knowledge of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ. To

him be the glory both now and to the day of eternity. Amen. " This text expresses our belief in God's

will for us. It also reflects our belief that He has made it possible for us to experience it. We accept, in

their fullest meaning, all commands and promises. They concern our growth into Christ in all things,

until we are perfect, and measure up to His fullness.

We are glad that we don't always have to be like babies, needing milk. We may, by use and growth,

become skilled in the word of righteousness. We should then be able to discern good from evil and

need strong meat. And none would grieve more than we at the thought of an end to the Christian life.

There could be no advance beyond it. But, we believe in a growth that produces maturity. We believe

A

in a development that, in fact, bears ripe fruit. We expect to reach the aim set before us, and if we do

not, we feel sure there must be some fault in our growing. No parent would be satisfied if, year after

year, their child remained a helpless babe. And no farmer would be pleased if his grain grew only to

the blade, but never produced the ear or the full corn in the ear.

Growth, to be real, must be progressive. The days, weeks, and months must bring a maturity in the

thing growing. But is this the case with a large part of that which is called growth in grace?

Doesn't the very Christian who longs for it, too often find that, at year's end, he is not as far in his

Christian experience as at the beginning? His zeal, devotion, and separation from the world are not as

complete as when his Christian life began.

I was urging a group of Christians to take an immediate, definite step into the Promised Land. A very

intelligent lady interrupted me. She thought her words would completely rebut my argument. She

exclaimed, "Ah! But, my dear friend, I believe in growing in grace.” “How long have you been

growing?” I asked. “About twenty - five years,” was her answer. “And how much more unworldly and

devoted to the Lord are you now than w hen you began your Christian life?” I continued, “Sadly!” was

the answer. "I fear I am not nearly so much so." Her eyes opened to see that, at least, her growth had

failed. It had done the opposite.

The trouble with her, and every other such case, is simply this, they are trying to grow into grace,

instead of in it. They are like a rosebush. The gardener should plant it in the hard, stony path to grow

into the flower-bed. But, it would reduce and wither instead of flourishing. The children of Israel

wandering in the wilderness are a perfect picture of this sort of growing. They had traveled for forty

years. They took many weary steps. They found little rest from their wanderings. Yet, at the end, they

were no nearer the Promised Land than at the start. At Kadesh Barnea, they were at the land's borders.

A few steps would have taken them into it.

Upon ending their wanderings in the plains of Moab, they were at its borders. But now there was a

river to cross, which there hadn't been at first. Their wanderings and fights in the wilderness had not

won them an inch of the Promised Land. To possess this land, one must first be in it. To grow in grace,

one must first be planted in it. But, once in the land, their conquest was very rapid. Once planted in

grace, the soul will grow in one month more than in years in any other soil. For grace is a most fruitful

soil, and the plants that grow therein are plants of a marvelous growth.

A Divine Gardener takes care of them. The Sun of Righteousness warms them. The dew from Heaven

waters them. Surely, it is no wonder they bear fruit. "Some a hundred-fold, some sixty-fold, some

thirty-fold." But, what does "growing in grace" mean? Few people understand what the grace of God

is. So, it is hard to answer this question. To say that it is free, unmerited favor, only expresses a little

of its meaning. It is God's wondrous, boundless love, poured out upon us without measure. It is not

based on our worthiness, but on His infinite, unfathomable love. Its heights and depths surpass all

knowledge. I sometimes think we change the meaning of "love" with God. We understand it well in its

human use.

But, if ever human love was tender, self-sacrificing, and devoted; if it could bear and forbear; if it could

gladly suffer for its loved ones; if it would pour itself out for their comfort and pleasure, then Divine

love is far more so. It is infinitely more tender, self-sacrificing, and devoted. It is glad to bear and

forbear, to suffer, and to lavish its best gifts on those it loves.

Take all the tenderness and love you know of, dear reader. Add the deepest love you have ever felt.

Then add the strongest love ever given to you. Next, pile on the love of all the world's loving hearts.

Now multiply it by infinity. You might then faintly glimpse the love of God in Christ Jesus. And this

is grace. To be planted in grace is to live in love. It means to envelop yourself in it, steep yourself in it,

and revel in it. It means to know nothing but love, and to grow in knowledge and faith in it. It means

to trust it completely and have no doubt that it will order all things well.

To grow in grace is opposed to all self-dependence, to all self-effort, to all legality of every kind. It is

to put our growing, as well as everything else, into the hands of the Lord and leave it with Him. We

should trust our Husbandman. His skill and wisdom are perfect. So, we won't question His methods or

His cultivation plan. It is to grow as the lilies or babes grow. To grow, without a care or anxiety. To

grow by a life force that must grow. To grow because we live and must grow. To grow because He

who planted us made us to grow.

Surely, this is what our Lord meant. He said, “And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the

lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory

was not arrayed like one of these. But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and

tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith?" Or, when

He says again, “And which of you by being anxious can add a single hour to his span of life?" There

is no effort in the growing of a child or of a lily. They do not toil or spin. They do not stretch or strain.

They make no effort to grow. They are not even aware that they are growing. But, by an inner life

force, they grow. God's providence, a gardener, the sun, and the rain nurture them.

And the result is sure. Even Solomon, our Lord, says, in all his glory, was not arrayed like one of these.

Solomon's array cost much toil and gold, but the lily's cost none of these. We may toil to make ourselves

beautiful spiritual garments. We may strain for spiritual growth. But we will achieve nothing. No man

can add a cubit to his stature by thinking. Our efforts can't match the beautiful dress the great

Husbandman gives His garden's plants. They grow under His care.

If I could make my readers see how helpless we are in growing, I believe it would relieve many lives.

Imagine a child obsessed with growing. He would not grow unless he tried to. He insisted on a

combination of rope and pulleys to stretch himself to the desired height. He might, it's true, waste his

days in a weary strain. But, there would be no change in the fact, "No man can add to his stature by

thinking." His years of labor would be wasted if they did not hinder the longed-for end.

Imagine a lily trying to clothe itself in beauty. It stretched its leaves and stems to grow. It tried to

manage the clouds and sunshine, to meet its needs. Yet, these two pictures show a truth. Many

Christians want to grow. They know they should. They feel a deep instinct to grow. But, they try to do

it by toiling and spinning. They wear themselves out with endless self-effort.

It is wear ying to watch. Grow, dear friends. But, please, grow in God’s way, the only true way. Be sure

to be rooted in grace. Then, let the Divine gardener cultivate you in His own way.

Expose yourselves to His presence in the sunshine. Let the dew of heaven fall on you. Then, see what

will happen. Leaves, flowers, and fruit must come in their season. Your Husbandman is a skilled one.

He never fails in His harvesting. Just don't hinder the shining of the Sun of Righteousness or the falling

of the dew from Heaven. A very thin covering may block the heat or moisture. The plant may wither

even in their midst. A slight barrier between your soul and Christ may cause you to fade like a plant in

a cellar or under a bushel. Keep the sky clear. Open every part of you to receive the blessings our

Divine Husbandman may bring.

Bask in the sunshine of His love. Drink in the waters of His goodness. Keep your face upturned to Him.

Look, and your soul shall live. You need to make no efforts to grow, but let your efforts instead be all

concentrated on this, that you abide in the Vine. The gardener who tends the vine will care for its

branches too. He will prune, purge, water, and tend them. They will grow and bear fruit that will last.

Like the lily, their glory will surpass even Solomon's.

What if you seem to yourselves to be planted at this moment in a desert soil where nothing can grow!

Trust fully in the great gardener. He will make that desert blossom and create springs in its sands. The

promise is sure. The man who trusts in the Lord, “He is like a tree planted by water, that sends out its

roots by the stream, and does not fear when heat comes, for its leaves remain green, and is not anxious

in the year of drought, for it does not cease to bear fruit.”(Jeremiah 17:8)It i s the great prerogative of

our Divine gardener. He can turn any soil into the soil of grace, the moment we put our growing into

His hands. He does not need to move us to a different field. Right where we are, with just the

circumstances around us, He makes His sun to shine and His dew to fall on us. He turns our greatest

obstacles into the best means of our growth. I care not what the circumstances may be, His wonder-

working power can accomplish this. And we must trust Him with it all.

Surely He is a man we can trust.

If He sends storms, winds, rains, or sunshine, we must accept it. We must trust, with unwavering faith,

that He will cultivate us and bring us to maturity. He knows the best way to do this. He controls the

elements to ensure our rapid growth. Let me entreat of you, then, to give up all your efforts after

growing, and simply to let yourselves grow. Leave it all to the Gardener, whose responsibility it is, and

who alone can manage it. No difficulties in your case can baffle Him.

Nothing in your past can mar His perfect work. Not the limiting of your growth, the dryness of your

life, or any deformity. If you will, put yourselves completely in His hands and let Him have His way

with you. His own gracious promise to His backsliding children a ssures you of this. “ I will heal their

apostasy ,” He says: “I will love them freely, for my anger has turned from them.

I will be like the dew to Israel; he shall blossom like the lily; he shall take root like the trees of Lebanon.

His shoots shall sp read out; his beauty shall be like the olive, and his fragrance like Lebanon.”(Hosea

14:4- 6) “They shall return and dwell beneath my shadow; they shall flourish like the grain; they shall

blossom like the vine; their fame shall be like the wine of Lebanon." (Hosea 14:7)

And again He says, " Fear not, you beasts of the field, for the pastures of the wilderness are green; the

tree bears its fruit; the fig tree and vine give their full yield."(Joel 2:22-26) And the floors shall be full

of wheat, and the fats shall overflow with wine and oil. I will restore to you the years that the swarming

locust has eaten, the hopper, the destroyer, and the cutter, my great army, which I sent among you. You

shall eat in plenty and be satisfied, and praise the name of the Lord your God, who has dealt wondrously

with you. And my people shall never again be put to shame.” (Joel 2:25 -26)

Oh! You could. But, you know what your Lord meant when He said, “And why are you anxious about

clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither toil nor spin"(Mathew 6:28 ).

These words show a life and a growth far different from the ordinary life and growth of Christians.

They show a life of rest and growth without effort. Yet, this life and growth have glorious results. To

every soul that becomes a lily in the Lord's garden, and grows as the lilies do, the same glorious array

will be given. They will know a mystical passage about their Beloved: "He feeds among the lilies."

We who fully trust believe in a growth in grace. It is a growth that brings desired results. It blossoms

into a flower and fruit, becoming a tree planted by rivers of water. It bears fruit in season. Its leaves do

not wither. It prospers in all it does. We rejoice to know that, in the Lord's heritage, many such plants

are growing up now. As the lilies grow by seeing the sun, they are changed into the same image by

beholding the Lord's glory, from glory to glory, by the Lord's spirit.

If you ask them how they grow so fast and well, they would say they don't worry about it. They hardly

notice their growth. Their Lord told them to abide in Him. He promised that if they did, they would

bear much fruit. They focus only on abiding, which is their part. They leave the rest to their good

Husbandman, who alone can manage it. You will find that such souls are not engaged in watching self,

but in looking unto Jesus.

They do not toil nor spin for their spiritual clothes. They leave it to the Lord to dress them as He pleases.

Self-effort and self-dependence are at an end with them. Their interest in self is gone, transferred over

into the hands of another. Self has become really nothing, and Christ alone is all in all to such as these.

And the blessed result is, that not

Even Solomon, in all his glory, was arrayed like these will be. Let us examine this subject practically.

We all know that growing is not a thing of effort, but is the result of an inward life, a principle of

growth. All the stretching and pulling in the world could not make a dead oak grow. But a live oak

grows without stretching. It is plain, then, that the key is to get within you the growing life. Then you

cannot help but grow. And this life is the life hid with Christ in God, the wonderful divine life of an

indwelling Holy Ghost. Be filled with this, dear believer. You must grow, whether you know it or not.

Do not worry about your growth. Just ensure you have the growing life.

Abide in the Vine. Let the life from Him flow through all your spiritual veins. Interpose no barrier to

His mighty life-giving power, working in you all the good pleasure of His will. Surrender completely

to His gentle guidance. Put your growing into His hands, as completely as you have put all your other

affairs. Suffer Him to manage it as He will. Do not concern yourself about it, nor even think of it.

Trust Him without reservation, and at all times.

Accept each moment's gift, from His dear hands. It is the needed sunshine or dew for your growth. Say

a continual "Yes" to your Father's will. Until now, you may have tried, as many do, to be both the lily

and the gardener, both the vineyard and the gardener. You have taken on the burdens and duties that

belong only to the Divine gardener. Only He can bear them. Henceforth consent to take your rightful

place and to be only what you really are. Say to yourself, "If I am only the garden, not the gardener; if

I am only the vine, not the gardener, then I must keep the garden and act its part."" I must not usurp the

gardener's place or try to act his part."

Do not choose your own soil or set your borders. Do not plant your own seeds, prune, or tend your

vines. Be content with what the Divine Husbandman arranges for you, and with the care He gives. Let

Him choose which plants and fruits to cultivate. If He wills it, let Him grow a potato as gladly as a

rose. And, let Him value everyday virtues as much as exalted passions. Be content with the seasons He

sends, and the sun and rain. Accept your growth, whether fast or slow. In short, be satisfied with all

His ways, even if we don't understand them.

There is infinite repose in this. As the violet rests in its nook, it contentedly accepts its daily portion. It

lets the rains fall, the suns rise, and the earth whirl, without one anxious pang. So, we must repose in

the present as God gives it to us. We should accept, without worry, our daily portion in His grand plan.

It is creative and redemptive.

The wind that blows can never kill the tree God plants. It blows east, it blows west. The tender leaves

have little rest. But any wind that blows is best. The tree God plants Strikes deeper root, grows higher

still, spreads wider boughs. For God's goodwill meets all its wants. No frost can blight the tree God

shields. The roots are warm beneath the soft snows. When spring comes, it knows, and every bud will

blossom. The tree God shields Grows on apace by day and night, Till, sweet to taste and fair to sight,

its fruit it yields.

No storm can blast the tree, God knows. No thunder, rain, lightning, or hurricane can. When they

spend, it remains. The tree God knows. Through every tempest, it stands fast. From its first day to its

last, it grows ever fairer.

If in the soul's still garden, a seed God sows a little seed, it will soon grow. And, all men will know it.

For heavenly land, He bids it blow. A seed God sows, and up it springs by day and night; through

life, through death, it grows right, forever grows.

fields.title: Chapter 10. Service
fields.body_html:
Christian service often starts as a burden, but through trust ing God’s will, it becomes a

joy. As believers surrender their will to God, they find freedom and strength in serving

Him. True service comes from yielding to God’s guidance, trusting Him for the results,

and letting go of self-reflection. This life of faith brings rest, freedom, and

power, as believers rely on God’s strength rather than their own.

erhaps, no part of Christian experience knows a greater change than in service. This is upon

entering into the life hid with Christ in God. In lower forms of Christian life, service can feel

binding. It is often a duty, and a trial and a cross. At first, some things may bring joy. But, they

become weary tasks. They are done faithfully, but with secret disinclination. There are many

wishes, both confessed and unconfessed, that they need not be done, or at least, not so often. The soul

finds itself saying, instead of the “May I” of love, the “Must I” of duty. The yoke, which was at first

easy, begins to gall, and the burden feels heavy instead of light.

One dear Christian expressed it once to me in this way. "After my conversion," she said, "I was full of

joy and love. I was so glad and thankful to do anything for my Lord. So, I eagerly entered every open

door." But, as my early joy faded and my love cooled, I began to regret my eagerness. I found myself

in services that were becoming very distasteful and burdensome. I could not give them up, since I had

begun them. It would excite great remark. Yet, I increasingly longed to do so. I was expected to visit

the sick, and pray beside their beds.

I was expected to attend prayer-meetings, and speak at them. I was expected to be always ready for

every effort in Christian work. The weight of these expectations bowed me down continually. At last,

it became unbearable to live the Christian life I had begun, and that everyone expected of me. I would

have infinitely preferred to scrub all day on my hands and knees rather than endure my daily Christian

work. I envied,” she said, “the servants in the kitchen, and the w omen at the wash- tubs.”

P

This may seem a strong statement. But, does it not evoke some of your own experiences, dear Christian?

Have you never gone to your work as a slave to his daily task, knowing it was your duty? You must do

it. But, like a rubber ball, you bounced back to your real interests and pleasures the moment your work

was done.

You know this was the wrong way to feel. You are ashamed of it, but you can't help it. You have not

loved your work. If you could have, you would have gladly given it up. Or, if this does not describe

your case, perhaps another picture will. You love your work in the abstract. But, in doing it, you find

many cares and responsibilities. You have doubts about your ability. This makes it a heavy burden.

You go to it, weary and bowed down, before the work has even begun.

You also distress yourself about your work. You are troubled if the results are not what you want. This,

too, is a constant burden. Now, the soul is entirely delivered from all these forms of bondage. It enters

fully into the blessed life of faith. First, it delights in any service. It has surrendered its will to the Lord.

He works in it to desire and do His pleasure. The soul now wants to do what God wants. It is always

nice to do what we want, no matter how hard or tiring it is. If a man is truly set on a thing, he will. He'll

ignore the obstacles in his way. He'll laugh at the idea of any opposition or difficulties hindering him.

How many men have, gladly and thankfully, searched the earth for wealth or to fulfill their ambitions?

They scorned any thoughts of the cross connected with it! How many mothers have congratulated

themselves on their sons' promotions to powerful government jobs? They have rejoiced. But, it may

have meant years of separation and hardship for their dear ones. Yet, these men and their mothers

would have called it an unbearable cross if Christ's service had required the same sacrifice of home,

friends, and ease.

It is altogether the way we look at things, whether we think they are crosses or not. I am ashamed to

think that any Christian would mourn for doing a thing for Christ, which a worldly man would do for

money.

What we need in the Christian life is to get believers to want to do God’s will, as much as other people

want to do their own will. And this is the idea of the Gospel. It is what God intended for us; and it is

what He has promised. In describing the new covenant in Heb. 8:6- 13 “ But as it is, Christ has obtained

a ministry that is as much more excellent than the old as the covenant he mediates is better, since it is

enacted on better promises. For if that first covenant had been faultless, there would have been no

occasion to look for a second. For he finds fault with them when he says: Behold, the days are coming,

declares the Lord, when I will establish a new covenant with the house of Israel and with the house of

Judah, not like the covenant that I made with their fathers on the day when I took them by the hand to

bring them out of the land of Egypt. For they did not continue in my covenant, and so I showed no

concern for them, declares the Lord. For this is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel

after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my laws into their minds, and write them on their hearts,

and I will be their God, and they shall be my people.”

“And they shall not teach, each one his neighbor and each one his brother, saying, ‘Know the Lord, for

they shall all know me, from the least of them to the greatest. For I will be merciful toward their

iniquities, and I will remember their sins no more. “In speaking of a new covenant, he makes the first

one obsolete. And what is becoming obsolete and growing old is ready to vanish away.

“He says it shall no more be the old covenant made on Sin ai. That is, a law given from the outside,

controlling a man by force. But it shall be a law written within, constraining a man by love. “I will put

my laws,” He says, “in their mind, and write them in their hearts.” This can mean nothing but that we

shall love His law, for anything written on our hearts we must love.

Putting it into our minds is the same as God working in us to “For it is God who works in you, both to

will and to work for his good pleasure. ” (Philippians 2:13)It means we will want what God wills. We

will obey His commands, not out of duty, but because we want to do what He wants. Nothing could

possibly be conceived more effectual than this. How often have we thought, "If I could get inside my

kids and make them want to do what I want, managing them would be so easy!" We have found, in

practice, that to deal with cross-grained people, we must avoid suggesting our wishes to them. We must

instead induce them to suggest their own. Then, we will face no opposition. We, a stiff-necked people

by nature, always rebel against an outside law. But we embrace a law that springs up within us.

God's plan is to possess a man's inner self. He wants to control and manage his will, and work it for

him. Then, obedience is easy and a delight. Service becomes perfect freedom. The Christian must

exclaim, "This happy service!" Who could dream earth had such liberty?” Then, dear Christian, if you

are in bondage, you must surrender your will to your Lord. Give Him complete control of it. Say, “Yes,

Lord, YES !” To everything. Trust Him to work in you to will. To bring your wishes and affections into

harmony with His lovely will. I have seen this done over and over, in cases where it looked beforehand

an utterly impossible thing.

In one case, a lady had long feared and hated a thing she knew was right. I saw her, in despair and

without feeling, give her will to her Lord. She began to say to Him, "Your will be done; your will be

done!” And in one short hour that very thing began to look sweet and precious to h er. It is wonderful

what miracles God works in wills that are utterly surrendered to Him. He turns hard things into easy

and bitter things into sweet. It is not that He puts easy things in the place of the hard, but He actually

changes the hard thing into an easy one. And this is salvation. It is grand. Do try it. You, who find daily

Christian living hard, will find that your Master will transform your bondage into the most delicious

liberty!

Or, if you love His will in theory, but find it hard to do, there is deliverance in the wonderful life of

faith. For in this life no burdens are carried, nor anxieties felt. The Lord is our burden-bearer, and upon

Him we must lay off every care. He says, in effect, be careful for nothing, but just make your requests

known to me, and I will attend to them all. Be anxious for nothing, He says, not even your service.

Above all, I should think, our service. We are utterly helpless in this. So, even if we were careful, it

would not matter. What have we to do with thinking whether we are fit or not!

The Master has the right to use any tool for His work. It is not the tool's place to decide if it is the right

one. He knows; and if He chooses to use us, of course we must be fit. And in truth, if we only knew it,

our chief fitness is in our utter helplessness. His strength can only be made perfect in our weakness. I

can give you a convincing illustration of this.

I once visited an asylum for people with intellectual disabilities. I watched the children doing dumbbell

ex ercises. We know that it’s hard for people with intellectual disabilities to control their movements.

They are usually strong, but they lack the skill to use that strength. So, they can’t do much. In the

dumbbell exercises, this problem was very clear. They made all sorts of awkward movements.

Occasionally, they would move in time with the music and the teacher’s instructions, but most of the

time, it was all out of sync .

One little girl, however, I noticed, who made perfect movements. Not a jar nor a break disturbed the

harmony of her exercises. And the reason was, not that she had more strength than the others, but that

she had no strength at all. She could not close her hands over the dumb-bells, nor lift her arms. The

master had to stand behind her and do it all. She yielded up her members as instruments to him, and

his strength was made perfect in her weakness. He knew how to do those exercises. He had planned

them. So, when he did them, they were done right. She did nothing but yield herself up utterly into his

hands, and he did it all.

The yielding was her part, the responsibility was all his. It was not her skill that was needed to make

harmonious movements, but only his. The question was not of her capacity, but of his. Her utter

weakness was her greatest strength. If this shows our Christian life, it's no wonder. Paul could say,

"Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me."

Who would not glory in being so weak and helpless, that the Lord Jesus Christ should find no hindrance

to the perfect working of His mighty power through us and in us?

Then, too, if the work is His, the responsibility is His, and we have no room left for worrying about it.

Everything in reference to it is known to Him, and He can manage it all. Why not leave it all with Him

then, and consent to be treated like a child and guided where to go. The most effective workers I know

have no anxiety about their work. They commit it to their dear Master. They ask Him to guide them

and trust Him for the wisdom and strength they need, moment by moment.

One might think they were too carefree, with such at stake. But, when you learn God's secret of trusting,

you will see the beauty and power of a life yielded to His work. You will cease to condemn. You will

wonder how any of God's workers can dare to bear burdens or responsibilities that He alone can bear.

There are one or two other bonds of service from which this life of trust delivers us. We find out that

we are not responsible for all the work in the world. The commands cease to be general, and become

personal and individual.

The Master does not map out a general course of action for us and leave us to get along through it by

our own wisdom and skill as best we may. He leads us step by step, giving us each hour the special

guidance needed for that hour.

His blessed Spirit in us brings to mind, when needed, the command. So, we need not think ahead. We

should simply take each step as it is revealed to us, following our Lord wherever He leads. “The steps

of a good man are ordered of the Lord, ” not his way only, but each separate step in that way. Many

Christians make the mistake of expecting to receive God’s commands all in a lump, as it were. They

think, because He tells them to give a tract to one person on a train, that they must always give tracts

to everyone. They burden themselves with an impossible command.

Once, a young Christian met a soul on a walk. The Lord had sent her to deliver a message. She took it

as a command to speak to everyone she met about their souls. This was, of course, impossible, and as

a consequence, she was soon in hopeless bondage about it. She was terrified to go outside. She lived

in constant shame.

At last, she told her distress to a friend. This friend, a servant of God, said she was mistaken. The Lord

has a special work for each worker. In a well-run household, each servant must not try to do the others'

work. The same goes for the Lord's servants. They are not obliged to do everything. He told her to seek

the Lord's guidance on her work. She should trust Him to show her whom to speak to. He assured her

that He guides His own sheep. He goes before them and makes a way for them.

She followed this advice. She laid her work on the Lord. The result was a happy path of daily guidance.

She was led into much blessed work for her Master. She did it all without a care, for He prepared the

way before her. Trusting God is like connecting the machinery to the steam engine. The power is not

in the machinery, but in the steam. The machinery is useless, disconnected from the engine. But if you

connect them, the machinery will run easily. It has great power behind it. So, the Christian life becomes

easy and natural. It develops the divine work within.

Most Christians are tense. Their wills clash with God's. The connection is not perfect. It takes effort to

move the machinery. But when the connection is made, the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus can

work in us with all its power. We are then free from the law of sin and death. We shall know the

glorious liberty of the children of God. We shall lead frictionless lives.

Another form of bondage is to service. The life of faith delivers the soul from it. It refers to the after

reflections that always follow any Christian work. These self-reflections are of two sorts. The soul both

congratulates itself on its success and is uplifted. Or, it is distressed over its failure and is cast down.

One of these is sure to come. Of the two, I dread the first more. The last causes greater suffering at the

time. But in the life of trust, neither will trouble us. We have committed ourselves and our work to the

Lord. We will be satisfied to leave it to Him and not think about ourselves at all.

Years ago, I found this sentence in an old book: "Never indulge, at the end of an action, in any self-

reflection, whether of self-congratulation or despair." Forget the things that are behind, the moment

they are past. Leave them with God.” It has been of unspeakable value to me. When the temptation

comes, as it always does, to indulge in these reflections, I turn from them at once. I refuse to think

about my work at all. I leave it to the Lord to overrule the mistakes and bless it as He chooses.

In short, for happy and effective service, just trust your work to the Lord and leave it there. Do not

pray, "Lord, guide me; give me wisdom; arrange for me." Then, rise from your knees and take back the

burden. Don't try to guide and arrange for yourself. Leave it with the Lord, and remember that what

you trust to Him, you must not worry over nor feel anxious about. Trust and worry cannot go together.

If your work is a burden, it is because you are not trusting it to Him. If you trust it to Him, you will

find the yoke He puts on you is easy. The burden He gives you is light. Even amid a life of ceaseless

activity, you will find rest for your soul.

But some may say that this teaching would make us into mere puppets. I answer, No, it would simply

make us into servants. A servant must not plan, arrange, decide, or supply materials. He must only

obey. It is for the Master to do all the rest. The servant is not responsible, either, for results. The Master

alone knows what results he wished to have produced, and so he alone can judge of them. Intelligent

service must, of course, sympathize with the Master's plans. But, there cannot be a full understanding.

The Master cannot shift his responsibility to the servant. With our limited view and great ignorance,

we can do little but accept God's will. We shouldn't expect to fully understand it. We must leave all

results to Him.

What seems like failure on the surface is often, on the unseen side, a great success. If we allow ourselves

to lament and worry, we will be foolish. We should be singing and rejoicing, not weeping. It is far

better to avoid all self-reflection. We should not think about ourselves at all, whether for good or ill.

We are not our own property, nor our own business. We belong to God. We are His instruments and

His business. He always attends to His own business. So, He will, of course, attend to us.

I once heard of a slave on a ship during a violent storm. While everyone else was scared, he whistled

happily. Finally, someone asked if he was afraid of drowning. He smiled and said, "Well, maybe I am.

But I don’t belong to myself, and it will only be my master’s loss." This attitude could help us avoid

many worries in our work. With a group of people fully dedicated to serving and trusting in our Master,

imagine what He could do. One person like this could defeat a thousand, and two could put ten thousand

to flight. Nothing would be impossible for them because, with the Lord, it doesn’t matter whether we

have many or few.

May God quickly raise such an army! And may you, my dear reader, enroll in this army today. Yield

yourself to God as one alive from the dead. May every part of you be His instrument of righteousness,

to be used by Him as He wishes.

fields.title: Chapter 11. Difficulties Concerning Guidance
fields.body_html:
Believers are encouraged to trust in God's promised guidance, despite struggles with

doubts about His will. God speaks through Scripture, the Holy Spirit's impressions,

personal judgment, and providential circumstances. These must align to confirm His

will. The chapter warns against self-deception and stresses testing impressions with

Scripture and common sense. Ultimately, believers are urged to trust God’s wisdom

and act promptly on His guidance while avoiding doubt.

ou have now begun, dear reader, the life of faith. You have given yourself to the Lord, to be

His wholly. He has taken you and begun to mold you into a vessel of His honor. Your deepest

desire is to be very flexible in His hands. You want to follow Him wherever He may lead you.

You trust Him to work in you to will and to do of His good pleasure. But you find a great difficulty

here. You do not know the voice of the Good Shepherd. So, you are in doubt about His will for you.

God is calling you to certain paths. Your friends express strong disapproval. And, these friends may be

older than you in the Christian life. They seem much more advanced, too. You can hardly bear to differ

from or distress them. You also feel very unsure about yielding to any duty they might disapprove of.

Yet, you cannot shake these impressions. You plunge into doubt and unease. There is a way out of all

these difficulties, to the fully surrendered soul. I would repeat, fully surrendered. Any will to resist

makes it hard to know God's mind on that point. So, first, ensure you truly want to obey the Lord in all

respects. If this is the case, your soul only needs to know God's will to consent to it.

Then, you cannot doubt His desire to make it known and to guide you.

There are many very clear promises in reference to this. Take, for instance, John 10:3- 4 “To him the

gatekeeper opens. The sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out,

when he has brought out all his own, he goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his

voice. ” John 14:26: But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will

Y

teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you." Also, James 1:56: “If

any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be

given him. But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea

that is driven and tossed by the wind. ” With such passages as these, and many more like them, we must

believe that Divine guidance is promised to us, and our faith must confidently look for and expect it.

This is essential; for in James 1:6- 7, we are told, “ But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the

one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind. For that person must not

suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord .

First, settle this point. Divine guidance has been promised. You will surely have it if you ask for it.

Let no doubt turn you from this.

Next, remember that our God has all knowledge and wisdom. Therefore, He may guide you to paths

where great blessings await you. But, to the short-sighted human eyes around you, those paths may

seem to lead to confusion and loss.

You must accept that God's thoughts and ways differ from man’s . Only He, who knows the end from

the beginning, can judge the results of any action. You must realize that His love for you may lead you

to go against your dearest friends' wishes.

You must learn from Luke 14 and similar passages, “If anyone comes to me and does not hate his own

father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters, yes, and even his own life, he cannot

be my disciple. Whoever does not bear his own cross and come after me cannot be my disciple. For

which of you, desiring to build a tower, does not first sit down and count the cost, whether he has

enough to complete it? Otherwise, when he has laid a foundation and is not able to finish, all who see

it begin to mock him, saying, ‘This man began to build and was not able to finish.’ Or what king, going

out to encounter another king in war, will not sit down first and deliberate whether he is able with ten

thousand to meet him who comes against him with twenty thousand? And if not, while the other is yet

a great way off, he sends a delegation and asks for terms of peace. So therefore, any one of you who

does not renounce all that he has cannot be my disciple.” ( Luke 14:26-33.)

To be a disciple of your Lord, you may need to forsake all you have. You may have to turn your back

on your family, or even your own life. If this is not clearly recognized, the soul may suffer. Often, a

child's path of obedience will displease those he loves most. If he cannot trust the Lord through this,

he will be lost.

Of course, this is in harmony with our duties of honor and love to one another in our various life

relationships. The closer we are to Christ, the more we will show His meekness and gentleness. We

will also be tender to our natural guardians and counselors. The Master's guidance will always show

itself by the Master's Spirit. If, in obeying Him, we act against our friends' wishes, our love and patience

will prove our motive. But, this point settled, we now ask how God's guidance will come to us. How

shall we know His voice?

There are four special ways God speaks: 1. the voice of Scripture, 2. the inward impressions of the

Holy Spirit, 3. our higher judgment, and 4. providential circumstances. If these four align, it is safe to

say that God speaks. I lay it down as a principle, which none can dispute. His voice will always be in

harmony with itself, no matter how many ways He may speak.

The voices may be many, the message can be but one. If God tells me in one voice to do or to leave

undone anything, He cannot possibly tell me the opposite in another voice. If there is a contradiction

in the voices, the speaker cannot be the same.

My rule for distinguishing the voice of God is to test it against this harmony. If I have an impression, I

must check if it aligns with Scripture. I must also see if my higher judgment approves it, and, as we

Quakers say, if "way opens" to carry it out. If either test fails, it is not safe to proceed. I must wait in

quiet trust until the Lord shows me the point of harmony. He will, if it is His voice that has spoken. For

we must not overlook the fact that there are other voices that speak to the soul. There is the loud and

clamoring voice of self that is always seeking to be heard. And there are the voices of evil, deceiving

spirits. They lie in wait to entrap every traveler who enters these higher regions of the spiritual life.

In the same epistle which tells us that we are seated in “ and raised us up with him and seated us with

him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus , ” (Eph. 2:6) , we are also told that we shall have to fight there

with spiritual enemies. “ For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against

the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness, against the spiritual forces of evil

in the heavenly places.” (Eph. 6:12). These spiritual enemies, whoever they are, must communicate

with us through our spiritual faculties. Their voices, therefore, will be, like God's, an inward impression

on our spirits.

So, just as the Holy Spirit may tell us, by impressions, the will of God, so will these spiritual enemies.

They will, by impressions, tell us their will, though not giving their name. It is plain, therefore, that we

need a test. We must try these inner impressions. It is to know whose voice is speaking. And that test

will always be the harmony to which I have referred. In a misguided attempt to honor the Divine Spirit,

some earnest Christians have ignored and even violated the Bible. They have disregarded clear signs

from Providence and outraged their own better judgment. God, who sees their sincere hearts, can and

does forgive. But, the consequences in this life are often very sad.

We must first test any voice claiming to be divine. It must align morally with God's mind and will, as

revealed in the Gospel of Christ. Whatever is contrary to this, cannot be Divine, because God cannot

contradict Himself. We cannot expect a direct revelation until we seek and obey God's will, as revealed

in the Bible. A great many fatal mistakes are made in this matter of guidance, by the overlooking of

this simple rule. If our Father has given us clear directions, He won't reveal anything more. No man

needs or could expect a direct revelation to tell him not to steal. God has already, in the Scriptures,

plainly declared His will about it. It seems so obvious that I would not mention it. But, I have met

Christians who overlooked it and became fanatical.

For the Scriptures are far more explicit even about details than most people think. And there are not

many important affairs in life for which a clear direction may not be found in God’s book.

Take the matter of dress, and we have 1 Pet. 3:3- 4 “ Do not let your adorning be external — the braiding

of hair and the putting on of gold jewelry, or the clothing you wear — but let your adorning be the hidden

person of the heart with the imperishable beauty of a gentle and quiet spirit, which in God’s sight is

very precious .” and 1 Tim. 2:9 - 10 “ likewise also that women should adorn themselves in respectable

apparel, with modesty and self-control, not with braided hair and gold or pearls or costly attire, but with

what is proper for women who profess godliness —with good works.”

Take the matter of conversation, and we have Eph. 4:29 “ Let no corrupting talk come out of your

mouths, but only such as is good for building up, as fits the occasion, that it may give grace to those

who hear . ” , and 5:4 “ Let there be no filthiness nor foolish talk nor crude joking, which are out of place,

but instead let there be thanksgiving .” Take the matter of avenging injuries and standing up for your

rights, and we have (Romans.12:19- 21) “ Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of

God, for it is written, “Vengeance is mine, I will repay, says the Lord.” To the contrary, “if your enemy

is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing you will hear burning

coals on his head.” Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good ,” and (Matthew. 5:38 -

48) “You have heard that it was said, ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ But I say to you, do

not resist the one who is evil. But if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also.

And if anyone would sue you and take your tunic, let him have your cloak as well. And if anyone forces

you to go one mile, go with him two miles. Give to the one who begs from you, and do not refuse the

one who would borrow from you. You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and

hate your enemy.’ But I say to you, Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that

you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the

good, and sends rain on the just and on the unjust. For if you love those who love you, what reward do

you have? Do not even the tax collectors do the same? And if you greet only your brothers, what more

are you doing than others? Do not even the Gentiles do the same? You therefore must be perfect, as

your heavenly Father is perfect.”

“ For this is a gracious thing, when, mindful of God, one endures sorrows while suffering unjustly. For

what credit is it if, when you sin and are beaten for it, you endure? But if when you do good and suffer

for it you endure, this is a gracious thing in the sight of God. For to this you have been called, because

Christ also suffered for you, leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps .”(1Peter.

2:19-21)

Take the matter of forgiving one another, and we have (Ephesians.4:32) “ Be kind to one another,

tenderhearted, forgiving one another, as God in Christ forgave you.”

Mark 11:25- 26 “And whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone, so

that your Father also who is in heaven may forgive you your trespasses .” Take the matter of conformity

to the world, and we have (Romans 12:20) “ Do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by

the renewal of your mind, that by testing you may discern what is the will of God, what is good and

acceptable and perfect. ” and (1 John 2:15- 17) “ Do not love the world or the things in the world. If

anyone loves the world, the love of the Father is not in him. For all that is in the world — the desires of

the flesh and the desires of the eyes and pride of life — is not from the Father but is from the world. And

the world is passing away along with its desires, but whoever does the will of God abides forever.

“ You adulterous people! Do you not know that friendship with the world is enmity with God?

Therefore, whoever wishes to be a friend of the world makes himself an enemy of God.”(James 4:4)

Take the matter of anxieties of all kinds, and we have (Matthew 6:25- 34) “Therefore I tell you, do not

be anxious about your life, what you will eat or what you will drink, nor about your body, what you

will put on. Isn't life more than food, and the body more than clothing? Look at the birds of the air:

they neither sow nor reap nor gather into barns, and yet your heavenly Father feeds them. Are you not

of more value than they? And which of you, by being anxious, can add a single hour to his span of life?

And why are you anxious about clothing? Consider the lilies of the field, how they grow: they neither

toil nor spin, yet I tell you, even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these. But if God

so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not

much more clothe you, O you of little faith? Therefore, do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’

or ‘What shall we drink?’ or ‘What shall we wear?’ For the Gentiles seek after all these things, and

your heavenly Father knows that you need them all. But seek first the kingdom of God and his

righteousness, and all these things will be added to you. “Therefore , do not be anxious about tomorrow,

for tomorrow will be anxious for itself. Sufficient for the day is its own trouble.

“ Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let

your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will

guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus.”( Philippians 4:6-7)

I only give these as examples to show how very full and practical the Bible guidance is. If you are

confused, first, check if the Bible addresses your question. Ask God to reveal His will to you through

the Scriptures. And whatever shall seem to you to be plainly taught there, that you must obey. Reading

and meditating on this record of God's mind and will enlightens us. The inspiring Spirit will do so. Our

obedience will then be, as if, a present, living word. It will be as if our Lord spoke it to us today from

Heaven. The Bible is an ancient message from God, sent to us long ago. It is also a present message,

sent to us now each time we read it.

"My words are spirit and life. You must obey them. It's a command, personal and present." But we

must remember, the Bible is a book of principles. It is not a group of unrelated sayings . Isolated texts

may be used to sanction things. These are opposed by Scripture's principles.

I recently heard of a Christian woman at a Western meeting. The text, "For we walk by faith, and not

by sight," brought it to mind. She felt it was a command to be literally obeyed. So, she blindfolded

herself and insisted on walking up and down the aisle to illustrate the walk of faith. She soon stumbled

and fell against the stove, burning herself. Then, she wondered at the mysterious dispensation.

Applying Scripture and her common sense would have saved her from the delusion.

The second test, therefore, is our own higher judgment, or common sense. It is as true now as in

Solomon's time. A "man of understanding shall attain unto wise counsels." His exhortation still binds

us: "Get wisdom, the principal thing. “Wi th all you're getting, get understanding." The Scriptures say

it is vital for God's children to use all their abilities on their journey through this world. They are to use

their outward faculties for their outward walk, and their inward faculties for their inward walk. They

might as well expect to be "kept" from stubbing their toes if they walk blindfolded. It's the same as

expecting to be "kept" from spiritual stumbling if they ignore their judgment and common sense.

I asked a "sound mind" Christian how she told false spirits from the Holy Spirit. She replied, "I rap

them over the head and see if they have any common sense." Some may say, "But we should not depend

on our human understanding in divine things." I answer that we should not depend on our unenlightened

understanding. We should rely on our judgment and common sense, which the Spirit of God has

enlightened. That is, God will speak to us through the faculties He has Himself given us, and not

independently of them. We must use our eyes when we walk, no matter how faithful we are.

Similarly, we must use our minds in our inner lives.

The third and last test is that of providential circumstances. If a “leading” is of God, a way will always

open for it. Our Lord assures us of this in John 10:4. It says, “When he has brought out all his own, he

goes before them, and the sheep follow him, for they know his voice. ” Notice here the expressions

“goes before,” and “ follows .” He goes before to open a way, and we are to follow in the way thus

opened. A Christian should not force his way and trample opposition. That is never a sign of a Divine

leading. If the Lord “goes before” us, He will open all doors for us, and we shall not need ourselves to

hammer them down.

The fourth point is this: We must test our impressions by the other three voices. We must also test those

voices by our inward impressions. If we feel a "stop in our minds" about anything, we must wait until

it is removed before acting. A Christian, who had quickly advanced in the Divine life, gave me this

secret: "I always mind the checks." We must not ignore our inner voice, nor ride roughshod over it,

any more than we must the other three voices of which I have spoken.

These four voices, then, will always be found to agree in any truly Divine leading. The voice of our

impressions, the voice of Scripture, the voice of our own sanctified judgment. The voice of providential

circumstances. If these four do not agree at first, we must wait until they do.

A divine sense of “oughtness,” derived from the harmony of all God’s various voices, is the only safe

foundation for any action. I have guarded the points of danger. So, please let me out. I long for the joy

of this direct communication of God's will to us. It seems to me to be the grandest of privileges. In the

first place, that God should love me enough to care about the details of my life is perfectly wonderful.

And that He would tell me all about it. And, to know how to live and walk to perfectly please Him,

seems almost too good to be true.

We never care about the little details of people’s lives unless we love them. We don't care what most

people do or how they spend their time. But when we love someone, we start to care. God's care for us

proves His love. It's a great blessing that He speaks to us about everything in our lives. This includes

our duties, pleasures, friendships, and all we do, think, or say.

You must know this in your own experience, dear reader. Only then will you find the joy and privilege

of a life hid with Christ in God. It is one of its most precious gifts. God promises to work in us to will

and to do of His good pleasure.

This means He will take control of our will and work it for us. His suggestions will come to us as

desires, not commands. They will originate in our will; we shall feel as though we wanted to do so and

so, not as though we must. This makes it a service of perfect liberty. For it is always easy to do what

we desire, no matter how difficult the circumstances. Every mother knows she could get perfect

obedience from her child. She just needs to control his will, making him want to do what she wants.

And this is what our Father does for His children in the new dispensation.

He writes His laws on our hearts and minds. We love them. Our affections and judgment, not our fears,

draw us to obey. The Holy Spirit usually guides by impressing a desire to do or avoid certain things.

In prayer, the soul feels a sudden suggestion about a duty. “I would like to do this or the other,” it

thinks, “I wish I could.” Or the suggestion may come as a question, “I wonder whether I had not better

do so and so?” Or it may be only at first in the way of a conviction that such is the right and best thing

to be done. The matter should be committed to the Lord. We must instantly choose to obey Him. If the

suggestion agrees with the Scriptures, a holy judgment, and the circumstances, we should obey it.

Immediate obedience is the safest and easiest course. When the Spirit speaks, it is easy to obey. But if

the soul hesitates and reasons, it becomes harder to obey.

The first convictions are usually right in a fully surrendered heart. God is faithful and will make His

voice heard above all others. Such convictions, therefore, should never be met by reasoning. Prayer

and trust are the only safe attitudes of the soul. But even these should be brief.

We must act before the time passes and we miss the blessing.

If the suggestion is unclear and doubt arises, we should wait for further insight. This is especially true

if our friends disagree. The Scripture rule is, “Whatsoever is not of faith is sin” which means plainly

that we must never act in doubt. A clear conviction of right is the only safe guide. But we must wait in

faith. We must fully surrender, saying, "Yes," to our Lord's will, whatever it may be.

Our troubles stem from a lack of will. Next, many doubt any real Divine guidance. God's children are

very skeptical here. They read the promises and feel the need. But, they cannot believe that someone

will guide them.

It's as if God wants us to obey His voice, but didn't know how to make us hear and understand Him. It

is, thus, very possible for God to speak, but for the soul not to hear, because it does not believe He is

speaking. No earthly parent or master could guide his children or servants if they did not believe him

or accept his voice as his true will. God, who spoke to the fathers in many ways, still speaks. He wants

to see if any souls will obey His will.

Every moment of our lives our Father is seeking to reveal Himself to us. “ Jesus said to her, “I who

speak to you am he.”(John 4:26) I that speak in your heart, in your circumstances, in your losses, in

your gains, in your sorrows, and in your joys, am He. "I speak everywhere and in everything." So, we

must have perfect faith that the Lord's voice is speaking to us. It will teach and lead us. He will give us

wisdom for our guidance. After asking for guidance, we must follow our strongest sense of what we

should do. A few rules can help us with this.

I. We must believe that God will guide us.

II. We must surrender our own will to His guidance.

III. We must hearken for the Divine voice.

IV. We must wait for the divine harmony.

When we are certain of God’s guidance, we must follow it without hesitation. He is our t rue home. The

path may be difficult and narrow, but nothing else can satisfy a heart that longs for Him. How little of

that path you have walked, my soul! Take courage, and let the thought of God draw you further. The

perfect way may be hard for the flesh, but it is not hard for love. If you were desperate for God, how

quickly you would move toward Him.

Do not give your duties to God reluctantly — let your hands be open and free. Fix your eyes on Jesus

and consider how freely He gave His love to you. True perfection requires only a heart that remains at

peace throughout the day, listening for the Spirit’s voice moment by moment. Keep your conscience

sensitive — do not ignore His quiet nudges. And go wherever His grace leads you.

fields.title: Chapter 12. Concerning Temptation
fields.body_html:
Temptation is not a sign of failure but a part of spiritual growth. It’s not a sin to be

tempted, only to yield to it. Discouragement is a trap, and trusting God with

temptation strengthens faith. Enduring temptation leads to spiritual growth and the

"crown of life" promised to those who persevere.

ome very big mistakes are made about temptation in this life of faith. First, people expect that,

after the soul rests in God, temptations will cease. They believe the promised salvation is from

both temptation and being tempted. When they find the Canaanite still in the land, and see the

great, walled cities, they are discouraged. They think they must have gone wrong and that this

cannot be the true land after all.

Next, they mistakenly see temptation as sin. They blame themselves for it, but it's the enemy's fault.

This leads to condemnation and discouragement. If it continues, it ends in sin. The enemy makes an

easy prey of a discouraged soul; so that we fall often from the very fear of having fallen. To solve the

first difficulty, I must refer to Scripture. It says the Christian life is a constant warfare. It also says we

must, especially when seated in heavenly places in Christ Jesus, wrestle against spiritual enemies there.

Their power and skill to tempt us must be far superior to any we've ever encountered.

Temptations usually grow tenfold in strength after we start the interior life, not decrease. Their power

must not lead us to doubt that we have found the true, abiding place. Strong temptations are generally

a sign of great grace, rather than of little grace. When the Israelites first left Egypt, the Lord did not

lead them through the Philistines' land, the nearest route. God said, “When Pharaoh let the people go,

God did not lead them by way of the land of the Philistines, although that was near. For God said, “Lest

the people change their minds when they see war and return to Egypt.” But, when they learned to trust

Him, He allowed their enemies to attack. In their wilderness journey, they met few enemies and fought

few battles. In the land, they faced seven great nations and thirty-one kings. They had to conquer walled

cities and defeat giants.

S

They could not have fought the Canaanites, Hittites, Amorites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites until

they had entered their land. Your temptations, dear Christian, may prove you are in the land you seek

to enter. They are unique to that land. Never let your temptations make you doubt that you are in the

promised "heavenly places."

The second mistake is not quite so easy to deal with. It's almost pointless to say that temptation is not

sin. Yet, most distress comes from not understanding this. The very suggestion of wrong seems to bring

pollution with it. The evil agency not recognized, the poor, tempted soul fears it must be very bad, and

far from God, to have had such thoughts. It is as though a burglar broke into a man's house to steal.

When the owner began to resist him, the burglar accused him of being the thief. It is the enemy's clever

trick to trap us.

He comes and whispers evil ideas to us: doubts, blasphemies, jealousy, envy, and pride. Then he says,

"Oh, how wicked you must be to think of such things!" It is plain that you do not trust the Lord. If you

did, these things would not have entered your heart. This reasoning seems true, so the soul accepts it.

It then feels condemned and discouraged. From there, it is easy to fall into sin. One of the most fatal

things in the life of faith is discouragement.

One of the most helpful is cheerfulness. A wise man once said that, in overcoming temptations,

cheerfulness was the key. It was the first, second, and third thing. We must expect to conquer. That is

why the Lord often told Joshua, “Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be

frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go ” (Joshua

1:9). And it is also the reason He says to us, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you. Not as

the world gives do I give to you. Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid” (John14:27) .

The power of temptation is in the fainting of our own hearts. The enemy knows this. He always tries

to discourage us at the start of his assaults, if he can.

Sometimes, we feel discouraged. We think it's righteous grief and disgust at ourselves for being
