Him. They knew Christ only “after the flesh,” is outside of them, their Lord and Master, but not yet

their Life.

Then came Pentecost. These disciples then knew Him as revealed within. They were one with Him,

their very indwelling Life. Henceforth, He was to them Christ within. He worked in them to will and

to do of His good pleasure.

He, by the law of the Spirit of His life, delivered them from the bondage to the law of sin and death,

under which they had been held. No longer was it between themselves and Him, a war of wills and a

clashing of interests. One will alone animated them, and that was His will. One interest alone was dear

to them, and that was His. They were made ONE with Him.

Surely, all can recognize this picture. But the final stage may not be fully reached. You may have left

much to follow Christ, dear reader. You may have believed in, worked for, and loved Him. Yet, you

may not be like Him. Allegiance, you know, and confidence you know, but not yet union. There are

two wills, two interests, two lives. You have not yet lost your own life that you may live only in His.

Once it was I and not Christ. Then it was I and Christ. Perhaps now it is even Christ and me. But has it

come to be Christ only, and not I at all? Perhaps you do not understand what this oneness means. Some

believe it is a great emotion or a feeling of oneness. They turn inward, examining their emotions. They

hope to find, in these, their union with God. But nowhere is the mistake of trusting to feelings greater

than here.

Oneness with Christ must, by nature, mean a Christ-like life and character. It is not what we feel, but

what we are that settles the question. No matter how strong our feelings, there can be no oneness

without a likeness of character with Christ. We must share a unity of aim, purpose, and thought. Our

actions must be similar, too.

This is common sense, and it is Scriptural too. We say two people are one. We mean their purposes,

actions, thoughts, and desires are alike. A friend may express great love and unity. But if their aims,

actions, and views are the opposite of ours, we can't feel any real oneness. This is true despite our

affection for each other. To be truly one with another, we must share everything. Our likes and dislikes,

joys and sorrows, hopes and fears, must all be the same. As someone says, we must look through one

another’s eyes, and think with one another’s bra ins. This is, as I said above, only plain common sense.

And oneness with Christ can be judged by no other rule. It is out of the question to be one with Him in

any other way than in the way of nature, character, and life. Unless we are Christ-like in our thoughts

and our ways, we are not one with Him, no matter how we feel. I have seen Christians with few Christ-

like traits. They were so emotional and ecstatic in their love for Christ that they believed they were

justified in claiming a close oneness with Him. I scarcely know a sadder sight. Surely our Lord meant

to reach such cases when He said, “Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom

of heaven, but the one who does the will of my Father who is in heaven.” (Mathew 7:21.)

He w as not making here any arbitrary statement of God’s will, but a simple announcement of the nature

of things. Of course it must be so. It is like saying, “No man can enter the ranks of astronomers who is

not an astronomer.” Emotions will not make a man an a stronomer, but life and action. He must be one,

not merely feel that he is one.

There is no escape from this inexorable nature of things, and especially here. We must be one with

Christ in character, life, and action. If not, we cannot be one with Him in any other way. There is no

other way. We must be "partakers of His nature" to share His life. His life and His nature are one.

But emotional souls do not always see this.

They feel so near to Christ and so united to Him that they think it must be real. They overlook the need

for a Christ-like character and walk. So, they build their hopes on their delightful emotions and exalted

feelings. They believe they must be one with Him to have such rich, holy experiences.

It is a fact that other causes can produce these emotions. They are not solely due to a divine influence.

The emotions depend largely on temperament and physical conditions. It is most dangerous, therefore,

to make them a test of our spiritual union with Christ. It may result in just such a grievous self-deception

as our Lord warns against in (Luke 6:46-49): “Why do you call me ‘Lord, Lord,’ and not do what I tell

you? Everyone who comes to me and hears my words and does them, I will show you what he is like:

he is like a man building a house, who dug deep and laid the foundation on the rock. And when a flood

arose, the stream broke against that house and could not shake it, because it had been well built. But

the one who hears and does not do them is like a man who built a house on the ground without a

foundation. When the stream broke against it, it immediately fell, and the ruin of that house was great.”

Our soul delights in calling Him, "Lord, Lord." But, are we doing what He said? He tells us this is the

important point, after all.

If, led by our feelings, we claim to abide in Him in meetings, among friends, or in our hearts before the

Lord, let us consider these words of the Holy Ghost: "He that says he abides in Him, ought himself so

to walk, even as He walked." Unless we are walking as He did, we cannot be abiding in Him, no matter

how much we may feel we are.

If you are one with Christ, you will be sweet to those who are cross with you. You will bear everything

and make no complaints. When reviled, you will not revile again. You will consent to be trampled on,

as Christ was, and feel only love in return. You will seek others' honor rather than your own. You will

take the lowest place and serve all, as Christ did. You will truly love your enemies and do well to those

who spitefully use you. In short, you will live a Christ-like life. You will show and feel, a Christ-like

spirit and walk among men as He did. This, dear friends, is what it is to be one with Christ. If this is

not your life, you are not one with Him. Your feelings, no matter how ecstatic, do not matter.

To be one with Christ is too wonderful and solemn a thing. It is too mighty an experience to be reached

by mere feelings. He was holy, and those who are one with Him will be holy also. There is no escape

from this simple and obvious Fact.

When our Lord tried to show His oneness with God, He said, “And he who sent me is with me. He has

not left me alone, for I always do the things that are pleasing to him.”(Joshua 8:29) “So Jesus said to

them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, the Son can do nothing of his own accord, but only what he sees the

Father doing. For whatever the Father does, that the Son does likewise. For the Father loves the Son

and shows him all that he himself is doing. And greater works than these will he show him, so that you

may marvel. For as the Father raises the dead and gives them life, so also the Son gives life to whom

he will. For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son, that all may honor the Son,

just as they honor the Fat her. Whoever does not honor the Son does not honor the Father who sent him”

(John 5:19-23)

The test of oneness, then, was the doing of the same works, and it is the test of oneness now. If our

Lord could say that, so must His disciples. He said to believe in Him only if He did the works of His

Father. He asked for no belief based on His claims.

It is forever true that "So, every healthy tree bears good fruit, but the diseased tree bears bad fruit. A

healthy tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a diseas ed tree bear good fruit” (Mathew 7:17 -18 ). It is not

that they will not, but they cannot. A soul united with Christ will, for sure, bear a Christ-like life. A

grapevine bears grapes, not thistles. I don't object to emotions, though. On the contrary, I believe they

are very precious gifts when they are from God, and are to be greatly rejoiced in. I object to using them

to test spiritual states, in ourselves or others. I don't want to base our faith on them. Let them come or

let them go, just as God pleases, and make no account of them either way. But, we must have the vital

marks of oneness with Christ. We must share a likeness in character, life, and walk. If we do, all will

be well. For “ Whoever says 'I know him' but does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth

is not in him, but whoever keeps his word, in him truly the love of God is perfected. By this we may

know that we are in him: whoever says he abides in him ought to walk in the same way in which he

walked.” (1John 2:4 -6)

It may be, my dear reader, that the grief of your life has been the fact that you have so few good feelings.

You try your hardest to get up the feelings that you hear others talking about, but they will not come.

You pray for them fervently and are often tempted to upbraid God because He does not grant them to

you. You are filled with unbearable anguish. You think your lack of emotion means your soul is not

united with Christ. You judge altogether by your feelings, and think there is no other way to judge.

Now my advice to you is to let your feelings go, and pay no regard to them whatever. They really have

nothing to do with the matter. They do not reflect your spiritual state. They only show your

temperament or current physical condition. People in very low states of grace often feel intense

emotions. We all know this from the scenes we have heard of or witnessed at camp-meetings and

revivals.

I once had a servant who was deeply involved in her church's revival meetings. Sometimes, she would

become so overwhelmed by the experience that she fainted. However, at other times, she showed little

evidence of spiritual commitment and did not live a moral life.

The Bible teaches, if nothing else, this: A Christ-like life must accompany any true experience of His

spirit. It could not be otherwise in the very nature of things. But I fear some Christians have separated

the two things so much that they now value their experiences over their walk. They care more about

their feelings than their character. A certain colored congregation in one of the Southern States was a

plague to the whole neighborhood. They openly disregarded even the ordinary rules of morality. They

stole, lied, and cheated, without a single prick of conscience. And yet their nightly meetings were times

of the gre atest emotion and “power.”

Someone finally spoke to the preacher about it. They begged him to preach a sermon on morality to

make his people see their sins. "Ah, misses," he replied, "I know the day is bad. But, it always brings

a coldness over the meetings when I preach about these things." You are helpless as to your emotions,

but you can have character if you will. You can be so filled with Christ as to be Christ-like. If you are

Christ-like, then you are one with Him in the only vital, essential way. Your feelings may say it's

impossible, but they are wrong.

Now that we've defined oneness with Christ, we must find how to achieve it. We must first of all find

out what the facts in the case are, and what our own relation to these facts is. If you read such passages

as ( 1 Corinthians 3:16), “ Do you not know that you are God’s temple and that God’s Spirit dwells in

you ?” Then, look at the chapter's opening. It shows to whom these wonderful words are spoken. They

are for babies in Christ, who were yet carnal and walked according to man. This soulunion, this glorious

mystery of an indwelling God, is the possession of even the weakest and most failing believer in Christ.

So that it is not a new thing you are to ask for, but only to realize that which you already have. It is

absolutely true for every believer in the Lord Jesus. His "body is the temple of the Holy Ghost, who is

in him, who is of God.”

It seems to me just in this way. It is as though Christ lived in a house, shut in a closet. The house's

dwellers don't know or notice Him. He longs to be known to them, to share their daily lives and

interests. But, He won't force Himself upon them. Only a voluntary companionship could satisfy His

love. The days pass over that favored household. They remain unaware of their great privilege. They

come and go about all their daily affairs with no thought of their wonderful Guest.

Their plans are laid without reference to Him. His wisdom to guide, and His strength to protect, are all

lost to them. Lonely days and weeks are spent in sadness, which might have been full of the sweetness

of His presence. But suddenly, the announcement is made, “The Lord is in the house!” How will its

owner receive the intelligence?

Will he call out a thankful greeting and open every door for his glorious Guest? Or will he shrink, afraid

of His presence, and seek a private corner to hide from His all-seeing eye?

Dear friend, I am glad to announce that the Lord is in your heart. Since your conversion, He has been

there. But you have lived in ignorance of it. Every moment might have been spent in the sunshine of

His sweet presence. Every step might have been taken under His advice. But because you did not know

it, and have never looked for Him, your life has been lonely and full of failure. But now that I announce

to you, how will you receive it? Are you glad to have Him? Will you throw wide open every door to

welcome Him in? Will you joyfully and thankfully give up the governance of your life into His hands?

Will you consult Him about everything, and let Him decide each of your steps, and mark out every

path? Will you invite Him to your innermost chambers, and make Him the sharer in your most hidden

life? Will you say, YES to all His longing for union with you, and with a glad and eager abandonment,

will you, then, hand yourself and all that concerns you over into His hands? If you will, then shall your

soul begin to know something of the joy of union with Christ.

And yet, after all, this is but a faint picture of the blessed reality. For it is far more glorious than to have

Christ in the heart or the house. It is to be united with Him as to be one with Him, one will, one purpose,

one interest, and one life. Human words cannot express such glory as this.

And yet I want to express it. I want to make your souls so unutterably hungry to realize it, that day or

night, you cannot rest without it. Do you understand the words, one with Christ? Do you catch the

slightest glimpse of their marvellous meaning? Does not your whole soul begin to exult over such a

wondrous destiny? For it is a reality. It means to have no life but His. To have no will but His. To have

no interests but His. To share His riches. To enter into His joys. To partake of His sorrows. To manifest

His life. To have His mind. To think, feel, act, and walk as He did. Oh, who could have dreamed that

such a destiny could have been ours!

Will you have it, dear soul? Your Lord will not force it on you. He wants you as His friend. A forced

union would ruin this. It must be yo ur choice. The bride must say a willing “Yes,” to her bridegroom,

or the joy of their union is utterly wanting. Can’t you say a willing “Yes,” to your Lord? It is such a

simple transaction, and yet so real! The steps are three. First, be sure that the Scriptures teach this

glorious indwelling of your God. Then, surrender your whole being to Him to be possessed by Him.

Finally, believe that He has taken possession and is dwelling in you. Begin to reckon yourself dead,

and to reckon Christ as your only life. Maintain this attitude of soul unwaveringly.

Repeat, "I am crucified with Christ, nevertheless I live, yet not I, but Christ lives in me," day and night.

Do this until it becomes your soul's breath. Put off thy self-life by faith and in fact continually, and put

on practically the life of Christ. Let this act become, by its constant repetition, the attitude of your

whole being. And, as surely as you do this daily, you will find your body continually bearing the dying

of the Lord Jesus.

Then, the life of Jesus will be made manifest in your mortal flesh. You must learn what salvation

means. You will see, with amazement, the Lord's secrets, of which you have hardly dreamed.

How have I made a mistake! God is my home. God Himself is here. Why have I looked so far for Him,

who is nowhere but near? Yet, God is never so far off as even to be near; He is within, our spirit is the

home He holds most dear. I thought myself Homeless, forlorn, and weary. I missed my joy. I walked

the earth, a weary soul, in God's sanctuary.

fields.title: Chapter 18. A Lesson In The Interior Life
fields.body_html:
True spiritual joy comes from trusting in God's unchanging nature, not from external

circumstances. Like the caterpillar that must die to become a butterfly, the soul must

let go of the self-life to embrace divine life. Through trials and loss, the soul learns to

find peace and joy in God alone. The key lesson is captured in the prophet’s words:

“Although... yet,” showing the triumph of rejoicing in Go d despite challenges.

t Christmas, many of our store windows show a significant picture. It is a dreary, desolate winter

scene. There is a dark, stormy sky, bare trees, and brown grass and dead weeds, with patches of

snow over them. On a leafless tree at one side of the picture is an empty and snow-covered nest, and

on a branch near sits a little bird. It is cold, dark, and desolate enough to daunt any bird, and drive it to

some fairer clime. But, this bird sits there, content. Its little head is bravely lifted to the sky, and a

winter song is about to burst from its tiny throat.

This picture, which always stands on my shelf, has preached me many a sermon. And the test is always

the same. It is in the two words at the head of this article, "Although" and "Yet."

“ Though the fig tree should not blossom, nor fruit be on the vines, the produce of the olive fail and the

fields yield no food, the flock be cut off from the fold and there be no herd in the stalls,”

(Habakkuk3:17). There come times in many lives when, like this winter bird, the soul finds itself

without comfort. All seems dark and wrong. Everything we trusted fails us. Promises seem unfulfilled,

and our prayers go unanswered. We find nothing left to rely on in earth or Heaven. And it is at such

times as these that the brave little bird with its message is needed. Although all is wrong everywhere,

yet there is one thing to rejoice in: God. He is the God of our salvation. He does not change. He is the

same good, loving, tender God yesterday, today, and forever.

A

We can rejoice in Him always, whether we have anything else to rejoice in or not. By rejoicing in Him,

I do not mean rejoicing in ourselves. I fear most people think this is what is meant. Their feelings,

revelations, and experiences form the basis of their joy. If none are satisfactory, they see no chance of

joy at all. But the lesson the Lord is trying to teach us all the time is the lesson of humility.

He commands us to look away from the self and its experiences. We must crucify the self and count it

dead. We must cease to care about the self. We should know and want nothing but God.

The reason for this is that God has destined us for a higher life than the self-life. That, just as He has

destined the caterpillar to be a butterfly, He has appointed its life to die. So, the butterfly may take its

place. Likewise, He has appointed our self-life to die so that the divine life may be ours instead. The

caterpillar destroys its grub form to become a butterfly. It dies that it may live. And just so must we.

So, the most essential thing now is to die to self and be reborn to a life in God. And it is for this reason

that the lesson of joy in the Lord, and not in self, must be learned. Every advancing soul must, sooner

or later, trust God. The bare God, if I may. It must trust Him for what He is, not for His promises or

gifts. It must learn to have its joy in Him alone, and to rejoice in Him when all else in Heaven and earth

shall seem to fail.

I believe the only way to reach this place is by the soul. It must face, in its own experience, the loss of

all things, both inward and outward. I don't mean that all one's friends must die, or all one's money be

lost. I mean that the soul shall find itself, from either inward or outward causes, abandoned, lost, and

empty of all consolation. It must come to the end of everything that is not God, and must have nothing

else left to rest on within or without. It must experience just what the prophet meant when he wrote

that “Although.”

It must go through the mud, fall off the edge, and be covered by the water . It must, at last, find,

among and below them, the present, living, loving, omnipotent God! Only then will it understand the

prophet's exulting shout of triumph. It will be able to join it : " yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will

take joy in the God of my salvation.”(Habakkuk 3:10) Then, and not until then, will it know the full

meaning of the verse that follows: “ GOD, the Lord, is my strength; he makes my feet like the

deer’s; he makes me tread on my high places .”(Habakkuk3:19) The soul often walks on what seem

high places. They are, however, largely self-made and emotional, with little of God in them. In

moments of loss and failure, these high places become edges. But the high places to which the Lord

brings the soul that rejoices only in Him can be touched by no darkness or loss. Their very

foundations are laid in the midst of an utter loss and death of all that is not God.

To find an unwavering experience, we must seek it only in the Lord. We must seek it apart from all

else, His gifts, and His blessings. We must seek it apart from all that can change with our earthly life.

Today's answered prayer may seem unanswered tomorrow. The once-fulfilled promises may no longer

feel real. The spiritual blessing that once brought joy may be lost. All we may have left is a hungry,

longing memory of it all. But when all else is gone, God is still left. Nothing changes Him. He is the

same yesterday, today, and forever, and in Him is no variableness, neither shadow of turning.

And the soul that finds its joy in Him alone can suffer no wavering. It is grand to trust in the promises,

but it is grander still to trust in the Promiser. The promises may be misunderstood or misapplied. When

we rely on them, they may seem to fail us. But no one ever trusted in the Promiser and was confounded.

The God behind His promises is infinitely greater than them. He can never fail us in any emergency.

The soul that trusts in Him knows perfect peace.

The little child does not always understand its mother's promises. But it knows its mother. Its trust is

based not on her word, but on herself. And just so it is with those of us who have learned the lesson of

this “Although” and “Yet.” There may not be a prayer answered or a prom ise fulfilled to our own

consciousness, but what of that? Behind the prayers and behind the promises, there is God, and He is

enough. And to such a soul the simple words, “God is”, answer every question and solve every doubt.

To the little trusting child, the simple fact of the mother’s existence is the answer to all its needs. The

mother may not make one single promise or detail any plan, but she is, and that is enough for the child.

The child rejoices in the mother, not in her promises, but in herself. To the child, as to us, there is joy.

It is the one unchangeable thing behind all that changes and can change. It is the mother's existence.

The child must be cared for while the mother lives. The child, instinctively if not intelligently, knows

this and rejoices in it. And while God lives, His children must be cared for. They should know this and

rejoice in it more than a human child would.

For what else can God do, being what He is? Neglect, indifference, forgetfulness, and ignorance are all

impossible to Him. He knows everything. He cares about everything. He can manage everything. He

loves us. What more could we ask? So, come what may, we will lift our faces to our God, like our

brave little bird teacher. In our darkest "Althoughs," we will sing our glad and triumphant "Yet."

All of God’s saints in all ages have done this. Job said, out of the depths of sorrow and trial which few

can equal, “ Though he slay me I will hope in him; yet I will argue my ways to his face .”(Job 13:15). In

his deepest ang uish, David could say, “Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death,

I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me.” (Psalm 23:4)

And again, "God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble."(Psalm 46:1). Therefore we

will not fear though the earth gives way, though the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea,

though its waters roar and foam, though the mountains tremble at its swelling. Selah there is a river

whose streams make glad the city of God, the holy habitation of the Most High. God is in the midst of

her; she shall not be moved; God will help her when morning dawns.

In his sorrows, Paul could say, "We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not

driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed; always carrying in the

body the death of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be manifested in our bodies.

For we who live are always being given over to death for Jesus ’ sake, so that the life of Jesus also may

be manifested in our mortal flesh. So death is at work in us, but life in you.” (2Corinthianss 4:812).The

soul that learned to rejoice in God alone can say all this and more.

Spiritual joy is not a thing, not a lump of joy, so to speak, stored away in one’s heart to be looked at

and rejoiced over. Joy is the gladness from having something good or knowing something pleasant.

And the Christian’s joy is simply his gladness in knowing Christ, and in his possession o f such a God

and Saviour. We do not on an earthly plane rejoice in our joy, but in the thing that causes our joy. And

on the heavenly plane, it is the same. We must " yet I will rejoice in the LORD; I will take joy in the

God of my salvation. "(Habakkuk 3:18.) No man or devil can take this joy from us. No earthly sorrows

can touch it.

A writer on the interior life says, in effect, that our spiritual journey has three very different regions.

Each is a necessary stage in our progress. First, there is the region of beginnings. It is a time of simple

joys and delights, strong hopes, and deep feelings. Many secrets reveal God. Next is a vast wilderness,

full of temptations and trials. It brings a loss of reason, dryness, and inner and outer darkness. If, after

a long trial, you endure the desert, a region of mountain heights awaits. There, you will find a union

with God, a detachment from earthly things, and a perfect contentment with His will. You will be

transformed into the image of Christ.

I cannot discuss if this order is true. But, I am sure of one thing. Many souls, who found joy in the

"Region of beginnings" here, later faced a desert experience that left them amazed and perplexed. And

I cannot but think such might, perhaps, in this explanation, find the answer to their trouble. They are

learning to detach from all that is not God. This is to unite their souls with Him, as shown in a picture

of the third and highest region of bliss.

The soul’s pathway is always through death to life. The caterpillar must die to become a butterfly. It

can only do so by giving up one life to live another. And neither can we. So, we may have to pass

through this desolate, deadly region to reach the calm mountain heights beyond. If we know this, we

can walk through the darkest times, sure that all is well, since God is God. Many who read this paper

have at least one of these desert "Althoughs." Some have many.

Dear friends, is the “Yet” there also? Have you learned the prophet’s lesson? Is God enough for you?

Can you sing and mean it, "You, O Christ, are all I want, more than all in you I find" If not, you need

the little bird to speak to you.

His song, as he sits on that bare, leafless tree in the howling winter storm, must become your song too.

Though the rain may fall and the wind blow, And the chill is the wintry blast; Though the cloudier sky

is still clouding, And the dead leaves tell that summer is passed; Yet my face I hold to the stormy

heaven, My heart is as calm as a summer sea; Glad to receive what my God has given, Whatever it

may be.

When I feel the cold, I can say, 'He sends it.' And His wind blows blessing, I surely know. For I've

never wanted but that He attends it. My heart beats warm, though the winds may blow. The soft, sweet

summer was warm and glowing. Bright were the blossoms on every bough. I trusted Him when the

roses were blowing. I trust Him now.

My faith would be small and weak if it wavered just because the roses have stopped blooming . Frail

was the trust that now should alter, doubting His love when the storm-clouds grow. If I trust Him once,

I must trust Him ever. His way is best, though I stand or fall. Through wind or storm, He will leave me

never, for He sends all."

fields.title: Chapter 19. How To Reign In The Interior Life
fields.body_html:
The kingdom of God is an inner, spiritual realm, not an external, physical one. Jesus

teaches that it is not a place to observe, but exists within those who live according to

God’s will. In this kingdom, individuals find freedom from external pre ssures and sin,

with Christ as the sovereign who bears all burdens. The true power of this kingdom

lies in inner peace and triumph over worldly struggles.

hen the Pharisees asked him when the kingdom of God would come, he answered, "It does not

come with observation."" Neither shall they say, 'Look, here!'" or, look there! For,

Behold, the kingdom of God is within you." The phrases "kingdom of God" and "kingdom of Heaven"

refer to the divine life in the soul. They are in Scripture. They mean simply the place or condition where

God rules, and where His will is done. It is an interior kingdom, not an exterior one. Its thrones are not

for human pomp and glory. They are for dominion over the things of time and sense. Its kings wear not

royal robes of purple and fine linen. They wear instead the inner garments of purity and truth. And its

reign is not in outward show, but in inward power.

Neither is it in one place rather than another, nor in one form of things above another. We should not

seek Christ in this mountain or at Jerusalem. That is not where to find Him and enter His kingdom. It

is not a matter of place at all, but one of condition. In every place, under every name, and in every

form, all who seek God and do good will find His kingdom within them. But this is very little

understood. Our childish literalism has led us to believe that a kingdom must be in a specific place. We

expected the kingdom of heaven to mean an outward victory of heaven over earth in some particular

location. We thought that to sit on a throne with Christ would mean to be publicly uplifted in power

and glory.

W

But, as Scripture's inner sense unfolds, we see that this would be a poor, superficial fulfillment of the

real meaning of these symbols. And the vision of their true significance grows before the "eyes that

see." At last, we know our Lord's words were truer than we had ever dreamed. The "kingdom of God

comes not with observation; neither shall they say, lord here! or, lord there!" for, behold, the kingdom

of God is wi thin you.”

Daniel 2:44 “And in the days of those kings the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never

be destroyed, nor shall the kingdom be left to another people. It shall break in pieces all these kingdoms

and bring them to an end, and it shall stand forever,” announces the kingdom. Isaiah 9:6-7 announces

the King: -- “ For to us a child is born, to us a son is given; and the government shall be upon his shoulder,

and his name shall be called Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God, Everlasting Father, and Prince of

Peace. Of the increase of his government and of peace, there will be no end, on the throne of David

and over his kingdom, to establish it and to uphold it with justice and with righteousness from this time

forth and forevermore. The zeal of the Lord of hosts will do this.”

This kingdom has the right to destroy all others. The law says the inward must rule the outward. If there

is peace within, no turmoil can affect the soul. But outward peace can't calm an inner storm. A happy

heart can walk, indifferent, through a sea of trouble. But internal anguish can't find joy in the best

surroundings. A man's inner self makes or unmakes his joy, not his possessions. Someone told

Diogenes, "The king has degraded you." “Yes , ” replied Diogenes triump hantly, “but I am not

degraded!” No act of kings or emperors can degrade a soul that retains its own dignity; no tyrant can

enslave an inwardly free man.

So, to have this divine kingdom within means all other powers to conquer or enslave are broken. The

soul reigns triumphant over them all. Men and devils may try to enslave one. But they are powerless

before the might of this interior kingdom. No longer will fashion, convention, or fear of man rule a

soul raised to a throne in this inward kingdom. Nor will the love of ease. Christians cringe and bow to

many tyrants. No sin or temptation can overcome, no sorrow can crush, no discouragement can hinder.

Let a man or woman have been bound in ever so tyrannical chains of sinful habits, this kingdom will

set them free. Circumstances may make men kings in the outside world. But, in the hidden life, men

become kings over circumstances. And, the soul that was once a slave to a thousand things, now finds

itself completely independent of them.

For the King in this kingdom is one whom nothing can affect or baffle. He it is who makes

circumstances. Since the government is on His shoulders, we cannot doubt that He will rule with perfect

justice. His subjects will want for nothing. The phrase "the government shall be upon His shoulder"

holds the secret of this wonderful kingdom. Upon His shoulder, not upon ours. The care is His. The

burdens are His. The responsibility is His. The protection is His. The planning, providing, controlling,

and guiding are all in His hands. No one can question as to His perfect fulfilment of every requirement

of His kingship. So, those in His kingdom are free from anxiety, burden, and trouble.

And by this deliverance they become kings. The government is not upon their shoulders, and they have

no business to interfere with it. Their King has assumed all responsibility. If He sees His subjects happy

and prosperous, He is content to bear all the weight and care of kingship. We often speak of the duties

of earthly kings. We pity them for the burdens of kingship. We recognize, even on an earthly plane,

that to be a king means, or ought to mean, the bearing of the burdens of even the meanest of his subject.

Even now, as I write, many hearts ache for the new Czar. He has taken on the heavy burden of the vast

Russian Empire.

We can learn, from every human heart, of kingship's duties. It means to be in a kingdom where God is

King. He has declared that all things shall be ordered with judgment and justice, forever. Surely no

care or anxiety can ever enter here, if the heart but knows its kingdom and its King! In John 18:36, our

King tells us the tactics of His kingdom: “ Jesus answered, “My kingdom is not of this world. If my

kingdom were of this world, my servants would have been fighting, that I might not be delivered over

to the Jews. But my kingdom is not from the world.”

Earthly kings and kingdoms gain supremacy through war. God's kingdom conquers by inward power.

Earthly kings subdue enemies; God subdues enmity. His victories must be interior before they can be

exterior. He does not subjugate, but he conquers. Even we, on our earthly plane, know this principle.

We do not value any victory over another that only reaches the body and has not subdued the heart. No

true mother cares for an outward obedience merely; nothing will satisfy her but the inward surrender.

Unless the center of the heart is conquered, the conquest seem worthless. And with God how much

more so? We are told, “But the LORD said to Samuel, “Do not look on his appearan ce or on the height

of his stature, because I have rejected him. For the LORD sees not as man sees: man looks on the

outward appearance, but the LORD looks on the heart.” (1samuel 16:7)

We speak of "subduing hearts." We do not mean to force a surrender. We mean that they are won and

willingly given to another. And it is after this fashion and no other that God subdues. So that to read

that “His kingdom rules over all” means that all hearts are won to His service in a glad and willing

surrender.

For again I repeat, His reign must be inward before it can be outward. And in truth, it is no reign at all,

unless it is within. If we think for a moment, we will see this must be so. It is impossible to imagine

God reigning in a kingdom where His subjects' actions are not controlled beyond their outward actions.

His kingdom is not of this world. It is a spiritual realm. Its power is over souls, not bodies.

So, it can only be set up once the soul is conquered.

Seen this way, all those declarations and prophecies become full of love and blessing. They say that

God will subdue His enemies and will rule them in righteousness and power! And how glorious with

hope does the voice of that great multitude heard by John sound out, saying, “Alleluia! For the Lord

God omnipotent reigns” In confirmation of all this we have two passages descriptive of this kingdom,

in (Romans.14:17) “ For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness

and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit.” , and (1 Corinthian s 4:20): “ For the kingdom of God does not

consist in talk but in power.”

Not outward things, but inward. Not what a man eats or drinks. Not where he lives. Not his nationality

or the customs of his race. Not even his thoughts or words. But what are the inward traits of his nature?

What is the power of his spirit? For these alone constitute this kingdom of God.

Not what I do, but what I am, is to decide whether I belong to it or not. This kingdom can be set up

only when we have and experience, inward righteousness, peace, joy, and power. So, no external

domination can achieve such results. Only the inner work of God's all-subduing spirit can.

I have learned a lot from the story of Odysseus and his journey, when he was sailing past the islands of

the sirens. These sirens could charm anyone who listened to their songs. They lured them to leap into

the sea. To avert this danger, Odysseus filled his crew's ears with wax. He did this so they would not

hear the fatal music. He then bound himself to the mast with knotted cords. They passed the isle in

safety. But, when Orpheus had to sail by the same island, he won a better victory. He made sweeter

music than the sirens and enchanted his crew with more alluring songs. So, they passed the dangerous

charmers, not only safely but with disdain. Wax and knotted cords kept Odysseus and his crew from a

fatal leap. But, inward delights let Orpheus and his crew triumph over temptation itself. And just so is

it with the kingdom of which we speak. It needs no outward law to bind it, but reigns by right of its

inward life.

So that it is said of those who have entered it, “Against such there is no law. “For it is a kingdom of

kings. The song we shall one day sing, nay, that we ought to be singing even now and here in this life,

declares this: " and from Jesus Christ the faithful witness, the firstborn of the dead, and the ruler of kings

on earth. To him who loves us and has freed us from our sins by his blood and made us a kingdom,

priests to his God and Father, to him be glory and dominion forever and ever. Amen (Revelation.1:5-

6.)

We who have entered this kingdom, or, rather, in whom this kingdom is set up, sit upon the throne with

our King and share His dominion. The world was His footstool, and it becomes our footstool also. He

reigned above the things of time and sense. A life lived in a higher, superior plane gave him that power.

So may we. We all know the saying that someone "rises above his surroundings." It means there is a

hidden power in that person. It controls his surroundings instead of being controlled by them. Our King

rose above His surroundings. We, who reign with Him, can do the same.

But, just as He was not a king in outward appearance, but only in inward power, so shall we be. He

reigned, not in that He had all the world's riches. But that He had none, and could do without them.

And so shall our reigning be. We shall not have all men bow to us, nor do all things bend to our will.

With all men opposing us and all things adverse, we shall walk in a royal triumph of soul through them.

We shall suffer the loss of all things, and by that loss be set forever free from their power to bind. We

shall hide in the King's will, an impregnable fortress. There, we shall reign in a perpetual Kingdom.

All this is contrary to man’s thought of kingship. The human heart can only grasp one idea. It is this:

that outward circumstances must bend to the soul that is on a throne with Christ. Friends must approve,

enemies must be silenced, and obstacles must be overcome. Affairs must prosper, or there can be no

reigning. If man had ordered Daniel's business, or the three Hebrews in the fiery furnace, he would

have said to win, they must change the kings' minds. Daniel should not have been cast into the lion's

den, and the Hebrew children should have been kept out of the furnace.

But God’s way was infinitely grander. He allowed Daniel to be cast among the lions. He wanted to

reign triumphant over them in their midst. He allowed Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego to be cast

into a burning furnace. He wanted them to walk through it without even the smell of fire on them. He

tells us, not to walk in paths without dragons and adders. But, we shall walk through the midst of them,

and "tread them under our feet."”

And how much more glorious a kingdom is this than any outward rule or control could be! To be a

king inside, but a slave outside, is a great triumph. It is the best our hearts can conceive. To be destitute,

afflicted, and tormented. To be stoned, torn apart, and slain with the sword. To wander in sheepskins

and goatskins, and in deserts, mountains, dens, and caves. Yet, through it all, to be kings in a kingdom

of righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Ghost. This is a kingdom that none but God could give,

and none but God-like souls could receive.

We have seen or heard of a few such kings. All hearts have acknowledged their unconscious effect. I

read about one of the members of the St. Cyr monastery. Their devotion made the monasteries and their

superiors hate them. They were cast out as evil from their community. One was sent as a prisoner to a

monastery where his enemies dwelt. There, he suffered cruel and degrading treatment. Although he

came from a noble background and was a former leader, he had to do the simplest tasks . He was forced

to carry a heavy burden on his back and made to beg with a sign on his chest saying he was the worst

of the worst. But, through it all, the saint's spirit triumphed. Nothing disturbed his calm or soured his

Christ-like sweetness.

For his persecutors, he never had anything but words of kindness and smiles of love. At last, by the

divine kingdom's great power, he won all hearts. He became the trusted friend and adviser, and the

beloved ruler of his former enemies who had once delighted in persecuting him. “Blessed are the meek,

for they shall inherit the earth” (Mathew 5:5) . By his meekness, he conquered and became king. At

one time, a dangerous criminal was sent to the monastery for imprisonment. He was so violent that no

bonds sufficed to bind him, and no strength could control him. At last, he was taken to the cell of a

brother from St. Cyr. They were shut up together. Even the stolid monks recognized that divine

meekness. It had a power to conquer that surpassed all they knew. The saint received the violent man

as a beloved brother and smiled upon him with heavenly kindness.

But the criminal returned it with abuse and violence. He broke the monk’s furniture and destroyed his

bed, he kicked him, beat him, and tore his hair, and spat upon him. He exhausted himself in his violence

against him. Through it all, the monk resisted nothing.

He spoke only words of love. Finally, the criminal, worn out with fury, paused to catch his breath. The

beaten and outraged man then smiled at his persecutor with deep love and compassion. It was as if he

wanted to comfort him for his misery. It was more than the criminal could bear. Hatred, revenge, and

anger he could repay in kind. But, he had no weapons against such love and meekness. His heart was

conquered. He fell at the feet of the saint and washed them with his tears, as he entreated forgiveness

for his cruelty, and vowed a lifelong loyalty to his service.

And from that moment all trouble with that criminal was over. He followed the saint about like a loving

and faithful dog, eager to do or to be anything the other might desire. When his prison term ended, the

gates opened. He could not be induced to leave, for he could not bear to leave the man who had saved

him by love. Of such a nature is kingship in this kingdom of heaven. Each soul can make the application

for itself, without need of comment from me.

In ( Mathew 5: 6-7), we have the King of this kingdom describing the characteristics of His kingdom

and giving the laws for Hi s subjects. “Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for

they shall be satisfied. “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall receive mercy. “Not the rich, or great,

or wise, or learned. But the poor in spirit, the meek, the merciful, the pure in heart, those who mourn,

and those who hunger and thirst. Also, the persecuted, reviled, and slandered. All such belong to this

kingdom. These kings are gentle, yielding, meek, and charitable. They reign with that power.

One Christian asked anoth er, “How can I make people respect me?” “I would command their respect,”

was the reply. This meant, not that he should demand, "Respect me!" But, he should act, live, and be,

so that all would respect him. Men can win a show of respect by being tyrannical. But, to rule their

hearts, they must try other methods.

Our Lord developed this thought to some who wished to share His throne. He called them to Him, and

said, “But Jesus called them to him and said, “You know that the rulers of the Gentiles lord it o ver

them, and their great ones exercise authority over them.”(Mathew 20:25). But it shall not be so among

you. Whoever wants to be great must be your minister. Whoever wants to be first must be the servant

of all. For even the Son of man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give his life a

ransom for many.”

From a human view, only one man reigns. He is the one who can be lord over those around him.

From the divine standpoint the soul that serves is the soul that reigns.

Not he who demands most, receives this inward crowning, but he who gives up most. What greater

leadership can be imagined than Christ's in the Sermon on the Mount? “But I say to you, do not resist

the one who is evil. But if anyone slaps you on the right cheek, turn to him the other also . ” If someone

sues you and takes your shirt, give them your coat too . And if anyone forces you to go one mile, go

with him two miles. (Mathew 5:39)

Surely only a soul that is in harmony with God can mount such a throne of dominion as this! But this

is our destiny. We are made for this purpose. We are born of a kingly race, and are heirs to this

Inexpressible kingdom; “ and if children, then heirs — heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ,

provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him .”(Romans 8:17) With that

we could realize this, and, see in every act of service or surrender, an upward step. It would lead us to

our kingdom and throne! I mean this in a very practical sense. I mean that our daily, humble tasks and

small sacrifices, if done well, will be steps up a ladder to our thrones. If we are faithful over the "few

things" of our earthly kingdom, we shall be made rulers over the "many things" of the heavenly

kingdom.

He who serves and suffers for Christ will reign with Him. He will be the "chiefest" in His kingdom of

love. Knowing this, who would hesitate to turn the other cheek? A kingdom and a throne are to be won.

Joseph was a type of all this. In slavery and in prison he reigned as king, as truly as when seated on

Pharaoh’s throne or riding in Pharaoh’s chariot. (See Gen. 39:6) “So he left all that he had in Joseph’s

charge, and because of him he had no concern about anything but the food he ate. Now Joseph was

handsome in form and appearance.”

(Genesis 39:22- 23.) “ And the keeper of the prison put Joseph in charge of all the prisoners who were

in the prison. Whatever was done there, he was the one who did it. The keeper of the prison paid no

attention to anything that was in Joseph’s charge, beca use the LORD was with him. And whatever he

did, the LORD made it succeed.” He became the greatest by being the least, the chiefest by being

servant of all.

Dear reader, are you ruling in this way, in this kind of kingdom? Are you the greatest in your small

world — at home, church, or in your social circle? Then be the least. Be the servant of everyone. If not,

your kingdom is not Christ’s kingdom, and your throne is not shared with Him. Accessing the secrets

and power of this inner kingdom is not a fantasy . It’s not just an imagined victory. It’s a real and true

way of reigning. It will make you rise above the world and its concerns. You will move through it,

unaffected by its praise or criticism. You will live in a place of peace and victory that the world can

neither give nor take away.

“For the kingdom of God is not in word but in power.” It is not a talk but a fact , and those who are in

it recognize their kingship and prove it by reigning. But perhaps thou will say, “How can I enter into

this kingdom , if I am not already in?” Let our Lord himself answer you:

“At that time the disciples came to Jesus, saying, 'Who is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven? ”

(Mathew 18:1) “And calling to him a child, he put him in the midst of them and said , 'Truly, I say to

you, unless you turn and become like children, you will never enter the kingdom of heaven. Whoever

humbles himself like this child is the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.”(Mathew 18:2 -3)

It is a kingdom of childlike hearts, and only such can en ter it. To be a “little child” means simply to be

one. I cannot describe it better than this. We all know little children.

We delight in their simplicity, trust, and carelessness. We admire their unquestioning obedience to

authority. To be the greatest in this divine kingdom, one must have the most of this child's trusting,

tender, and obedient heart. It is guileless and self-forgetting.

“Not everyone who says to me, ‘Lord, Lord,’ will enter the kingdom of heaven, but the one who does

the will of my Fa ther who is in heaven.”( Matthew 7:21 ) .It is not saying, but doing, that will avail us

here. We must be a child, or we cannot sit on the child’s throne. And to be a child means to do the

Father’s will, since the very essence of true childhood is the spirit of obedience united to the spirit of

trust.

Become a little child. Set aside your greatness, self-assertion, and wisdom. Give up your strength and

self-dependence. Consent to die to your old self. Be born again into the kingdom of God. The only way

out of one life into another is by a death to one and a new birth into the other. It is the old story,

therefore, reiterated so often and in so many different ways, of through death to life. Die, then, that you

my live. Lose your own life that you may find Christ’s life.

They can only enter the butterfly's kingdom by dying to its caterpillar life, and then becoming a

butterfly. Likewise, we can only enter God's kingdom by dying to the kingdom of self, and then rising

to life in Christ. Let go of everything natural. This includes your ideas, plans, and thoughts. Instead,

accept God's plans, ways, and thoughts. Do this faithfully and persistently. You shall, at last, sit on His

throne and reign with Him in an eternal kingdom. It will break and consume all other kingdoms, and

stand forever.

There is no other way. This kingdom can't be entered through pride, appearance, or power . It can only

be entered by littleness, helplessness, childlikeness, babyhood, and death. Only he who humbles

himself shall be exalted. To share Christ's throne, we must first follow Him in suffering, loss, and

crucifixion. If we suffer with him, we shall also reign with Him.

Not as an arbitrary reward for our suffering, but as the result that will follow in the very nature of

things. Christ's loss must bring Christ's gain. His death must bring His resurrection. To follow Him in

the regeneration will, without fail, bring the soul that follows to His crown and throne. In a volume of

sermons for children, I have found a vivid illustration of this royal kingdom: –

A young boy from one of the refuges in England had risked his life to save his friend. The Queen of

England had sent him a medal through one of her earls. His friends pushed him forward to receive it,

as he was shy and nervous and tried to step away.

Look at the honorable chairman. He had come from the House of Lords, where earls, dukes, and

distinguished men like lawyers, judges, statesmen, and warriors were gathered. Royal princes were

also there. Yet, all peer though he was, he was moved. He murmured, "I have the honor," and pinned

the lifesaving medal on the child's jacket. His heart was full. He paused to swallow down something

that would rise in his throat before he could go on.

There is the 'glory and honor' of statesmen, warriors, and lawyers. But the glory of selfless lifesaving

excels all. That was the wondrous glory won by this boy." He had plunged into the stream and shared

a drowning boy's risk. That little hand, look at it there, steadying him by holding the table, had come

out holding the saved.

“Why has self -forgetfulness such mighty power? How was it that a twelve-year old boy could bow

down an audience of grown men before him? What gave to that brow, that it’s stubby crown of carroty

hair, a glory and honor more than the luster of gold and jewels?

Why did that small body in its little breeches and jacket, wiping its tears on the rough little sleeve, grip

thousands of hearts? Why did it make them, for a time, loyal subjects of its kingdom?

Why was all this so? It was so because that little boy had been like Christ, in his spirit of selfless

sacrifice for others." He had some of the beauty we are meant to worship. It is the glory that makes

angels shout. All of heaven falls and adores. They say, " saying with a loud voice, Worthy is the Lamb

who was slain, to receive power and wealth and wisdom and might and honor and glory and

blessing!”( Revelations 5:12) .The Lamb that was slain is the mightiest King ever. All who share His

spirit are in His kingdom. This kingdom is not a place, but a character. So, those without that character

cannot be in it.

We pray daily, “Your kingdom come.” Do we know what we are praying for? Do we comprehend the

change it will make in us if it comes in us? Are we willing to be so changed? What is the kingdom of

God but the rule of God? And what is the rule of God but the will of God? Therefore, when we pray,

“Your will be done on earth as it is in heaven,” we have touched the secret of it all. A group of savages

might take over a kingdom by force, but to truly control its civilization, they must follow its rules. The

same is true for the kingdom of heaven. It only grants its power to those who obey its laws. “ The one

who conquers, I will grant him to sit with me on my throne, as I also conquered and sat down with my Father

on his throne . ”( Revelation 3:21 ) “He always reigns who sides with God,” says an old writer. And again,

“He who perfectly accepts the will of God, dwells in a perpetual kingdom.”

Are you reigning after this fashion and in this sort of a kingdom? Are you the most important by being

the servant of all? Are you a king over your circumstances, or do your circumstances reign over you?

Do you triumph over your temptations, or do your temptations triumph over you? Can you sit on an

inward throne in the midst of outward defeat and loss?

Can you conquer by yielding, and become the greatest by being the least? If you can’t answer yes to

all these questions, then you can’t come into his kingdom. "Whatever yo ur lot or men's opinions, you

are among those whom our Lord calls 'the greatest in the kingdom of heaven.'"

fields.title: Chapter 20. The Chariots Of God
fields.body_html:
God's chariots are spiritual vehicles, often disguised as trials or hardships that carry

the soul to victory and spiritual growth. Unlike visible, earthly chariots, these divine

chariots are unseen and require faith to recognize. By embracing life’s challenges as

Through God’s means of uplifting us, we can rise above difficulties and experience spiritual

triumph. Trusting in God’s invisible power leads to true victory.

“The chariots of God are twice ten thousand, thousands upon thousands; the Lord is among them; Sinai

is now in the sanctuary. (Psalm 68:17.)

hariots are for transportation and moving forward. Earthly chariots carry their riders to their

destinations, overcoming all obstacles. God's chariots carry their souls. No words can express the

glorious places to which that soul shall arrive who travels in the chariots of God. And our verse tells

us t hey are “very many.” All around us on every side they wait for us; but we, sadly,

we do not always see them. Earth’s chariots are always visible, but God’s chariots are Invisible.

“So he sent there horses and chariots and a great army, and they came by night and surrounded the city.

When the servant of the man of God rose early in the morning and went out, behold, an army with

horses and chariots was all around the city. And the servant said, “Alas, my master! What shall we do?

He said, “Do not be afraid, for those who are with us are more than those who are with them. “Then

Elisha prayed and said, “O Lord, please open his eyes that he may see.” So the Lord opened the eyes

of the young man, and he saw, and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire all

around Elisha.” (2 Kings 6:14 -17)

C

This is the prayer we need to pray for ourselves and for one another, “Lord, open our eyes that we may

see.” For the world all around us is full of God’s horses and chariots, waiting to carry us to plac es of

glorious victory. But they do not look like chariots. They look instead like enemies, sufferings, trials,

defeats, misunderstandings, disappointments, unkindnesses. They look like massive cars of misery,

waiting to crush us. But they are chariots of triumph. They can take us to the heights of victory our

souls long for.

If we would “ride on the high places of the earth , ” we must get into the chariots that can take us there;

and only the “chariots of God” are equal to such lofty riding as this . (Deuteronomy 32:12-13)

“The Lord alone guided him ; no foreign god was with him. He made him ride on the high places of

the land, and he ate the produce of the field, and he suckled him with honey out of the rock, and oil out

of the flinty rock.”

“Then you shall take delight in the Lord, and I will make you ride on the heights of the earth. I will

feed you with the heritage of Jacob, your father, for the mouth of the Lord has spoken. (Isaiah 58:14).

We may make out of each event in our lives either a Juggernaut car to crush us, or a chariot in which

to ride to heights of victory. It all depends upon how we take them; whether we lie down under our

trials and let them roll over and crush us, or whether we climb up into them as into a chariot, and make

them carry us triumphantly onward and upward.

“And as they still went on and talked, behold, chariots of fire and horses of fire separated the two of

them. And Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven. And Elisha saw it and he cried, “My father, my

father! The chariots of Israel and its horsemen! And he saw him no more. Then he took hold of his own

clothes and tore them in two pieces.”(2Kings 2:11 - 12).Whenever we mount into God’s chariots , the

same thing happens to us spiritually that happened to Elisha. We shall have a translation. Not into the

heavens above us, as Elisha did, but into the heaven within us, which, after all, is almost a grander

translation than his. We shall be carried up away from the low earthly groveling plane of life, where

everything hurts and everything is unhappy, up into the “heavenly places in Christ Jesus,” where we

shall ride in triumph over all below.

“And raised us with him and seated us with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus ,” (Ephesians

2:6). These “heavenly places” a re interior, not exterior, and the road that leads to them is also interior.

But the chariot that carries the soul over this road is generally some outward loss, or trial, or

disappointment; some chastening that does not indeed seem for the present to be joyous, but grievous;

but that nevertheless afterward yielded the peaceable fruits of righteousness to them that are exercised

thereby.

“And have you forgotten the exhortation that addresses you as sons? My son, do not regard lightly the

discipline of the Lord, nor be weary when reproved by him. For the Lord disciplines the one he loves,

and chastises every son whom he receives. It is for discipline that you have to endure. God is treating

you as sons. For what son is there whom his father does not discipline? If you are left without discipline,

in which all have participated, then you are illegitimate children and not sons. Besides this, we have

had earthly fathers who disciplined us, and we respected them. Shall we not much more be subject to

the Father of spirits and live? For they disciplined us for a short time as it seemed best to them, but he

disciplines us for our good, that we may share his holiness. For the moment, all discipline seems painful

rather than pleasant, but later it yields the peaceful fruit of righteousness to those who have been trained

by it.”( Hebrews 12:5-11).

Look upon these scoldings , no matter how grievous they may be for the present, as God’s chariots sent

to carry your souls into the “high places” of spiritual achievem ent and uplifting, and you will find that

they are, after all, “paved with love.”

“King Solomon made himself a carriage from the wood of Lebanon. He made its posts of silver, its

back of gold, its seat of purple; its interior was inlaid with love by the daughters of Jerusalem.” (Song

of Solomon 3:9-10 ). Your own individual chariot may look very unlovely. It may be a cross-grained

relative or friend; it may be the result of human malice, or cruelty, or neglect; but every chariot sent by

God must necessari ly be paved with love, since God is love, and God’s love is the sweetest, softest,

tenderest thing to rest one’s self upon that was ever found by any soul anywhere. It is His love indeed

that sends the chariot.

“Was your wrath against the rivers, O Lord ? Was your anger against the rivers, or your indignation

against the sea, when you rode on your horses, on your chariot of salvation? You stripped the sheath

from your bow, calling for many arrows. Selah, you split the earth with rivers. The mountains saw you

and writhed; the raging waters swept on; the deep gave forth its voice; it lifted its hands on high. The

sun and moon stood still in their place at the light of your arrows as they sped, at the flash of your

glittering spear. You marched through the earth in fury; you threshed the nations in anger. You went

out for the salvation of your people, or the salvation of your anointed. (Habakkuk.3:8-13)

Here, the prophet tells us that it was God’s displeasure against the obstacles that beset the path of His

people that made Him come to their rescue, riding in His “chariots of salvation.” Everything becomes

a “chariot of salvation” when God rides upon it. The “clouds” that darken our skies and seem to shut

out the shining of the sun of righteousness are, after all, if we only knew it, His chariots, into which we

may mount with Him, and “ride prosperously” over all the darkness.

“Gird your sword on your thigh, O mighty one, in your splendor and majesty! In your majesty ride out

victoriously for the cause of truth and meekness and righteousness; let your right hand teach you

awesome deeds!”(Psalm 45:3 - 4). “He rode on a cherub and flew; he came swiftly on the wings of the

wind.” ((Psalm 18:10). “There is none like God, O Jeshurun, who rides through the heaven s to your

help, through the skies in his majesty.” (Deuteronomy 33:26). A late writer has said that we cannot, by

even the most vigorous and toilsome efforts, sweep away the clouds, but we can climb so high above

them as to reach the clear atmosphere overhead; and he who rides with God rides upon the heavens far

above all earth-born clouds.

“O kingdoms of the earth, sing to God; sing praises to the Lord, Selah to him who rides in the heavens,

the ancient heavens; behold, he sends out his voice, his mighty voice. Ascribe power to God, whose

majesty is over Israel, and whose power is in the skies.”(Psalm 68:32 -34 ) . This may sound fanciful,

but it is really exceedingly practical when we begin to act it out in our daily lives.

I knew a lady who had a very slow servant. She was excellent in every way and very useful. But her

slowness irritated her naturally quick mistress.

The lady would get angry with the girl twenty times a day. And, twenty times, she would regret it and

try to control her anger. But it was in vain. Her life was made miserable by the conflict. One day, it

occurred to her that she had, for a long while, been praying for patience. Perhaps this slow servant was

the very chariot the Lord had sent to carry her soul into patience. She immediately accepted it as such,

and from that time used the slowness of her servant as a chariot for her soul. And the result was a

victory of patience that no slowness of anybody was ever able to disturb.

At one of our conventions, I knew a sister who had to sleep in a room with two others because of the

crowd. She wanted to sleep, but they wanted to talk. The first night, she was disturbed. She lay there,

feeling frustrated and upset, long after the others had quieted down. She could have slept. But the next

day, she heard about God’s chariots. That night, she decided to see the talking sisters as her chariots.

They would help her learn sweetness and patience. She lay there, feeling peaceful and calm. But it got

very late, and they should all have been as leep. So, she quietly said, “Sisters, I’m lying here riding in

a chariot.” This brought complete silence. Her chariot had carried her to victory, both inside and out.

If we choose to ride in God’s chariots, not our own, we would experience the same.

“ Woe to those who go down to Egypt for help and rely on horses, who trust in chariots because they

are many and in horsemen because they are very strong, but do not look to the Holy One of Israel or

consult the Lord! And yet he is wise and brings disaster; he does not call back his words, but will arise

against the house of the evildoers and against the helpers of those who work iniquity. The Egyptians

are man, and not God, and their horses are flesh, and not spirit. When the Lord stretches out his hand,

the helper will stumble, and he who is helped will fall, and they will all perish together. (Isaiah 31:1-

3)

“Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the Lord our God. They collapse

and fall, but we rise and stand upright. ” (Psalm. 20:7 -8). Our constant temptation is to trust in the

“chariots of Egypt.” We can see them. They are real and look substantial. But, God's chariots are

invisible and intangible. It's hard to believe they are there. Our eyes are not opened to see them.

“By your messengers you have mocked the Lord, and you have said, ‘with my many chariots I have

gone up the heights of the mountains, to the far recesses of Lebanon; I felled its tallest cedars, its

choicest cypresses; I entered its farthest lodging place, its most fruitful forest.” We try to reach the high

places with the “multitude of our chariots.” We first depend on one thing, then another. We do this to

improve our spirit and gain spiritual victories. We “go down to Egypt for help.” (2 Kings 19: 23).

And God is obliged often to destroy all our own chariots before he can bring us to the point of mounting

into His.

“And in that day, declares the Lord, I will cut off your horses from among you and will destroy your

chariots ;”( Micah 5:10). “An d to overthrow the throne of kingdoms. I am about to destroy the strength

of the kingdoms of the nations, and overthrow the chariots and their riders. And the horses and their

riders shall go down, everyone by the sword of his brother.” (Haggai. 2:22) .We rely too much on a

dear friend to aid our spiritual growth. So, the Lord must separate us from that friend. We believe our

spiritual growth relies on a favorite preacher's ministry. Now, we are mysteriously removed. We see

our prayer-meeting or Bible-class as our main source of spiritual strength. Now, we are unable to attend

it. And the “chariot of God,” which alone can carry us to the places where we hoped to be taken by the

instrumentalities upon which we have been depending, is to be found in the very deprivations we have

so mourned over. God must burn up with the fire of His love every chariot of our own that stands in

the way of our mounting into His.

“For behold, the Lord will come in fire, and his chariots like the whirlwind, to render his anger in fury,

and his rebuke with flames of fire.”(Isaiah. 66:15) .Let us be thankful, then, for every trial that will

help to destroy our chariots, and will compel us to take refuge in the chariot of God, which stands ready

and waiting beside us.

“For God alone, O my soul, wait in silence, for my hope is from him. He only is my rock and my

salvation, my fortress; I shall not be shaken. On God rests my salvation and my glory; my mighty rock,

my refuge is God. Trust in him at all times, O people; pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge

for us. Selah.” (Psalm. 62:5 -8).We have to be brought to the place where all other refuges fail us, before

we can say, He only. We say, He and something else.

"His, and my experience," or "my church relationships," or "my Christian work"; and all that comes

after the "and" must be taken away from us, or must be proved useless, before we can come to "He

only."” As long as visible chariots are at hand, the soul will not mount into the invisible ones.

“Sing to God, si ng praises to his name; lift up a song to him who rides through the deserts; his name

is the Lord; exult before him!” (Psalm. 68:4).If we want to ride with God “upon the heavens,” we have

to be brought to an end of all riding upon the earth.

“Your procession is seen, O God, the procession of my God, my King, into the sanctuary.” (Psalm.

68:24). To see God’s goings, we must get into the sanctuary of his presence; and to share in His goings

and go with Him, we must abandon all earthly goings.

“A man’s steps are from the Lord; how then can man understand his way?”(Proverbs.20:24). “My

steps have held fast to your paths; my feet have not slipped.”(Psalm. 17:5).

“I waited patiently for the Lord; he inclined to me and heard my cry.”(Psalm.40:1). When we m ount

into God’s chariot our goings are “established,” for no obstacles can hinder its triumphal course. All

losses therefore are gains that bring us to this.

“But whatever gain I had, I counted as loss for the sake of Christ. Indeed, I count everything as loss

because of the surpassing worth of knowing Christ Jesus my Lord. For his sake I have suffered the loss

of all things and count them as rubbish, in order that I may gain Christ and be found in him, not having

a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the

righteousness from God that depends on faith.” (Philippians.3:7 -9). Paul understood this, and he gloried

in the losses which brought him such unspeakable gain.

“So to keep me from becoming co nceited because of the surpassing greatness of the revelations, a

thorn was given me in the flesh, a messenger of Satan to harass me, to keep me from becoming

conceited. Three times I pleaded with the Lord about this, that it should leave me. But he said to me,

“My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.” Therefore I will boast all

the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me. For the sake of Christ,

then, I am content with weaknesses, insults, hardships, persecutions, and calamities. For when I am

weak, then I am strong.” (2 Corinthians.12:7 -10)

Even the "thorn in the flesh," the messenger of Satan sent to trouble him, became just a chariot for his

willing heart, taking him to victories he could not have reached otherwise. To "take pleasure" in one’s

struggles — what is that if not turning them into the greatest of chariots?

Joseph dreamed of his future triumphs and reign. But, to the eye of sense, the chariots that carried him

there were bitter failures. It was a strange road to a kingdom. It went through slavery and a prison. Yet,

there was no other way for Joseph to reach his triumph. His dream, Gen. 37:5- 10 “Now Joseph had a

dream, and when he told it to his brothers they hated him even more. He said to them, “Hear this dream

that I have dreamed: Behold, we were binding sheaves in the field, and behold, my sheaf arose and

stood upright. And behold, your sheaves gathered around it and bowed down to my sheaf.” His brothers

said to him, Are you indeed to reign over us? Or are you indeed to rule over us? So they hated him

even more for his dreams and for his words. Then he dreamed another dream and told it to his brothers

and said, Behold, I have dreamed another dream. Behold, the sun, the moon, and eleven stars were

bowing down to me. But when he told it to his father and to his brothers, his father rebuked him and

said to him, what is this dream that you have dreamed? Shall I and your mother and your brothers

indeed come to bow ourselves to t he ground before you?”

His chariots, Genesis. 37:19- 20 “They said to one another, “Here comes this dreamer. Come now, let

us kill him and throw him into one of the pits. Then we will say that a fierce animal has devoured him,

and we will see what will b ecome of his dreams.” Genesis 27:28 “May God give you of the dew of

heaven and of the fatness of the earth and plenty of grain and wine.” Genesis 39:19 -20

“As soon as his master heard the words that his wife spoke to him, “This is the way your servant treated

me,” his anger was kindled. And Joseph’s master took him and put him into the prison, the place where

the king’s prisoners were confined, and he was there in prison.” And Joseph’s master took him and put

him into the prison, the place where the ki ng’s prisoners were confined, and he was there in prison;

how he rode in his chariots, Genesis. 39:1- 6 “Now Joseph had been brought down to Egypt, and

Potiphar, an officer of Pharaoh, the captain of the guard, an Egyptian, had bought him from the

Ishmaelites who had brought him down there. The Lord was with Joseph, and he became a successful

man, and he was in the house of his Egyptian master. His master saw that the Lord was with him and

that the Lord caused all that he did to succeed in his hands. So Joseph found favor in his sight and

attended him, and he made him overseer of his house and put him in charge of all that he had. From

the time that he made him overseer in his house and over all that he had, the Lord blessed the Egyptian’s

house for Joseph’s sake; the blessing of the Lord was on all that he had, in house and field. So he left

all that he had in Joseph’s charge, and because of him he had no concern about anything but the food

he ate.”

Genesis 39:21- 23 “ But the LORD was with Joseph and showed him steadfast love and gave him favor

in the sight of the keeper of the prison. And the keeper of the prison put Joseph in charge of all the

prisoners who were in the prison. Whatever was done there, he was the one who did it. The keeper of

the prison paid no attention to anything that was in Joseph’s charge, because the LORD was with him.

And whatever he did, the LORD made it succeed .” His triumph.

And now a word as to how one is to mount into these chariots. My answer would be simply this: Find

out where God is in each one of them, and hide yourself in Him. Or, in other words, do what the little

child does when trouble comes, who finds its mother and hides in her arms. The real chariot, after all

that, that takes us triumphantly through is the carrying of God.

Isaiah. 46:4 “Even to your old age I am he, and to gray hairs I will carry you. I have made, and I will

bear; I will carry and will save.” The baby carried in the chariot of its mother’s arms rides triumphantly

through the hardest places and does not even know they are hard.

Isaiah. 63: 9 “ In all their affliction he was afflicted, and the angel of his presence saved them; in his

love and in his pity he redeemed them; he lifted them and carried them all the days of old.”.And how

much more w e, who are carried in the chariot of the “arms of God.” Get into your chariot, then. Take

each thing that is wrong in your lives as God’s chariot for you. No matter who built the wrong, it is

now God's chariot for you. It must carry you to a heavenly place of triumph. Shut out all the second

causes, and find the Lord in it. Say, “Lord, open my eyes that I may see, not the visible enemy, but thy

unseen chariots of deliverance.”

Accept His will in the trial, whatever it may be, and hide yourself in His arm s of love. Say, “Your will

be done; Your will be done!” over and over.

Shut out every other thought but the one thought of submission to His will and of trust in His love.

Make your trial your chariot. Then, your soul will "ride upon the heavens" with God in a way you never

dreamed possible.

I have no doubt. If our eyes were opened, we would see our homes, businesses, and streets filled with

the "chariots of God." There is no need for any of us to walk for lack of chariots.
