That cross inmate of your household, who has made life a burden, may henceforth be a glorious chariot.

It will carry you to the heights of heavenly patience and longsuffering. Your misunderstanding,

mortification, unkindness, disappointment, loss, and defeat are chariots. They wait to carry you to the

heights of victory you have longed for.

Then, with thankful hearts, mount into them. Lose sight of all second causes in the shining of His love.

He will carry you in His arms, ensuring your safety and celebrating victory over it all.

fields.title: Chapter 21. Without Me You Can Do Nothing
fields.body_html:
Living in constant union with Christ means doing all things for His glory, recognizing

His presence in both spiritual and everyday tasks. Without Christ, we can do nothing.

True divine union involves relying on Him for strength, transforming even mundane

actions into acts of worship and bringing peace and rest.

bout The Life Of Divine Union In its practical Aspects. Not long ago, I was driving with a

preacher from the Religious Society of Friends through our lovely Philadelphia Park. Our talk

turned to the fruitlessness of much modern church preaching. We had, of course, discussed the

lack of the Holy Ghost. But, we felt it did not explain everything. We both knew many Spirit-

baptized preachers who had no fruit from their ministry. I suggested that one reason might be this.

Many ministers, when preaching or discussing religion, adopt a different tone and manner. This style

removes religion from ordinary life. It fails to reach the hearts of those who live for simple pleasures

and duties.

"Now, for instance," I said. "If, in your preaching from the Friends' gallery, you could use the same

tone and manner as you present one, how much more effectual and convincing your preaching would

be." "Oh, but I could not do that," was the reply. "The preacher's gallery is so much more solemn a

place than this." "But why is it more solemn?"” I asked. "Is it not God's presence that makes the gallery

and pulpit solemn? And, is it not here as well?" "Is it not just as solemn to live our daily lives as it is

to preach? Should we not do the one to His glory as much as the other? I then added, as the subject

opened before me, "I believe a large part of the difficulty lies in the unscriptural and unnatural divorce

between our so-called religious life and our so-called temporal life. It's as if our religion were separate

from us. It's a garment to put on and off as we wish.

A

On Sundays, and in church, we seek and worship God. So, we must show our religious life in a solemn

way. But, our strained gravity and decorum deprive it of half its power. But on Mondays, we seek our

own interests. So, we shed our work life and, with relief, live it. This is more natural and powerful.

The thoughts that started remained with me and gathered strength. Soon after, I attended a meeting.

The leader read John 15:5. The words, "am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and

I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing," amazed me.

I had read those words hundreds of times. I thought I understood them. But now, they seemed newly

inserted in the Bible. They were ablaze with wondrous meaning.

"There it is," I said to myself. Jesus himself said so. Apart from Him, we have no real life, whether

temporal or spiritual. Therefore, all living or doing without Him is 'nothing,' as God, who sees all, calls

it. Then, I wondered if anyone truly believed this. If they did, did they apply it in their daily lives? In

an instant, I saw that the secret of divine union lay in its practical side as much as in any inner

revelations. If I do nothing, literally nothing, apart from Christ, I am, of course, united to Him in a

continual, unquestionable oneness. But if I live and work apart from Him, I have no real union, no

matter how exalted my emotions about it may be.

It is to consider this aspect of the subject, therefore, that the present paper is written. I am sure that the

wide divorce I spoke of, between things spiritual and things temporal, has done more than almost

anything else to hinder a true union with God. It has made religion seem so outside of common life that

it is almost unattainable to most people. It has made the experience of Christians stiff and unnatural. It

seems to shut them out from the free, happy, childlike ease that belongs to the children of God.

I feel, therefore, that it is of vital importance for us to understand the truth of this matter. The thought

that makes it clearest to me is this: our oneness with Christ contains the whole thing in a nutshell. If

we are one with Him, then of course, in the very nature of things, we can do nothing without Him. For

that which is one cannot act as being two. If I do anything without Christ, then I am not one with Him

in that thing. Like a branch severed from the vine, I am withered and worthless. The branch should

know it depends on the vine for its growth, fruit, and climbing. But it might feel it could grow and

climb over a fence or around a tree. So, it might sever its connection with the vine for that part of its

life.

Of course that which sought an independent life would wither and die in the very nature of things.

And just so is it with us who are branches of Christ the true vine. We can do nothing, great or small,

without withering and death. The same is true for a branch of the natural vine. It will show us, at once,

how fatal is the divorce I have spoken of, to the oneness with Christ, for which our souls hunger. We

all know, more or less, that we cannot live our religious life without Him. But, in our socalled temporal

life, who thinks our daily tasks should be done for Christ? Tasks like keeping house, doing business,

making calls, darning stockings, sweeping, trimming a bonnet, or entertaining guests.

Only those who abide in Him and do them in His strength can do them rightly.

If it is Christ in the Christian leading the prayer meeting, then they are one. So, it must also be Christ

in the Christian who is to keep the house and make the bargain. So, one duty is as religious as the other.

It is the man that makes the action, not the action the man.

If we "acknowledge God in all our ways," we will make our daily life as solemn and sweet as our

religious occasions. We should do everything, even eating and drinking, for His glory.

If our religion is truly our life, it must be in everything we do. No act, however human or natural, can

escape its control and guidance. If God is always with us, He is with us in our business and social times

as much as in our religious times. His presence is as solemn in one moment as in another.

If we for ‘In him we live and move and have our being’; as even some of your own poets have said,

‘for we are indeed his offspring " (Acts 17:28), then we can do nothing without Him, whether we know

it or not. And facts are stubborn things, thank God, and do not alter for all our feelings. In Psalm 127:1-

2 ‘’unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the Lord watches over the

city, the watchman stays awake in vain. It is in vain that you rise early and go late to rest, eating the

bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep. ” We have a very striking illustration of this

truth. The Psalmist says, "Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it labor in vain. Unless the

Lord keeps the city, the watchman wakes in vain." It is vain for you to rise early, to sit up late, and to

eat the bread of sorrows; for so He gives His beloved sleep.” The two things, done in vain unle ss the

Lord is in them, are purely secular. They are simple business matters on the human plane of life. The

lesson is only impressive for this: It proved God's presence in temporal things. Those were undeniable

facts.

In truth, the Bible is full of this fact, and the only wonder is how any believer in the Bible could have

overlooked it. God is present in all daily life, from building cities to counting hairs and noting a

sparrow's fall. He is the mainspring of it all. In all we do, even eating and drinking, we must do it for

Him and His glory. We are urged to live and walk in the light, so our works, both temporal and spiritual,

show they are "wrought in God."

This brings unspeakable comfort to every loving Christian heart. It turns all of life into a sacrament. It

makes the kitchen, workshop, nursery, and parlor as sacred a place of service to the Lord as the prayer

meeting, mission board, or charity visit.

A dear young Christian mother and housekeeper came to me, sorely grieved, because of her busy,

worldly life. “There seems,” she said, “to be nothing spiritual about my life from one week’s end to the

other. My large family of little children is so engrossing that I have no time for anything but attending

to them and my household duties. Each night, I go to bed sick at heart. I have felt separated from my

Lord all day and could do nothing for Him.” I told her what I wrote above. I assured her that all would

change if she would see and acknowledge God in these homely duties. She must recognize her total

dependence on Him to do them.

Her heart welcomed the good news with gladness. Months later, she told me that, from then on, life

had become a transformed and glorified thing. It was now filled with the Lord's presence and the

sweetness of serving Him.

Another Christian, a young lady from a fashionable family, came to me. She was in grief. Much of her

life, she felt separated from God and sensed no presence of Him. I told her to avoid anything that could

cause such a separation. But she assured me it was impossible. The things she meant were not wrong.

“For instance,” she said, “it is my duty to visit my mother. Yet, nothing separates me so much from

God as visits”

“But how would it be,” I asked, “if you visited as service to the Lord and for His glory?” “What!” she

exclaimed, “visits for God? I never heard of such a thing.” “But why not?” I asked, "If it is right to

make visits at all, it ought to be done for God. We are commanded to do all for His glory. If it is not

right, you ought not to do it." As a Christian,” I continued, “you must not do anything that you cannot

do for Him.” “I see! I see!” she exclaimed, after a little pause, “and it makes all life look so different!

“Nothing can separate me from Him but sin. But, any act done to His glory will draw me closer and

make His presence more real.”

These two instances will illustrate my meaning. I'm sure thousands of weary souls would be

transformed if they realized and acted on these truths. An old spiritual writer says, to become a saint,

we need not change our works. We must only aim them at God. We must do them for His glory, in His

strength. Before, we did them for ourselves, with our own power. This means what our Lord meant

when He said, "Without me you can do nothing."

There is another side to this truth. It is comforting. The Psalmist develops it in the verses I quoted. “It

is vain,” he says, “to rise early, to sit up late, and to eat the bread of sorrows.” Or, in other words,

“What is the use of all this worry and strain? “W ork will amount to nothing unless God is in it. If he

is, what folly to fret or be burdened? "His presence means He assumes care and responsibility for it

all." Ah, it is vain indeed, and I wish all of God's children knew it! We mothers ought to know it. "Our

ways with our children would teach us, if we had the 'eyes to see.' How many mothers have risen early,

sat up late, and eaten the bread of sorrows, just to give sleep to their beloved children?"

And how grieved their hearts would have been if, after all their pains, the children had refused to rest.

I can appeal to some mother hearts, I am sure, as thoroughly understanding my meaning. Memories

will arise of the rosy boy coming in at night, tired from play. His knees were out, and his coat was torn.

We stayed up late and rose early to patch it all. We wanted the cause of all the mischief to rest

undisturbed in happy childhood sleep.

How vain, and worse, would it have been for that beloved darling to have sat up late, risen early, and

eaten the bread of sorrows? His mother was doing it for him just so he wouldn't have to. If this is true

of mothers, it must be more so of their Maker. He came among us in bodily form to bear our burdens,

carry our sorrows, and do our work, so we might "enter into His rest."

“For whoever has entered God’s rest has also rested from his works as God did from his. ”(Hebrews

4:10). He has learned, at last, a lesson. Without Christ, he can do nothing. But, he can do all things

through Christ, who strengthens him. So, he has given up all self-effort. He has abandoned himself to

God to work in him to do His will. This and this only is the rest that remains for the people of God.

Scientific men are seeking to resolve all forces in nature into one primal force. Unity of origin is the

present cry of science. Light, heat, sound are all said to be the products of one force differently applied,

and that force is motion. All things, say the scientists, can be resolved back to this. I cannot say if they

are right or wrong. But, the Bible reveals a grand primal force behind motion. It is God's force. God is

at the source of everything, God is the origin of everything, and God is the explanation of everything.

Without Him was not anything made that was made, and without Him is not anything done that is done.

It is no mystery. It is a simple fact. Our Lord says, "Without me you can do nothing." Of Himself, He

said, “I can do nothing on my own." He meant that He and His Father were so one that any independent

action was impossible. It must be a glorious necessity between our souls and Christ. That is why He

said we could do nothing without Him. It means He has made us one with Himself. So, we cannot act

independently towards Him, as He could not towards His Father.

Dear Christian, do n’t you see here a glimpse of a wonderful glory? Let’s believe that without Him, we

can truly do nothing. We must believe it because it’s true. But let’s recognize this truth and start living

by it from now on. Let’s turn away from living apart from Christ. From now on, let’s acknowledge

Him in everything we do. Everything we do should be as a service to Him, for His glory. We rely on

Him alone for wisdom, strength, patience, and everything else we need to live well.

As I said before, it is not so much a change of acts that will be necessary, as a change of motive and of

dependence. The house will be kept, the children cared for, and the business run, perhaps as before.

Outwardly, it will be the same. But, inwardly, God will be acknowledged, depended on, and served.

There will be a great difference between a life of ease in His presence and a life of painful effort apart

from Him.

Bringing God into our affairs will yield many benefits. We will gain divine wisdom in their conduct.

There will be a greater speed in accomplishing them. We will see a surprising increase in our resources.

We will better grasp the true nature of things. And, we will expand in ways that will amaze our cramped

souls.

I mean this literally. The house will be nicer and easier to maintain. The children will learn faster. The

stockings will be mended quickly. The hosts will be better at entertaining guests. The servants will be

easier to manage. The deal will be more satisfying. And life will be sweeter and more peaceful. God

will be i n every moment of it, and when He’s present, everything goes well. In this simple way, the

soul will develop the habit of "abiding in Christ." His presence will become the most real thing in our

lives, and we will have a quiet, private connection with Him that brings us joy.

A child of God may ask, "What is the quickest way to reach the highest union with God in this life?"

There is no quicker way than the one I have been declaring. By the homely path of everyday duties

done thus in God and for God, the sublimest heights are reached. Not as a reward, but as a natural

result. If we abide in Him and refuse to leave Him, we shall be where He is. All that He is will be ours.

If you wish to know, dear reader, the divine union in your soul, start today to practice what I have

suggested.

Offer every moment and every action of your life to God. Say to Him, “Lord, I do this in you and for

your glory. You are my strength, my wisdom, and everything I need. I rely only on you.” Refuse to

live even for a single moment or do anything without Him. Keep doing this until it becomes a habit for

your soul. Soon, you will understand the deep desires of your soul, and they will be fulfilled in the

constant presence of Christ, your life within.

fields.title: Chapter 22. The One Hundred And Thirty-Ninth Psalm
fields.body_html:
In Psalm 139, we are reminded that God is always with us, no matter where we are or

what we're facing. His presence is constant, and He understands us completely,

offering love and care like a devoted parent. No darkness or difficulty can separate us

from Him, and His continual presence provides peace, security, and strength in every

circumstance.

our great hospitality surrounds us like a boundless sea. We cannot lose ourselves where all is

home, nor drift away from you.”

Very few of us understand the full meaning of the words in Matthew. 1:23, “Behold, the virgin shall

conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel . ” This short sentence reveals the world's

greatest truth. God, the Almighty Creator of Heaven and Earth, is not a distant god in a glorious Heaven.

He lives with us, in our poor, helpless lives, as close as we are to ourselves. This seems so incredible

to the human heart that we are slow to believe it. But, the Bible teaches it as fact, from cover to cover.

Any honest mind cannot deny this.

In the very beginning of Genesis we read of the “presence of the Lord God amongst the trees of the

garden.” Since then, He is always revealed to us. He has a daily, close relationship with His peop le

everywhere. In Exodus we find Him asking them to make Him a “sanctuary that He might dwell among

them.” He is recorded as having "walked" with them in the wilderness, and as "taking up His home"

with them in the Promised Land. He taught them to rely on Him as an ever-present Friend and Helper.

They should consult Him about all their affairs and give Him their lives. And finally, He came in Christ

in bodily form. He dwelt in the world as a man among men. He made Himself bone of our bone and

flesh of our flesh. He took upon Him our nature. He revealed to us, in the most real way, a great and

blessed truth. He intended to be with us always, even unto the end of the world.

Y

Those who believe this truth will find its solution. It will solve all their life's troubles. As a little girl, I

remember that, in trouble, my parents' arrival always relieved me. When I heard one say, "Daughter, I

am here," every burden dropped and every anxiety stilled. It was their simple presence that did it. They

did not need to promise to relieve me. They did not need to tell me their plans. Their presence was all

the assurance I required. It meant everything would be set right and all would go well for me.

After their arrival, I only wanted to see how they would do it.

They must be exceptional parents. Their children are very confident. I think they were. But our God is

exceptional. So, the application is absolute. His presence is all we need.

It would be enough for us, even if we had not a single promise nor a single revelation of His plans. The

Bible says, "I will be with you." It has stilled all questions and fears. Who can doubt it? He meant to

assure us that His infinite wisdom, love, and power are on our side. Over and over again in my

childhood, have the magic words, “Oh, there is mother!” It brought me relief and comfort. In my later

years, I've heard, "Oh, there is God!" spoken with reverence.” brought me a far more blessed

deliverance. With Him present, what could I have to fear? He has said, “ Keep your life free from love

of money, and be content with what you have, for he has said, 'I will never leave you nor forsake

you .”(Hebrews 13:5). So, I may boldly say, The Lord is my helper. I will not fear what man shall do

to me. I still recall the inspiring sense of security that came with my father's presence. I never feared

anything when he was by. And surely with my Heavenly Father by, there can be no possible room for

fear.

I seek to make clear and definite the fact of "Emmanuel, God with us." Its practical help and comfort

inspire me. I am sure that few of God's own children truly believe it. They may say they do. They may

repeat a thousand times, in a devout tone, "Oh, yes, we know that God is always present with us, but,

and in this "but," the whole story is told. There are no “buts” in the vocabulary of the soul that accepts

His presence as a literal fact. Such a soul is joyously triumphant over every suggestion of fear or of

doubt. It has God, and that is enough for it. His presence is its certain security and supply, always, and

for everything.

I beg my readers to turn with me to the 139th Psalm. There, we will find a blessed revelation of this

truth. The central thought of the Psalm is to be found in verses 7 to 12, “Where shall I go from your

Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed

in Sheol, you are there! If I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea,

even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me. If I say, “Surely the darkness

shall cover me, and the light about me be night,” even the darkness is not dark to you; the night is bright

as the day, for darkness is as light with you.”

This passage is the strongest proof of His constant presence with us, wherever we are or whatever we

do. People seek to be in the Lord's presence. But they cannot escape it. There is no place in the universe

where He is not. Not in heaven, hell, or the farthest sea. No darkness can hide from Him, even for a

moment. The reason is, He "has possessed our reins." It means He is not only with us, but within us.

So, He must accompany us wherever we go.

We must accept it as true. Our Lord's words, "Look, I am with you always, even unto the end of the

world," were not just a beautiful sentiment. They are an undeniable fact. He is with us, and we cannot

get away from Him.

In thick darkness, we may see nothing. We may think, often think that He does not see us. But our

Psalm assures us that the darkness hides not from Him. In fact, darkness and light are both alike to

Him. We are as present to His view and as plainly seen in our darkest spiritual depths as in our brightest

light. The darkness may hide Him from us, but it does not hide us from Him. Nor does any spiritual

distance or wandering take us from His presence. Not even if we sink into sin in our wandering. In the

uttermost parts of the sea, or wherever we may be, He is ever present to hold and to lead us. There is

not a moment nor a place where we can be left without His care.

Sometimes, confusion makes us unaware of the loving care of our nurses. A child in confusion might

cry out for its mother, and its sad cries will break her heart. Meanwhile, she is holding the child's hot

hand, cooling its fevered head, and caring for it with a mother's love. The sickness may hide the mother

from the child, but it doesn't hide the child from the mother.

And just so it is with our God and us. Our doubts, fears, sorrows, and sins cannot hide us from Him.

But they often hide Him from us. He has said that the darkness and light are alike to Him. If our faith

accepts this, we can trust in dark times. Though we cannot see or feel Him, our God cares for us. He

will never leave us.

Whether, however, this abiding presence of our God will be a joy to us or a sorrow will depend upon

what we know about Him. If we think of Him as a stern tyrant, intent only on His own glory, we shall

be afraid of His continual presence. If we see Him as a loving Father, we'll be glad. He wants only our

happiness. So, we'll be thankful to have Him with us always. For the presence and the care of love can

never mean anything but good to the one beloved.

The Psalm we are considering shows us that God's presence is love. It brings us infinite comfort and

rest. He says in verses 1 to 5, “O Lord, you have searched me and known me! You know when I sit

down and when I rise up; you discern my thoughts from afar. You search out my path and my lying

down and are acquainted with all my ways. Even before a word is on my tongue, behold, O Lord, you

know it altogether. You hem me in, behind and before, and lay your hand upon me.”

Our God knows us and understands us, and is acquainted with all our ways. No one else in all the world

understands us. People may misinterpret our actions and misjudge our motives. Our natural

characteristics are not taken into account, nor our inherited tendencies considered. No one makes

allowances for our ill health; no one realizes how much we have to contend with. But our Father knows

it all. He understands us. His judgment considers every part of our character, both conscious and

unconscious. It also considers what controls our actions. Only an all comprehending love can be just,

and our God is just. No wonder Faber can say:

Nowhere on Earth are its sorrows felt more than in Heaven. Nowhere are its failings judged more

kindly. Some of you may fear His justice, thinking it would be against you. But do you not see? It is

all on your side, just as a mother's justice is, because He knows our frame and remembers that we are

dust. No human judge can ever do this, and to me, this comprehension of God is one of my most blessed

comforts. Often, I do not understand myself; all within looks confused and hopelessly tangled. But I

remember that He has searched me. He knows me. He understands my perplexing thoughts. So, I may

leave the whole mess to Him to unravel.

And my soul sinks at once, as on downy pillows, into a place of the most blissful rest. Then, because

of His complete knowledge of our needs, what comfort it is to be told that He knows our down sitting

and our uprising. He compasses our path, and takes note of our lying down. Our God does for us what

a mother does for her foolish, careless, ignorant, but dearly loved little ones. When a mother is with

her children, she thinks of their comfort and well-being always before her own. They must have

comfortable, draught-free seats. She must endure any discomfort. Their beds must be soft and their

blankets warm, let hers be what they may.

Their paths must be smooth and safe, even though she is obliged to walk in rough and dangerous ways.

Her own comfort, as compared with that of her children, is of no account in a loving mother’s eyes.

Surely, our God is not less capable of a self-sacrificing love than the mothers in this world. He must be

better and greater on the line of love and self-sacrifice than any mother He ever made. He has assured

us that He knows our down sitting and uprising. He compasses our path and our lying down. So, we

can be sure, in all the little details of our lives, we get the very best that His love, wisdom, and power

can provide. I mean this in a very literal sense. I mean that He cares for our seats and our beds. He sees

that we each have the best kind for our highest development.

And just on this last point is where He is so much better than any mother can be. His love is a wise love

that sees the outcome of things and cares more for our highest good than for that which is lower. A

mother's weak love can't see beyond a child's comfort. It can't bear to cause any discomfort. But God's

strong, wise love can permit some pain. It is for the sake of the future glory that will come from it.

At home and abroad, let us trust God. He knows all about our daily lives. So, let Him choose our seats,

beds, and other small things.

For we are told in our Psalm that He “besets” our path. We have some of us have known what it was to

be “beset” by unwelcome and unpleasant people or things. But we never thought, perhaps, t hat we were

beset by God. He loves us so much that He cannot leave us alone.

No coldness or rebuffs can drive Him away. Yet it is gloriously true! Moreover , He besets us “behind”

as well as before. Just as a mother does. She goes after her children. She picks up all they dropped and

clears away their rubbish.

We mothers start this in the nursery with the blocks and toys. We do it all our lives. We try to fix what

our children have left undone or wrong. It takes a lot of effort and trouble, but our love makes that

effort seem small compared to caring for our children. What good mother would ever turn away a sad,

crying child? Or refuse to help a boy untangle his kite strings? Even if the knots and tangles are his

fault, her love understands and feels for those mistakes. So, she works even harder to help fix them.

Our God does all this, and more, for us from infancy. He does it long before we are aware of it, until

the end of our earthly lives. We have seen Him before us, perhaps, but we have never thought of Him

as behind us as well. Yet, it is a blessed fact. He is behind us. He longs to make crooked things straight,

untangle our knots, and atone for our wrongs. If any of us has a troubling past, let us be happy. The

God who is behind us will set it all straight if we commit it to Him. He can even make our mistakes

work together for good. Ah! It is a grand thing to be surrounded by God.

Then again, what comfort in verses 14 to 16: "I praise you, for I am fearfully and wonderfully made.

A Wonderful work are your works; my soul knows it very well. My frame was not hidden from you

when I was being made in secret, intricately woven in the depths of the earth. Your eyes saw my

unformed substance; in your book were written, every one of them, the days that were formed for me,

when as yet there was none of them.”

We often dislike, more than we admit, how we were made. Our mental or moral “make - up” does not

suit us. We think that if we were created with less of this or more of that, we'd be more successful. If

we were less impulsive or more enthusiastic, we could better serve God. We could also be more

satisfactory to ourselves and to Him. We believe that if we were more like someone we admire, it

would help too. And we are tempted sometimes to think that with our miserable make-up, it is hopeless

to expect to please Him.

If we truly realized that God made us, we would see the folly of all this at once. But, we feel that He

had little hand in it. We think we were put together haphazardly, leaving our characters to chance. We

believe in creation in the general, but not in the particular, when it comes to ourselves. This Psalm

shows that God oversaw our creation. He managed even the smallest details. Figuratively, he wrote

down what each "member" was to be when none existed yet. So, we are, by nature, what God wants.

He made us do a special work. I mean, of course, our natural characteristics, not the perversion of them

by sin on our parts.

There is something very glorifying to the Creator in this way of looking at it. Genius always seeks to

express itself in many ways. No true artist repeats himself. Each painting or statue is a new expression

of his creative power. An art exhibition should not have two identical pictures. If it did, it would lower

the value of art. The same is true for us, as we are "God's workmanship." His creative power expresses

itself differently in each one of us.

And in the individual "make-up," which sometimes troubles us, there is a unique power. Without it, the

day of the exhibition, when we are to praise His glory, would be incomplete. He asks only this: since

He made us, He should manage us. He alone understands us, so only He can do it.

The man who makes an intricate machine is best suited to manage and repair it. Anyone else who

meddles is likely to spoil it. Given our complex minds and our poor control of them, we should be

thankful to hand them to their Creator and leave them in His hands. We can be sure He will make the

best of us. Even with our "peculiar temperaments" and flaws, we will be made into vessels of honor.

We will be sanctified and fit for the Master's use, ready for every good work.

I once read a saying from an old Quaker writer that stayed with me: "Be content to be just what God

made you." It helped me understand my thoughts. I believe that to truly submit to God, we must accept

ourselves as He created us, just as we accept our daily circumstances. If we did not exist, a part of

God’s creation would be missing. His work would be incomplete. Besides, com plaining about

ourselves is like complaining about the One who made us, which must hurt Him. Let’s be content and

trust the Divine Potter to shape us as He sees best and use us as He chooses.

Verses 17 and 18 bring out another view of God’s continual pr esence with us, and that is, that He is

always thinking about us, and that His thoughts are kind and loving thoughts, for the Psalmist calls

them precious. “How precious also are thy thoughts unto me, O God! How great is the sum of them!

If I should count them, they are more in number than the sand: when I awake, I am still with thee.”

So many people are tempted to think that God is not paying any attention to them. They believe their

interests are beneath His notice. They feel too unworthy to hope for His attention. But they wrong Him

grievously by such thoughts. A mother pays as much attention to her smallest infant as to her oldest

children. She is as interested in its little needs and pleasures as in theirs. I am not sure, but she is more.

She thinks of the one who needs them most. He who made the mother's heart will care for His most

helpless creatures. He hears the young lions when they cry. Not a sparrow can fall to the ground without

Him. We are worth more than many sparrows. So, we need not fear neglect for a moment.

Creating anything requires constant care from the Creator. Omnipotence's glory is that it can do

everything at once. It can tend to the smallest details and the grandest tasks. "Only an infinite greatness

can hold all things. A greatness less than infinite would crush us."

I don't know why we see a man or woman as weak for neglecting small details in favor of big tasks.

Yet, we accuse our God of doing the same thing. But if any of my readers have been guilty of this folly,

let it end now. “How precious to me are your thoughts, O God! How vast is the sum of them!

If I were to count them, they would be more than the sand. I awake, and I am still with you.”

The rest of the Psalm shows a perfect harmony between the soul and God. It is where this life of simple

faith has begun. The soul unites with God, knowing that He is always present and cares. It loves what

He loves and hates what He hates. It eagerly asks Him to search and test it, so no part of it is out of

harmony with Him.

In His presence, darkness must flee. The heart will feel it cannot endure having any corner hidden from

His light. “For, you make known to me the path of life; in your presence there is fullness of joy; at your

right hand are pleasures forevermore.” (Psal m 16:11 ) An old woman, in a desolate part of England,

made a lot of money selling ale and beer to travelers at her lonely cottage. But her conscience troubled

her about it. She wanted to be a Christian and go to Heaven when she died. But, she felt that, if she did,

she'd have to give up her profitable business. She thought that would be too much to bear. So, she was

torn between the two.

One night, at a meeting she attended, a preacher spoke about the joy of God's constant presence. He

said knowing this truth brings great happiness. Her heart was filled with excitement at the thought that

this could be true for her. Forgetting all about the beer, she simply and sincerely accepted it as a

wonderful reality. As the preacher kept speaking, she cried in her he art, “Lord Jesus, I didn’t know you

were always with me! Lord, how amazing it is to know that you are always here with me, taking care

of me! I will never feel lonely again !

When the meeting ended, she walked home across the fields. The joyful thought kept repeating in her

heart, "Ah, Lord Jesus, you are coming home with me tonight." She said, "Never mind, Lord Jesus, old

Betty won’t ever let you go again now. I know you are here with me.

Her faith in God’s presence grew stronger, and she felt more joy ful with each step. By the time she

reached her cottage door, her heart was full of happiness. As she walked in, the first thing she saw was

a big pot of beer on the table, ready to be sold. A thought came to her: “The Lord won’t like that pot of

beer.” Her heart quickly responded, “Then it must go.” The pot was heavy, so she knelt beside it and

prayed, “Lord, You have come home with me. You will live in this cottage, and I know you don’t want

this beer here. Please give me the strength to pour it out.” God gave her strength, and soon the beer was

running down the road. Then she went back inside, knelt, and thanked the Lord for helping her. She

added, “Now, Lord, if there is anything else in this cottage that you don’t like, show me, and I will get

rid of it too. Isn’t this a perfect example of the message at the end of our Psalm?

"Lord, don’t I hate those who hate you? Am I not troubled by those who oppose you? I hate them

completely and see them as my enemies.

Search me, O God, and know my heart. Test me and know my thoughts.

If there is anything wrong in me, show me, and lead me on the right path forever Just as light drives

out darkness, so does the realized presence of God drive out sin. The soul that by faith abides in His

presence knows a very real and wonderful Deliverance.

And now I trust that some will ask, “How can I find this presence to be real to myself?” I will close,

so, with a few practical directions. First, convince yourself from the Scriptures that it is a fact. Facts

must always ground our experiences. Without them, the experiences are worthless. It is not the feeling

that causes the fact, but the fact that produces the feeling. What every soul needs, first of all, is this.

God's own words must convince them, beyond question. They must know, as an unalterable fact, that

His presence with us is constant.

Then, this point settled, we must make it real. We must "practice His presence," as an old writer said,

always and everywhere, in everything. You must obey the Scripture command. It says, "In all your

ways acknowledge Him." So, at every hour and moment, say, "The Lord is here." Do everything, even

eating and drinking, in His presence and for Him. Literally, “whether, therefore, you eat or drink, or

whatsoever you do, do all to the glo ry of God.” By this continual "practice of His presence," the soul

gains a habit of faith. It becomes, finally, as hard to doubt His presence as it was to believe it at first.

This requires no great effort, just an unwavering faith. It is not studied reasoning or elaborate

meditations that will help you here. The soul must, by simple faith, recognize that God is present. It

must then, in freedom and simplicity, talk to Him about everything, all the time. He does not need great

things of us. He asks for so little. A little remembrance of His presence. A few words of love and

confidence. A brief lifting of the heart to Him as we go about our daily tasks. A constant appeal to Him,

a present and loving friend. A desire to live in a sense of His presence, and to let our hearts "dwell at

ease" because of it. The least remembrance is welcome to Him. It helps make His presence real to us.

Whoever remains faithful in this exercise will soon discover a blessed realization. Of all I've tried to

tell in this book, and of far more that I cannot, I hope you will understand, beyond words, those

wonderful words about our Lord: "They must call Him Emmanuel, which means, 'God with us."

THE END

fields.title: Chapter 1
fields.body_html:
Understanding Libraries

hat a library is and what it does

Setting up a library starts with understanding what a library truly is. It is not simply a

room filled with books, but a vibrant, active space that holds knowledge, stories, and

opportunities. Think of it as a doorway to discovery. Your library should bring together the

different kinds of resources your community needs: children’s storybooks, students’ textbooks,

magazines, newspapers, maps, DVDs, and even digital resources such as eBooks and online

journals. When these materials are gathered and arranged in a clear, simple structure, the library

becomes a gateway that helps people learn, explore new ideas, and grow in ways they may never

have imagined.

But a good library is more than the materials on its shelves—it is also the experience it offers. As

you set up your library, consider how it will serve the people who use it. Create areas where

children can enjoy stories, students can study comfortably, and adults can read quietly or search

for information that supports their daily needs. If possible, provide computers or Wi-Fi so that

even those without access at home can learn and connect. Above all, ensure the library is warm,

safe, and welcoming. When people feel comfortable, they are more likely to return, take part in

activities, and discover the joy of reading and learning.

Because of these important services, libraries play a unique role in every part of society:

In schools,

Libraries help students and teachers succeed. They provide textbooks, storybooks, research

materials, and digital tools that support the curriculum. They teach learners how to find

information, think critically, and develop a lifelong love of reading. A school library is often the

heart of academic life, encouraging curiosity and helping pupils build strong learning habits.

W

In communities,

Libraries act as centres for learning, connection, and social support. They help job seekers create

CVs, and offer people a comfortable place to read, learn new skills, or participate in activities.

In organisations,

Libraries support professional growth and informed decision-making. Whether in a company,

government office, hospital, or NGO, a library provides reliable information that helps

professionals carry out research, plan projects, and improve services. These specialised

collections ensure staff have the knowledge they need to excel.

In families,

Libraries bring learning into the home. Parents can borrow books for their children, find

educational materials, or join family-friendly activities like storytelling sessions, reading clubs,

or homework support programs. For some families, the library is a safe, free, and inspiring place

to spend time together.

Different Types of Libraries

Even though all libraries share the same purpose — to provide access to information — they

serve different groups and therefore operate in different ways.

Public Libraries

These are open to everyone and are usually funded by the government or community. They offer

book lending, internet access, children’s programs, literacy training, and community events.

Their mission is to serve the public equally, regardless of age, education level, or income.

Academic Libraries

Found in colleges and universities, they support advanced study and research. Their collections

include textbooks, scholarly journals, academic databases, and research tools. Trained librarians

help students and researchers find in-depth information for assignments, dissertations, and

scientific work.

School Libraries

Located in primary, secondary, and high schools, these libraries help learners grow academically

and personally. They provide age-appropriate books, curriculum resources, reading programs,

and support for research skills. Their goal is to encourage reading, support classroom learning,

and help young people become independent learners.

Special Libraries

These libraries serve specific groups and have highly focused collections. They can be found in

hospitals, law firms, museums, government departments, NGOs, or corporations. Their resources

are tailored to the unique needs of the organisation — for example, medical journals in a hospital

library or legal texts in a law library.

Core Principles That Guide All Good Libraries

Despite their differences, all good libraries are built on the same foundation of values:

Organization

Materials are arranged in a clear, logical way so people can find what they need quickly. This

includes proper shelving, cataloguing, and classification.

Access

Libraries work to ensure that everyone — regardless of age, background, or ability — can freely

use their resources and services. This includes eliminating barriers such as cost, distance, or lack

of technology.

Service

Libraries exist to help people. Trained staff guide users, answer questions, assist with

technology, and help them find the information they need.

Fairness and Inclusion

A library must be a place where everyone feels welcome. Collections should represent different

cultures, points of view, management, and interests. Services should be accessible to all.

Knowledge Sharing

Libraries preserve and share the knowledge of society. They do this by lending materials, hosting

programs, supporting research, and creating spaces for learning and community discussion.

fields.title: Chapter 2
fields.body_html:
Library Administration & Governance

How to Lead, Organise, and Guide Your Library Successfully

eading a library is a task that combines leadership, service, and discipline. When you take

responsibility for a library — whether it is a school library, a community library, or a small

organisational resource centre — you are taking on more than a room full of books. You are

stepping into a leadership role. Your decisions will shape how the library feels, how it functions,

and how well it serves the people who depend on it. This is to help you understand how to run

your library with confidence, clarity, and purpose.

1. The Role of a Librarian: What You Are Responsible For

Far beyond issuing books, a librarian is responsible for:

• Organising the collection: arranging books, maintaining order, and making sure

everything is easy to find.

• Helping users: answering questions, guiding research, assisting with computers, and

supporting reading.

• Planning programs: storytime sessions, reading clubs, study workshops, or community

activities.

• Maintaining the space: keeping it clean, safe, welcoming, and accessible.

• Managing records: tracking borrowed books, updating user information, and keeping

simple statistics.

• Protecting the collection: repairing books, preventing damage, and ensuring materials

are used responsibly.

Imagine a library without a librarian.

Books would be misplaced. Borrowers wouldn’t know where things are. Damaged books would

go unnoticed. The library would feel confusing instead of helpful.

Example

L

A student walks in looking for a history textbook for their exam. The librarian doesn’t just point

at a shelf—they guide the student, check availability, offer alternatives, and suggest other helpful

resources, such as past papers or online materials.

In simple terms, the librarian is the heart of the library , keeping everything running smoothly.

2. Library Leadership or Committees: Who Makes the Big Decisions?

Some libraries — especially school, public, or organisational libraries — have a leadership team,

governing board, or committee. These people help guide the library’s long-term direction.

They are responsible for:

• Setting the overall vision

• Approving budgets

• Supporting the librarian’s work

• Making decisions about big purchases

• Establishing policies

• Planning development or expansion

• Ensuring the library serves its community fairly

Think of governance as the “steering wheel.”

The librarian may run the daily engine, but the committee helps steer the library in the right

direction—deciding where the library wants to go and how it plans to get there.

3. Policies and Procedures: The Rules That Keep the Library Running

Every good library needs policies and procedures .

These are simply the written rules and step-by-step instructions that help everyone understand

how things work.

Policies (The Rules)

Policies explain what should happen. Examples include:

• Borrowing rules (how many books, for how long)

• Fines or penalties for lost books

• Opening and closing times

• Behaviour expectations

• Use of computers or the internet

• Donation guidelines

Policies help maintain fairness, protect the collection, and keep the library organised.

Procedures (The Steps)

Procedures explain how things should be done. For example:

• How to register a new user

• How to issue and return books

• How to handle damaged materials

• How to close the library at the end of the day

• How to record statistics

If you set good procedures, the library runs smoothly even when different staff or volunteers take

turns working.

4. Staff and Volunteer Roles: How Everyone Contributes

Not every library has a large team, but many have at least a few helpers. Each person plays a

valuable role.

Here are common roles:

Librarian or Library Manager

Leads daily operations, supports users, and manages the collection.

Library Assistant

Helps with shelving, issuing books, guiding users, and basic administration.

Volunteers

Support activities like reading sessions, shelving, and organising events — especially in

community or church libraries.

ICT/Technology Support

Helps with computers, digital catalogues, and internet services (in libraries that use technology).

Security or Custodial Support

Keeps the environment safe and clean.

Your library may have only one staff member, but it’s important to understand these roles —

they help clarify responsibilities and identify areas where help is needed.

5. Planning, Goal Setting, and Measuring Progress

To grow a strong library, you need a plan.

This plan does not have to be complicated — even a simple one-page document can guide your

work for the entire year.

Your library’s plan should include:

• What you want to achieve (goals)

• How you will achieve it (strategies)

• What resources do you need (budget, staff, materials)

• When you expect to complete it (timeline)

Examples of simple goals include:

• Increasing membership

• Improving the children’s corner

• Buying new textbooks or storybooks

• Starting a reading club

• Providing weekly ICT lessons

Measuring Progress

At the end of each month or term, you can track things like:

• Number of users

• Books borrowed

• New materials added

• Programs run

• Feedback from users

Planning is like planting seeds.

You may not see the results immediately, but each action grows into a stronger, more helpful

library. These simple records help you see what is working — and what needs improvement.

6. Professional Ethics and Standards: How Library Workers Should Behave

As a library worker, you hold a position of trust.

People come to you for help, guidance, and sometimes private information. It is important to act

professionally and ethically.

Good library ethics include:

• Respecting all users: treating everyone fairly and kindly

• Protecting privacy: not sharing private information about users

• Being honest and reliable: following rules, returning money, and keeping clear records

• Staying neutral: not judging people based on what they read or believe

• Promoting learning: encouraging reading, curiosity, and discovery

• Caring for resources: using materials responsibly and teaching others to do the same

Example

If a user forgets their library card, the librarian should follow the identification procedure—not

bend rules for friends or relatives.

Ethics are like the moral compass of the library—they guide behaviour and ensure trust. These

principles help build a library that people trust and return to.

fields.title: Chapter 3
fields.body_html:
Managing Library Collections

How libraries take care of their books and materials.

library is only as strong as the collection it keeps. The books, magazines, digital

materials, and other resources you gather will shape how your library serves its people.

Managing these materials is not a one-time task—it is a journey that continues as long as your

library is alive. In this chapter, we walk together through the process of building, organising,

protecting, and refreshing a library collection that people can trust and enjoy.

Choosing and Acquiring Books

Every collection begins with a choice. When you select a book for your library, you are making a

promise: a promise that this book will help someone learn, grow, imagine, or solve a problem.

That is why choosing materials with care is so important.

Start by understanding the needs of the people who will use your library. A school library will

choose storybooks, readers, textbooks, and subject guides. A community library may choose

books on farming, health, business, language learning, and children’s reading materials. A

special library may focus on medical, legal, or technical knowledge. When you know your users,

you know what to collect.

Libraries receive books in many ways. Some are purchased using a budget or donations. Others

come through requests from organisations or government programs. Many community and

school libraries receive donated books from well-wishers. Donations can be a blessing, but they

must be checked carefully. A library should not become a storage place for unwanted or outdated

items. Accept only books that are clean, relevant, and in good condition. A single useful book is

more valuable than a box full of unsuitable ones.

Cataloguing and Classification: Giving Each Book a Home

A

When new books arrive, the next step is to help them “introduce themselves” to the library. This

process is called cataloguing. Here, you record important details like the title, author, subject,

and year of publication. These details become part of your library’s catalogue—the master list of

everything the library owns.

Once a book is described, it needs a place to live on the shelves. This is where classification

comes in. By grouping books according to their subjects, you create an organised map that helps

people find what they need. A science book, a storybook, and a history book all get their own

unique “address.” When a book has a clear title, users can find it easily without confusion.

Good cataloguing and classification save everyone time. They make the library simpler to use,

especially for children, new readers, and community members who may be interacting with a

library for the first time.

Processing New Books: Preparing Them for Use

Before a book reaches the shelves, it needs a little attention—almost like a new student preparing

for the first day of school. This preparation is called processing.

Processing may include stamping the library’s name inside the book, adding a spine label with its

call number, covering it with protective plastic, and giving it a barcode or unique number for

tracking. These small details make a big difference. They protect the book, help you keep

records, and ensure that each item can be borrowed, returned, and easily found again.

Processing is the final step before a book becomes part of your library family.

Arranging Books on the Shelves

A well-arranged shelf is an invitation. When books are neat, accessible, and clearly labelled,

people feel comfortable exploring the library on their own.

Shelve books according to their call numbers so that they follow a natural order. Place children’s

books on lower shelves where young readers can easily reach them. Create welcoming spaces for

storybooks, textbooks, novels, and subject areas. Newspapers and magazines can be displayed

separately so readers can quickly pick up the latest issue.

Some librarians set aside special areas for “New Arrivals” or “Recommended Reading.” These

small touches make the library feel alive and changing, not static.

When your shelves are tidy, users sense that the library is cared for—and they care for it in

return.

Preserving Books: Helping Them Last Longer

Books age the way people do—slowly, quietly, and sometimes unexpectedly. Preservation is the

work of protecting your collection so it remains useful for many years.

Keep books in a clean, dry, well-ventilated space. Avoid direct sunlight, which fades covers and

weakens pages. Dust shelves regularly. Teach users, especially children, to turn pages gently and

return books properly. Repair small tears early so they do not become big ones later.

Often, preservation requires more attention than money. A little care every day keeps your

collection healthy.

Weeding: Removing What No Longer Serves the Library

A good library grows not only by adding books, but also by removing those that no longer help

the community. This process is called weeding. Some books become outdated, especially in

subjects like science, health, or technology. Others may become too worn out to continue using.

Some may simply sit untouched for years.

Weeding keeps your shelves relevant, attractive, and easy to search. It prevents users from

relying on wrong or outdated information. Think of weeding as pruning a tree—it helps the

library stay strong and vibrant.

When removing books, always follow a simple rule: keep what is useful, safe, and relevant. Let

go of what no longer supports your mission.

Keeping Inventory: Knowing What You Own

A responsible librarian always knows the state of the library’s collection. Inventory is the

process of checking each book against your records to confirm that it still exists, is in the right

place, and is in good condition.

Inventory helps you track missing items, repair damaged ones, and decide what needs to be

purchased. It also helps you communicate clearly with donors, administrators, or partners about

the true size and condition of your collection.

Doing an inventory once or twice a year keeps your library organised and trustworthy.

Bringing It All Together

Managing a library collection is an act of care. You choose materials thoughtfully, organise them

with purpose, protect them with love, and update them responsibly. When you do these things

consistently, your library becomes much more than a room of books—it becomes a resource

your community can depend on, year after year.

A well-managed collection invites people to learn, explore, and discover. And that is the gift

every library is meant to offer.

fields.title: Chapter 4
fields.body_html:
Library Services & User Experience

Everything a library does for its users.

good library feels alive. It feels welcoming. It feels like a place where every person—

whether a child, a student, a parent, or an elder—can discover something useful,

comforting, or inspiring.

In this chapter, we explore the many services a library offers and the kind of environment that

makes users feel valued and supported.

Creating a Welcoming Environment

The moment someone enters your library, their experience begins. A clean, organised, friendly

space invites people to stay longer, explore more, and return again. You don’t need fancy

furniture or expensive decorations. Sometimes, even simple touches make a difference: neatly

arranged shelves, clear signs, a quiet reading corner, or a friendly greeting from the librarian.

A welcoming library is one where users feel seen and respected. Children feel free to ask

questions. Adults feel comfortable seeking help. Students feel safe settling down with their

books. When people feel at home, they learn better.

Circulation Services: Borrowing and Returning Books

Circulation is at the heart of library activity. This is the process that allows users to borrow

materials, enjoy them at home, and bring them back for others to use. A clear, simple borrowing

system helps everyone understand how the library works.

Some libraries use membership cards or registers; others use digital systems. Whatever method

you choose, consistency matters. Record borrowing carefully, set reasonable return dates, and

encourage users to take responsibility for the materials they borrow. This helps build trust and

ensures that the collection remains available for everyone.

A

When borrowing works well, the library becomes more than a place to read—it becomes a place

that shares.

Reference and Information Services

People come to the library with questions. Some want to know how to start a business. Others

need information for schoolwork. Some may be looking for health advice, job opportunities, or

community programs. Reference services help users find reliable answers to their questions.

The librarian plays an important role here. You don’t need to know everything, but you should

know where to look . A good librarian guides users to the right shelf, the right book, or the right

website. Sometimes, the most powerful thing you can say is, “Let me help you find that.”

Reference service turns the library from a room of books into a bridge connecting people with

the information they need most.

Reader Advisory and Encouraging Reading

Many users, especially children or new readers, don’t always know what to read next. Reader

advisory is the gentle art of helping them choose books they will enjoy or benefit from.

You might recommend a storybook to a child who loves adventure, guide a student toward

material that strengthens their subjects, or help an adult discover books that support their work or

personal development.

When the librarian takes time to understand the reader, reading becomes a journey that both of

you share.

Literacy Programs and Learning Activities

Libraries play an important role in strengthening literacy and learning. These programs can be

simple or structured, depending on the resources available. A few examples include:

• story hours for children

• reading clubs for youth

• homework support groups

• writing workshops

• basic computer classes

• book discussions for adults

You do not need a big budget to run meaningful programs. A library volunteer, a group of

enthusiastic students, or a community member with a skill to share can bring life to your library.

These activities turn the library into a learning centre—a place where knowledge grows through

participation, not just reading.

Supporting Special Groups

Different groups in the community have different needs, and a good library recognises this.

Children often need colourful spaces, easy-to-read books, and patient guidance. Teenagers

benefit from safe study areas, internet access, and engaging activities. Adults appreciate

newspapers, practical guides, and informative workshops. Seniors may prefer large-print books

or quiet reading spaces.

When your library considers the needs of each group, it becomes a place where everyone finds

something for themselves.

Digital Access and Technology Support

In today’s world, many people rely on libraries for digital access—especially in communities

where technology is limited or expensive. Offering computer access, internet services, or even a

single tablet can open doors for learners, job seekers, and families.

Some people use the library to type assignments. Others come to apply for jobs, research online,

or improve their digital skills. If your library has the tools, you might also guide users on how to

create email accounts, search safely, or use basic software.

Providing technology does not replace books—it expands what the library can offer.

Community Engagement and Partnerships

A library thrives when it is connected to the community around it. You can invite local leaders,

teachers, parents, and organisations to share their knowledge or partner in activities.

Collaborations with schools can strengthen learning. Partnerships with NGOs can bring

resources or training. Involving youth groups can bring energy and creativity into the library.

A library that works with its community quickly becomes a centre of shared growth.

Overall User Experience

At the centre of all these services is one simple truth: people return to places where they feel

respected and supported. A good library listens to its users, understands their challenges, and

creates a space where learning becomes enjoyable.

When a child discovers a story they love, when a student finds material for a research project,

when an adult gains a skill that changes their life— that is the true measure of the library’s

success.

A library that cares about its users becomes much more than a place to read.

It becomes a place to grow.

fields.title: Chapter 5
fields.body_html:
Technology in Libraries

How simple technology that supports modern library work.

n the modern age, wisdom requires leveraging the tools available to us. Technology is not a

replacement for human connection, but a powerful instrument that multiplies the efforts of

your staff and expands the reach of your ministry of information. The transition to digital tools

might feel overwhelming, but remember the principle: simple technology enables deep service.

This chapter will guide you through the foundational technologies that support efficient, modern

library work. Our focus is on systems that bring order, clarity, and security to your records,

ensuring that the precious resources under your care are managed with excellence.

1. The Core Engine: The Library Management System (LMS/ILS)

Every successful library needs a centralised system to manage its entire operation. This system,

often called a Library Management System (LMS) or Integrated Library System (ILS), is the

heart of your digital work.

Principle: Centralised Order

The LMS replaces separate paper ledgers, card catalogues, and spreadsheets with one unified

record. This unification saves time, eliminates errors, and gives you a single, clear view of your

entire collection and all your users.

• What it Does:

o Cataloguing: It stores the permanent, official record for every book, magazine, or

digital item you own.

o Circulation: It tracks who has borrowed what, when it is due, and automatically

manages holds and due dates.

o Patron Records: It keeps secure records of your members, including their contact

information and borrowing history.

I

Application: Choosing Your System

Do not let the complexity of large commercial systems discourage you. Many excellent, low-cost

or free open-source solutions exist that are tailored for small to medium libraries. The key is to

choose a system that is simple to learn, backed by good online documentation, and scalable as

your library grows.

2. The Doorway to Discovery: Digital Catalogues

The Online Public Access Catalogue (OPAC) is the face of your collection. It is the digital

system that allows users to search your holdings without needing to speak to a staff member.

Principle: Empowered Search

A digital catalogue transforms searching from a physical task (walking the aisles) into an

intellectual one (typing keywords). It empowers users to be self-sufficient and find exactly what

they need, even if they don't know the precise title.

• Enhanced Searching: Users can search by keyword (a topic, a phrase), author, subject,

or genre. It is far more flexible and faster than a traditional card catalogue.

• Availability: The catalogue immediately shows the user if a book is on the shelf, on loan,

or available at another branch, saving them time and frustration.

• Remote Access: Ideally, your OPAC is available online, meaning a student can check if

a book is available from their home before making the journey to the library.

Action: Catalogue Your Collection with Discipline

The best system is only as good as the data entered into it. Ensure your staff is trained in

consistent data entry (metadata). Every book must have accurate subject headings and

descriptions so that the catalogue can find it reliably. Good data entry is an act of service to the

future user.

3. Tools for Daily Operations: Computers and Basic Software

Basic computing power forms the foundation of modern library work, extending beyond

circulation and cataloguing.

Principle: Efficiency and Communication

Every computer in your back office should be used to increase staff efficiency and improve

external communication.

• Office Software: Utilise basic word processing (for policies, reports), spreadsheets (for

budgets, collection analysis), and presentation software (for training and community

programs). Again, use free and open-source alternatives if funding is limited.

• The Internet & Email: The internet is essential for professional development, contacting

vendors, and communicating with patrons and stakeholders. Treat your library email as a

professional communication tool, responding to user queries with clarity and promptness.

• Staff Training: Invest the time to ensure all staff members are proficient in the basic use

of a computer, file organisation, and security awareness. This eliminates delays and

builds confidence.

4. Expanding the Horizon: Online Resources and E-Content

The library’s collection now extends far beyond its four walls. Online resources, databases, and

e-books allow you to offer access to materials you could never afford to purchase physically.

Principle: Infinite Shelf Space

Online resources allow you to provide access to vast amounts of specialised information that

your physical space cannot hold. This expands your relevance to researchers, students, and

professionals.

• Databases: These are crucial for academic and research work. Even accessing free,

publicly available government databases or educational resource aggregators can

significantly enhance your reference capabilities.

• E-Books and E-Journals: Partner with consortia or utilise platforms that provide shared

access to digital collections. E-books meet the needs of digital learners and allow for

instantaneous access.

• Curation: Your role is to guide the user through the information chaos of the internet.

Curate a list of trusted, high-quality, free online resources and feature them prominently

on your library website or public access computers.

5. Small Steps to the Future: Low-Resource Automation

You do not need massive funding to begin automating certain tasks. Automation is the

delegation of routine, repetitive work to a machine or a system.

Principle: Freeing Up Staff for Service

Every minute your staff spends manually stamping books or calculating overdue dates is a

minute taken away from helping a user. Automation frees staff time for high-value work: reader

advisory, reference interviews, and community engagement.

• Basic Automation Targets (Low Cost):

o Email Reminders: Configure your LMS to automatically send email

notifications for overdue books or hold pickups.

o Self-Check: Simple barcode scanners and a dedicated computer station can allow

patrons to check out books themselves (with supervision), reducing lines at the

main desk.

o Inventory: Use your LMS features to perform a cyclical inventory audit rather

than a massive annual shutdown.

6. Upholding Trust: Data Protection and Backup

Technology introduces risks alongside opportunities. As the keeper of the community’s

information, you are also the steward of their personal data. This stewardship requires rigour and

a deep sense of responsibility.

Principle: Trust and Preservation

The wisdom to protect your users’ data and your library’s records is non-negotiable. Loss of data

is the loss of institutional memory and community trust.

• Protecting User Data:

o Confidentiality: Train your staff that a user’s borrowing history is strictly

confidential . It is private and must never be discussed or shared.

o Access: Use strong passwords and limit staff access only to the data required for

their specific job functions (Principle of Least Privilege).

• Backing Up Records:

o The 3-2-1 Rule: Maintain at least 3 copies of your critical data (your cataloguing

records, patron data, and financial files). Store these copies on at least 2 different

types of media (e.g., hard drive and cloud storage). Ensure at least 1 copy is

stored offsite (the cloud is an ideal solution).

o Regular Testing: Regularly test your backup procedure to ensure you can restore

the data if the main system fails. A backup is useless if it cannot be recovered.

Final Challenge for the Manager

The technology discussed here is simply a chisel in the hands of a skilled craftsman. It is not

meant to replace the human touch, but to make the human touch more effective and more

frequent. Use technology with intentionality, ensuring it always supports your ultimate mission:

to serve and empower the users of your library.

fields.title: Chapter 6
fields.body_html:
Library Operations & Facility Management

The daily practical work inside the library.

aily operations reflect discipline, consistency, and care. Opening procedures prepare the

space; closing procedures secure it. Staff must practice courtesy, clarity, and calm conflict

resolution, guided by policy and rooted in respect.

Wisdom understands that a well-managed building and a well-trained staff are requirements for

effective service. If the floor is dirty, the lights are dim, or the rules are unclear, the user's focus

shifts from the pursuit of knowledge to the distraction of discomfort.

This chapter addresses the practical, day-to-day work that builds a foundation of excellence.

These routines—from opening the doors to balancing the budget—are acts of stewardship that

honour the resources entrusted to you. Discipline in the small things leads to success in the

great things.

1. The Daily Rhythm: Opening and Closing Procedures

A library must operate with the precision of a clock. Your opening and closing routines establish

the tone for the day and ensure the facility is secure for the night.

Principle: Preparation and Security

• Opening: The goal is to transition from a closed space to a welcoming, fully functional

public service point before the first user arrives.

o Turn on all necessary lights and equipment (computers, self-check machines).

o Conduct a quick security sweep (check emergency exits, restrooms).

o Staff briefing: Review the day's programs, address any ongoing issues (like a

faulty copier), and assign posts.

o Ensure the circulation desk is fully stocked and ready for transactions.

• Closing: The process must be thorough, ensuring the safety of staff, users, and the

collection.

D

o Provide clear warnings to users (e.g., "The library closes in 15 minutes").

o Secure all cash and valuable equipment.

o Perform a final collection sweep: Check books returned just before closing, clear

reading tables, and ensure all windows and doors are locked.

o Data Integrity: Run the end-of-day reports on the LMS/ILS and verify that all

transactions are safely backed up.

2. Managing the Human Element: User Relations and Conflict

The staff-user relationship is the most delicate and vital part of library operations. Courtesy must

be the default, but you must be prepared for the exceptions.

Principle: Courtesy and Clarity

Good service is based on dignity and respect for every person who enters the building. This

principle must hold even when faced with challenging behaviour.

• Handling Users Politely: Train staff to use positive language, maintain eye contact, and

practice active listening. A simple "I'd be happy to help you find that" is more welcoming

than "What do you want?"

• Managing Conflict and Disruptions:

o De-escalation: Approach conflict with calm authority. The goal is to manage the

behaviour, not judge the person. Speak quietly and clearly, and never argue in

public.

o Policy Reliance: When addressing disruptions (e.g., noise, misuse of property),

rely on a clearly documented library policy. "Our policy states that all food must

be kept outside the reading area" is far stronger than "I don't allow food in here."

o Knowing Limits: Train staff to know when to seek management intervention or,

in rare cases, when to call security or law enforcement. The safety of the staff and

other users is paramount.

3. The Physical Environment: Safety, Cleanliness, and Organisation

A library that is clean and safe communicates respect for its users and its resources. This is a

perpetual task that requires constant vigilance.

Principle: Order and Accessibility

A well-organised space is a key to independent discovery. A safe space is a mandate for

hospitality.

• Cleanliness: Establish a clear daily and weekly cleaning schedule. Focus particularly on

high-touch areas (door handles, computer keyboards, restrooms). A clean environment

encourages better community behaviour.

• Safety & Security:

o Clear Pathways: Ensure all aisles are clear, with no obstacles that could cause

trips or falls. Emergency exits must always be accessible and clearly marked.

o Incident Reporting: Implement a simple system for reporting maintenance issues

(e.g., a broken chair, a flickering light) immediately. Addressing minor issues

quickly prevents major problems later.

• Organisation (Shelf Reading): Daily "shelf reading" (checking that books are in their

correct order on the shelves) is non-negotiable. A misfiled book is a lost book. Train staff

to treat this task as essential inventory control.

4. Designing the Experience: Space Planning and Arrangement

The physical arrangement of the library influences user behaviour and comfort. Your facility

should reflect the needs of your community.

Principle: Function and Flexibility

• Comfort and Function: Designate areas for specific activities: quiet zones for study,

collaborative zones for group work, and comfortable zones for leisure reading. Use

lighting and furniture to delineate these spaces.

• Accessibility: Review your floor plan constantly to ensure it meets the highest standards

of accessibility. Are the shelves too high? Is the signage clear? Are pathways wide

enough for mobility aids? The arrangement of your space must not impose a barrier on

any potential user.

• Signage: Invest in clear, professional signage. Signage acts as a silent reference guide,

helping users navigate the collection and understand library rules without needing staff

assistance.

5. Sustaining the Vision: Basic Financial and Budgeting Practices

Financial integrity is the bedrock of institutional trust. Good library management requires simple,

rigorous attention to incoming funds and outgoing expenditures.

Principle: Transparency and Stewardship

You must know exactly where the money comes from and where it is going. Your budget is the

financial expression of your mission.

• Budgeting Basics: Develop a simple, two-part budget:

o Operating Costs: Fixed, recurring expenses (salaries, utilities, rent).

o Collection/Program Costs: Flexible expenses for buying books, supplies, and

running programs.

• Cash Management: Establish clear protocols for handling fines, fees, and donations. All
