transactions must be recorded immediately and reconciled daily. Never allow staff

handling cash to also be responsible for final reconciliation.

• Reporting: Prepare a simple monthly financial report for your governing board or

stakeholders. This report should clearly show income, expenditure, and the remaining

funds, demonstrating responsible stewardship.

6. Proving the Impact: Statistics and Reporting

You cannot manage what you do not measure. Statistics and reports are the evidence that your

work is successful and are crucial for securing future funding.

Principle: Evidence and Advocacy

Reports must translate daily activities into a compelling narrative of progress and community

value.

• Key Statistics to Track:

o Circulation: Total books borrowed (the most fundamental measure).

o Usage: Number of visits (gate count) and use of public computers/Wi-Fi.

o Program Attendance: Number of people attending story time, classes, or events.

o Reference Questions: Number of in-depth queries handled by staff.

• Preparing Reports: Use your statistics to tell a story: "Attendance at our digital literacy

class increased by 40% this quarter, leading to three users reporting they found

employment using skills learned here." Reports should be concise, data-driven, and

focused on the outcomes , not just the activities.

Final Challenge for the Manager

The highest wisdom is knowing that facility management is not a distraction from service, but a

condition for service. Run your building with excellence, manage your finances with integrity,

and use your data to advocate with power. Manage the house well, and the knowledge within

it will prosper.

fields.title: Chapter 7
fields.body_html:
Starting or Reviving a Library

A Call to Build and Restore

s you arrive at this final chapter, you stand at the doorway of action. Everything you have

learned so far—about organisation, service, discipline, and community—now becomes the

foundation for something real. Whether you are beginning a library from an empty room or

breathing life back into one that has been forgotten, your work is sacred. You are building a

place of learning, shaping a space for growth, and restoring hope where it may have faded.

A neglected library is not a defeat. It is an invitation—an opportunity to rebuild with clarity,

wisdom, and renewed purpose. And a brand-new library is a chance to plant something that

generations will benefit from. This chapter gives you a clear, steady path forward for both

beginnings and restorations.

Starting a New Library

Laying a Strong Foundation

Creating a library from scratch is one of the most rewarding tasks you can undertake. At the

beginning, everything is open. You can choose the right systems, set clear values, and establish a

culture of service from day one.

Understanding Your Mission

Every library begins with a mission. Ask yourself:

Who am I building this library for, and what needs will it meet?

Maybe you want to support children’s literacy, help students succeed in exams, or give adults a

place to learn new skills. When your purpose is clear, your decisions become easier—what books

to buy, what programs to run, and how the space should feel.

Preparing the Space

A

Choose a location that people can reach easily—somewhere safe, clean, and welcoming. Even a

small room can become a powerful resource if it is well-lit, organised, and inviting.

Shelves, tables, a few chairs, and a small registration area are enough to begin. Start small, but

start intentionally.

Finding Resources

Every new library needs an initial collection. You may buy some books, receive donations, or

partner with schools and organisations. Aim for materials that truly fit your users—not just

whatever happens to come your way.

And if your budget is limited, that’s perfectly fine. One computer for registration, one printer,

and a few essential supplies are enough to begin operating responsibly.

Setting Simple Policies

Your first policies should be short, clear, and easy to explain.

For example:

• Who can borrow books

• How long can they keep them

• How to treat library materials

• How to behave in the library

Think of policies as gentle boundaries that help the library run peacefully.

Organising and Launching

Process each new book carefully. Stamp it, label it, add it to your catalogue, and shelve it

correctly. When your collection is ready, practise your circulation steps. Make sure staff or

volunteers know how to issue and return books, search the catalogue, and assist users politely.

Starting a library is less about perfection and more about consistent, thoughtful action.

Reviving a Failing Library

Restoring Order, Purpose, and Life

Sometimes, a library loses its way. Books become outdated or damaged. Records fall behind.

Users stop visiting because the space no longer meets their needs. If this is the situation you face,

do not be discouraged. Revival is possible—and it begins with honest assessment.

Step 1: Understanding What Went Wrong

Walk slowly through the library with open eyes.

Ask simple but important questions:

• Are the books still useful?

• Are they organised properly?

• Do people still visit? Why or why not?

• Are staff motivated and trained?

• Are digital systems being used or ignored?

You cannot fix what you have not seen clearly.

Step 2: Clearing, Cleaning, and Rebuilding

Begin with the collection. Remove the books that no longer serve. Outdated science, torn

materials, irrelevant topics—these weigh the library down. Freeing shelf space makes room for

better things.

Next, refresh the physical space. Clean the shelves, repair broken furniture, replace blown bulbs,

and repaint if possible. A freshly cleaned library sends a strong message: something new is

beginning.

Then, restart your systems. Re-catalogue where necessary. Reset passwords. Update records.

Simplify your procedures so that staff do not feel overwhelmed.

Finally, retrain your team. Encourage kindness, attentiveness, and responsibility. The attitude of

the staff can revive a library faster than any new book can.

Step 3: Reintroducing the Library to the Community

Once the basics are restored, it is time to reopen the doors with confidence. Remind the

community that the library is here for them. Share new policies, new opening hours, or special

programs. Even a single well-planned activity—story time, a digital skills class, or a reading

challenge—can bring excitement back.

Revival is not about making everything perfect. It is about restoring trust, order, and hope.

Common Mistakes and How to Avoid Them

Even the most passionate library managers fall into avoidable traps. Here are some lessons that

protect you from unnecessary struggle.

Buying Books Nobody Needs

A library serves the community, not the personal tastes of the manager. Always choose materials

based on real users and real needs.

Weak or Inconsistent Organisation

If cataloguing and shelving are done carelessly, books become invisible. A misplaced book is a

lost book. Keep your systems simple, consistent, and disciplined.

Too Many Rules

Policies should help people, not chase them away. Keep rules light, clear, and easy to

understand.

Waiting Instead of Reaching Out

A library should not hide. Visit schools, talk to leaders, and remind the community of the

services you offer. An active library has an active voice.

Ignoring Backup and Safety

Always protect your catalogue and digital records. One computer crash should never destroy

years of work.

Mistakes are normal. The wise manager learns from them early and adjusts quickly.

Growing the Library Over Time

Steady, Sustainable Development.

Growth does not happen overnight. It is built one wise decision at a time.

Begin by expanding the collection slowly—based on what people actually borrow. If students

love storybooks, buy more storybooks. If adults borrow business guides, strengthen that section.

Let usage guide growth.

Next, expand your services. Can you run a mobile reading day at a nearby school? Can you start

a small reading corner in a church or community centre? Growth does not always mean a bigger

building; sometimes it means a wider reach.

And do not underestimate volunteers. Retired teachers, youth leaders, university students, or

parents can bring energy and skills that elevate your library without adding cost.

Finally, seek partnerships and grants only when they fit your direction. A library grows best

when it grows with purpose.

Conclusion

Your Work is a Gift to the Future

You have reached the end of this guide, but the real work is ahead. Building or reviving a library

is not just an administrative duty—it is an act of service. Every catalogued book, every organised

shelf, every child helped, and every adult guided is a seed planted for the future.

Your library will shape minds, support families, empower communities, and open doors that may

stay open for a lifetime.

Stand firm in wisdom.

Serve with patience.

Lead with clarity.

And build something that lasts.

Your library may begin as a room of books, but with dedication and heart, it will become a place

of transformation for generations to come.

END

fields.title: Chapter 1
fields.body_html:
The Spirit is a Real Person

efore we can understand what the Holy Spirit does, we have to understand who He is . The Holy Spirit isn’t just some kind of “power” or “energy” from heaven. He’s a real, living Person, God Himself, and He deserves our love, trust, worship, and full surrender.

When you start seeing the Holy Spirit as your Friend and Helper , not just a “force,” your Christian life changes. Real Christian living means spending time with Him every day, listening to His guidance, and letting Him work in and through you.

Knowing Him, Not Just His Power

Many people make mistakes about the Holy Spirit because they try to understand His work before they truly know Him . It’s impossible to understand what the Holy Spirit does if you don’t first know Him.

We need to decide: is the Holy Spirit just an “influence” from God, or is He a Divine Person, just as real as God the Father and Jesus? If He is a Person (and He is), then He deserves our worship, trust, and love.

Some people think the Holy Spirit is a kind of “power”, that's not it, the Holy Spirit is a Person who wants to guide you.

The Spirit’s Presence Changes Us

The Holy Spirit is a Person of infinite power, wisdom, and holiness, and He lives in every believer.

The Bible shows clearly that the Holy Spirit is a Person. A “person” isn’t just a body with hands and feet; it’s someone who knows , feels , and chooses . The Holy Spirit has all of these characteristics:

• He knows. 1 Corinthians 2:10-11 says the Holy Spirit “searches” and “knows” even the deep things of God. That’s not just energy; that’s a thinking Being.

• He chooses. In 1 Corinthians 12:11, the Holy Spirit chooses who gets which spiritual gifts. He’s not a tool for us to use, He’s God deciding how best to use us.

B

• He loves. Romans 15:30 speaks of “the love of the Spirit.” We often thank God the Father for His love and Jesus for His sacrifice, but when’s the last time you thanked the Holy Spirit for loving you, for chasing you down when you were lost and opening your eyes to Jesus? Without His patience and love, none of us would be saved.

• He feels pain.

Ephesians 4:30 warns us not to “grieve the Holy Spirit.” You can’t grieve a power, but you can grieve a Person. Just like you wouldn’t want to hurt your mom or best friend, knowing the Spirit lives in you makes you think twice about sin.

What He Does Only a Person Can Do

Over and over, the Bible shows the Holy Spirit doing things only a person can do:

• He searches and reveals God’s truth (1 Corinthians 2:10).

• He speaks to the churches (Revelation 2:7).

• He prays for us when we don’t know what to pray (Romans 8:26).

• He testifies about Jesus (John 15:26).

• He teaches us (John 14:26).

• He leads us (Romans 8:14).

• He gives orders and assignments (Acts 13:2; Acts 16:6-7).

Our Comforter and Friend

When Jesus was about to leave His disciples, they felt scared and lost. But He promised them “another Comforter, the Holy Spirit, to be with them forever (John 14:16-17). The Spirit isn’t just “power” to help you live for God; He’s God Himself living with you and in you .

Treat Him like a Person

The Bible says people can:

• Rebel against the Spirit (Isaiah 63:10).

• Insult the Spirit (Hebrews 10:29).

• Lie to the Spirit (Acts 5:3).

• Blaspheme the Spirit (Matthew 12:31-32).

Most Christians say with their mouths that they believe in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, but in practice, they treat the Spirit like a power instead of a Person.

The Secret of Real Christian Living

Every week, you may hear the blessing from 2 Corinthians 13:14: “The grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit be with you all.” But have you ever really experienced the fellowship (friendship, partnership, closeness) of the Holy Spirit?

This is the secret of a strong, joyful Christian life:

• To know the Holy Spirit as your Friend.

• To walk with Him daily.

• To let Him lead and guide every area of your life.

fields.title: Chapter 2
fields.body_html:
The Deity of the Holy Spirit

n the last chapter, we learned that the Holy Spirit is a real Person. But now we need to ask: What kind of Person is He? Is He just a powerful being, or is He actually God ? The Bible makes it very clear that the Holy Spirit is God Himself . Let’s look at five major proofs.

1. The Holy Spirit Has God’s Attributes

The Bible gives the Holy Spirit the qualities that only belong to God:

• Eternal (forever): Hebrews 9:14 calls Him the eternal Spirit.

• Everywhere (omnipresent): Psalm 139:7-10 says you can’t escape His presence— whether in heaven, the sea, or the depths of the earth, He’s there.

• All-knowing (omniscient): 1 Corinthians 2:10-11 tells us the Spirit knows everything, even the thoughts of God. John 14:26 says He will teach us all things, and John 16:12-13 shows He guides us into all truth and even tells what’s coming.

• All-powerful (omnipotent): Luke 1:35 shows His power when the angel tells Mary that the Holy Spirit will cause Jesus to be born.

2. The Holy Spirit Does God’s Works

Only God can do certain things. The Bible says the Spirit does them too:

• Creation: Job 33:4 says, The Spirit of God has made me. Psalm 104:30 adds, When You send Your Spirit, they are created. Genesis 1 also shows the Spirit active in creation.

• Giving Life: John 6:63 says the Spirit gives life. Romans 8:11 shows He gives life to our mortal bodies. Even in Genesis 2:7, where God breathed life into Adam, the fuller New Testament revelation shows the Spirit’s role.

• Prophecy (God’s messages): 2 Peter 1:21 says people spoke God’s words as the Spirit guided them. In the Old Testament, 2 Samuel 23:2-3 says, The Spirit of the Lord speaks by me.

So, the Spirit creates, gives life, and delivers God’s words—all things that only God can do.

I

3. The Holy Spirit Is Identified With Jehovah (God)

In the Old Testament, many verses speak about Jehovah (God). The New Testament applies some of those same verses to the Holy Spirit.

• Example 1: Isaiah 6 describes Jehovah speaking. But in Acts 28:25-27, Paul says it was actually the Holy Spirit speaking through Isaiah.

• Example 2: In Exodus 16:7, Israel’s complaints were against Jehovah. But Hebrews 3:7- 9 says their rebellion was against the Holy Spirit.

This shows the Holy Spirit isn’t just representing God; He is God.

4. The Holy Spirit Is Equal with the Father and the Son

The Bible puts the Holy Spirit’s name right alongside the Father and the Son, showing He is their equal:

• 1 Corinthians 12:4-6: Spirit, Lord, and God are all listed together in equality.

• Matthew 28:19: Jesus commands baptism in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

• 2 Corinthians 13:14: Paul blesses believers with the grace of Jesus, the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit.

No created being or angel could be placed alongside the Father and Son like this. Only God Himself could.

5. The Holy Spirit Is God

Finally, Acts 5:3-4 makes it clear. Peter tells Ananias that when he lied to the Holy Spirit, he wasn’t lying to people; he was lying to God.

So, without a doubt, the Holy Spirit is not just some power or influence; He is God Himself, a Divine Person.

fields.title: Chapter 3
fields.body_html:
The Holy Spirit Is Different from the Father and Jesus

o far, we have seen that the Holy Spirit is a real Person, and not just any person, but fully God. Now another big question comes up: Is the Holy Spirit the same as the Father or Jesus? Or is He distinct from them?

When we carefully look at what the Bible says, it’s very clear: the Holy Spirit is not the same as the Father or the Son—He is a separate Person.

Let’s check out some examples:

• At Jesus’ baptism (Luke 3:21–22), all three Persons showed up. Jesus was in the water, the Holy Spirit came down like a dove, and the Father spoke from heaven, saying, “You are my beloved Son; with you I am well pleased.” You can see it: three distinct Persons, all present and active at the same time.

• In Matthew 28:19 , Jesus told His disciples to baptize people “in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.” Notice how He lists them separately, yet together, showing they’re all equally God but not the same Person.

• In John 14:16 , Jesus says, “I will ask the Father, and He will give you another Helper, to be with you forever.” Here we see Jesus (the Son) asking the Father, and then the Father sending the Holy Spirit. Three Persons, working in unity.

• In John 16:7 , Jesus makes it even clearer. He tells His disciples that it’s better for them if He leaves because then the Holy Spirit will come. Jesus was going back to the Father, but the Spirit was coming to take His place on earth.

• In Acts 2:33 , after Jesus rose from the dead and went to heaven, the Bible says He was exalted to the right hand of the Father. From there, He received the Holy Spirit from the Father and poured Him out on the believers. Again, three Persons in action.

All of these verses show the same thing: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three distinct Persons. They talk to each other, send each other, and work with each other, but they are all fully God, united in perfect harmony.

S

fields.title: Chapter 4
fields.body_html:
The Holy Spirit’s Role under the Father and the Son

ven though the Holy Spirit is fully God, He chooses to take a supportive role to the Father and the Son. He points people to Jesus and carries out the will of God the Father. This isn’t about being “less important,” but about unity and teamwork within the Trinity.

Just like Jesus was fully God but still submitted to the Father while on earth, the Holy Spirit also works in a way that shows His connection and obedience to both the Father and the Son.

The Bible makes this clear:

• Sent by the Father and the Son In John 14:26, Jesus said: “But the Helper, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, he will teach you all things and bring to your remembrance all that I have said to you.” Here, the Spirit is sent by the Father, but in Jesus’ name. In John 15:26, Jesus adds: “But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me.” So, the Father sends the Spirit, and the Son also sends Him. That shows teamwork and unity, not competition.

• His Names Show His connection The Spirit is sometimes called “the Spirit of God” (Romans 8:9) and also “the Spirit of Christ.” In Acts 16:7, He’s even called “the Spirit of Jesus.” These names show that His role is deeply tied to both the Father and the Son.

• He Speaks What He Hears John 16:13 says: “When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his own authority, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come.” The Holy Spirit doesn’t just come up with His own message. He passes on what He hears from the Father and the Son.

E

• He Glorifies Jesus John 16:14 says: “He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you.” The Spirit doesn’t try to make Himself the center of attention. His mission is to make Jesus known and honored, just like Jesus made it His mission to glorify the Father.

From all this, we see that while the Holy Spirit is completely God, He has chosen a role where He works under the direction of the Father and the Son. But this doesn’t mean He’s “less than them,” it’s about unity. In fact, just as Jesus lived and worked on earth in the power of the Holy Spirit, we see that they all work together perfectly in love and purpose.

fields.title: Chapter 5
fields.body_html:
The Holy Spirit: Who He Is and What He Does

he Bible gives the Holy Spirit 25 different names, and each one shows us something amazing about Him. The Spirit is God living in the world and in believers, making God real in our hearts. He’s closely connected to Jesus and helps us know Him personally. As our promised Comforter, He guides, empowers, and changes us to live holy lives.

I. The Spirit

The simplest name for the Holy Spirit is just “The Spirit.” In Hebrew and Greek, this word means “breath” or “wind.”

1. Breath:

• John 20:22 says, “Jesus breathed on them and said, ‘Receive the Holy Spirit.’”

• Genesis 2:7 shows God breathing life into Adam.

This teaches us that the Holy Spirit is God’s own life coming into us. When we receive the Holy Spirit, we’re receiving God Himself inside of us.

2. Wind:

• John 3:6-8 compares the Spirit to the wind: “The wind blows where it wants, and you can hear it but not see it.”

The Holy Spirit is:

• Sovereign: He does His own thing. We can’t control Him, but we can cooperate with Him.

• Invisible but real: We can feel His presence and see His work, even if we can’t see Him.

• Essential: Just like air and wind are necessary for life, the Spirit is necessary for spiritual life.

• Life-giving: Ezekiel 37:8-10 shows that the Spirit can bring even dry bones to life—He makes us spiritually and physically alive!

T

• Irresistible: Just like a powerful storm can’t be stopped, a Spirit-filled person can’t be resisted.

II. The Spirit of God

Sometimes the Bible calls Him the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 3:16). This just emphasises that He comes from God, with all His divine power.

III. The Spirit of Jehovah

In Isaiah 11:2, the Holy Spirit is called the Spirit of Jehovah. This shows He is God’s covenant Spirit, the one who stays true to His promises.

IV. The Spirit of the Lord Jehovah

Isaiah 61:1-3 calls Him the Spirit of the Lord Jehovah. This is even more personal—it shows the Spirit’s connection to God as Lord and Covenant Keeper for His people.

V. The Spirit of the Living God

2 Corinthians 3:3 calls Him the Spirit of the living God. This name tells us that the Holy Spirit makes God real to us, not just a concept. He makes God someone we can know and experience personally.

VI. The Spirit of Christ

Romans 8:9 calls Him the Spirit of Christ. Why?

1. He’s Christ’s gift: Jesus gives the Holy Spirit to believers.

2. He reveals Christ: John 16:14 shows that the Spirit points us to Jesus.

3. He forms Christ in us: Ephesians 3:16-17 says the Spirit makes Christ live in our hearts.

VII. The Spirit of Jesus Christ

Philippians 1:19 calls Him the Spirit of Jesus Christ. This emphasises that the Spirit comes from the Man Jesus, who was raised and exalted.

VIII. The Spirit of Jesus

Acts 16:6-7 shows the Spirit of Jesus guiding the early church. He directs believers in their mission and decisions.

IX. The Spirit of His Son

Galatians 4:6 calls Him the Spirit of His Son. This name reminds us that the Spirit makes us children of God. We’re not slaves—we’re sons and daughters who can say, “Abba, Father!”

X. The Holy Spirit

Luke 11:13 reminds us that God will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. This name emphasizes His holiness. He is pure, and when we invite Him into our lives, He transforms us.

XI. The Holy Spirit of Promise

Ephesians 1:13 calls Him the Holy Spirit of promise. He is God’s promise to us—the gift Jesus said we should wait for after He went back to heaven.

XII. The Spirit of Holiness

Romans 1:4 calls Him the Spirit of holiness. He is not only Holy, but He also makes us Holy too.

XIII. The Spirit of Judgment & XIV. The Spirit of Burning

Isaiah 4:4 shows two names:

• Spirit of Judgment: He shows us our sins and helps us see them as God sees them. Spirit of Burning: He purifies, refines, energises, and transforms us, like a fire in our hearts.

XV. The Spirit of Truth

John 14:17 calls Him the Spirit of truth. He teaches us all truth and guides us in God’s ways.

XVI. The Spirit of Wisdom, Counsel, and Knowledge

Isaiah 11:2 shows He gives:

• Wisdom & Understanding

• Counsel & Might

• Knowledge & Fear of the Lord

In short, He equips us with the smarts, strength, and reverence we need to live for God.

XIX. The Spirit of Life

Romans 8:2 calls Him the Spirit of life. He sets us free from sin and gives spiritual life.

XX. The Oil of Gladness

Hebrews 1:9 calls Him the oil of gladness. He fills us with joy that can’t be taken away, even in hard times.

XXI–XXII. The Spirit of Grace & Supplication

• Spirit of Grace: Hebrews 10:29 shows He gives us God’s grace to live for Him.

• Spirit of Grace and Supplication: Zechariah 12:10 shows He teaches us how to pray and connects us to God deeply.

XXIII. The Spirit of Glory

1 Peter 4:14 calls Him the Spirit of glory. He gives us God’s glory as we live for Him and endure challenges.

XXIV. The Eternal Spirit

Hebrews 9:14 calls Him the eternal Spirit. He is infinite, eternal, and divine; our God is forever, and the Spirit lives in us now.

Before Jesus went back to heaven, He had already been the disciples’ helper. Whenever they were in trouble, they went straight to Him. For example:

• Once, the disciples didn’t know how to pray, so they asked Jesus, “Lord, teach us to pray.” Jesus taught them the prayer we now call the Lord’s Prayer (Luke 11:1–4).

• Another time, Peter was sinking in the water and shouted, “Lord, save me!” Jesus immediately reached out and caught him (Matthew 14:30–31).

In every hard situation, they turned to Him. Now that Jesus is in heaven, we have someone just as Divine, wise, strong, loving, and tender, always ready to help us, the Holy Spirit. Even better, He lives in our hearts and will help us if we trust Him.

If we really understand the Holy Spirit as our helper, loneliness disappears. How could we ever feel alone when the best Friend ever is right with us?

Dr. Torrey shared from his own life. For eight years, he was separated from his family because of his work. That kind of loneliness would have been unbearable—except for the Holy Spirit. He remembered walking alone on the deck of a stormy ship in the South Seas. His family was so far away, the officers were busy, and he felt alone. But then he realised: the Holy Spirit was walking beside him. And that was enough.

Once, at a Bible conference, a doctor thanked him. The doctor often drove long distances in the night through storms and felt lonely, but now he understood that the Holy Spirit was always with him, and that made him fearless.

Dr. Torrey shared another story. One night, he had to walk four miles along a dark lake path during a thunderstorm. It was dangerous, but he remembered what he had taught about the Holy Spirit as a Friend. He thought, “He’s walking with me,” and he went forward without fear.

Even a young woman in London overcame her fear of the dark because she believed the Holy Spirit was always with her. She went into a completely dark room alone and felt no fear; she even described the room as glowing with His presence.

The helper also helps with insomnia. Dr. Torrey suffered from it for two terrible years. One night, tired and sad, he remembered teaching about the Holy Spirit as a Friend. He prayed and opened his heart to Him. Instantly, joy filled him—and he fell asleep. From then on, whenever insomnia returned, he simply trusted the Holy Spirit.

The Holy Spirit even heals broken hearts. Many people experience deep loss and loneliness when loved ones die. But the Holy Spirit can fill every empty, aching part of our hearts. Dr. Torrey told of a widow in Glasgow. On the anniversary of her husband’s death, she came to a meeting and found hope in the thought of the Holy Spirit as her Friend. Years later, she said He continued to satisfy and fill her heart.

This help extends to our work for God, too. Dr. Torrey himself wasn’t naturally confident. As a boy and even as a college student, he was shy. But once he understood that the Holy Spirit was there to guide him, everything changed. Preaching became a joy, not a fear.

The Holy Spirit helps in all parts of Christian life:

• When we pray (Romans 8:26–27)

• When we study the Bible (John 14:26; John 16:12–14)

• When we share faith with others (Acts 8:29)

• When we teach or preach (1 Corinthians 2:4)

• When we face temptation (Romans 8:2)

• Even when we die (Acts 7:54–60)

Let’s never forget: the Holy Spirit is our helper , always by our side to guide us, help us, and take our part in everything.

fields.title: Chapter 6
fields.body_html:
The Holy Spirit and the World around Us

he Holy Spirit doesn’t just work in people—He’s involved in the whole universe! He helped create the world and keeps everything alive. Many people think the Holy Spirit only cares about humans, but the Bible shows His work is everywhere.

The Holy Spirit has a three-part role in the material universe:

1. The Holy Spirit Created Everything

The Bible shows that the Holy Spirit was part of creation:

• Psalm 33:6 : “By the word of the Lord the heavens were made, and by the breath of his mouth all their host.”

• Job 33:4 : “The Spirit of God has made me, and the breath of the Almighty gives me life.”

This means the Spirit helped create the stars, the earth, animals, and people. The Father, Son, and Holy Spirit all worked together in making the world (Genesis 1:1-3; Colossians 1:16; Hebrews 1- 2).

2. The Holy Spirit Keeps Everything Alive

Creation doesn’t just exist on its own. The Holy Spirit sustains all life :

• Psalm 104:29-30 : When God takes away His Spirit, life ends. When He sends His Spirit, everything is renewed.

The Spirit not only keeps humans alive, but also the entire universe. Nothing survives without Him. This is why the world isn’t God—it’s God’s creation, alive because of His Spirit.

3. The Holy Spirit Develops Life

The Holy Spirit also transforms the world from chaos to order :

• Genesis 1:1-3 : The Spirit hovered over the waters before God said, “Let there be light.”

• Genesis 2:7 : God breathed life into man, making him a living being.

T

Through the Spirit, creation moved from simple matter to plants, animals, humans, and eventually, God’s perfect plan in Jesus Christ. The Bible shows a step-by-step development , not random evolution: lower forms of life become higher forms through God’s Spirit.

fields.title: Chapter 7
fields.body_html:
The Holy Spirit Convicting the World of Sin,

Righteousness, and Judgment

he Holy Spirit is God’s helper who shows people what is right and wrong. He helps us see our mistakes, especially not trusting Jesus, shows us how good Jesus is, and reminds us that one day everyone will have to answer for their choices. We can’t understand this on our own; it only happens when the Holy Spirit helps us.

1. Realising Our Mistakes

Our journey to knowing Jesus starts when we see that we really need Him. The Holy Spirit helps us notice the wrong things we do. Jesus said in John 16:8-11 that the Spirit will help people understand sin, right choices, and God’s ways. The first example of this is in Acts 2:36-37. Peter told the people that Jesus was Lord and the One they had rejected and even killed. When they heard this, they felt deep guilt and asked, “What should we do?” The Holy Spirit had done His work—helping them see their mistakes.

Even if Peter had said the same thing before, it wouldn’t have worked. But with the Holy Spirit, His words have power. Only the Holy Spirit can truly help someone realise their mistakes. Our hearts can trick us, and we often don’t notice our own faults, but we see everyone else’s easily.

That’s why trying to make someone see their mistakes by arguing or reasoning doesn’t always work. Friends, teachers, or pastors can use the Bible and logic, but without the Holy Spirit, hearts don’t change.

For example, a worker in Chicago tried for two hours to show an engineer his mistakes, but nothing happened. When Dr. Torrey trusted the Holy Spirit to work, the man quickly realized his mistakes and asked God for help.

The Holy Spirit can even reach the hardest hearts. No one is too proud, too busy, or too good for Him to help. Everyone needs Him to open their eyes to their mistakes.

Realising Jesus is perfect

2. Seeing Jesus is Right

The Holy Spirit also helps people see that Jesus always did what’s right. Even though some people didn’t believe in Him, Jesus is perfect and approved by God. His resurrection shows everyone that He is completely right in God’s eyes (Ephesians 1:21).

T

3. Understanding God’s Judgment

The Holy Spirit helps people understand that there is right and wrong and that bad things have consequences. He shows that the devil—the one who tries to lead people away from God—has already been defeated through Jesus’ death and resurrection. The cross wasn’t just Jesus being punished; it was also a victory over the devil.

Talking about judgment can feel scary because people don’t like thinking about punishment. But the Holy Spirit helps us see why it’s serious. Dr. Torrey said that when he experienced the Holy Spirit, he finally understood how important God’s judgment is and knew what the Bible teaches.

The Holy Spirit works through believers to convince the world of sin, righteousness, and judgment. On the Day of Pentecost, He came to the disciples and used them to reach the 3,000 people who were saved. The Spirit still works through us today.

The main sin He points out is unbelief in Jesus. It’s not stealing, lying, or other moral failures that are the key sin, though they are sins too. The biggest issue is whether someone believes in Christ. Many people even see unbelief as a sign of intelligence or superiority. But the Holy Spirit shows it for what it really is: rebellion against God.

fields.title: Chapter 8
fields.body_html:
The Holy Spirit Bearing Witness to Jesus Christ

hen our Lord was talking to His disciples on the night before His crucifixion of the Comforter who, after His departure, was to come to take His place, He said, “But when the Helper comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, who proceeds from the Father, he will bear witness about me. And you also will bear witness, because you have been with me from the beginning.” (John 15:26, 27 KJV), and the Apostle Peter and the other disciples, when they were strictly commanded by the Jewish Council not to teach in the name of Jesus said, “And we are his witnesses of these things; and so is also the Holy Ghost, whom God hath given to them that obey him” (Acts 5:32 KJV).

It is clear from these words of Jesus Christ and the Apostles that it is the work of the Holy Spirit to bear witness concerning Jesus Christ. We find the Holy Spirit's testimony to Jesus Christ in the Scriptures; besides this, the Holy Spirit bears witness directly to the individual heart concerning Jesus Christ. He takes his Scriptures and interprets them to us and makes them clear to us. All truth is from the Spirit, for He is “the Spirit of truth,” but it is especially His work to bear witness to Him who is the truth, that is, Jesus Christ (John 14:6).

It is only through the testimony of the Holy Spirit directly to our hearts that we ever come to a true, living knowledge of Jesus Christ (1 Corinthians 12:3). No amount of mere reading the written Word (in the Bible) and no amount of listening to man's testimony will ever bring us to a living knowledge of Christ. It is only when the Holy Spirit Himself takes the written Word, or takes the testimony of our fellow man, and interprets it directly to our hearts that we come to see and know Jesus as He is.

On the day of Pentecost, Peter gave all his hearers the testimony of the Scriptures regarding Christ and also gave them his testimony. He told them what he and the other Apostles knew by personal observation regarding His resurrection, but unless the Holy Spirit Himself had taken the Scriptures which Peter had brought together and taken the testimony of Peter and the other disciples, the 3,000 would not on that day have seen Jesus as He was and received Him and been baptised in His name.

The Holy Spirit added His testimony to that of Peter and that of the written Word. Mr. Moody used to say in his terse and graphic way that when Peter said, “Let all the house of Israel therefore know for certain that God has made him both Lord and Christ, this Jesus whom you crucified (Acts 2:36), the Holy Spirit said, ‘Amen’ and the people saw and believed.” And it is certain that unless the Holy Spirit had come that day and through Peter and the other Apostles borne His direct testimony to the hearts of their hearers, there would have been no saving vision of Jesus on the part of the people.

W

If you wish men to get a true view of Jesus Christ, such a view of Him that they may believe and be saved, it is not enough that you give them the Scriptures concerning Him; it is not enough that you give them your testimony, you must seek for them the testimony of the Holy Spirit and put yourself into such relations with God that the Holy Spirit may bear His testimony through you. Neither your testimony, nor even that of the written Word alone, will effect this, though it is your testimony, or that of the Word, that the Holy Spirit uses. But unless your testimony and that of the Word is taken up by the Holy Spirit and He testifies, they will not believe. This explains something which every experienced worker must have noticed. We sit down beside an inquirer and open our Bibles and give him those Scriptures which reveal Jesus as his atoning Saviour on the cross, a Saviour from the guilt of sin, and as his risen Saviour, a Saviour from the power of sin.

It is just the truth the man needs to see and believe to be saved, but he does not see it. We go over these Scriptures, which to us are as plain as day, again and again, and the inquirer sits there in blank darkness; he sees nothing, he grasps nothing. Sometimes we almost wonder if the inquirer is stupid, that he cannot see it. No, he is not stupid, except with that spiritual blindness that possesses every mind unenlightened by the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 2:14). We go over it again, and still he does not see it. We go over it again, and his face lightens up and he exclaims, “I see it. I see it,” and he sees Jesus and believes and is saved and knows he is saved there on the spot. What has happened? Simply this, the Holy Spirit has borne His testimony, and what was dark as midnight before is as clear as day now.

This also explains why it is that one who has been long in darkness concerning Jesus Christ so quickly comes to see the truth when he surrenders his will to God and seeks light from Him. When he surrenders his will to God, he has put himself into that attitude towards God where the Holy Spirit can do His work (Acts 5:32). Jesus says in John 7:17, “If anyone's will is to do God's will, he is saved there on the spot. What has happened? Simply this, the Holy Spirit has borne His testimony, and what was dark as midnight before is as clear as day now. This also explains why it is that one who has long been in darkness concerning Jesus Christ so quickly comes to see the truth when he surrenders his will to God and seeks light from Him.

When he surrenders his will to God, he has put himself into that attitude towards God where the Holy Spirit can do His work (Acts 5:32). Jesus says in John 7:17, “If anyone's will is to do God's will, he will know whether the teaching is from God or whether I am speaking on my authority.” When a man wills to do the will of God, then the conditions are provided on which the Holy Spirit works, and He illuminates the mind to see the truth about Jesus and to see that His teaching is the very Word of God. John writes in John 20:31, “but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.” John wrote his Gospel for this purpose, that men might see Jesus as the Christ, the Son of God, through what he records, and that they might believe that He is the Christ, the Son of God, and that thus believing they might have life through His name.

The best book in the world to put into the hands of one who desires to know about Jesus and to be saved is the Gospel of John. And yet many a man has read the Gospel of John over and over again and not seen and believed that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God. But let the same man surrender his will absolutely to God and ask God for light as he reads the Gospel and promise God that he will take his stand on everything in the Gospel that He shows him to be true and before the man has finished the Gospel he will see clearly that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and will believe and have eternal life. Because he has put himself into the place where the Holy Spirit can take the things written in the Gospel and interpret them and bear His testimony.

I have seen this tested and proven time and time again all around the world. Men have come to me and said to me that they did not believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and many have gone further and said they were nonbelievers and did not even know whether there was a personal God. Then I told them to read the Gospel of John, which presents the evidence that Jesus was Christ and the Son of God. Oftentimes, they have told me they have read it over and over again, and yet were not convinced that Jesus was the Christ, and the Son of God. Then I have said to them, “You have not read it the right way,” and I have got them to surrender their will to God (or in case where they were not sure there was a God, have got them to take their stand upon the right to follow it wherever it might carry them).

Then I have had them agree to read the Gospel of John slowly and thoughtfully, and each time before they read to look up to God, if there were any God, to help them to understand what they were to read and to promise Him that they would take their stand upon whatever He showed them to be true, and follow it wherever it would carry them. And in every instance, before they had finished the Gospel, they had come to see that Jesus was the Christ and the Son of God, and had believed and been saved. They had put themselves in that position where the Holy Spirit could bear His testimony to Jesus Christ, and He had done it, and through His testimony, they saw and believed.

If you wish men to see the truth about Christ, do not depend upon your powers of expression and persuasion, but cast yourself upon the Holy Spirit and seek for them His testimony, and see to it that they put themselves in the place where the Holy Spirit can testify. This is the cure for both disbelief and ignorance concerning Christ. If you are not clear concerning the truth about Jesus Christ, seek for yourself the testimony of the Holy Spirit regarding Christ. Read the Scriptures, read especially the Gospel of John, but do not depend upon the mere reading of the Word, but before you read it, put yourself in such an attitude towards God by the absolute surrender of your will to Him that the Holy Spirit may bear His testimony in your heart concerning Jesus Christ. What is mostly needed is a clear and full vision of Jesus Christ, and this comes through the testimony of the Holy Spirit.

One night, a number of our students came back from the Pacific Garden Mission in Chicago and said to me, “We had a wonderful meeting at the mission tonight. There were many drunkards and outcasts at the front who accepted Christ.”

The next day I met Mr. Harry Monroe, the superintendent of the mission, on the street, and I said, “Harry, the boys say you had a wonderful meeting at the mission last night.” “Would you like to know how it came about?” he replied. “Yes.” “Well,” he said, “I simply held up 63 Jesus Christ and it pleased the Holy Spirit to illumine the face of Jesus Christ, and men saw and believed.” It was a unique way of putting it, but it was an expressive way and true to the essential facts in the case. It is our part to hold up Jesus Christ, and then look to the Holy Spirit to illumine His face or to take the truth about Him and make it clear to the hearts of our hearers, and He will do it, and men will see and believe. Of course, we need to be so walking towards God so that the Holy Spirit may take us as the instruments through whom He will bear His testimony.

fields.title: Chapter 9
fields.body_html:
How the Holy Spirit Makes Us New

eing “born again” isn’t something we can do by ourselves. It’s something the Holy Spirit does in us. He gives us a new life inside, helping us think differently, feel differently, and make better choices. The Bible is His guide, but only He can make it real in our hearts. Being “good,” going to church, or trying really hard to fix yourself can’t do this on its own. Even someone who seems far from God can be changed by the Holy Spirit.

The Apostle Paul writes: "He saved us, not because of what we did, but because of His mercy. He saved us through the washing of rebirth and renewal by the Holy Spirit." (Titus 3:5)

Jesus also told Nicodemus: "No one can enter God’s kingdom unless they are born of water and the Spirit." (John 3:5)

This shows that being born again in your heart is important.

What is regeneration? Regeneration is the impartation of life, spiritual life, to those who are spiritually dead through their trespasses and sins (Ephesians 2:1). The Holy Spirit imparts this life. The written Word is indeed the instrument which the Holy Spirit uses in regeneration. We read in 1 Peter 1:23, “Since you have been born again, not of perishable seed but of imperishable, through the living and abiding word of God.” We read in James 1:18, “Of his own will he brought us forth by the word of truth, that we should be a kind of first fruits of his creatures.” These passages make it plain that the Word is the instrument used in regeneration, but it is only as the Holy Spirit uses the instrument that the new birth results. “It is the Spirit who gives life.” (John 6:63).

Paul teaches that just reading the Bible isn’t enough. God’s Spirit needs to make the words alive in our hearts. Without Him, even the truth can be hard to understand. But when the Spirit works, the truth becomes alive and changes us.

Being born again means getting a new nature from God (2 Peter 1:4). Everyone is born with a nature twisted by sin:

• A mind that can’t fully see or understand God (1 Corinthians 2:14).

• A heart that loves the wrong things and hates the right things (Galatians 5:19-21).

• A will that wants to please itself instead of God (Romans 8:7).

B

When the Holy Spirit regenerates us, He gives:

• A mind that sees and thinks like God (1 Corinthians 2:12-14).

• A heart that loves what God loves and hates what He hates (Galatians 5:22-23).

• A will that delights in doing God’s work (John 4:34; John 6:38).

No amount of preaching or studying the Bible can create this change—it’s the Spirit alone who makes a person a new creation.

The Bible compares it to a seed. The human heart is the soil, the Word of God is the seed, and the Spirit is the one who makes it grow (Luke 8:11; 1 Peter 1:23; James 1:18). You can plant the seed, but it’s the Spirit who quickens it and produces life in the heart.

Real-life examples: Some people seem completely hopeless, addicted, lost, or broken, but when they hear God’s Word and the Spirit touches them, they can be transformed into a new creation. Their thoughts, hearts, and actions change, and they start living in a way that pleases God.

This is called sudden regeneration. It means not just changing how you look on the outside, but being completely new on the inside. The Bible shows it, and it happens all the time. The Holy Spirit can bring life to hearts that feel far away from God.

The Holy Spirit’s work shows us that:

• Education can’t save us.

• Being good can’t save us.

• Going to church, reading the Bible, or praying can’t save us.

But here’s the good news: anyone can be born again. You can become like Jesus, loving what God loves and hating what He hates. The Spirit can give you His life, and you can be completely renewed.

fields.title: Chapter 10
fields.body_html:
The Holy Spirit: Fullness and Forever Joy

he Holy Spirit lives inside everyone who believes in Jesus. He gives joy, peace, and strength that last, not like temporary happiness from money, popularity, games, or entertainment. When we pay attention to Him and follow His leading, He fills our hearts with real satisfaction.

1. The Holy Spirit Lives in Every Believer

Every Christian is a home for God’s Spirit . The Bible says in 1 Corinthians 6:19 that our bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit.

Even when we make mistakes, He doesn’t leave us. We don’t have to invite Him to come—He is already there. Our job is to listen to Him, obey Him, and let Him guide us in how we think and live.

2. The Holy Spirit Gives Lasting Satisfaction

Jesus said in John 4 that those who receive the water He gives will never be thirsty again. He was talking about the Holy Spirit.

Earthly things fade fast, but the Spirit is like a never-ending fountain :

• He comforts us when we’re hurting.

• He gives peace in sadness.

• He brings hope when everything feels dark.

As Isaiah 61:3 says, He replaces sadness with joy and beauty.

3. The Spirit Helps Us Let Go of Empty Pleasures

When the Holy Spirit fills our hearts:

• We don’t crave unhealthy or distracting pleasures,

• Not because we’re forced to give them up,

• Not because we’ve found something better .

D. L. Moody once said he could go to the theatre anytime he wanted, but he just didn’t want to. That’s the kind of change the Spirit brings: new desires, new joy, new freedom.

T

4. Removing the Things That Block His Joy

Things like sin, stubbornness, or ignoring God can block the Spirit’s joy in our lives when we:

• Confess,

• Obey,

• And surrender, the Holy Spirit fills us again with peace and power.

fields.title: Chapter 11
fields.body_html:
The Holy Spirit Sets Us Free From Sin

n our own, we cannot overcome sin. Even Paul tried to obey God’s law by his own strength, but he kept failing. He discovered that there were two forces at work in him, God’s law telling him what to do, and another power in him pulling him toward sin. This led to frustration and defeat.

But Paul also discovered the answer is the Holy Spirit.

Romans 8:2 teaches that the Holy Spirit sets us free from the power of sin. When we stop depending on our own willpower and instead rely on the Spirit, He gives us strength to live the way God wants. The normal Christian life is not constant failure, it is daily victory through the Spirit.

We still have the flesh and temptation, but the Spirit gives us the power to resist and obey God. This victory does not come from ourselves, and if we become proud, neglect prayer, or ignore God’s Word, we can fall.

The Holy Spirit works through Scripture. The more we stay in God’s Word and depend on Him in prayer, the more we walk in freedom from sin.

O

fields.title: Chapter 12
fields.body_html:
The Holy Spirit Forms Christ within Us

e cannot become like Jesus by trying really hard. The Holy Spirit is the One who forms Christ’s character in us and helps us live like Him from the inside out. In Ephesians 3:16– 19, Paul prays that believers will be strengthened by the Spirit so Christ may live deeply in their hearts.

The Spirit does four major things in this process:

1. Christ dwells in us

The Spirit doesn’t just visit us, He settles deep within us. Instead of us trying to imitate Jesus in our own strength, the Spirit makes Christ live His life through us. 2. He roots and grounds us in love

The Spirit builds our lives on love, love toward God and others. Since Jesus is love, becoming like Him means growing in love. 3. He helps us understand Christ’s love

Christ’s love is huge—too big for our minds to fully grasp—but the Spirit helps us experience and appreciate it personally. 4. He fills us with the fullness of God

The Spirit’s work is a lifelong process of making us more like God in character and maturity. Day by day, He keeps shaping us until we reflect more of God’s fullness.

W

fields.title: Chapter 13
fields.body_html:
The Holy Spirit Producing Christ-like Character in Us

rue Christian character is the fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23). We cannot produce this fruit by our own effort. It is the Holy Spirit who forms Christ-like character in us.

He replaces the works of the flesh—selfishness, anger, jealousy—with love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.

Character is not produced by forcing ourselves to be better, any more than fruit grows by pulling on a branch. Fruit comes when the tree has life and the right conditions. Likewise, spiritual fruit comes when the Spirit lives in us, and we yield to His control.

It is not our struggle, but His work. When we stop depending on ourselves and fully let the Holy Spirit govern our lives, the fruit of the Spirit appears naturally and continually.

T

fields.title: Chapter 15
fields.body_html:
The Holy Spirit Confirming Our Sonship

he Holy Spirit doesn’t just guide us, He also tells us that we are God’s children. Romans 8:15-16 says, “You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father.’ The Spirit bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God.”

When we accept Jesus as our Saviour, surrender to the Spirit, and live in obedience, the Spirit fills our hearts with a deep sense of being God’s children. It’s more than just calling God “Father” with our lips; we actually feel it in our hearts.

Imagine a child who has never spoken before finally saying ‘Papa.’ In the same way, when we call God “Abba, Father” from our hearts, the Spirit fills Him with joy because He loves to hear His children recognise Him as their Father.

So the journey is clear:

1. Accept Jesus as Saviour.

2. Surrender your life to the Holy Spirit.

3. Walk in obedience and trust Him.

4. Let the Spirit fill you with a real sense of being God’s child.

When all these steps happen, you experience the freedom, confidence, and joy of being a true child of God.

T

fields.title: Chapter 16
fields.body_html:
The Holy Spirit as a Teacher

he Holy Spirit teaches believers by bringing to mind the words of Christ when needed and guiding them into all truth, revealing deep spiritual realities that human wisdom cannot grasp. He helps believers understand Scripture by illuminating its meaning and empowers them to communicate God’s truth effectively, emphasizing that true understanding and teaching depend on the Spirit’s guidance rather than human knowledge alone.

Our Lord Jesus in His last conversation with His disciples before His crucifixion said, “But the Comforter which is the Holy Ghost, whom the Father will send in My name, He shall teach you all things, and bring all things to your remembrance, whatsoever I have said unto you” (John 14:26 KJV). Here we have a twofold work of the Holy Spirit, teaching and bringing to remembrance the things which Christ had already taught. We will take them in the reverse order.

I. The Holy Spirit brings to remembrance the words of Christ. This promise was made primarily to the Apostles and is the guarantee of the accuracy of their report of what Jesus said; but the Holy Spirit does a similar work with each believer who expects it of Him, and who looks to Him to do it. The Holy Spirit brings to our mind the teachings of Christ and the Word just when we need them for either the necessities of our life or of our service.

Many of us could tell of occasions when we were in great distress of soul or great questioning as to duty or great extremity as to what to say to one whom we were trying to lead to Christ or to help, and at that exact moment the very Scripture we needed some passage it may be we had not thought of for a long time and quite likely of which we had never thought in this connection was brought to mind. Who did it? The Holy Spirit did it.

He is ready to do it even more frequently if we only expect it of Him and look to Him to do it. 92 It is our privilege every time we sit down beside an inquirer to point him to the way of life to look up to the Holy Spirit and say, “Just what shall I say to this inquirer? Just what Scripture shall I use?” There is a deep significance in the fact that in the verse immediately following this precious promise, Jesus says, “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you.” It is by the Spirit bringing His words to remembrance and teaching us the truth of God that we obtain and abide in this peace. If we simply look to the Holy Spirit to bring to mind Scripture when we need it, and just the Scripture we need, we shall indeed have Christ's peace every moment of our lives.

One who was preparing for Christian work came to me in great distress. He said he must give up his preparation, for he could not memorize the Scriptures. “I am thirty-two years old,” he said, “and have been in business now for years. I have gotten out of the habit of studying, and I cannot memorize anything.” The man longed to be in his Master's service, and the tears stood in his eyes

T

as he said it. “Don't be discouraged,” I replied. “Take your Lord's promise that the Holy Spirit will bring His words to remembrance, learn one passage of Scripture, fix it firmly in your mind, and then another, and look to the Holy Spirit to bring them to your remembrance when you need them.” He went on with his preparation.

He trusted the Holy Spirit. Afterwards, he took up work in a very difficult field, a field where all sorts of errors abounded. They would gather around him on the street like bees, and he would take his Bible and trust the Holy Spirit to bring to remembrance the passages of Scripture that he needed, and He did it. His adversaries were filled with confusion, as he met them at every point with the sure Word of God, and many of the most hardened were won for Christ.

II. The Holy Spirit will teach us all things. There is a still more explicit promise to this effect two chapters further on in John 16:12-14. Here, Jesus says, “I still have many things to say to you, but you cannot bear them now. When the Spirit of truth comes, he will guide you into all the truth, for he will not speak on his authority, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are to come. He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you.” This promise was made in the first instance to the Apostles, but the Apostles themselves applied it to all believers (1 John 2:20-27). It is the privilege of each believer in Jesus Christ, even the humblest, to be “taught of God.” 93 Independent of human teachers, “You have no need that anyone should teach you” (1 John 2:27). This, of course, does not mean that we may not learn much from others who are taught of the Holy Spirit.

If John had thought that he would never have written this epistle to teach others. The man who is the most fully taught of God is the very one who will be most ready to listen to what God has taught others. Much less does it mean that when we are taught of the Spirit, we are independent of the written Word of God; for the Word is the very place to which the Spirit, who is the Author of the Word, leads His pupils and the instrument through which He instructs them (Ephesians 6:17; John 6:33; Ephesians 5:18-19; Colossians 3:16). But while we may learn much from men, we are not dependent upon them. We have a Divine Teacher, the Holy Spirit.

We shall never truly know the truth until we are taught directly by the Holy Spirit. No amount of mere human teaching, no matter who our teachers may be, will ever give us a correct, exact, and full apprehension of the truth. Not even a diligent study of the Word, either in English or in the original languages, will give us a real understanding of the truth. We must be taught directly by the Holy Spirit, and we may be thus taught, each one of us. The one who is taught will understand the truth of God better, even if he does not know one word of Greek or Hebrew, than the one who knows Greek and Hebrew thoroughly and all the cognate languages as well, but who is not taught of the Spirit. The Spirit will guide the one whom He thus teaches “into the truth.” The whole sphere of God's truth is for each one of us, but the Holy Spirit will not guide us into all the truth in a single day, nor in a week, nor in a year, but step by step.

There are two special lines of the Spirit's teaching mentioned:

(1) “He will declare to you the things that are to come.” Many say we can know nothing of the future, that all our thoughts on that subject are guesswork. Indeed, we cannot know everything about the future. There are some things which God has seen fit to keep to Himself, secret things which belong to Him (Deuteronomy 29:29). For example, we cannot “know the times, or the seasons” of our Lord's return (Acts 1:7), but there are many things about the future which the Holy Spirit will reveal to us.

(2) “He will glorify me, for he will take what is mine and declare it to you.” This is the Holy Spirit's special line of teaching with the believer, as with the unbeliever, Jesus Christ. It is His work above all else to reveal Jesus Christ and to glorify Him. His whole teaching centers on Christ. From one point of 94 view or the other, He is always bringing us to Jesus Christ. Some fear to emphasize the truth about the Holy Spirit in case Christ Himself be mocked and put in the background, but no one magnifies Christ as the Holy Spirit does. We shall never understand Christ, nor see His glory, until the Holy Spirit interprets Him to us.

No amount of listening to sermons and lectures, no matter how able, no amount of mere study of the Word, even, would ever give us to see “the things of Christ”; the Holy Spirit must show us, and He is willing to do it, and He can do it. He is longing to do it. The Holy Spirit's most intense desire is to reveal Jesus Christ to men. On the day of Pentecost, when Peter and the rest of the company were “filled with the Holy Spirit,” they did not talk much about the Holy Spirit; they talked about Christ.

Study Peter's sermon on that day; Jesus Christ was his one theme, and Jesus Christ will be our one theme, if we are taught of the Spirit; Jesus Christ will occupy the whole horizon of our vision. We will have a new Christ, a glorious Christ. Christ will be so glorious to us that we will long to go and tell everyone about this glorious One whom we have found. Jesus Christ is so different when the Spirit glorifies Him by taking of His things and showing them to us.

III. The Holy Spirit reveals to us the deep things of God, which are hidden from and are foolishness to the natural man. We read in 1 Corinthians 2:9-13, “What no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love Him.” These things God has revealed to us through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches everything, even the depths of God. For who knows a person's thoughts except the spirit of that person, which is in him? So also no one understands the thoughts of God except the Spirit of God.

Now we have received not the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God, that we might understand the things freely given to us by God. And we impart this in words not taught by human wisdom but taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual.” This passage refers primarily to the Apostles, but we cannot limit this work of the Spirit to them.

The Spirit reveals to each believer the deep things of God, things no human eye has ever seen, no ear has ever heard, and that have never entered into the heart of man; these are the things God has prepared for those who love Him. It is evident from the context that this does not refer solely to heaven or the things to come in the life hereafter. The Holy Spirit takes the deep things of God, which God has prepared for us, even in the life that now is, and reveals them to us.

IV. The Holy Spirit interprets His revelation. He imparts power to discern, know, and appreciate what He has taught. In the next verse to those just quoted we read, “The natural person does not accept the things of the Spirit of God, for they are folly to him, and he is not able to understand them because they are spiritually discerned.” (1 Corinthians 2:14). Not only is the Holy Spirit the Author of revelation, the written Word of God: He is also the Interpreter of what He has revealed. Any profound book is immeasurably more interesting and helpful when we have the author of the book right at hand to interpret it to us, and always our privilege to have the author of the Bible right at hand when we study it.

The Holy Spirit is the Author of the Bible, and He stands ready to interpret its meaning to every believer every time he opens the Book. To understand the Book, we must look to Him, and then the darkest places become clear. We often need to pray with the Psalmist of old, “Open my eyes, that I may behold wondrous things out of your law” (Psalm 119:18). It is not enough that we have the revelation of God before us in the written Word to study, we must also have the inward illumination of the Holy Spirit to enable us to understand it as we study.

It is a common mistake, but a most noticeable mistake, to try to understand a spiritual revelation with the natural understanding. It is the foolish attempt to do this that has landed so many in the bog of so-called “Higher Criticism.” To understand art, a man must have a beautiful sense as well as the knowledge of colours and paint, and a man to understand a spiritual revelation must be taught of the Spirit. A mere knowledge of the languages in which the Bible was written is not enough. A man with no good sense might as well expect to appreciate the Sistine Madonna, because he is not colour blind, as a man who is not filled with the Spirit to understand the Bible, simply because he understands the vocabulary and the laws of grammar of the languages in which the Bible was written.

We might as well think of setting a man to teach art. He understood that painting was to set a man to teach the Bible because he had a thorough understanding of Greek and Hebrew. In our day we need not only to recognize the utter insufficiency and worthlessness before God of our righteousness, which is the lesson of the opening chapters of the Epistle to the Romans, but also the utter insufficiency and worthlessness in the things of God of our wisdom, which is the lesson of the First Epistle to the Corinthians, especially the first to the third chapters. (See, for example, 1 Corinthians 1:19-21, 26, and 27.)

The Jews of old had a revelation by the Spirit, but they failed to depend upon the Spirit Himself to interpret it to them, so they went astray. So Christians today have a revelation by the Spirit,

and many are failing to depend upon the Holy Spirit to interpret it to them, and so they go astray. The whole evangelical church recognizes, theoretically at least, the utter insufficiency of man's righteousness. What it needs to be taught in the present hour, and what it needs to be made to feel, is the utter insufficiency of man's wisdom. That is perhaps the lesson which this twentieth century of majestic intellectual conceit needs most to learn. To understand God's Word, we must empty ourselves utterly of our wisdom and rest in utter dependence upon the Spirit of God to interpret it to us.

We do well to lay to heart the words of Jesus Himself in Matthew 11:25, “I thank you, Father, Lord of heaven and earth, that you have hidden these things from the wise and understanding and revealed them to little children.” Several Bible students were once discussing the best methods of Bible study, and one man, who was learned and scholarly, said, “I think the best method of Bible study is the baby method.” When we have entirely put away our righteousness, then and only then, we get the righteousness of God (Philippians 4:7, 9; Romans 10:3). And when we have entirely put away our wisdom, then we get the wisdom of God. “Let no man deceive himself,” says the Apostle Paul. “If anyone among you thinks that he is wise in this age, let him become a fool that he may become wise” (1 Corinthians 3:18). And the emptying must precede filling, the self-poured out that God may be poured in.

We must daily be taught by the Spirit to understand the Word. We cannot depend on the fact that the Spirit taught us yesterday. Each new time we come in contact with the Word, it must be in the power of the Spirit for that specific occasion. That the Holy Spirit once illumined our minds to grasp a certain truth is not enough. He must do it each time we confront that passage. Andrew Murray has well said, “Each time you come to the Word in study, in hearing a sermon, or reading a religious book, there ought to be as distinct as your intercourse with the external means, the definite act of selflessness, denying your wisdom and yielding yourself in faith to the Divine teacher” (“The Spirit of Christ,” page 221).

V. The Holy Spirit enables the believer to communicate to others in power the truth he has been taught. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 2:1-5, “And I, when I came to you, brothers, did not come proclaiming to you the testimony of God with lofty speech or wisdom. For I decided to know nothing among you except Jesus Christ and him crucified. And I was with you in weakness and fear and much trembling, my speech and my message were not in plausible words of wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, so that your faith might not rest in the wisdom of men but in the power of God.” In a similar way, in writing to the believers in 1 Thessalonians 1:5, “Because our gospel came to you not only in word, but also in power and in the Holy Spirit and with full conviction.

You know what kind of men we proved to be among you for your sake.” We need not only the Holy Spirit to reveal the truth to chosen apostles and prophets in the first place, and the Holy Spirit in the second place to interpret to us as individuals the truth He has thus revealed, but in

the third place, we need the Holy Spirit to enable us to effectively communicate to others the truth which He Himself has interpreted to us. We need Him all along the line. One great cause of real failure in the ministry, even when there is seeming success, and not only in the regular ministry but in all forms of service as well, comes from the attempt to teach by “enticing words of man's wisdom” (that is, by the arts of human logic, persuasion and eloquence) what the Holy Spirit has taught us.

What is needed is Holy Ghost power, “demonstration of the Spirit and power.” 98 There are three causes of failure in preaching today. First, some other message is taught than the message which the Holy Spirit has revealed in the Word. (Men preach science, art, literature, philosophy, sociology, history, economics, experience, etc., and not the simple Word of God as found in the Holy Spirit's Book, the Bible.) Second, the Spirit-taught message of the Bible is studied and sought to be grasped by the natural understanding, that is, without the Spirit's illumination.

How common that is, even in institutions where men are being trained for the ministry, even in institutions which may be altogether orthodox. Third, the Spirit-given message, the Word, the Bible studied and understood under the Holy Ghost's illumination, is given out to others with “enticing words of man's wisdom,” and not in “demonstration of the Spirit and of power.” We need, and we are dependent upon the Spirit, all along the line. He must teach us how to speak as well as what to speak. He must be the power as well as the message.

fields.title: Chapter 17
fields.body_html:
Praying, Thanking, and Worshipping in the Spirit

he Holy Spirit not only dwells in us—He directs us in prayer, thanksgiving, and worship. He enables us to pray according to God’s will, to give thanks sincerely, and to worship in spirit and in truth.

The Spirit guides our prayers. Often, we do not know what to ask or how to ask it. Our wisdom fails, and words escape us. But the Spirit Himself intercedes for us, shaping our unspoken desires and aligning them with God’s purposes (Romans 8:26). Thus, our prayers become not merely the expression of our wishes, but the expression of His will.

The Holy Spirit inspires the believer and guides him in thanksgiving as well as in prayer. We read in Ephesians 5:18-20, “And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit, addressing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord with your heart, giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.” Not only does the Holy Spirit teach us to pray, but He also teaches us to render thanks.

One of the most prominent characteristics of the Spirit-filled life is thanksgiving. On the Day of Pentecost, when the disciples were filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke as the Spirit gave them utterance, we hear them telling the wonderful works of God (Acts 2:4,11), and today, when any believer is filled with the Holy Spirit, he always becomes filled with thanksgiving and praise. True thanksgiving is “to God, even the Father,” through, or “in the name of” our Lord Jesus Christ, in the Holy Spirit.

The Spirit leads us in worship. True worship is not outward display or mere emotion. It is the recognition of God’s character and works, expressed through prayer, thanksgiving, sacrifice, and obedience. The Holy Spirit guards us from worship that is only excitement of the flesh, and enables worship that is in spirit and in truth (John 4:23–24). Only as we depend upon the Holy Spirit can our prayers be right, our thanksgiving sincere, and our worship acceptable to God.

T

fields.title: Chapter 18
fields.body_html:
The Holy Spirit Sends Us Where We’re Meant to Go

he Holy Spirit actively guides believers to specific kinds of work. He helps us know exactly what God wants us to do, not by miracles or random signs, but through prayer, patience, and listening closely to Him.

In Acts 13:2-4 , we read that while the early Christians were worshipping and fasting, the Holy Spirit told them to set apart Barnabas and Saul for the work God had called them to. They prayed, laid hands on them, and sent them off. God’s Spirit didn’t just call them into general Christian service, He showed them the specific work they were meant to do.

Today, many people wonder, “Should I go to China, Africa, or India?” Only the Holy Spirit can answer that. No one else, not your parents, teachers, or friends—can make that decision for you. God knows where He wants you, and He will make it clear if you’re willing to listen.

Some try to follow their own plans or just go wherever they feel like. Others wait for approval from humans. But the Holy Spirit wants to guide us, not people.

How does the Holy Spirit call? Sometimes, He guides us in ways we don’t notice at first. He might guide your thoughts, open doors for you, or put certain people in your path. The key is: He will guide you if you listen and are ready.

How do we respond to the Holy Spirit’s call?

1. Desire it: Want to know God’s plan for your life.

2. Seek it: Spend time praying, worshiping, and listening.

3. Wait for it: Be patient. God’s timing is perfect.

4. Expect it: Believe that He will show you what to do.

The Holy Spirit can guide us in all aspects of our lives. If you don’t know what to choose, don’t panic. God’s guidance is clear, and He will make it obvious if it’s His will. We don’t need to force signs or miracles. We just need to surrender our will to Him, ask Him for wisdom, and follow step by step.

T

fields.title: Chapter 19
fields.body_html:
The Holy Spirit and Your Body

he Holy Spirit doesn’t just help our minds and hearts—He also works in our bodies. Romans 8:11 tells us that the Spirit who raised Jesus will also give life to our mortal bodies. That’s not just a future promise, but a present reality. Yes, right now, He can make alive in you what is not working, yes, right now. Believe it, pray to God, and receive your healing. Hallelujah!

Jesus healed people through the Spirit (Matthew 12:28, Acts 10:38). James 5:14 even talks about anointing with oil as a symbol of the Holy Spirit bringing healing. The Spirit can give us strength, health, and energy, especially in moments of weakness or sickness.

That doesn’t mean Christians never get sick, but that doesn’t mean Christians should ever be sick! The Bible says that those who dwell in Zion shall not say, “I am sick, and guess what, Christians are now in Zion.

T

fields.title: Chapter 20
fields.body_html:
The Baptism with the Holy Spirit

ne of the most important words in the Bible about the Holy Spirit is “baptised with the Holy Spirit.” John the Baptist first used it. He said, “I baptise you with water, but the one coming after me will baptise you with the Holy Spirit and fire” (Matthew 3:11).

Later, our Lord Jesus said the same thing in Acts 1:5: “John baptised with water, but you will be baptised with the Holy Spirit soon.”

When this happened on the Day of Pentecost (Acts 2:3-4), the Holy Spirit came on the disciples, they were filled with Him, and they began speaking in other languages as the Spirit enabled them. Even Peter said that the Holy Spirit fell on Cornelius and his family, showing that this experience is the same for everyone (Acts 10:44-46; Acts 11:15-17). Other ways the Bible talks about this include:

• “Receive the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:38; Acts 19:2-6)

• “The Holy Spirit came on them” (Acts 19:2-6)

• “Gift of the Holy Spirit” (Hebrews 2:4; 1 Corinthians 12:4, 11, 13)

What is the Baptism with the Holy Spirit?

1. It’s a real experience you can know.

The Bible shows it’s something real. You can know if you have received it. In Acts 19:2, Paul asked the disciples at Ephesus, “Did you receive the Holy Spirit when you believed?” They hadn’t. So it’s possible to believe in Jesus and still not be baptised with the Holy Spirit. 2. It’s different from being born again.

Being born again makes you a child of God. The baptism with the Holy Spirit gives power for service . A person can be saved but not yet filled with the Spirit. 3. It’s for service, not just happiness.

The main purpose isn’t just to feel joy, though joy often comes. The baptism with the Holy Spirit gives power to serve God effectively . It prepares you for the work He has called you to do, whether that’s preaching, teaching, helping, or raising your family in faith.

O

What does it do?
