“Nothing tends more to cement the hearts of Christians than praying together. Never do

they love one another so well as when they witness the outpouring of each other's hearts

in prayer.”

“It was very common to find Christians, whenever they met in any place, instead of

engaging in conversation, to fall on their knees in prayer.”

“What are our Bibles good for, if we do not lay hold on their precious promises, and use

them as the ground of our faith when we pray for the blessing of God?”

“If you find yourself strongly drawn to desire a blessing, you are to understand it as an

intimation that God is willing to bestow that particular blessing, and so you are bound to

believe it.”

Prayer and the Word of God

“God says He is more ready to give His Holy Spirit to them that ask Him than parents

are to give bread to their children. Here we are bound to believe that we shall receive it

when we pray for it. You have no right to put in an “if” and say, “Lord, if it be Thy will,

give us Thy Holy Spirit.” This is to insult God.”

“Prayer is an essential link in the chain of causes that lead to a revival. Truth by itself

will never produce the effect without the Spirit of God, and that Spirit is given in answer

to prayer.”

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“Be filled with His Spirit, and He will give you objects enough to pray for. He will give

you as much of the spirit of prayer as you have strength of body to bear.”

“But as I turned and was about to take a seat by the fire, I received a mighty baptism of

the Holy Ghost. Without any expectation of it, without ever having the thought in my

mind that there was any such thing for me, the Holy Spirit descended upon me in a

manner that seemed to go through me, body and soul. I could feel the impression, like a

wave of electricity, going through and through me. Indeed it seemed to come in waves

and waves of liquid love.”

“Prayer is not the foe to work, it doe s not paralyse activity. It works mightily; prayer

itself is the greatest work.”

fields.title: Chapter 9. Rees Howells (1879 – 1950)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

Rees Howells was born in 1879 in the small coal-mining village of Brynamman in South Wales.

He grew up in a working-class Welsh family and as a young man emigrated to the United States,

where he contracted typhoid fever and, near death, made a promise to God: “If you let me live, I

will give you my life.” He recovered, returned to Wales, and was swept into the Welsh Revival

of 1904 – 1905 under Evan Roberts.

Following his radical conversion and a deeper consecration of himself to God, Howells entered a

remarkable journey in which the Holy Spirit began to teach him what he called “true

intercession” — prayer involving identification with the need, agony of soul, and the gaining of

spiritual authority. He tested these principles first in local ministry and then as a missionary in

South Africa, where revival accompanied his work.

In 1924, Howells founded the Bible College of Wales in Swansea, which became a centre of

prayer and intercession. The college trained missionaries and sent them to the nations, living

entirely by faith. During the years leading up to World War II, Howells became increasingly

burdened for world events and shifted his intercession from local concerns to national and

international affairs.

During World War II (1939 – 1945), Howells and his college community prayed every evening

from 7 p.m. to midnight, plus additional hours in the morning. They interceded specifically for

key turning points in the war — Dunkirk, the Battle of Britain, North Africa, and others. Many

believe their intercessions were decisive in those moments. Rees Howells died in February 1950,

and his biography, Rees Howells: Intercessor by Norman Grubb, has since inspired generations

of intercessors worldwide.

A Great Answer to Prayer

Of all the answered prayers in Howells’ life, none is more dramatic than the evacuation of

Dunkirk in May 1940. As Hitler’s armies drove the Allied forces back to the b eaches of northern

France, over 300,000 British and French soldiers were trapped, with the German tanks closing in.

Invasion of Britain seemed certain.

On 21 May 1940, Howells wrote in his diary: “The situation looked extremely black for Britain.

It was an hour of near panic.” He and his college community cried out to God with agonising

intercession. On 28 May, as the prayer warriors prayed together, a deep peace settled over them.

One student prayed at the end of the meeting: “I feel sure something has happened.”

On 29 May, the evacuation of Dunkirk began. Inexplicably, on 23 May, the German High

Command had issued a halt order for all ground troops — an order that remains unexplained by

military historians to this day. At the same time, the English Channel, normally rough, fell to an

extraordinary calm, allowing small civilian boats to cross and bring the soldiers home. Over

338,000 men were rescued. Air Chief Marshal Lord Dowding, Commander of Fighter

Command, later said: “Even during the battle one realis ed from day to day how much external

support was coming in. At the end of the battle one had the sort of feeling that there had been

some special Divine intervention.” Rees Howells believed it was the direct answer to prayer.

Key Scriptures

Isaiah 62:6 – 7 — “You who make mention of the LORD, do not keep silent, and give Him

no rest till He establishes and till He makes Jerusalem a praise in the earth.”

Ezekiel 22:30 — “I sought for a man among them who would make a wall, and stand in

the gap before Me on b ehalf of the land, that I should not destroy it; but I found no one.”

Romans 8:26 — “The Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray

for as we ought, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for

words.”

His Words on Prayer

“There are three things to be seen in an intercessor which are not necessarily found in

ordinary prayer: identification, agony, and authority.”

“The intercessor must become responsible for the prayer that the Holy Spirit gives them.

They must “pray through” until the prayer is answered.”

“Before God will use you in intercession, it will cost you. The intercessors love God so

much that they want to obey. They will pay the price because of their love for the

Saviour.”

“Once the Holy Spirit has called an intercessor to a spiritual conflict, the intercessor

must carry on to completing the task, no matter what the cost — and it will be costly.”

“Prayer is not an exercise, it is the life.”

Prayer and the Word of God

“The path of the intercessor i s the way of the cross. It is also the way of fellowship with

Jesus on a very deep level. It is a sacrifice of love. The intercessor has the sentence of

death — death to self — in himself.”

“As the crucifixion of self proceeds, intercession begins. You ar e never forced into

prayer. The intercessor needs to be willing to enter into a new place of intercession with

God.”

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“The intercessor must become responsible for the prayer that the Holy Spirit gives

them.”

“As their prayers gr ew more fervent, they also felt the increasing presence of the Holy

Spirit among them. The Spirit was the engine of all true intercession.”

“God help us to know the Spirit and to reverence Him as the Spirit of prayer!”

fields.title: Chapter 10. Billy Graham (1918 – 2018)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

William Franklin Graham Jr. was born on 7 November 1918 on a dairy farm near Charlotte,

North Carolina. He grew up during the Great Depression, learning the value of hard work and a

simple faith. In the autumn of 1934, at the age of fifteen, he attended a series of revival meetings

led by the travelling evangelist Mordecai Ham. One evening, under deep conviction, he walked

to the front and gave his life to Christ.

After attending Bob Jones College, the Florida Bible Institute, and Wheaton College (where he

met his future wife Ruth Bell, daughter of medical missionaries to China), Graham was ordained

and began pastoral work. In 1945 he joined Youth for Christ and began preaching at rallies

across America and in postwar Europe.

In September 1949, Graham opened a series of revival meetings in Los Angeles. Planned for

three weeks, the tent meetings were extended to eight weeks as the city was gripped by what

newspapers called the greatest religious revival in the history of Southern California. Over

350,000 attended, and 3,000 publicly committed their lives to Christ. Almost overnight, Billy

Graham became a national figure.

Over the following six decades, Graham preached the Gospel in live crusades to an estimated

215 million people in 185 countries, with many millions more reached through radio, television,

and film. He counselled twelve US presidents. He was the first major evangelist to insist on

racially integrated crusades in the American South. The Billy Graham Evangelistic Association,

which he founded in 1950, continues its work around the world. Graham died at his home in

Montreat, North Carolina, on 21 February 2018, at the age of 99.

A Great Answer to Prayer

The Los Angeles crusade of 1949 was born out of extraordinary prayer. A cross-denominational

revival prayer network with over one hundred and twenty clergy had been meeting and praying

for a city-wide awakening for months before Graham arrived. More than one thousand prayer

groups across Los Angeles were interceding specifically for the crusade.

In the months before the crusade opened, Graham himself had retreated to the San Bernardino

mountains in a personal crisis of faith — wrestling with intellectual doubts about the Bible. On

his knees before God, he placed his open Bible on a tr ee stump and said, in essence, “Lord, I

cannot answer all the questions. But I accept this Book as Your Word by faith.” A deep peace

settled over him. He arose and went to preach.

The results surpassed all expectation. Country music star Stuart Hamblen was converted and his

changed life became front-page news. When media magnate William Randolph Hearst — for

reasons no one has fully explained — sent the telegram to all his editors “Puff Graham,” the

crusade exploded into national prominence overnight. Thousands came to faith in those eight

weeks. Graham always said it was entirely the work of prayer.

Key Scriptures

Romans 10:14 — “How then shall they call on Him in whom they have not believed?

And how shall they believe in Him of whom they have not heard? And how shall they

hear without a preacher?”

2 Timothy 4:2 — “Preach the word; be ready in season and out of season; correct,

rebuke and encourage — with great patience and careful instruction.”

John 3:16 — “For God so loved the world that He gave His onl y Son, that whoever

believes in Him should not perish but have eternal life.”

His Words on Prayer

“Prayer is for every moment of our lives, not just for times of suffering or joy. Prayer is

really a place, a place where you meet God in genuine conversatio n.”

“In the Bible God speaks to us; in prayer we speak to God. Both are essential.”

“You cannot pray for someone and hate them at the same time.”

“True prayer is a way of life, not just for use in cases of emergency. Make it a habit, and

when the need a rises you will be in practice.”

“Heaven is full of answers to prayer for which no one ever bothered to ask.”

Prayer and the Word of God

“Pray frequently as you read the Bible and you will discover a fellowship with God.

Prayer and Bible study are inseparably linked. Effective prayer is born out of the

prompting of God's Spirit as we read His Word.”

“The Spirit of God takes the Word of God and makes the child of God. Read your Bible

daily. Do not be content to skim through a chapter merely to satisfy your conscience.

Hide the Word of God in your heart. It comforts, guides, corrects, encourages — all we

need is there.”

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“Rely constantly on the Holy Spirit. We know that the Holy Spirit prays for us, and what

a comfort that should be to the weakest of us. Stand aside and let Him take over all the

choices and decisions of your life.”

“The Spirit -filled life is not abnormal; it is the normal Christian life. Anything less is

subnormal; it is less than what God wants and provides for His children.”

“It is never a question of how much you and I have of the Spirit, but how much He has of

us.”

fields.title: Chapter 11. Henry Blackaby (1935 – 2024)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

Henry Thomas Blackaby was born on 15 April 1935 in Williams Lake, British Columbia,

Canada. H e earned his bachelor’s degree in history and English from the University of British

Columbia and his theological degrees from Golden Gate Baptist Theological Seminary in

California. He served as a music director, education director, and pastor in California before

answering a very specific call that changed his life.

In 1970, a Canadian pastor approached Blackaby with a challenge: “The only hope for Canada is

if Canadian pastors come back home.” Blackaby heard this as a word from God. He and his wife

Marilynn moved to Saskatoon, Saskatchewan, to pastor Faith Baptist Church — a tiny, dying

congregation of ten people.

What happened over the next twelve years was nothing short of miraculous. The church grew

dramatically, planted thirty-eight daughter churches and mission posts, and became the epicentre

of the remarkable Saskatoon Revival of 1971 — a city-wide awakening that transformed entire

denominations. During those years, Blackaby developed the principles that would become

Experiencing God.

His book Experiencing God: Knowing and Doing the Will of God, co-written with his son

Richard and Claude King in 1990, has sold over seven million copies and been translated into

more than forty-five languages. It has been described as one of the most influential Christian

books of the twentieth century. Blackaby went on to serve the Southern Baptist Convention's

Home Mission Board as Director of Prayer and Spiritual Awakening, travelling the world to call

the Church back to God. He died on 10 February 2024 at the age of 88.

A Great Answer to Prayer

Before the Saskatoon Revival of 1971 broke out, Henry Blackaby and a group of Saskatoon

pastors had been meeting together every week for two years, praying specifically for God to send

revival to their city. They had no guarantee that anything would happen. But they prayed and

they waited.

On 13 October 1971, twin evangelists Ralph and Lou Sutera arrived for what was planned as a

week-and-a-half of meetings at Ebenezer Baptist Church. But God had different plans. Within

days, the meetings could not be contained. The congregation moved to a larger church, and that

was overflowed in two nights. They moved to the largest church in the city — 1,600 seats — and

ran double services nightly. Finally, the Saskatoon Centennial Auditorium was rented, with

2,400 seats, and still it was full.

Entire denominations were transformed. The Christian Missionary and Alliance denomination

reported a one hundred percent increase in conversions in that first year. Baptised church

members discovered they had never been truly born again. Families were reconciled. Debts were

paid. Enemies were forgiven. Blackaby said that the entire DNA of his life was changed during

the revival — and the principles he lived through those days became the message he spent the

rest of his life proclaiming to the world.

Key Scriptures

Jeremiah 29:13 — “You will seek Me and find Me, when you seek Me with all your

heart.”

John 14:21 — “Whoever has My commandments and keeps them, he it is who loves Me.

And he who loves Me will be loved by My Father, and I will love him and manifest Myself

to him.”

Isaiah 55:8 – 9 — “My thoughts are not your thoughts, neither are your ways My ways,

declares the LORD. For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are My ways higher

than your ways and My thoughts than your thoughts.”

His Words on Prayer

“Prayer is designed to adjust you to God's will, not to adjust God to your will.”

“All revival begins, and continues, in the prayer meeting. In times of revival, thousands

may be found on their knees for hours, lifting up their heartfelt cries, with thanksgiving,

to heaven.”

“Prayer is a relationship, not a religious activity.”

“When God answers your prayer, He receives the glory, your faith is increased, and you

have a fresh experience of Hi s love.”

“Prayerless leaders are like ship captains without compasses; they can make their best

guess at which direction to go, but they have no assurance they are heading the right

way. Prayer keeps leaders focused on the one absolutely consistent factor in life — God.”

Prayer and the Word of God

“God speaks by the Holy Spirit through the Bible, prayer, circumstances, and the church

to reveal Himself, His purposes, and His ways. If you have trouble hearing God speak,

you are in trouble at the very heart of your Christian experience.”

“When you want to know how God wants you to reach your city, or be involved in His

work, ask Him. His promise is to always answer when we pray according to His will.”

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“God speaks by the Holy Spiri t through the Bible, prayer, circumstances, and the church

to reveal Himself, His purposes, and His ways.”

“Prayer is not solely about making requests, but about aligning our desires with God's

plans for us. The Spirit prompts us to seek out what God has in store.”

“Revival is a divinely initiated work in which God's people pray, repent of their sin, and

return to a holy, Spirit-filled, obedient, love- relationship with God.”

fields.title: Chapter 12. Bill Bright (1921 – 2003)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

William R. Bright was born on 19 October 1921 in Coweta, Oklahoma, the sixth of seven

children of a cattle-ranching family. Until eighth grade he attended school in a one-room

schoolhouse. After distinguished academic achievement at Northeastern State University, he

moved to California and built a successful confections business. He was introduced to the Gospel

through the ministry of Henrietta Mears at Hollywood Presbyterian Church, and in 1945

surrendered his life completely to Christ.

While studying at Princeton and Fuller theological seminaries, Bright felt an overwhelming call

from God. He and his wife Vonette signed what they called a “slave contract” — literally a

written surrender of all their rights and ambitions to Jesus — and in 1951 launched Campus

Crusade for Christ at the University of California, Los Angeles.

Within months, hundreds of students at UCLA had given their lives to Christ, including the

student body president, the campus newspaper editor, and several athletes. By the end of the

1950s, Campus Crusade had spread to dozens of campuses. The ministry grew to become one of

the largest Christian organisations in the world, with 26,000 staff and 225,000 volunteers in 191

countries.

In 1952, Bright wrote The Four Spiritual Laws — a simple gospel presentation that has been

distributed to over 2.5 billion people. In 1979, he produced the Jesus film, which by his death

had been translated into over 1,400 languages and viewed by more than five billion people. In

1996 he received the Templeton Prize for Progress in Religion — worth $1.1 million — and

donated the entire sum to promote prayer and fasting. Bill Bright died on 19 July 2003.

A Great Answer to Prayer

The campus breakthrough at UCLA in 1951 was the seed from which everything else in Bright's

ministry grew. It was entirely the product of prayer. When Bright launched Campus Crusade

with a handful of volunteers, there was no precedent for this kind of student ministry and no

guarantee of success. He and Vonette prayed earnestly before every meeting, every conversation,

every outreach.

Within months, the student body president of UCLA, the campus newspaper editor, and several

top athletes had committed their lives to Christ. The transformation of these high-profile students

sent shockwaves through the campus. Word spread. The movement grew. Within a decade it had

become a national and then international force.

But the greatest answered prayer in Bright's life was the Jesus film. It took years of prayer, fund-

raising by faith, theological preparation, and logistical work to produce. When it was released in

1979, it was initially shown in just a few countries. Bright prayed that it would reach the world.

Over the following decades, God answered that prayer far beyond what Bright could have

imagined: the film has now been seen by more than five billion people in over 200 countries, and

hundreds of millions of people have prayed the prayer of salvation after watching it. It is the

most watched film in human history.

Key Scriptures

Matthew 28:19 – 20 — “Go therefore and make discip les of all nations, baptising them in

the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all

that I have commanded you.”

Acts 1:8 — “But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and

you will be My witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of

the earth.”

1 John 5:14 – 15 — “This is the confidence that we have toward Him, that if we ask

anything according to His will He hears us. And if we know that He hears us in whatever

we ask, we know that we have the requests that we have asked of Him.”

His Words on Prayer

“Show me a church or a Christian organisation that emphasises prayer, and I'll show

you a ministry where people are excited about Jesus Christ and are witnessing for Hi m.”

“I believe the power of fasting as it relates to prayer is the spiritual atomic bomb that our

Lord has given us to destroy the strongholds of evil and usher in a great revival and

spiritual harvest around the world.”

“Fasting with a pure heart and mo tives brings personal revival and adds power to our

prayers. Personal revival occurs because fasting is an act of humility.”

“Fasting and prayer can bring about a change in the direction of our nation, the nations

of the earth, and the fulfilment of the G reat Commission.”

“Not only do you have the ear of the greatest Person in the universe, but as you kneel in

your place of prayer, you have the privilege of being used of God to help change the lives

of individuals and nations.”

Prayer and the Word of God

“His promise is that He will always answer when we pray according to His will: “This is

the confidence which we have before Him, that, if we ask anything according to His will,

He hears us” (1 John 5:14–15). Lay hold of this promise and pray accordingly.”

“Fasting and prayer are the only disciplines that fulfil the requirements of 2 Chronicles

7:14: “If My people who are called by My name will humble themselves, and pray and

seek My face, and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven.””

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“Fasting reduces the power of self so that the Holy Spirit can do a more intense work

within us.”

“We are filled with the Holy Spirit by faith alone. Pray: “Dear Father, I need You. Fill

me with the Holy Spirit as You commanded me to be filled and as You promised in Your

Word that You would do if I asked in faith.””

“Through fasting and prayer, the Holy Spirit can transform your life. Fasting and prayer

can effect change on a much grander scale when God's people seek His face with broken

and repentant hearts.”

fields.title: Chapter 13. Loren Cunningham (1935 – 2023)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

Loren Duane Cunningham was born on 30 June 1935 in the oil boom town of Taft, California,

into a family with generations of Christian ministers. From early childhood, prayer and faith

were woven into the fabric of his life. His parents were Assemblies of God ministers who

modelled radical trust in God.

In June 1956, at the age of twenty, Cunningham was kneeling in prayer in a missionary’s home

in the Bahamas, asking God for a message to preach that evening, when he received a

remarkable vision. He saw a map of the world come alive, with waves crashing on the continents

and turning into young people — thousands upon thousands of young men and women from

every nation, going to every nation, preaching the Gospel. He had no idea how to interpret it or

what to do with it, but he wrote it down.

Four years later, in 1960, Cunningham founded Youth With A Mission (YWAM) in Lausanne,

Switzerland, at the age of twenty-four, with his wife Darlene. YWAM broke the mould of 1960s

missions by welcoming young people who were not career missionaries to serve short-term,

unsalaried, interdenominationally, on any continent. The movement grew with remarkable speed.

In 1978, Cunningham co-founded the University of the Nations in Kailua-Kona, Hawaii. By the

time of his death on 6 October 2023 at the age of 88, YWAM had grown to over 20,000 full-time

staff from more than 150 nations serving at over 2,000 locations in 191 countries. Cunningham

was the first person in history to travel for the sake of the Gospel to every sovereign nation,

dependent country, and more than 100 territories on earth.

A Great Answer to Prayer

Shortly after founding YWAM, Cunningham needed a farm to serve as the first permanent base

for the growing ministry. He had no money, no donor, and no realistic prospects. He did what he

always did: he prayed. Then, in an act of bold faith, he went to an auction and bought a barbed

wire, a milk can, and a hay wagon — farm items — before the farm existed.

His young students were bewildered. “What are these for?” they asked. “God is going to give us

a farm for YWAM,” he replied simply. Shortly after, a man came to Cunningham and said three

words: “I want to give you a farm.” It was exactl y the farm they needed. That farm became the

mother base of the entire global movement, and it all began in prayer and faith.

But the greatest answered prayer in Cunningham’s life was the fulfilment of the 1956 vision

itself. He spent sixty-seven years watching that vision come true — wave after wave of young

people from every nation going to every nation with the Gospel of Christ. He saw millions of

young people mobilised for missions through YWAM, and he died knowing that the vision was

still unfolding.

Key Scriptures

Mark 16:15 — “Go into all the world and preach the gospel to every creature.”

John 10:27 — “My sheep hear My voice, and I know them, and they follow Me.”

Acts 13:2 — “While they were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit said,

“Set apart for Me Barnabas and Saul for the work to which I have called them.””

His Words on Prayer

“Hearing God is not all that difficult. If we know the Lord, we have already heard His

voice — after all, it was the inner leading that brought us to Him in the first place. But

we can hear His voice and still miss His best if we don't keep on listening.”

“Guidance is first of all a relationship with the Guide.”

“We get caught in our boxes — but when we pray outside of them, ask God, the

impossible CAN be d one.”

“We followed the Three Steps to Hearing God: First, we took Christ's authority to silence

the enemy. Second, we asked the Lord to clear from our minds any presumptions and

preconceived ideas. Third, we waited, believing He would speak in the way and in the

time that He chose.”

“The Lord will lead us into victory, but success itself is the most dangerous obstacle to

properly hearing the voice of God.”

Prayer and the Word of God

“When a critical mass of people have the Bible and apply what it teaches in their lives, a

nation is transformed. The Book is the key to everything.”

“This is what hearing God is all about — getting to know Him better. Prayer is not

primarily a technique for getting things; it is the language of relationship with the

Father.”

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“Every great historical move of the Spirit I had studied began with times of confession

and deep repentance. God's power is released after a time of cleansing.”

“Whenever we came to a crossroads in the mission, we prayed until the Holy Spirit

spoke. Then we obeyed. That is the only way to build anything that will last.”

“To know God and to make Him known — that is YWAM's call. And to know God, you

must pray.”

fields.title: Chapter 14. Derek Prince (1915 – 2003)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

Derek Prince was born in Bangalore, India, in 1915, to British parents. He was educated at the

elite Eton College and then Cambridge University, where he was elected to a prestigious

fellowship at King's College for his philosophical dissertation at the age of twenty-four. He

described himself at the time as an atheist.

When World War II broke out, Prince joined the Royal Army Medical Corps as a conscientious

objector. As a self-assigned philosophical exercise, he began to read the Bible. In 1941, while

stationed in a milit ary barracks, he had what he described as a “supernatural experience” — a

meeting with Jesus Christ. He later wrote: “Out of this encounter I formed two conclusions: first,

that Jesus Christ is alive; second, that the Bible is a true, relevant, up-to-date book. These

conclusions altered the whole course of my life.” Two weeks later he was baptised in the Holy

Spirit.

The morning after his conversion, the man who had never prayed in his life could not stop

praying. He was posted to North Africa and Palestine, where during his wartime service he met

Lydia Christiansen, a Danish woman running an orphanage for eight girls in Ramallah. They

married in 1946, and Prince instantly became the father of eight daughters. He gave up his

Cambridge fellowship, was ordained, and founded a Pentecostal church in London.

From London, the Princes moved to Kenya, where Prince led a school and planted churches. He

subsequently moved to the United States and Canada, eventually settling in Jerusalem in 1981 —

a city he loved with a profound biblical conviction. He wrote over fifty books and 600 audio

teachings, translated into more than 100 languages. He died in Jerusalem on 24 September 2003,

one of the most widely-heard Bible teachers of the twentieth century.

A Great Answer to Prayer

The most dramatic answered prayer in Derek Prince’s life was his own conversion — an

unsolicited, unexpected encounter with the living Christ while reading the Bible alone in a dark

army barracks. Prince had not been seeking God. He had been studying the Bible as a

philosopher studies an ancient text. But God broke through, and the man who had gone to sleep

as an atheist woke up as a believer.

Prince often spoke of his grandmother, who had prayed for him faithfully throughout his

irreligious years at university. He believed with absolute conviction that her years of prayer for

him had prepared the ground for that extraordinary encounter.

Later in his ministry, while serving as a school principal in Kenya in the late 1950s, Prince

prayed for people to be raised from the dead on two separate occasions — and both times God

answered. These experiences deepened his understanding of the authority available to believers

in prayer. He spent the remainder of his life teaching believers that prayer is not a religious

formality but a weapon of war, a tool of healing, and a means of advancing the Kingdom of God

on earth.

Key Scriptures

Ephesians 6:17 – 18 — “Take the sword of the Spirit, which is the Word of God, praying

at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication.”

Romans 8:34 — “Christ Jesus who died — more than that, who was raised to life — is

at the right hand of God and is also interceding for us.”

1 Timothy 2:1 — “I urge, then, first of all, that petitions, prayers, intercession and

thanksgiving be made for all people — for kings and all those in authority.”

His Words on Prayer

“Prayer is limitless. It's our intercontinental ballistic missile. We can launch it from

anywhere and make it reach anywhere.”

“The people who really rule the world are those who know how to pray.”

“Truth is not obtained cheaply. It demands much time given to prayer and study of the

Scriptures, followed by practical application in our daily lives.”

“What kind of spiritual sacrifices does God expect us to offer? Ju st as Jesus offered up

prayers and petitions during His life on earth, so should we. When we learn to pray, then

we are qualified to rule.”

“If you are praying in faith, you say: “The answer is ten years nearer than when I started

praying.””

Prayer and the Word of God

“The great revelation of the will of God is the Word of God. And the Word of God is

packed from beginning to end with divine promises. The will of God is not hidden from us

— it is revealed in Scripture. Pray the promises.”

“God has provide d us three main spiritual weapons: the Word of God, the name of Jesus,

and the blood of Jesus. We launch these weapons through prayer, praise, preaching, and

testimony.”

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“We cannot effectively serve God without the Holy Spirit.”

“Fasting deals with the two great barriers to the Holy Spirit that are erected by man's

carnal nature — the stubborn self-will of the soul and the insistent self-gratifying

appetites of the body.”

“The night before my conversion I hadn't known how to pr ay. The next day I couldn't

stop praying. Even if I got a mug of water I had to pause and thank God for the water

before I could drink it. Prayer was now as natural as breathing. That is the work of the

Holy Spirit.”

fields.title: Chapter 15. Timothy Keller (1950 – 2023)
fields.body_html:
Who Was He?

Timothy James Keller was born on 23 September 1950 in Allentown, Pennsylvania. He grew up

in a Lutheran family but did not come to a living faith until his time at Bucknell University in the

late 1960s, where he became a Christian through involvement with InterVarsity Christian

Fellowship. He went on to earn his Master of Divinity at Gordon-Conwell Theological Seminary

and his Doctor of Ministry at Westminster Theological Seminary.

Ordained in the Presbyterian Church of America, Keller served for nine years as pastor of West

Hopewell Presbyterian Church in Hopewell, Virginia, before joining the faculty of Westminster

Theological Seminary as Professor of Practical Theology. In 1989, against almost all human

advice, he and his wife Kathy moved to New York City in response to a call from their

denomination to plant a church in Manhattan.

Redeemer Presbyterian Church began with fewer than fifty people meeting in borrowed space.

Within a decade it had grown to thousands of weekly worshippers. By the time Keller retired as

senior pastor in 2017, Redeemer drew over 5,000 people each Sunday to multiple services, had

planted over one hundred churches in the New York metropolitan area, and had become a model

of urban church ministry studied by pastors worldwide.

Keller’s books — including The Reason for God, The Prodigal God, and Prayer: Experiencing

Awe and Intimacy with God — have sold millions of copies and been translated into scores of

languages. He co-founded The Gospel Coalition and Redeemer City to City, which has trained

church planters in global cities on every continent. In 2020 Keller was diagnosed with pancreatic

cancer, which he faced with extraordinary faith and transparency. He died on 19 May 2023, aged

72.

A Great Answer to Prayer

The planting and growth of Redeemer Presbyterian Church in Manhattan is, by almost any

measure, a remarkable answer to prayer. In 1989, New York City was not considered fertile

ground for evangelical Christianity. The culture was aggressively secular, the pace of life

brutally relentless, and the social pressure against religious commitment intense. Most church

planting attempts in Manhattan had failed or remained tiny.

Keller and his wife prayed, studied, and prepared for years before moving to the city. They

approached the task with theological rigour and cultural intelligence, trusting God to open hearts

in what seemed like the hardest soil in America. God answered abundantly. The church grew

from fifty to five hundred to five thousand — drawing young professionals, artists, academics,

and sceptics who were encountering the Gospel perhaps for the first time.

Keller also testified that his battle with cancer, rather than destroying his prayer life, deepened

and transformed it. He wrote that facing death forced him to be still before God in a way his busy

ministry had never permitted. The cancer taught him that prayer is not a technique for getting

results but an encounter with the living God in which the soul is remade. He faced his final years

with a joy and confidence that many who knew him described as one of the most powerful

testimonies they had ever witnessed.

Key Scriptures

Matthew 6:6 — “When you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your

Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in s ecret will reward you.”

Philippians 4:6 – 7 — “Do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer

and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the

peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds

in Christ Jesus.”

Romans 8:26 — “The Spirit helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray

for as we ought, but the Spirit Himself intercedes for us with groanings too deep for

words.”

His Words on Prayer

“Prayer is awe, intimacy, struggle — yet the way to reality. There is nothing more

important, or harder, or richer, or more life-altering. There is absolutely nothing so

great as prayer.”

“Prayer is the only entryway into genuine self -knowledge. It is also the main way we

experience deep change — the reordering of our loves. Prayer is how God gives us so

many of the unimaginable things He has for us. It is the way we know God, the way we

finally treat God as God. Prayer is simply the key to everything we need to do and be in

life.”

“We know God will answer us when we call because one terrible day He did not answer

Jesus when He called. Jesus’ prayers were given the rejection that we sinners merit so

that our prayers could have the reception that He merits.”

“Prayer is th e way to experience a powerful confidence that God is handling our lives

well — that our bad things will turn out for good, our good things cannot be taken from

us, and the best things are yet to come.”

“To fail to pray, then, is not to merely break some religious rule — it is a failure to treat

God as God.”

Prayer and the Word of God

“Our prayers should arise out of immersion in the Scripture. We should plunge ourselves

into the sea of God's language, the Bible. Listen, study, think, reflect, and ponder the

Scriptures until there is an answering response in your heart — and then that response,

offered back to God, is truly prayer.”

“What is essential in prayer is not that we learn to express ourselves, but that we learn to

answer God. Real prayer begins when God speaks first — in His Word, through His

Spirit — and we respond.”

Prayer and the Holy Spirit

“Prayer is continuing a conversation that God has started through His Word and His

grace, which eventually becomes a full encounter with Him.”

“A triun e God would call us to converse with Him, because He wants to share the joy He

has always had within Himself. Prayer is our way of entering into the happiness of God

Himself.”

“Prayer turns theology into experience. The doctrines of Scripture must become the fuel

for prayer, or they will merely remain knowledge in the head. When the Spirit takes truth

and drives it into prayer, the fire is lit.”

CONCLUSION

What These Men Leave to Us

You have now walked through the lives of fifteen men who prayed. They came from different

centuries, different continents, different denominations, and different backgrounds. Some were

scholars and some were uneducated. Some pastored great churches and some served in obscurity.

Some are celebrated names in church history and some are known only to those who search

deeply for the hidden heroes of the faith. But every single one of them discovered the same truth:

that prayer is not one activity among many, but the foundation on which all genuine ministry is

built.

Look at what prayer did in their lives. It brought the revival Andrew Murray's father had prayed

for over thirty years. It filled D. L. Moody with the power of the Holy Spirit on a New York

street and sent him to preach to millions. It turned the tide of World War II through a small

company of intercessors in a Welsh Bible College. It planted a church in the hardest city in

America and grew it to five thousand people. It brought rain to a remote Chinese island when an

idol's followers challenged the living God. It converted a Cambridge atheist through a Bible read

alone in an army barracks. It turned a dying congregation of ten people in the Canadian prairies

into a church that planted thirty-eight daughters.

Prayer works. Not as a magic formula. Not as a technique. Not as a religious duty performed to

earn God's favour. Prayer works because God is real, God is present, God is listening, and God is

powerful. Prayer works because Jesus Christ is at the right hand of the Father, ever living to

make intercession for us (Heb rews 7:25). Prayer works because the Holy Spirit within us “helps

our weakness” and “intercedes for us with groanings too deep for words” (Romans 8:26). When

we pray, we are not speaking into an empty sky. We are speaking to the Creator and Sustainer of

the universe, the One who holds every nation in the palm of His hand, the One who loved us

enough to send His only Son to die for us.

The Common Thread

Looking at these fifteen men together, several patterns emerge that are worth naming.

First: they were all men of the Word. Not one of them prayed in isolation from Scripture.

Andrew Murray insisted that the Word and the Spirit must be united in prayer. E. M. Bounds

declared that the Word of God is “the food by which prayer is nourished and made strong.” A. R .

Torrey taught that “prayer that is born of meditation upon the Word of God is the prayer that

soars upward most easily to God's listening ears.” Timothy Keller described prayer as

“continuing a conversation that God has started through His Word.” For all fifteen men, the

Bible was not separate from prayer — it was the language of prayer, the fuel of prayer, and the

foundation of prayer.

Second: they were all men who depended on the Holy Spirit. They did not trust in their own

eloquence, their theological training, their organisational ability, or their natural gifts. Spurgeon

said, “Prayer is the creation of the Holy Spirit.” Moody prayed until God came and overwhelmed

him on a New York street. Torrey taught that entering God's presence is only possible by the

Holy Spirit's power. Finney experienced the Spirit descending “in waves of liquid love.” Rees

Howells spent his entire ministry under the direct guidance and anointing of the Holy Spirit. For

all of these men, the Holy Spirit was not a doctrine to be discussed but a Person to be depended

upon.

Third: they were all men who paid a price. Prayer is not easy. It is not convenient. It costs time,

energy, sleep, comfort, and pride. E. M. Bounds rose at four in the morning every day for thirty

years. Rees Howells and his community prayed every evening until midnight during the darkest

years of the war. Andrew Murray lost his voice for two years in the crucible of surrender.

Watchman Nee spent twenty years in prison. Jonathan Edwards was dismissed by his own

congregation. Charles Finney was mocked and opposed. Derek Prince gave up a brilliant

academic career. Timothy Keller faced cancer with prayer as his only weapon. None of them told

us prayer was easy. They told us it was worth it.

Fourth: they were all men whose prayers outlived them. The prayers of Andrew Murray's father

for revival were answered in 1860, decades after those prayers began. E. M. Bounds’ prayer for a

praying Church was answered through eight books published after his death. Rees Howells

interceded for the State of Israel before it existed, and the nation was reborn in 1948, two years

before he died. Loren Cunningham received a vision in prayer in 1956 that he spent sixty-seven

years watching unfold. Billy Graham prayed for lost souls at every crusade, and the fruit of those

prayers continued to ripple through individuals, families, and communities long after each

meeting ended. Prayer is not limited by the lifetime of the one who prays. It reaches into eternity.

A Word to Ugandan Pastors

You are serving God in one of the most spiritually strategic places on earth. Uganda sits at the

heart of the African continent, a nation with a history of Christian martyrdom, revival, and the

extraordinary blessing of the Holy Spirit. The missionaries who came to Uganda in the

nineteenth century paid a tremendous price. The Uganda Martyrs died with the name of Christ on

their lips. The East African Revival of the twentieth century sent waves of Holy Spirit power

through Uganda and beyond. You are the heirs of all of that.

But the inheritance of the past is not enough. Every generation must meet God afresh. The fire

on the altar must be renewed every morning. And in your generation, the challenges are great:

poverty and suffering among your people, family breakdown, political pressure, false teaching,

spiritual warfare, the pull of material prosperity and personal ambition. Only a deep and

sustained prayer life will equip you to face these challenges and lead your congregation through

them.

You are also uniquely positioned for global influence. Uganda has given the world remarkable

Christian leaders, preachers, and evangelists. Ugandan missionaries serve across Africa and

beyond. Ugandan churches are sending churches. As you build your prayer life, you are not only

serving your local congregation — you are building foundations for the global mission of the

Church.

The fifteen men in this book were not super-humans. They were ordinary people who took God

at His word. They prayed because they believed that God hears. They persisted because they

believed that God answers. They sacrificed comfort and convenience because they believed that

prayer is worth more than anything else they could do. Every one of them would say to you

today: “You can do this. You must do this. The world you are trying to reach is waiting for you

to pray.”

CALL TO ACTION

A Charge to the Pastors and Teachers of Uganda

This book is not meant to sit on a shelf. It is meant to send you to your knees. As you close these

pages, the question is not “What did I learn?” but “What will I do?”

Here are seven practical commitments you can make in response to what you have read:

1. Establish a Daily Prayer Appointment

Every man in this book set aside specific time for prayer. Some prayed for hours each morning.

All of them were deliberate and disciplined. Choose a time — whether it is thirty minutes at

dawn, an hour at midday, or an evening vigil — and protect it. Tell your family. Guard it from

interruption. And keep it even on the days you do not feel like praying, for those are often the

days your prayer matters most.

2. Ground Your Prayers in Scripture

As you pray, bring your Bible with you. Read a passage first. Let God speak before you speak.

Pray the promises back to God. Let the words of the Psalms become your own words. Let the

prayers of Paul in Ephesians 1 and 3 shape the way you pray for your congregation. Let the great

prayers of the Bible — Moses, Daniel, Nehemiah, Jesus — teach you what prayer looks like

when it moves heaven.

3. Pray for the Filling of the Holy Spirit

Ask God every day for a fresh filling of the Holy Spirit. Not just for gifts and power — though

those are real and important — but for the character of Christ to be formed in you. Ask the Spirit

to show you what to pray for, to giv e you the burdens of God’s heart, and to intercede through

you for the things that matter most to God.

4. Pray for Your Congregation by Name

Take a list of the people in your congregation and pray through it regularly. Pray for their

marriages, their children, their work, their struggles, and their faith. When people bring you

prayer requests, keep a record and follow up. Let your congregation know that you pray for them

by name. This is one of the most powerful things a pastor can do.

5. Build a Culture of Prayer in Your Church

Spurgeon said the Monday evening prayer meeting was the engine of everything Metropolitan

Tabernacle accomplished. Rees Howells’ prayer community gathered every evening. What is the

prayer life of your congregation? Establish a regular prayer meeting. Teach on prayer from the

pulpit. Share answered prayers publicly to build faith. Invite your elders and deacons to pray

together before every meeting. Let prayer be the air your church breathes.

6. Find or Become a Prayer Partner

Almost every man in this book had people who prayed with and for him. Charles Finney had

Father Nash. Loren Cunningham had a community of YWAM intercessors. Henry Blackaby had

a group of Saskatoon pastors who prayed together for two years before the revival came. Find

one or two other pastors or elders who will commit to pray with you regularly. And pray for one

another specifically, honestly, and persistently.

7. Intercede for Uganda and the Nations

Your prayers are not limited to your congregation. The God you pray to is the God of the

nations. Pray for Uganda — for its leaders, its families, its schools, its churches, its missionaries.

Pray for Africa. Pray for the unreached peoples of the earth. Pray for the coming of the Kingdom

of God in every nation. As Rees Howells discovered, the scope of prayer is as wide as the heart

of God.

A Final Word

Andrew Murray wrote: “The man who mobilises the Christian church to pray will make the

greatest contribution to world evangelisation in history.”

E. M. Bounds declared : “Around us is a world lost in sin, above us is a God willing and able to

save; it is ours to build the bridge that links heaven and earth, and prayer is the mighty

instrument that does the work.”

Timothy Keller concluded: “There is absolutely nothing so great as prayer.”

These men were right. Prayer is the greatest work. It is the most important thing you will do

today, and tomorrow, and every day of your ministry. It is the thing that makes everything else

you do alive with the power of God. And it is available to you right now.

So close this book. Find a quiet place. Open your Bible. And pray. Not because you have to.

Because the God of Andrew Murray and Charles Spurgeon and Watchman Nee and D. L. Moody

and all the rest — that same God — is waiting to meet you there.

“And whatever you ask in prayer, you will receive, if you have faith.”

Matthew 21:22

To God Alone Be the Glory

fields.title: Chapter 10
fields.body_html:
Conclusion: The Chief Shepherd Still Calls ..................................................................................... 36

Scripture Appendix: God’s Word on the Pastoral Calling .............................................................. 38 

Dedication

This book is dedicated to every pastor, elder, and shepherd

who carries the weight of souls with quiet faithfulness.

To those who study late, visit the grieving, counsel the lost,

and preach the Word whether or not the season feels fruitful —

who have learned that the calling itself is the reward.

To those who aspire to lead Christ-centred, disciplined lives

and to grow into the image of the Good Shepherd —

tenderly, courageously, and faithfully.

And to every congregation whose faithfulness has made

their pastor’s joy complete.

“I will give you shepherds after my own heart, who will lead you with knowledge and

understanding.”

— Jeremiah 3:15 (NIV)

Introduction: The Weight and the Glory of the Pastoral

Calling

There is no calling quite like it. The pastor stands at the intersection of the eternal and the

ordinary — one foot in the theological library, the other in the hospital room; one hand on the

Scripture, the other on the shoulder of someone whose world has just fallen apart. He is

simultaneously a student, a preacher, a counsellor, a comforter, a leader, and a servant. He

carries the weight of souls. He is responsible, under God, for the spiritual nourishment and

protection of people who will one day stand before the Almighty — and he knows it. The men in

this book felt that weight, accepted it, and by the grace of God discharged it with a faithfulness

that history has not been able to forget.

The pastoral calling is not a human invention. It flows directly from the heart of God, who

revealed Himself, across the whole span of Scripture, as a shepherd. The imagery is everywhere.

Isaiah heard the divine promise: “He tends his flock like a shepherd: He gathers the lambs in his

arms and carries them close to his heart; he gently leads those that have young” (Isaiah 40:11,

NIV). Before He gave the church its human under-shepherds, God established His own

shepherding character as the pattern they would be called to imitate. Every pastor who has ever

wept with a grieving widow, searched for a wandering soul, or patiently fed the spiritually

starving was doing so as a reflection of the God who is Himself the first and greatest Shepherd.

God was not reluctant to hold human shepherds accountable for the care of His flock. Ezekiel

recorded some of the most piercing words in the prophetic literature — words addressed not to

pagans but to Israel’s own leaders: “Woe to you shepherds of Israel who only take care of

yourselves! Should not shepherds take care of the flock? You eat the curds, clothe yourselves

with the wool and slaughter the choice animals, but you do not take care of the flock. You have

not strengthened the weak or healed the sick or bound up the injured. You have not brought back

the strays or searched for the lost” (Ezekiel 34:2–4, NIV). This divine indictment is also, read

from the opposite direction, the most comprehensive job description for faithful pastoral ministry

ever written. The good shepherd does precisely everything here described as neglected.

What is a good pastor? He is not primarily a motivational speaker, a nonprofit executive, or a

spiritual entertainer. He is a man called by God to feed, protect, lead, and love a specific group of

people entrusted to his care — not for a season of personal ambition but for the long haul of

faithful ministry. The ten men in this book were not uniformly gifted, equally educated, or

similarly temperamented. Chrysostom thundered from the great pulpit of Constantinople and was

exiled for refusing to flatter the powerful. George Herbert composed poetry in a country village

and died at thirty-nine having transformed it. Richard Baxter visited every home in

Kidderminster with a catechism and a burning conviction that no soul in his parish should perish

for want of a shepherd’s attention. Dietrich Bonhoeffer ran an illegal underground seminary and

went to the gallows rather than compromise the integrity of the church he had served.

The apostle Paul’s charge to the Ephesian elders remains the definitive description of what the

pastoral calling demands: “Keep watch over yourselves and all the flock of which the Holy Spirit

has made you overseers. Be shepherds of the church of God, which he bought with his own

blood” (Acts 20:28, NIV). Two things are inseparable in this command: the pastor must first

keep watch over himself — his own soul, his own walk with God, his own integrity — and then

over the flock. A man cannot give what he does not possess. A shepherd whose own soul is

malnourished will soon be unable to feed those in his care. The men in this book understood this.

Their pastoral fruitfulness was inseparable from their personal devotion.

Peter’s instruction to elders carries both the weight of command and the warmth of invitation:

“Be shepherds of God’s flock that is under your care, watching over them — not because you

must, but because you are willing, as God wants you to be; not pursuing dishonest gain, but

eager to serve; not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock. And

when the Chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the crown of glory that will never fade away”

(1 Peter 5:2–4, NIV). That final promise — the unfading crown from the Chief Shepherd’s own

hand — is what sustained these ten men through decades of invisible, costly, often thankless

ministry. They were not working for human applause. They were working for an audience of

One.

These chapters are not hagiographies. They do not pretend these men were without flaw or

failure. Several of them made serious mistakes; some were imperfect in ways their own writings

acknowledge with painful candor. What they shared was not perfection but a profound

seriousness about the pastoral calling — a conviction that to be entrusted with the care of souls

was the most solemn responsibility a human being could bear, and a determination to discharge

it, by the grace of God, with everything they had.

These pages are written for pastors and for those who love them. They are written for

seminarians who are still deciding what kind of minister they will be, for elders who wonder

whether the quiet faithfulness of their ministry matters, and for church members who want to

understand the calling of the man who stands before them week by week. Above all, they are

written for anyone who aspires to shepherd — in whatever form, at whatever scale — in the

spirit of the One who said, “I am the good shepherd.”

fields.title: Chapter 1
fields.body_html:
Shepherd

Who He Was

John Chrysostom was born around 347 AD in Antioch, Syria, the son of a military officer, and

received the finest classical education his era could provide before his conversion to an ascetic

Christian life under the bishop Meletius. He spent several formative years as a monk in the

Syrian desert before returning to Antioch, where his gifts as a preacher drew enormous crowds

and earned him the posthumous title by which history remembers him: Chrysostom, “Golden-

Mouthed.” In 398 AD, the Emperor Arcadius appointed him Archbishop of Constantinople

against his will, and Chrysostom accepted the role with the same directness he brought to

everything: he immediately sold the extravagant furnishings of the episcopal palace and used the

proceeds to build hospitals for the poor, dismissed corrupt clergy, and began preaching — to the

empress and the beggar with identical plain-spokenness — every Sunday. His refusal to flatter

the powerful resulted in two exiles, the second of which killed him; he died in 407 AD on a

forced march in the mountains of Pontus.

His Vision for the Pastoral Calling

Chrysostom’s masterpiece on pastoral ministry, “On the Priesthood,” written early in his career,

remains one of the most penetrating analyses of the pastoral calling in Christian literature. Its

central argument is deceptively simple: the care of souls is the most demanding, the most

consequential, and the most dangerous of all human occupations. It demands more than

medicine, more than law, more than statecraft, because its territory is the eternal soul, and its

failures are measured not in earthly loss but in loss that cannot be undone. Chrysostom did not

write this to discourage pastors but to call them to a level of seriousness commensurate with the

stakes.

The foundation of Chrysostom’s pastoral vision was the understanding that the congregation was

not the pastor’s audience but his flock — a living body for which he was, under Christ,

responsible. He drew the sharpest possible contrast between the pastor and the hireling from

Jesus’ own words: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.

The hired hand is not the shepherd and does not own the sheep. So when he sees the wolf

coming, he abandons the sheep and runs away.” (John 10:11–12, NIV). The test of the true

shepherd, Chrysostom taught, came not when the ministry was easy and the congregation was

growing, but when the wolves arrived — when standing firm cost something real. He himself

passed this test at the cost of his life.

Chrysostom was equally insistent that faithful preaching was the non-negotiable center of

pastoral ministry. A shepherd who did not feed the flock with the Word was a shepherd in name

only. He preached verse by verse through entire books of the Bible in an era when that practice

was unusual, convinced that the congregation needed the whole counsel of God, not a curated

selection. He took Paul’s charge with absolute literalism: “Preach the word; be prepared in

season and out of season; correct, rebuke and encourage — with great patience and careful

instruction” (2 Timothy 4:2, NIV). His own sermons, preserved in eighty-nine homilies on

Matthew and sixty-eight on Genesis among hundreds of others, were the living embodiment of

this command. They were not rhetorical performances but pastoral acts — careful, sustained,

patient feeding of a flock.

His pastoral theology of the poor was among his most distinctive and demanding contributions.

Chrysostom believed that the way a congregation treated the poor was a direct measure of how

seriously it had understood the gospel. His homily on Matthew 25 — in which he drew out the

staggering implication that Christ was present in the person of every hungry, thirsty, and

homeless person — was among the most socially urgent pastoral sermons in Christian history.

He wrote: “Do you wish to honour the body of Christ? Do not ignore him when he is naked. Do

not pay him homage in the temple clad in silk only then to neglect him outside where he suffers

cold and nakedness.” He grounded this not in social theory but in Paul’s declaration: “There is

neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there male and female, for you are all one

in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28, NIV). The pastoral community that took this verse seriously, he

argued, could not be indifferent to the material suffering of any of its members.

Chrysostom was also the great pastoral theologian of courage. He watched too many pastors

around him perform a careful calculus of how much truth they could afford to preach without

offending those whose patronage sustained the church. He found this kind of ministry beneath

contempt. The pastor’s obligation was not to his social standing but to the souls in his care, and

those souls needed the truth even — especially — when the truth was unwelcome.

He held to Paul’s warning with unflinching consistency: “For the time will come when people

will not put up with sound doctrine. Instead, to suit their own desires, they will gather around

them a great number of teachers to say what their itching ears want to hear” (2 Timothy 4:3,

NIV). Chrysostom refused to be one of those teachers. His two exiles were the price he paid for

that refusal, and he paid it without complaint.

His final pastoral legacy was the example of his own death. Driven by soldiers through the

mountains in the bitter autumn cold, too weak to walk, he died with the same words on his lips

that had opened his ministry: “Glory be to God for all things.” It was a pastoral death in the

fullest sense — a dying that preached. He had taught his congregation throughout his ministry

that suffering was not a contradiction of God’s love but a participation in Christ’s. Now he

showed them what that looked like in a man who believed it. He had lived Paul’s testimony: “I

have learned to be content whatever the circumstances” (Philippians 4:11, NIV). He had. And he

had taught his flock, by word and by example, to do the same.

A Prayer:

Lord Jesus, the Good Shepherd, give us the courage of Chrysostom — to preach

the Word when it is welcome and when it is not, to stand between our people and

the wolves regardless of the cost, and to love the poor not as a project but as

Yourself. Make us shepherds who are willing to lay down our comfort, our

reputation, and our ease in the service of the flock You have entrusted to our care.

Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 2
fields.body_html:
Servants

Who He Was

Gregory was born around 540 AD in Rome into one of the city’s most distinguished aristocratic

families, and by his early thirties had risen to become the Prefect of Rome — the highest civil

office in the city. At the height of his civic career, he underwent a dramatic conversion to the

monastic life, transforming his family’s estate on the Caelian Hill into a monastery and spending

five years in the contemplative life he had always preferred. Against his own wishes, Pope

Pelagius II drew him out of the monastery for diplomatic service and then, in 590 AD, the clergy

and people of Rome elected Gregory himself as pope. He accepted with genuine grief —

describing himself in his letters as having been dragged from the contemplative life into “the sea

of the world” — but went on to govern the Western church for the next fourteen years with a

competence and pastoral wisdom that made him, in the judgment of history, not merely “Great”

but the defining model of Christian pastoral leadership for the next thousand years. He styled

himself “Servant of the servants of God,” a title still used by the papacy today.

His Vision for the Pastoral Calling

Gregory’s pastoral treatise, the “Liber Regulae Pastoralis” (Book of Pastoral Rule), written in the

first months of his papacy, is perhaps the single most influential handbook on pastoral ministry

in Christian history. King Alfred the Great translated it into Old English. It shaped the

understanding of ministry across the medieval church. Its central insight — that the pastor must

know each sheep differently and therefore minister differently to each one — remains as

challenging and true today as when Gregory wrote it. Good pastoral care, he argued, is not the

application of a single method to all people, but the discernment of what each person, in their

particular condition, most needs from God.

Gregory’s foundational pastoral conviction was rooted in the shepherd imagery of the Hebrew

prophets, particularly the great shepherd-chapter of Ezekiel. The divine promise in Ezekiel 34

was, for Gregory, not merely a prophetic description of Christ but a blueprint for what human

under-shepherds were to imitate: “I will search for the lost and bring back the strays. I will bind

up the injured and strengthen the weak, but the sleek and the strong I will destroy. I will

shepherd the flock with justice” (Ezekiel 34:16, NIV). Each verb in this verse was for Gregory a

pastoral obligation: to search, to bring back, to bind up, to strengthen, to exercise justice. The

good pastor was active, not passive — going out to the lost rather than waiting for them to return,

binding wounds rather than ignoring them, strengthening the weak rather than merely celebrating

the strong.

The most practically transformative dimension of Gregory’s pastoral teaching was his insistence

on differentiated care. The frightened person needed encouragement; the arrogant person needed

correction. The poor person needed comfort; the rich person needed warning. The healthy person

needed instruction; the sick person needed patience. Applying the same pastoral approach to all

of these was not pastoral wisdom but pastoral laziness. He found the model for this

differentiation in Paul’s description of his own ministry: “To the weak I became weak, to win the

weak. I have become all things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some” (1

Corinthians 9:22, NIV). This was not inconsistency or sycophancy — it was pastoral

intelligence, the skill of knowing what medicine was needed for what condition.

Gregory’s theology of pastoral humility was equally profound. He held the highest office in the

Western church and chose for his title words that deliberately inverted the logic of human power:

“Whoever wants to become great among you must be your servant, and whoever wants to be first

must be your slave — just as the Son of Man did not come to be served, but to serve, and to give

his life as a ransom for many” (Matthew 20:26–28, NIV). Gregory believed that pastoral

authority was not diminished by humble service but constituted by it. The bishop who used his

office to accumulate privilege was not exercising pastoral authority; he was evacuating it. The

servant of the servants was, precisely in his servanthood, the most truly authoritative figure in the

room.

Gregory also understood the pastoral office as demanding the highest standard of personal

spiritual life. The pastor could not call his flock to a depth of devotion he himself had not

entered. This was not merely a matter of credibility but of capacity: a man who had not spent

time in contemplative prayer could not lead others into it, and a man who had not wrestled with

his own sin could not speak with genuine authority to the sin of others. Gregory grounded this in

Paul’s instruction to Timothy, which he regarded as the most important pastoral exhortation in

the New Testament: “Watch your life and doctrine closely. Persevere in them, because if you do,

you will save both yourself and your hearers” (1 Timothy 4:16, NIV). Life and doctrine together:

the pastoral office demanded excellence in both, and neither could substitute for the other.

His personal pastoral style — accessible, attentive, patient, and formidably competent — was

itself a teaching. He wrote over eight hundred letters that survive, many of them pastoral

responses to specific individuals in specific crises. He responded to the plague, organized food

distribution, negotiated with the Lombards, reformed the liturgy, and sent missionaries to

England — all while sustaining a personal spiritual life that he described as always being

interrupted and never being abandoned. He embodied Peter’s vision of pastoral leadership: “Not

lording it over those entrusted to you, but being examples to the flock” (1 Peter 5:3, NIV). He

was the example — in service, in humility, in competence, and in the willingness to be spent for

the sake of those in his care.

A Prayer:

Lord, You are the Shepherd who searches, binds up, and strengthens. Make us

pastors in Your image — not servants of our own comfort or reputation, but

servants of Your servants. Give us Gregory’s discernment to know what each soul

needs, his humility to stoop to every need, and his perseverance to sustain the

caring over the long years of ministry. Let us be examples to the flock by

becoming nothing less than what we preach. Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 3
fields.body_html:
Who Made the Ordinary Holy

Who He Was

George Herbert was born on April 3, 1593, in Montgomery, Wales, into a distinguished English

family and received a brilliant education at Westminster School and Trinity College, Cambridge,

where he was eventually appointed Public Orator — a position that brought him into regular

contact with the court of King James I and seemed to promise a career of worldly prominence.

He resisted the call to pastoral ministry for years, reluctant to leave the prestige of public life, but

in 1630, at the age of thirty-six, he accepted the small country rectorship of Bemerton in

Wiltshire, near Salisbury. He had at most three years left to live — he died of tuberculosis in

1633 at thirty-nine — but those three years produced what many regard as the most beautiful

body of devotional poetry in the English language and a prose guide to country pastoral ministry,

“A Priest to the Temple, or The Country Parson,” which remains a model of pastoral humility,

attentiveness, and creativity to this day.

His Vision for the Pastoral Calling

Herbert’s understanding of pastoral ministry was inseparable from his sacramental imagination:

the conviction that the ordinary materials of human life — a meal, a field, a broom, a bed —

were capable of carrying the weight of divine meaning. This was not mysticism but incarnational

theology: the God who had taken on flesh and dwelt in a village was the God who was present in

the daily textures of his parishioners’ lives, and the pastor’s task was to help them see Him there.

The country parson was not a figure who descended periodically from spiritual heights to address

the mundane; he was one who lived among his people and helped them discover the sacred in

their midst.

Herbert’s portrait of the country parson in his prose work is striking in its emphasis on pastoral

presence. The pastor must be known to his people not as an occasional visitor or a Sunday

institution but as a neighbour, a friend, and a fellow laborer in the same soil. He drew on Paul’s

tender image of the nursing mother: “Just as a nursing mother cares for her children, so we cared

for you. Because we loved you so much, we were delighted to share with you not only the gospel

of God but our lives as well” (1 Thessalonians 2:7–8, NIV). This sharing of life — not merely of

information — was, Herbert believed, what distinguished pastoral ministry from lecturing. The

pastor who shared his life with his people loved them in the way Paul described: not as an

audience to be instructed but as children to be nurtured.

He insisted in The Country Parson that the pastoral home should itself be a sermon. The parson’s

household was to be governed by prayer, hospitality, simplicity, and godly order, so that anyone

who entered it felt the presence of a different set of values from those that governed the world

outside. The parson’s wife was his partner in this ministry; his children were its first fruits; his

table was open to the poorest parishioner. Herbert grounded this conviction in Paul’s

requirements for the overseer: “An overseer is to be above reproach, faithful to his wife,

temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to teach, not given to drunkenness” (1

Timothy 3:2–3, NIV). These were not abstract virtues for Herbert but practical habits of daily

life — each one, practiced consistently, shaping the home into a visible argument for the gospel.

Herbert’s pastoral poetry — collected in The Temple , published posthumously — was itself a

pastoral instrument. He wrote poems that gave his parishioners language for experiences they

had felt but could not articulate: the experience of spiritual dryness, of feeling unworthy of God’s

love, of struggling to pray, of discovering that God had been present in circumstances they had

assumed He had abandoned. His great poem “Love (III)” — in which Love (Christ) welcomes

the reluctant soul to the table despite its protests of unworthiness — captured in fourteen lines

what Paul took a chapter to unfold: “For God so loved the world that he gave his one and only

Son, that whoever believes in him shall not perish but have eternal life” (John 3:16, NIV).

Herbert’s pastoral genius was in translating these enormous truths into the textures of human

experience that his parishioners actually lived.

He was also a pastor of great personal patience with the struggling, the slow, and the spiritually

confused. He wrote in The Country Parson that the parson must never show frustration with

those who do not understand quickly, must never make them feel stupid for their questions, and

must always remember that he himself was once ignorant of the things he now knows. He found

his model for this in Paul’s instruction: “And the Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome but

must be kind to everyone, able to teach, not resentful. Opponents must be gently instructed, in

the hope that God will grant them repentance leading them to a knowledge of the truth” (2

Timothy 2:24–25, NIV). Gentleness in instruction was not a pastoral nicety for Herbert but a

theological conviction: the God who had been patient with him required him to be patient with

others.

Herbert died at thirty-nine with a short ministry behind him and a handful of poems sent to a

friend with the instruction that they be published only if he thought they might help “some poor

dejected soul.” They have been helping poor dejected souls for nearly four hundred years. He

had discharged the pastoral calling in the way Paul described: “We proclaim him, admonishing

and teaching everyone with all wisdom, so that we may present everyone fully mature in Christ”

(Colossians 1:28, NIV). He had proclaimed, admonished, and taught — in sermons, in prose, in

verse, and in the daily texture of a life lived among his people. The maturity he labored for in

others was achieved in himself by the grace of the God he served.

A Prayer:

Lord of the ordinary and the holy, teach us to find You in the textures of everyday

life and to help others find You there too. Where we are tempted to consider small

ministries beneath us, give us Herbert’s contentment with the particular flock You

have given us. Make our homes sermons, our tables open, our patience

inexhaustible, and our words — however few — capable of helping some poor

dejected soul find their way to You. Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 4
fields.body_html:
Who Visited Every Door

Who He Was

Richard Baxter was born on November 12, 1615, in Rowton, Shropshire, England, the son of a

gentleman farmer whose own late conversion to genuine Christian faith shaped young Richard’s

understanding of what real religion looked like. Largely self-educated in theology through

voracious reading, he was ordained and in 1641 became the minister of Kidderminster — a town

of two thousand people that by his own account was, when he arrived, almost entirely irreligious.

By the time he left fourteen years later, the town had been transformed: almost every house had a

family altar, the streets rang with the sounds of singing, and the congregation had grown to such

numbers that the church could not contain them. He accomplished this not by dramatic revival

meetings but by systematic, patient, personal pastoral visitation of every family in the town. His

book

“The Reformed Pastor,” published in 1656, remains the most searching examination of pastoral

duty in the English language.

His Vision for the Pastoral Calling

Baxter’s pastoral vision was built on a single, burning conviction: every soul in the parish was

his responsibility before God. Not the souls who attended faithfully. Not the souls who were easy

to reach. Every soul. This was not a pious aspiration for Baxter but a methodological

commitment he discharged by meeting with every family in Kidderminster — roughly eight

hundred families — once per year, catechizing them personally, assessing their spiritual state,

and addressing whatever he found with teaching, exhortation, and prayer. He described this work

as the heart of his ministry, more important than any sermon he preached.

The theological foundation of Baxter’s pastoral urgency was the doctrine of the watchman from

Ezekiel — one of the most searching passages in the whole of Scripture for those who hold

pastoral responsibility: “When I say to a wicked person, ‘You will surely die,’ and you do not

warn them or speak out to dissuade them from their evil ways in order to save their life, that

wicked person will die for their sin, and I will hold you accountable for their blood. But if you do

warn the wicked person and they do not turn from their wickedness or from their evil ways, they
