will die for their sin; but you will have saved yourself” (Ezekiel 3:18–19, NIV). Baxter took this

with deadly seriousness. The blood of souls who perished for want of a shepherd’s warning

would be required of the shepherd. This was not a comfortable doctrine, but Baxter did not seek

comfort in his theology — he sought fidelity.

His most famous line from The Reformed Pastor crystallizes his entire pastoral philosophy: “I

preached as never sure to preach again, and as a dying man to dying men.” This was not

hyperbole. Baxter was ill for most of his ministry, frequently certain that he was close to death,

and he preached accordingly. Every sermon was potentially his last. Every visit to a family might

be the last opportunity to speak to that soul before it stood before God. This urgency was not

manufactured anxiety but a theological conviction that time was short and eternity was long, and

that the pastor who forgot this fact was unworthy of his calling. He took Paul’s charge with

complete literalism: “In the presence of God and of Christ Jesus, who will judge the living and

the dead, and in view of his appearing and his kingdom, I give you this charge: Preach the word;

be prepared in season and out of season” (2 Timothy 4:1–2, NIV). It was always the season.

Baxter was equally insistent about the pastor’s own spiritual state as a prerequisite for effective

pastoral ministry. He opened The Reformed Pastor with a searching section on the necessity of

personal godliness in the minister, arguing that a pastor who neglected his own soul was not

merely personally compromised but pastorally disabled. He quoted Acts 20:28 and then

unpacked its first clause with piercing intensity: “Keep watch over yourselves and all the flock of

which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers” (Acts 20:28, NIV). "Yourselves" came first. A

man who could not keep watch over his own soul had no business claiming to watch over others.

This was not an optional preliminary to pastoral ministry; it was its precondition.

His model of catechetical visitation — meeting with families in their homes, working through

questions about faith and salvation, identifying misunderstandings and addressing them with

Scripture — was driven by a theology of every-member accountability that he found in the New

Testament pattern of mutual instruction. He loved Paul’s confidence in the Roman congregation:

“I myself am convinced, my brothers and sisters, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled

with knowledge and competent to instruct one another” (Romans 15:14, NIV).

The goal of his personal pastoral work was precisely this — to bring his parishioners to the point

of being able to instruct and exhort one another. He was working toward his own relative

redundancy. When every home in Kidderminster could sustain its own spiritual life, he had done

his job.

Baxter’s pastoral legacy was the proof that genuine, systematic pastoral work transforms

communities. He did not wait for revival to come to Kidderminster; he believed that faithful

pastoral labor was the ordinary means by which God brought revival, and he labored

accordingly. His confidence rested on God’s own promise through Jeremiah: “I will give you

shepherds after my own heart, who will lead you with knowledge and understanding” (Jeremiah

3:15, NIV). The shepherd God gives after His own heart leads with knowledge and

understanding — not raw enthusiasm, not institutional management, but the patient, informed,

personally attentive leadership of a man who knows his sheep by name. Baxter knew every

family in Kidderminster. He knew their names, their struggles, their questions, and their spiritual

condition. And through that knowledge, God transformed the town.

A Prayer:

Lord, make us shepherds who feel the weight of every soul in our care. Deliver us

from the comfortable deception that faithful preaching alone discharges the

pastoral calling, and drive us out of our offices and into our people’s homes. Give

us Baxter’s urgency — to preach as dying men to dying men — and his patience,

to visit, to catechize, to pray, and to work as though the next visit might be the one

that opens a door that has been closed for years. Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 5
fields.body_html:
Tended His Flock

Who He Was

Jonathan Edwards was born on October 5, 1703, in East Windsor, Connecticut, the son of a

Congregational minister and the grandson of the formidable Solomon Stoddard of Northampton.

He entered Yale at thirteen, graduated at seventeen, and by 1727 had joined his grandfather’s

congregation in Northampton, Massachusetts, as associate pastor. He succeeded Stoddard in

1729 and remained in Northampton for over twenty years until his congregation dismissed him

in 1750 in a bitter dispute over communion practice — a rejection he bore with remarkable

grace. He spent the following years as a frontier missionary to Native Americans at Stockbridge

before being elected president of the College of New Jersey (now Princeton) in 1757. He died in

1758, six weeks after his installation, of a smallpox inoculation gone wrong, at the age of fifty-

four. He is widely regarded as the greatest theologian and philosopher that America has

produced, but he was, first and throughout, a pastor.

His Vision for the Pastoral Calling

Edwards’ pastoral vision was inseparable from his theological vision, because he believed that

the deepest pastoral act was the communication of truth about God in all its depth and beauty and

terror. A congregation that understood who God was — truly, deeply, not merely notionally —

would love Him appropriately, fear Him appropriately, and live accordingly. The pastor’s

primary task was therefore theological: to bring his people into genuine, transforming knowledge

of the God they professed to worship. Sermons that did not engage the mind and the heart

together, he believed, produced only a superficial religion that would not survive the pressures of

the world.

Edwards’ understanding of his pastoral role was shaped by Paul’s magnificent description of the

minister’s comprehensive aim: “He is the one we proclaim, admonishing and teaching everyone

with all wisdom, so that we may present everyone fully mature in Christ. To this end I

strenuously contend with all the energy Christ so powerfully works in me” (Colossians 1:28–29,

NIV). “Fully mature in Christ” was not a modest target. It required nothing less than the

comprehensive transformation of the whole person — mind, will, affections, and habits — in

conformity with the image of Christ. Edwards worked toward this goal in Northampton for over

two decades, preaching, teaching, counseling, and writing, always aiming at maturity rather than

mere attendance.

The revival of 1734–1735 in Northampton, which Edwards documented in A Faithful Narrative

of the Surprising Work of God , presented him with the pastoral challenge he was perhaps best

equipped to meet: how to distinguish genuine spiritual awakening from emotional counterfeit.

His response was the most careful and theologically sophisticated pastoral discernment of

religious experience that the Protestant tradition had yet produced. He found his categories in

Scripture: “Do not quench the Spirit. Do not treat prophecies with contempt but test them all;

hold on to what is good, reject every kind of evil” (1 Thessalonians 5:19–22, NIV). He refused to

quench the Spirit by dismissing everything unusual as mere enthusiasm; he also refused to accept

everything emotional as therefore genuine. His Treatise Concerning Religious Affections remains

the definitive pastoral guide to this kind of discernment.

Edwards also understood the pastoral office as demanding the most complete and unflinching

proclamation of the whole counsel of God — including the doctrines that made polite society

uncomfortable. His famous sermon “Sinners in the Hands of an Angry God” is often caricatured

as theological sadism, but it was in fact a pastoral act of desperate love: the attempt to break

through the complacency of a congregation that was dangerously comfortable with a religion that

cost them nothing. He was doing precisely what Paul charged: “For I have not hesitated to

proclaim to you the whole will of God” (Acts 20:27, NIV). The whole will of God included

judgment, and a pastor who omitted it was not protecting his congregation from unnecessary

discomfort but exposing them to eternal danger.

His pastoral care in the aftermath of his 1750 dismissal is one of the most revealing episodes of

his ministry. He had been rejected by the congregation he had served for twenty-three years. The

dismissal was painful, public, and, by most historical assessments, unjust. Yet he left

Northampton without bitterness, commended his congregation to God’s mercy, and continued to

pray for them. He had absorbed what he had preached: that God’s sovereignty extended even

over the disappointments of faithful men, and that the pastor’s peace did not depend on

congregational approval. He rested in the character of God as Paul described it: “And we know

that in all things God works for the good of those who love him, who have been called according

to his purpose” (Romans 8:28, NIV). His frontier years at Stockbridge, in which he produced

some of his greatest theological work in obscurity and hardship, were the fruit of that faith.

His enduring pastoral legacy was his proof that theological depth and pastoral care are not in

tension but are inseparable. The congregation that was fed only emotional experience without

theological substance would be swept away when difficulty came. The congregation that was

given only dry doctrine without pastoral warmth would starve. Edwards gave his people both —

not always perfectly, but always seriously — because he believed that Paul’s description of

mature faith required both: “Speaking the truth in love, we will grow to become in every respect

the mature body of him who is the head, that is, Christ” (Ephesians 4:15, NIV). Truth and love

together: that was Edwards’ pastoral vision, and it remains the vision that every faithful minister

must recover in every generation.

A Prayer:

God of all truth and all love, give us Edwards’ courage to preach the whole

counsel of Your Word without editing the parts that make us uncomfortable, and

his wisdom to discern what is genuinely of Your Spirit. Teach us to aim, in every

pastoral act, at the full maturity of Christ in the lives of those we serve. And

where we are dismissed or disappointed, let us rest in Your sovereignty and

continue to pray for those who once rejected us. Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 6
fields.body_html:
Who Shepherded with Grace

Who He Was

John Newton was born on August 4, 1725, in London, the son of a ship captain, and spent his

early adult years in the brutal world of the Atlantic slave trade — first as a pressed sailor, then as

a crewman, and finally as the captain of slave ships. A terrifying storm in 1748 precipitated the

crisis that began his conversion, and he was ordained as a Church of England minister in 1764,

serving as curate of Olney in Buckinghamshire until 1780. He co-authored with William Cowper

the famous

“Olney Hymns,” including “Amazing Grace,” and corresponded with hundreds of individuals

across England — producing some of the warmest and most practically wise pastoral letters in

the English language. He spent the last twenty-seven years of his ministry as rector of St. Mary

Woolnoth in London, where he continued to preach and counsel until near his death in 1807 at

the age of eighty-two.

His Vision for the Pastoral Calling

Newton’s pastoral identity was inseparable from his personal history. He was, by his own

lifelong testimony, the greatest evidence for the proposition that God’s grace was greater than

any sin — a fact he could not allow himself to forget and would not allow his congregation to

forget. His famous self-description in his will — “John Newton, Clerk, once an infidel and

libertine, a servant of slaves in Africa, was, by the rich mercy of our Lord and Saviour Jesus

Christ, preserved, restored, pardoned, and appointed to preach the faith he had long laboured to

destroy” — was not false modesty but the controlling narrative of his entire pastoral ministry. He

had been the chief of sinners. He therefore had the deepest possible sympathy for the struggling.

The pastoral letters Newton wrote across his long ministry constitute one of the richest bodies of

practical spiritual direction in the English language. They were remarkable for their combination

of doctrinal precision and pastoral warmth — never separating the two, never allowing doctrine

to become cold or warmth to become sentimental. He operated from the apostolic pattern Paul

described: “We were gentle among you, like a mother caring for her little children” (1

Thessalonians 2:7, NIV). This gentleness was not the gentleness of someone who had never

known real darkness, but of someone who had known it deeply and had been reached anyway.

He could write to those in spiritual despair with genuine authority: he had been there.

One of Newton’s most distinctive pastoral contributions was his theology of the slow work of

grace in the Christian life. He was unimpressed by rapid and dramatic spiritual claims, and he

counselled patience with both himself and others in the long, uneven process of sanctification.

He famously compared himself to a person half-rescued from a mud-pit: not yet out, but at least

facing the right direction and moving toward cleaner ground. He found the scriptural basis for

this patience in Paul’s own testimony: “Not that I have already obtained all this, or have already

arrived at my goal, but I press on to take hold of that for which Christ Jesus took hold of me”

(Philippians 3:12, NIV). This was not an excuse for complacency but a safeguard against the

despair that came from expecting instantaneous transformation. The shepherd who understood

this could hold his flock through the long middle years of the Christian life with steady, patient

hope.

Newton also brought to his pastoral ministry an unusual capacity for bearing with those he

disagreed with. He was a Calvinist who refused to use his Calvinism as a weapon; he was an

evangelical who maintained pastoral relationships with those of very different theological

convictions. He grounded this irenic disposition in Paul’s instruction to Timothy: “And the

Lord’s servant must not be quarrelsome but must be kind to everyone, able to teach, not

resentful. Opponents must be gently instructed, in the hope that God will grant them repentance

leading them to a knowledge of the truth” (2 Timothy 2:24–25, NIV). Newton practiced this

gentleness not because he had no convictions but because he had learned from his own history

that God worked through patience, not through argument, and that a wounded conscience was

more likely to be healed by kindness than by doctrinal correctness.

His pastoral ministry of presence — visiting the sick, the dying, the confused, and the grieving

— was sustained across eight decades by the simple conviction that every soul he met had been

bought by the same blood that had bought his own. He never lost his astonishment at having

been forgiven. That astonishment was the wellspring of his pastoral compassion. He loved Paul’s

language about the ministry of comfort: “Praise be to the God and Father of our Lord Jesus

Christ, the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our troubles,

so that we can comfort those in any trouble with the comfort we ourselves receive from God” (2

Corinthians 1:3–4, NIV). Newton had received the comfort. He spent his life distributing it.

He continued to preach at St. Mary Woolnoth well into old age and near-blindness, famously

saying when urged to retire: “What! Shall the old African blasphemer stop while he can speak?”

His ministry was a demonstration that pastoral faithfulness is not constrained by age,

background, or personal history — that the grace which redeems the vilest sinner is also the

grace that qualifies the most unlikely shepherd. He embodied the truth Paul wrote to the

Corinthians: “But by the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace to me was not without

effect” (1 Corinthians 15:10, NIV). Grace was not without effect in John Newton. It made him

one of the most compassionate and effective pastors of his century.

A Prayer:

Amazing God, whose grace is greater than any sin we have committed or any

darkness we have inhabited, make us pastors who never lose our astonishment at

having been forgiven. Where we are tempted to pastor from the height of our

holiness, bring us back to the memory of what we were before Your grace found

us. Give us Newton’s gentleness with the struggling, his patience with the slow,

and his inexhaustible readiness to comfort with the comfort we have ourselves

received. Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 7
fields.body_html:
Young Shepherd of Dundee

Who He Was

Robert Murray M’Cheyne was born on May 21, 1813, in Edinburgh, Scotland, the youngest of

five children in a godly middle-class family. He was converted in his early twenties, educated at

Edinburgh University and New College, and ordained in 1836 at the age of twenty-three as the

first minister of St. Peter’s Church in Dundee — a new church in a working-class district of

approximately four thousand people. He ministered there for just seven years before dying of

typhus in 1843 at the age of twenty-nine, having never recovered full health after a period of

serious illness in 1838–1839. In those seven years he transformed St. Peter’s, wrote hymns that

are still sung today, undertook a mission to the Jews of Palestine, and built a prayer movement

that outlasted him. Andrew Bonar’s “Memoir and Remains of Robert Murray M’Cheyne,”

published after his death, became one of the most widely read Christian biographies of the

nineteenth century and a formative influence on generations of ministers.

His Vision for the Pastoral Calling

M’Cheyne’s understanding of pastoral ministry was summed up in the most famous sentence he

ever wrote, addressed to a young ministerial student: “The greatest need of my people is my

personal holiness.” This was not a prescription for a withdrawn, other-worldly pietism; it was a

pastoral theology of the most practical kind. If the congregation was fed spiritually by the

minister, then the spiritual temperature of the congregation was inevitably shaped by the spiritual

temperature of the man. A cold-hearted minister produced a cold-hearted congregation. A man in

genuine communion with God carried that communion into the pulpit with him, and the

congregation felt it.

M’Cheyne grounded this conviction in Paul’s personal exhortation to Timothy, which he

regarded as the most important pastoral counsel in the New Testament: “Don’t let anyone look

down on you because you are young, but set an example for the believers in speech, in conduct,

in love, in faith and in purity. Until I come, devote yourself to the public reading of Scripture, to

preaching and to teaching. Do not neglect your gift… Watch your life and doctrine closely.

Persevere in them, because if you do, you will save both yourself and your hearers” (1 Timothy

4:12–16, NIV). Life and doctrine together, inseparably: the watching of the life first, and then its

overflow into the doctrine. M’Cheyne rose early every morning to spend the first hours of the

day with God before he met with his people, convinced that an unhurried morning with the Lord

was the single most important pastoral preparation he could make.

His pastoral preaching was distinctive in its Christ-centredness. He believed that every passage

of Scripture pointed ultimately to Christ and that every sermon, whatever its text, should bring

the congregation to the Saviour. He was not interested in moralizing or practical self-

improvement separated from the person of Christ; he wanted his people to know and love and

trust the Lord Jesus with a depth of personal intimacy that transformed their lives from the inside

out. He took to heart Paul’s declaration of pastoral method: “For I resolved to know nothing

while I was with you except Jesus Christ and him crucified” (1 Corinthians 2:2, NIV). This was

not intellectual narrowness but pastoral wisdom: in the crucified Christ was the full width of

human need — forgiveness, healing, hope, identity, purpose, and eternal life. Everything his

congregation needed was there.

M’Cheyne’s pastoral care extended with particular tenderness to the young of his congregation.

He invested heavily in the children and young people of St. Peter’s, building Sunday schools,

catechism classes, and young people’s meetings, convinced that the spiritual formation of the

next generation was among the most urgent pastoral priorities. He had been converted young

himself and understood that the grace which caught him early could catch others early too. He

found his model in Paul’s personal investment in Timothy: “I have been reminded of your

sincere faith, which first lived in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice and, I am

persuaded, now lives in you also” (2 Timothy 1:5, NIV). Faith transmitted through personal

relationship across generations was the pattern — and M’Cheyne worked to be that kind of

transmitter to the young of Dundee.

His illness in 1838 — which removed him from his congregation for almost a year and which he

described with anguish in his diary — was one of the most formative pastoral experiences of his

life. In the weakness of that year he came to understand in his body what he had previously

understood only in his theology: that the power of ministry did not originate in human strength,

and that a weak minister trusting in a strong God could accomplish more than a vigorous

minister trusting in himself.

He found in Paul’s experience the language for his own: “But he said to me, ‘My grace is

sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.’ Therefore I will boast all the more

gladly about my weaknesses, so that Christ’s power may rest on me” (2 Corinthians 12:9, NIV).

The greatest revival in St. Peter’s history occurred while M’Cheyne was absent — led by

William C. Burns during his convalescence. He received this news with humble joy,

understanding it as a confirmation that the work had never been his to begin with.

M’Cheyne died at twenty-nine. He left behind him a transformed congregation, a body of hymns,

a pattern of personal devotion that has shaped ministers across the world, and a famous Bible-

reading plan that his friend Andrew Bonar published and which is still in use today — carrying

readers through the whole Bible in a year, the Old Testament once and the New Testament twice.

He had planted in seven years what many ministries do not plant in fifty. He embodied Peter’s

vision of what the pastoral life produces: “But you are a chosen people, a royal priesthood, a

holy nation, God’s special possession, that you may declare the praises of him who called you

out of darkness into his wonderful light” (1 Peter 2:9, NIV). He had declared those praises. His

congregation declared them after him. And the declaration has not stopped.

A Prayer:

Holy Lord, remind us that the greatest thing we can do for our congregations is to

be holy ourselves. Where we have substituted activity for communion, busyness

for devotion, or technique for holiness, restore us. Make us like M’Cheyne — men

whose first hours belong to You, whose preaching is saturated with Christ, and

whose greatest ambition is not a large ministry but a holy one. And let us trust

that if the work is truly Yours, it will outlast us. Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 8
fields.body_html:
Who He Was

Aiden Wilson Tozer was born on April 21, 1897, on a farm in Newburg, Pennsylvania, and

converted to Christianity at age seventeen after hearing a street preacher in Akron, Ohio. He was

entirely self-educated in theology — he never attended seminary or college — and was ordained

as a minister in the Christian and Missionary Alliance in 1920. He served as pastor of Chicago’s

Southside Alliance Church from 1928 to 1959 — thirty-one years — and then at Avenue Road

Church in Toronto until his death in 1963 at sixty-six. He edited

“Alliance Life” magazine for many years and authored over forty books, the most celebrated of

which is

“The Pursuit of God” (1948), widely regarded as a Christian classic. He was known as a

“prophetic voice” in the evangelical church of his era — a man willing to say what others would

not, who saw the church’s compromises clearly and named them plainly.

His Vision for the Pastoral Calling

Tozer’s pastoral vision was that of the prophet-pastor: the man who does not merely manage a

religious institution but guards the spiritual integrity of the community he serves. He was deeply

concerned throughout his ministry that American evangelicalism was in danger of exchanging

the authentic pursuit of God for a comfortable religious experience that demanded nothing and

transformed no one. His books and sermons were acts of pastoral alarm — urgent, sometimes

sharp, always rooted in the conviction that the church of Jesus Christ was meant to be something

far more serious and far more glorious than what most of its members had settled for.

Tozer’s foundational pastoral text was also his personal biography: Paul’s great declaration in

Philippians that the consuming purpose of his life was not achievement but knowing: “I want to

know Christ — yes, to know the power of his resurrection and participation in his sufferings,

becoming like him in his death, and so, somehow, attaining to the resurrection from the dead”

(Philippians 3:10–11, NIV). The pastor’s first obligation was not to build a program, grow a

congregation, or produce publishable results but to know God. Everything else — preaching,

counseling, administration, evangelism — was downstream from that knowing.

The pastor who was not himself in genuine pursuit of God was dispensing borrowed capital, and

it would eventually run out.

He was prophetically alert to the encroachment of entertainment culture on the church’s worship.

As early as the 1950s, he identified a drift toward spectacle and away from genuine encounter

with God — a drift that substituted the thrill of religious experience for the substance of divine

encounter. He found the corrective in Jesus’ own declaration about the nature of true worship:

“Yet a time is coming and has now come when the true worshippers will worship the Father in

the Spirit and in truth, for they are the kind of worshippers the Father seeks. God is spirit, and his

worshippers must worship in the Spirit and in truth” (John 4:23–24, NIV). Spirit and truth: both,

together, inseparably. Entertainment could produce neither. Only the Spirit of God, working

through the truth of God’s Word, could produce the worship that God was actually seeking.

Tozer’s pastoral theology of the presence of God was rooted in his personal experience of

seeking God in the depths of contemplative prayer. He read widely in the Christian mystics —

Brother Lawrence, François Fénelon, Teresa of Ávila, Meister Eckhart — and found in them a

tradition of experiential knowledge of God that he believed the evangelical church had largely

abandoned. He held up Isaiah’s vision as the standard against which all genuine pastoral ministry

should be measured: “In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord, high and exalted, seated

on a throne; and the train of his robe filled the temple” (Isaiah 6:1, NIV). The pastor who had

seen the Lord as Isaiah had seen Him — in His holiness, His majesty, His consuming presence

— would never be satisfied with offering his congregation anything less. That vision was the

foundation of all genuine pastoral prophetic ministry.

He was equally concerned with what he identified as the “snare of popularity” in pastoral

ministry — the constant temptation to say what would be received well rather than what needed

to be said. Tozer read his culture carefully and was not deceived by numerical growth. He

understood Paul’s warning as a description of a perpetual pastoral danger, not merely a future

one: “For the time will come when people will not put up with sound doctrine. Instead, to suit

their own desires, they will gather around them a great number of teachers to say what their

itching ears want to hear. They will turn their ears away from the truth and turn aside to myths”

(2 Timothy 4:3–4, NIV).

The popular pastor, he warned, was often the most dangerous kind — not because his

congregations were large but because their size could give the false impression that everything

was well when the Spirit had long since moved on.

His personal pastoral simplicity was itself a teaching. He lived modestly, gave away his

royalties, refused to negotiate his convictions for the sake of institutional advancement, and spent

hours each week alone with God in a way that shaped and sustained everything he preached. He

had taken to heart the great command at the heart of the Shema: “Love the Lord your God with

all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind and with all your strength” (Mark

12:30, NIV). He pursued God with all four of these: with heart in devotion, with soul in

surrender, with mind in study, and with strength in discipline. He was not a perfect man. But he

was a man seriously in pursuit of a perfect God — and his pursuit called his congregation to the

same.

A Prayer:

Consuming God, deliver us from the pastoral safety of saying only what our

congregations want to hear. Give us Tozer’s courage to speak what the Spirit is

actually saying, even when it is uncomfortable. Renew in us the hunger to know

You — not merely to know about You — and let our pursuit of Your presence be

the invisible fire that warms everything we do in ministry. Where we have made

the church too easy, too comfortable, and too entertaining, restore the weight of

Your glory. Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 9
fields.body_html:
Counted the Cost

Who He Was

Dietrich Bonhoeffer was born on February 4, 1906, in Breslau, Germany, into a cultured, upper-

middle-class family of physicians, lawyers, and academics. He showed exceptional intellectual

gifts from childhood and completed his theological doctorate at the University of Berlin at the

age of twenty-one. After a formative year in New York at Union Theological Seminary and

Abyssinian Baptist Church in Harlem — where he encountered an African-American

Christianity of spiritual depth that he believed German Lutheranism had largely lost — he

returned to Germany to teach, preach, and eventually lead the illegal “Confessing Church”

seminary at Finkenwalde in defiance of the Nazi-controlled German church. He was arrested by

the Gestapo in April 1943, imprisoned for two years at Tegel Prison in Berlin, and executed by

hanging at Flossenbürg concentration camp on April 9, 1945 — three weeks before the end of

the war. His books, including “The Cost of Discipleship” and “Life Together,” have shaped

Christian thought across the world for eight decades.

His Vision for the Pastoral Calling

Bonhoeffer’s pastoral vision was born in a crisis. The German church of the 1930s was, with

notable exceptions, capitulating to National Socialism — allowing the state to dictate its

doctrine, purge its Jewish-Christian members, and press its ministry into the service of national

ideology. Bonhoeffer’s response was to insist, at increasing personal cost, that the church of

Jesus Christ owed its ultimate obedience not to the state but to its Lord, and that pastoral ministry

meant, in conditions of crisis, the willingness to suffer for that confession rather than

compromise it.

His foundational text for pastoral ministry was the account of Christ’s call in the synoptic

Gospels, which he unpacked at length in The Cost of Discipleship . The call of Jesus was absolute

and unconditional: it demanded a break with every prior loyalty, every prior security, every prior

identity. Bonhoeffer identified what he called “cheap grace” — the preaching of forgiveness

without repentance, baptism without church discipline, and the Lord’s Supper without confession

— as the most dangerous corruption facing the German church.

Against it he set the words of Jesus: “Whoever wants to be my disciple must deny themselves

and take up their cross and follow me. For whoever wants to save their life will lose it, but

whoever loses their life for me will find it” (Matthew 16:24–25, NIV). The pastor who preached

cheap grace was not offering his congregation a gentle version of Christianity; he was offering

them a counterfeit that would fail them at the very moment they most needed the real thing.

His Life Together — a short, luminous account of the community life at his Finkenwalde

seminary — was his pastoral theology of Christian community. He argued that the Christian

community must be built not on human affinity, shared temperament, or institutional

convenience but on the Word of God and on the person of Jesus Christ alone. Any community

built on human foundations would eventually collapse when human failings became too great to

bear. Only a community grounded in Christ could sustain genuine forgiveness, genuine honesty,

and genuine love. He found the pattern in Paul’s description of the body: “Just as a body, though

one, has many parts, but all its many parts form one body, so it is with Christ” (1 Corinthians

12:12, NIV). The pastor’s task was to build that body — not to create a collection of satisfied

individual consumers.

Bonhoeffer’s pastoral courage in the face of state pressure was one of the most searching

exhibitions of pastoral integrity in the twentieth century. He had the opportunity to remain in the

safety of America when the war began; instead he returned to Germany, knowing what it might

cost him. He believed that the pastor’s authority rested ultimately on his willingness to suffer for

the truth he proclaimed — that a shepherd who ran when the wolves came was not a shepherd at

all. He held to Hebrews’ charge to congregations: “Have confidence in your leaders and submit

to their authority, because they keep watch over you as those who must give an account. Do this

so that their work will be a joy, not a burden, for that would be of no benefit to you” (Hebrews

13:17, NIV). He gave his congregation reason for confidence by being the kind of shepherd

described here — one who kept watch at the cost of his own freedom and, ultimately, his life.

His prison writings, collected in Letters and Papers from Prison , display a pastoral sensibility

that continued to function even in conditions designed to destroy it. He wrote letters of genuine

spiritual direction to family and friends from his cell. He led worship services for fellow

prisoners and guards. He found in Paul’s prison letters — Philippians, Colossians, Ephesians —

not merely consolation but a model of pastoral ministry conducted from within the most

constraining circumstances imaginable. He had absorbed what Paul testified: “I can do all this

through him who gives me strength” (Philippians 4:13, NIV). The all things he could do through

Christ included dying well, which he did — according to the camp physician who witnessed his

execution — with composure and serenity that astonished even the guards.

His legacy is the legacy of the pastor who refused to separate theological conviction from ethical

action, who understood that the church’s silence in the face of injustice was itself a pastoral

failure, and who paid for this understanding with his life. He had preached Amos and Micah with

great power; he died exemplifying what he had preached. He had taken Peter’s vision of the

pastoral calling with complete seriousness: “Be shepherds of God’s flock that is under your care,

watching over them — not because you must, but because you are willing, as God wants you to

be” (1 Peter 5:2, NIV). He was willing. He was willing to the end.

A Prayer:

Lord Jesus, who laid down Your life for Your sheep, make us shepherds willing to

do the same. Where the church is tempted to offer cheap grace, give us

Bonhoeffer’s courage to preach the cost of discipleship. Where the world’s

pressure pushes us toward comfortable silence, give us voices that cannot be

quieted. And where the pastoral calling leads us through its own valley of

shadows, sustain us with the certainty that You have walked it before us. Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 10
fields.body_html:
Healed Souls

Who He Was

David Martyn Lloyd-Jones was born on December 20, 1899, in Cardiff, Wales, the son of a dairy

farmer who later moved the family to London. He showed extraordinary academic gifts and

trained as a physician, becoming in his mid-twenties the junior assistant to Sir Thomas Horder,

physician to the royal family and the most distinguished clinician in England. He appeared

destined for the heights of British medicine. Instead, in 1927, he resigned his medical career,

took a dramatic cut in income, and became pastor of a small, struggling Congregational church

in Aberavon, South Wales — a working-class mining community. He served there for eleven

years before accepting the call to Westminster Chapel in London in 1938, where he preached for

the next thirty years to congregations of several thousand people. His Friday-night Bible studies

and his long expository sermon series — including thirteen years on Paul’s letter to the Romans

— produced a body of published sermons that remains among the most widely read in the

English-speaking world. He died in 1981 at eighty-one.

His Vision for the Pastoral Calling

Lloyd-Jones’ pastoral vision was shaped by his medical training in ways that he acknowledged

throughout his ministry. The physician’s method — careful diagnosis before prescription,

attention to underlying causes rather than surface symptoms, refusal to offer a remedy that

addressed only the presenting complaint while leaving the deeper disease untouched — was, he

believed, precisely the method required of the faithful pastor-preacher. The congregation that

was given comfort without diagnosis was like a patient sent away with pain medication when

what they needed was surgery. The pastor-physician’s first obligation was to the truth of the

condition, not to the comfort of the patient.

Lloyd-Jones’ deepest conviction about preaching — which he regarded as the primary pastoral

act — was that it was not merely the communication of information or even of doctrine but an

event in which God Himself spoke through His Word to the gathered congregation. He had a

theology of the preached Word as the living voice of God, grounded in Paul’s description of the

gospel’s reception in Thessalonica: “And we also thank God continually because, when you

received the word of God, which you heard from us, you accepted it not as a human word, but as

it actually is, the word of God, which is indeed at work in you who believe” (1 Thessalonians

2:13, NIV). The Word was at work — not the preacher, not the sermon, but the Word itself,

living and active in those who received it. The preacher’s task was to get out of the way of that

working and let the Word do what only the Word could do.

His great sermon series, particularly his exposition of Romans, was a sustained act of pastoral

care for the whole person. He believed that doctrinal preaching, properly done, was not the

opposite of pastoral warmth but its deepest expression — because the people who understood the

doctrines of grace, justification, and sanctification most clearly were the people best equipped to

endure suffering, resist temptation, and sustain faith under pressure. He grounded this in Paul’s

own statement of method: “For I am not ashamed of the gospel, because it is the power of God

that brings salvation to everyone who believes: first to the Jew, then to the Gentile. For in the

gospel the righteousness of God is revealed” (Romans 1:16–17, NIV). The gospel in its full

doctrinal richness was not a liability to be managed but a power to be released. His thirty years

of expository preaching were thirty years of releasing that power.

Lloyd-Jones was deeply concerned, like Tozer, with what he saw as the trivialization of Christian

worship in the mid-twentieth century. He believed that the church had progressively substituted

human activity for divine encounter — that prayer meetings had become planning meetings,

worship services had become performances, and evangelism had become salesmanship. He

called the church back to Acts’ description of the earliest community: “They devoted themselves

to the apostles’ teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to prayer. Everyone was

filled with awe at the many wonders and signs performed by the apostles” (Acts 2:42–43, NIV).

Awe was the missing ingredient. A church that had lost its awe before God had lost something

essential, and no amount of programming or activity would replace it.

He was equally insistent that the pastor must preach the whole counsel of God, including its most

demanding and uncomfortable dimensions. He found Paul’s Miletus address to the Ephesian

elders the most searching passage in the New Testament for any man in pastoral office: “For I

have not hesitated to proclaim to you the whole will of God. Keep watch over yourselves and all

the flock of which the Holy Spirit has made you overseers. Be shepherds of the church of God,

which he bought with his own blood” (Acts 20:27–28, NIV).

The whole will of God: not a curated selection, not the pleasant portions, not the parts that would

generate a positive response, but everything — preached with the full authority of a man who

understood that the price paid for these souls was the blood of the Son of God.

Lloyd-Jones’ pastoral life at Westminster Chapel was one of sustained, unhurried, deep

engagement with his congregation through preaching, personal counseling, and prayer. He was

often described by those who knew him as a man whose presence carried a quality of spiritual

weight — not severity, but gravity, the gravity of a man who lived before God and knew it. He

had absorbed what the author of Hebrews commanded: “Therefore, since we are surrounded by

such a great cloud of witnesses, let us throw off everything that hinders and the sin that so easily

entangles. And let us run with perseverance the race marked out for us, fixing our eyes on Jesus,

the pioneer and perfecter of faith” (Hebrews 12:1–2, NIV). He ran with perseverance. He fixed

his eyes on Jesus. He finished the race. And the congregation he left behind was richer for every

year he had served them.

A Prayer:

Lord of the Word and the Spirit, make us pastors who are not ashamed of the full

gospel and who refuse to offer our congregations comfortable substitutes for the

real thing. Give us Lloyd-Jones’ patience for the long work of expository

preaching, his diagnostic eye to see what our people truly need, and his holy

gravity — the weight of a man who knows he stands between the living Word and

its dying hearers. May our ministries be measured not by size but by faithfulness

to the whole will of God. Amen.

Conclusion: The Chief Shepherd Still Calls

You have now spent time with ten men who understood the pastoral calling with a seriousness

that rebukes every comfortable version of ministry that has arisen since their day. Chrysostom

sold the bishop’s palace and went to his death rather than flatter the powerful. Gregory governed

the Western church with the title “Servant of servants.” George Herbert transformed his small

parish in three years and died before he could see the harvest. Richard Baxter visited every

family in Kidderminster and watched a town become a congregation. Jonathan Edwards

preached the whole counsel of God to his people for twenty-three years and was dismissed for

doing so with integrity. John Newton spent a lifetime distributing the grace that had, against all

reason, found him. Robert Murray M’Cheyne poured out a holy ministry in seven years and died

at twenty-nine. A.W. Tozer spent thirty-one years in one Chicago church refusing to preach what

the age wanted to hear. Dietrich Bonhoeffer returned from safety into danger, built a community

of genuine discipleship, and died with serenity on the gallows. Martyn Lloyd-Jones preached the

whole letter to the Romans over thirteen years and trusted the Word to do what only the Word

could do.

What do these ten men call us to? They call us, first and above all, to seriousness about the

pastoral office. The care of souls is not a profession to be managed or a career to be advanced. It

is a calling to be discharged, at whatever personal cost, with faithfulness to the One who issued

it. The flock does not belong to the pastor; it was bought with blood that is not his, entrusted to

him by a Shepherd whose standards are those of a Father who gave His Son for each individual

sheep. To handle that responsibility carelessly is an act of theological negligence that these ten

men would not recognize as pastoral ministry at all.

They also call us to the comfort of a promise. The Chief Shepherd is still present. The same God

who equipped Chrysostom to face exile, who gave Gregory wisdom to care for eight hundred

different kinds of people, who sustained M’Cheyne in illness, who walked with Bonhoeffer into

the darkness of Flossenbürg — that God is the God who calls every pastor today and promises to

equip every person He calls. The author of Hebrews expresses it with breathtaking completeness:

“Now may the God of peace, who through the blood of the eternal covenant brought back from

the dead our Lord Jesus, that great Shepherd of the sheep, equip you with everything good for

doing his will, and may he work in us what is pleasing to him, through Jesus Christ, to whom be

glory for ever and ever” (Hebrews 13:20–21, NIV). The great Shepherd of the sheep is present.

He is equipping. He is working. The pastoral calling is not a solo venture between a man and his

congregation; it is a collaboration between a human under-shepherd and the divine Chief

Shepherd, who never sleeps, never abandons His flock, and never runs out of the grace His

servants need.

Perhaps you are reading this book as a pastor who is exhausted. The work is long, the fruit is

sometimes invisible, and the weight of the souls in your care presses on you in ways that others

around you cannot fully understand. The ten men in this book knew that weight. They did not

carry it by being extraordinary; they carried it by returning repeatedly to the One who had called

them to carry it, distributing it into hands strong enough to bear it. They prayed, they studied,

they stayed, and they trusted.

Perhaps you are reading this as someone who is not yet in pastoral office but who feels the first

stirrings of a call. The same Shepherd who called these ten is still calling. He is still looking for

men and women who will receive His flock with reverence, tend it with patience, guard it with

courage, and return it to Him at the last with the words “Here are the ones You gave me, and I

have not lost one of them.” That is the pastoral ambition worth having.

The call has not changed. The flock still needs feeding, protecting, and leading. The wolves are

still real. The wandering sheep are still wandering. And the Chief Shepherd is still speaking the

same commission He has spoken in every generation: “Take care of my sheep” (John 21:16,

NIV). Three words. Enough for a lifetime. The ten men in this book gave their lifetimes to it.

May we do the same.

“I will give you shepherds after my own heart, who will lead you with knowledge and

understanding.”

— Jeremiah 3:15 (NIV)

Scripture Appendix: God’s Word on the Pastoral

Calling

The following scriptures on pastoral ministry and shepherding are cited throughout this book. All

quotations are from the New International Version (NIV) unless otherwise indicated.

Introduction

Isaiah 40:11 — “He tends his flock like a shepherd: He gathers the lambs in his arms and

carries them close to his heart; he gently leads those that have young.”

Ezekiel 34:2–4 — “Woe to you shepherds of Israel who only take care of yourselves! Should

not shepherds take care of the flock? You eat the curds, clothe yourselves with the wool and

slaughter the choice animals, but you do not take care of the flock. You have not

strengthened the weak or healed the sick or bound up the injured. You have not brought back

the strays or searched for the lost.”

Acts 20:28 — “Keep watch over yourselves and all the flock of which the Holy Spirit has

made you overseers. Be shepherds of the church of God, which he bought with his own

blood.”

1 Peter 5:2–4 — “Be shepherds of God’s flock that is under your care, watching over them

— not because you must, but because you are willing, as God wants you to be; not pursuing

dishonest gain, but eager to serve; not lording it over those entrusted to you, but being

examples to the flock. And when the Chief Shepherd appears, you will receive the crown of

glory that will never fade away.”

fields.title: Chapter 1
fields.body_html:
John 10:11–12 — “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the

sheep. The hired hand is not the shepherd and does not own the sheep. So when he sees the

wolf coming, he abandons the sheep and runs away.”

2 Timothy 4:2 — “Preach the word; be prepared in season and out of season; correct,

rebuke and encourage — with great patience and careful instruction.”

Galatians 3:28 — “There is neither Jew nor Gentile, neither slave nor free, nor is there

male and female, for you are all one in Christ Jesus.”

2 Timothy 4:3 — “For the time will come when people will not put up with sound doctrine.

Instead, to suit their own desires, they will gather around them a great number of teachers to

say what their itching ears want to hear.”

Philippians 4:11 — “I have learned to be content whatever the circumstances.”

fields.title: Chapter 2
fields.body_html:
Ezekiel 34:16 — “I will search for the lost and bring back the strays. I will bind up the

injured and strengthen the weak, but the sleek and the strong I will destroy. I will shepherd

the flock with justice.”

1 Corinthians 9:22 — “To the weak I became weak, to win the weak. I have become all

things to all people so that by all possible means I might save some.”
