after the “pattern shown to Moses in the Mount” (Exodus 25:9, 40) and that therefore it was itself a

prophecy and an exposition of the truth of God. It was not mere architecture. It was the Word of

God done into wood, gold, silver, brass, cloth, skin, etc. And Bezaleel needed as much special

inspiration to reveal the truth in wood, gold, silver, brass, etc., as the apostle or prophet needs it to

reveal the Word of God with pen and ink on parchment. There is much reasoning these days about

inspiration that appears at first sight very learned, but that will not bear much rigid analysis with

the exact statements of the Word of God. There is nothing in the Bible more inspired than the

tabernacle, and if the Destructive Critics would study it more, they would give up their ingenious

but weak theories as to the composite structure of the Pentateuch.

2. Truth hidden from man for ages and which they had not discovered and could not discover by

the unaided processes of human reasoning, has been revealed to apostles and prophets in the

Spirit. We read in Ephesians 3:3- 5, “ By revelation, as I have written briefly. When you read this,

you can perceive my insight into the mystery of Christ, which was not made known to the sons of

men in other generations as it has now been revealed to his holy apostles and prophets by the

Spirit. ” The Bible contains truth that men had neve r discovered before the Bible stated it. It

contains truth that men never could have discovered if left to themselves.

Our heavenly Father, in great grace, has revealed this truth to us, His children, through His

servants, the apostles and the prophets . The Holy Spirit is the agent of this revelation. Many tell us

today that we should test the statements of Scripture by the conclusions of human reasoning or by

the “Christian consciousness.” The foolishness of all this is evident when we bear in mind that t he

revelation of God exceeds human reasoning, and that any consciousness that is not the product of

the study and absorption of Bible truth is not a Christian consciousness. The fact that the Bible

contains truth that man has never discovered is stated in the Scriptures, but we know it also as a

matter of fact.

There is no one of the most distinctive and precious doctrines taught in the Bible that men have

ever discovered apart from the Bible. If our consciousness differs from the statements of this

Book, which is so plainly God's Book, it is not yet fully Christian and the thing to do is not to try

to pull God's revelation down to the level of our consciousness but to tone our consciousness up to

the level of God's Word.

3. The revelation made to the prophets was independent of their thinking. It was made to them by

the Spirit of Christ, which was in them. And it was a subject of inquiry to their mind as to its

meaning. It was not their thought, but His. We read in 1 Peter 1:10- 12, “Concerning this salvatio n,

the prophets who prophesied about the grace that was to be yours searched and inquired carefully,

inquiring what person or time the Spirit of Christ in them was indicating when he predicted the

sufferings of Christ and the subsequent glories. It was revealed to them that they were serving not

themselves but you, in the things that have now been announced to you through those who

preached the good news to you by the Holy Spirit sent from heaven, things into which angels long

to look. ” These words make it clear that a Person in the prophets, and independent of the prophets,

and that Person is the Holy Spirit, revealed truth which was independent of their thinking, which

they did not altogether understand themselves, and regarding which they needed to make diligent

search and study. Another Person than themselves was thinking and speaking, and they were

seeking to understand what He said.

4. No prophet's utterance was of the prophet's own will, but he spoke from God, and the prophet was

carried along in his utterance by the Holy Spirit. We read in 2 Peter 1:21, “For no prophecy was ever

produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.”

Then, the prophet was simply an instrument in the hands of another, as the Spirit of God carried him

along, so he spoke.

5. It was the Holy Spirit who spoke in the prophetic utterances. It was His word that was upon the

prophet's tongue. We read in Hebrews 3:7, “Therefore, as the Holy Spirit says, 'Today, if you hear his

voice.” Again, we read in Hebrews 10:15- 16, “And the Holy Spirit also bears witness to us; for after

saying, 'this is the covenant that I will make with them after those days, declares the Lord: I will put my

laws on their hearts, and write them on their minds.”

We read again in Acts 28:25, “And disagreeing among themselves, they departed after Paul had made

one statement: ' The Holy Spirit was right in saying to your fathers through Isaiah the prophet, etc.’ ”

Still, we read in 2 Samuel 23:2, “The Spirit of the Lord speaks by me; his word is on my tongue.” In

these passages, we are told that it was the Holy Spirit who was the speaker in the prophetic utterances

and that it was His word, not theirs, that was upon the prophet's tongue. The prophet was simply the

mouth by which the Holy Spirit spoke. As a man, that is except as the Spirit taught him and used him,

the prophet might be as weak as other men are but when the Spirit was upon him and he was taken up

and carried along by the Holy Spirit, he was perfect in his teachings; for his teachings in that case were

not his own, but the teachings of the Holy Spirit.

When thus carried along by the Holy Spirit, it was God who was speaking and not the prophet. For

example, there can be little doubt that Paul had many mistaken beliefs about many things, but when he

taught as an Apostle in the Spirit's power, he was perfect, or rather the Spirit, who taught through him,

was faultless and the consequent teaching was perfect as God Himself. We do well, therefore, to

carefully distinguish what Paul may have thought as a man and what he did teach as an Apostle.

In the Bible, we have the record of what he taught as an Apostle. Some think that in 1 Corinthians 7:6,

25, “Now as a concession, not a command, I say this ... but I gi ve my judgment as one who by the

Lord's mercy is trustworthy,” Paul admits that he was not sure in this case that he had the word of the

Lord. If this is the true interpretation of the passage (which is more than doubtful), we see how careful

Paul was when he was unsure to note the fact, and this gives us additional certainty in all other passages.

It is sometimes said that Paul taught in his early ministry that the Lord would return during his lifetime,

and that in this he was mistaken. But Paul never taught anywhere that the Lord would return in his

lifetime.

He indeed says in 1 Thessalonians 4:17, “ Then we who are alive, who are left, will be caught up together

with them in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we will always be with the Lord .” A s he was

still living when he wrote the words, he did not include himself with those who had already fallen asleep

in speaking of the Lord's return. But this is not to assert that he would remain alive until the Lord came.

At this period of his ministry, he entertained the hope that he might remain alive and consequently lived

in an attitude of expectancy, but the attitude of expectancy is the true attitude in all ages for each

believer. It is possible that Paul expected that he would be alive to the coming of the Lord, but if he

expected that, he did not teach it. The Holy Spirit kept him from this as from all other errors in his

teachings.

6. The Holy Spirit in the Apostle taught not only the thought (or “concept”) but the words in which the

thought was to be expressed. We read in 1 Corinthians 2:13, “And we impart this in words not taught by

human wisdom but taught by the Spirit, interpreting spiritual truths to those who are spiritual.” This

passage teaches that the words, as well as the thought, were chosen and taught by the Holy Spirit. This is

also a necessary conclusion from the fact that thought is conveyed from mind to mind by words, and it is

the words which express the thought, and if the words were imperfect, the thought expressed in these

words would necessarily be imperfect and, to that extent, be untrue.

Nothing could be clearer than Paul's statement, “ in words taught by the spirit .” The Holy Spirit has

Himself expected all the modern ingenious and wholly unbiblical and false theories regarding His work

in the Apostles. The more carefully and precisely we study the wording of the statements of this

wonderful Book, the more we will become convinced of the marvelous accuracy of the words used to

express the thought. Often, the solution to an apparent difficulty is found in studying the exact words

used. The accuracy, precision, and perfection of the exact words used are amazing.

To the superficial student, the doctrine of verbal inspiration may appear questionable or even absurd;

any regenerated and Spirit-taught man, who considers the words of the Scripture regularly, will become

convinced that the wisdom of God is in the very words, as well as in the thought which the words

endeavor to convey. A change of a word, letter, a tense, a case, or number, in many instances, would

land us into contradiction or untruth, but taking the words exactly as written, difficulties disappear and

truth shines forth. The Divine origin of nature shines forth more clearly in the use of a microscope as we

see the perfection of form and adaptation of means to the end of the minutest particles of matter.

Similarly, the Divine origin of the Bible shines forth more clearly under the microscope as we notice the

perfection with which the turn of a word reveals the absolute thought of God.

But someone may ask, “If the Holy Spirit is the author of the words of Scripture, how do we account

for variations in style and wording? How do we explain, for instance, that Paul always used Pauline

language and John Johannean language, et c.?” The answer to this is very simple. If we could not

account for this fact, it would have little weight against the explicit statement of God's Word with

anyone humble and wise enough to recognize that there are a great many things which he cannot

account for, which could be easily accounted for if he knew more. But these variations are easily

accounted for.

The Holy Spirit is quite wise enough and has quite facility enough in the use of language in revealing

truth to and through any given individual, to use words, phrases, and forms of expression and idioms

in that person's vocabulary and forms of thought, and to make use of that person's uniqueness. Indeed,

it is a mark of the Divine wisdom of this Book that the same truth is expressed with absolute accuracy

in such widely variant forms of expression.

7. The utterances of the Apostles and the prophets were the word of God. When we read these words, we

are not listening to the voice of man, but to the voice of God. We read in Mark 7:13, “thus making voi d

the word of God by your tradition that you have handed down. And many such things you do.” Jesus

had been setting the law given through Moses over against the legalistic traditions, and in doing this, He

says in this passage that the law given through Mo ses was “ the word of God .” In 2 Samuel 23:2, we

read, “The Spirit of the Lord speaks by me; these words are on my tongue.” Here again , we are told that

the utterance of God's prophet was the word of God. Similarly God says in1 Thessalonians 2:13 “And

we also thank God constantly for this, that when you received the word of God, which you heard from

us, you accepted it not as the word of men but as what it is, the word of God, which is at work in you

believers.” Here , Paul declares that the word which he spoke, taught by the Spirit of God, was the very

word of God .

fields.title: Chapter 22. The Work Of The Holy Spirit In Jesus Christ
fields.body_html:
Jesus Christ is the perfect example of the Holy Spirit’s complete work in a person’s life. He was

conceived, empowered, led, taught, and even raised from the dead by the Holy Spirit, accomplishing His

ministry through the Spirit's power. This same Spirit is available to believers today for living

victoriously, serving God, and overcoming sin.

Jesus Christ Himself is the one perfect manifestation in history of the complete work of the Holy

Spirit in man.

1. Jesus Christ was begotten of the Holy Spirit. We read in Luke 1:35. “And the angel answered her,

'The Holy Spirit will come upon you, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you; therefore

the child to be born will be called holy the Son of God.” As we have already seen, in regeneration the

believer is begotten of God, but Jesus Christ was begotten of God in His original generation. He is the

only begotten Son of God (John 3:16). It was entirely by the Spirit's power working in Mary that the Son

of God was formed within her. The regenerated man has a physical nature received from his earthly

father and a new nature conveyed by God. Jesus Christ had only the one holy nature, that which in man

is called the new nature. Nevertheless, He was a real man as He had a human mother.

2. Jesus Christ led a holy and spotless life and offered Himself without spot to God through the working

of the Holy Spirit. We read in Hebrews 9:14, “How much more wi ll the blood of Christ, who through the

eternal Spirit offered himself without blemish to God, purify our conscience from dead works to serve

the living God.” Jesus Christ met and overcame temptations as other men may meet and overcome them,

in the power of the Holy Spirit. He was tempted and suffered through temptation (Hebrews 3:18), He

was tempted in all points like we are (Hebrews 4:15), but never once in any way did He yield to

temptation. He was tempted entirely apart from sin, but He won His victories in a way that is open for

all of us to win victory, in the power of the Holy Spirit.

3. Jesus Christ was anointed and fitted for service by the Holy Spirit. We read in Acts 10:38, “How God

anointed Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. He went about doing good and healing

all who were oppressed by the devil, for God was with him.” In a prophetic vision of the coming

Messiah in the Old Testament we read in Isaiah 61:1 “ The Spirit of the Lord God is upon me, because

the Lord has anointed me to bring good news to the poor; he has sent me to bind up the

brokenhearted, to proclaim liberty to the captives, and the opening of the prison to those who are

bound ” In Luke's record of the earthly life of our Lord in Luke 4:14, we read “And Jesus returned in the

power of the Spirit to Galilee, and a report about him went out through all the surrounding country.”

Similarly, Jesus said of Himself when speaking in the synagogue in Nazareth, “ The Spirit of the Lord is

upon me, because he has anointed me to proclaim good news to the poor. He has sent me to proclaim

liberty to the captives and recovery of sight to the blind, to set at liberty those who are oppressed, to

proclaim the year of the Lord's favor. ” (Luke 4:18 -19.). All these passages contain the one lesson that it

was by the special anointing with the Holy Spirit that Jesus Christ was qualified for the service to which

God had called Him. As He stood in the Jordan after His baptism, “The Holy Ghost descended in a

bodily shape like a dove upon H im,” and it was then and there that He was anointed with the Holy

Spirit, baptized with the Holy Spirit, and equipped for the service that lay before Him. Jesus Christ

received His equipment for service in the same way that we receive ours, by a definite baptism with the

Holy Spirit.

4. Jesus Christ was led by the Holy Spirit in His movements here upon earth. We read in Luke 4:1,

“And Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from Jordan and was led by the Spirit in the

wilderness.” Living as a man here upon earth and setting an example for us, each step of His life

was under the Holy Spirit's guidance.

5. Jesus Christ was taught by the Spirit who rested upon Him. The Spirit of God was the source of

His wisdom in the days of His flesh. In the Old Testament prophecy of the coming Messiah we

read in Isaiah 11:2- 3, “ And the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him, the Spirit of wisdom and

understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, the Spirit of knowledge and the fear of the Lord

And his delight shall be in the fear of the Lord. He shall not judge by what his eyes see, or decide

disputes by what his ears hear .” Further on in Isaiah 42:1, we read, “Behold my servant, whom I

uphold, my chosen, in whom my soul delights; I have put my Spirit upon him; he will bring forth

justice to the nations. Etc .” Matthew tells us in Matthew 12:17 -18 that this prophecy was fulfilled

in Jesus of Nazareth.

6. The Holy Spirit abode upon Jesus in all His fullness, and the words He spoke as a result were

the very words of God. We read in John 3:34, “For he whom God has sent utters the words of God,

for he gives the Spirit without measure .”

7. After His resurrection, Jesus Christ gave commandments unto His Apostles whom He had

chosen through the Holy Spirit. We read in Acts 1:2, “ Until the day when he was taken up, after he

had given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he had chosen .” This relates to

the time after His resurrection, and so we see Jesus still working in the power of the Holy Spirit

even after His resurrection from the dead.

8. Jesus Christ performed His miracles on earth in the power of the Holy Spirit. In Matthew 12:28,

we read, “But if it is by the Spirit of God that I cast out demons” It is through the Spirit that

miracle working power was given to some in the church after our Lord departed from this earth (1

Corinthians 12:9-10), and in the power of the same Spirit, Jesus Christ performed His miracles.

9. It was by the power of the Holy Spirit that Jesus Christ was raised from the dead. We read in

Romans 8:11, “If the Spirit of him who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised

Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells

in you.” The same Spirit who is to quicken our mortal bodi es and is to raise us in some future day

raised Jesus. Several things are evident from this study of the work of the Holy Spirit in Jesus

Christ: First of all, we see the completeness of His humanity. He lived and He thought, He

worked, He taught, He conquered sin and won victories for God in the power of that very same

Spirit whom it is our privilege also to have.

In the second place, we see our utter dependence upon the Holy Spirit. If it was in the power of the Holy

Spirit that Jesus Christ, the only begotten Son of God, lived and worked, achieved and triumphed, how

much more dependent are we upon Him at every turn of life and in every phase of service and every

experience of conflict with Satan and sin?

The third thing that is evident is the amazing world of privilege, blessing, and victory that is open to us.

The same Spirit by which Jesus was originally begotten is at our disposal for us to be begotten again of

Him. The same Spirit by which Jesus offered Himself without spot to God is at our disposal that we may

also offer ourselves without spot to Him. The same Spirit by which Jesus was anointed for service is at

our disposal that we may be anointed for service. The same Spirit who led Jesus Christ in His

movements on earth is ready to lead us today. The same Spirit who taught Jesus and imparted to Him

wisdom and understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, and the fear of the Lord is here to teach us.

Jesus Christ is our pattern (1 John 2:6), “the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29). Whatever

He realized through the Holy Spirit is for us to realize today.

THE END

fields.title: Chapter 1
fields.body_html:
Created to Lead

The Biblical Foundation of Male Spiritual Leadership

"The Lord God took the man and put him in the Garden of Eden to work it and

take care of it. And the Lord God commanded the man, 'You are free to eat from

any tree in the garden; but you must not eat from the tree of the knowledge of

good and evil, for when you eat from it you will certainly die.'"

— Genesis 2:15–17

To understand what God asks of a man, we must go back to the beginning. Before polygamy was

introduced by Lamech in Genesis 4, before the Fall, before sin entered the human story, God

designed a world, and He designed a man to lead it.

Notice how the Bible tells the story. In Genesis 1, male and female are created together on the

same day, both in the image of God, both given dominion over the earth. This is our foundation: a

man and a woman are equal in dignity, equal in value, equal in their bearing of God's image. No

husband should ever treat his wife as less than himself. No father should ever treat his daughters

as less than his sons. In the image of God, we are the same.

But in Genesis 2, God gives us a closer look at how He arranged the first family, and here we see

something important. God formed Adam first. He placed Adam in the garden. He gave the

command about the tree to Adam, before Eve was even created. He gave Adam the work of naming

the animals. Then He said, "It is not good for the man to be alone," and He made Eve from Adam's

side — not from his head to rule over him, not from his feet to be trampled, but from his side to

walk beside him.

From this order, the apostle Paul draws a conclusion in the New Testament. Writing to Timothy,

he says, "For Adam was formed first, then Eve" (1 Timothy 2:13). Paul is teaching that God's

design for male leadership in the home and church is rooted not in culture, not in sin, not in who

is bigger or stronger, but in creation itself. Before the Fall, God had already given the man a

particular responsibility.

And what was that responsibility? The text is clear. Adam was placed in the garden "to work it

and take care of it" (Genesis 2:15). The Hebrew word for "take care of" (shamar) means to guard,

to keep, to protect. Adam was to be a worker and a watchman. He was to cultivate and to protect.

This is still the calling of every man — to build up, and to guard.

Now watch carefully what happened in Genesis 3. The serpent came to Eve. She listened. She took

the fruit. She ate. And then the Bible says something that many men have never noticed: "She also

gave some to her husband, who was with her, and he ate it" (Genesis 3:6).

Who was with her? Adam. Where was he when his wife was being deceived by the serpent?

Standing right there. Doing what? Nothing. Saying nothing. Leading nothing. Protecting nothing.

He was silent when he should have spoken. He was passive when he should have acted. He was a

coward when he should have been a man.

Brothers, this is the first sin of masculine leadership, and it is still our most common failure. Not

that we are too aggressive, but that we are too passive. Not that we lead too much, but that we lead

too little. Our wives are being deceived by the lies of this age, and we are standing next to them

saying nothing. Our children are being discipled by social media, bad friends, and worse teachers,

and we are sitting on the sofa scrolling our phones. Our churches are being weakened by

compromise, and we are silent in the pew.

And then notice what Adam did when God confronted him. He blamed his wife. "The woman you

put here with me — she gave me some fruit from the tree" (Genesis 3:12). He even blamed God.

A passive man becomes a blaming man. He will not take responsibility for his home, for his church,

for his sin. He points his finger at his wife, at his boss, at the government, at the missionaries, at

anyone but himself.

But observe this closely. When God came looking in the garden, whom did He call? "The Lord

God called to the man, 'Where are you?'" (Genesis 3:9). God did not call Eve first, even though

Eve sinned first. God called Adam. Why? Because Adam was the head. Adam was the one who

had been given the command. Adam was responsible. In the same way, when judgment came on

the human race, Paul tells us it came "through one man" — through Adam, not through Eve

(Romans 5:12). The woman sinned first, but the man was held accountable.

This is sobering for us, brothers. God holds men accountable for what happens in their homes,

their churches, their communities. We cannot escape it by blaming our wives. We cannot escape

it by blaming our culture. We cannot escape it by blaming our fathers who did not teach us. The

Lord is asking you, today, "Where are you?"

But thanks be to God, the story of Adam is not the last word. The Bible tells us of a second Adam

— the Lord Jesus Christ. Where the first Adam failed, the last Adam succeeded (1 Corinthians

15:45). Where the first Adam was silent, Christ spoke truth. Where the first Adam hid, Christ

stepped forward. Where the first Adam took from his bride and ruined her, Christ gave Himself

for His Bride to save her. Where the first Adam brought death, Christ brought life.

Every man who trusts in Jesus is united to the second Adam. Your failure in leadership is not the

end of your story. The grace of Christ covers your cowardice, and the Spirit of Christ gives you

power to lead. You do not lead in your own strength. You lead in His.

So hear the call, brother. God created you to lead — not to dominate, not to oppress, not to boss

your wife around, not to beat your children — but to cultivate and to guard. To build up your

family spiritually. To watch over your home. To go to God first before the enemy comes to your

wife. To take responsibility when things go wrong. To model Christ.

You were created for this. Will you rise up?

A Prayer

Father, I confess that I have been more like the first Adam than the second. I have

been silent when I should have spoken. I have been passive when I should have led.

I have blamed others for what You have given me to carry. Forgive me, Lord. Wash

me in the blood of Jesus, the second Adam, who succeeded where I failed. Fill me

with Your Holy Spirit, that I may lead my home, my church, and my community as

You have called me. Teach me to cultivate what You have entrusted to me. Teach

me to guard it. And when You come looking for me, may I no longer be found hiding.

Here I am, Lord — send me. In the name of Jesus Christ, Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 2
fields.body_html:
The Inner Man

Character Before Charisma

"The Lord does not look at the things people look at. People look at the outward

appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart."

— 1 Samuel 16:7

When the prophet Samuel went to the house of Jesse to anoint a new king over Israel, he saw Eliab,

the oldest son — tall, strong, handsome, the kind of man we would quickly call a leader. Samuel

said to himself, "Surely the Lord's anointed stands here before the Lord." But God corrected him.

"Do not consider his appearance or his height, for I have rejected him. The Lord does not look at

the things people look at. People look at the outward appearance, but the Lord looks at the heart"

(1 Samuel 16:6–7).

Brother, this is where true spiritual leadership begins: not in your arms, not in your wallet, not in

your title, not in your degree, not in your clan, but in your heart. God will not use a man whose

heart is rotten, no matter how impressive he looks on the outside. And God will use a man whose

heart is right, no matter how unimpressive he looks on the outside.

We live in an age that worships charisma. The loud preacher draws the crowd. The flashy

businessman is envied. The man with the biggest car is respected. But God is not impressed with

any of this. God is looking for character.

What is character? Character is who you are when no one is watching. Character is what you do

when the lights are off, when you are alone in a hotel room in a different city, when your phone is

in your hand and no one will ever know, when the money is on the table and the accountant has

left the room. Character is the fruit of the Spirit — love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness,

faithfulness, gentleness, self-control (Galatians 5:22–23) — grown slowly in the soil of your heart

over years of walking with Jesus.

The apostle Paul, when he listed the qualifications for an elder in the church, said almost nothing

about gifting and almost everything about character. Read 1 Timothy 3 slowly. An elder must be

"above reproach, faithful to his wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable, able to

teach, not given to drunkenness, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of money" (1

Timothy 3:2–3). Notice: able to teach appears only once in this long list. The rest is character. If

you cannot keep your temper at home, you are not qualified to lead anywhere else.

The same pattern appears in Titus 1, where Paul says an elder must be "blameless, faithful to his

wife, a man whose children believe and are not open to the charge of being wild and disobedient"

(Titus 1:6). God looks at how a man is doing as a husband and father before He considers him for

leadership in the church. Your home is your first ministry. If your character is not being formed

there, it is not being formed at all.

Consider the life of Archbishop Janani Luwum of Uganda. He was born in 1922 in Acholi, in the

north of our country. He was converted as a young schoolteacher and was deeply shaped by the

East African Revival. What made him great was not that he had a famous name or a powerful

position — both of those came later. What made him great was that for decades before he ever

stood before Idi Amin, he was walking with Jesus, confessing his sin, loving his wife Mary

Florence, and raising his children in the fear of the Lord. By the time Amin tried to intimidate him

in 1977, Luwum had the inner man of a lion. He said, "I can see the hand of God in this. Even if I

die, I will not be afraid." When his moment came, he did not flinch, because his heart had been

prepared long before in secret.

Charisma can carry you to the top. Only character can keep you there.

The apostle Peter understood this. In 2 Peter 1, he gives us a beautiful chain of virtues: "make

every effort to add to your faith goodness; and to goodness, knowledge; and to knowledge, self-

control; and to self-control, perseverance; and to perseverance, godliness; and to godliness, mutual

affection; and to mutual affection, love" (2 Peter 1:5–7). Notice the verb: "make every effort."

Character does not happen by accident. It is cultivated, like a garden, by daily labor in prayer, in

the Word, in confession, in obedience.

Augustine of Hippo, the great North African father of the Church, spent the first years of his adult

life chasing sinful pleasures, ambition, and worldly wisdom. He had brilliance, but he lacked

character. It was only when he met Christ in a garden in Milan, weeping and crying, "Take and

read, take and read," and opening his Bible to Romans 13, that the Lord began to form in him the

inner man that would later write the Confessions and The City of God and shape the Church for

centuries. Augustine is a reminder to every African man: your past does not disqualify you, but

your character must be rebuilt from the inside out.

Let me ask you some hard questions, brother. When you are alone on your phone, what do you

look at? When your wife disagrees with you, how do you respond? When a woman who is not

your wife smiles at you, what do you do with your eyes? When the bribe is offered, what do you

say? When your child disobeys, do you correct with patience or explode with rage? When the

offering plate comes around, do you give, or do you grip? When someone insults you, do you

return evil or bless?

These small moments, multiplied over years, are who you really are. These are the inner man. No

title from men can replace it. No amount of noisy religion can disguise it. God sees it. Your wife

sees it. Your children see it. And one day, the whole of heaven and earth will see it.

But here is the good news. You are not left alone to build your character. "God's divine power has

given us everything we need for a godly life through our knowledge of him who called us by his

own glory and goodness" (2 Peter 1:3). In Christ, you have everything you need. The Holy Spirit

lives in you. The Word of God is given to you. The Church of God surrounds you. The means of

grace are available to you. If your character is weak, it is not because God has withheld anything.

It is because you have not pressed into what He has already provided.

So do not be discouraged. Begin today. Begin with confession. Begin with the Word. Begin with

prayer. Begin in the secret place. And let God slowly, patiently, build in you a man whose outside

and inside match — a man whose wife trusts him, whose children honor him, whose church can

rely on him, and whose Savior can say, "Well done, good and faithful servant."

A Prayer

Father, You see what no one else sees. You know what no one else knows. You have

looked into my heart, and You have seen the truth about me. Where I am a

hypocrite, expose me. Where I am proud, humble me. Where I am lazy in my soul,

stir me up. Lord Jesus, You were tempted in every way as I am, yet You were without

sin. Form Your character in me by the power of Your Holy Spirit. Make my outside

and my inside the same. Make me a man of integrity — whole, undivided, true. Help

me to build my inner man in the secret place, so that when my moment comes, I will

not fall. In Your holy name I pray, amen.

fields.title: Chapter 3
fields.body_html:
The Man Who Prays

Power on His Knees

"Therefore I want the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands without

anger or disputing."

— 1 Timothy 2:8

There is one practice that has defined every great man of God in the Bible and every great man of

God in church history: he prayed. Not occasionally. Not desperately only in emergencies. Not

merely in public to be heard. He prayed — deeply, daily, privately, persistently.

Abraham prayed. When God told him He was about to destroy Sodom, Abraham stood before the

Lord and interceded for a city full of strangers (Genesis 18:22–33). Moses prayed. When Israel

made the golden calf and God threatened to destroy them, Moses lay on his face for forty days and

nights (Deuteronomy 9:18). David prayed. Read the Psalms — they are a man's prayer journal

soaked in tears, praise, confession, and faith. Daniel prayed. Three times a day, with his window

open toward Jerusalem, even when it cost him the lions' den (Daniel 6:10). Nehemiah prayed.

Before he spoke to the king, before he laid a single stone, he lifted his heart to God (Nehemiah

2:4).

And above them all, our Lord Jesus Christ prayed. The Son of God, perfect in every way, needing

nothing, rose before dawn to pray (Mark 1:35), went up into the mountains alone to pray (Luke

6:12), prayed all night before choosing the twelve apostles, prayed for Peter, prayed for His

disciples, prayed for you and me in John 17, and prayed in Gethsemane until His sweat became

like drops of blood. If the Son of God needed to pray, how can we — weak, sinful, foolish —

imagine we can lead without prayer?

A man who does not pray is not a spiritual leader, no matter what he calls himself. He may be a

good provider, a strong disciplinarian, a respected businessman. But if he is not on his knees before

God, he is leading his family into darkness while stumbling himself.

Paul's instruction to Timothy is striking. He says, "I want the men everywhere to pray, lifting up

holy hands without anger or disputing" (1 Timothy 2:8). Paul singles out men. Not because women

do not pray — they pray powerfully, and we know it — but because Paul is telling us that visible,

leading, holy-handed prayer in the worship of the church is the duty of men. And if we will not

pray publicly in the gathering of God's people, it is usually because we are not praying privately

in our own closets.

Let me speak directly to husbands and fathers now. Your wife is praying for you. Your mother has

been praying for you since before you were born. The women of your church are on their knees

for the men. They are carrying the spiritual weight of the home while we discuss politics and

football. This must change.

When was the last time you prayed with your wife? Not a quick prayer before food, but a real

prayer — holding her hand, confessing your sins, praising God, interceding for your children,

asking for His will to be done in your home? Peter warns husbands to treat their wives with

understanding, "so that nothing will hinder your prayers" (1 Peter 3:7). Think about that. How you

treat your wife can block your prayers from being heard. Many of our prayers have hit the ceiling

because there was unrepented sin against the woman in our own bed.

When was the last time you laid hands on your children and prayed a blessing over them? Jacob

blessed his sons before he died (Genesis 49). Jesus took children in His arms and blessed them

(Mark 10:16). A father's blessing is a powerful thing in Scripture. Do not withhold it. Lay hands

on your children at night, pray over them by name, speak God's favor over their lives. Many of our

sons and daughters have gone astray because a father's blessing was missing.

The East African Revival, which touched Rwanda, Uganda, Kenya, Burundi, and Tanzania in the

1930s and 40s, was fundamentally a prayer movement. Simeon Nsibambi of Uganda and Dr. Joe

Church, a missionary in Rwanda, would meet in a room in Kampala and pray for hours. Men

gathered in small huts at dawn to cry out to God, to confess their sins, to walk in the light with one

another. William Nagenda, who later became one of the greatest preachers of the revival, was a

man marked by prayer. Festo Kivengere — who would later preach the gospel from Uganda to

America and Europe — was a man of prayer. These were not professional clergymen at first. They

were ordinary Ugandan men who decided that they would not lead their families or their nation

without first falling on their knees. And from their prayers, a continent was shaken.

George Müller of Bristol, England, ran orphanages for thousands of children in the 1800s without

ever asking anyone for money. When the cupboards were empty and breakfast was about to be

served, he would gather the children and pray. Over and over, the food arrived — sometimes a

baker knocking at the door saying, "God woke me in the night and told me the orphans needed

bread," sometimes a milkman whose cart had broken down outside and who asked if they could

use the milk before it spoiled. Müller kept records of over fifty thousand specific answers to prayer

in his lifetime. He said, "The business of my life is to trust the Lord." Brother, if a man in England

could trust God like that, can you not trust Him for your small shop in Kampala, your farm in the

village, your job in Nairobi, your family in Dar es Salaam?

Let me give you a simple pattern for prayer as a husband and father. First, pray alone each morning.

Even fifteen minutes, before your phone comes on, before the radio goes on. Open your Bible,

read a Psalm, turn it into prayer, confess your sins, praise God, lay out your day. Second, pray with

your wife each night, or at least several times a week. Short is fine at the start. The point is to take

her hand and say, "Let us pray." Third, pray over each child by name, ideally at bedtime. Ask God

to save them, to keep them pure, to give them wisdom, to call them to serve Him. Fourth, pray

with your family at meals — more than just "bless this food," but true thanksgiving. Fifth, join a

praying community — in your church, with a few brothers, in a men's group. Do not try to be a

praying man alone.

Do not wait until you feel like it. Do not wait until you are holy enough. Do not wait until life

slows down. Begin now. Poorly is better than not at all. A stumbling, sincere prayer from a sinful

man is more precious to God than the smoothest speech from a hypocrite.

There is great power in a praying man. His wife walks through the day with a covering over her.

His children grow up with a spiritual inheritance. His business is touched by the hand of God. His

church is strengthened. His nation is moved. And on the day of judgment, he will not be ashamed,

because he will have walked with his God.

A Prayer

Father, teach me to pray. I confess I have prayed too little, too shallowly, too

selfishly. I have been quicker to scroll my phone than to seek Your face. Quicker to

complain to others than to cry out to You. Quicker to plan my day than to consecrate

it. Lord Jesus, You who prayed all night on the mountain, teach me. Holy Spirit,

who intercedes for us with groans, pray through me. Make me a man whose wife

can say, "My husband prays for me." Make me a father whose children know, "Papa

prays for us." Make me a brother in the church who can stand and lift holy hands.

And where revival is needed in my home, my village, my nation, let it begin on my

knees. In the mighty name of Jesus, amen.

fields.title: Chapter 4
fields.body_html:
Loving Her as Christ Loved the Church

The Husband's Calling

"Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave himself up

for her to make her holy, cleansing her by the washing with water through the

word."

— Ephesians 5:25–26

There is no higher standard for a husband in all the Bible than this: love your wife as Christ loved

the Church. And there is no clearer demonstration of that love than a cross.

Paul gives us this command in Ephesians 5, in a passage that has become controversial in our day

but is in fact one of the most beautiful pictures of marriage ever written. He says, "Wives, submit

yourselves to your own husbands as you do to the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife as

Christ is the head of the church." Many men stop reading there and puff out their chests. "Did you

hear that, woman? I am the head. You must submit." But Paul does not stop there, and neither

should we. He keeps writing. "Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave

himself up for her."

Brother, look at the model Paul gives us. The head of the wife is like Christ, the head of the Church.

And how does Christ lead His Church? By giving Himself up for her. By taking her sin on His

own body. By being crucified in her place. By washing her, not with power, but with sacrifice. By

speaking the Word of God to her gently, patiently, daily. By preparing her as a radiant bride,

without spot or wrinkle.

If this is the model, then "headship" has nothing to do with bossing your wife around. It has

everything to do with laying down your life for her. The husband is the head not as a dictator but

as a servant-leader. Not as a master but as a protector. Not as a man who takes but as a man who

gives, gives, and gives again until he has nothing left.

Let us be honest about our culture, brothers. In many parts of East Africa, we have inherited

practices that are not Christian, though they wear Christian clothes. The harshness some men show

toward their wives, the physical violence that is still too common, the silence about bride price that

turned the wife into a purchase, the expectation that a wife is a servant to fetch water and bear

children but not a partner to share life — these are not the gospel. They are not the way of Christ.

They are corruptions of a good creation, and they must be repented of.

The apostle Peter wrote, "Husbands, in the same way be considerate as you live with your wives,

and treat them with respect as the weaker partner and as heirs with you of the gracious gift of life,

so that nothing will hinder your prayers" (1 Peter 3:7). Three things shine here. First, live with her

— not leaving her alone while you drink with friends, not away from home for months, but with

her, sharing life. Second, be considerate — which in the Greek means "according to knowledge,"

meaning take time to know her heart, her fears, her joys, her body, her soul. Third, treat her with

respect. She is an heir with you of eternal life. She will be a queen in the kingdom of heaven. Treat

her now as you would treat a queen.

And do not forget that the ancient world Peter wrote to was harsher than ours. Wives could be

divorced for burning dinner. Husbands ruled like kings. Into this Peter brings the gentleness of

Christ. If the early Church could reform Roman marriage, the gospel can reform our marriages

too.

I want you to notice one more thing in Ephesians 5. Paul says Christ cleanses the Church "by the

washing with water through the word" (Ephesians 5:26). How does a husband participate in his

wife's sanctification? By bringing the Word of God to her. This is why a husband must be a man

of the Word. How will you wash your wife with Scripture if you do not know Scripture? How will

you speak life over her in her discouragement if you cannot open the Bible? How will you remind

her of the promises of God when she is fearful if the Bible is dusty on the shelf?

Martin Luther, the great German reformer, loved his wife Katharina deeply. He called her his

"morning star," his "dear rib," and he relied on her as a true partner. Luther wrote, "There is no

more lovely, friendly, and charming relationship, communion, or company than a good marriage."

He read Scripture with her. He prayed with her. He joked with her. He grieved with her when their

daughter Magdalene died. Luther the theologian was also Luther the husband, and the same gospel

he preached in the pulpit he lived in the kitchen. This is our call.

Let me speak even more practically. Husband, when was the last time you told your wife you love

her? Not assumed it. Not showed it through providing money. Said it, looked her in the eye, with

tenderness? When was the last time you apologized to her — not offered a defensive "sorry if you

were offended" but a true confession, "I was wrong, please forgive me"? When was the last time

you asked her about her fears, her hopes, her dreams, not about food or children or bills, but about

her heart?

Your wife is not your housemaid. She is your sister in Christ before she is your wife. She is going

to stand beside you in the resurrection. She is a fellow heir of the grace of life. Lead her toward

Jesus, not toward exhaustion. Serve her as Christ served the Church.

I know some of you reading this are thinking, "But you do not know my wife. She is difficult. She

does not respect me. She does not cook like my mother. She does not listen." Brother, Christ did

not wait for the Church to be lovely before He loved her. "While we were still sinners, Christ died

for us" (Romans 5:8). He loved us when we were His enemies. If He only loved those who deserved

it, none of us would be saved. So also, you are called to love your wife not because she deserves

it, but because Christ does. Your love for your wife is an act of worship to Jesus.

And to the young men who are not yet married, let me say this. Do not enter marriage lightly. Do

not marry a woman because she is beautiful. Beauty fades. Do not marry a woman because she is

rich. Riches fly. Do not marry a woman because your parents chose her for you without your

consent. Marry a woman who fears the Lord (Proverbs 31:30), whose character you have observed

over time, whom you can love as Christ loves the Church — for life. And before you take that

vow, ask yourself: am I ready to die for her? Because that is what the vow means.

Finally, let me remind you of the promise. When a husband loves his wife as Christ loved the

Church, something miraculous happens. The wife blooms. The home becomes peaceful. The

children feel secure. The church is strengthened. The watching world sees a picture of the gospel.

Your marriage is a stage on which the love of Jesus is displayed. Do not ruin the play. Love her

well.

A Prayer

Lord Jesus, You loved Your Bride the Church and gave Yourself up for her. You

washed her, cleansed her, spoke tenderly to her, and are preparing her for glory.

Forgive me for the ways I have failed to love my wife like You. Where I have been

harsh, soften my heart. Where I have been absent, bring me home. Where I have

been silent, give me words of life. Where I have exploited my authority, teach me

servant-leadership. Fill me with Your Spirit, that I may love my wife not as the

world loves but as You love — sacrificially, patiently, tenderly, for her

sanctification and Your glory. And make our marriage a living picture of the gospel

in a dark and watching world. In Your name I pray, Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 5
fields.body_html:
Raising Arrows

The Father's Sacred Duty

"Children are a heritage from the Lord, offspring a reward from him. Like arrows

in the hands of a warrior are children born in one's youth. Blessed is the man

whose quiver is full of them."

— Psalm 127:3–5

Of all the gifts God gives a man, few are greater than children. And of all the responsibilities God

gives a man, none is weightier than fatherhood.

The psalmist compares children to arrows in the hand of a warrior. Think carefully about that

picture. An arrow is not aimless. An arrow is sharpened, shaped, fitted, aimed, and released toward

a target. A warrior who throws arrows blindly is no warrior at all. A father who brings children

into the world but does not shape them, sharpen them, aim them at the glory of God is a warrior

with a quiver he cannot use.

Yet how many of our homes today are full of unformed arrows? Fathers have brought children

into the world and then abandoned their shaping to the mother, to the school, to the church, to the

television, to the streets. Our nations are overrun with young men who have never been fathered.

They know how to survive, but they do not know how to live. They know how to take, but they do

not know how to love. They have seen anger, but they have not seen tenderness. They have been

beaten, but they have not been blessed. And they grow up to be like the men who made them.

This cycle must be broken, and God has put the axe in your hand.

The foundational passage on fatherhood in the Bible is Deuteronomy 6:4–9. Every Jewish father

knew it by heart. Every Christian father should know it by heart too. "Hear, O Israel: The Lord our

God, the Lord is one. Love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with

all your strength. These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. Impress

them on your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road,

when you lie down and when you get up. Tie them as symbols on your hands and bind them on

your foreheads. Write them on the doorframes of your houses and on your gates."

Notice carefully, father. Before you can impress God's word on your children, it must be on your

own heart. A man cannot give what he does not have. If the Bible is not shaping you, it will not

shape your children through you. This is the first work of fatherhood — to be a man of the Word

yourself.

Then notice the times: when you sit at home, when you walk along the road, when you lie down,

when you get up. That is, all the time. Fatherhood is not a Sunday morning event. It is not

outsourced to the pastor. It is the quiet, daily, thousand-times-repeated work of teaching your

children who God is, why He made them, what He has said, and how they should live. In the

evening around the fire. In the morning at the breakfast table. On the boda-boda ride to school. In

the garden as you dig together. Everywhere, always, you are discipling them.

Paul writes to the Ephesians, "Fathers, do not exasperate your children; instead, bring them up in

the training and instruction of the Lord" (Ephesians 6:4). There are two sides to this. The negative

side: do not exasperate. Do not provoke them to anger by your harshness, your unfairness, your

absence, your favoritism, your drunkenness, your rage. Many fathers in our culture have

exasperated their children through physical and verbal abuse, and it is one of the chief reasons our

young people walk away from the church. They associate God the Father with their earthly father,

and if their earthly father was a terror, they run from God too. This must not be.

The positive side: bring them up in the training and instruction of the Lord. The word "training"

means discipline, shaping, molding — it is an active, intentional forming of character. The word

"instruction" means teaching, explanation, warning. A father must do both. He must teach them

and he must shape them. And he must do it "of the Lord" — not according to his own preferences

or his own frustrations, but according to what the Lord has commanded.

Discipline is part of love. "The Lord disciplines the one he loves, and he chastens everyone he

accepts as his son" (Hebrews 12:6). A father who does not discipline his children does not love

them. But discipline is not abuse. Biblical discipline is done in love, not in rage. It is done for the

child's good, not for the father's relief. It is followed by restoration, not by lingering bitterness. It

is always tied to teaching, so the child understands not just that he is being punished, but why his

behavior is wrong.

In our African culture, the cane has been used freely for generations. I will not debate every cultural

practice here, but I will say this: many of us crossed a line from biblical discipline into cruelty,

and our children have carried those scars into adulthood. Hear the Word of God: "Fathers, do not

embitter your children, or they will become discouraged" (Colossians 3:21). If your child is afraid

of you more than they love you, something is wrong.

Let me give you some practical aims for your children. Aim them at Christ. The first goal of

fatherhood is their salvation. Pray it over them every day. Teach them the gospel over and over.

Do not assume they are Christians just because they were born into a Christian home. Lead each

child to personal faith in Jesus.

Aim them with wisdom. Proverbs was written by a father, Solomon, for his son. Read Proverbs

together. Teach them about the choice between the way of the wise and the way of the fool,

between diligence and laziness, between purity and adultery, between the fear of the Lord and the

folly of the scoffer.

Aim them at usefulness. Teach them to work with their hands. Teach them to serve others. Teach

them to manage money. Teach them to be humble. Teach your sons how to treat women — in how

you treat their mother. Teach your daughters what a godly man looks like — in who you are. Your

life is the curriculum. Your words are secondary.

Aim them at the local church. Do not let them see Christianity as a family-only affair. Take them

to church every week. Introduce them to godly mentors. Let them see you serving, giving,

worshipping, submitting to other leaders. If they see that church is important to you, it will be

important to them.

Brother, consider the father in the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15). When his younger son

returned in shame and rags, the father ran to him, embraced him, kissed him, restored him. That is

the heart of God. And that is the heart a father must have. Sometimes our children will disappoint

us. Sometimes they will break our hearts. The call of a father is not to write them off, but to watch

the road with eyes full of hope, ready to run when they turn home.

Your children did not ask to be born. God gave them to you, and He will ask you one day what

you did with them. Not what you bought for them, but what you built into them. Not how many

you had, but what they became. Be a father worth having. Aim your arrows well. And one day, by

God's grace, your quiver will be full of arrows flying for the glory of God.

A Prayer

Heavenly Father, You are the Father from whom every family in heaven and on

earth takes its name. You have given me children as a heritage and a responsibility.

Forgive me for every time I have been too busy, too harsh, too distant, too angry,

too silent. Forgive me for exasperating them instead of shepherding them. Give me

the grace to disciple them — to read Your Word with them, to pray with them, to

correct them with love, to model Christ before them. Save my children, Lord. May

not one of them be lost. Use me as Your instrument to shape them into arrows that

will fly far and hit the target of Your glory. In the name of Jesus Christ, our elder

Brother, Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 6
fields.body_html:
Strength Under Control

Gentleness as a Mark of True Manhood

"Come to me, all you who are weary and burdened, and I will give you rest. Take

my yoke upon you and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart, and

you will find rest for your souls."

— Matthew 11:28–29

What kind of man is Jesus? The King of kings. The Lord of lords. The Lion of Judah. The One

who spoke galaxies into being. The One before whom every knee will bow. And how does He

describe Himself? "I am gentle and humble in heart."

This is astonishing, brother. The strongest being in the universe calls Himself gentle. The One with

all authority in heaven and on earth calls Himself humble. If Jesus is the perfect Man — and He is

— then the perfect man is gentle. Not weak. Not soft. Not a coward. But strong in such a way that

he does not need to prove it by crushing others.

We have a serious problem in our culture. Many men confuse manhood with harshness. They think

that to be respected, they must shout. To be obeyed, they must threaten. To be feared, they must

hit. They raise their voices at their wives, backhand their children, bark at their workers, and call

it "being a man." But this is not manhood. This is brokenness. It is a man out of control trying to

pretend he is in control.

Look again at Jesus. He cleared the temple with a whip (John 2:15). He rebuked demons and

silenced storms. He stared down Herod and called him "that fox" (Luke 13:32). He was not soft.

And yet the same Jesus took little children in His arms and blessed them. The same Jesus wept at

the tomb of Lazarus. The same Jesus knelt and washed His disciples' feet, including the feet of

Judas who would betray Him. The same Jesus said from the cross, "Father, forgive them, for they

do not know what they are doing" (Luke 23:34). Strength and gentleness were not enemies in Him.

They were friends.

Paul calls gentleness a fruit of the Spirit (Galatians 5:22–23). You cannot produce it yourself. You

can try to fake it for a while, but it will break under pressure. True gentleness is grown in a man

only by the Holy Spirit working in him over time. The more a man walks with Jesus, the gentler

he becomes. The more he sees his own sin and the depth of grace he has received, the less harsh

he is with others. A proud man is always harsh. A humble man is almost always gentle.

Moses is called "a very humble man, more humble than anyone else on the face of the earth"

(Numbers 12:3). This is the same Moses who led millions out of Egypt, who confronted Pharaoh,

who smashed the tablets, who judged Israel. He was no weakling. But he was humble. He led from

his knees more than from his shoulders. And God entrusted him with everything.

I want to speak honestly about something that grieves the heart of God in many of our homes:

domestic violence. Brother, if you have ever hit your wife, listen to me. That is not manhood. That

is not biblical headship. That is sin. The hand that God gave you to bless her, to work for her, to

protect her, you have used to wound her. The body that Christ has given as His own temple, you

have bruised. This is not a small matter. It is a sin against your wife, against God, and against the

picture of Christ and His Church that your marriage is supposed to display.

There is grace for you. But grace comes with repentance. You must confess it — to God, to her,

to your pastor, to a trusted brother in the church. You must submit to counsel and accountability.

If you are in a pattern of violence, you must get help now. Not tomorrow. Now. "An angry person

stirs up conflict, and a hot-tempered person commits many sins" (Proverbs 29:22). God will not

hold back His judgment from a man who harms the one he vowed to protect.

And fathers, hear me: the same applies to how you treat your children. The cane has its place

within biblical, measured correction, but many of our fathers have crossed far over that line.

Children who grow up afraid of their father's hand often struggle for years to know a gentle God.

They imagine that God the Father is like Papa — unpredictable, angry, a terror. What a lie we have

told them by our rage. Let us undo it by our gentleness from this day forward.

Think of Festo Kivengere, the great Ugandan evangelist. During the reign of terror under Idi Amin,

after Archbishop Janani Luwum was murdered, Kivengere fled to Kenya for his life. He later wrote

a book with a startling title: "I Love Idi Amin." Imagine that. A Ugandan bishop, whose friend

was murdered by the dictator, saying publicly that he loved him. This was not a weakness. It was

the strength of the gospel. Kivengere wrote, "On the cross, Jesus said, 'Father, forgive them, for

they do not know what they are doing.' As evil as Amin was, I knew that I must love him." That is

gentleness rooted in resurrection power. That is manhood under the lordship of Jesus.

Let me give you the marks of a gentle man.

A gentle man listens more than he speaks. He does not shout down his wife in an argument. He

does not interrupt his children to have the last word. He listens carefully. He considers. He speaks

truth, but he speaks it in love (Ephesians 4:15).

A gentle man keeps his word. His yes is yes and his no is no (Matthew 5:37). He does not need to

swear, because he does not need to be loud to be believed.

A gentle man controls his temper. "Whoever is slow to anger is better than the mighty, and he who

rules his spirit than he who takes a city" (Proverbs 16:32). A man who can conquer a city but not

his own temper has conquered nothing. A man who can rule his own spirit is a true king.

A gentle man forgives. He does not hold grudges. He does not wait to avenge every insult. He

remembers how much he has been forgiven by Christ, and it softens him toward others.

A gentle man is approachable. His wife is not afraid to tell him something has gone wrong. His

children run to him, not away from him. His employees can speak the truth to him without fear.

His friends can rebuke him in love.

A gentle man prays under pressure. When the storm comes, he does not explode. He goes to his

knees. The first response of a gentle man to trouble is prayer, not panic, not rage.

Brother, our land is full of hard men. We do not need any more of them. We need gentle men —

men like Christ. Men whose strength is under His control. Men whose wives are honored, whose

children are treasured, whose employees are respected, whose enemies are loved. Such men

change a village. Such men change a nation.

A Prayer

Lord Jesus, You are gentle and humble in heart. You are strong beyond measure,

and yet You never crushed a bruised reed or snuffed out a smoldering wick. Forgive

me for the harshness in my words, the rage in my eyes, the cruelty in my hands.

Tame my temper, Lord. Break my pride. Teach me the true strength of gentleness.

Make me a man in whose presence my wife feels safe, my children feel loved, my

enemies feel respected. Let Your Spirit bear the fruit of gentleness in me, that those

who meet me may see something of You. In Your gentle and mighty name, amen.

fields.title: Chapter 7
fields.body_html:
By the Sweat of Your Brow

Working Hard and Providing Well

"Anyone who does not provide for their relatives, and especially for their own

household, has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever."

— 1 Timothy 5:8

These are sobering words. The apostle Paul does not say a man who fails to provide is a weak

Christian, or a struggling Christian, or a Christian who needs encouragement. He says such a man

has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.

Why such strong language? Because provision is one of the most basic callings of a man. Long

before a man leads spiritually, he must provide materially. Long before he teaches the Bible to his

family, he must put food on their table. These are not competing duties — they go together. A man

who preaches a great sermon on Sunday but whose children go to bed hungry on Monday has

failed. God has called him to both.

Work is not a curse. This is important for us to understand, because many men think of work as

punishment, something to escape through winning the lottery, finding a rich marriage, or receiving

remittances from a relative abroad. But in Genesis 2, before Adam sinned, God placed him in the

garden "to work it and take care of it" (Genesis 2:15). Work came before the Fall. Work is part of

how God made us. Work is dignifying. Work is worship.

What the Fall did was make work harder. God said to Adam, "By the sweat of your brow you will

eat your food" (Genesis 3:19). The soil now produces thorns. The business now faces corruption.

The field now suffers drought. The office now has conflict. But work itself remains a gift. When

we labor with our hands and our minds, we are imaging our Creator, who labored for six days and

rested on the seventh.

The book of Proverbs has stern warnings about the lazy man. "Go to the ant, you sluggard; consider

its ways and be wise! It has no commander, no overseer or ruler, yet it stores its provisions in

summer and gathers its food at harvest" (Proverbs 6:6–8). "A little sleep, a little slumber, a little

folding of the hands to rest — and poverty will come on you like a thief and scarcity like an armed

man" (Proverbs 6:10–11). "The sluggard does not plow in season; so at harvest time he looks but

finds nothing" (Proverbs 20:4).

Brother, in our East African context, we must confront a spirit of idleness that sits on many young

men. They gather at the trading center and complain that there are no jobs. Some of them have

phones in their hands and half a day to burn. They wait for handouts. They dream of going abroad

to Dubai or America, but they will not dig the garden at home. They complain that life is unfair

while the fields around their house lie untended. The Bible's answer to this is simple and strong:

work.

Paul said to the Thessalonian church, "For even when we were with you, we gave you this rule:

'The one who is unwilling to work shall not eat.' We hear that some among you are idle and

disruptive. They are not busy; they are busybodies. Such people we command and urge in the Lord

Jesus Christ to settle down and earn the food they eat" (2 Thessalonians 3:10–12).

This is not harshness against the poor. The Bible commands us to care for the widow, the orphan,

the disabled, the elderly, those truly unable to work. That is true religion (James 1:27). But for the

able-bodied man who refuses to work, there is no Christian welfare. Get up. Plant. Trade. Learn a

skill. Drive a boda-boda. Start small. Be faithful. God blesses faithful hands.

And when God does give you work, do it with all your heart. "Whatever you do, work at it with

all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters" (Colossians 3:23). Do not be the

kind of worker who only works when the boss is looking. Do not steal time, steal materials, steal

credit. Do not take bribes. Do not cheat customers. Your work is your testimony to the world.

Many people will never hear a sermon, but they will meet you at the market, at the office, at the

shop. Is your work a signboard for Christ?

Let me speak also to men who have money. You are not exempt from this chapter. A rich man can

be just as lazy as a poor man — sometimes more so. Solomon said, "A sated man loathes honey,

but to a hungry man every bitter thing is sweet" (Proverbs 27:7). Wealth tests a man's soul. If God

has given you success, you must still work. Your work may be different — leading a company,

discipling younger men, serving on church boards, giving generously — but it must be real work,

not self-indulgence.

Consider George Müller of Bristol, who I mentioned earlier. He trusted God for daily provision

for thousands of orphans, yet he worked incredibly hard. His prayers did not replace labor. His

prayers fueled labor. He was up at dawn, he handled correspondence, he managed staff, he

preached, he wrote, he traveled thousands of miles. Prayer and work are not opposites in the

Christian life. They are partners.

Consider also the apostle Paul. Though he was an apostle and had the right to be supported by the

churches, he worked with his own hands as a tentmaker (Acts 18:3, 1 Thessalonians 2:9). He did

not want to be a burden. He wanted to model the dignity of labor. He said to the Ephesian elders,

"You yourselves know that these hands of mine have supplied my own needs and the needs of my

companions" (Acts 20:34).

Now let us think about provision in the African context. A Christian man in East Africa often has

more than just his immediate family to consider. There is the wider family — aging parents,

younger siblings in school, cousins with needs. This can become a heavy burden, but it is also a

beautiful calling. Paul said, "Anyone who does not provide for their relatives, and especially for

their own household." Relatives first, then household first among them. Your nuclear family must

come before the wider family in your budget — otherwise you are robbing your wife and children

to please your relatives. But you are not free to ignore those relatives either. Balance, wisdom,

generosity, and limits all together.

Set goals. Work with a plan. "The plans of the diligent lead to profit as surely as haste leads to

poverty" (Proverbs 21:5). Have a budget. Know what comes in and what goes out. Save something,

even a little. "In the house of the wise are stores of choice food and oil, but a foolish man devours

all he has" (Proverbs 21:20). Avoid debt where possible. Plan for your children's school fees. Plan

for old age. Plan to give generously to God's work.

Give the first portion to God. The principle of the tithe runs through the Old Testament and is

honored throughout the New. Honor the Lord with the first and best of what you earn (Proverbs

3:9). A man who will not tithe to his local church cannot claim to trust God with his money. It is

a simple test of the heart.

Finally, do not love money. "The love of money is a root of all kinds of evil. Some people, eager

for money, have wandered from the faith and pierced themselves with many griefs" (1 Timothy

6:10). You can work hard without worshiping money. You can pursue excellence without being

ruled by greed. You provide so your family is fed and God is honored — not so you can boast

against your neighbor. Many Christian men in our region have been destroyed by the prosperity

gospel, a false teaching that turns Jesus into a business deal. Flee that false gospel. Work hard.

Trust God. Be content. Give generously. And let your life be a rebuke to both the sluggard and the

greedy.

Brother, put your hand to the plow and do not look back. Your family is watching. Your neighbors

are watching. Your Lord is watching. Work as unto Him, and He will bless the work of your hands.

A Prayer

Lord God, You who labored for six days and rested on the seventh, teach me the

dignity of work. Break the spirit of laziness in me. Break the spirit of greed in me.

Give me strength for my hands, wisdom for my mind, integrity for my dealings. Let

me work not for bread alone but as an act of worship to You. Provide for my

household, O God. Let my wife and children never lack what they need. Use my

hands to serve my family, my church, and the poor. Make me generous where I have

been grasping. Make me diligent where I have been idle. And may the sweat of my

brow be a sweet offering to You. In Jesus' name, Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 8
fields.body_html:
The Watchman at the Gate

Protecting Your Home

"After I looked things over, I stood up and said to the nobles, the officials and the

rest of the people, 'Don't be afraid of them. Remember the Lord, who is great and

awesome, and fight for your families, your sons and your daughters, your wives

and your homes.'"

— Nehemiah 4:14

When Nehemiah led the returning exiles to rebuild the walls of Jerusalem, enemies surrounded

them. Sanballat and Tobiah mocked them, then plotted to attack them. Nehemiah's response is a

masterclass in godly manhood. He armed the men. He set watchmen on the walls. He stationed

fighters at every gap. And he called out the charge: "Fight for your families, your sons and your

daughters, your wives and your homes."

Brother, God has made you a watchman at the gate of your home. There are enemies — you cannot

pretend otherwise. There is the enemy of the flesh, within us. There is the enemy of the world,

around us. There is the enemy of the devil, against us. You stand on the wall, and your household

stands behind you. You must watch, and you must fight.

Protection is one of the most basic callings of a man. It goes back to Adam, who was placed in the

garden to "work it and take care of it" (Genesis 2:15). The word "take care of" in Hebrew is the

same word used for watchmen, for those who guard. Adam was to protect the garden, and

especially, he was to protect Eve from the serpent. He failed. We have often failed too. But God

still calls us to this work, and He gives us grace to do it.

There are three levels of protection a man must provide for his household: physical, emotional,

and spiritual. Let us look at each.

First, physical protection. You are the first line of defense for your wife and children against any

physical threat — whether an intruder in the night, a dangerous road, a toxic environment, a health

crisis. A man does not hide behind his wife when danger comes. He steps in front. A man does not

send his children into harm while he sits safe. He leads them through.

Many of us do this instinctively when danger is obvious. But there are subtler physical threats we

must guard against too. Does your family have clean water? Is your home secure? Do your children

walk safe routes to school? Is your wife exhausted because she carries burdens you could share?

Physical protection is not only about chasing thieves. It is about building a safe, healthy, livable

home.

Second, emotional protection. This is where many of us fail most seriously, often without realizing

it. Your home should be the safest place in the world for your wife and children — not only safe

from outside enemies, but safe from you. If your temper rages inside your own home, you have

not protected your family. You have become the very thing they need protection from.

A man who protects his family emotionally watches what comes out of his mouth. "The tongue

has the power of life and death" (Proverbs 18:21). Your words can build up your wife or tear her

down. Your words can bless your children or curse them. Many of us carry wounds to this day

from words a father spoke decades ago. Guard your tongue. Speak life.

A man who protects his family emotionally watches who comes into the home. Not every guest is

a blessing. Not every relative is safe around your daughters. Not every friend is a good influence

on your sons. You are the gatekeeper. If someone brings a spirit of drunkenness, lust, violence, or

mockery into your house, it is your duty to keep them out. Do not be afraid to offend people when

the safety of your family is at stake.

A man who protects his family emotionally listens when they speak of fear or pain. Do not dismiss

your wife's concerns as "women's talk." Do not laugh when your son tells you what frightened

him. Take them seriously. Their hearts are in your hands.

Third, spiritual protection. This is the deepest and most important. The apostle Paul writes, "Our

struggle is not against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the

powers of this dark world and against the spiritual forces of evil in the heavenly realms" (Ephesians

6:12). There is a real devil. There are real demons. There are real spiritual attacks on your wife,

your children, your home. And you are called to stand as a watchman on that wall.

How do you protect your family spiritually? First, by covering them in prayer. The devil does not

fear your theology; he fears your prayers. Pray over every room of your home. Pray at the door as

your children leave for school. Pray by their beds at night. Pray with your wife before you fall

asleep. Prayer is the invisible armor over your family.

Second, by guarding what enters the home through media. The television, the internet, the

smartphone — these are open doors, and the devil walks through them freely if no watchman is at

the gate. Fathers, you must decide what your children watch, what apps they have, what songs they

listen to. This is not oppression. This is love. "I will not look with approval on anything that is

vile," said David (Psalm 101:3). Your home should be the same. You will answer to God for what

you allowed to enter.

Third, by guarding the teaching your family receives. In our day, there is no shortage of false

teachers. Prosperity preachers sell salvation. Self-appointed prophets claim private revelations.

Cults dress up like churches. You must be a Berean (Acts 17:11), testing everything by Scripture,

and you must help your family do the same. Do not let your children be discipled by whatever loud

voice shouts the latest on social media. Disciple them yourself. Take them to a faithful, Bible-

preaching local church. Read solid Christian books with them. Answer their questions carefully.

Consider the Maccabees, the Jewish warriors of the intertestamental period, who defended their

faith against the Greek king Antiochus Epiphanes. When Antiochus tried to force them to worship

idols and abandon the Scriptures, one family — Mattathias and his sons — stood up. They said,

"Let everyone who is zealous for the law and who stands by the covenant follow me!" (1

Maccabees 2:27). Mattathias, a father, risked everything for the spiritual protection of his

household and his nation. His son Judas "Maccabeus" became famous for defending the people of

God. Though they lived before Christ, their zeal for the Lord is a picture of what a watchman father

looks like.

Consider the early Ugandan martyrs. When Kabaka Mwanga demanded that the young Christian

pages renounce their faith and submit to his perverse demands, Mukasa, Lwanga, and the others

refused, even knowing it would cost them their lives. Their refusal was not only for themselves —

it was for the faith of a whole generation. They protected the gospel by their blood. Their watch

cost them everything, and because of it, the Church in Uganda stands today.

Brother, you may never face martyrdom. But you will face daily skirmishes. A coworker invites

you to a corrupt deal — the enemy is at the gate. A sensual advertisement pops up on your phone
