— the enemy is at the gate. A teacher tells your child that the Bible is a fairy tale — the enemy is

at the gate. A friend mocks your faith — the enemy is at the gate. At each of these gates, a

watchman is needed. That watchman is you.

Do not sleep on the wall. Do not wander off to your own pleasures and leave the walls unmanned.

Do not trade the safety of your home for the pleasures of the flesh. Stand firm. Pray. Fight the good

fight of faith. And when you are weary, remember the words of Nehemiah to tired men: "Our God

will fight for us" (Nehemiah 4:20).

A Prayer

Mighty God, You are a wall of fire around Your people. Teach me to be a watchman

at the gate of my home. Make me alert to the schemes of the devil. Make me brave

against the threats of this age. Make me quick to pray over my wife, my children,

and every corner of my house. Where I have let evil through the gates, forgive me.

Where I have slept on the wall, awaken me. Where I have become the danger my

family needed protection from, convict me and change me. Let my home be a

fortress of Your peace, and let Your angels encamp around us. In the name of Jesus

Christ, the Lord of hosts, amen.

fields.title: Chapter 9
fields.body_html:
Accountability

No Man Stands Alone

"As iron sharpens iron, so one person sharpens another."

— Proverbs 27:17

One of the great lies a man can believe is that he does not need other men. He thinks he is strong

enough, wise enough, holy enough to walk the Christian life alone. He will come to church on

Sunday, but he will not open his life to anyone in particular during the week. He has no one who

knows his struggles. He has no one who can correct him. He has no one who can pray specifically

over his secret battles. He is an island, and he is sinking.

Brother, the devil loves a lone man. He picks off the stragglers. He destroys the isolated. He

whispers to the private man that no one understands him, no one would forgive him, no one can

help him. And slowly, steadily, the lone man is eaten by sins he never meant to let grow.

The Bible is clear that God has made us for community, and especially that men need other men.

"As iron sharpens iron, so one person sharpens another" (Proverbs 27:17). Iron does not sharpen

itself. A knife left alone grows dull. A man left alone grows dull — in his love for Christ, in his

holiness, in his zeal, in his courage. He needs the scraping, the grinding, the honest friction of

another iron man.

David had Jonathan. "In everything Jonathan did, he had great success, because the Lord was with

him" (1 Samuel 18:14), and the bond of their souls was such that "Jonathan became one in spirit

with David, and he loved him as himself" (1 Samuel 18:1).

When David was hunted by Saul in the wilderness, Jonathan came to him and "helped him find

strength in God" (1 Samuel 23:16). Every man needs a Jonathan — a brother who helps him find

strength in God when life has crushed him.

Paul had Timothy and Titus and Silas and Barnabas and Luke. He was an apostle, a man of

tremendous spiritual power, and yet he did not travel alone. He wrote his deepest affections to

these men. Read 2 Timothy — it is a dying man's letter to his son in the faith, full of love and

honesty. Paul, in his last days, said, "Only Luke is with me" (2 Timothy 4:11), and he asked

Timothy to come quickly. Even the great apostle needed companions.

Jesus Himself, though He was the Son of God, gathered the Twelve and was especially close to

Peter, James, and John. He did not lead alone. He did not die alone. He lived His earthly ministry

surrounded by brothers.

If Jesus, David, and Paul all needed brothers, who are you to think you can live alone?

The most essential element of accountability is honesty. Until a man is willing to be honest with

at least one other brother, he cannot grow. James writes, "Therefore confess your sins to each other

and pray for each other so that you may be healed. The prayer of a righteous person is powerful

and effective" (James 5:16). There is healing in confession. Not to a priest in a dark box, but to a

brother in the light of day. When you say out loud to another Christian man, "I have been struggling

with lust," or "I have been drinking in secret," or "I have been cheating on my taxes," or "I have

been harsh with my wife and I do not know how to stop," something powerful happens. The sin's

hiding place is exposed. The darkness flees. The healing begins.

Here in our region, the East African Revival was marked precisely by this kind of honesty. When

the Spirit fell on Rwanda and Uganda in the 1930s, men began to confess their sins publicly. Some

had stolen from their employers; they went to pay back what they had taken. Some had slept with

women not their wives; they went to ask forgiveness. Some had grudges with fellow believers;

they went to reconcile. They called it "walking in the light," based on 1 John 1:7: "If we walk in

the light, as he is in the light, we have fellowship with one another, and the blood of Jesus, his Son,

purifies us from all sin." And revival spread like fire. This kind of honesty is the fuel of revival,

and without it, our churches will stay weak no matter how many programs we run.

So, brother, find at least two or three men in your local church and bind yourself to them. Do not

pick only your closest personal friends — pick men you respect spiritually, men who will tell you

the truth even when it hurts. Meet with them regularly. Some meet weekly, some monthly, some

every other week. Whatever schedule fits, commit to it and keep it. Do not cancel the meeting

because you are "too busy." You are never too busy to save your soul.

When you meet, go beyond small talk. Ask each other hard questions. The Methodist bands, started

by John Wesley in the 1700s, used a set of probing questions that still convict today. They asked

each other things like: "What known sins have you committed since our last meeting? What

temptations have you met with? How were you delivered? What have you thought, said, or done,

of which you doubt whether it be sin or not?" Wesley's movement transformed England partly

because men were not allowed to hide.

And brothers, some of you need to ask forgiveness from other men. You have offended a brother

in the church and have been avoiding him for years. This is not Christianity. Jesus said, "If you are

offering your gift at the altar and there remember that your brother or sister has something against

you, leave your gift there in front of the altar. First go and be reconciled to them; then come and

offer your gift" (Matthew 5:23–24). If something stands between you and another believer, it also

stands between you and God. Go to him. Humble yourself. Make it right. The relief on the other

side is worth it.

Accountability is also about receiving correction. Proverbs says, "Whoever heeds discipline shows

the way to life, but whoever ignores correction leads others astray" (Proverbs 10:17). "Do not

rebuke mockers or they will hate you; rebuke the wise and they will love you" (Proverbs 9:8). Can

a brother correct you? If you become angry and defensive every time someone points out a fault,

you are a fool, not a leader. The wise man welcomes correction, even when it stings. He says,

"Thank you for loving me enough to tell me. Let me pray about this. Let me repent of this."

Husbands, listen here too. Your wife is often your best accountability partner. She sees what no

one else sees. She can tell when your prayer life is weak. She can tell when your heart is hard.

Receive her observations with grace. Do not be the husband who demands submission but refuses

correction. A humble husband invites his wife's insight into his soul.

Finally, submit yourself to the authority of your local church. Not just attendance, but membership.

Place yourself under the shepherding of biblical elders. Be willing to be disciplined if you fall into

serious sin. The book of Hebrews says, "Have confidence in your leaders and submit to their

authority, because they keep watch over you as those who must give an account" (Hebrews 13:17).

A man who will not submit to any spiritual authority on earth is a law unto himself — and such a

man is dangerous to his family and to the church.

No man stands alone. Not David. Not Paul. Not Jesus. Not Kivengere. Not Luwum. Not you. Find

your brothers. Let them see you. Let them sharpen you. And together you will stand when alone

you would fall.

A Prayer

Father, I confess that I have tried to walk this road alone. I have kept my sins hidden

in the dark where they have grown in power. I have avoided honest friendships

because I feared exposure. I have rejected correction because I loved my pride.

Forgive me, Lord. Give me at least one brother, and if possible many, with whom I

can walk in the light. Make me honest. Make me teachable. Make me quick to

confess and quick to forgive. Use iron in my life, even when it grinds, to make me

sharp for Your service. And knit me deeply into the body of Christ, so that I may

stand and not fall. In the name of Jesus, amen.

fields.title: Chapter 10
fields.body_html:
Men in the Church

Eldership and Service

"To the elders among you, I appeal as a fellow elder and a witness of Christ's

sufferings who also will share in the glory to be revealed: Be shepherds of God's

flock that is under your care, watching over them — not because you must, but

because you are willing, as God wants you to be; not pursuing dishonest gain, but

eager to serve."

— 1 Peter 5:1–2

God has ordered His Church with shepherds. From the earliest days, the apostles appointed elders

in every city (Acts 14:23, Titus 1:5). These men — mature, proven, biblically qualified — are

given the task of shepherding God's people. Not to be kings, but servants. Not to enrich themselves,

but to feed the flock. Not to dominate, but to lead by example.

Brother, spiritual leadership in the home and spiritual leadership in the church are not two separate

lives. They flow from the same well. The man who shepherds his wife and children well is the

kind of man God chooses to shepherd His Church. And the man who serves faithfully in his local

church is strengthened to serve better at home. The home prepares the man for the church; the

church equips the man for the home.

Let us look carefully at who can be an elder in the Church of Christ. Paul writes to Timothy: "Here

is a trustworthy saying: Whoever aspires to be an overseer desires a noble task. Now the overseer

is to be above reproach, faithful to his wife, temperate, self-controlled, respectable, hospitable,

able to teach, not given to drunkenness, not violent but gentle, not quarrelsome, not a lover of

money. He must manage his own family well and see that his children obey him, and he must do

so in a manner worthy of full respect. (If anyone does not know how to manage his own family,

how can he take care of God's church?) He must not be a recent convert, or he may become

conceited and fall under the same judgment as the devil. He must also have a good reputation with

outsiders, so that he will not fall into disgrace and into the devil's trap" (1 Timothy 3:1–7).

Notice first: "whoever aspires to be an overseer desires a noble task." It is right and good for a man

to aspire to eldership in the Church. This is not an ambition born of pride but a holy desire to serve

God's people. If the Lord has put this desire in you, do not suppress it. But also do not rush it. Most

of the qualifications in this list require years of faithful living to develop.

Notice second: this is a list of character, not a list of gifts. The only gift mentioned is "able to

teach." Everything else is about who the man is. He is above reproach — his life has no dirty secret

waiting to explode. He is faithful to his wife — "a one-woman man," as the Greek literally says,

meaning he is devoted to her alone. He is temperate — not ruled by appetites. He is self-controlled

— his mouth, his temper, his desires are governed by the Spirit. He is respectable — his life

commands honor without demanding it. He is hospitable — his home is open, his table welcomes

guests. He is not given to drunkenness — this is crucial in our East African context where alcohol

destroys so many homes. He is not violent but gentle. He is not quarrelsome. He is not a lover of

money.

Notice third: he must manage his own family well. Paul says if a man cannot shepherd at home,

he cannot shepherd in the church. The home is the testing ground. Many men in our churches want

the title of elder, the microphone, the respect, the influence — but they have not first proved

themselves at home. Their wives fear them. Their children are wild. Their households are in

disorder. Such men are not yet ready. Go home, shepherd your wife, raise your children in the

Lord, and let the fruit ripen before you grasp for the position.

Notice fourth: he must not be a recent convert. In our rapidly growing churches across East Africa,

this warning is often ignored. We give pulpits to men who have been born again for only a year or

two. Sometimes we give them to men who have never been truly converted at all but who have

charisma and money. This produces pride in the young leader and disaster in the flock. Let maturity

grow. Let character be tested. Let trials be endured. Then lift a man up.

Notice fifth: he must have a good reputation with outsiders. The neighbors who know you — the

market woman who sells you tomatoes, the boda-boda rider who has driven you, the employee

under you — they know if you are a true Christian or only a Sunday one. If the world thinks you

are dishonest, a womanizer, a cheat, a bully, you are not qualified to lead the church, no matter

how loud you are in worship.

Now, brother, perhaps you are not an elder and never will be. Perhaps you do not aspire to that

office. That is fine. Not every man is called to eldership. But every man is called to serve the local

church. Hear this clearly: if you are a Christian man, your church needs you, and you need your

church.

Think of the church as a body (1 Corinthians 12). Every member contributes something. If the

ushers are always the same women, where are the men? If the cleaning of the building falls on the

widows, where are the men? If the small group leaders are always the pastor's wife and her friends,

where are the men? If the Sunday School teachers are all women, who is modeling Christ for the

little boys? If the finances of the church are handled by one tired person, where are the faithful

men to bring their wisdom?

Serve where you are needed. Teach if you can teach. Give if you can give. Sing if you can sing.

Fix things if you are handy. Visit the sick. Welcome the newcomer. Pray at prayer meeting. Help

with youth events. Disciple a younger man. Support your pastor. Bring a meal to the bereaved

family. The body is built up when every part does its work (Ephesians 4:16).

Honor your pastors. Hebrews says, "Have confidence in your leaders and submit to their authority,

because they keep watch over you as those who must give an account. Do this so that their work

will be a joy, not a burden, for that would be of no benefit to you" (Hebrews 13:17). Your pastor

is a man like you, with his own struggles. He needs your prayers, your encouragement, your honest

support. Do not gossip about him. Do not undermine him. Do not tear him down behind his back.

If you disagree with him, go to him privately in love.

A word of warning also: do not idolize him. The pastor is a man, not a messiah. Do not build your

faith on his personality. In our region, we have seen too many one-man churches where the pastor

is treated like a king or a prophet, where no one can question him, where the money flows into his

pockets and the building never gets finished. This is not biblical Christianity. Elders — plural —

lead the church (Acts 14:23, Titus 1:5). A healthy church has a plurality of qualified men, not a

single unaccountable ruler. If your church does not have this, pray for it, work toward it, and

perhaps, with humility and patience, help build it.

Consider Athanasius, the great African bishop of Alexandria in the 300s. He is known as

"Athanasius against the world" because he stood for the deity of Christ when most of the church

had drifted into the Arian heresy. Five times he was exiled by emperors who wanted him to

compromise. Five times he returned. He was faithful to the truth of Scripture no matter the cost.

And because one African man would not bow, the Church today still confesses that Jesus is fully

God. One faithful elder can change the course of history. Do not think your service is too small to

matter.

Consider also the humble pastor in a small village church in Uganda or Kenya or Tanzania. He

will never be famous. He will never write a book. His name will not be remembered in fifty years.

But he prays for his flock. He preaches the Word faithfully Sunday after Sunday. He visits the

sick. He buries the dead. He marries the young. He catechizes the children. He will hear one day

from Jesus, "Well done, good and faithful servant." That is glory enough. Do not despise such

men. Do not leave them alone. Stand with them.

Brother, commit to a local church. Be a member, not a visitor. Be a servant, not just a consumer.

Be present in the joys and the hardships. Be there when the roof leaks and when there is no money

for the power bill. Be there when the youth are wild and need godly men. Be there when an elder

falls into sin and the church weeps. Be there when revival comes and when seasons are dry. "They

devoted themselves to the apostles' teaching and to fellowship, to the breaking of bread and to

prayer" (Acts 2:42). So must you.

A Prayer

Father, thank You for Your Church, the body of Christ, the pillar and foundation

of the truth. Forgive me for the times I have been a consumer rather than a servant,

a critic rather than a builder, a drifter rather than a member. Give me a heart for

Your local church. If You are calling me to eldership, prepare me and do not let me

run ahead of Your timing. If You are calling me to other service, make me faithful

in the smallest task. Help me honor my pastors, support my brothers, and build up

the body. Make me a man of whom it may be said, "He loved the Church of God."

In the name of Jesus, the Chief Shepherd, Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 11
fields.body_html:
The Teacher at Home

Family Worship and Discipleship

"These commandments that I give you today are to be on your hearts. Impress

them on your children. Talk about them when you sit at home and when you walk

along the road, when you lie down and when you get up."

— Deuteronomy 6:6–7

The pulpit of the home is greater than the pulpit of the church. This is not because the church pulpit

is unimportant — it is vitally important — but because the home pulpit reaches ears that hear you

six days a week, not one. Your wife and your children will hear more sermons from you at your

dinner table than they will ever hear from the greatest preacher in Africa. The question is not

whether you are teaching them. You are. The question is, what are you teaching them?

If you do not pray with them, you are teaching them prayer is unimportant. If you do not open the

Bible with them, you are teaching them the Bible is unimportant. If you do not worship God in the

home, you are teaching them worship is for Sunday only. If you never correct them when they

dishonor God in speech or action, you are teaching them God's name is not to be feared. You teach,

whether you mean to or not. Every father is a pastor of his home, either a faithful one or a negligent

one.

Moses told the fathers of Israel to "impress" God's commandments on their children. The Hebrew

word is intense — it means to sharpen, to pound in, to engrave. This is not a casual mention. This

is intentional, repeated, patient teaching. It is the work of years, not moments.

And when does this teaching happen? "When you sit at home and when you walk along the road,

when you lie down and when you get up" (Deuteronomy 6:7). That is, always. In four broad times:

at home, on the road, at night, in the morning. This covers a day.

Let me paint a picture for you of what family discipleship can look like. I am not giving a law here,

only a shape. Adapt it to your household, your stage of life, your rhythms. But do something.

In the morning, before you scatter to work and school, gather for a short time around the Word.

Read a portion of Scripture — maybe a chapter, maybe just a few verses — and pray together for

the day. It does not have to be long. Ten or fifteen minutes is enough. The consistency matters

more than the length.

At meals, pray — not the same rote prayer every time, but real thanksgiving. Discuss the day. Ask

your children questions about what they are learning. Listen to your wife tell you about her

morning. Eat together. Technology down. Screens off. Hearts open.

On the road — meaning in the car, on the walk to school, on the boda-boda, wherever you travel

together — talk about God as you go. "Do you see the sunset? What kind of God makes that?"

"Do you remember what the pastor preached about yesterday? What did you think?" "Why do we

help that beggar? What does the Bible say?" The road is a classroom for the father.

At night, gather again for family worship. This is the main meal of your spiritual table. Read

Scripture, sing a hymn or chorus, pray, perhaps use a catechism to teach the faith. Bless your

children one by one before they go to bed. Put your hand on each child's head and pray, "Lord,

bless my son. Lord, bless my daughter. Keep them in the faith. Protect them this night. Make them

useful to You." Those words will echo in their souls for a lifetime.

Then pray with your wife before you sleep. Confess any sins from the day. Forgive if there has

been friction. Intercede for the children, for the family, for the church. End the day as you began

it — under the mercy of God. If this sounds overwhelming, take heart. You will not do it perfectly.

You will miss days. Your wife will carry it some days. Your children will roll their eyes at some

points. That is fine. You are not trying to create a flawless religious performance. You are trying

to weave the gospel into the fabric of your home. The occasional miss is not the issue. The pattern

over years is what shapes souls.

Let me recommend a few practical tools. The Psalms are the prayer book of the Bible and a

wonderful starting point for family reading. Begin in Psalm 1 and work slowly through. The

Gospels — Matthew, Mark, Luke, John — are where your children will meet Jesus; read them

repeatedly. Proverbs is full of practical wisdom; read a chapter a day, matching the day of the

month. Simple catechisms, like the children's catechism or an age-appropriate confession of faith,

can give your family the skeleton of Christian doctrine. Good hymnals or songbooks put theology

into song that children remember for life.

Think of Timothy, the young pastor in the New Testament. Paul says to him, "I am reminded of

your sincere faith, which first lived in your grandmother Lois and in your mother Eunice and, I am

persuaded, now lives in you also" (2 Timothy 1:5). Then later: "But as for you, continue in what

you have learned and have become convinced of, because you know those from whom you learned

it, and how from infancy you have known the Holy Scriptures" (2 Timothy 3:14–15). From

infancy. Lois and Eunice had been teaching Timothy the Scriptures since he was a baby. This is

the mother's blessing, but it should also be the father's legacy. What are you teaching your infant?

What is being poured into your toddler? Do not wait until they are teenagers and then expect them

to love Jesus. Begin now, with the youngest in the home.

And do not despair if your children are already grown and you feel you missed the window. You

did not. You can still repent, apologize to your adult children for past failures, and begin leading

them now. Many men, in their fifties and sixties, have been the most powerful spiritual leaders to

their adult children — precisely because they humbled themselves and started late with grace. It is

better to begin late than never.

Jonathan Edwards, the New England pastor of the 1700s, had eleven children with his wife Sarah.

He prayed for each of them daily. He read the Bible with them. He walked the grounds of his home

with them, catechizing, discussing, laughing, teaching. A study of the descendants of Jonathan and

Sarah Edwards found over a thousand graduates, pastors, professors, judges, authors, and public

servants. That is what happens when a father takes family discipleship seriously. A century later,

his great-great-grandchildren were still being shaped by the habits of prayer that began at his

hearth.

And do not forget the children of Festo Kivengere and other Ugandan revival fathers. Many of

them became pastors, teachers, and faithful servants of the Lord themselves. The fire did not die

with the fathers — it was passed. Fathers in East Africa, pass the fire.

Let me close with a warning and encouragement. The warning: your children will see through

hypocrisy. If you teach the Bible at night but live in contradiction by day, they will notice. They

will wait until they are old enough to reject the faith, and they will throw it out as something their

father only performed. Do not teach what you are not trying to live. Apologize to them when you

fail. Show them a father who is being sanctified, not a father who pretends to be already perfect.

The encouragement: God can do more with a sincere, stumbling father than you can imagine. He

is the One who works in your children. You plant and water, but He gives the growth (1 Corinthians

3:6–7). Be faithful. Be patient. Be persistent. And trust the God who loves your children more than

you do.

A Prayer

Lord God, You are the great Teacher. You taught Israel through Moses, You taught

Your disciples as You walked along the road, You teach me still through Your Word

and Spirit. Make me a teacher in my own home. Forgive me for the times I have left

the spiritual instruction of my family to others. Give me a love for Your Word. Give

me patience to teach line by line. Give me wisdom to answer my children's

questions. Give me grace to live what I teach. Let our home be a small church

where Your Name is loved, Your Word is read, and Your Son is adored. Let my

children, when they are old, rise up and call Your name blessed because their father

taught them to know You. In Jesus' name, amen.

fields.title: Chapter 12
fields.body_html:
The Battle Within

Fighting Sin and Walking in Purity

"Flee from sexual immorality. All other sins a person commits are outside the

body, but whoever sins sexually, sins against their own body."

— 1 Corinthians 6:18

We have spoken much about leadership outside of ourselves — in the home, in the church, in the

community. Now we must speak about the hardest leadership of all: the leadership of ourselves.

The war within. The fight for personal holiness.

Brother, you cannot lead others into places where you refuse to go yourself. You cannot call your

wife to purity if you are feeding on pornography in secret. You cannot teach your sons self-control

if you are mastered by alcohol. You cannot instruct your daughters about modesty if your eyes

wander when you walk down the street. The battle within comes before the battle without. Jesus

said, "You hypocrite, first take the plank out of your own eye, and then you will see clearly to

remove the speck from your brother's eye" (Matthew 7:5).

Let us speak honestly about some specific sins that devastate men, especially in our East African

context.

First, sexual sin. Sexual immorality has been a stumbling block for men since the Garden of Eden,

and our generation has no shortage of it. Adultery is everywhere. Pornography is in every pocket

that carries a smartphone. Polygamy, though sometimes dressed in cultural clothing, often feeds

the same selfish desires. Young men sleep with girlfriends and call it "just how things are."

Older men keep girls on the side and think their wives do not know. Pastors fall. Deacons fall.

Elders fall. The newspapers are full of scandals.

The Bible's command is simple: "Flee from sexual immorality" (1 Corinthians 6:18). Not debate

it. Not flirt with it. Not enjoy the edges of it. Flee. Joseph ran from Potiphar's wife so fast he left

his cloak behind (Genesis 39:12). That is the pattern. When the temptation comes, your legs are

your best friend.

Why flee? Paul gives the answer: your body is a temple of the Holy Spirit (1 Corinthians 6:19).

You are not your own. You were bought at a price. Christ paid for every cell of your body with

His blood. To defile what He has bought is to sin not only against your wife, not only against the

woman involved, not only against your children, but against Christ Himself.

Practically, how do we flee? Set guardrails. Do not meet alone with a woman who is not your wife,

especially not in private settings. Do not text late at night with a woman who is not your wife. Do

not keep pornographic material anywhere — on your phone, on your computer, in your mind.

Install accountability software. Confess to a brother when you have stumbled. Do not romanticize

your past sins by telling the old stories. Keep your mind and your eyes under the rule of the Spirit.

"I made a covenant with my eyes not to look lustfully at a young woman," said Job (Job 31:1).

Make that same covenant today.

Second, alcohol. This is a particular plague in East Africa. Home-brewed spirits, local beers,

waragi, imported whiskeys — they have destroyed more African homes than almost any other

single sin. A man goes out after work "just for one drink." He comes home drunk at midnight. His

wife smells it. His children see it. His Sunday sermon dies on his lips.

Scripture does not forbid the moderate use of wine (Psalm 104:15, 1 Timothy 5:23). But it

repeatedly condemns drunkenness. "Do not get drunk on wine, which leads to debauchery. Instead,

be filled with the Spirit" (Ephesians 5:18). "Wine is a mocker and beer a brawler; whoever is led

astray by them is not wise" (Proverbs 20:1). "Woe to those who rise early in the morning to run

after their drinks, who stay up late at night till they are inflamed with wine" (Isaiah 5:11).

Let me speak clearly. If alcohol has any grip on you at all — if you need it to relax, if you cannot

stop at one, if you spend money on it your family needed for food, if you have ever been drunk in

front of your children, if your wife has begged you to stop — then you must put it down completely.

Not reduce. Not manage. Stop. The Bible calls it "not given to drunkenness" as a qualification for

leadership (1 Timothy 3:3). Many men in our region cannot lead because they cannot rule their

cups.

Third, anger. We have spoken of this in the chapter on gentleness, but it returns here as a deep sin

to fight. "In your anger do not sin. Do not let the sun go down while you are still angry, and do not

give the devil a foothold" (Ephesians 4:26–27). Uncontrolled anger in a man gives the devil a

direct doorway into his home. Many of our fathers passed rage down to us like an inheritance. We

can break that chain. We can refuse to pass it to our sons.

Fourth, the love of money and corruption. In our culture, bribery is so common it has almost

become invisible. Small gifts to get a job done. Larger payments to avoid traffic tickets. Business

deals built on kickbacks. Government contracts that line private pockets. Some of this is simply

theft from the poor, dressed up in polite language. The Bible is uncompromising: "Whoever loves

money never has enough; whoever loves wealth is never satisfied with their income" (Ecclesiastes

5:10). "A greedy man brings ruin to his household" (Proverbs 15:27). "The Lord detests dishonest

scales" (Proverbs 11:1).

If you are in a position where you can give or take bribes, there will be a cost to doing it God's

way. You may earn less. You may be passed over. You may be laughed at. But "better a little with

righteousness than much gain with injustice" (Proverbs 16:8). You cannot serve God and money

(Matthew 6:24). Choose today whom you will serve.

Fifth, pride. This is the root of all the others. Pride is the sin that turned an angel into the devil.

Pride says, "I know better than God." Pride says, "The rules do not apply to me." Pride says, "I do

not need accountability." Pride says, "I am the head — obey me." Pride is sneaky, and it hides in

everything, even our humility. "God opposes the proud but shows favor to the humble" (James

4:6). Brother, take note: God opposes the proud. Not just dislikes. Opposes. Actively works

against. Do not let pride sit unchallenged in your heart.

How do we fight these sins? Not by trying harder alone. Willpower fails. Resolutions break. The

pattern is always the same: repent, confess, run to Christ, be filled with the Spirit, find a brother to

walk with you, stay close to the means of grace.

The Gospel is the engine of your holiness. It is not that Jesus saved you by grace and now you

must become holy by sweat. No — "he who began a good work in you will carry it on to

completion until the day of Christ Jesus" (Philippians 1:6). The same grace that saved you

sanctifies you. You fight sin from a place of acceptance, not for acceptance. Your Father already

loves you. Your failures do not drive Him away. They drive you to Him.

Consider Augustine of Hippo once more. He struggled with sexual sin for years. He famously

prayed, "Lord, grant me chastity — but not yet!" He knew what was right, but he could not walk

in it. When he finally broke through, it was not by his own strength. He was weeping in a garden,

heard a child's voice saying "take and read," opened the Bible, and read Romans 13:13–14: "Let

us behave decently, as in the daytime, not in carousing and drunkenness, not in sexual immorality

and debauchery, not in dissension and jealousy. Rather, clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus

Christ." The light flooded in. The chains snapped. The power of the gospel broke through.

Your breakthrough will come the same way. Not by grit, but by grace. Not by hiding, but by

bringing your sin into the light. Not by self-righteousness, but by the righteousness of Christ laid

hold of by faith. "It is for freedom that Christ has set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not let

yourselves be burdened again by a yoke of slavery" (Galatians 5:1).

So fight, brother. Fight every day. Fight with your Bible open. Fight with your knees bent. Fight

with brothers beside you. Fight with your wife aware. Fight with the Holy Spirit as your strength.

And know this: in Jesus Christ, you are on the winning side.

A Prayer

Holy God, You are light, and in You there is no darkness at all. I confess I have

walked in dark places. I have loved sins that You hate. I have fed desires that will

destroy me. Have mercy on me, a sinner. Wash me whiter than snow. Break the

power of every sin that has bound me — every lust, every bottle, every outburst,

every bribe, every secret pride. Crucify my flesh with its passions and desires. Fill

me with Your Holy Spirit. Give me brothers to fight beside me. Make me a man who

walks in the light, who confesses quickly, who runs to Christ when he falls. And in

the end, present me faultless before the presence of Your glory with great joy. In

the name of Jesus, who is mighty to save, amen.

fields.title: Chapter 13
fields.body_html:
Vision and Stewardship

Setting Godly Goals

"Then the Lord replied: 'Write down the revelation and make it plain on tablets so

that a herald may run with it.'"

— Habakkuk 2:2

A man without vision is a drifter. He may work hard, but he does not know where he is going. He

may make money, but he does not know what for. He may raise children, but he does not know

what he wants to pass to them. Life happens to him, rather than him living life on purpose.

Solomon wrote, "Where there is no vision, the people perish" (Proverbs 29:18, in the older

translation). The newer translations put it, "Where there is no revelation, people cast off restraint."

Both ideas are true. A man who has not heard from God about his life, and who has not put his

vision on paper, lives without direction and often without restraint.

God is a God of plans. "For I know the plans I have for you," declares the Lord, "plans to prosper

you and not to harm you, plans to give you hope and a future" (Jeremiah 29:11). If God plans for

your life, should you not also plan with Him? Many Christian men mistake "waiting on the Lord"

for passivity. They do nothing and call it faith. But biblical waiting is active. Nehemiah prayed for

four months before he acted (Nehemiah 1–2), but when he acted, he had a plan. He counted the

days, surveyed the walls, organized the workers, assigned the gates.

Brother, have you set godly goals for your life? Not the world's kind of goals — a bigger car, a

bigger house, a bigger title — but goals shaped by Scripture and aimed at the glory of God?

Goals for your walk with Christ? Goals for your marriage? Goals for your children? Goals for your

work? Goals for your giving? Goals for your local church? Goals for your nation?

Let me help you think in categories.

Spiritual goals. Where do you want to be with Christ in one year, five years, twenty years? Do you

have a plan to read through the Bible? Do you have a plan to memorize Scripture? Do you have a

plan for prayer? Do you have books you intend to read to grow in theology and pastoral wisdom?

Ask God to show you the man He wants you to become spiritually, and then ask Him how to get

there.

Marriage goals. What kind of husband do you want to be in ten years? What does your wife most

need from you this year — healing from some past wound? More time? More prayer? Better

communication? Sit down with her and ask. Then write it down. Without a goal for your marriage,

you will drift into mediocrity.

Family goals. What do you want to pass to your children? Not just money — character, faith,

skills, a love of learning, a love of the Church, a heart for the lost. Name what you want them to

know, what you want them to believe, what you want them to be. Then design your fatherhood

toward those goals.

Work goals. What is God calling you to do with your hands and your mind? If you are an employee,

how will you become excellent? If you are a business owner, what ethical and profitable path lies

ahead? If you are a farmer, what is the plan for this season's planting and for five years from now?

Do not drift in your work. Plan it.

Financial goals. What is your plan for saving, giving, investing, and providing? Proverbs says,

"The plans of the diligent lead to profit as surely as haste leads to poverty" (Proverbs 21:5). Have

a household budget. Set aside for your children's school fees. Give to your local church regularly.

Save for emergencies. Plan for old age. Avoid ruinous debt. These are not optional for a godly

man.

Service goals. How do you want to serve God's people? What gifts has He given you, and how

will you use them? Maybe you want to disciple three young men next year. Maybe you want to

help plant a church. Maybe you want to start a ministry for widows in your community. Dream

with God. Write it down.

Habakkuk was told to "write down the revelation and make it plain on tablets, so that a herald may

run with it" (Habakkuk 2:2). Write your vision. Get it on paper, or on your phone, or in a notebook.

There is something holy about writing. It forces you to think clearly. It makes the vision survive

when your memory fails. It lets you review and adjust. Begin today. Just a page. A few lines under

each category. You can refine it over time.

Then pray over your vision regularly. Lay it before the Lord. Say, "Father, if this is not from You,

kill it. If this is from You, bring it to pass. I submit every goal to Your will." "Commit to the Lord

whatever you do, and he will establish your plans" (Proverbs 16:3). Remember also, "Many are

the plans in a person's heart, but it is the Lord's purpose that prevails" (Proverbs 19:21). Your goals

are not God's orders to Him. They are your honest desires submitted to His sovereign hand.

Stewardship is the twin of vision. If God has given you a life, you are to steward it. If He has given

you money, time, talents, children, a wife, influence — all these are on loan. "Now it is required

that those who have been given a trust must prove faithful" (1 Corinthians 4:2). The parable of the

talents (Matthew 25:14–30) is clear: the Master will return and ask what you did with what He

gave you. The man who buried his talent in fear was called wicked and lazy. The men who invested

and multiplied were welcomed into the joy of their Master.

Do not bury your talents, brother. Do not sit on your hands because you feel small. Do not say, "I

am only a farmer, a driver, a clerk, a young man." God gave you your talents. Use them. Start

where you are. Trade faithfully. Grow what He has given.

A simple tool: every Sunday evening, look at the week ahead. What are your priorities? Your Bible

reading plan? One concrete way you will serve your wife this week? One thing you will teach your

children? One person you will disciple or encourage? One hour you will give to the local church?

One person you will pray for by name? Plan it. Then do it. A year of such weeks changes a life.

Consider William Wilberforce, the English Christian statesman of the late 1700s. He set himself

"two great objects": the abolition of the slave trade and the reformation of manners (moral renewal

of society). He wrote these goals down. He pursued them for decades. He did not live to see all the

fruit, but he changed the British Empire. One man with a clear, God-given vision can move

mountains.

Consider also our African brothers who have done the same. Samuel Ajayi Crowther, a Nigerian

who was rescued from a slave ship as a boy, set himself to translate the Bible into his mother

tongue and to plant the Church among his people. He did it. Today the Yoruba church is one of

the strongest in Africa partly because a man set a godly goal and worked toward it for the rest of

his life.

Dream big dreams for God, but be faithful in small daily steps. "Do not despise these small

beginnings, for the Lord rejoices to see the work begin" (Zechariah 4:10). The oak tree is in the

acorn. The revival is in the prayer meeting of three men. The great marriage is in the daily kindness

of a husband. The godly son is in the bedtime prayer of a father. Plant well and the harvest will

come.

A Prayer

Father, You are the God who plans from eternity past to eternity future, the God

who numbered my days before one of them came to be. Give me Your vision for my

life. Break me free from drifting. Break me free from mediocrity. Break me free

from burying my talents in fear. Show me what You are calling me to do, to become,

and to leave behind. Give me the discipline to write down what You reveal. Give

me the wisdom to plan carefully. Give me the faith to trust You with the outcome.

Let my life not be wasted. Use every year, every week, every hour for Your glory.

And at the end of my days, may I hear from You, "Well done." In Jesus' name, Amen.

fields.title: Chapter 14
fields.body_html:
A Legacy That Outlives You

Leaving a Godly Heritage

"A good person leaves an inheritance for their children's children, but a sinner's

wealth is stored up for the righteous."

— Proverbs 13:22

You will die, brother. I do not say this to be dark. I say it because the Bible says it. "It is appointed

for man to die once, and after that comes judgment" (Hebrews 9:27). Your days are numbered

(Psalm 90:12). The length of your life is a secret kept by the One who gave it to you. Some men

get eighty years. Some men do not see their fortieth birthday. Some men are cut down at twenty-

five, leaving a young wife and small children. None of us know.

But this much we do know: you will leave something behind. Every man does. The question is not

whether you will leave a legacy. The question is what kind.

Solomon tells us, "A good person leaves an inheritance for their children's children." Notice the

horizon. Not just for your children, but for your children's children — the grandchildren you may

or may not live to see. A godly man thinks generationally. He is not building only for his lifetime.

He is building for generations he will not meet on this side of eternity.

What kind of legacy should a godly man aim for? Let us consider three levels: material, moral,

and spiritual.

First, a material inheritance. Scripture does honor the passing of material goods. "Houses and

wealth are inherited from parents," says Proverbs 19:14.

A father who leaves his family with nothing when he could have planned better has not served

them well. This does not mean you must become rich. It means you must be faithful. If you have

a small plot of land, can you leave it free of debt? If you have a small business, can you leave it in

good health? If you have little to leave, can you leave a legacy of honest dealing with those you

owed? Some men leave debts and lawsuits behind them — that is a curse to their children. Some

leave paid-up accounts and quiet consciences — that is a blessing.

Plan for what happens when you die. Write a will. In many African contexts, when the husband

dies without a will, the extended family may come and take what was meant for the widow and

the children. Protect your household. A will is not lack of faith; it is an act of love. "The prudent

see danger and take refuge, but the simple keep going and pay the penalty" (Proverbs 27:12).

Second, a moral inheritance. This is more valuable than money, and many poor men have left

enormous moral wealth to their descendants.

A moral inheritance is the memory of integrity. It is your children saying, "Papa never lied to us."

It is your neighbors saying, "Your father never cheated me." It is your wife saying, "Your father

never once raised his hand against me." A reputation for honesty is a shelter that covers your

children's children.

A moral inheritance is also the memory of love. It is your grown son remembering, "Papa took me

fishing. Papa prayed for me at my bedside. Papa told me he was proud of me." It is your grown

daughter remembering, "Papa treated Mama with respect. Papa hugged me. Papa told me I was

beautiful in the Lord." Children who are loved well by their fathers are anchored for life.

A moral inheritance is the shape of how you lived. Your working hard. Your faithfulness to one

wife. Your kindness to the poor. Your refusal to take bribes. Your laughter in your home. Your

songs on the road. Your tears at the funeral of a friend. Your courage at the funeral of a child.

These memories are currency your children will spend for the rest of their lives.

Third, and most important, a spiritual legacy. This is the treasure that outlives every other. "Houses

and wealth are inherited from parents, but a prudent wife is from the Lord" (Proverbs 19:14) —

how much more is a prudent faith? Money is eaten by inflation and sometimes by corrupt officials.

Land can be stolen. Buildings can burn. Reputations can fade. But a grandchild who knows Jesus

because his grandfather prayed for him — that is a legacy no fire can touch, no thief can steal, no

government can confiscate.

Think again of Timothy, who had the faith that "first lived in your grandmother Lois and in your

mother Eunice" (2 Timothy 1:5). Three generations of faith. A grandmother who loved Jesus, a

mother who loved Jesus, a grandson who became a pastor and apostolic helper because of them.

This is a family we do not hear much about by name, but their legacy shaped the Church forever

through Timothy's ministry.

Think of the Wesley family. Susanna Wesley, mother of John and Charles, raised nineteen children

in a small English parsonage. She taught them the Scriptures. She prayed for them daily. Two of

them — John and Charles — shook the world through the Methodist revival, which reached across

England, America, and yes, eventually the continent of Africa. Susanna could not have known that

her patient mothering would one day result in churches planted in Uganda. But that is how legacy

works. A mother's prayers in 1710 became a missionary's boat sailing in 1870 became an African

pastor's sermon in 2026.

Think of the East African Revival fathers — Nsibambi, Nagenda, Kivengere, and many more

whose names are not as famous but whose prayers and lives touched generations. Kivengere lived

to see his preaching impact churches on three continents. His legacy is not a monument of stone;

it is souls in glory, churches still preaching the gospel, children of converts still walking with Jesus.

And think of the Ugandan martyrs. Young men, most of them teenagers and young adults, burned

alive at Namugongo in 1886. They did not leave behind material wealth. Many had no children.

But look what they left behind: a Church. A century and a half later, more than 80% of Uganda

professes the name of Christ because of the witness of those young men. Their blood became seed,

just as Tertullian said centuries earlier, "The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church." Every

June 3rd, Catholics and Protestants alike still remember them. The smallest spiritual legacy is

larger than the grandest earthly one.

So what will your legacy be?

Brother, begin now to live with your end in mind. Every day, ask, "If I died tonight, what would

my wife remember? What would my children inherit? What would my church say at my funeral?

What would the Lord Jesus say when He meets me?" This is not morbid. This is wisdom. "Teach

us to number our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom" (Psalm 90:12).

Live in such a way that when you are old, you can sit and look at your grandchildren and know

that you planted well. Live in such a way that when you die, your children say, "Our father loved

Jesus, and he loved us." Live in such a way that long after the last person who remembers your

face has also died, your great-great-grandchildren are still walking with the Lord because of the

family you planted for Him.

The trees you plant today will give shade to generations who will never know your name. Plant

well.

A Prayer

Eternal Father, the generations come and go, but You remain forever. My days are

a breath; Your years have no end. Teach me to live with eternity in view. Let me

not waste my one short life on trivial things. Let me lay down a spiritual heritage

that will echo through my family long after my bones rest in the earth. Give me

grace to love my wife so well that my granddaughters will expect to be loved well.

Give me grace to teach my children so faithfully that my great-grandchildren will

sing Your praises. Let the trees I plant give shade to many. And may my name be

found written in the Book of Life when the final day comes. In the name of Jesus

Christ, the Resurrection and the Life, Amen.

CONCLUSION

Rise Up, Men of God

A Call to Action and Closing Prayer

We have come to the end of this journey, brother, but your journey is only beginning.

We began by looking at the hungry land around us — hungry for godly men. We looked at God's

creation design, at the inner man, at the power of prayer, at the husband's calling to love, at the

father's duty to disciple, at the gentleness of true strength, at the dignity of work, at the watchman's

duty of protection, at the iron of accountability, at service in the local church, at the pulpit of the

home, at the war within against sin, at the vision of a well-planned life, and at the legacy that

reaches far beyond our own grave.

Fourteen chapters. Fourteen calls. Fourteen areas where God has spoken. And now the book closes,

and the question presses: what will you do?

Reading is easy. Applying is hard. Books can be set on a shelf and forgotten, or they can be the

match that lights a fire. Which will this book be for you?

Let me lay before you a simple call to action. Not complicated. Not overwhelming. Just a

beginning. Take what follows and make it your own, with your pastor, with your wife, with your

brothers in the faith.

First, make sure you are a Christian. I ask this of every reader, because no one can lead spiritually

who has not first been made alive by the Spirit of God. Have you come to the end of yourself and

found only Jesus is enough? Have you repented of your sins and trusted in Christ alone for

salvation? If you have never done this, do it today. Right where you are. "If you declare with your

mouth, 'Jesus is Lord,' and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be

saved" (Romans 10:9). Do not read another chapter of your life without settling this.

Second, commit to a few specific changes. Not all fourteen at once — you cannot carry all of it at

the same moment. But pick two or three areas where the Lord has most convicted you, and begin

there. Perhaps it is morning prayer. Perhaps it is speaking gently to your wife. Perhaps it is putting

away alcohol. Perhaps it is starting family worship. Perhaps it is joining a men's accountability

group. Pick two or three and commit before God, in writing if possible, with a witness if possible,

to begin.

Third, go to your wife and tell her. Do not promise what you cannot deliver. Simply say, "I have

been reading about what God expects of me as a husband and father. I see that I have failed in

some areas. I am asking God to change me, and I am asking you to pray for me." Most wives, on

hearing such words from their husbands, will weep tears of joy and will pray down heaven upon

you. A humble husband is a powerful husband.

Fourth, go to your children, one at a time, and speak to them. If you have harmed them, confess it.

If you have been absent, tell them you are coming home. If you have never blessed them, lay your

hand on their head tonight and bless them by name. "The Lord bless you and keep you; the Lord

make his face shine on you and be gracious to you; the Lord turn his face toward you and give you

peace" (Numbers 6:24–26). That old blessing, spoken over your children tonight, may echo in

them for eighty years.

Fifth, find a brother. Do not walk alone. Today, tomorrow at the latest, reach out to one godly man

in your church and ask him to meet with you regularly. Tell him, "I am trying to become the man

God is calling me to be. Will you walk with me? Will you pray with me? Will you ask me hard

questions?" You may be surprised how many men have been waiting for someone to ask them.

Sixth, plant yourself deeply in a local church. Not just attendance — membership, service,

submission to elders, participation in the body. Be there in the joys and the struggles. If your

current church is not preaching the gospel faithfully and teaching the Word carefully, pray about

this with your wife and seek a church that does. But do not be a drifter. The Church is the bride of

Christ. Love what He loves.

Seventh, write your vision. Following Habakkuk's instruction, sit down this week — even for thirty

minutes — and write what God is calling you to in each area of life. Spiritual. Marriage. Children.

Work. Finance. Service. Let it be imperfect. Refine it over time. But get something on paper. Pray

over it. Act on it.

Eighth, pick up this book again in one year. Read it again. See where God has changed you. See

where you still need to grow. Let it be a marker on your journey. Share it with another man who

needs to read it.

And now, my brother, hear the final word.

East Africa — Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda, Burundi, South Sudan, Ethiopia, and beyond

— is waiting for men like you, men who will rise from their knees with the name of Jesus on their

lips and the courage of the Spirit in their hearts.

Our grandfathers in the faith — Charles Lwanga at Namugongo, Simeon Nsibambi on Namirembe

Hill, Festo Kivengere in exile, Janani Luwum before the dictator — they fought the good fight.

They finished the race. They kept the faith (2 Timothy 4:7). They have passed the torch.

Now it is your hand that holds it.

Will you take up the torch, or will you let it fall?

The devil hates a rising man. He will oppose you. He will tempt you. He will try to use your own

past failures to convince you it is hopeless. Do not listen. "Greater is he who is in you than he who

is in the world" (1 John 4:4). The same Christ who conquered death conquers your fear. The same

Spirit who raised Jesus from the dead will raise you from your spiritual sleep.

Rise up, husband. Your wife has been praying for this day.

Rise up, father. Your children have been waiting for you to lead.

Rise up, brother. The church of God needs your shoulder beside theirs.

Rise up, man of Africa. The nations are watching. Heaven is watching. The Lord Jesus Christ is

watching. And one day you will stand before Him and give an account.

May you stand on that day, not trembling in shame, but joyful, weary but not ashamed, your hands

rough from faithful labor, your family standing behind you, your brothers beside you, your Savior's

words ringing in your ears: "Well done, good and faithful servant. Enter into the joy of your Lord."

Amen, and Amen.

Closing Prayer

Our Father in heaven, hallowed be Your name. Your kingdom come, Your will be

done, on earth as it is in heaven. Lord Jesus Christ, You who walked the earth as

the perfect Man, the true Husband of the Church, the great Son of the Father, we

lift our eyes to You now. Holy Spirit, without whom nothing true can be done, we

ask You to fall fresh upon us. We come before You, Father, as men. Some of us are

young, some old. Some married, some still waiting. Some have fathered children

well, some have failed them deeply. Some have walked with You for years, some

are only just beginning. But all of us, in this moment, bow before You and say: we

are Yours. Forgive us for the years we have lived for ourselves. Forgive us for the

wives we have not loved as Christ loved the Church. Forgive us for the children we

have not discipled, the homes we have not led, the churches we have not served, the

sins we have not confessed, the brothers we have not supported. Wash us in the

blood of Jesus. Clothe us in His righteousness. Fill us with His Spirit. And send us

out as men. Make us men who pray before they speak. Men who confess before they

accuse. Men who love before they demand. Men who serve before they command.

Men who work hard and trust You for the harvest. Men who stand as watchmen at

the gates of our homes. Men who plant ourselves in Your Church and do not drift

away. Men who fight the battle within and walk in the purity Your Son bought with

His blood. Men of vision. Men of faithfulness. Men who leave behind a legacy that

will sing Your praises for generations. For our wives, O Lord, have mercy. For our

children, make us the fathers You have called us to be. For our churches, raise us

up as servants and elders. For our nations — Uganda, Kenya, Tanzania, Rwanda,

Burundi, South Sudan, Ethiopia, Sudan, the Congo, and all of Africa — send us a

revival like the fire that fell in the 1930s, a fire that humbles men, purifies families,

strengthens churches, and shakes whole nations. We long to see it. We pray for it.

We will be ready for it. Bless the wives who are reading this prayer beside their

husbands, those who have prayed for years and are about to see the answer. Bless

the single men who are preparing for a holy marriage one day. Bless the widowers

who feel alone. Bless the young men who have no father in the home, and be their

Father Yourself. Bless the elders of the Church who are weary in shepherding.

Bless the pastors who plead in empty sanctuaries. Bless the evangelists who still

walk the village paths with Bibles in hand. And when our days are done, Lord, let

us stand before You with joy. Let none of our family be missing at the Wedding

Supper of the Lamb. Let our labor not be in vain. Let our lives sing of Your goodness

long after our graves have grown quiet. We ask all this in the mighty, glorious,

saving, sanctifying name of the Lord Jesus Christ, our Savior, our Lord, our

Brother, our King. Amen.

THE END

fields.title: Chapter One. The Morning Hour
fields.body_html:
LORD, in the morning you hear my voice; in the morning I prepare a sacrifice for you and watch." — Psalms 5:3 .

“ The Lord God has given me the tongue of those who are taught, that I may know how to sustain with a word him who is weary. Morning by morning he awakens; he awakens my ear to hear as those who are taught.” — Isaiah 50:4.

From the earliest ages, God's servants have thought of the morning as the time fitted for the worship of God. It is still regarded by all Christians both as a duty and a privilege to devote some portion of the beginning of the day to seeking fellowship with God. Many Christians, especially the Student's Christian Association, observe The Morning Watch; the Y. P. C. E. Society speaks of it as the Quiet Hour; others use the name of the Still Hour or the Quiet Time.

All these, whether they think of a whole hour or half an hour, or a quarter of an hour, unite with the Psalmist in what he says, "O LORD, in the morning you hear my voice."

“O

In speaking of the extreme importance of this daily quiet time of prayer and meditation on God’s Word, Mr. Mott has said: “Next to receiving Christ as Saviour, and claiming the baptism of the Holy Spirit, we know of no act attended with larger good to ourselves or

others, than the formation of an encouraged resolution to keep the morning watch, and spend the first half-hour of the day alone with God.” At first sight, the statement appears too strong. The act of receiving Christ as Saviour is one of such infinite consequences for eternity, the act of claiming the Holy Spirit is one that works such a revolution in the Christian life, that such a simple thing as the firm determination to keep the morning watch hardly appears sufficiently important to be placed next to them.

However, if we think of how impossible it is to live out our daily

lives in Christ as our Savior from sin, or to maintain a walk in the leading and power of the Holy Spirit, without daily, close fellowship with God, we soon shall see the truth of the sentiment. This is because it simply means the fixed determination that Christ shall have the whole life, that the Holy Spirit shall in everything be fully obeyed. The morning watch is the key to the position in which the surrender to Christ and the Holy Spirit can be unceasingly and fully maintained.

To realise this, let us first look at what ought to be the object of the morning watch. The morning watch must not be regarded as an end in itself.

It is not sufficient that it gives us a blessed time for prayer and Bible study, and so brings us a certain measure of refreshment and help. It is to serve as a means to an end. And that end is to secure the presence of Christ for the whole day. Personal devotion to a friend

or a pursuit means that that friend or pursuit shall always hold their place in the heart, even when other engagements occupy the attention. Personal devotion to Jesus means that we allow nothing to separate us from Him for a moment.

To abide in Him and His love, to be kept by Him and His grace, to be doing His will and pleasing Him- this cannot possibly be an intermittent thing to one who is truly devoted to Him. “I need Thee every hour,” “Moment by moment I am kept in His love.” These hymns are the language of life and truth. “In Thy name shall they

rejoice all the day,” “I the Lord do keep it; I will wter it every mom

These are words of Divine power. The believer cannot stand for one moment without Christ. The personal devotion to Him refuses to be content with anything less than to abide always in His love and His will. Nothing less is the true scriptural Christian life. The importance and blessedness and true aim of the morning watch can only be seen as nothing less than its first object.

The clearer the object of our pursuit is, the better we shall be able to adapt the means to its attainment. Consider the morning watch now as the means to this great end:

I want to secure absolutely the presence of Christ all the day, to do nothing that can interfere with it. I feel at once that my success for the day will depend upon the clearness and the strength of the faith that seeks, finds and holds HIM in the closet. Meditation, prayer,

and the word will all be used as subordinate and auxiliary to this: the link for the day between Christ and I must be renewed and firmly fastened in the morning hour. At first, it may appear as if the thought of the whole day, with all its possible cares, pleasures, temptation, may disturb the rest I have enjoyed in my quiet devotion. It is possible; but it will be no loss.

True religion aims at having the character of Christ so formed in us that even in our most common acts, His temper and disposition shall show themselves. The spirit and the will of Christ are meant so to

possess us that in our oneness with men, in our relaxation, in our business, it shall be a second nature to us to act according to them. All this can be, because Christ Himself, as the Living One, lives in us. Be not disturbed if at first the aim appears too high or difficult, and occupies too much of your time in the hour of private prayer. The time you give it will be richly rewarded. You will return to prayer and scripture with new purpose and new faith.

As the morning watch begins to have its effect on the day, the day will react in its first half-hour, and fellowship with Christ will have a new meaning and a new power. It will especially have its influence on the spirit in which you keep the morning watch.

As the grandeur of the aim-unbroken fellowship with God in Christ through the day and the true nature of the means to secure it- a definite conscious meeting with Christ and a securing His presence for the day-possesses us, it will be seen that the one essential thing

is, whole-hearted purpose: the fixed determination, whatever effort or self-denial it may cost, to win the prize. In study or on the sport field, every student knows what need there is of vigorous will and determined purpose if we are to succeed.

Religion needs, and indeed deserves, not less but more of intense devotion. If anything, surely the love of Christ needs the whole heart. It is this fixed determination before everything to secure Christ’s presence that will overcome every temptation to be unfaithful or superficial in the keeping of our pledges. It is this will

that makes the morning watch itself a mighty means of grace in strengthening character, and nerving us to say No to every call for self-indulgence. It is this will that will enable us at once, when we enter the inner chamber and shut the door, to be there with our whole heart, ready at once for our oneness with Christ. And it is the determination that from the morning watch on, will become the keynote of our daily life.

In the world, it is often said: Great things are possible to any man who knows what he wills, and wills it with all his heart.

The student who has made personal devotion to Christ his watchword, will find in the morning hour as the place where his insight into his holy calling is renewed day by day; where his will is braced up to walk worthy of it; and his faith rewarded by the

presence of Christ waiting to meet him, and take charge of him for the day. We are more than conquerors through Him who loves us. A living Christ waits to meet us.

fields.title: Chapter Two. The Door Shut — Alone With God
fields.body_html:
ut when you pray, go into your room and shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you...” Matthew 6: 6.

Man was created for fellowship with God. God made him in His own image and likeness, that he might be fit for this, capable of understanding and enjoying God, entering into His will, and delighting in His glory. Because God is the everywhere-present and All-pervading One, he could have lived in the enjoyment of an unbroken fellowship amidst whatever work he had to do.

Sin robbed us of His fellowship.

Nothing but this fellowship can satisfy the heart of either man or God. It was this Christ who came to restore; to bring back to God His lost creature, and bring back man to all he was created for. Oneness with God is the consummation of all blessedness on Earth as in Heaven. It comes when the promise, so often given, becomes a full experience: “I will never leave you nor forsake you”, and when we can say:

BThe Father is always with me, this oneness with God is meant to be ours all day, whatever our condition or the circumstances that surround us. But its enjoyment depends upon the reality of the oneness in the inner chamber. The power of maintaining close and

glad fellowship with God all day will depend entirely upon the intensity with which we seek to secure it in the hour of secret prayer. The one essential thing in the Morning Watch or the Quiet Hour is — Fellowship with God. It is this that our Lord teaches us to be the inner secret of secret prayer: “Shut the door and pray to your Father who is in secret” Matthew 6:6.

The first and chief thing is to see that there in secret you have the Father’s presence and attention. Know that He sees and hears you. Of more importance than all your requests, however urgent, of more

importance than all your earnestness and effort to pray aright, is this one thing- the childlike, living assurance that your Father sees you, that you have now met Him, and that with His eye on you and yours on Him, you are now enjoying actual oneness with Him.

Christian, there is a terrible danger to which you stand exposed in

your inner chamber. You are in danger of substituting Prayer and Bible Study for living fellowship with God, the living interchange of giving Him your love, your heart, and your life, and receiving from Him His love, His life, and His spirit.

Your needs and their expression, with your desire to pray humbly and earnestly and believingly, may so occupy you, that the light of His countenance and the joy of His love cannot enter you.

Your Bible Study may so interest you, and so waken pleasing religious sentiment, that yes, the very word of God may become a

substitute for God Himself, the greatest hindrance to fellowship because it keeps the soul occupied instead of leading it to God Himself. And we go out into the day’s work without the power of an abiding fellowship, because in our morning devotions the blessing was not secured. What a difference it would make in the life of many if everything in the closet was subordinate to this one thing: I want to walk with God through the day; my morning hour is the time when my Father enters into a definite engagement with me and

I with Him that it shall be so. What strength would be imparted by the consciousness: God has taken charge of me, He is going with me Himself; I am going to do His will in His strength all day; I am ready for all that may come! Yes, what a nobility would come into life if secret prayer were not only an asking for some new sense of comfort, light, or strength, but the giving away of life just for one day into the sure and safe keeping of a Mighty and Faithful God!

Pray to your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you.” Where the secret fellowship with the Father in spirit and in truth is maintained, the public life before men will carry the reward.

The Father who sees in secret takes charge and rewards openly. Separation from men, in solitude with God is the sure, and the only way to live in oneness with men in the power of God’s blessing.

fields.title: Chapter Three. The Open Door — The Open Reward
fields.body_html:
ut when you fast, anoint your head and wash your face that your fasting may not be seen by others but by your Father who is in secret. And your Father who sees in secret will reward you." Matthew 6: 17-18.

" Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John and perceived

that they were uneducated, common men, they were astonished. And they recognized that they had been with Jesus." Acts 4:13.

" When Moses came down from Mount Sinai, with the two tablets of the testimony in his hand as he came down from the mountain, Moses did not know that the skin of his face shone because he had

been talking with God. Aaron and all the people of Israel saw Moses, and behold, the skin of his face shone, and they were afraid to come near him. But Moses called to them, and Aaron and all the leaders of the congregation returned to him, and Moses talked with them.Afterward, all the people of Israel came near, and he commanded them all that the LORD had spoken with him in Mount Sinai. 33. And when Moses had finished speaking with them, he put

a veil over his face." Exodus 34: 29-33.

" B

The transition from fellowship with God in the morning hour to oneness with our fellowmen is often difficult. If we have met God, we long to maintain the sense of His presence, and our surrender to

Him. We go out to the breakfast table, where, perhaps in the bosom of our own family, the atmosphere is all at once changed, and as the presence of men and the visible asserts itself, we begin to lose what we had found. Many young Christians have been perplexed with the question how to keep their heart filled with that of which they do not feel at liberty, or has not the opportunity, to speak. Even in religious circles, it is not always easy to have free oneness, through lack of fervor or boldness, on that which would give the greatest profit and pleasure. Let us strive to learn how our oneness with men, may be, instead of a hindrance, a help to the maintenance of a life of

continual fellowship with God.

The lessons which the story of Moses with the veil on his face teach, are very suggestive. Close and continued fellowship with God will in due time leave its mark and make itself manifest before men. Moses was not that his face shone: the light of God shining from us

will be unconscious; it will but deepen the sense of our being an earthen vessel (1 Corinthians 2:3, 4 and 2 Corinthians 4). The sense of God’s presence in a man may often cause others to fear, or at least feel at ease in his company.When others observe what is to be seen in him, the true believer will know what it is to veil his face, and prove by humility and love that he is indeed a man of like passions with those around him.

And yet, through all, there will be the proof, too, that he is a man of God, who lives in, and has dealings with, an unseen world.

The same lessons are taught by what our Lord says about fasting.

Make no show of your fasting, so that you appear not unto men to fast; meet them in the joy and kindness of God’s gentleness, as the

Father’s beloved and loving child. Count upon God, who has seen you in secret, to reward you openly, to give you grace in oneness with men, to maintain your communion with Him, and make them know that His grace and light are on you.

The story of Peter and John confirms the same truth: they had been with Jesus not only while He was on Earth, but as He entered into the Heavenlies, and had received His spirit. They simply acted out what the spirit of Christ taught them; even enemies could see by their boldness that they had been with Jesus.

The blessing of oneness with God may easily be lost by entering too deeply into oneness with men. The spirit of the inner chamber must be carried out in a holy watchfulness throughout the day. We know not at what hour the enemy may come. This continuance of the morning watch may be maintained by a quiet self-restraint, in not giving the reins to nature.

It has, in a religious home circle, often sought help, in each one repeating a text at the breakfast table on some fixed subject, giving easy occasion to the religious conversation. When once the abiding sense of God’s presence and of oneness with Him- “Continue in the

fear of the LORD all the day.”- has become the aim of the morning hour, with the deepest humility and the most loving oneness with those around us, grace will have been sought and found to pass on into the day’s duties with the continuity of fellowship kept unbroken. It is a great thing to enter the inner chamber, shut the door, and meet the Father in secret. It is a greater thing to open the door again, and go out, in an enjoyment of that presence which nothing can disturb.

To some, such a life does not appear needful; the strain is too great;

one can be a good Christian without it. To those who seek to be men of one thing, who feel that if they are to be true and mighty to influence the church and the world around them they must be full of God and His Presence, everything will be subordinate to the one question: How to bear in the earthen vessel the heavenly treasure, the power of Christ resting on us all the day.

fields.title: Chapter Four. Moses And The Word Of God
fields.body_html:
n regard to the connection between prayer and the word in our private devotion, the expression of a convert from heathenism has often been quoted: I pray, I speak to God; I read in the Bible, and God speaks to me. There is a verse in the history of Moses, in which this thought is beautifully brought out. We read, Numbers 7: 89, "And when Moses went into the tent of meeting to speak with the LORD, he heard the voice speaking to him from above the mercy seat that was on the ark of the testimony, from between the two cherubim; and it spoke to him.” When he went in to pray for himself or his people, and to wait for instructions, he found one waiting for him. What a lesson for our morning watch.

A prayerful spirit is a spirit to which God will speak. A prayerful spirit will be a listening spirit waiting to hear what God says. In the

oneness with God, His presence and the part He takes must be as real as my own. We want to ask what is needed so that our Scripture reading and praying may be such true fellowship with God.

First, get into the right place. “Moses went into the Tabernacle to speak with God.”

IHe separated himself from the people, and went where he could be with God alone. He went to the place where God was to be found. Jesus has told us where that place is. He calls us to enter into our closet, shut the door, and pray to our Father who sees in secret.

Anywhere where we really are alone with God may be to us the secret of His presence. To speak with God needs separation from all else. It needs a heart intently set upon and in full expectation of meeting God personally, and having direct dealings with Him. Those who go there to speak to God will hear the Voice of the one speaking to them.

Next, get into the right position. Moses heard the Voice of One speaking from off the mercy seat. Bow before the mercy seat. There the consciousness of your unworthiness will not hinder you, but be a

real help in trusting God. There you may have the assured confidence that your upward look will be met by His eye, that your prayer can be heard, and that His loving answer will be given.
